An oddity among bullet hells in which the player can gather a huge armada of higly specialized, highly disposable kamikaze ships. Hitogata Happa's mechanics inspire in me a wild ambivalence. It is absurd, demanding, and masochistic in ways that no other shooter would dare. This game brings so many gimmicks to the table along with such a relentless difficulty that at first pass it seems like some kind of sick joke, but  I can't help but feel a certain fondness for its vaulting imagination.  In between the whimsical dolls named after tea leaves and the massive German flying machines there's a mechanically tight game with plenty of heart that just begs to be replayed again and again. After all, success really comes down to bringing the proper tool for the job, and knowing how to use it.

God, oh my god. I'm trying to wrap my brain around this mess of a game. This game reminds me of my overly drunk, always screaming uncle. He would walk into our home, which didn't belong to him, and begin to throw furniture around the room like a crazed gorilla. He would do this on and off for a year until my mom sat him down and began to do the same thing he would do in front of him, this time he was sober, though. He realized how wrong it was and began to change his ways, but this is when he did something much worse than what he did before. There was a loud noise outside my room and even though I was scared as it was very late at night, I left my room to see what the sound was. To my suprise, I saw him standing over the dead body of my pet dog, Ruckus. He had a shotgun in hand and looked up to me in the midst of night with blood all over his body and a smile on his face. I watched him run off into the woods behind my house and never saw him again. The police continued to look but only found small pieces of a much bigger puzzle, this included shotgun shells and torn pieces of clothing which matched my description of him that night. My point is that this game is mysterious, and mystical. I give it a 10/10 despite the fact that I have barely played it.

What an enormous disappointment.
Act 1 was enjoyable though perhaps not as great as I had hoped. And I had read that Tim Schaffer, lead designer, had said that people should replay Act 1 before playing Act 2 so that you don't forget all the callbacks.
And I did.
What a terrible waste of time.
Act 2 throws away so many story elements that made Act 1 intriguing. And so making me play Act 1 *again* and then tossed aside a bunch of the story felt like a complete betrayal. And the sad thing is that Act 2 retroactively makes Act 1 feel much worse... because all of the intriguing setups have terrible payoffs and therefore make the setups no longer enjoyable in retrospect.
Act 2 is like the Matrix sequels. Matrix 2 didn't seem that horrible until Matrix 3 came out. If Matrix 3 had been amazing, people would remember Matrix 2 somewhat fondly. But since Matrix 3 was terrible, people simply wish The Matrix had never got a sequel at all.
I guess this is my roundabout way of saying that I wish Broken Age didn't get made and I hadn't wasted my time playing it.

Natural Selection 2 is a very cool concept "indie" game which melds first-person shooter with real-time strategy.  It's essentially strictly player vs. player, as the tutorial/training which implements AI is very buggy.  NS2 is otherwise your run-of-the-mill humans vs. aliens game with the typical offsetting balances.  Playing as the commander provides a different feel from any other RTS game, as the performance of your field units is not consistent, since player skill varies from one player to the next.  Also, the commander can provide a small amount of direct support to field units, other than simply providing leadership and direction.
Although I do recommend Natural Selection 2 for those who enjoy RTS and FPS games, be advised that there is a steep learning curve since the game is almost entirely PvP.  There are rookie friendly servers, but that doesn't guarantee anything.  For the most part, you'll be jumping in head-first into a gauntlet of experienced soldiers in a slaughterhouse.  Expect to do poorly up front unless you have amazing luck and repeatedly land on elite teams which can carry you.

Trust me, Phantom Trigger is by far the most exciting hardcore neon slasher game you’ll ever find yourself playing! Because it’s the only game in this completely made-up genre.
In all seriousness though, Phantom Trigger can be considered a very solid pixel art action game that manages to do a lot of things right and in a quite unique way despite its apparent resemblance to another well-known indie hit.
If you, like me, ended up on this store page thanks to the art style, I can ensure you won’t be disappointed. The pixel art here is as good as it gets and you’ll find yourself fighting your way through wonderful neon-inspired scenarios magnificently drawn using vibrant colors and smooth animations to depict some singular figures. The sounds are spot on with nice synth-music and fitting effects that offer a very precise feedback of both yours and your opponent’s attacks.
Gameplay-wise the game is solid and relies on a heavily combo-based combat system that you are forced to master as soon as possible in order to survive the waves of enemies that try to make your life miserable right from the get-go. The enemies themselves are various enough and new types, with their own attacks, are introduced all game long. A few simple puzzles are also a nice addition to frequently shift the pace of the game.
The entire title is almost entirely focused on collecting stuff that eventually gives you access to that area boss battle and this, with the nice addition of appropriate sounds and music, helps giving the moment you face a boss a very epic tone. The fight itself develops around spotting a boss’ weak point while avoiding its attacks with no chance to do any damage. Once you find it, it's a walk in the park until the boss is gone.
The most surprising aspect in a game like this, though, it’s how meaningful the narrative background is: what you see happening during your playthrough is there for a reason and represents the delirious fantasies of a mentally ill man, whose inner demons are in a perpetual fight with his true self.
Phantom Trigger is a game that I thoroughly enjoyed and that I definitely recommend.

I've been seeing a lot of negative reviews for this game and I feel like a lot of them are unfair.
For one, the writing is fantastic. The characters are interesting and the tone is humorous but without sacrificing an interesting story.  The voicework also helps with that. They really pulled an all star cast together.
Most of the problems people seem to have come from Act 2. As someone who just purchased the game and played it straight throught, I didn't notice a huge change between acts. The changes felt like the natural progression of a narrative. Act one does a lot of the set up of the world and characters, and act 2 advances the narrative and lets you interact with things from a different perspective. I can see why people like Act 1 better. When you are seeing everything for the first time it does feel a bit more exciting, and witnessing a character's quirks is of course going to be better initially, but it wouldn't make narrative sense for the game to continue that way.
I will say that the puzzles seemed to get tougher in act 2, but they didn't seem too terrible. There was one puzzle that felt a little unfair, but I can overlook that for the sake of a fun story.
Keep in mind that this review is coming from someone who generally doesn't play adventure games.

Hard West was developed by CreativeForge Games and published by Gambitious Digital Entertainment. It was released on November 18th, 2015 for $19.99. A review copy was provided for The Hidden Levels. Initially a Kickstarter project, 4,398 backers pledged $94,183 CAD to fund development.
Hard West is a turn based strategy action title with some similarities to X:COM and other tactical shooter type games. The movement and combat mechanics are streamlined and the game plays very well. Artistically the game is very thematic, showing off a western style and some interesting illustrations. While stability was a slight issue, there are various graphic settings that can be adjusted to ensure smooth play. The replay value is moderate due to some variance in certain characters surviving events. There is also an option to turn the difficulty up or down for each scenario.
What I enjoyed:
Screaming theme – Hard West is extremely thematic and stylized with a western theme. There are additional layers to the thematic aspect including gold mining and battling Mexican cartels. The theme is very well constructed and fits every aspect of story and game play. It is clear that during development making this western theme scream was a high priority.
Tactical is practical – There is something to be said for turn based games of this nature. Allowing players to spend time picking what they hope will be the perfect move for each character is engaging and thought provoking. A major benefit of these types of games for my personal situation is that my toddler often wants attention randomly. Turn based games afford the ability to walk away for a bit and come back to them at your convenience.
Simply elegant – One of the outstanding aspects of Hard West is that the game mechanics are streamlined and simple. This is not to say the game isn’t difficult, just that manipulating your characters and their items or upgrades is very easy to comprehend. The system of playing cards which give your characters various abilities and bonuses is a fantastic example of the elegance of design. These cards along with weapons and gear are very easy to change or set up due to an intuitive interface for each character.
What I disliked:
Environmental challenges – The area that I found to be a bit of a let down was that most of the battle environments seemed very similar. The layouts were different at times, but the option of sunny Mexican villa or burning western landscape was somewhat redundant. There is certainly room for expansion in this game and if development does explore that option, more unique environments would be a necessary addition.
Jammed revolver – At one point in my preview video there was a full crash, seemingly due to rendering both the first and second floor of a building at once. These little stutters were seen a handful of times. I was reverted back to the start of an entire mission in the case of the crash which is always a bit of a let down. The issues while distracting are not debilitating and shouldn’t keep anyone from finishing the game.
Covered sight – The mechanics are fairly solid minus an occasional miscalculation or bug in the combat system. There were a couple of instances where the percentage for hit was below 20% but there was clear line of sight and no cover for the enemy. This was not common enough to be a major issue. I will say it ruined my tactical advantage in the instances that it did occur.
Tactical turn based games are generally fun and provide a substantial amount of thought to play. Hard West is worthy of being mentioned alongside a title like XCOM. It may not have the depth in terms of long term character advancement but it’s a solid experience with a fantastic theme. If you like western themes or tactical shooting games of this type then this game is certainly one to enjoy.
Score: Buy it now

After being granted an ice sword from a living tree, you embark on a quest of... something. You don’t really know what’s happening, until you reach specific areas which trigger story moments. The story gets really interesting and kept me intrigued the whole way through. Phantom Trigger is a “Neon Slasher” so expect vibrant visuals, energetic electronic music and lots of hack & slashing. Unfortunately, the combat gets very dull and repetitive with the game throwing a constant unrelenting barrage of enemies, and not providing enough incentive or player progression to compenste. It’s a moderately fun game but lacks motive.
- The visuals are very colourful and vibrant, and encapsulates a wondrous neon aesthetic. The lighting is done well and the environmental effects are quite good. The levels themselves lack a bit of variety, but each level is very distinct and unique both visually and gameplay-wise. The levels are filled to the brim with bloodthirsty monsters, and the design of the monsters is very creative.
- The sounds are great and there’s solid feedback for every attack, action and combo. The sounds are full of energy and neon vibes and I enjoyed them throughout the entirety of the game. Similarly, the music is also great and the boss music is suitably epic.
- Each level involves reaching the end and defeating a boss before returning back to the main camp. The level design is alright but lacks deviation, and the few puzzles thrown in, though did help with the game’s pace, were just not enjoyable. I do like a bit of puzzles but this is just pure brain-straining memory tests. Along the levels you can find items to give to NPCs back at the camp, but I have no idea what the point is, as I made every NPC disappear from the camp at the start of the game, and they never came back. :(
You have 3 weapons: a short and nimble ice sword, powerful fiery knuckles and a long energy whip. The whip can be used to propel environmental objects at enemies, but the controls for doing so felt weird and even though I used the whip at every available chance, I never got accustomed to the weird handling. I hated when certain bosses required the use of the whip, but the boss’ large hit-box is thankfully fairly forgiving. You can also do a teleport dash which is very useful and at times essential. There are no combos for each individual weapon alone, as each consecutive attack is identical in damage, which I found disappointing. Performing combos is straightforward and easy, but every combo is only 3 attacks with the 3rd being a special attack. With every attack being so similar, and a very small number of combos (only 7, of which 3 are functionally identical), the combat gets very dull and lacklustre later in the game.
All your weapons can be levelled naturally as you use them, and you can also gain experience from finding special mirrors along the game. Your weapons will never improve though; the sole purpose of levelling them is to unlock combos that require weapons to be above a certain level. You’ll never gain any skill points or be able to progress your character in any way whatsoever. Apart from a couple new combos, which aren’t particularly interesting, the only thing to compensate for the increasing difficulty is your increasing skill. However, there is nothing to compensate for the increasing repetition and shallow combat as you fight enemy after enemy. It got to the point where on the final level, since all my weapons were max level, I had asked myself: why am I even fighting? And from then on I speedily teleported through the entire level and only battled when the game physically forced me to.
Despite the combat being lacklustre, the combat and difficulty is balanced well, and making the most of combos requires some timing and skill to pull off. I also (mostly) enjoyed the boss fights. They were creatively designed, and instead of being a huge and generic damage-sponge enemy, they were more about finding out how to damage them. I enjoyed these boss fights as they weren’t just pure combat, and they sometimes required you to think. The last boss however, was immensely underwhelming and was painfully unenjoyable. The boss does nothing significant, instead the boss fight involves being locked in a room and forced to fight seemingly endless waves of enemies. This felt closer to a survival mode than a boss fight, and I had already tired by the shallow combat and so this fight was a drag.
- The gameplay takes place in some sort of alternate reality, and at certain points the game briefly switches realities and follows another person named Stan. You find out that Stan has a fatal illness, and opted for an experimental treatment as opposed to expensive surgery. After which, his memory seems to have been affected and you cannot even remember who he is. At least, that’s what it initially seems like. The story gets slowly revealed through snippets along the game, and there’s some interesting twists thrown in. It’s succinct, but maybe suffers somewhat from vagueness and lack of explanation. Nonetheless, I was pleasantly surprised by the story and found it to be one of my favourite aspects of the game.
- The game runs fine and smoothly, however there were multiple bugs that broke the game forcing me to relaunch. I encountered a glitch where the screen stopped following the character, and another where I restarted after dying but was still dead, and another where the game just got stuck. While I did have to relaunch, the checkpoints ensured I didn’t lose much if any progress.
- No tutorial whatsoever, but it’s easy enough to learn the controls. There’s only WASD and the mouse, so a quick glance at the combo menu will be all you need.
- the game is around 6 hours long, though it would probably have been more enjoyable if it was shorter (and cheaper). Unless you’re an achievement hunter, there isn’t really any reason to replay the game.
- None
$15 is a little much for this game honestly. Initially it’s a fun and attractive neon world, with vibrant visuals, energetic music and creative design. However, the shallow combat and limited progression mars the latter half of the game. If you can snag this on at least a half price sale, only then would I recommend getting it.
There’s some fun to be had, but $15 for a 6 hour game marred by shallowness and repetition just isn’t worth it in my opinion.

According to developers
is a "Slasher" with RPG and Roque-like elements. I never heard of the "Slasher" genre and the game has little to no elements from RPG or Roque-like \(-_-)/ As far as I am a concerned this is a hack&slash game with a very simple combat and no control over customization of skills. Unfortunately, this game has a lot of glitches and questionable design choices specifically when it comes to combat. Phantom Trigger has some really cool visuals but the levels tend to be very bloated with effects. Honestly, it has a lot of great ideas but they came together like a trainwreck. The only thing that pushed me to barely recommend it was a well done psychological story.
I encountered numerous glitches from going through walls to enemies that get stuck in walls while you have to kill them to progress. Needless to say, some of the achievements like killing all enemies are impossible with those glitches. Fortunately, I have not encountered any game breaking glitches but some people have (although I had to restart from last checkpoint several times) Framerate was getting low in few places when there is too much on the screen. Game settings are extremely limited.
The game does not rely much on numbers.It is mostly a reflex based system that does not motivate you to kill enemies (you can skip about 80% of them). The combat is not very deep to carry itself without much RPG elements. You can unlock several cool combos but I found them to be kinda unnecessary. Special attacks on a third hit often put you at high-risk low reward situation. I made a suggestion to transfer some of the interesting moves to cooldown abilities which I think could improve the game. I don't hate the feel of the combat as much as I hate the progression in combat. Developers need to figure out how to keep it interesting because it got really freaking boring to activate everything through 3 hit combos. There is also a neat color system where you can only damage some enemies with a specific attack of the same color.

Phantom Trigger is a hardcore action-adventure game set in a mysterious world, where you control the hero and three main weapons :
A sword ( blue)
A whip ( green )
And knuckles ( red )
Using the three weapon types wil level them up ( represented by meteres in the top left )
Also, destroying crystals of the weapon's color will increase it's level.
But why?
Well, higher level on a weapon opens up more combo attacks to perform with them.
For instance : attack with the blue sword twice, and then attack with the whip ; and you get an attack that freezes foes into solid ice.
Attack with sword twice, and then dash - you get a move that dashes through enemies while also slowing them down.
There are quite a few combos to open up this way.
\And the color of the weps comes into play with more than just simple leveling up, they also use it in boss battles ( where you need to use the proper color affintiy to deal damage )
In puzzles, where you have to repeat a pattern with the right weps, and in the right order.,
And in some battles,where the enemies will change affinity, casuing you to switch weps to deal damage to them at all, it makes you think outside of your normal attack patterns.
The game can be rather difficult, but you can adjust difficulty on the fly in game . I don't find this release build to be too difficult, the Alpha and Beta versions were far more crippling in terms of difficulty
The story is cryptic, the environments are beautifully crafted, and the effects of (distortions and glitches ) are really well done, and add alot of atmosphere to the game.
All in all, if you enjoy games like HLD where skill is a requirement, and you will die often and learn from mistakes, then you might enjoy this one as well.

I recommend this game, but not without reservation. I enjoyed Phantom Trigger. It isn’t without its shortcomings, but it is a very polished and fun game. It took me around 5 hours to beat it on the hardest difficulty, but I didn’t feel like that was a bad thing. I actually quite enjoyed the tightness of the gameplay and felt that the developers went the direction of short and fun, rather than long and tedious. You can play through it again for different endings and the like, but the initial experience is quite short.
The first three hours of the game are by far the best. Enemies are introduced at a great pace, you acquire new and interesting skills, the story is engaging, combat is phenomenal, the NPCs are unique and varied, and you are faced with interesting biomes and puzzles. On top of all of this, the music and sound design are superb, and the art is beautiful. Phantom Trigger is a work of art in so many ways.
So where do my reservation lie? My reservations lie with the end game. I maxed out all of my weapons with two hours of game left and met most if not all the enemy types by this point. So for the last jaunt of my playthrough, I wasn’t experiencing anything really new or novel and my enjoyment started to wear thin. It got to the point that during the last level I would simply dash past all of the enemies, knowing full well they couldn’t do anything to me, and only fought when forced.
So even with these shortcomings, the first three hours were so good and so original that I can’t help but recommend this game.

Fallout Shelter, the other Fallout game.
Fallout Shelter is a free-to-play mobile platform game, released by Bethesda Softworks in 2015, just before the release of Fallout 4, as a sort of teaser for things to come. In 2017, the mobile game was released on Steam.
One of the fundamentals of a Fallout game, is the music; where would we be wandering without some classic tunes? In the menu, you can hear some jazzy music playing in the background. There is no music playing in the background while you actually play though; however, in any menu tab you open, you will be greeted with some jazzy music. Slightly disappointing, not being able to listen to the ingame music while you actually play.
There are no accusation to be made in the graphics department of the game. For a mobile game, the graphics are great, casual, pleasant to look at. Comparing the graphics to games on PC, well, there are certainly worse graphics than what Fallout Shelter offers. Even on the PC platform, the graphics still meet a satisfactory standard with no crime punishable.
Originally, being a mobile game, the game itself needs to be easy to enjoy. No confusions with controls or gameplay, no need to look up on the internet how to do this or that. Passing its mobile game criteria of being an easy, casual game is also eligible on the PC platform. No one likes a game with difficult controls. With Fallout Shelter, there is no controls, only your mouse which would’ve exchanged your thumbs if you were to be playing this game on a mobile device. Fallout Shelter is now one of the many other “clicker” games, needing only a mouse to do everything.
But can Fallout Shelter offer a persisting amount of entertainment on a PC?
As a mobile game, it has distinguished itself a worthwhile title. But moving a mobile game to a PC platform is moving an U/10 into an U/20’s match. It may have skills in its area, it may even be able to show them skills in the new field, but it just can’t compete compared to the games, specifically designed for the PC.
You turn your computer on, you get into the game, you click on your vault rooms to collect what resources and profit they have made to make your vault and the dwellers inside sustained, and then you're finished.
It’s fine on a mobile platform, where you only need to pull the device out of your pocket, but for the demands of the game, you need to turn your computer on. Wait for everything to load and startup. Enter the game. Click on everything that needs clicking. And then you’re done. That’s all you need to do.
All you do in it, is click on a few rooms to gather resources and supplies like power, water, medical supplies etc. Maybe send someone outside your safe haven to gather some pre war materials, clothing and defensive weaponry. That’s all you do. It’s a repeated cycle of doing those things. Every Time you get into the game, that’s all you can do. And on a PC, that gets quite boring after awhile.
It lacks a required depth, storyline, mission. It’s too small for the PC platform. You enter the game, and you’ve already done everything that the game has to offer in a matter of no time at all. After you’ve done everything, you’re simply just playing the game to meet your vaults mundane requirements, and all that is, is clicking on maybe five-six things. After that initial playthrough, the game loses its charm, its creativity; you’re not playing the game for any purpose, except to perform some mundane task to keep your vaults dwellers happy.
Concluding this review, the game is great on the mobile platform, for something casual to play while you're waiting or are bored somewhere. But on a PC platform, the game is too small, it lacks depth and a persisting entertainment. After five minutes of game time, you’ve pretty much done everything, and everything after that is doing the same thing.

The art style reminded me of quite a few other titles that I really loved, but after a few minutes, I wasn't sure if my reverence was appropriate. The story, while mildly interesting, was delivered almost too subtly, through small clips spread out through the game. Not necessarily a bad thing, but it was rather strange and disjointed. The combat is clearly the star of the show in this game. It seems pretty good, but the main issue I had was the lack of a tutorial. Everything seems to be left for you to figure out alone, which definitely adds a retro feel to the game, but there's a reason that drop-in games fell out of style in recent years. We have so many choices for games these days, especially niche indie titles, so to find yourself confused and flailing around can quickly cause you to lose interest. I think the majority of the problem I had with the game was the controls. I feel like both the whip and the dash should be tied to the mouse cursor. All-in-all, I had fun, and I think it's worth a play if you see it on sale. Give it a shot for yourself!

Virginia is possibly one of the finest games I have ever played. The story is told in such a way that you may always understand the plot, but you always understand how Anne (the protagonist) feels. It subverts the idea that video games are about player agency and control by using user interaction as a method of conveying feeling in the same way that cinematography or a musical score can. The way that Virginia will instantly tie many confusing threads together in a moment of realization is stunning, but also the way it can smoothly transition between the absurd and the mundane leaves you questioning the reality of some of the event. With Virginia, Variable State has not only tapped into the unique properties of video games for telling stories, they have mastered it.

It's not perfect, just like any game, but this is one of, if not the, best game in my library. It's a multiplayer shooter/RTS hybrid, as in; if you're the commander, you have a top down view and can build structures, order troops, and more. Although the two teams, (alien and marine) are completely different, it is balanced better than any game in existence that offers aesymmetical gameplay. The marines are more like your standard shooter, but there's no aim down sights, like many of the best tactical shooters such as CS, but the aliens are the most fun, with their in-mouth view. With the aliens, you can evolve to different species, you start off as a skulk, then, (in order of cost) Gorge, the healer, the Lerk, A flying Creature, The Fade, with it's deadly claws and blink ability. Then there is the Onos, the tank. All these are brought with resources, which you get for capturing res towers and holding them. It's the best multiplayer game I've ever played.

This one though is different.  Everything that the other two get right, THIS one gets wrong.  Uninteresting attack patterns, extremely repetetive (and short) level design, stupid control issues (really?  There's no "slow movement" button here?  In a bullet-hell shmup? when there WAS one in the other two?), cheap boss attacks (the first boss: If you DONT know that he's going to do the arm swipe as his first attack, and if you dont ALREADY know just where to be when he does it, you WILL die 1 second into the fight.  Gets worse from there.) and one of the worst game mechanics I've ever heard of in this type of game.
See, here's the main gimmick:  You've got all of these different dolls that you control instead of ships.  You can switch them out when one dies, and you essentially get nine lives to go with.  All of them have different abilities and blah blah blah.  None of THAT matters, though, you see.  While that all sounds cool, it's obliterated by that particular gameplay mechanic that I mentioned up above.  You cant just shoot things in this or use special powers on them, nooooooooooo.   What you have to do is kill yourself.  No, really.  Bosses in particular CANNOT be beaten without doing this.... numerous times on each.  You fill up this "flow" meter by shooting stuff, and when it's powered up, ramming yourself into an enemy of any sort will cause the doll to violently explode, doing massive damage to anything caught in the blast.
Bosses take next to no damage from anything else, so you A: have to do this against them, and B: have to have enough remaining lives when you reach each one.
But the problem with this is simple:  This is a danmaku shmup.   Bullet-hell.  Where the idea of RAMMING something exists.  Think about that for a second.  You've got chaotic, and most importantly, DENSE patterns coming out from these things, and you have to RAM THE SOURCE OF THEM.  In other words, you must successfully plow directly through the areas with the highest bullet density (since it's where the shots are coming from) and successfully ram the boss without taking a hit.  Yeah.  Good luck with that one.
Typically, getting really close to enemies... and I dont mean right next to them, but just a short distance away... in a bullet-hell game is quite the challenge for most players.  There are plenty of games of this type where the closer you are to an enemy when it pops, the more points you get.  Which makes sense due to the challenge of getting close without taking a hit.  But that's an OPTIONAL thing.... you dont HAVE to do it.  And you can learn it in bits and pieces.  As you go through the game in question, you'll learn the patterns and learn how everything works, and you spot different ways of getting close to some things to pop them, and so on.
Well, in THIS game, you *have* to do it, and getting close isnt good enough.  Gotta actually collide with the thing.  AFTER surviving long enough to charge up the Flow meter.
Yeah.  Saying that this is frustrating is an understatement.
This developer has made a number of interesting and creative shmuppy games, and for the most part all of them are very good, which of course includes Gundemonium Recollection and GundeadliGne, the other two in this 3-pack.  But THIS game is the exception.  And I haaaaaaaate having to say that, as this is one of those developers that I have alot of respect for otherwise.
But even a great dev can make a mistake from time to time.

Nuclear Throne is an excellent rogue-lite shoot-em-up that offers addicting gameplay and endless replayability.
The gunplay in Nuclear Throne is fast, visceral, and extremely satisfying. A wide variety of weapons each provide unique experiences and strategies, and limited ammo forces you to be constantly changing weapons and adapting your tactics to what you have available. Coupled with a selection of character providing gameplay altering specialties, and you never feel locked into a single "best" playstyle. This variety and the games rapid-fire pacing put the gunplay front and center, drawing attention away from relatively small and straightforward procedural levels.
Nuclear Thrones visuals are as bold and compelling as it's gunplay. Bright colors, energetic animations, and a charming pixel-art style contribute to a enjoyable arcade-style feel. The visual distinction is overall excellent, and art choices never interfere with the players ability to tell what is going on in the game. Indeed, the art direction always conveys the events of the game flawlessly, and makes watching Nuclear Throne almost as compelling as playing it.
Overall, Nuclear Throne is an arcade-style shooter that succeeds in being both adrenaline-pumping and endlessly charming. It's a must-buy for anyone who who enjoys fast-paced roguelikes or arcade games.

Western is not a genre we stumble upon in gaming world on a daily basis. Therefore, we're always happy to lick scorched blood and whiskey off our dust covered, dry lips. For me personally, the beginning and the end of western video games is Outlaws, there are multiple reasons why and I don't think anyone is interested in hearing the whole list.
CreativeForge Games and its Hard West were two unknowns to me, but the premise sounded promising. It mentioned cowboys, occult and X-Com, so it was enough for me to pick it up.
Hard West is single player TBS with RPG elements. Game consists of eight scenarios loosely connected by a story that didn't quite deliver. It wasn't enough western nor occult to fully occupy my brain. It would be unfair to say that some aspects weren't good, but as a whole, I was more 'meh' than 'yay' about this one, and when I am 'meh' as a person who READS and PLAYS ANYTHING and EVERYTHING and often gets overly excited by extreme stupidity, well... it's bad.
You unlock scenarios as you play. Scenarios could be interpreted as mini universes inside a bigger one, each revolving around central character. There's fighting and choice-and-consequences entwined: you fight in a missions, then you move around the map represented as a buffalo skull picking different options and influencing your game in different ways. Every scenario contains different mechanism - some ask of you to feed your players, other are allowing you to predict the outcomes via clairvoyance. When the time to fight comes again, you enter something I call battle screen where you equip each character with different guns and consumable items you earn by fighting, trading or completing objectives.
Hard West introduces several interesting systems which unfortunately fail to help the game rise above the average. Poker hands is one of these systems. You can equip each character with up to five cards. Each card is a perk by itself, improving luck, sight or shooting skills. When you combine cards together, you may assemble a poker hand. High card, pair, flush and so on, each of these hands deal another set of bonus improvements to characters. While this sounds great, it proved to be of little use in the game. I didn't feel too much difference between carefully and randomly picked hands. Another system that creates pressure on players is luck system. When the enemy's bullet misses you, your luck goes down, so at certain point you need to move away to stay alive. It would be great, tense and hard to have enemies push forward with this system, but unfortunately, enemy AI is horrenous and most of the time, you're dealing with enemies that take awkward positions and shoot without any tactics on their mind. Game also introduces ricochet shots, typical part of any decent cowboy movie, but most of the time, you won't utilize these. Shooting pans and anvils is not something you need to do in this game, no matter if you're able to do this.
Fighting missions are why Hard West gets compared to X-Com. I didn't spot any other similarities. And to be quite honest, thanks to clunky controls and bad camera positions, Hard West feels pretty cheap. I am almost certain this one was built in Unity because as I've played it reminded me of Wasteland 2 (which I love, by the way) and all of the bad moments that I've encountered while traveling and fighting in radioactive desert. What I've liked about X-Com is the fluidity of the fight, the movement, the complete experience. It makes me happy to see weapons inspired by Wild West's real and -state-of-prototype instruments of death, but it just isn't enough. To add insult to injury - there's no option to save mid mission, so at certain points you're doomed to 40 minute fights. If you exit and/or die, you need to start again and that causes quite a frustration.
What I've really liked about the game is its audio. Music is appropriate and mystical in a way. Weapon sounds wear "Standard Quality" badge and the narrator, a guy named Death - he's FANTASTIC. Really, a ♥♥♥♥ing awesome job. Death personally kept me on pushing through the storyline in the moment where I just wasn't willing to continue.
Another huge disappointment for me personally was implementation of occult elements in the game. The whole experience felt like this:
Offices of CreativeForge Games.
Team member 1: I don't know, these western guys aren't really convincing. We need something more...
Team member 2: How about we make some of them worship Satan? Hail Satan! Pentagrams!!!
Since Western-meets-Horror is one of the selling points, I was thinking we will get something DarkToweresque, but it turned out that shallow characters couldn't even be saved with addition of cults and ocassional demon spawns. Mostly because demons in this game are SO stereotypical they have red skin and horns. Really? I mean, really?
When you're done with the campaign, you'll realize another and major flaw: replayabilty is none. OK, you can always try to get higher difficulty or beat the game in Iron Man mode. Sadly, the fact you can't transfer your loadouts and earned cards from one to another scenario and combined them all together makes the second playthrough nothing short of forced grind fest.
Hard West promised a lot. I've expected even more because you can't really resist and stop drooling when someone says they'll deliver X-Com type of game with Western and Satanic themes. It turned out Hard West isn't that hard nor way too western, not to mention how desperately 'unevil' it is. It's a cheap looking game with some great elements and it wouldn't be fair to recommend it at the current (14,99) nor its regular price (19,99) when X-Com and its DLC's prices are dropping like flies every now and then.
In case you really need your western'n'cult fix, wait for a discount to get it.

With charming art and animation, together with stellar voice-acting, Broken Age is an enjoyable adventure.
However, the combination of a somewhat lackluster story and puzzles that sometimes become quite head-scratching does deflate the experience a bit.
Occasionally the story gets a bit interesting with the two protagonists' experiences mirroring each other. Also, while the story itself isn't very deep, the characters that you meet along the way are well-written and often funny. While never causing me to wipe tears of laughter from my eyes, Broken Age often made me smile.
If you're looking to enjoy lovely visuals, well-written dialogue and excellent voice-acting, this is the point'n'click adventure for you. If you're looking for an engaging and thought-provoking story, I'm afraid this game simply doesn't offer that.

Each of you probably heard or played in such a famous game Civilization.
Actions Civilization 3 begins as well as in all other parts: in ancient times. You are the leader of your people. And there are not a few of them!

Also, when creating a map, you can choose the size of the map (from small to huge) and the landscape of the terrain (from small islands to one large continent). The game begins with the fact that you have a worker and a settler. With the help of a settler you are establishing the city - your capital.
After this, the race between civilizations begins. You will learn different technologies: from writing to nuclear weapons, building more cities than rivals, exchanging technologies, building various wonders of the world: the Great Pyramids, the Great Wall of China, Hanging Gardens, the Colossus and much more. The only thing that I do not understand how in Moscow can be the Colossus, and the Great Pyramids and the Great Wall of China. In this regard, the creators of course lost. In Civilization 3 you lead a variety of wars. First, you attack ordinary foot soldiers, then they turn into legionnaires.
Also at your disposal will be aviation, cruisers and many other modern innovations. In cities you will build various buildings that improve the life of the population.
In each city there is a certain number of people. If you are a strong player, then opponents will offer you peace with them, offer gifts, and if you are very weak, they will demand technology, gold, cities for your life.

The majority of the time the dash, if it works, will leave you either too far from an enemy to continue the fight or just drop you slap bang in the middle of a damage inducing obstacle.
Aesthetically speaking it's not terribly interesting. Art style is identical to Hyper Light Drifter without any of the charm. Music is a very familiar ambient mush that is both unobtrusive and yet boringly repetitive, I'm reasonably sure the first and second areas had the exact same score.
What I got from the story was... weak. I'm guessing the writers were dealing with English as a second language, which can have it's own charm to it, but when the game itself is this mediocre it simply becomes another area worth criticising. Much of the dialogue is very disjointed and can make little sense from one sentence to another which could work in a sort of pseudo David Lynch, dream like way but again, other things are needed to prop up such a feature.
Ultimately I was hoping to feel that "imitation is the sincerest form of flattery" when it came to this and Hyper Light Drifter. There is a good game in here somewhere, a little love and attention given to the mechanics and various features would do wonders. However, as it stands, this comes off as little more than a cynical wannabe. Save yourself the hassle and buy the game that, I will generously say, "inspired" this one.

I was a little hesitant to buy this game after reading some of the reviews about the lack of persistence, lack of player overwatch, and enemies running up point blank. However, for me, this appeared to be blown out of proportion. Let's review those criticisms first.
This is part of the game mechanics, essentially. The game features various abilities, items, and statuses. Each scenario, you start with a certain set of these. A lot of times the starting circumstances are thematic. Personally, it was enjoyable to rebuild your posse's abilities, and try new combinations of abilities and gear.
Basically, the enemy gets a circle, that if you enter, you will get shot automatically. The player does not. First, this is to prevent the PLAYER from running up point blank and shooting the enemy. Secondly, you are smarter than the AI, so it needs aids like this to keep the challenge. Third, it helps the "puzzle" aspect of tactics. Manuevering is extremely important in this game, so the overwatch zones challenge you to think about how you want combat to move, and how you are going to flank.
This almost never happened to me. I think what it might be, is the AI trying to position, then coming around a corner very close to one of your characters. Instead of backtracking to cover, like you might do, the AI instead takes a shot that is likely to hit, and does full damage (as cover reduces damage). Usually, the way this occured for me was the AI running out into the open at medium range from my characters. My characters luck (a form of expendable defense) usually protected them from these attacks, which resulted in the AI enemy getting gunned down, sans cover.
OK, onto the review...
Combat mechanics - Imagine the typical tried and true XCOM mechanics, plus a few twists, and it moves faster (only 1-2 hits to kill your average guy). First, you have LUCK, which causes enemy shots to miss, but then depletes in proportion to their hit chance (in other words, the better the shot, the more luck is burned off to protect your character). When a character uses certain items, or gets hit, they regen luck. Luck is also spent to perform certain special abilities, meaning you have to choose between defense and (typically) offense. Secondly, if you have partial cover you take less damage... and full cover even less (and the same for the enemy).
RPG Mechanics - This was really enjoyable. Your character does not level up, but instead gets weapons, usable items, a talisman, and playing cards. This last one is really important. Your characters can have up to 5 cards equipped. Each provides a passive bonus, some provide and active bonus, and (here's my favorite part) if you can arrange a type of poker hand (like 2 of kind, full house, straight, etc.) you get additional passive bonuses. These, combined with your characters natural stats, and equipped gear allow you to create awesome combos.
Level Design - The levels are great. They are complex enough to provide a variety of strategy. The best part is that most missions have some sort of objective to complete, and a lot of them have secondary objectives that give you bonuses. Lastly, certain missions start off out of combat, where your characters can sneak around the guards, completing objectives before combat even starts (which is initiated by your actions).
The Campaign - First, it tells several stories, each of which help flesh out the main story line and give you an idea of what happened before, after, and during the main campaign. My favorite part was how most of the campaigns had their own system of how it worked. In one campaign you have to keep track of men and food while leading an expidition. In another you have to research different things, and use tools to track down an important quest item. It reveals how flexible the game engine really is.
The World - It is a great marriage between Clint Eastwood and HP Lovecraft. I love it love it love it.
Line of Sight - Every XCOM style game I have ever played suffers from this, so it's not a huge negative in my mind. However, you will find the enemy making shots you swore were impossible, or set your characters up to be behind cover when they take full damage.
The writing - I didn't want to put this down as bad, even though it technically is, because it didn't stop me from enjoying the game. So, the story is great, but occassionally the writing just breezes through details. You will get lines like "And then you used your powers to kill everyone ever." WOT. That's not an actual line from the game, but I'm paraphrasing to illustrate these odd lines found throughout the game.

Phantom Trigger begins with the main character Stan suffering from an abrupt seizure before quickly transitioning to an alternate reality in which we control a scarfed individual called The Outsider. From here, it divulges into 2 plot lines, one as The Outsider traversing the strange world, the other depicting the events involving Stan after the seizure (these are delivered through flashbacks) and it’s a shame that the latter is stifled by the former.
Stan early on makes is clear that he doesn’t want use surgery to solve his condition/disease and opts instead for the more dangerous and experimental route. The game expands on the selfishness of this decision by showing the impact on his familial relationships but by contrast, it doesn’t take the time to properly explain the link between Stan’s condition and how that correlates with what’s happening in the alternate reality. We know that they’re closely related but we don’t know how or why that’s become the case.
These questions also don’t get answered by the characters in the strange world since most of them only speak in cryptic dialogue that merely alludes to a bigger picture. By the time the rather abrupt ending brings the game to a conclusion, their lack of character development and actual narrative impact made them feel lackluster at best. The game could have really explored something interesting with this setup but handling the delivery this way made it a predictable adventure for anyone who recognizes the initial premise.

Let’s address the elephant in the room. Phantom Trigger is similar to Hyper Light Drifter in that fans of one are likely to enjoy the other but there are also enough differences to see this as more than a clone or reskin. The core gameplay loop involves going through 4 worlds and clearing the enemies within them until you eventually meet the boss at the end of the level. Again, if you’ve played HLD, this explore-each-map bit is really familiar.
Due to this repetitive nature, enjoyment of the gameplay boils down to the execution of combat and the variety provided, so a lot of this review will zone in on these two aspects. Phantom Trigger uses a 3 weapon system alongside a dash mechanic, a sword for quick slashes, a whip to pull enemies towards you and a pair of claws for slower but more powerful blows. Each of these weapons level up in parallel as they gain experience with every strike and you’ll be able to use certain moves (or combos) once you’ve levelled up the associated equipment. Naturally, since the more powerful combos require multiple high-level weapons, the game encourages you not to be a one trick pony.
Now, one of the title’s biggest strengths is its fast-paced nature. Since enemies hit quite heavily, the game promotes a playstyle dependent on reflexes and quick thinking and that rush of being so close to death only gets more intense as your engagements increase in difficulty. Also, by including combos with different effects like freezing foes in place, it also adds a layer of depth needing proper positioning to make use of these moves. It’s also equally important not to overcommit when attacking and you’ll realize how easy it is to do that when you’re not used to how the delay between dashes and attacks increase as you get further into your 3-hit combo.
By allowing these mechanics to interact with one another, the title creates this ruthless but equally rewarding dynamic, requiring you to think things like “what combo’s the best for this situation”, “what position I should take” and “how many hits can I deal safely”, all within a few seconds. However on the flip side, the gameplay really disappoints in the variety provided for 2 major areas.
The first is the enemy diversity since you’ll only get 1-2 genuinely new foes per level. Everyone else is either the same or just a combined version of 2 enemies you’ve already faced before in the game’s attempt to have this illusion of variety. The second is in the combos provided. From the total 7, 5 of them are almost repeats of one another. While they may be slightly different in aspects like their range or sequence (sword-whip-claw as compared to sword-claw-whip), it’s not enough to give them their own unique use cases. As a result, what you have is a combat system that’s only enjoyable for as long as it remains fresh and that only lasts for like a couple of hours which isn’t great considering the game takes about 5-6 to complete.
1) Great Presentation – would still give overall polish to HLD but this is no slouch
2) Good initial gameplay setup with the fast-paced nature and difficulty
1) Underdeveloped story and characters – you will not get answers to most of the important plot questions
2) Combat does not have the longevity to last 5-6 hours
While I only have one major point of criticism in how the game actually plays, that’s because Phantom Trigger is a title that I really enjoyed, for the first 2 hours. Past that, I struggled to find something to keep that feeling going because it just didn’t have anything left to give. When you’re going up against wave upon wave of the same enemies throughout all the maps, using what is essentially the same combos over and over again, the additional 3-4 hours to complete it become a real slog, especially since the story doesn’t give you the answers you’re looking for either. I wouldn’t recommend this title at full price, best to wait for a sale till it’s about 10 dollars before pulling the trigger.

Mafia III was one of my most anticipated games of 2016. What made the Mafia series was its own blend of uniqueness concentrating on pure character development and really making the player emphasis everything you did. Its true that Mafia III so far has caught my eye regarding the story and has demonstrated the character well but after awhile you will grow tired of constant interruptions from cut scenes whenever something gets interesting. The first few hours literally plays out like a Netflix drama but it gets more annoying in the end if anything as your constantly getting introduced to new characters and backstory.
The engine they have used in Mafia 3 is horrible, capped at 30 FPS at launch was the least of its issues when even on the highest settings and having to put your graphics card in the toaster for three hours produces some of the worst textures in any AAA game this year, its really bad. Even on the highest settings this game is just dead set ugly with texture pop in's, a horrible sky box and awful car damage to detail. The only decent graphics in this game are the animations when your shooting people as blood will pop out from injuries but combat itself is rather clunky. The game does not feel very keyboard friendly, its obviously intended to be used by a controller but even then it feels stiff and unpolished.
Missions were another good element of the previous Mafia's, branding a sort of uniqueness every time however Mafia 3 has taken a more open world approach by giving the player missions to take over districts for three different mob bosses. They are repetitive to say the least and you will be constantly going back to the same places to kill / interrogate the same people. One instance was when I killed a minor boss near the window to complete the objective to only have to then drive all the way back to get the last boss mission to then DRIVE BACK TO THE SAME PLACE and have a different looking main boss IN THE EXACT SAME POSITION AS THE LAST!! Seriously 2k, your mission designs in this game is lazy. Mafia 3 reminds me more or less like a Ubisoft tittle.. if I wanted to play Farcry 4 I would of played that bloody game. Lazy lazy lazy..
You also have the ability to wire tap phone boxes much like Ubisofts towers, which in turn reveals the hidden objectives.. well done great innovation there!
I'm not running a fantastic beast machine, but I can damn well play almost any new game that has came out this year so far on mostly top settings in 1920x1080 without issues. Mafia 3 for me plays less then 30 on 1080p in the lowest settings possible, it was poorly optimized and no way at all ready to be released on PC or any platform for that matter. The amount of bugs, crashes and down write terrible game play has left me sour for 2K. If you enjoy this game, good for you but for me its a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt of what used to be a very good series and I don't even think i'll have the patience to play any more.

Virginia clearly isn't a game for everyone. It mostly appeals to people, who like to use their imagination. It's a story driven game, just like a game from the Telltale Series (The Walking Dead, Tales from the Borderlands, etc.). But while the Telltale games let you make (very) little choices, Virginia is absolutely linear. This game truly is a visual novel.
The short story itself (about 2h playthrough) is confusing and leaves the player with a lot of questions behind. But while some may see this as something negative, I personally like this kind of storytelling. You have to interpret stuff. It's like a X-Files episode (there are even two FBI-Agents, which investigate a mysterious case), where you're mostly left in the dark about what is going on.
Beside the mysterious story, the game itself is very colorful and the visuals are pretty. The gorgeous Soundtrack fits great into the whole atmosphere.
To summarise: If you can bear linear gameplay, but like visual storytelling of a mystical plot, where not everything is explained in detail - this game is worth a try.

I'm so sad that I have to give this game a bad review, but that's what I think of it.
In Virginia you play as Anne Tarver an FBI agent who investigates a disappearance of a young boy in a small town Kingdom of Virginia.
I first learned of the game while going through upcoming game section and fell in love with the art style and the fact that was influenced by X-Files and David Lynch. I couldn't wait to play it and was excited beyond belief. But after I played it, I was disappointed and in the end I have not much positive to say about Virginia.
But however I will start with the good. The art style is absolutely amazing. It's absolutely breathtaking. I fell in love with it and is one of the reasons why I bought the game in the first place (excluding X-Files and David Lynch).
The soundtrack is also amazing. Simply put the orchestral score is amazing and is some of the best this year.
The atmosphere is also really good. and helps build tension in some later segments of the game, but this is where I have to stop with the good and get on with the bad.
The story is the probably the biggest gripe I have with the game. The story is muddled and it makes no sense and the ending is also very bland. The story has too many jumps from one place to another and I honestly didn't think that was a good idea.
When the story jumps from one place to another it becomes tedious just to keep up with the plot.
Now as for the other points the game is also not very David Lynchy. It was almost advertised as a game inspired by Twin Peaks and I have to admit it's not even close to being anything close to Twin Peaks. Later in the game there are some moments which people might associate with Twin Peaks, I really don't see it.
The game is also incredibly short around an hour long and it really shows that the game had to wrap up quickly as the ending doesn't really make sense ( I do understand the final scene, but won't say anything on it here since that's heavy spoiler territory).
In the end I have to say that Virginia is incredibly disappointing, and is only worth checking out if you are incredibly interested and only on a sale, otherwise don't bother.

Many people asked me about the game „Orion: Dino Horde“. So I have written a review now. ^^
First I have to say that the game has just 36/100 Metascore. But the Metascore was for the game "Dino Beatdown", not for "Orion: Dino Horde" and the game hasn’t only changed the name, its totally different now.
For many people it’s still not a good game, because of a not perfect graphic (uff.. for me the graphic looks alright – I would give for it 7/10 points. – You can take a look at my Screenshots), some bugs (really the most Shooter Multiplayer Games have bugs/glitches…) and the not so realistic weapon sounds or I DON’T KNOW WHY!
Really…

For me it’s like a mix out of “Primal Carnage” (Jurassic Park Style) and “Killing Floor” plus you have more possibilities in this game. The aim of the game depends on the mission you choose (but in general it’s about shooting dinosaur (1st Person shooting view / 3rd Person Hybrid Gameplay), surviving and protecting the base).

(lots of enemies)
(protecting base, activating objects and surviving the growing waves of dinosaur)
(like in “Primal Carnage” there are 2 teams “Dinosaurs” and “Humans” who play against each other and switch after that)
You can play it
You can choose the difficulty (Noob, Easy, Normal, Hard, Insane, Redikulous) you want to play and one out of 40+ possible maps!
During the game you earn Credits to buy other weapons (50+ weapons, Tech & Gear) and (depending on the game mode) you can also use 7 different vehicles.
But you also earn EXP with killing dinosaur which increases your level. Yeah your level – there is also a level system in this game and the different human classes have all unique abilities.
He has a Jetpack which makes him able to fly for a while (That’s freaking awesome! It’s so funny when the T-Rex is really nearly to eat you and you just fly away BYE BYE T-REX lol). But back to the topic the Assault starts with a CV-10 Pistol (better weapons you get with killing and purchasing). His Grenade is “Frag Grenade”.
The Recon has the ability to use his cloak which makes him invisible for the enemies for some seconds. He starts with the CV-10 Silenced Pistol and uses the EMP Grenades.
The Supporter people have medic guns. They can heal themselves or other teammates whenever they want but they really need it because they can’t just fly away. They start with the M-40 Magnum and have Smoke Grenades. I like those Smoke Grenades because when you get into trouble with the Supporter because you have to reload your weapon but you can’t - because too many dinosaur are attacking you - and you are just healing yourself the whole time, it’s possible to throw such a Smoke Grenade and the dinosaur run away. Good time for reloading and healing. ^^
You unlock more abilities with a higher level (for example less fall damage or more jump height). The current maximum reachable level is 50.

Oh it’s just HEAVEN for achievement hunters! There are 250+ achievements and the most of them are not that hard to get. There is really for everything an achievement.. for kills with all weapons, healing, flying, riding, surviving and and and.
So all in all.. what should I say… this game offers much and makes a lot of fun! Sure it’s not perfect (e. g. weapon sound isn’t realistic) but who cares.. which game is really that realistic? In Left for Dead 2 you can shoot through a wall but not through a TENT! LOL So I tell you to give this game a try and maybe you join my games and we smash those dinosaur together! ^.~

Date of Review: 04.2016
Playtime ~600hrs (Actual play time according to Hive Stats)
NS2 is a blend of strategy and shooter. I will not say "unique", since the word seems overused nowadays. What they tried to implement are two 2 factions that actually have very different playstyles while still staying moderately balanced. It is also uncommon in the way that the development team keeps the game updated and running, partially relying on community effort to do so.
Within the game the Marine faction represents the standard FPS gameplay of tactical movement and long range engagements. The Marines move slower through the map, but have a distinctive firepower advantage and can set up outposts a lot more quickly than the aliens. The Marine commander will have to juggle a lot betweeen setting up bases, maintaining resource income and supporting frontline troops. Marine field players will need to coordinate with the commander and each other in order to hold as much ground as they can without spreading their forces too much
The Alien faction has many lifeforms that have short range attacks and low hitpoints, especially in the beginning of the game. They rely on stealth and synergies between their abilites to ambush and overwhelm marines or sneak behind enemy lines to quickly destroy key structures. The Alien Commander can focus a lot more on supporting his team and can even leave his position in the Hive vacant for some time to assist in attacking or defending. Alien field players need to pick wisely when to invest resources in higher lifeforms and balance between doing the most possible damage and keeping their valuable lifeforms alive.
As an advise for new players I recommend to visit servers with a lower playercount first. The game is designed around teams with 6-8 players, which further increases the steep learning curve on some of the high playercount servers. Also, I advise them not to be afraid of trying to play aliens at first. While playing as marine may be more familar to many, there are many things to learn and keep in mind at once that simply do not matter for alien players. Going for a high skill server while learning is okay, however keep in mind that on servers with a high average skill the atmosphere can become a bit competetive.
Strenghts:
- The game has a strong emphasis on teamplay and tactical gameplay. While personal skill is also important the team with the better coordination, even if it just by a part of the team, can have a big impact on the outcome.
- Both sides have a unique feel and playstyle to them, and a variety of weapons to cater to different preferences of playstyle.
- A very unique atmosphere that is supported by map design and faction design alike.
- Different map designs encourage different approaches in playstyle, both personal and as a team.
- The "community development team", hired by the developers to maintain the game, produces regular patches in coordination with the community to fix performance and gameplay issues.
Weaknesses:
- The Netcode could need some serious improvement, with long range weapons facing against short range weapons differences in latency can have a huge negative impact when playing. I recommand searching servers with a latency (ping) of less than 100 (my experience suggests less than 50).
- The playerbase is stable, but small. There is a number of well populated servers, however it is possible you come online at a time where all the "good" servers are full. With your ping in mind, try out for yourself whether you want to wait for a slot on a server in your region or try your luck on one with a higher latency, or with more/less skilled players than you.
- For a new player, the amount of things to learn can be overwhelming at first, especially on marines. There are a number of gameplay mechanics that are not immediately clear to the player and need to be learned. Be not afraid to ask, even if some of the experienced players may sound harsh, there is always someone who will be willing to help.
- The same goes for commanding. There is a lot about commanding that is not immediately apparant, so you might not want to try it right off the bat. However, messing around in offline sandbox mode might be good to get an idea of "what that commander is doing" while you are out fighting, even if you are not interested in commanding.
I recommend NS2 to anyone ready to invest some time into learning the game before actually having fun. There are a few initial hurdles to overcome if you want to play successfully. However once you become more accustumed to the mechanics this game can be fun and challenging to skilled and less skilled players alike. Also, my personal experience with the players in NS2 is that there are quite a few helpful ones that you can get along with very well, although you may need to take the initiative talk to them first. Many players are not used to the amount of communication NS2 requires for both teams, so this factor might also require some effort from the side of the new player.
A simple and unrelenting challenge, incredibly addictive.

Nuclear Throne is comparable to Isaac on methamphetamines, packed with bullet hell nonsense and a crazy assortment of weapons, perks and interesting, unique characters. The gameplay consists of point-to-shoot style combat and when you die, you start again with unlocks acquired along the way. To top this off the pixel art is lovingly crafted, with cute, lively sprites (that only drive you to kill them) and with excellent visuals comes excellent audio with this spaghetti-western styled soundtrack that plays intensely under furious mouse clicks and flying bullets.
I honestly recommend this game to anyone looking for an EXTREMELY challenging, yet equally rewarding experience.

Personal, Biased Review, with some Factual Tidbits:
Absolutely amazing!  For those who grew up with or have experience with old Windows operating systems (Windows 95 in paticular) it should be a very nostalgic experience.  Even if you haven't used Windows 95, it's still a blast to play!  By putting "Advisors" in the game (Advisors are people to advise you in specific fields; one helps with economics, one with war, etc.), the developers made the game beginner-friendly, and fun for all ages.  The only downside is that alot happens at one time, and everything can get a bit overwhelming (20 of your cities could be rioting while you're in a war with Ghandi's India (it happens), all of your resources could be gone, while your treasury's funds are slowly depleting and the world hates you), which makes the game a bit tedious at times.
Technical Stuff:
Graphics: 5/10
One must remember while playing that this game was made for Windows 95/98/Me, and doesn't have very good graphics.  However, they get the job done, and the leader animations are quite ahead of their time.
Story: 10/10
Many people will say there is no story.  But that's the name of the game.  There is no story because you CREATE your own story.  History follows your actions and the story evolves the more you play and make tough decisions.
Sound: 3/10
Personally, I like the music in the game, but the actual music plays in constant loops of 3-6 songs depending on the era, and seeing how the games can drag on for ten hours or more, I have to dock the game for this one. The SFX is okay, but there's nothing groundbreaking (just how groundbreaking can SFX get, anyways?).
Gameplay: 7/10
Using the mouse constantly can get very tiring, and the keyboard shortcuts can be hard to remember.  As the game drags on, the gameplay can get overwhelming on tedious, and it can be quite depressing when the end of the game seems like forever away The advisors are nice touch for beginners, though.
Replayability: 10/10
With around thirty different civilizations to choose from, each with their own abilities and strategies, this game is as open-ended as it gets.  No game is the same, and depending on what civilizations you're up against, and what civilization you are, you'll have to adapt your strategy.
Overall: 7/10 "Amazing"
With the advisors, the game is made easier for beginners, but only hardcore players will stick around to see whether or their civilization will stand the test of time.  The game's sound and graphics are lacking (it was released for Windows 95), but that is made up for with great gameplay, although it can get tedious at times, and maximum replayability.
Final Word:
A great game, and one of my personal favorites.  My civilization may not stand the test of time, but this game definitely will.  'Nuff said.

Or, last option, have them "collect things"? I originally thought Endurance was the dump stat to end dump stats, but apparently it effects the HP gained upon level up, which I'll take at face value. But I don't think it does anything else, besides run the Nuka Cola bottler, the only room that does that, not like you'd know that until you had 80 (or 100, I forgot) dwellers, because the dumb game doesn't let you know. Seriously, what's the benefit in hiding this stuff? Let me know all the numbers. I'm just going to go on the wiki to look at the numbers myself if you don't let me peek behind the curtains.
Speaking of stats and applications, what do stats do in combat/quests? Hotline Miami: Do you like hurting other people?
“Do you like hurting other people?” is probably the single most memorable line from Hotline Miami. In an industry filled with blood, violence, gore, and hundreds of thousands of murders… A game has never asked me this simple question.
And that really made the question stand out, because while I don’t like hurting other people… I do like playing video games that glorify killing… And that made me question  myself. It put me into the headspace of actually physically harming these top down representations of human beings.
But it didn’t stop me from slitting their throats and kicking their skulls in. They’re just pixels after all.
I avoided Hotline Miami for a really long time. It came out back in 2012 and I was a significantly different person back then. I found that the game bothered me, and I felt it was disturbing. Why? I don’t really know. It just seemed excessive to me. Fast forward four years, and after avoiding the game and not giving it a chance I found that I owned it via a Humble Bundle I had purchased. So I decided, “Might as well!” I then installed the game and finished it in the same day… And purchased Hotline Miami 2 the following afternoon.
I was both excited and uneasy going into it. I played through the first level, and after completing it and seeing the game tally up my score I said to myself, “Okay, I get it.”
And then I was hooked.
The sound track, the visceral gameplay, the fast gameplay loop of death and restart… It was great!
It also helps that the game is coy, it doesn’t tell you much. Unlike the violence which is front and center, the story is very subtle as to be near non existent. There’s just enough to keep you interested and pique your curiosity. It’s like a mini-skirt, long enough to cover everything, but short enough to keep things interesting. I can’t believe I just wrote that-- but it’s true.
I found that the mystery behind the events of the game were really what enthralled me. The gameplay is very well balanced, and while it is sometimes frustrating it never felt unfair. If I was having trouble, it’s because I wasn’t utilizing everything at my disposal or I was approaching the situation from the wrong angle.
This has been used many times to describe Hotline Miami, but it’s like a fast action puzzle game. And I find that to be a very apt description. Adjusting your strategy to take down a particularly tough room and getting slightly better at it each time is very satisfying. And when you finally pull it off you feel like an apex predator, pouncing from the shadows on an unsuspecting gazelle. Although in this case I guess it would be the Gazelle doing the pouncing.
You have just enough vision to plan your attack a few seconds before you engage the hapless enemies, and you have to be near perfect with your execution. Otherwise you have to start over… Which you will do a lot. Like, a lot. But there are barely any loading times, and when you die you’re instantly back in the action-- with fairly reasonable check-points as well! Plus the great soundtrack will pull you in and make it a seamless experience.
By far my favorite song was Daisuke, by El Huervo.
Overall if you haven’t checked out Hotline Miami by now I would say give it a go. If you were reluctant because it was so violent, well I found that I had a double standard. Somehow ripping someone’s head off in Mortal Kombat was okay, but hitting them with a lead pipe isn’t. This game really isn’t as bad as it comes off in trailers. Everything happens so fast that you barely have time to even think about what you’re doing, or pay close enough attention to the actual deaths.
And as it turns out, that might be the whole point of the game.
The few moments where the game really makes you watch someone be killed, can be gross. I cringed a few times. But it’s nothing that wasn’t already in God of War.
If you’re like me and had reservations, check out Hotline Miami. It’s very good.

Wanted to love this game. After many, many, restarts and partial playthroughs I just ended up calling it quits. Played FO1 and 2, and Tactics when they were first released and they sit high on my list of "fond of old games." This, I did not care for at all. Enemies zerg you (that's the extent of the AI). In FO Tactics they at least had the sense to flank you, take cover, hide, runaway, switch weapons appropriately, etc. You'd think that would be something we'd see in the 21st century. Not here. They run at you or shoot, then you shoot back, repeat.
The stat system is broken (not using that word as a euphamism or perjorative, there are stats that matter and those that don't. And your stats don't effect your skills at all beyond intelligence).  There are only a few viable builds to complete the game. The skills are so convoluted and could have been easily reduced by half. For instance you have: Alarm Disarming, Lockpicking, and Safe Cracking. Is there any reason these couldn't be under one skill instead of three? No. Then you have: Hard A*s, Kiss A*s, Smart A*s, Barter, and Leadership, aren't these all subsets of a larger skill like persuasion/speech or based on charisma? Well, no, not in Wasteland 2. Why are they convoluted? Probably to compensate for a game design that allows for so few actions in game beyond "kill person in this manner" or "successfully interact with this object for a reward."
Weapons and armor have arbitrary penalties that exist only to impose penalties. For instance, did you know that an "assault rifle" loses all efficiency at five feet and  a board with a nail in it works MUCH better? I didn't know that, but after playing WL2 I do. Further energy weapons do lots of damage to you if they hit your armor, but if they hit your bare skin they don't do much on any damage at all. Logic! It's the guise of strategy, not actual strategy. It's strategic like rock, papers, scissors.
This game has a lot of heart. It tries very hard an certainly has charm. Yet I've played browser based games with more depth, complexity, strategy, and sophistication. Really wanted something to take me back to those first days playing FO1/2 and Tactics. Instead it's better to just play those instead of WL2. Or, if you really want a strategy based around functional abilities, gear (that you build or collect), multiple means of achieving you goal, and competent AI go play XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within.
I want my money back.
