WL2 has an Immersive atmosphere and quality voice acting. Weather is not dynamic nor are there day/night cycles but you will find different weather conditions in some areas.
Your rangers will gain experience and levels quickly. This will make them more deadly and survivable. You will see some familiar weapons in this game. But how they are implemented is for game mechanics. While not realistic, the weapons are fun and you will want a mix of weapon types used by your team, e.g. not all using energy weapons.
Energy weapons and armor... it may take some time to understand how these work. Why and when they don't work and against whom. Some question whether armor should be removed before some battles (I left mine on). While the implementation may lack refinement, it still works. Take your hits, adjust your strategy and learn to be more effective in battle. Prioritize some enemies and use you action points more effectively, e.g. move to cover and/or crouch. Friendly fire can happen so watch your line of sight.
Throwing grenades to a platform above your rangers or even over a fence doesn't work. You need line of sight and to be at the same level as your enemy or above them. But grenades and rockets do go where you tell them and can be very effective.
Many say there are areas that are bugged, like LA and the Bastion, maybe. You may find these comments when searching for solutions. But I question if these comments are based either upon the demo or an older revision, as they have not been updated. While there are many times you might question why you can't perform a particular action regarding a quest, they can be satisfactorily completed. There are also different methods for completing most quests.
How you play and in particular who you aid in your journey has an affect not only in the end-game summary but the final battle. Do you need/want allies at the final battle or are you baddass enough to take 'em all on by yourself? Play how you like and when you have won the game, play it again!

Coming to terms with the missed potential of Virginia is one of the most deflating experiences I've had in 25 years of gaming. Virginia is somehow completely narcissistic and utterly ashamed of itself at the same time.
- References that are this thinly veiled border on plagiarism, no matter how nostalgic they are.
- Lynch's metaphors and surrealism serve a purpose beyond obscuring paper-thin archetypes.
- Listening to a radio play in a cinema would be a frustrating experience. So is watching a film that that thinks it is a video game, especially when overwrought cinematic elements encroach so much on player control.
This game nails so many things that its fatal flaws are all the more painful. If you want to make a film, make a film. If you want to make a video game, embrace the medium - don't try and hide it behind film language. If you can't cope with the idea that a player might look in the wrong direction at the wrong time, it's time put down Unity and pick up a camera.
The only thing innovative about this game is the way it belittles and encumbers the medium.
I'll rewrite this review when I've calmed down.

Awesome game.  Expect to fail a lot, as there is a learning curve, but I found it a very enjoyable and rewarding experience, hardly ever frustrating.  You will learn something about rocketry and orbital mechanics, especially if you take advantage of the wealth of resources that the community has put together outside of the game.  Whipping out your calculator to calculate delta-v's makes you feel like a wizard!  As an added bonus, whenever you fail, you are often treated to a nice explosion (and remember: Jebediah signed up for this!).
In KSP, essentially a sandbox game, your imagination is the limit!  There is so much to do.  I've visited most of the planets (Eloo mission in the works) and at over 200 hours, I feel that I've barely scratched the surface of all you can do in KSP.
Also, mods.  So many mods to add in elements that you feel are lacking in the stock game.  The game has gotten some negative reviews from people nervous about Take Two ruining the modding aspect of the game, but I personally think this is unfounded.  GTA and KSP could not be more different; it's foolish to expect the same the result, especially when the devs have always encouraged and supported mods.
Highly recommended

Story wise, this game doesn't like to waste your time. It does a lot of flash forwards (which may bother some people) but personally, I like things that don't waste my time with fillers. Especially in short titles like this one.
Sound designers were also hard at work. I played it on both surrounds headsets and speakers and I have to say, it was pretty impressive (mainly because I wasn't expecting this sort of quality from an indie game) Oh and the music. I think it's the most important character (yes you read it right) of the game. It literally carries the story.
Visually speaking, the image is shrunk to 21:9 aspect ratio to give you a cinematic feel. It even suggests you set the fps limit to 30 for that very reason. But if you're using a 21:9, then it's a different story. The image is full size and (personally) 30 fps cap is not neccesary. That being said, I don't think the main reason behind the 30 fps limit was the "cinematic feeling" because in some scenes, I saw frames dipping down to low 20's with a single 980. It wasn't a big issue though.
Anyway, I digress. All and all it was a nice 2 hour experience. There aren't many games like this.
It's also priced right (unlike *cough*nomansky*cough*) It doesn't pretend to be a 60$ title and I think the reason behind this game getting mixed reviews on store page is because people have unimaginable expectations.
That's not the developers fault. And that's why I'm bothering to write a review.

Mafia III was one of my most anticipated games of 2016. What made the Mafia series was its own blend of uniqueness concentrating on pure character development and really making the player emphasis everything you did. Its true that Mafia III so far has caught my eye regarding the story and has demonstrated the character well but after awhile you will grow tired of constant interruptions from cut scenes whenever something gets interesting. The first few hours literally plays out like a Netflix drama but it gets more annoying in the end if anything as your constantly getting introduced to new characters and backstory.
The engine they have used in Mafia 3 is horrible, capped at 30 FPS at launch was the least of its issues when even on the highest settings and having to put your graphics card in the toaster for three hours produces some of the worst textures in any AAA game this year, its really bad. Even on the highest settings this game is just dead set ugly with texture pop in's, a horrible sky box and awful car damage to detail. The only decent graphics in this game are the animations when your shooting people as blood will pop out from injuries but combat itself is rather clunky. The game does not feel very keyboard friendly, its obviously intended to be used by a controller but even then it feels stiff and unpolished.
Missions were another good element of the previous Mafia's, branding a sort of uniqueness every time however Mafia 3 has taken a more open world approach by giving the player missions to take over districts for three different mob bosses. They are repetitive to say the least and you will be constantly going back to the same places to kill / interrogate the same people. One instance was when I killed a minor boss near the window to complete the objective to only have to then drive all the way back to get the last boss mission to then DRIVE BACK TO THE SAME PLACE and have a different looking main boss IN THE EXACT SAME POSITION AS THE LAST!! Seriously 2k, your mission designs in this game is lazy. Mafia 3 reminds me more or less like a Ubisoft tittle.. if I wanted to play Farcry 4 I would of played that bloody game. Lazy lazy lazy..
You also have the ability to wire tap phone boxes much like Ubisofts towers, which in turn reveals the hidden objectives.. well done great innovation there!
I'm not running a fantastic beast machine, but I can damn well play almost any new game that has came out this year so far on mostly top settings in 1920x1080 without issues. Mafia 3 for me plays less then 30 on 1080p in the lowest settings possible, it was poorly optimized and no way at all ready to be released on PC or any platform for that matter. The amount of bugs, crashes and down write terrible game play has left me sour for 2K. If you enjoy this game, good for you but for me its a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt of what used to be a very good series and I don't even think i'll have the patience to play any more.

Many people asked me about the game „Orion: Dino Horde“. So I have written a review now. ^^
First I have to say that the game has just 36/100 Metascore. But the Metascore was for the game "Dino Beatdown", not for "Orion: Dino Horde" and the game hasn’t only changed the name, its totally different now.
For many people it’s still not a good game, because of a not perfect graphic (uff.. for me the graphic looks alright – I would give for it 7/10 points. – You can take a look at my Screenshots), some bugs (really the most Shooter Multiplayer Games have bugs/glitches…) and the not so realistic weapon sounds or I DON’T KNOW WHY!
Really…

For me it’s like a mix out of “Primal Carnage” (Jurassic Park Style) and “Killing Floor” plus you have more possibilities in this game. The aim of the game depends on the mission you choose (but in general it’s about shooting dinosaur (1st Person shooting view / 3rd Person Hybrid Gameplay), surviving and protecting the base).

(lots of enemies)
(protecting base, activating objects and surviving the growing waves of dinosaur)
(like in “Primal Carnage” there are 2 teams “Dinosaurs” and “Humans” who play against each other and switch after that)
You can play it
You can choose the difficulty (Noob, Easy, Normal, Hard, Insane, Redikulous) you want to play and one out of 40+ possible maps!
During the game you earn Credits to buy other weapons (50+ weapons, Tech & Gear) and (depending on the game mode) you can also use 7 different vehicles.
But you also earn EXP with killing dinosaur which increases your level. Yeah your level – there is also a level system in this game and the different human classes have all unique abilities.
He has a Jetpack which makes him able to fly for a while (That’s freaking awesome! It’s so funny when the T-Rex is really nearly to eat you and you just fly away BYE BYE T-REX lol). But back to the topic the Assault starts with a CV-10 Pistol (better weapons you get with killing and purchasing). His Grenade is “Frag Grenade”.
The Recon has the ability to use his cloak which makes him invisible for the enemies for some seconds. He starts with the CV-10 Silenced Pistol and uses the EMP Grenades.
The Supporter people have medic guns. They can heal themselves or other teammates whenever they want but they really need it because they can’t just fly away. They start with the M-40 Magnum and have Smoke Grenades. I like those Smoke Grenades because when you get into trouble with the Supporter because you have to reload your weapon but you can’t - because too many dinosaur are attacking you - and you are just healing yourself the whole time, it’s possible to throw such a Smoke Grenade and the dinosaur run away. Good time for reloading and healing. ^^
You unlock more abilities with a higher level (for example less fall damage or more jump height). The current maximum reachable level is 50.

Oh it’s just HEAVEN for achievement hunters! There are 250+ achievements and the most of them are not that hard to get. There is really for everything an achievement.. for kills with all weapons, healing, flying, riding, surviving and and and.
So all in all.. what should I say… this game offers much and makes a lot of fun! Sure it’s not perfect (e. g. weapon sound isn’t realistic) but who cares.. which game is really that realistic? In Left for Dead 2 you can shoot through a wall but not through a TENT! LOL So I tell you to give this game a try and maybe you join my games and we smash those dinosaur together! ^.~

This game shares quite a lot in common with Shadow of Mordor. Which should be expected because it is a sequel after all..
I enjoyed this game, moreso than its predecessor. It has a better story and more unique/tougher combat thanks to more Orc captain attributes. Every captain is different from the last, so it doesn't start feeling like you're fighting the same exact Uruk captain, except with a different name and apparel.
I am neutral on the siege mechanic; yes, it's fun for the first couple of times you conquer a stronghold. But, after that, it loses its charm and starts becoming borderline tedious and boring.
The end game is not worth it, in my opinion. I, myself, did not attempt to go through the end game (Act 4). Having to go through mission after mission defending your strongholds from sieges, with little variance between said sieges was not at all appealing to me. Sieges were already repititious enough as is. I don't want to (nor do I need to) fight through however many end game sieges to witness the final, special cutscene thanks to it being uploaded online.
Despite its flaws and occassionally tedious siege missions, if you are a LoTR fan as I am, you'll absolutely love this game. Lore doesn't always correspond with the books, but it's still a great story nonetheless.
In conclusion, I advise picking this game up on sale because it really doesn't offer enough to be considered a full game. It's more like a DLC for Shadow of Mordor - a revamped story and some different mechanics. If you enjoyed its predecessor, you'll enjoy this installment.

I'm a huge fan of narrative game experiences ("walking-simulators") and was excited to play through this. The premise and idea are promising but the actual experience itself is average at best and mediocre at worst. The lack of any dialogue was a bold choice but combined with a cinema-like narrative structure it only left me confused and frustrated. There was also an annoying lack of detail in environments, I enjoy exploring and learning more about the characters and this gave me absolutely none of that. Additionally, there were weird cultural mistakes about America because this was created by a British game studio (the English-style breakfasts being the most notable example). That sounds nit-picky and petty (and it is), but if a developer wants to create to a linear, narrative, film-like experience then they need to really pay attention to the little things.
Ultimately it feels like a film that has been unsuccessfully shoehorned into a game. The developer seemed like they were uninterested in utilizing the strengths of the medium and just wanted to make a movie instead.

Alan Wake is one of these games that takes you by surprise. I really enjoyed playing it even if I encountered several difficulty walls that prevented me from finishing it (read below).
The main character is a writer à la Stephen King, going on vacation to solve a writer's block issue, and immediately confronting his inner demons in the most terrifying way, along with the disappearing of its wife.
The story is delivered mostly during cinematics (and this time, it's not a problem since the story is solid and the character is a writer). Then the player goes from safe place A to safe place B wandering into darkness and escaping light-sensitive foes.
The game succeeds in capturing the powerlessness of the character, with a constant balance between fight of flight. And rewards exploration in a good way (weapons, ammunition, novel pages, tv serials, etc.)
But what is really good about the game, is that the gameplay and the world makes sense regarding the main character. Burning foes with your light before shooting or evading them is a very nice game mechanic. Setting the horror in a otherwise peaceful environment is very powerful.
Alan Wake is a very good example of an action / adventure game made right, along with a solid character and story. Play it !
So, about the difficulty walls :
#1 I was blocked in the forest with not enough ammunition to deal with darkened foes and had to restart from the beginning. The second time I've played, I moved passed that stage and went pretty far in the game.
#2 I had some trouble to pass the stage where I drive a car on a road with multiple foes around. I find it frustrating to be forced to learn a new mechanic (driving) while struggling my way out. Hopefully I went through after several tries
#3 Actually, I'm stuck in the forest again, in a place with 3 switchable lamptorches on the ground and surrounded by foes. I can manage to kill the first ones by luring them into the light, but am usually killed while moving to another lamp. It is very frustrating because I want to know how the story ends, but the "easy mode" isn't easy anymore. Maybe I haven't learned how to play properly...
So I still have mixed feelings about this, especially the "not so" easy mode. When I play in "easy mode" it's mostly to learn mechanics and enjoy the story without too much challenge. I cannot begin to comprehend the fact that developers will break this agreement midway, like if playing in easy mode wasn't noble or something...  If I want a challenge, I play in medium or hard mode depending on my skills.
Nethertheless, Alan Wake is a very good game based on a single and effective concept with strong execution.

I have mixed feelings about Broken Age. I don't think it deserves a thumbs down, but I'm not sure it deserves a thumbs up either.
As a crowdfunding backer, I played act 1 when it was first released and I liked it. The characters are fun and amusing (particularly Curtis, the hipster-ex-lumberjack-turned-metalworker) and the art is pretty. Most of the puzzles are a little bit on the easy side, which some people might not like, but personally, I prefer that over wandering around and figuratively beating my head against the wall trying to figure out what to do next...
... which is exactly what act 2 is full of. Some puzzles are just completely unintuitive and you practically have to stumble across the answer. Others require you to switch back and forth between Shay and Vella to find the solution, which only makes sense in-fiction through a very weak and underexplored plot point. The game also never once indicates that this is something you should do; you can play through the entirety of Shay or Vella's side of act 1 without any knowledge of the other character's chapter, and then act 2 spontaneously expects you to know that you'll need to alternate between them to find the solutions to the opposite character's puzzles.
So, in conclusion, I would recommend act 1, and once you come that far, you might as well finish up act 2, despite its problems, including a sudden and unsatisfying ending.

Hard West, developed by CreativeForge Games, is a turn based strategy RPG set in a brutal and unforgiving period where a man’s life is worth less than a wad of chewing tobacco; The Wild West. You’ll play as a series of poor souls who were unlucky enough the cross paths with the Devil himself. Overcoming the hardships and tortures of life is only a meager victory compared to the supernatural horrors plaguing the West.
Now, before anything, I think it’s safe to say that Hard West has rightfully taken its place on my list of favorite turn based strategy games. It draws some clear inspiration from X-COM, yet it’s nothing close to a copycat. This game is entirely fresh and adds its own little spins to the genre.
So, as you’d expect, gameplay is pretty solid. Players are equipped with a limited amount of actions, which are spent on movement, the consumption of an item, or attacking. The game offers a series of abilities which can either be purchased or found randomly as you traverse the ruined landscapes. The combination of 1800’s lifestyle and demonic upbringings is not something I’ve seen before in a game, so the results are… surprising: Anything from fanning your revolver to controlling the powers of Satan is available to you.
Also, Hard West has a more lenient feel to it, opposed to other turn based strategy games. It's hard to explain it properly, but maneuvering my characters and setting up flanking positions and whatnot felt so fluid to me. You can utilize almost every inch of the battleground to their favor, and the variety of ways to win a fight is staggering.
As for cons, one thing is SERIOUSLY irking me, and I’ve noticed a fair amount of other reviews bring this up, too. There is no checkpoint/save system when in combat. Fights could last a very long time, depending on the player’s strategies, and if a main character is killed nearing the end of a battle by some stray bandit, you’ve gotta start ALL OVER again. This has happened to me a handful of times, and I could only quench my rage by shutting the game down and taking a break.
Secondly, I've encountered a bug when the enemy is taking their turn in a battle. Sometimes... they just wont do anything, and I end up locked on the 'ENEMY'S TURN' screen. Had to restart a single battle three times before it finally fixed itself. This game's issues are few, but damn, they can be annoying.
I really hope the devs patch this bug, but apart from those gripes, I'm really loving this game.
If you want an intense and addictive turn based strategy game with a hint of satanic horror, Hard West is the place to go.

A very competent XCOM:EU mechanics imitiating turn based tactics game. It is heavily focused on flanking which works very well and is rewarding to do. However with the unique "luck" system, accuracy by volume is very viable, and that is a nice touch.
The setting takes the cake here. A generic western would have been boring, but the supernatural elements are executed perfectly to keep the player interested. The narrator's voice is a pleasure to listen to.
The game plays out in several 1-3 hour scenarios that connect to each other to form an overarching storyline. I'm hopeful for add-on scenarios, since the layout is perfect for that.
Some people complain about the lack of overwatch and no saving in missions, but I find them to be fitting with the theme and the setting.
My only real complaint is that the combat missions have no procedural elements in them, so it is very easy to find a certain tactic for a mission that works every time. Its more like a puzzle game in that sense.
So in conclusion: I'd highly recommend this game for anyone interested in the genre of turn based tactics. With such low price its almost a steal.

This game is unique.  In the parlance of our times, its 'genre' doesn't really exist anymore.  Once, there was a time in gaming when titles did not have to contain certain genre tropes in order to be easily classified and immediately accessible.  So you would do well to consider what this game is, and what it is not, and adjust your expectations accordingly.
This game is fan service of the highest order.  The original Wasteland game lives and breathes inside of this one.  This is the master class on how to update a title with current technology without sacrificing the spirit of the original.  If you loved the original Wasteland, you may buy this title immediately without reservation.  It will blow your mind.  This game is for you.  They made it for you.  Praise them, and thank them for closing the loop. We have come full circle from our gaming origins, and we may now rejoice in exploding our foes like blood sausages.
However, it is important to note:
THIS IS NOT A TACTICAL SQUAD BASED RPG.  This is an update of a title from an era of gaming where, due to technical limitations, it was difficult to even render your party members as seperate icons.  So obviously if you are looking for compelling, deep and complex tactical turn based combat (as I often do) then there are dozens of other titles that do it better.  Its just not a priority for this game, this game is about narrative, it is from a time when narrative was king.  Comparisons to X-Com and whatnot are missing the point.
Anywho.  The writing is brilliant, the world is vibrant, the nostalgia is soul shattering, the humor is mature and hilarious.  It didn't make me feel bad about myself the way Fallout did.  If narrative is your jam, you're gonna love it, the wonky camera won't hamper your enjoyment.  If you're under 30, be warned you will have to click your mouse more than you're used to.

Surprisingly, the game isn't as good at telling a story as it is at suggesting moods and creating moments fixed in time. An exceptionally unique impression is set from the quiet locale, the entirely silent cast, the phenomenal orchestral score, the cinematic editing and the overall dream-like strangeness of events.
Its singular ambiance and approach to storytelling are the main reasons this game should be played. It is the expressed culmination of everything previous interactive narratives strove to achieve, elevated tenfold, yet with many of the same drawbacks associated with the genre.
The game flows smoothly with very few interactions, with the player acting more as a witness than a direct influence. Many scenes jump cut without intervention; others simply expect you to perform the one available action. Sometimes you'll be sitting at a café while nothing happens for several perfect seconds, and though this may sound dull it is actually quite effective at conveying an appropriate state of mind, simultaneously meaningful and banal.
The engaging yet linear story offers no choice to make except for minor subplots tied to obscure achievements. There are some collectible flowers and feathers that have a slight influence over your apartment's decoration but they're inconsequential diversions.
Unfortunately, the game derails spectacularly on its last day, as it trades its delicately crafted crescendo of subtle surrealism for all-out batshit crazy weirdness. The final sequences introduce many elements that will hardly make any sense without a commendable mental effort to discern meaning hidden in symbolism and hallucinations. It is not immediately clear what is real or imagined. This sudden change of pace may easily be dismissed as ineffectual or incohesive and ends the experience on a sour note, or suggests a second playthrough for proper understanding.
Visual default settings locked at 30 fps are dizzying beyond belief but thankfully this can be fixed through the options menu. Minimalist low-poly art style reminiscent of vector illustrations is very well presented. Shaky camera is a bit excessive.
The game throws a few obvious nods to the X-Files by incorporating distinct replicas of its iconic locations, setting it uncomfortably halfway between respectful homage and conspicuous plagiarism. Oddly since they state a few other influences, these references come without acknowledgement by the developers.
For best results, approach Virginia with an open mind and a taste for artistic storytelling.

Coincidentally, I lived in Virginia for 20 years and loved watching David Lynch films while I was there, so I knew this game would hit a sweet spot for me. I adore narrative-driven exploration games like this, and Virginia is no exception. There isn't a traditional "fail-state" per se, but for me the fail state would be
ruminating on the symbolism, metaphors, and themes that Virginia presents.
If it's one thing the game falls short on, it's that the characters fall a little flat. The plot, themes, and environments take center stage spectacularly in this tale, but part of what made Twin Peaks so memorable and amazing were the characters. I wish we had an Agent Cooper of our own in the game (probably the best protagonist in all of television, so it's big shoes to fill).
If you abhor "walking simulators" with minimal interactivity, then you probably won't like this game. If you want an interesting cinematic exploration game with a thought-provoking story, gorgeous score, and unforgettable visuals, then you have to try Virginia.

This is a game of wild artistic vision. It sheds convention in favor of uniqueness. You can see that as pretentious or inventive, and that will shape how you ultimately feel about this "game". Virginia showed me something I have never seen before, and for that I have no qualms with my time and money spent.
The aesthetic is unique and striking. The orchestrated soundtrack calls back to classic films of the 80s and 90s. The plot is complex and layered. There is some real humanity to the characters. This is a tough story. You play as a black female FBI agent working in a backwater town in Virginia in the early 90s. There is an oppressive atmosphere of a very different culture and time for America.
That being said, the plot self destructs in a way that I can only describe as beautiful and maddening. Virginia ramps up time and time again to what you expect to be a resolution, only to be thrust back down with more questions and hard cuts to other times/places/people.
If you want a video game that is traditional, convential, and sensible, Virginia is not for you. If you want a plot with branching paths and character choices and dialogue, Virginia is not for you.
If you want a creative vision that inspires far more questions than answers, if you like the idea of being buried in symbolism and atmosphere, if you're tired of story beats and character arcs being manufactured and just handed over to you, then set aside your expectations and just let Virginia show you its crazy, crazy vision of life and how the decisions we make can change us forever.

The best way I have found to describe Spintires is
. The main, and only goal, of the game is to pickup lumber from point A and haul it to point B (more variety in the map goals would be appreciated).
From this description of the game I bet your thinking 'this game sounds dumb'. But wait there's more! Well, there's mud. Lots of mud. The game includes a fantastic engine that is able to simulate the deformation of mud under the chassis and wheels of your truck and the way your truck reacts to this deformation is satisfying and just great to watch. It adds a nice (if sometimes frustrating) challenge to the task of getting to your goals.
The game also looks nice, not amazing, but enough to engross you into the world... of mud. The main issues that I personally have with this game is that it doesn't really allow for exploration due to the fact if you stray off the 'roads' you will get stuck.
Additionally, the map is obscured by 'cover' when you start a level, this (for me) is just frustrating. Just give me the whole map; without it there is no way of planning your routes without it and when you play hardcore you cannot reset your vehicles to the garage. Thus there has been many points where I just have to start again as the starting vehicle gets stuck and there is no way to recover it (this can cost upto an hour or more of game time and progress being lost).
Also, as an additional point, just stay away from water... there is no way of predicting depth until your truck has stalled and is being carried downriver to its demise.
Overall, I would suggest watching some gameplay on Youtube (or your video streaming site of choice) before purchasing this game. I personally enjoy this game, however I can see why others may not.

Natural Selection 2 is a game you really have to play for a little while before you really get it, at least that’s how it was for me. The trailers and pictures I’ve had seen of the game didn’t really make me that interested and I pretty much just forgot about it for a long time before I finally bought it on a whim, but man am I glad i did! Teamwork, strategy and unique gameplay with a mix of fps and rts. These are the things that make this game really special. Teamwork, because there is no one man army in this game. You need the team to pull together to win the game. Strategy, while this is an first-person shooter it’s also an real-time strategy with each team having a commander. The commanders job is to guide and coordinate the team to gain control of resources, key locations and use those resources to reseach new equipment to fight the enemy.
Maps are well made, large and beautiful in its own way. Aliens and marines each have unique abilities. As a marine I feel like I’m in a very well made aliens movie as I and my teammates move up checking every corner for aliens that want nothing more than to tear us to pieces. As an alien you are the animal lurking around in the shadows waiting for you prey. Either as an alien or marine it's intense, going from silence to fast paced action in an instant, while also having a lot of depth because of its rts elements. Point is, this game is just amazing!

Death is better than Hell (as the name appears on the store page and not a typo in this review) is the first game to hit Steam from developer/publisher Polina Alekseevna. It’s a top-down dungeon crawler-esque action title that pits you against NekroSkeletus and its underground minions. At first glance it looks like a simple non-isometric rpg title from the four-eighty-six era of PCs kind of in the vein of Dungeons & Dragons, albeit a very basic one. In this case, however, those looks are incredibly deceiving.
While the footage and images on the store front show a mildly competent creation, it’s far from one. First of all the keyboard control scheme is ludicrous at best. You move around with the arrow keys while you attack using the space bar, q for an alternate attack (which is a dash forward with your sword), and e to use mana which brings back a small amount of life. Thankfully this isn’t too much of a problem given the hit detection box surrounding your foes seems to be random, and your alternate attack happens sporadiclly after eight to ten normal ones.
And then there are the enemies themselves. The common hordes of spiders, bats, and skeletons will rush you if you get within their line of sight, which is expected. However, they also will just stand there if you take two steps away, or just not even attack. Sometimes they randomly bombard you, and then do nothing or move slower the next time. And with the ever changing hit detection you can be feet from them and hit, facing away and hit, or be right on top and not even make contact at all.
All that said, the goal is to defeat all enemies in the fairly small dungeon and find the steps to advance. Given the aforementioned issues, what seems simple becomes a frustrating nightmare regardless how good you are at these types of games. After only a few floors (if you even make it that far) your interest will quickly wain due to the glaring faults of the title that is on sale at the time of writing this for a dollar snd nineteen cents. Sadly, it isn’t even worth that, let alone the regular asking price of two dollars (both US currency) until further improvements have been made to the controls, hit detection, and enemy ai.

This game is incredibly difficult to review because half of it - Act 1 - was all but flawless and the other half  - Act 2 -was subpar. It's definitely still worth playing, and I still loved and enjoyed it a lot, but Act 2 not only fell totally flat, it also ruined the entire rest of the game.
Broken Age starts out with a host of interesting, amusing, complex, and excellently-voiced characters and even more great puzzles. I'm absolutely awful at puzzle games, so I found myself cheating by using a guide more often than I'd like to admit, but I always felt like the solutions made perfect sense; anyone who plays and loves puzzle games on a regular basis will love those featured in Act 1, which are tricky but completely logical. The plot of Act 1 was similarly dazzling, and the twist at the end - like most of Act 1's puzzles - made perfect sense but still made my jaw drop.
Then we enter Act 2, and things begin to change for the worse.
The puzzles become insanely difficult - not because any of them are that hard to solve, but because none of them are intuitive at all. They become significantly less about making connections and thinking cleverly and a lot more about wandering around clicking on things you've already clicked half a hundred times and offering random people random objects until something finally works. I honestly have no idea how anyone managed to solve half of Act 2's puzzles - especially those featured in the highly frustrating finale, which requires you to switch back and forth between characters helplessly trying to figure out what the hell it is you're supposed to be doing, why what you're doing isn't working, and how to make it work. The constant need to rewire Hexipals (basically little robots with varying functions depending upon how they're wired) is irritating and frustrating beyond belief, especially the miniscule, impossibly well-hidden clues given to you to figure out the order in which the wires need to be connected barely help at all. Not to mention all the disappointing plot points and gaping plot holes the second act introduces into the once-awesome story.
TL;DR: Broken Age Act 1 was absolutely fantastic and shouldn't be missed. Broken Age Act 2 kind of sucked and probably should be avoided at all costs.

Very good game for the price. Sure, it's a turn-based strategy with a Wild West theme (or rather, Weird West) but this is not an X-Com wannabe with a simple WW reskin. The game plays very differently, and pleasantly so. You can grant your posse members various abilities by assigning them poker cards, and some of these abillities are especially interesting and provides tactical depth and variety. Imagine being able to ricochet your shot through several objects before killing your target, or being able to regenerate when not under sunlight.
I also enjoyed the "luck" mechanic. It really gives meaning to phrase &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck". :)
If you read the negative comments, common complaints are the use of checkpoints (i.e. you can't save mid fight) as well as the game being broken into scenarios, with each scenario being independent (i.e. you can't carry over your characters or equipment from one scenario to the next, except for certain unlockable equipment). While the use of checkpoints can be inconvenient, I don't find it much of an issue. Yes, it can be time consuming when you have to replay a fight from the beginning when one of your key character is killed, but I believe it is designed as a such to encourage effective planning and strategy, especially on missions that allow your posse to "set up" their placement before commencing the fight. You will be constantly outnumbered and outgunned, so rushing in with your guns blazing usually means failure. Thus, unless you devise a viable strategy, be prepared to keep replaying the same mission many times.
As for the independent scenarios, each one has an interesting mechanic and story to tell. The varied scenario mechanics, ranging from gold mining to science research to temple raiding expedition, are both refreshing and creative, so much so, they feel like  standalone mini-games in themselves. I am only half-way through the campaign, but thus far, each scenario has kept engaged and asking me for more.
All in all, this is a very solid turn-based strategy game with high production value. In my book, it's a solid 8.5/10 and definitely worth the price if you enjoy TBS games.

Awesome game.  Expect to fail a lot, as there is a learning curve, but I found it a very enjoyable and rewarding experience, hardly ever frustrating.  You will learn something about rocketry and orbital mechanics, especially if you take advantage of the wealth of resources that the community has put together outside of the game.  Whipping out your calculator to calculate delta-v's makes you feel like a wizard!  As an added bonus, whenever you fail, you are often treated to a nice explosion (and remember: Jebediah signed up for this!).
In KSP, essentially a sandbox game, your imagination is the limit!  There is so much to do.  I've visited most of the planets (Eloo mission in the works) and at over 200 hours, I feel that I've barely scratched the surface of all you can do in KSP.
Also, mods.  So many mods to add in elements that you feel are lacking in the stock game.  The game has gotten some negative reviews from people nervous about Take Two ruining the modding aspect of the game, but I personally think this is unfounded.  GTA and KSP could not be more different; it's foolish to expect the same the result, especially when the devs have always encouraged and supported mods.

I looked forward to this game for a long time, and will admit that once I got it did not fall in love with it and so have put very limited time into it, so take my game experience with that grain of salt.  Many people have clearly loved it, and so maybe you will too, but I feel let down and consider this a title that for me has lived up neither to its hype or even to its promises.
Clearly a lot of care and attention to detail went into crafting this game, as well as a long process of interacting with the community during development, and I am impressed with the features.  That they did not add up to a fun and immersive experience for me may have been primarily due to a dislike for the camera handling.  I found early on that I preferred a wide view most of the time, but the camera handles poorly for that.
I also believe that the bar was set reasonably high for visual quality, but again I feel like the look achieved was not equal to the sum of the components, and possibly that has to do with the Unity engine.
I have generally good feelings that Fargo's team was revived by this project and has leveraged the enthusiasm for this revival to  continue on with new projects as well as encouraging other developers doing interesting projects, but otherwise am not too excited to have been a day 1 kickstart supporter.
Some 32 months after the project was officially funded we have not seen the mod tools kit that was promised.  I realize that Fargo was honest in projecting that mod tools would require further time and it will probably come someday, but at this stage of the game's shelf life I'm about ready to declare that a broken promise.  This may seem like a moot point since I haven't cared much for the game, but it is disappointing nonetheless.

It's a story driven walking simulator, it is about 2 hours long. There is a huge chunk of the gamer market that this game is NOT going to please.
I enjoyed it, and I'm planning a second play through. But I really enjoy short, story driven walking simulators.
You play as a black female FBI investigator, working on both a missing person case, and investigating a fellow agent for possible corruption. The story is told in a series of jarring, sudden flash backs, with immediate scene changes, in a surreal "acid-trip" manner with a minimalist art style. There is no spoken dialogue; only body language. The story is multi-layered and complex, "dreams within dreams," and that is part of the charm. You almost need others playing the game with you, so you can talk about the story together to piece it all together.
It's not for everyone, but it is my sort of game.

Hitogata Happa is a Japanese bullet hell shoot’em up that will not only test your patience but your skill and reaction time as well. I have played lots of bullet hell games on steam, but none can hold a candle to how hardcore Hitogata Happa is. The bullet patterns are absolutely insane and the fantastic musical score will get you pumped as you wade through endless walls of impassable bullets. Unlike other games, Hitogata Happa offers you a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of ship variety. Each ship has its pros and cons which require practice for an understanding of how they work. Boss fights are epic and they all have extra mechanics that make them extra fun to fight. Sadly, no matter how much I love this game, it’s not for everyone. It is very hard; the first boss fight will rage quit most people. However, if you are a fan of Japanese bullet hell, this is the best you are going to get until TouHou makes it to steam.

-The menu and character progression options.... The menu has lots of LONG DELAYS you can't avoid. Want to open the inventory? Gotta do an animation! Want to recycle an orc? Gotta wait 15 seconds while he yells and falls over! Want to recycle gear? Gotta click the button for 3 seconds (cough, console port scars, cough).
-Who the #@%!'s idea was it to make "hold esc" the button for bringing up the army screen (console port scars)??
-It takes a stupid amount of time to open loot boxes (I know, we'll get to those). If you buy 15 loot boxes, you'd think you're just going to open them, right? Wrong! Painstakingly open each one, and "load" for about 5 seconds between them. Then, about 2% of the things you get are even useful AT ALL. So how do you get rid of the 98% useless stuff? You guessed it! More recycling that takes FOREVER. And you can't even do that in 1 menu! You have to scross through each individual inventory (sword, dagger, bow, ring, cloak, chest) and hold the recycle button on each individually. DRIVES ME CRAZY!
-Loot boxes! Why developers think this is a compelling game feature is beyond me!

There's plenty of other reviews out there that can give you the scoop on all the features of this game, so I won't attempt to add to that already voluminous dialogue. What I will do is tell you a story about just one of my experiences with the game:
I was hauling a medium-sized load of logs to the drop-off point. My truck of choice for this job was a nice three-axle number called the C255. With locking differentials and six wheel drive, this thing was pulling the load with ease. This truck builds confidence – the kind of confidence that persuades a person to take a shortcut.
It looked safe enough at first: gentle rolling hills covered in deep emerald-green grass. However, the beauty of this pastoral scene belied the agonizing brown muck that lay just inches below those damp blades grass. Before I knew it, the C255 was buried up to the fenders. Those fat lumpy tires churned away at the mud like a mixer in cake batter, but the truck wouldn't budge. I tried reversing, turning, then forward again, over and over, and nothing worked. A scan of the surroundings for a winch anchor was fruitless. I was stranded in the middle of beautiful field of green grass that disguised the truck-swallowing mud beneath. A situation like this called for extreme measures.
The answer was the E7310. I call this bad boy the Behemoth. It's an 8x8 that's as big as two city buses and this thing does. not. get. stuck. Period. Which is good, because all it's really good for is rescuing other trucks that are stuck. Once I arrived on the scene, it was a simple matter of hooking up a tow line and away we go. It was at this point that I was reminded of an old saying about “best laid plans.”
In my eagerness to see how effective the Behemoth would be at towing my log truck out of the muck, I forgot to adjust the steering on the towed vehicle. As I'm pulling it out of the mud, one of the wheels gets hung on a rock, and the whole thing goes crashing over on its side. And there, scattered across those rolling green hills, were my precious logs. Oh, bother.
Fortunately, I had an answer for this as well. I brought in a third truck, another three-axle called the C4320. This one had the perfect attachment for my dilemma: a crane. With this handy-dandy I had the C255 upright and reloaded lickety-split, and the logs were delivered without further incident.
Now, if a person were to experience the above-described scenario in real life, it would make for a pretty craptacular day. But doing it in this game, I was having a ball. This was truly one of my all-time best gaming moments. This game takes something that would drive a man to spit nails and makes it fun. Really fun. And that's what makes this game special.

Alan Wake has been delivered to us in 2010 and still manages to be a pearl in an ocean of similar releases.
As you embody the best seller writer Alan Wake, you will gradually discover the misteries surrounding Bright Falls, an apparently friendly country town.
From the first moments of the game, you will realise how apparences are mere masks that hide the truth.
Armed with a flashlight, guns and flares, Alan will become part of this mistery.
Alan Wake mixes and perfectly blends various genres: horror, shooter, puzzle, telltale. This mixture is all linked thanks to an involving atmosphere and such a brilliant use of every media aspect (the OST is actually part of the plot, not to mention Poets of the Fall as singers).
All the hidden collectibles, references, side-games and achievements enhance and enforce the replayability factor.
What I really love of Alan Wake is the complex plot; without getting into details and possible spoilers, I can tell it feels like watching and controlling a very well done adaptation of a great book.
The graphic engine helps to get into Bright Falls, even though some motion captures could have been better (not complaining, considering it is a 2010 release).
The only small complain (more like a personal opinion) I could make concerns the controls and the camera view: in tight places and among many enemies it can be a bit of a challenge to move around without falling or bumping over an obstacle, but again, it's just a subjective view, and not really affecting that much the gameplay.
There is no reason why I should not recommend Alan Wake; every type of gamer can play it with satisfactory results. It's that kind of game you wish could never have an end.

I've been a big fan of Double Fine's games for a good number of years now, and I knew there was a lot of hype surrounding this game. I decided not to play the game until the whole thing was out, just so I'd be able to experience the whole story. So...does this game live up to the standards of some of Double Fine's previous works?
Well...yes and no.
I'll start with all the good things about this game. First of all, this game is visually beautiful. It really does look like a painting brought to life. All the characters stand out, and they each have their own designs and distinguishing characteristics. Speaking of the characters, I really liked the voice work in this game. It was fun hearing the likes of Elijah Wood, Jack Black, Richard Horvitz, Jennifer Hale, Masasa Moyo, and David Kaufman all in one game. All the dialogue contains that Double Fine charm that you can find in their other games.
But then you get into things like the story, and some of the puzzles, and that's where things start to feel a little...sloppy. The puzzles in the first half are, for the most part, easy to figure out on your own (at least for me). But then in the second half, there are puzzles that require you to go back and forth, trying to pick up on very miniscule clues and doing a lot of memorizing. And while the game's overall story starts off pretty interesting, it just sort of runs out of gas by the second half, and gives us a lot of plot holes. Namely (SPOILER ALERT!)...so, we're just supposed to ignore that Shay's parents lied to him about being artificial intelligences for most of his life?
So, in the end, if you're a fan of Double Fine's other games, you should probably give this game a shot. Is it visually and audibly appealing? For sure. Is the game's story as good as, say, "Psychonauts," "Costume Quest," or "The Cave"? Well...no. But if you can get past that part of it, "Broken Age" is still a pretty solid game which, sadly, seems to be the victim of too much hype. Overall, I'd recommend it.

I found Broken Age through the Double Fine Adventure series. I've always loved behind the scenes documentaries about creative enterprises like movies and games.  So I much more interested in the process than they actual game.  But I quickly reached a point where DFA made me so interested in the project that I had to stop, buy the game and play through before I finished DFA.
I haven't play an adventure game in more than a decade, so I came to Broken Age without the nostalgia people have for Monkey Island or Grim Fandango.
But within ten minutes I was in.  The art style is gorgeous, the story is compelling, and the twist at the end of Act I was fantastic.
The puzzles in Act II were beyond my frustration tolerance for an enjoyable experience and if it were a different game I would have put it down.  But the story and the art style completely got it's hooks into me that I had to finish it, even though it meant leaning on a walkthrough from time to time.  It is a great accomplishment for the studio that was further enriched by the documentary.
Thanks to Tim Schaffer and all the folks at Double Fine for giving one of my best gaming experiences of the year.

So i bought Hard West after looking at a gameplay demo..it's a split decision because there are a lot of flaws in the game..but for only 10-15 dollars depending on currency rate, i guess i can recommend the game because there are still some fun to be had playing the game..
pros:
- the game art and animation is well done..probably on the same level to shadowrun series
- the music and voice over is also very well done and brings a good atmosphere to the game
- gameplay wise, quite strategic..even if it borrows x-com elements a lot..a lot of variety with the guns and magic..some battles are somewhat unbalanced to favor the enemies (see below)
- the lore of wild west meets magic and demons is quite interesting
cons:
- some battles are very outnumbering..but still can be done with good positioning..one most fatal/lazy mechanism is this: the enemies have a sort of x-com style overwatch counterattack which automatically attack when you come near them..but the players DON'T! i'm sure they can program this system to work with the players..but it seems that they are too lazy to include it to the system..making battles unbalanced due to this..
- bullets don't have physics..such as really bouncing of walls or hitting bystanders by accident..the bullets simply fly to the targeted enemy and does a rng whether it will hit or miss that enemy..if there is a bystander directly in the middle of the gunfight, the bullet will never hit them..also the bullets will only ricochet by a skill, no accident fire of bullets bouncing off objects and hitting someone..it seems that bullets physics are a forgotten technology since jagged alliance 2..
- characters items and money and cards don't carry on to the next chapter..this is a bit of an odd design choice..perhaps it's made to balance the game, but it seems useless to actually hoard inventory or money if they are going to be gone anyway..
- a save system mid-battle would be nice
- there is a bug sometimes which makes the map screen goes blank..i had to restart the game to make it normal again
still..the game is quite fun for it's price so i can vote recommend..but its probably a 60%/40% percentage of recommend or not..

I decided to open up my horizons and explore what's so apparently fascinating about storydriven games. Unfortunately for Virginia, I already did a few years ago thanks to the incredible Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. I would think that, by now, the Starbreeze's masterpiece would serve as an example on how you should be able to marry both the narrative and the game mechanics without forcing any form of emotions and let the player express their own feeling. Virginia doesn't do that which is extremely disappointing.
The one thing that I would call a redeeming factor is the original soundtrack which is, in my opinion, very good. In fact, I never get bored of hearing orchestral music when it's done right. I can appreciate heavy guitar like I can appreciate a good symphony. Saying no to an orchestra is like saying no to bacon but I digress. I can also applaud the (I think it is) handdrawn opening screen representing some locations like a map.
The rest, and it's my opinion, just falls incredibly flat and I would even suggest that this product could have told its story way better in another form of medium. I can definitely report a significant lack of interactivity. In fact, it's done in a more primitive way than the classic point & click products such as Myst, The Broken Sword or even Phantasmagoria. The Broken Sword II is a game that I really enjoyed back then. But here, we have a serious lack of respect for the player with terrible transitions and, certainly the worst offense, doors that are locked as soon as you open them. While you could lead your own investigation in a game like L.A. Noire, you're not given a choice or an opinion. You're technically forced to feel a certain way. The actions from the main character made me hate her and this isn't normal. There's a complete disconnection with the player. Even museums seem more interactive and at least you can learn a thing or two for the same price.
While I could recommend this product to a specific crowd, those who enjoyed heavily-restricted storydriven games, I cannot recommend it to anyone else. In my honest opinion, this shouldn't be on sale as a game... because it's not a game. There's no real challenge, there's no player agency, there's no failure state, there's no respect for the player. This product wasn't built with the player in mind. I hate losing my time and money... and I clearly did even if I wanted to give this product a chance because... maybe I was going to appreciate it. But I don't. I can't even classify it as a bad game because... it's not a game. Again, why is Steam or any platform selling it?
And yes, I did finish the story.

What an interesting game.
Virginia is a game about choices and the results of making choices, but the gameplay gives the player few choices. This is a game structured like a movie with sequential jump scenes and a linear storyline. The player uses the FPS mechanic to control an FBI agent on a case. The presumed case is about a missing boy but the actual case is an internal affairs investigation of your partner.
There is little player control and few ways to interact with the game world. You are locked into the story and will be transitioned from scene to scene with little or no control. While such lack of control has apparently bothered a lot of others (read the reviews) it does work as a counter-metaphor to the story being told inside the game.
The very interesting feature of this game is that the entire story is told visually and without dialog, either written or spoken. The player must infer the story and the character’s motivations and feelings through observation. Both the graphic style and the music enhance this style of story telling and really add to the players experience.
Good games should be designed to evoke one or more feelings in the player. Games like Fallout 4 appeal to players that like exploration and building. Games like the new Doom appeal to players that want fast-paced combat and excitement. Game like Virginia appeal to players that want to experience the story.
The plot of the story (avoiding spoilers), uses Magical Realism and is similar to games like Kentucky Route Zero. Since understanding and appreciating the story requires careful observation by the player, some people are unhappy that it was not told more explicitly through dialog. However, I believe that adding dialog would not make this game work as well as it does. In fact, at the very end of the story a lot of threads are pulled together by looking to the right rather than looking to the left.
The developers of this game, by using a visual story telling style rather than spoken and written dialogs, assume a level of participation by the player. This is a risky bet by the developers and likely explains the strong game review scores but the poor player review scores.
Virginia is a very interesting game in how it visually tells its story and it takes a number of chances with its assumption about the players. I hope it works out and we see more game like this.

I would like to preface this review by saying that I was honestly fairly excited for this game. Not because I was disillusioned by some gimmicky gameplay grandeur, but because it has dinosaurs in it. Dinos are the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and they're my favorite monster/animal. It's a shame that ORION couldn't live up to anything particularly special, or, good for that matter.
The Co-op is finnicky, the horde mode is too easy, the gun balance is terrible, the graphics are horribly optimized, and the textures are of a low resolution. If you can slog through most of the game on the surface it looks awful, but after playing with it for a bit, you can clearly see some decent (even good) ideas thrown in.
The vehicle options are cool, some of the guns are awesome, and playing as some of the dinos is fun. It just doesn't feel thought out and the execution is exceptionally poor. Some of the dinos are glitchy, and don't play or attack correctly. Some vehicles are nothing more than road kill simulators, and the weapon imbalance stated earlier gives me zero incentive to try-out or use any of the other more interesting guns. All-in-all, ORION: Dino Horde was a poorly developed game with some cool ideas just feel dropped half-way through. It's unfortunate for us dino-lovers. Perhaps we'll get a good dino game one day, but it's not today.

Nuclear Throne is a frantic top-down roguelike in a post-apocalyptic world, containing lots of guns to shoot from and lots of enemies to shoot at. It features a dozen of characters with different starting abilities, a leveling system that lets you choose one of four mutations from the pool every level, and several Crowns that alter your playstyle.
The base of this game consists of clearing levels of crowds of enemies. Your foes may not be tough from the start, but after a short while you'll be facing against hails of bullets, and your lifebar is always short. Luckily, you can compensate that with your own firepower.
One the the most prominent aspect of the game is the wide range of weaponry that starts off pretty simple but gets more and more ridiculous the further you get: from revolvers, shotguns and wrenches to gatling bazookas, double miniguns and super plasma cannons. But to see such fine items of destruction you gonna need to get far enough on your path to the legendary Throne.
Because the game is
. It is not for the faint of heart or those with a short temper. Not once will you feel invincible (and if you will, the game will soon prove you wrong). During your first 10 hours death will be par for the course of learning the game, and reaching the Throne for the first time will feel like a triumph; and something that happens once in a blue moon, as there is seemingly always something that stops you dead on your way that you could not predict or control.
After getting some experience under your belt though, the way you play becomes a mix of tough decisions - which perk to take, which weapon to keep, play it safe or go guns blazing? Most of your deaths will be because of your own miscalculations or sloppyness, the occurences of "I was doomed from the start" are quite rare.
As for more mundane aspects, the graphics is pretty nice and every element is visually distinct. The control shceme is very simple, consisting of pretty much 8 buttons. The sound is juicy and the music fits very nicely into the atmospere of the setting.
The game also has a bunch of secrets. For most of them you'll probably have to look into the wiki, alas.
Overall, Nuclear Throne is considered one of the pillars of its genre not without a good reason. It sure is recommended for fans of action-filled roguelikes where your success depends on your reflexes and abilities to make the best out of your situation.
If you dare, try and reach the Throne.
The Throne definitely exists.

If I had to describe Alan Wake in one word, the word would be “Fantastic”. The game is really unique in a few aspects. In the game you play as Alan Wake who is writer from New York. He's not a soldier, he has no combat training, he is clumsy, slow, and last guy you'd pick as video game hero in every possible way. The plot alternates between a manuscript, a dream, flashbacks, and Alan being awake. This can be a little confusing, and I admit after beating the game I'm still not sure what happened. I think this is actually a plus, because it gives you a reason to replay the game, and find the rest of the manuscript. It's almost as if you put Stephan King, & the Twilight Zone in a blender.  The cutscenes, and voice acting are very well done. The story is presented in a series of six episodes, and with each episode you get the “Previously on Alan Wake” cutscenes to lead you in to the next. It's like your controlling a TV episode of the X-files. The game play is survival horror. You always be scrounging for supplies like batteries, flares, bullets, and it typically seems you have just enough to get by. The combat centers around using light from flashlights, flares, generators, or flash grenades to essentially weaken your enemies. The “Taken” are possessed with the darkness, and can only be killed when the light has removed their shield. The scenery is beautiful, the game looks great even on low settings. The lighting and effects, are all on point. The music is a perfect fit, some instrumentals, some alternative indie bands. I can't find anything negative to say about Alan Wake, I enjoyed every minute of the experience, and I'm glad I got a chance to play it. Wait, why are you still reading this? Go add this to your wishlist, or library!

Please read other reviews to realize how good the game is - it is great, in my opinion and it costs $16 at the time of this review, so just get it, if you like old school TBS.
What I primarily want to address in this review is something that I see a lot of people say -
A. No overwatch for your team, but the enemy has it- First of all there is NO overwatch in the game, however enemies do get "attacks of opportunity" if you move within a certain radius of their location -  they get a free shot at you.
But -
1. The game clearly shows you by means of a red circle the extent of each enemies attack of opportunity radius, and
2. If you approach the enemy from behind their is no attack of opportunity, so try to out maneuver them.
EDIT: As of 11/30/2015, with a new patch the devs have confirmed that enemies too will stay out of your area of influence, i.e. you also get an attack of opportunity if the enemy steps into your area of influence, except that they wouldn't -  so that is fair.
Not every game needs to be XCOM and I applaud the devs for doing things differently.
B. Enemies running up to you at the end and one-shotting you:
1. The game has items (consumables, vests and totem like objects) and skills that increase defense and HP, use them!!
2.  Not every character is essential to the game's progress, protect ones that are and sacrifice, if necessary, the rest.
As for the save, I can understand why the devs chose to implement the checkpoint system - it takes the tension to a whole new level. It ensures that like XCOM, I do not dash, I use one movement on peripheral characters to first get an idea of what is in the general area before I dash with the others, if I dash at all. I generally have AP remaining on most characters when I end my turn - better safe than sorry.

A "newcomer" to the tactical genre, "Hard West" takes some of the elements from XCOM and twists them around, adding as it goes. What comes out is a fresh idea of a story-driven, innovative tactical game with RPG elements and an awesome setting in the "Weird West" (It's like West... just weirder... and with demons... and rituals... and it fits GREAT!).
Let me point out what makes "Hard West" so exemplary:
- The "luck" system that governs all the shooting. No longer can you miss those 90% Chance to Hit shots 3 times in a row. Now all of your missed shots take some of the enemy's "luck" and once its value is lower than your Chance to Hit, you WILL hit. That's it... It's simple yet very satisfying and adds more tactic to the old genre that usually was just based on chance.
- You can change the environment to create new covers. Did you ever find it irratitng that a table cannot be overturned to give you cover. Well, now it can :D
- Awesome abilites. The abilites that your characters can use are simply awesome. Ever wanted to shoot 6 people at once in one second? Just "Barrage" the s^%t out of them. Want to make a battle into "sudden death"? Use "Equalization" and change EVERYONE's HP to 1.
- The story. The plot is just the right amount of cliche & some twists that make the "weird west" setting even more unique. It's immersive and the entire game is based on it, so it's VERY DIFFERENT from XCOM.
- Wacky weapons. The game takes some strange designs from times long past and introduces them to the game. And it's amazing! Ever wanted to shot a 9 barreled shotgun in somebody's face? Well, now you can!
- Experience system is based on cards. An wesome idea to customize your characters using poker cards. Each cards improves the character's statistics but also gives him an ability. HOWEVER you can combine cards into poker hands that give powerful bonuses. Great idea!
There is much much more I could tell you about this game. It also has its flaws, of course, but which game doesn't? The cons are vastly outmatched by the pros.
Want to experience something new and fresh? Get "Hard West" now!

Originally I had some crashes with this game version (Steam), but managed to fix it. The info is at the end of the review. Civilization III Complete was one of the games I spent the most time with, and really enjoyed it. For me, it's easily one of the best 4X games ever made (at least in the time I type it).
If you did not play Civilization 3 in the past and are wondering if you should buy it - below is some basic info that should encourage you to do that.
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
The pluses:
+ Lots of civilizations, each plays differently
+ Lots of different units + special military unit for each civilization
+ The AI scripts are demanding (unlike in most modern games)
+ Resources on map force you to play strategically
+ Depending on the size and type of the maps, games might differ quite a lot
+ You can play in really big maps
+ The game has fine mods that you can find on the internet
+ It's hard to stop playing it
------------------------------------------------------
The minuses:
- It's hard to stop playing it
- At higher difficulties the military victory is the most viable option (only)
- When you control most of the map it's just boring killing of the remaining weaklings
- At the industrial age, you probably control most of the map
- At higher difficulties AI is cheating
- Civilizations are not balanced (some are really good, some - really bad)
- After you learn to use workers and diplomacy, it's not that hard (but still fun)
- Old 2D game, so in native desktop resolution units and fonts might be too small
- Old 2D game, so in native game resolution units might be too big (and no widescreen)
======================================
For native desktop resolution in game:
1. Go to the Conquests folder in your Civ 3 folder conquests.ini
2. Put "keepRes=1" in conquests.ini file (without "")
======================================
Those settings should fix crashes in Windows 7 64 bit.
1. Go to the Conquests folder in your Civ 3 folder
2. Rename LSANS.FOT to -LSANS.FOT
If that does not help:
Set Windows compatibility to Windows XP Service Pack 2 and run program as administrator.
If the game runs too slow delete keepRes=1 from ini file (in Windows XP mode the game is slower)
======================================
That's it. You can now go buy the game.

If you're a fan of the original Fallouts (1 & 2) or isometric rpgs like them then you will love this game, I cannot recommend it enough. The story lasted me 40 hours and was fantastic the whole way through, I felt like my choices actually had impact.
Graphically the game's not that special though it gets the job done, but you shouldn't let that deter you as the gameplay more than makes up for it.
Gameplay revolves mostly around turn based combat with a squad of up to 7 controlled characters (4 created, 3 followers)and when not fighting you'll be engaging in dialogue with many characters, solving their problems and upholding the law as a desert ranger, or not if a bit of anarchy takes your fancy. At high difficulty levels it can prove a good challenge but if you're new to the genre you shouldn't have much trouble on the lower difficulty.
There is a lot of freedom in the game, many choices in your missions that can alter the ending and how the game flows, if you felt like it you could just shoot a rocket at some npc you don't like, there are no 'critical characters' that cannot die, if you wanted to you could wipe out entire factions and it will be reflected in the ending.
Nearly every choice you make in every quest is reflected in the ending you recieve increasing replayability, you can also bring one or all of the characters you finish with into a new game as a sort of new game+
I cannot stress how much I enjoyed this game, I played it for hours on end everytime I started it up and found it very difficult to put down, if you're a fan of this genre you won't regret playing it.

I have to preface this by saying my taste in games is not as mainstream as some and the things that make this game outstanding to me might be considered flaws to others. The depth of character design choices is wonderful, though I'll admit id like more portraits and aesthetic options to make use of.
The combat system is wonderfully simple but tactically complex and feels just like Fallout 1 or 2 brought up to date and I have found (at least on seasoned difficulty) that encounters have been fair and in the first 15 hours I havent been seriously threatened with the exception of a boss fight, which is how it should be. I am not saying this is an easy game and I will admit I really took my time learning the character creation system before I committed to starting the game and I am sure if you don't take your time or you are not familiar with the mechanics this game i the difficulty curve could be much greater. For me this is a very rewarding approach and I found the character creation process a lot of fun.
I love the little details and the fact that the developers chose not to dumb things down and take out what some might call surperfulous bits like water consumption on the world map from the game. I love the depth of dialouge options, having keywords to choose from and the ability to choose who is asking what- it might not have an effect (with the exception of hard♥♥♥♥♥smart♥♥♥♥♥ kiss♥♥♥♥♥choices) but it gives a feeling of role-play and brings my characters to life for me. This is a game that lets you play your party how you imagine them for better or worse and from what I have experienced the story can cope and really lets you play ball.
Overall Wasteland 2 is an exceptional game if you are a lover of classic western rpgs or are of an older tabletop rpg generation. It doesn't ride on nostalgia to be good, though it certainly has a bit of that feel to it. This is just a well done game that proves that graphics (though they are perfectly good in my opinion) don't make an rpg and that you don't need to dumb something down for the least common denominator to make sales goals. If you put something out that relies on a deep and well used ruleset (so far no skill is useless), an interactive story, freedom of choice and a good honest challenge (without being frustratingly difficult) are what matter most.

Pros: Dinosaurs, Music, Multiplayer
Cons: Repetitive, Balance, Community
ORION: Dino Horde entertains for a while with its virtually endless number of dinosaurs.  The soundtrack to the slaughter fits well, though the sound effects and narrator less so.  Multiplayer, especially with friends, adds much to the fun.
However, the gameplay itself is boringly repetitive after the first hour or so.  Dinosaurs' simple AI will only ever rush players and every vehicle seems to have the same turret.
The game is balanced poorly in many different respects: long respawn times in Survival and Conquest modes, infinite instant respawns of powerful player-controlled dinosaurs in Rampage mode, and other issues.
The number of online players reaches about fifty on weekends at most, so most other gamemodes are never played.  Grinding achievements will require a buddy and quite a bit of time for completionists.
ORION: Dino Horde offers a little enjoyment slaughtering waves of mindless reptiles.

I came into this really hyped for this game. Loved Mafia 2 and with the improvements that were being advertised this looked like a real upgrade.
Unfortunately the game really disappoints in the tech department to the point that I cannot recommend it right now. Which is such a shame because the set up is great, the characters are fleshed out, the dialogue is fantastic, the main missions are good, the shooting is really punching, the violence is violent!
I am running this game on a 6600k with 32GB RAM and a gtx1080 in 4k and I am getting barely 30fps after the weekend patch. The textures are incredibly low res, the lighting is awful. I can't figure out if this game is supposed to have this washed out 60's technicolor film look or not, there is some kind of filter applied and it does not do the game any good. I get a line running at each end of the screen in some moments which again I can't figure out is a tech issue or is suppose to be this effect that shows that this shown on worn out film!?
Mission markers are buggy, there will be markers for missions that are clearly not available any more, you go to the waypoint and there is nothing there...
OK, that's the bad stuff out of the way. On the plus side, Lincoln is a good character, up there with Vitto. Donovan is a good side-kick and provides a lot of the comic relief, so needed in a game which doubles down on race and social issues. Everybody else is really playing this really straight up and there is really no other humour. Which is a shame because I remember Mafia 2 being really light-hearted in spots and having a really good balance between gory violence and enjoyable banter.
For me right now, this game is a weak 6/10 with all the tech issues on the PC side. There is so much potential. Let me just mention the Baron Saturday Fun House mission at the start of the game, that one mission shows what potential there is here, but it is really weighted down by bugs and just poor optimization.
Keeping checking the forums for an improvement, because if this gets properly patched, it is definitely worth getting stuck in, but right now I can't recommend it at full price

----SoM was great because you could do anything at any time. Total freedom. Not so in the sequel.

-The menu and character progression options.... The menu has lots of LONG DELAYS you can't avoid. Want to open the inventory? Gotta do an animation! Want to recycle an orc? Gotta wait 15 seconds while he yells and falls over! Want to recycle gear? Gotta click the button for 3 seconds (cough, console port scars, cough).

-It takes a stupid amount of time to open loot boxes (I know, we'll get to those). If you buy 15 loot boxes, you'd think you're just going to open them, right? Wrong!
