I bought this game because it was on sale and well rated critically, but I didn't really think I would like it that much. I'm not a huge fan of shooters and I had never played a horror game in my life, so I was honestly a little nervous even to try the game. Overall, I'd say Alan Wake absolutely won me over, and I'd list it as one of my 15 or 20 favorite games of all time.
Alan Wake is layed out as if it were a playable TV series, split into 6 "episodes" and 2 special "episodes". I found this format extremely enjoyable, and each episode was the perfect length for a solid long evening of gameplay without dragging on TOO long for a single sitting. (Of course, you don't have to finish the episodes in a sitting, but that's what I found myself doing)
The story is nothing revolutionary, but I was satisfied with the narrative. It paces everything about right, first dropping you in a mystery with no clear leads, only more questions. The first hour or two of the game are more about surviving the evil forces emanating from the dark lake than actually solving the mystery, but soon you start picking up clues that legitimately move you towards your goal of finding your missing wife. You do feel the danger of the dark forces attacking you - I never rolled my eyes upon appearance of new enemies as one might with a less intense game; it was always cause to brace for a tough battle.
That moves us on to the combat system. And maybe it was just my inexperience with shooters, but the combat in this game was pretty difficult for me (not that that is a BAD thing). Okay, sure, at its heart it's a simple system - basically every enemy in the game can be defeated with the one-two punch of light followed by bullets - but it's no quick task to break enemies' darkness shields with your flashlight, so when you're dealing with multiple baddies it's a bad idea to try to finish off the first before starting on the second. Towards the end of the game I finally mastered the dance of simultaneously keeping enemies at bay and destroying them, but I certainly took more deaths along the way than it's cool to admit. At any rate, though it was tough, combat was never TOO frustrating, nor was it ever boring (the difficulty kept me invested here - if you're better at it than me the lack of diverse enemies might wear on you though). You'll pick up a few extra light-based weaponry options as you go, as well as the occasional chance to use surroundings to help you out, but combat never strays too far from a light-em-up/mow-em-down core.
I wouldn't call this game "scary" as much as "extremely tense", which was perfect for me. If you're a bit stronger-minded then me in the horror regard and find the early levels lacking, I will note that Special 1: The Signal is a standout in that regard. No, still no jumpscares or gruesome creatures, but being hounded and harassed by a demented version of the main character was a dark, somewhat terrifying experience that will probably be what I think of when I think of this game in 10 years.
The game's ending before the specials is very confusing. The Specials clean it up a bit but it can still be a little hard to piece together. But as a whole the journey mattered more than the destination and I still thought the story was good.
Overall, I'd say give it a shot regardless of how this game's genre relates to what you normally play or like.

Ah, the first game in my alphabetical backlog clear... Complete.
Alan Wake is a writer. He and his wife go on a retreat to a creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing cabin in the middle of a backwater town, Bright Falls, ostensibly as a vacation. Soon enough his wife is kidnapped by an evil presence, he's lost a week of his life to amnesia, the pages of a book he can't remember writing are telling the future, and crazy shadow people are trying to kill him.
As Alan, you'll shine light on stuff. Sometimes for a few seconds, sometimes for five or maybe even six. The stuff will then flash, either accomplishing a task or making said stuff vulnerable to a writers greatest tool: his ♥♥♥♥ing gun. This is the basic mechanic of the game, dark = bad, light = good. Enemies wear the darkness like a shield, and the game does a good job of getting creative with light sources to help you disperse it. The classic explosive barrel, fireworks, and an entire lighthouse are at your disposal at various points to aid you in your battles against the creeping blackness. This is basically the framework of the entire game, and I found the combat slightly tedious by the time the credits had rolled.
There are few different weapons in the game, but they all function roughly the same way. The gunplay is standard third person shooter fare, with a nifty dodge function that feels pretty satisying when you pull it off at the perfect time. Alan isn't a soldier tough guy - his name is Alan, for christ's sake - he's a writer, and he feels suitably flimsy and fragile.
The selling point of this game is the atmosphere. Creepy and uncomfortable, obviously inspired by the likes of Twin Peaks (Alan's coffee addiction, the town itself) and the Twilight Zone (in true Remedy style, TV's littered around the game play episodes of "Night Falls" a TZ rip off that Alan wrote a few episodes of, all in full motion video) the location and the people are well executed and suitably weird. Though I feel it may suffer somewhat from its video game format, as the antagonistic Dark Presence is very, unsurprisingly, present throughout the entire game, making the story and the events seem kinda cheesy and overplayed.
Still, a good game. Not great, but good. The DLC episodes are worth a go if you enjoy the gameplay, but don't add much to the story.

This is a different game for a different kind of gamer. It's one focused on making sure you plan carefully and don't make mistakes rather than setting the fastest time. Getting stuck and losing loads, tipping over, having to deal with vehicles less than adequate at the job when you're starting, going into the wrong mud pit...it's all a part of the game, and it never feels unfair or forced like some...other *coughneedforspeedgridautosport* driving games. You screw up and it's your own damn fault. The graphics are well-rendered and at times stunning when it comes to visual effects and terrain deformation.
Still, it needs a bit more polish, especially in the UI department. it's a mess, the camera's wonky, and it feels unfinished in this part of the game. more, different kinds of loads would be appreciated as well as more usefulness when it comes to the largest truck in the game. The saving system needs an overhaul as well, particularly for multiplayer.
Still, this remains the best simulation of off-road, deep mud driving there is, and will (literally) provide hours of challenge for even the most seasoned sim driver. If you want something different, this is one that won't disappoint in that regard.

TL;DR Great atmosphere, fluid gameplay, well made storyline (alot of extra info given through world items) and good difficulty.
Alan Wake is the protagonist of his own story, trapped inside the pages he writes when he blacks out. At the start, you arrive in Bright Falls to relax and get some inspiration for your next book ''Departure'', when a bunch of weird things happen. People posessed by darkness and evil appear to try and end Alan's life, and he must fight through it to save his wife.
The game overral has a great atmosphere, giving you a jist of the story through dialogue and giving you the rest through hidden pages/TV's/Radios. It's dark, and you fend off enemies with your greatest weapon: LIGHT! (oh and guns too). The game is very well written and narrated as it's done by Alan himself (they really went full out by modeling a character from a real guy). The game also has a bunch of small jumpscares scattered throughout the game in the form of 2 second cutscenes with lound noises, but I guess you get used to it. The gameplay part is fun and Wake moves fluidly through Bright Falls.
Overall, I would definitly recommend this to any fan of good storytelling and mystery. It was the best(or close to) from it's genre in the Xbox 360 Generation.

I purchased Hard West expecting a turn-based strategy game with RPG elements, choice-driven story and intuitive gameplay. Instead, I was given an entirely convoluted version of Chess with a meak story that, to me, looks more of an Alpha than a full release.
At certain points in the game, it was painfully obvious that the developers had rushed to finish their product. Animations are janky and disjointed, most character models seem to be palette-swaps of each other, a linear story masquerading as a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure, and the gameplay isn't anywhere near as fine-tuned as the developers have claimed. With a lack of a proper save feature, the game requires the player to devote several hours of time to something that would fare much better as a casual game.
So, I leave this with a downvote for now. If the developers continue to work on it and adress the problems highlighted by the community, I may remove this review.

Fantastic game that feels like an amalgamation of XCOM, Sunless Sea, Desperados & Quentin-Tarantio-movies.
The story is presented through single scenarios that must be unlocked, but not necessarily be played in chronological order. Each scenario is closed in itself and presents a part of the main storyline, the prologue or side-stories. All of them will ultimately run together for the final scenario.
The game focusses strongly on the narrative side, most of the events are presented through text. You will be able to roam a portion of the Weird West and interact with landmarks, towns, etc. through which you can buy/sell equipment and also delve deeper into the Weird West.
Combat is well-thought out, the system of cover and the weapons-damage dependent on it requires you to move a lot and try to flank the enemies. Sadly, they will do the same and are quite smart at catching you off-guard, which is more often than not the end because characters (enemy or PC) can survive about 2-3 shots at the very most.
Thankfully, you can customize your characters fixed stats by equipping trinkets or poker cards, which will also unlock abilities. Should you get and actual poker hand, you'll get extra bonusses.
The characters are intriguing and the storylines hold many suprises and are generally well written and interesting. It's amazing how they eventually string together for the finale.
I definitely recommend this game, go get it while it's on sale!
Oh yeah, you have only one autosave, so whatever you do, you did it ^^ Ain't no turning back when you hustle with the devil

I backed this game on Kickstarter when it was a tangent of an idea, the thought of "Let's make one of those games like we used to". Let me get the first things out of the way: I don't feel like I wasted my money.
The first act of the game is amazing. Puzzles are a little uninspired and the gameplay is essentially clicking on things until you stumble across the solution. It's fairly simple, which for those who like puzzle point and click games is not a downside at all.
The story of Act 1 is well told, the ideas run deep, the story is well told. The world is well developed, the characters decent enough as characters and as metaphors. Each took classic stories and ideas and presented them in unique lights, the characters and situations serving as metaphors of teenage life.
But as you might notice, I said this game is not recommended. After how strong Act 1 is, it seems like a shoe-in for a game that should be bought. Sadly, Act 2 undoes everything good act one did, from characters to story to undoing the very metaphors and ideas. The puzzles get odder as well, many of the puzzles requiring knowledge the other has when both characters are separated and have no communication with the other. From a story standpoint alone, the characters unable to progress to their next puzzle because the other one has not unlocked a specific spaceship door, or one character relying on the wiring diagram the other has in their repaired robot simple makes no sense. Act1 makes the game amazing from many angles, while Act 2 goes and undoes everything good Act 1 did.
As the game goes and creates these great ideas and then simply tosses all of them aside for a fairly boring ancient and deep conspiracy, it feels like all investment into the game and all the great ideas are simply thrown aside with a simple "Oh, we didn't really mean that, just ignore it please".

Pros: Dinosaurs, Music, Multiplayer
Cons: Repetitive, Balance, Community
ORION: Dino Horde entertains for a while with its virtually endless number of dinosaurs.  The soundtrack to the slaughter fits well, though the sound effects and narrator less so.  Multiplayer, especially with friends, adds much to the fun.
However, the gameplay itself is boringly repetitive after the first hour or so.  Dinosaurs' simple AI will only ever rush players and every vehicle seems to have the same turret.
The game is balanced poorly in many different respects: long respawn times in Survival and Conquest modes, infinite instant respawns of powerful player-controlled dinosaurs in Rampage mode, and other issues.
The number of online players reaches about fifty on weekends at most, so most other gamemodes are never played.  Grinding achievements will require a buddy and quite a bit of time for completionists.
ORION: Dino Horde offers a little enjoyment slaughtering waves of mindless reptiles.

I went into Virginia really wanting to like it but there are so many glaring issues from the getgo. I love storydriven games,I love "walking simulators", I love subdued gameplay and character stories. I love Dear Esther, Gone Home, Twin Peaks, the X-files and I'm a huge sucker for low poly aestethics. I should be THE target audience. But I found myself hating it only a few minutes in. It's SUCH a wasted opportunity.
They could have told the story though dialogue but they didn't. The lack of any voice acting give nothing of substance to the few characters I met. Not even the protagonist.
They could have told the story through enviromental storytelling but they didn't. The low poly aesthetics, while sometimes (and just sometimes) pretty don't convey any sense of place in the world. No notes to look at, no newspaper clippings to give context. Everything is the bare minimum and tells us nothing of the world.
They could have told the story through body and facial animations but they didn't. Everyone is just a expressionless puppet and there is no character or life to any animation. Again, it's the BARE minimum.
From a team that spent TWO YEARS on this, I would expect polish. It's alright to take your time on a story but Jesus! Why? Why do this? Why spend so much time on something with such a glaring lack of vision or polish? You can't have a big dramatic swelling of music when looking at a town that looks like it was made in 5 minutes in Blender. You can't CUT every five seconds like in a movie to progress the story faster. You can't just make a game because it's cheaper or easier than a movie. There is NO reason this should be a game and again, this is from someone who adores Gone Home.

If there was ever a game to be labeled as an "experience", Virginia is the one. Note how I didnt say "interactive experience".
Virginia is a game, however the creators have used the game medium to tell the story they wished to tell and they have done that marvelously. The enviroments are well designed and play off the art style while the pacing is clearly inspired by the works they credit.
In terms of a game there is little to do. You progress through scenes by interacting (moving the analogue stick and pressing A/X is the entirety of your input potential) with key elements. Going into Virigina it being a first person story driven game I expected a few gamified elements, and to satisfy these cravings there are collectable feathers and flowers. However, these only add a subtle cosmetic touch to some scenes and outside of the game they yeild nothing.
This is more a fact that an opinion. Virginia may be a game, but is one that makes use of the interaction by letting you move through the story, It knows it. It does it well, and you will finish the game with plenty of your own thoughts and ideas bubbling away.
It's and experience more than a game, and that isn't always a bad thing.

This game is only for a certain kind of person that has fun in mostly singleplayer RPG (or MMO-lite) experiences customizing, leveling, and looting to go up in powerlevel for a sense of competitiveness with yourself and other people.
The controversies surrounding lootboxes (something the devs themselves made completely irrelevant if you actually play the game) and the "grind", are complete BS. Take it from someone that was able to play this game entirely for free thanks to a friend, and I still went around to go and buy the game for myself to show the Monolith Devs the support for their fun content.
Now, don't get me wrong. I think Warner Bros as publishers are complete scum, the concept of microtransactions preys on the vulnerable, the fact this game only has one black dude in the entirety of the story (so far), and that post-chapter 2 Talion has no dialogue outside of cutscenes is bad and laughable. The cons, for myself, end there.
The entire game, including the late-game "grind" to unlock the true ending, can be completed in a solid 10 hours of straight playtime. This is if you were playing on Nemesis Difficulty and absolutely gave not a single♥♥♥♥♥♥about anything else the game had to offer beyond the story. That's the short summary.
Ransacking and building up your fortresses is extremely fun. Dicking around with orcs until they became super-powered and creating your own personal stories with them is honestly the biggest highlight of the game and it's extremely fun. The online game modes that offer competitive play with your personal fortresses and helping people revenge vendettas for loot is extremely fun. The side quests (if you care for that sort of thing) are really funny. The gameplay value of this game is just genuinely phenomenal and offers a lot of replay value even when you finish the game.
On the topic of loot-boxes, they're all unnecessary, and the ones that actually mean anything can be purchased with in-game currency that's earned, which I'm sure hundreds of people heard on various new sites can be exploited if you're bad at the game. I've never once had to touch or use them for anything until after I had completed the game and felt like clearing my Mirian. My garrison quickly filled up to 300 orcs, and I was left spending 15 solid minutes trying to delete orcs before I decided to never touch this part of the game ever again. (Seriously Monolith, implement a feature to delete in bulk.)
This game is really fun for the competionist type of person, which I am, though some parts felt short and others (the legendary gear sets) felt a little too long. I have high hopes going forward with future DLC content that this game will be made even greater.
My only worry is that they will finish the current 2017-18 DLC year and completely forget about the game and eventually drop support.

So, you don't really feel that "Oh sweet an upgrade" moment. Also, the skills, once you find your play style getting skill points becomes useless after level 25. You are just buying useless skills you won't use after that point. I actually got tired of buying skills after leveling.
I wish I could tell the different tribes apart just by looking at them, like using different markings. The grunts and orcs don't really look like Uruk Hai either. Just plain af, I think even the grunts should look like they come from a tribe. I hate that after a certain point your orcs are undead, wtf is that? Is this for the Halloween feel? Honestly, do not know what they were going for here. Luckily it is toward the end.
Shadow Wars is so repetitive after round 5 I have to take several days break because I do not want to enter into the siege/defend grind again. It seriously becomes unbearable. Also, you see this giant map, right? Well, sorry but only like 1/10th of it is accessable because it's based around the fortress on the map. I was hoping it would be as open as skyrim or even half that. Each section is small enough to not get a good feel of open world. Fast travel to this continent for this fortress, or go to this fortress in the other continent. Like I said, no "real" open world feel. However, I am the type of person to run around and explore, there is none of that in this game. Truly, you have seen it all just 20 mins into a new region.
Conclusion: I hope this helps you decide on buying, I reccommend soley because I did have fun and enjoyed the gameplay. The actual combat/story. I just notice there is SO MUCH FU*KING POTENTIAL WITH THIS SERIES I MEAN CMON GUYS. That's all. Get it on sale.

Just finished my playthrough of Wasteland 2. I put well over a 100 hours into, so I guess it wasn't terrible.
Still, it's fairly rough. It's ugly as sin. It's fairly buggy. Feels like the developers were intoxicated with the ability to make huge maps, so everything is twice the size it needs to be. The UI / interface / whatever goes out of its way to annoy you at times. The writing is unexceptional at best.
On the other hand: Once you go through half the game and end up in California, you start getting involved hub areas with multiple solutions and interesting characters. Everything is filled with callbacks to the original Wasteland (and apparently if you'were a fan of the original Wasteland, this game is exactly the sequel you were looking for). It's ambitious, to say the least.
Still, if you're looking for an old school RPG... go with Dragonfall. Or wait for Pillars of Eternity. But once you're done with those, you can give Wasteland a try. It's not all bad, just not very good.

This game has multiple angles to it. If you are a marine or alien, that game is essentially search-and-destroy. If you are commander, the game becomes an RTS where you have no direct control over the units. Technology unlock progresses through the game as your commander dedicates the resources you capture to bringing in phase gates (teleporters), better guns, better armor, better ammunition, mechs and jetpacks. On the alien side, you have carapace, poison glands, worm holes (actual holes not time-space bending holes), evolutionary progression and structures built by a type of alien. The Khara alien species has the ability to morph into different forms, all of which have very different playing styles. Again, all this costs resources. The income is split between the other players and the commander. The commander does the research while the other players buy the upgrades. Basically, if you played the old mod for HL, this is the same game at the core.
NS2 has a steep learning curve, especially for the aliens, which is why this game was never a heavy-weight in terms of players. The alien abilities rely on coming in from all directions to overwhelm the marines and the marines depend on other factors for their buffs when they are away from base. The quality of your commander can mean the difference between victory or defeat to an absolute degree. You can kick them if they are not up to the task. The UI is actually designed in a very compact manner to have as many uses as possible without having that many menus.
All that being said, the community is OK. Most of the players appear to be older and more mature and willing to help out noobies to a degree. Just remember to ask questions and stay with the group when in any doubt. Loners get shot/eaten very fast.

1.) When you move and stop, you take an extra step. This makes movement less precise and makes any platforming much harder than it should be.
2.) You need to explore in order to get a lot of the achievements, but the game punishes exploration by spawning additional mobs to fight. This means getting the collectibles will make the game harder, evne some of the hidden chests do this, because it takes more ammo to deal with the new mobs than you get from the chest.
3.) Too often the game takes away all of your supplies. Sometimes there's a game reason. Other times there's not. I understand if I'm detained by the police, they are going to take away my guns. But why wouldn't I take my shotgun, flare gun, flash bangs, etc. on the final mission?

I'd say the normal difficulty is your standard Mega Man difficulty with the Mibibli difficulty being it's own beast. Not impossible, however there are some instances of cheap deaths or "begginer's traps". Also the flaw or positive depending if you like it, of chosing which level to pick first since this game does let you choose levels in any order you want. It's not as if, you can choose the hardest level early on, you can only choose one set of levels at a time till you go to the next set, but some levels are harder than others. If you want a fair platformer with a difficulty that gets harder over time, this game can repel you away with its choose what level you want to tackle first even though one level can be harder than the other. It's trial and error for what to go for first, to some that's an issue but for people like me it's one of the joys of the first playthrough. Other small things include not being able to pause the game, no audio settings and no controller support (although you can map your keys with third party software, but its a small extra hassle). There is also one stage with a computer theme and it wasn't clear to me what the gimmick was,but it seems others got it quick when I handed it to a friend. It might be a personal thing but, because I didn't understand I was stuck there for a good couple hours the first playthrough.
With the negatives out of the way the positives are really strong, for one this game is pretty meaty, it has quite a few of levels, well worth the price. All the levels are designed to teach you a mechanic in a safe enviorment and test you on the next. It's for the most part all wonderfully designed. After you finish the first set of bosses you go on to the next and upon defeating them they give you powers. Some of these power you find your self using all the time, while others find yourself not using at all.These powers are different weapons or abilities. You hold up or down to scroll between weapons which is good because it takes a second to change a weapon, although sometimes you wish there was a seprate button to switch faster, but its not like it takes long to change weapons in the first place. Anyways the weapons and abilities you find good are really good and help a lot with the hard stages. The bosses can vary from easy to hard which usually reflects how hard the level is so more often than not you'll pick an easy level with a easy boss and not vice versa most of the time anyway.
The sound direction is satisfying, shooting an enemy and hearing the 8 bit explosion just feels good, the jump sounds makes a good sound. In general the sound effects make the game feel more fun and I really appriciate it for that. Speaking of sound the soundtrack is one of the best in video game history and I stand by that. It's mostly 8 bit but its not restricted to 8 bit and will show it's true colors when it want's to. I whole heartly recomend the soundtrack if anything.

I do think this has excellent production values for the price range, and a lot of care & imagination went in to it so all credit to the devs.
There's just 3 things keeping me from giving it the thumb's up & possibly from persisting with it:
* As others have said; the lack of a save system is a bit of a downer, especially as the battles can be long (and more than a bit tedious in the case of the lengthy stealth ones) and you're basically making uninformed 'story' decisions on the world map.
* It's a let-down to have no overwatch option (though all AI's do!), or defensive options of any kind - as others have said, a suicidal run-up-for-point-blank-shot by the AI basically trumps everything from a strategic point of view.
* I read up quite thoroughly before buying, but saw no mention of the campaign system; basically the game is split up into chapters that you can replay endlessly, and NOTHING you do persists between runs (except unlocking 3 signature items on a universal vendor from each chapter).
Personally I found this massively disappointing, as it really removed any sense of role-playing and gravitas from the 'story' decisions you make; there's zero weight to ANYTHING you do (aside from triggering those 3 unlocks), so long as you can make it through the mandatory battles.
This also (for me at least) detracts from the 'poker hand' system of character upgrade cards; you only get so many in a run-through - mostly random - so you can't count on any kind of synergy, and by the time you might assemble a 'hand' anyway you'll likely only get to play it for one battle then the chapter is over & it's gone forever.

Where to start - this game has some phenomenally well-written story in choose-your-own-adventure style on the tactical map, with twists that follow basically every decission you ever made in the scenario. The main story-line (dealing with Warren, from the "Hard Times" scenario all the way to the last scenario in the line to the right, a total of four scenarios) has been a blast to play, and I have yet to tackle the remaining four scenarios (and I reckon it will take me double, or even triple, the amount of time to clear everything on hard+injuries+ironman mode). The game has that strong Deadlands vibe to it (the devs have admitted that they've drawn inspirations from the popular Wierd West pen & paper game), and mixes it well with your Spaghetti Western tropes of a man searching for vengeance, or money... or death in general.
The lack of save feature doesn't bother me at all - on the countrary, it just lengthens the experience even further by allowing you to replay the scenarios on harder difficulties (with optional injuries and ironman mode), hunting for the remaining relics that are often the rewards for your decissions. The dead-zone (overwatch) feature that AI has is also an additional challenge and I welcome it (tip: if you move to a place without previous line-of-sight of the enemy, there won't be a deadzone a.k.a you won't get shot, and the enemy will be intimidated by your pressence, thus allowing you to land a free 100% shot between his eyes just like they like to do).
Finally, if I had to nitpick to find a flaw in the game, I would say that the ocassional freezes when entering the barter screen and lack of more content are the cons. The first can easily be remedied with an optimization patch, and more content will surely come in form of DLC (keepin' my fingers crossed for a full-blown expansion of 4 more scenarios, or even a sequel). As a fan of Spaghetti Westerns and Deadlands, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to everyone who enjoys an ominous, grim story bundled with some true grit tactical combat.

TBoI is an evil little game that takes a fairly dim view of Judaism and Christianity. Once I got desensitized to it, what I found was one of my new favorite games.
Simply, it's one part Legend of Zelda and two parts Smash TV, with a massive amount of unique item collection and "leveling" to make sure it's addictive... which it is. Every game is different, thanks to random dungeons and items, making TBoI incredibly replayable, albeit pretty difficult for the first 10 or 20 playthroughs.
The bad:
Without any instructions, and vague/cryptic power-up descriptions, many collectibles can seem useless, when they are in fact deeply strategic. So keep the wiki handy. To complicate things, since it's made in Flash, the engine is horribly inefficient. Unless you have a monster CPU, expect slowdown on basically every screen. Last, given that a full playthrough can take a couple solid hours, the lack of a save system means leaving TBoI on pause A LOT.
But:
YOU SHOULD ABSOLUTELY OWN THE GAME (and "Wrath" expansion!).

When I first started playing ORION: Prelude, I noticed how my graphics card didn’t really enjoy it all that much. Although I don’t notice my graphics card struggling anymore (either because some bug was fixed, or I simply don’t notice anymore) the game play is pretty straight forward, as far as first person shooters go.
You see Dinosaur, you shoot them into extinction. End of story. However, the multitude of different methods with which you may choose to slaughter our scaly-friends really deserves mentioning. You can choose from sniper rifles, flamethrowers, laser rifles, automatic rifles, cryoblades, cryoknifes, oh my! That coupled with being able to go into stealth, heal yourself/friends, or use a jetpack makes for a very enjoyable dynamic game experience.
I feel that it’s important to note: if you do not like the FPS genre this game is probably still a skip for you. Because it’s still very much a FPS, just a bit more refreshing with more options and interesting challenges.
I don’t have much to say about the Achievements at this time, because I’m still working on getting more of them. Many of the achievements are very grindy, and the others will require a friend or two to complete. I don’t really think that highly of grinding achievements, but it kept me playing. If you’re achievement driven I’d suggest caution if considering to play this game.
On a side note, many of the names of the achievements have really amused me; there are many references, my all time favorite being “guy on the toilet”. Just look it up, and look up the requirement. It’s pretty hilarious.
ORION: Prelude’s standard price is $14.99, once again I come to my same problem and values. I think this game is really great when you play with friends, if you’re on your own; it’s not even close to being worth the buy. If you really want to try it out. The game occasionally goes on for free on the weekends. That’s an okay time to check it out to see if you like it. If you do, I recommend waiting for a sale on the game, there was a 90% sale once, that’s when my brother brought this game for me.

Pro’s:  I enjoyed playing this game, I thought it was decent for a FPS it has some quirks to work out, the game is fun to play with other people, there are a lot of guns, it let me pew pew with a bow, I’ve murdered thousands of dinosaurs (I had dreams of being eaten by a T-Rex as a child).
Con’s: The price seems high, but the value in my eyes is close to fair… but only if you really like FPS’s or have friends to play with already. The graphics are intense on computers, the achievements are grindy, there’s no story.
Once again, I really did enjoy playing this game. And I’ll look forward to finishing out my 1,000 dinosaurs killed with ____ weapon achievements, but it’s not really for everyone. Good luck, and dodge when you reload!

TL;DR at bottom
If you liked the first one, you will like this one.  The game can be grindy at a time but there are a lot of cool experiences with the Nemesis system, although as the game goes on they become less interesting and the really cool ones happen less often.  The story is okay, I never really enjoyed the first one for its story, but its not terrible. I would say its a slight improvement over the first in terms of Story Telling.  The real gem is the Nemesis system, and of course wholesale Orc slaughter.
I have put in an enjoyable 105 hours.  If you like to 100% games it is a fairly easy one to do, a bit of grinding at the end would be the worst part.
Personally I hardly even noticed the lootboxes.  Yes, when you pause you can see a small window in the bottom left corner advertising the expansion passes and loot crates along with the community challenge.  Personally I spend so little time in the menu it doesn't really matter.  As for the lootboxes, they are entirely worthless in my opinion.
Spending real money on them would be absurd as the game throws basically an endless amount of the ingame currnecy at you and the ones earned through Online Conquests/Vendattas usually contain gear worse than what you already have.  As for the Orcs, I often have to kill off Orcs I have so many of them, so buying Orcs would just be redundant.
TL;DR -  If you like the first game, you will like this one.  It is a slight improvment in terms of story and gameplay, with a massive improvement to the Nemesis system.  Lootbox outrage is nothing more than outrage for the sake of outrage,  you will never have to buy a single lootbox in the game - not even with the endless amounts of ingame currency.

Virginia is well worth investing two hours and £7 in. Its jump-cut pacing and dialogue-free story eliminate the two biggest flaws suffered by its peers: dropping out of flow due to excessive amounts of walking or listening.
You won't make any meaningful choices or solve any puzzles while playing. The level of interactivity is instead pitched to keep you engaged with the world without becoming distracted from the considerable task of interpreting it. Characters, locations, and events all whizz by at a pace that would be astounding in a traditional game, yet Virginia makes the onslaught manageable and even exhilarating.
Each scene adds something new to the unfolding narrative, and most are completely unique. World design and animation are superb throughout, with the game's posterised look helping to break up low detail areas. Most scenes keep things flowing smoothly with very clear signposting, and on the few occasions when I did become lost there were only a few seconds of fumbling required. The plot itself is perhaps best described as "diffuse", but I was able to follow it and enjoy the unusual perspective offered by a female protagonist.
Technically there is less to praise. The posterisation shader is dependent on the location of the camera, resulting in distracting bands of colour sometimes crawling over surfaces as you move around. A 30fps cap is in place by default and you are warned when disabling it that the game is meant to be experienced at that speed; this is bizarre and I suspect a fig leaf to cover up performance problems. It isn't even enough, with more than a few scenes dipping below 20fps on my more than capable system.
Nevertheless, Virginia is the best walking simulator yet made. It escapes the criticisms implicit in the genre's name by successfully expanding the model first explored by
from twenty minutes to two hours of densely packed entertainment. I'd far rather see more of this than the current torrent of 95%-filler survival games.

Kerbal Space Program has been one of my favorite games for several years, since pre-release up to now.  A wealth of content is tempered with a sharp learning curve, as the game fully embodies the phrase that 'the fun is in the journey'. Probably a result of my lack of ambition, but in all of my hours playing I've only very recently made stable orbits around Eve and Duna; and since the Kerbol system is a mirror of our own, these correlate to Venus and Mars. You can reach this point far earlier than I did with a little more motivation, and learn a lot along the way with guides and videos.
The game is an accurate simulation of orbital mechanics and ideas, but it can be as easy or as difficult as you want it to be. You can strap a load of rocket boosters onto a capsule and brute force your way out into the wild unknown, or meticulously calculate your orbits and crunch the numbers to create realistic and highly efficient missions. An active modding community (
) helps to add new and varied content if you find yourself getting bored with the game, from Faster-Than-Light machines to modular surface bases, and more that I couldn't even fathom.
It can be hard for beginners. But give it some time, learn the basics and it won't be long until you're converting entire worlds to suit the needs of the Kerbal Empire, or whatever you can think up. I vividly remember the first time I reached a stable orbit, an unprecedented achievement, and soon you'll be running missions to the Mün in your sleep, or beyond.

The liberties taken here with The Lord of the Rings setting are absolutely ridiculous. The energy that could be harvested from Tolkien spinning in his grave (were that a thing) could power a large city. But at the same time, it’s the Lord of the Rings setting that makes this game so rewarding for me. Would the gameplay mechanics I like (the open world with multiple questlines, fantastic skill upgrades, and actions that impact across regions) be just as fun set in a different universe? Perhaps. But the Middle Earth set pieces such as Minas Tirith, Gondorian soldiers, fallen rangers, traitorous stewards, Ringwraiths,  Haradrim defectors… it’s too tempting for me to resist. The liberties taken may be ridiculous, but there's enough lore used that is also treated with a fan’s respect and passion to make up for it to me.
UPDATE: After the storylines are done, the game features a fourth act that many describe as a grind. I've found it to be not worth the effort I need to put into it to succeed. I wish the developers had included it as an optional mode presented after the credits roll, instead of an epilogue that you can simply choose to not slog your way through.

Virginia wears its influences fine, and I particularly enjoyed the song that oh-so narrowly skirts Twin Peaks copyrights, but if you're looking for the Lynch or X-Files Walking Simulator, this is not it. I could not wait for it to end, and when the game informed me I was on the "Final Day," I cheered (mind you, this was about 90 minutes in). The ending, of course, collapses on a string of climaxes, but by then, I was already waiting to turn the game off.
You can tell a ton of work went into some environments, while others were left fairly vacant. You'll slowly walk through many hallways that do nothing to advance the narrative nor elevate any palpable tension. And while I was pleasantly surprised by the idea of finding items that cosmetically enhance particular scenes, there is otherwise no reason to spend any additional time in each environment. For an FBI agent, I found very few clues (at least when I was actually in control).

TL;DR: Decent story, interesting world, mediocre dialogues. Relatively boring battles/gameplay. Decent sound and graphics, but limited customization and very ugly character models.  Would have fared better without the high expectations from the kickstarter. Close to a positive recommendation, but not quite: 5/10.
The sequel to the inspiration for Fallout... talk about high expectations. Add to this the fact that it was a super-successful Kickstarter project that promised to put the creative people back in charge of their own projects, and it's easy to see why so many hopes for the future of PC roleplaying rest(ed) on this game. I found it somewhat disappointing in many details small and large, unfortunately. Would I have liked it without the hype? I will never know. Does it matter for this review? No. A game that carries so much baggage needs to be reviewed with it in mind.
Story/World:
Meh. As so often, it is difficult to say anything without too many spoilers. The world is an... interesting place. Unlike Fallout, it places less emphasis on realism and does not take itself too seriously, allowing for some weird and fascinating factions and places, which are fun to explore. Unfortunately, while there are some gems, the size of the world means that no place has much depth and really catches your heart. Did I feel at home and connected to Ranger Citadel? No. Did I care that a lot of old acquaintances showed up, helped and died in the final battle? No. Did I really care for the epilogues for the places I had visited? No. So: While the game presents a varied and interesting world, it failed to pull me in.
Additionally, they sat a bit heavily on the predecessor (old characters, old locations, old stories that are repeated again and again) which I did not play, making it hard for me to get invested.
Dialogues were a mixed bag as well. Some good, but also a lot of repetition of the same pieces of information over and over again.
The roleplaying came down to a handful of choices (Do I help this person? Which of those two factions do I support?). My characters lacked, unfortunately, a character.
The main story is actually very short. Weird robots show up. Now go and fight them. It's nice and consistent, without plot holes, but the ending
Sound:
Nice enough, but could have been more varied.
Graphics:
I usually don't care too much about graphics, but some things really disturbed me here from the very beginning. Character models are
. What's more, there are a very limited number of character portraits, all of which are used as NPC portraits as well, so you quite often have two identically-looking people talking to each other. Finally, the descriptions of characters in the world very often don't match their portrait at all. Takes me out of the story.
That said, the maps are done with great care and are quite beautiful.
Gameplay:
Yeah... that was what almost made me give up on the game in between. There are a few minor things that bugged me (area map is a screenshot, allows no notes, shows no locations), but the big thing is the combat. This is where you spend most of your game.
the combat is pretty damn
: There is a basic cover mechanic, but many places in which you will find yourself starting battles are devoid of cover at least for your group. Thus, many battles end up being about choosing who to shoot. Throw in some small-ish things like unclear sight lines/weapon ranges especially when the battle goes over two levels and the whole affair becomes less an intricate chess game between you and the (mediocre) AI and more a tedious excercise in mopping up without using too many resources.
Then there are the crates. And the safes. And the holes. And the toasters. Everything wants to give you items, which are absolutely necessary in the beginning and absolutely superfluous in the end. But if you're anything like me, you will STILL open the next safe - just in case of the very occasional plot-relevant item. Makes the game go even slower and becomes, at times, an excercise in quick-saving and quick-loading.
Finally, while the game throws loads of skills at you, there is no deep character building here. One weapon skill, one auxiliary skill (or three for the skill monkeys) per person, done.
In summary, while the game amused me and made me smile at times, it did not make me think and it did not make me care for its world or characters. At least one of those I expect from a roleplaying game. Thus: Not recommended.
Addendum: Reading it again, this review sounds exceptionally negative. It wasn't really meant to be; most of the issues I mentioned bothered me, but not as much as in other games. It's just that a lot of things that don't bother me too much add up to make this game pretty mediocre - maybe 5/10.

TL;DR at the bottom
Pros:
+This game can run on ANY computer. Literally just try it, it'll work
+Devs are actually listening to the community
+Fun characters with diverse play-styles
+Character custimization that expands beyond just how the character looks (explained later on)
+Fun maps
Cons:
-Really buggy game. Sound glitches where you'll hear a weapon firing indefinitely, visual bugs like t-posing characters, and sometimes (extremely rarely) abilities just not working
-Bad matchmaking system
-Only able to queue with a party of 2 in competative
-Balance issues (but the dev team listens to the community and usually do the appropriate nerfs)
So, let's start off with what the game is itself. It is a fps moba type game that bases itself around the different champions (just think of it like overwatch). Two 5-man teams fight to push a payload (Payload), capture a point (Siege), or to be the last surviving team (Survival). At the start of each match, you and your team will select which characters they want to play. There are flank characters which do high damage and have high mobility at the cost of being squishy, tanks which take the most damage and deal low to medium damage, support characters which heal and do medium damage, and damage which do medium to high damage and have medium mobility.
When you and your teammates have selected a character,
. You are locked into this character, but not to fear! There are loadouts and legendary cards for your characters in order to fit different play-styles and situations. There are also 'burn cards' which you can buy in-game with currency you get for killing, healing, or staying on the objective. Burn cards act very much like items do in other moba games, and you buy them to counter what your enemies have. Loadouts are made before you join a game with different cards, and Legendary cards are chosen at the beginning of each game. Some examples of the loadout cards are more health, more mobility, and cooldown reduction. Some examples of the Legendary cards are Maeve's getting an elimination resets one of her abilities and Ghrok's activating ghost walk instead of dying.
. The meta revolves around these different loadouts and legendary cards and how they can change a character. For example, Pip is normally a healer that does some pretty decent damage and slows enemies. However, it is possible to play him like a flank character with these different loadouts and legendary cards.
The only thing bad with the loadouts being able to change a character so much is it makes the loadouts nearly vital to a character. This is where most of the negative reviews will come in: The essence system. As of OB44, essence has been added into the game as a new type of currency. Previously, loadout cards were bought with gold and legendary cards didn't even exist. Now, loadout cards AND legendary cards are bought with essence. New players start 36000 essence, and founders 76000 essence. The cards cost anything between 5000-500 essence depending on the rarity of the card, and the legendary cards cost 12000 essence (quickly nerfed from it's original price of 18000 essence). "But how do I get essence?" you may ask. You get essence from duplicate cards from the three cards that radiant chests give you. So, say you have Card A. You get a radiant chest and from the three-card drop you get Card A. You'll get a certain amount of essence depending on the rarity of Card A. These radiant chests cost 2500 gold but cost less the more you buy in bulk. You can earn 2500 gold in about 5 matches. Sounds like a pretty botched system? That's because it is. This is the major flaw in the game at the current state. However, you may still buy cards - with essence. While you dont have to pray to rngesus to give you whatever card you want, you do have to pray to get duplicate cards.
TL;DR In all, this game is fairly good but does have its downsides. The essence system is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ but if you can put up with that and the (sometimes funny) bugs, you'll love this game. It has amazingly fun gameplay that revolves around teamwork. The characters are fun, and the ever-evolving meta is interesting and deep. Overall, it is a solid 8/10 (maybe a 7/10 because of the essence system) and worth your time to try. If the game weren't so buggy, and the essence system wasn't so♥♥♥♥♥♥I would easily give this a 10/10.

Brutal yet surprisngly fun game
There isn't much platforming per say, most of the gameplay consists of dodging enemy fire (like in SHMUPs) and avoiding deadly obstacles. Game is pretty brutal, there is a health system but you get killed in 2-3 hits, spikes and botomless pits are instant death, and health pickups are placed behind additional obstacles. At the same time it feels very fair, there are no untelegraphed or undodgeable attacks. It still takes some time to figure out enemy or level mechanics (each level has different sprites for deadly spikes, which can be somewhat unexpected). Levels aren't too long and usually have 2 checkpoints so you won't lose too much time by dying.
There is a good variety in level mechanics, almost every level has an interesting gimmick. For example, there is an underwater level where all jumps are higher, or a DDR-themed level where all projectiles are move hints you should press to avoid damage. Same goes for enemies, they have mechanical differences instead of stat differences.
Visually game is nothing special, it looks OK though a few times it's hard to tell which object is a spike or an enemy until you touch it, but it's not much of a big deal. Music is actually quite fitting and enjoyable. There is no plot.
. Keyboard controls are tight, but I wish the game didn't stay too true to old two-button controller scheme. Later in the game you get a dash ability which is used by pressing Jump + Shoot + Move at the same time and timely use of it is quite vital in some places, but it takes time to get used to the combination. Also there are no buttons for specific weapons, so weapon switch takes time. It's not much of a big deal until you get to level rush (optional bonus level).
Took me around 6 hours to beat. For current price quite a steal as long as you like these kinds of games.

An absolutely brilliant exercise in turn-based strategy.  Hard West succeeds in creating a very real and very dangerous game which never ever becomes too easy, only easier than it was before.  The game's luck mechanic removes the RNG from things like cover, special abilities, and attacks, making every single facet of this game predictable, observable, and controllable.  The scenarios are all very well-designed and require extensive thinking and judicious use of your characters' special abilities in order to master and overcome otherwise impossible odds.
Narratively the game presents an arch story of villains, villains, and a single lone hero who is also a bit of a villain himself.  It's a pitch-black story of revenge and brutality in the vein of "High Plains Drifter", wrapped in a keen appreciation for and understanding of cowboy folklore and western mysticism--battle-ready priests, noble gamblers, good-hearted nuns, and more acts of Satan than you can shake a stick at.  This is all compounded by the introduction of a Fallout 1-style overworld, dotted with queer characters, strange encounters, and more.
Some bugbears in the form of game stability, lack of replay value, and lack of saving after a mission are painful, and sabotage what is otherwise a near-on peerless tactical experience.  Should be played by fans of XCOM, fans of Westerns, and fans of good games in general.

This game is revolutionary in the realm of off-road driving simulators as I don't believe there is anything else out there quite like SpinTires.  There is a very impressive realism to the terrain and with the environment all together.  And it can get very unforgiving to the novice explorer.  There is a fair array of trucks to drive and the majarity of them are off-road purpose built, russian military trucks that look quite unstoppable.
There is more to this game then just getting stuck waist high in sucking mud, high centering on large rocks or fallen trees or swamping out the engine in deep waters.  You can winch yourself out of tough places.  Plow over trees that get in your way.  Keep in mind, the bigger the truck your driving, the bigger the tree you can crush.  Run fuel and repair supplies to broken down trucks.  Open up other garage places and even haul logs to lumber mills.  In fact, the main objective is to haul lumber to the mills through the most challenging terrain imaginable.  And if that's not enough, you can team up with up to 3 of your friends and tackle the challenge together.
The game currently does have some draw backs though.  The camera still needs some work as it can get difficult to see where you want to look.  Especially when your in a tight group of trees, on a steep hill or working with the crane.  The manual transmission mode is awkward and clumsy but you will get use to it over time.  And the multiplayer mode is very lacking.  Yes, you can help your friends by winching them out of tight places or giving them fuel or repairs.  But you can't see their lights, hear their trucks engines or see what they have done to the terrain after they have driven over it.  You can't help your friends load lumber and you can't see your friends trucks that they have abandoned.  Only the trucks they are currently using.
Over all, the game is pretty well put together and while being played in hardcore mode, can offer a challenge to even the most seasoned off-roaders.  Given all that I have said, there is a certain level of fun to this game that will have you coming back for more.  And if the creators of this game do something to address the issues I had mentioned above, it would make this game so much more enjoyable.

I jumped on Broken Age near release. I'm a huge fan of Double Fine and a large portion of the cast in this game. I was also interested in playing another game with the 'painted' style graphics as well as trying other types of point-and-click adventures. This game was released in 2 acts. Act one was amazing; such an intriguing tale matched with great dialogue and fun problem solving. It took me a good chunk of time to make it to the end without cheating! Now about Act 2..
I've seen a lot of hate for Act 2 so don't let that scare you away from the game, but.. There was a solid delay in the release of Act 2 and because of that I found the well crafted story that was half-told and full of mystery from Act one, well, a little hard to remember. I didn't totally forget what happened but almost all character sentimate was lost and I was very much detatched from all of the characters that I know I loved at the end of Act 1. This doesn't effect the person purchasing this game after release of both acts though. Where I feel act 2 gets most of it's hate is the way the story changes and even the puzzles. You get the answers to the questions raised in Act 2 but if you're like me at all you're not totally happy with what you get. Without giving anything away it's a bit dissapointing and super underwhelming. It seemed like an utter lack of creativity compared to Act 1. Also, the puzzels do very much increase in difficulty during progression of the game but in Act 2 the answers to the puzzles make the story completely unbelievable. This is fiction but the puzzles around the end can only be solved by a player who is taking advantage of having the perspectives of both protagonists which leaves you wondering how the characters could have ever figured any of this out. By the end they're practically working together without any communication at all just because you, the player, are controlling them.
Anyway, that's how I feel about Broken Age. I still give it a thumbs up even though the second half did not meet the expectations set by the first the game as a whole was very good and half-way stellar. I definitely recommend it, especially now that both Acts have been released.

Most RPGs and games in general try to hide the plot and world from the player. They try to dumb things down and can the story into as compact of a thing as they can. But not this one. The Witcher 2 dumps your stupid♥♥♥♥♥in the middle of it's world and doesn't even give you a pat on the♥♥♥♥♥and a nudge in the right direction. The game will start throwing earls, barons, dukes, kings, lands, wars, races, racial tensions, past events, and all kinds of crap at you and tell you to sort it out on your own.
The gameplay is fun but it really takes a back seat to the storyline and atmosphere. It's more Game of Thrones than it is Lord of the Rings, which is not bad. The immersion and the way the game handles it's spider-web of plotlines and interactions reminds me a LOT of Baldur's Gate.
Decisions you make in the beginning chapters of the game, things you say to certain NPCs, impact the rest of the story in a huge way and you'll never know what kind of decision you made until it's happening. There is no meter to tell you if you're giving the good answer, or the evil one. You just pick whichever one seems to fit what you want and hope for the best. It turns the game into a huge moral gray blob. Top it with the fact that there are really no good or bad guys and you have an awesome story to play with.
Combat is fun. Targeting can be a little clunky, but it isn't so bad as to be anything game-breaking. Carrying two different swords - a steel one for humanoid enemies, and a silver one for monsters - is interesting. The rune system can be a little tricky to learn, but once figured out it is handy.
Highly recommended. If you count yourself an RPG fan of any sort, you owe it to yourself to play this. It is as essential to your experience of the genre as Dragon Age: Origins, Ultima 7, Baldur's Gate, Morrowind, Skyrim, or the original Mass Effect.

Sid Meier's Civilization III Complete is a turn based strategy game developed by Firaxis Games and released Oct 30, 2001.
The "Story" is more so in the individual experience you have playing these types of games. You're put into a random world with random NPC's (unless you try to determine the world and nations by selecting them...) the key defining elements are how you interact with the game's NPC's.
My personal story is I kept to myself, and then people started threatening me, and I'm not going to take any of that from easy difficulty NPC's, so they declared war on me and I fought them until the game ended.
I've played Civilization Call to power, and I've played Civilization 4... Civilization 3 is different then both, but difficult to articulate how it's different... the game feels slower paced, I can't wage war as effectively by bombardment as I can in civ call to power or civ4.
The game just hasn't clicked with me in the way Civ5 did immediately. the User interface has a serious case of the 2000's
There are scenarios and tons of special mod or DLC packs which are included in Civ3. If you're looking to burn some time playing a strategy game, Civilization 3 can easily eat up that time with the crazy amounts of content it has.
The dilemma I have with Civ3, is that I prefer Civ5, and Civ call to power... but that doesn't mean Civ3 is bad... it's quite good and chalk full of content. Especially for the low price... But while playing I just find myself thinking "man, I'd rather be playing Civ5".
I think it's nice to have Civ3 as a backup for my laptop when I'm on trips, or for a new/old challenge.

In its current state, the game is incredibly simple, as in, there's not much to it. There is 'technically' character customization, but it's hardly anything at the moment. The gameplay is casual, to say the least. This game is incredibly easy for anyone who has any skill at an FPS, however even so the game handles like a dream, and it's incredibly well optimized.
Pros
- One of the smoothest FPS' I've ever played
- Easy
- Surprisingly good looking considering how well it runs
- Simple/Easy to understand (In terms of gameplay and functionality)
- Casual (Play at your leisure, and it's not overly stressful compared to other FPS')
- Despite being Russian made, has surprisingly good English translations
Cons
- Simple (In terms of overall features)
- Few maps
- Little variation if any in gameplay
- Community is primarily Russian and Korean despire being marketed towards English audiences as well (Not neccessarily a bad thing, but it can be frustrating connection-wise)
- No real challenge
All in all, it's not a bad little shooter, but it's definitely got some work to be done before it's anything worth talking about. Give it a try, you'll probably have some fun, but you'll probably get bored of it in like an hour or two.

Now for a disclaimer I didn't play this game until both acts had been released so I don't have the many years of waiting that had happened to many others who expected more from Tim Schafer. I have the review split in two below:
Act 1:
Honestly, I really enjoyed this. I found the puzzles not too simple, but solvable and quite a lot of fun. The two different characters are very interesting, both wanting to go against the curve of their surroundings and free themselves.  The many different characters are well written and voice acted too with a twist at the end which I sadly saw coming as I had seen Zero Punctuation's review of Act 2. I still quite enjoyed it though.
Act 2:
The sequal was quite interesting as both teens try to get to grips with what has just been revealed to them and they have to work hard to get out of the situation and reveal a diabolical plan. Unlike the first game, you need control of both characters to complete puzzels on either side (as if they were mentally linked, but they aren't) with one of the most ANNOYING puzzels I have ever seen in a Double Fine game. Luckily there were a few guides online that helped me out with this, leading to a interesting and somewhat symbolic ending.
Now, unlike everyone else I didn't play the first part before the release of the second part. As a full game, it's fine and works well. However, if I were waiting for this second part I would be VERY dissappointed. Not to get into any spoilers, but the ending was cut a little short. The villains never get killed or take one, but it ends it with the whole "hope" message like RAGE which also♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off as it's like reading a story and then someone tore out the last few pages before the hero's confrontation with the villain.
All in all, now I would say it's worth the money but considering the kickstarter behind it, the amount of time it's taken and other issues like with Spacebase DF9 being incomplete I'd say not to support Double Fine's games unless they're COMPLETE as they have proven that even given a year they can't finish a game that they had recieved a stupid amount of money over.

This is a very decent game, despite all the negativtiy surrounding the Micro-transactions, a short yet slightly grinding story, but honestly, this game really does live up to the expectations from what they showed us from the gameplay trailer, and among other aspects, I do wish the battles were bigger and bolder, and maybe an occassional betrayal in the middle of the fight, just to spice things up, but I digress, The game shouldn't be attacked due to some of the minor features they added, The mico-transaction is nothing but an option, and you can still beat the whole game without getting a lootbox, even so, it is nice to spend your mirian on something once you upgraded the fortresses, and it can't be any worse then Battlefront 2, Shadow of War has given us many memroable and great orcs or trolls, you can't deny that you want to keep them like your little generals, play army and then smash a couple of heads along the way, but hey, thats why we're getting unlimited siege and an Orc rebellion mode, its not a bad game it just made a few key mistakes that aren't neccessary for getting to the end, I mean its not like Asura, where you have to pay the DLC to get the real ending. The story could've used more depth and maybe something to fill in the time before  we reached Act IV: Shadow wars, make it less grindy, but hey, the developers had to use what time they had to do what they can. can't blame them for making the story what it is, but it ties in to the Tolkien universe and Lord of the ring movies swimingly. Though it would be nice to lay siege Mina-tiras as one of the nine, only to be beaten by Aragorn, but hey beggers can't be choosers. Finally the nemesis system is pretty damn impressive, at least the orcs actually see us as a very bigger threat then we were in Shadows of Mordor, I mean all we did was topple a Orcish heirarchy, here, we toppled the same heirarchy but just added battles and spies and toppled a whole fortress to the ground, all while decapitating an Overlord to replace it with another equally crazed Orc, and the Betrayals are a neat touch, I mean its a better upgrade and gives us the players a better chance to get rid of orcs we can't keep and replace them with better orcs in the later on as we progress the missions and time. Overall, The game could use a bit of work in the story department, not gonna lie on that, But Given on how much we were given with the side quests, the Stories made with our orc followers and enemies, and with major battles and strategy to take a fort, I would defiently recommend the game to people, But if you want to do some ACTUAL gambling and none of that RNG nonsense on the Micro-transactions, Just play the Arena matches and set some bets, at least thats Gambling done right, TWO orcs go in, and Only One....Will be replaced, that is all.

My all-time favorite multiplayer FPS.
At this point, balance is about as even as it's going to get for an FPS with asymmetrical teams, and the developers (both Unknown Worlds and the Community Dev Team) have added a significant amount of content in a number of rather sizable updates. The community is still quite active and is far less dickish than most, which, to me, is a rarity in this age of games going out of style once they're no longer the flavor of the month.
The gameplay, while obviously an FPS, is very much dependent upon the strategic layer, and vice versa. What this means is that the commander's role is absolutely vital to the success of the players on foot, and their capability to win their encounters affects whether or not he can expand; it's not like Nuclear Dawn or some other RTS/FPS hybrids where one element is gimped or neutered while the other is fleshed out.
My only complaint would be the devs' tendency to change things unnecessarily every other week, with minor balance patches or changes throwing the whole game out of whack. The game as it is now is NOT the same game it was at launch, not by a long shot. If you can keep pace with the changes and roll with the punches, however, it's excellent fun.
One crucial tip for new players would be to use your microphone, if you have one (I know you do). Communication with your team is key. Don't be afraid to pipe up on voice, and always keep an eye on your map (bound to the C key by default).

Alan Wake is a really enjoyable survival "horror" game. The way the game is presented (as a TV show) actually fits perfectly into the quality of the story. It's a made for TV kind of scary, and that's not a bad thing. Every horror game doesn't need to be a scary as possible or a total gore fest. There is nothing wrong with more mild scares & the use of suspense to create tention. Though I only have 3+ hours in the Steam version, I played it all the way through on the 360. (Holy Crap does the 360 version run like assy-poo-poo)
Score: 7.5/10
Pros:
-Engaging story
-Well done voice acting
-scares that aren't just cheap/lame jump scares
-quality suspense
-beautiful lighting effects
-impressive & atmospheric visuals/graphics
-fun story
-fun/funny/interesting NPC's
Cons:
-irritating combat (not broken or anything just frustrating sometimes)
- Uninspired enemies (ooooh smoke Zombie people, so origional)
-too many collectables
-one or two of the NPCs are obnoxious (your agent Dave for example)
-bland weapons (not necessarily the games fault, it is set in the "real" world.
Alan Wake is definitely worth picking up. Not at full price but anything under $20 is a worthwhile proposition. This is a great survival horror game for "beginners", kids, or anyone very easily scared. It looks great, it has a fun story & over all good voice work. By no means is Alan Wake perfect, but its fun and worth you time at the right price. Only the meanest, most bitter gamers wouldn't enjoy playing this game. Give it a shot. If you hate it, feel free to come back to my comment & yell @ me. With refunds now being a thing, you have nothing to lose. You'll know if you're gonna like it before 2 hours.

PROS:
~Super rich detail in everything.
~Maps are huge.
~Ability to create your own 4 person squad from the get go.
~The ability to have a max of seven people in your party! How awesome is that!?

CONS:
The game is extremely well done, and the only issues I could possibly have with it are not being able to zoom in on the map display, which can make missing parts of maps an easy thing to do, leaving you wandering back and forth until you get frustrated. Then again, I may not have noticed where I was supposed to go. Either way, it's an extremely minor thing, especially when the maps for most places are quite huge, many consisting of other areas you have to travel to in order to search the area fully. The other thing I would have liked is voice acting for everything. But I suppose I am spoiled like many others these days, where pretty much every game out now has voice acting throughout.
Overall, two little things that don't deter from my experience whatsoever.

Mibibli's quest is a colorful, humorous platforming adventure that brings us back to what made some of the classic balls-hard platformers like Mega Man tick, while still adding and improving in its own flambouyant style. It's got responsive controls, clever mechanics, and challenging levels, holding true to the NES's style of gameplay. It also has beautifully accurate-to-the-NES graphics, an amazing chiptune soundtrack that goes perfectly with each level, and a certain retro styling to it that I've honestly never felt anything similar to. One of the only issues I had was that the controls are quite restricted. There are no customization options, and no gamepad support. Despite these things, Mibibli's Quest is still a fantastic adventure that I would go on any day. A rad retro throwback, Mibibli's Quest is an addictive one-player platformer bringing us back to the greats of platforming that I would reccomend to any fans of the classics of the genre. This game scores a smooth 9/10.

I haven't quite completed the game yet, but after 12 hours I think I'm qualified to give a review. I''m really taking my time with this one and have already replayed the same scenarios a couple of times before moving on to the later ones.
Pros:
-Interesting Storyline
-Awesome aesthetic
-Well thought-out tactical gameplay
-Choices matter
-Very punishing at times
Cons
-Very punishing at times
I see some people complaining about the lack of a save function, but I think that's entirely intentional. These scenarios are meant to be played through multiple times as there are a lot of different ways to go about it. It's pretty easy to ♥♥♥♥ up and lost a character or let debuffs go on unchecked for too long, but in my opinion that's part of the appeal. You can't save constantly and just go back when you make a bad decision; you'll have to start the whole scenario over. Luckily the scenarios aren't too long and considering how many different ways you can go about completing them, it's fun to go back to square one and approach it from a different angle if you feel you've made the wrong choices.
I started on the lowest difficulty (still a challenge if you're not versed in tactical turn-based gaming), but I quickly moved on to the normal difficulty which was immensely satisfying.
If you don't like turn-based tactical games then there's probably no way you'll like this, but as far as strategy RPGs go this is one of my favorites already. People are comparing it to XCOM, and I think that's a fair comparison, but I actually liked the narrative and level structure in this game a lot more than I liked XCOM (I did really like XCOM).
It feels oldschool while still being innovative and fresh. I think it's a must-have for people who like tactical strategy RPGs, and worth checking out if you have a soft spot for Wild West games.
I should mention that this game was gifted to me for free from a random person online, and I knew very little about this going in so my expectations weren't very high. I do however think that if I had been excited about this game before it came out, it would have satisfied me. I'd go as far as to say that I would purchase any DLC that comes out in the future, as I can see myself playing and replaying these scenarios for some time to come.

This game has it's own character. The two different ways of playing (tactical combat missions and world map story telling) are a big part of this character. So, potential interested player, be warned: This is a story heavy game and you will do a lot of reading (or skipping and missing out on a big part of the game). There is only one voice actor, though considering the price tag, this should not surprise anybody. The rest is up to you.
The tactical missions seem all doable and with a little bit of trial and error, quite manageable. The character abilites (gained via the interesting card system) can have a huge influence on the way fights take. The weapons get quite strong during the game, some might be even overpowered (a rifle doing 13 damage, while most enemies have 3-6 hitpoints). The cover system is quite important for surviving and the AI seems to try to flank you, so movement is important. Once you are used to the controls, it plays really well. A lot of people seem to be upset about the missing overwatch ability on player characters (the AI has something like that). But you don't really need it. The moment I realised that my characters don't have such an ability, I adapted and changed my tactics. No problem.
The world map part, that contains most of the story, is ok. You move from one point of interest to the next, though most of the time you can decide to take detours befor going to the marked point to continue the story. There are many choices to be made and they might even influence the tactical missions. Each time you reach a point of interest, there is something to read and sometimes quite a lot. There are some riddles and each scenario has it's own special way of progressing, though it is not too hard to figure out. I'd like to see a change to the UI though. Because there is a lot of stuff happening from time to time that shows up in the lower left corner. You get notified that something has happened to a character, you gained an object or money. And sometimes it is too much that shows too fast.
I really like the story and the way it is presented. The idea of using only half of the scenarios for the main story and framing it with an equal amount of other scenarios is interesting, though it shifts the focus away from the protagonist. Character development happens only within a scenario and the story. You have to start again with every scneario, though there is a mechant travelling from scenario to scenario that sells some items, that you aquired in previous scenarios. The card system really helps to tailor the characters you have in the way you want to have them. Every character can use every weapon and every ability, allthough they start with different stats and injuries or story events might alter those further.
The savepoint mechanic is. what it is. I'd like to be able to save when I have to leave due to real live issues. Other than that, I can live with the approach of accepting the consequences of your choices. In a certain way it fits the story. The game is quite taxing for the GPU. I had to activate V-sync to not feel like sitting next to a plane. The fans were working really hard. I have read, that the game tries to give you as high FPS as possible. This might be the issue. There are some black screens and long loading times from time to time. This might be fixed in a patch, we will have to wait and see.
TL:DR: The game is well worth the $20.
