Today, Kickstarter has been used by a number of different developers to crowdfund their games. I would like to say that Broken Age was the game that started this trend (which, by the way, I am very happy to see). Tim Schafer, the co-developer of Day of the Tentacle and developer of Grim Fandango, asked for $400k to make a small game as well as a documentary about the development process. He got waaaaay more and started to make a full-length point-and-click adventure game.
This was in February 2012. As scope increased, so did the development time and the game took a long time to get done. Double Fine also ran out of money and decided to split Broken Age in two acts in order to make some money whilst developing the last part of the game. I was one of the backers and I worried immensely about the future of the game. In the end I was happy to see a full game released. But how was the results?
First of all, the graphics are beautiful. I love the hand-painted feeling in the game and the imaginative scenes that we get to explore. Everything is just gorgeous. The music goes hand-in-hand with the graphics and the result is a very smooth and calming ambience.
The theme of the game is growing up and taking control of your life. Our main protagonists are Vella and Shay:
Vella is a young woman who has been selected to be sacrificed to the beast that regularly visit her village, threatening to kill everyone if it doesn’t get young maidens.
Shay is a young man who stuck on a spaceship where the ship’s mother does everything to keep him safe and out of harm’s way.
Neither of them have any control of their lives and they desperately want to break out of their situation.
Broken Age is divided into two acts which were released months apart, and the difference in gameplay is very distinct between the two acts. In both acts, you will solve puzzles in order to advance the story. After the first act Double Fine Productions were criticised for not making the puzzles difficult enough. They were easy, story-based and required very few steps to solve.
In the second act, Double Fine had listened to their fan base and upped the difficulty of the puzzles. The second part of the game has more classic adventure game puzzles with some far-fetched solutions. I had to bring out pen and paper and take notes to solve some of them, and I must say I enjoy this difficulty level much more than the first part.
Unfortunately, you can’t please everyone. With act 2 released, now the critique was that the game was too difficult and that the puzzles were not fun anymore.
Either way, if you love beautiful graphics and a nice story I would definitely recommend Broken Age. Just be warned that there may be some difficult puzzles waiting ahead. If you instead want difficult puzzles you will need to play for an hour or so before you will have your challenge.
I am very happy that I backed this game when it was released on Kickstarter because I truly believe it has made a difference in the gaming industry. However, if I were to recommend just one point-and-click game to you, I would have to recommend Deponia instead.
The documentary is very worth seeing so if you have the time and are curious about how to make a computer game: check it out on YouTube!

Even with a beautiful art style, animation, and voice acting, Broken Age turns into a dreadful game. The puzzles start out whimsical and somewhat charming, eventually becoming frustrating and downright asinine.  The gameplay relies heavily on backtracking, trial and error, and obtuse "logic".  You will be forced to run circuits throughout the same 6-8 scenes over and over and over again, deseperately seeking to stumble upon some absurd situation, or item-combining nightmare, for which no precendent was set.  This leaves you swinging blindly most of the time, just trying to trigger the next element to some puzzle that really has nothing to do with anything.
There is some genuinely funny humor in places, but it is peppered in among cliches, and contrived circumstances built seemingly to make a joke.  The dialog and voice acting is otherwise top-notich, though the quality of Act 2 overall, especially in cutscenes, did not feel well-honed, giving it a sense that the project was rushed.  There are some good ideas in places, such as with sharing puzzle solutions between protagonists, but they are executed in such a frustrating way that makes playing the game an exercise in patience and tolerance.
Perhaps all of the shortcomings of the puzzles and backtracking could be overlooked if the payout of the story delivered something surprising or exciting, but it never does.  The only twist in the game comes early in Act 1, and the rest of the narrative just leans on absurd puzzle situations without actually delivering an interesting overall story.  For as odd, and deeply imaginative as the setting and situations are, the story falls flat and doesn't deliver any incentive to see it through.  There is just no payout, and that's what makes this the most disappointing.  If you must play this, do it with a walkthrough at the ready.

Broken Age, when looked at as two seperate parts, starts out very promising and then starts to decline around the beginning of Act Two.
Act One is short and sweet. It introduces the characters and world with a beautiful, handdrawn, storybook-like aesthetic. It presents enough plot elements to keep you interested and intriged enough to see the Act to its conclusion. It explores themes centered around coming of age and rebellion as well as the potential dangers associated with each. A number of interesting characters are introduced and it evokes a sense of Schafer's classic titles.
Insert a year and a bit of waiting. Now take everything established in the first game and swap the characters. Very few new locations (usually single, one-off rooms), only a few new characters and a number of awkward puzzles to lengthen playtime. Also, the story goes a bit off the rails.
The fundemental problem with Broken Age Act Two is that the more of its story it reveals, the more ridiculous it becomes. When you finally learn the antagonist's motivation for everything you realize it has almost nothing to do with the core themes presented in Act One. It's underwhelming in every regard.
This would all be forgivable if the gameplay was worthwhile. While some of the puzzles are clever and funny, others are an exercise in tedium. The worst part is that some puzzles play by their own rules. For example, I had an idea of how to complete the knot untying puzzle before I presented the necessary items to complete it. Because I remembered a previous knot and requested instructions to untie it
I had all the items, the solution was no longer valid. The correct order was to have all the items first
present them to the NPC
look at the knot
go back to the NPC...
... then do this two more times (at least there was a fast travel)...
... Why did it have to be three times?
Then the wiring/rewiring and final puzzle was a royal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If the order you had wasn't
for the final puzzle, you had to restart, rewire, reswitch, and reposition yourself until you got it right. If you made a single mistake you had to start from the very beginning.
It also brings into question how two characters in seperate areas are able to reference things from the other's perspective. You could argue that Shay remembered the wiring pattern from looking at his mom's photograph, but how could he possibly know the wiring pattern for the bot that Vella fixed?
Yes, "video game logic". I know.
All-in-all I have mixed feelings about this game. As a complete package I would recommend a buy to Point-And-Click adventure fans but only when it goes on sale. As for the general consumer: avoid. If you want a better example of Schafer's work, play Monkey Island 1, 2, and 3, Full Throttle, Psychonauts or Grim Fandango. Despite its pretty design, Broken Age is hardly worth your money or time.

This was one of the best game purchases I've ever made. I grabbed it during a holiday sale, but even at full price it's only $8.00 with the expansion pack.
I believe this game could be accurately compared to the original Legend of Zelda (NES) in terms of format; the top-down room-by-room style will surely remind any fans of the LoZ of that game's dungeons. Functionally The Binding of Isaac is similar to Geometry Wars, in that the user's left hand controls character movement and the right hand controls attacking (with space and shift thrown in for item use).
BoI's visuals are smooth, unique, and totally disturbing. The soundtrack is amazing; a different track for every level that never seems to get old. In fact, the soundtrack is one of my favourite parts of the game.
The game itself is very easy to learn but pretty difficult to master. Just as you get comfortable with it and have beaten it a number of times, it hits you with a difficulty increase to keep things fresh.
There are dozens of enemies and bosses to be encountered, and hundreds of items to get your hands on (After 30 hours of play I've still found less than 50% of them). The levels are randomized every playthrough, so the game always feels exciting.
Admittedly, BoI is pretty disturbing, with mature subject matter and graphics and design elements that are not for the squeamish. The game's storyline draws parallels to the Biblical tale of the same name, and has religous references throughout. Despite this, it's (REALLY) not something you'd find loaded onto a computer in a Christian or Catholic school. Some people will certainly find this game's subject matter to be quite off-putting. If you feel this may apply to you, do a little personal research about the game before you considering dropping the money for it.
I'm sure it goes without saying that I recommend this game. I've got about 30 hours of playtime as I'm writing this, and it's still climbing. Actually, I think I'll play it right now.

When a game is as beautiful and full of potential as Virginia is, it's difficult to admit that its flaws outweigh its better aspects. I wanted to like this game, but I feel like I'd be lying if I were to recommend it.
The art and music work well together to fashion a stunning world from an aesthetic standpoint, but upon closer inspection that world falls apart. The lack of interactivity in the environments are more reminiscent than a sparse model home than the life-filled spaces of Gone Home or Firewatch. Unfortunately, it doesn't have the same charm of other "walking simulators" to carry it. The game's soundtrack is ambitious, but inadequately implemented (more on this in a moment). The game's scenes are jarringly short, which ends up as a bit of a paradox, as the game's pacing makes it feel like one long scene rather than a fulfilling narrative. At the length of a fairly short movie by today's standards, Virginia still dragged. The soundtrack tries to match the game's pacing, and succeeds for some of the quieter moments, but the tense scenes feel too thinly stretched, going on for far too long for the music's urgency to have the same impact.
From a gameplay standpoint, there isn't exactly much to talk about. Your control over the main character is criminally shallow, leaving a unsatisfying disconnect. Often in environments there's only one thing to interact with, and there's no feeling of exploration when you're being railroaded through the story with even less agency than similar titles. It's difficult to call Virginia a "walking simulator" when you aren't even doing much of that, but "clicking simulator" sounds too close to point-and-click adventures, so I suppose I must settle for "watching simulator." This brings an issue to mind: I'd much rather be watching this story as a movie than playing it as a game, especially given how little gameplay there actually is. Were this an animated film, perhaps it would have faired better, but as a game--even as a narrative experience--it's sorely lacking in giving any sense of fulfillment.
Much of the unfulfilled feeling this game leaves lies in the story. Now, I'm not dead set on narratives requiring traditional structures, and I love movies that incorporate strong visual storytelling (Upstream Color comes to mind), but Virginia's narrative has an indirectness that leads to confusion rather than good old fashioned min♥♥♥♥ery. The developers did, indeed, set out to make a confusing game, but rather than being a complex mystery Virginia ends up as a scattered, unfocused, vague mess. Trust me, I got the major points of the story. It isn't that hard to piece together. However, what the game presents is, again, unsatisfying. I believe a lot of this is due to the lack of voice acting. While the NPCs were characterized well, Anne herself feels criminally shallow for the weight attributed to her story. The player doesn't identify with her because her motivation's don't align with ours in the slightest. Were there some narration, perhaps this wouldn't have been so jarring, but as it stands this alienation doesn't add anything to the game.
I feel like this game could have been more. Had the player been given more agency, there would have been a better connection to the story rather than the unshakable feeling of being an outsider. The visual style doesn't make up for the lifeless environments, and the music is largely hit or miss, with more of the latter in the long run. The story felt rushed and the pacing dragged, and the game's world isn't fleshed out enough to feel its own.
To sum it up in a word, Virginia was unsatisfying. Perhaps I'm missing the point. But perhaps the game just needs to make its point better.

Speaking as a movie lover, Virginia is a pretty fascinating story. Imagine if David Lynch directed the pilot episode of The X-Files. It has some great visuals and a soild score. It's worth it to at least watch a stream if you're into this kind of story.
As a gamer, and as someone who loves "walking sims" and artistic games, there is no reason that this should have been told as a game instead of movie. You have no agency, there is no sense of exploration, you can't affect any outcome, and you never have any option to choose. You pretty much walk through a series of very linear levels with usually only one object to interact with at any given time.
Virginia is an interactive experience the same way that turning pages in a book is an interactive experience.
Watch a stream if you're interested, because you are missing out on nothing by watching instead of playing this game.

In the hours I spent wandering Bright Falls's many forests, it became easier and easier to realize something. I had scared myself more than the wandering wackos with axes who were out for my blood had. Sure, I had jumped a few times when I'd rounded a corner to see some shadowy stalker making his way towards me, weapon in hand, but even more times I had jumped when I flashlight cast some odd shadow on a tree.
This happened more often than not because Alan Wake knows how to create something that most recent "horror" or "thriller" releases have long forgotten, that being atmosphere. And oh what an atmosphere it is. Whether exploring during the day, or on a casual stroll down murderer filled trails, Alan Wake establishes firmly that there are indeed things lurking in the dark. Those things are being controlled by something beyond your realm of understanding, and they've taken you're wife. They could emerge from anywhere, and be anyone and for I can compliment it without fear.
It helps that the game's setting is so well realized, whilst wearing its influences on its sleeve. Anyone familiar with Twin Peaks and its quirky little town are likely to feel right at home in Bright Falls, and they won't feel surprised to learn that the town has its fair share of dark secrets and zany inhabitants. As writer's block suffering writer Alan Wake, you'll make your way through Bright Falls's streets, the nearby forests, and a few other locales that I won't spoil, in search of your wife, who was mysteriously spirited away in the night. As events continue on it becames clear that for some reason, things are playing out according to a manuscript that Alan apparently wrote, despite not recalling having ever done so.
It's an interesting enough mystery to pull you along through the game's eight TV-show-esque "episodes", which is how the game splits up its levels. Each one has its own arc while adding to the games overarching plot, and opens with a "Previously on Alan Wake..." segment, and closes with a "The End" card. Its an odd set-up that for the most part works if you're willing to go along with it, though I could hardly blame you for feeling at odds with the game seemingly telling you to take a break for a bit, or for it repeating what you've just seen a minute prior as it tries to catch you up on events. The game's first six "episodes" are where the bulk of the story is held, and feels much more consistent than the latter two, which were originally post-release DLC when the game was first finding its feet on the Xbox. Those latter two present the game at its strangest, and prove to be tougher to follow by comparison, whereas the main episodes feel far more consistent, slowly ramping up the strangeness while keeping the player with a more set and understandable goal as they go after their protagonist's lost wife.
In the process you'll be gunning down shadow-shielded humans, Poltergeist-esque inanimate objects, and other obstacles with a mixture of light and good old fashioned ballistics. That's due to the fact that each enemy has been empowered by the game's mysterious Darkness, an entity you'll be facing down any time you happen to pass through dark areas. To actually harm your foes, you'll be wearing them down with your flashlight, before unloading your weapon into them. In between sections of combat, players might be asked to perform feats of platforming, or minimal environmental puzzle solving.
This proves to be where the game stumbles the most. While for the most part combat works well enough, there will still be times where enemies manage to close in enough on the player that the aiming goes wonky, and you'll almost always miss your mark. Other times things will fly by you, requiring you to quickly fling the camera in the direction that they flew off in the hopes of catching them with your flashlight before they zoom off again, with the chance of hitting and killing you.
The game's few instances of platforming also prove to be difficult, due in no small part to Alan's small hops. It can prove frustrating to think you'll be able to make a jump, before being required to try it a few times due to having failed, whether to imprecise controls or needing to be at a more proper distance for making longer leaps.
Those issues don't destroy the game, though, and pop up few enough times that they barely dent the majority of the experience. Said experience will prove to be quite the strange trip for anyone willing to take it, with the game likely leaving you with more questions than it has answers to give, which the game's smaller "sequel" American Nightmare only addresses in small ways. With no larger Alan Wake sequel in sight, be prepared to leave Bright Falls having hopefully enjoyed your stay, but with no ticket back, for now.

Mafia 3 was obviously pushed to the public to soon, and it shows in the stability and performance of the game. Bugs and crashes are prevalent and break the game-play way to often... which is a shame, as the game is amazing fun.
Video:
Text:
Now, lets tackle the big issue: PC Performance is horrid. Frequent bugs and various crashes to desktop. There is NO excuse for this. This is a very valid reason not to purchase the title at this time.
But... as a game is more than merely it's performance, there is a lot more to be said about Mafia 3 that is is great.
So lets start with the setting & story, where most of my love for this game comes from. As the setting in fictional 1960s USA is phenomenal in visuals for the city and construction, technology displayed is mostly time-period coherent and everything from various guns and weapons to the look and feel of cars fits quite well. And even though you as a player have little to no customization available to you - the NPCs in the world do look the part, from Cop to cleaning lady. everything fits, and stepping into a diner for the first time made me feel like i was transported into a old gangster movie.
Also, the almost casual way that the game deals with racism and segregation fits so well as to be scary realistic, it's what you'd expect to happen when a segment of your population is considered "less" by common society. This goes from interactions in shops, with people on the street and even how cops deal with you.
Now, unlike most other open world games this title is very focused on the story that is much enriched by the world that was created. Very good overall and made me feel like i was playing the witcher in it's quality and depth.
The lack of NPC's in the world at large as well as a decided lack of meaningful things to do outside of the story progression in the world is a big problem though.
The lack of NPC's is clearly a constraint to shore up the shoddy performance by limiting how many NPC's are on screen for the consoles / weak PC port, but sadly this means you often find streets, shops and buildings that feel like they should be stuffed to the brim - but end up feeling like a burial in progress. But the lack of meaningful stuff to do in the world, that provides more than a bit of fluff collectibles or a pittance in money, is a bigger problem for the open world title.
And this feels like content was cut to make it to release, and will be nickle and dimed to the players in future DLC.
Overall i really enjoyed the game, but with the PC performance issues, it remains hard to recommend buying the title in its current state.

Nuclear Throne is a post-apocalyptic roguelike-like (roguelite) top-down shooter. Its filled to the brim with irradiated mutants to blast, tons of powerful weapons (that can sometimes do more harm to you than enemies), and fast gameplay.
What started as a curious playthrough or two evolved into a slight addiction over the proceeding weeks. My goal was simple. I wanted to reach the Nuclear Throne and complete the game. The slight issue became that the game is pretty difficult. Nevertheless, I pushed myself further and set goals each time I made it that one step further. Unlocking new content, discovering secrets, and developing strategies.
While the game itself seems shallow on the surface, especially coming from and playing things like Enter the Gungeon; it takes awhile to discover the wealth of content that the game actually offers. While one may fault the game to hide a lot of this content away through cryptic means, it does add a lot depth for those seeking more content after getting their fill of beating the game, which I did end up doing (multiple times in fact).
So, about that difficulty thing; well, there's no denying it's a punishing game. In fact, many of your deaths will eventually feel like they are out of your control, especially once you get into the later levels. The procedural randomization that generates the layouts can feel unfair at times. You do get better at expecting certain things and developing strategies against these rare RNG nightmares, but it’s never in your full control. Luckily, I think that's where the faults end, at “rare unfair spawns”.
The rest of the game is top notch. The audio, the visuals, the style, the atmosphere and world it creates through its quirkiness. Although its sadly locked at 30 frames per second and in a 4:3 aspect ratio, these become very small nitpicks after playing it a bit.
While I was obviously late the party with this one, I ended up really enjoying the speed and frenetic gameplay that Nuclear Throne offers, even over its successors in the genre.

One thing I liked is that the black female character is more important and relevant than the white male character (usually you'd expect the male-white-character-is-the-hero-and-saves-helpless-girl cliché).
Even so, I don't recommend the game. I could maybe recommend only Act 1 and the feeling of wondering what Act 2 could have been rather than actually experiencing it. Okay so here's the deal. The first half of this game? Amazing. Second half? NOT worth the wait and a complete drag to pull yourself through.
The first half of this game throws us into two completely seperate worlds. The fantasy realm of Vella and the sci-fi world of Shay. Both are works of art visually and plot wise, with mechanical creatures covered in kid-friendly yarn and controls made out of baby toys to sacrifices to ancient monsters and snakes who hate the sound of tubas.
The characters are interesting enough, with plenty to say and the protragonists willing to chatter on about almost anything you click on. Plus the mid game reveal? It will have you on the edge of your seat.
Sounds good right? Then you get to the second half...
WHICH immediately strips the game of most of its most charming qualities, re-uses almost all the stages from the last half (there is only one new stage you really explore) and ties everything together with a rather shoddy villain collaberations which I really feel was a last minute descision.
Especially the fact that they plucked a character who had minor screen time in the first act and settled her into the villain conglamorate where they REALLY stuck out with how different their character design was from EVERYONE ELSE and reused the same exact lines they used during their limited screen time before rather than have the voice actor come back and at least change the inflection of the voice to be more dramatic.
Also the puzzles in the scond half are an absolute chore, there is a difference between a good puzzle, and a tedius one. Many of the puzzles in this game are defintely the latter in the second half, and also pull you out of the storyline as they require info from one protragonist be used with the other protragonist with no communication between them they just "magically know the answer" due to you (the players) intervention.
All in all, if its on sale I guess get it but know that only half of the game is really worth playing and the final resolution will feel cheap and unfullfilling despite the first halfs quaint charm. Definitely not worth full price.

-Difficulty is quite serious. For now, hard feels actually hard. Far harder than Dragonfall on very hard or Wasteland 2 on ranger in Arizona
-AI seems decent. Enemies are good in flanking. Usually when enemies are leaving cover they do it to make more damages to the player, althrough sometimes they stay in the open carelessly. Also they don't know how to effectively fight against players using top building floors.
-No hp sponges. 2-3 bullets and both enemies and players die
-First mission after tutorial has a good encounter design. (defending a house)
-There is a possibility to start the tutorial as a tutorial or as a normal mission. There is written a promise that it is short and to the point which is true. The best part: if player declines playing it as a tutorial then he must deal with a quite strong opponent on the start which is not attacking during tutorial:)
-As most enemies and player can't stand more than 2 hits, positioning is vital. Fighting is deadly and fast. Enemy can quickly turn tables with a good shot.
-Encounter design is fantastic. Had a rescue mission which looked as it was supposed to be done with minimal killing. Game respected my choice to kill everybody and after eliminating everyone on the map mission was successful without a need to complete an objective of opening the prison doors. Had an optional mission which starts the player surrounded and outgunned. It was thrilling and challenging. Maps are small, often reused, but different enemy placement makes encounters feel distinct.Big number of covers and hight places offers many approaches on how to tackle objectives.
-Ricochet ability is fun.
-Luck mechanic is really interesting. It works as a mana pool for abilities, but it protects from being hit. The more severe a hit chance is the more luck it takes to stop it. Luck is automatically used for that purposes. Being hit and losing hp replenish some of it.
-There is some environment manipulation. Could open wells doors to improve its cover. Environment can be destroyed like windows.
-Abilities are presented as cards which can be assigned to characters. Looks like 1 ability cannot be used by 2 different characters. You can take 5 of them on missions. Depending on which one you have chosen, you can get a passive buff on top of their standard uses. I suppose those bonuses are poker inspired.
-Rotating camera is horrible. Don't understand why they can't bind it to the mouse. It's worse than Wasteland 2 camera. Also when the enemy from different hight attack, camera should change the height, now it is always on the same level when it was left during player turn.
-Height seems to influence aim and range.
-Enemies can do overwatch. It looks player cannot use it. I had many times when I was begging for overwatch.
-The biggest surprise: CYOA. This part is good enough it would be acceptable if it was a game in itself. There are many C&C moments which actually include consequences! Game autosaves, so I didn't retry anything but results were enough specific it seems highly unlikely both options led to the same outcome. In scenario I played the main goal was collecting gold, which was quite complex with many tools, ways to do it and hidden mines. Got even an optional mission.
-Writing and story are really good. Love the character of the devil who is a mysterious, well dressed gentleman who appears and disappears on the whim tempting people.
-Game has a nice aesthetic and art direction.
-Looks like there are secondary objectives/consequences to missions (having to pay gold if hired merc dies)
-Always had luck with bugs but so far haven't encountered any. Enemies think a little too much before turn. Game runs smooth, but I have a good pc.
-There is an ironmode and a mode in which being low on hp gives debuffs, but there is more xp.(or skill points, whatever is used)
Had a good feeling when buying it, but (as for now) it surpassed expectations. I recommend this. We may have got a sleeper hit.

This was one of the best game purchases I've ever made. I grabbed it during a holiday sale, but even at full price it's only $8.00 with the expansion pack.
I believe this game could be accurately compared to the original Legend of Zelda (NES) in terms of format; the top-down room-by-room style will surely remind any fans of the LoZ of that game's dungeons. Functionally The Binding of Isaac is similar to Geometry Wars, in that the user's left hand controls character movement and the right hand controls attacking (with space and shift thrown in for item use).
BoI's visuals are smooth, unique, and totally disturbing. The soundtrack is amazing; a different track for every level that never seems to get old. In fact, the soundtrack is one of my favourite parts of the game.
The game itself is very easy to learn but pretty difficult to master. Just as you get comfortable with it and have beaten it a number of times, it hits you with a difficulty increase to keep things fresh.
There are dozens of enemies and bosses to be encountered, and hundreds of items to get your hands on (After 30 hours of play I've still found less than 50% of them). The levels are randomized every playthrough, so the game always feels exciting.
Admittedly, BoI is pretty disturbing, with mature subject matter and graphics and design elements that are not for the squeamish. The game's storyline draws parallels to the Biblical tale of the same name, and has religous references throughout. Despite this, it's (REALLY) not something you'd find loaded onto a computer in a Christian or Catholic school. Some people will certainly find this game's subject matter to be quite off-putting. If you feel this may apply to you, do a little personal research about the game before you considering dropping the money for it.
I'm sure it goes without saying that I recommend this game. I've got about 30 hours of playtime as I'm writing this, and it's still climbing. Actually, I think I'll play it right now.

I wish Steam had a more nuanced option than "Yes" or "No" because I would use it for this game.
Let me begin with some things that affected my view of the game that might not affect yours. I was a Kickstarter backer, and backed Double Fine Adventure (Broken Age) for an amount quite a bit higher than the suggested retail price. I did so because my three all-time favorite adventure games (Monkey Islands 2, Monkey Islands 1, Day of the Tentacle) were all by Tim Schafer.  Unfortunately, the result -- this game I am reviewing -- does not match their quality. And no, it is not just nostaligia, because Broken Age compares poorly against The Book of Unwritten Tales (1 & 2 both highly recomended) which is "modern." So part of the reason for my disappointment in Broken Age is that it did not meet the high expectations I had going in to it.
Now to the game itself, starting with the art. Zooming into the screenshots will show that the game has a distinct, almost impressionistic, art style to it -- see for example the visible brush stokes in some of the backgrounds. Obviously art is subjective, but I did not find the art to taste. Honestly, I would have prefered whatever effort  that went into the art style put instead into creating more locations, more puzzles, more plot, more ....   anything other than snooty art. Your milage may vary.
Part 1 was widely criticized for having overly easy puzzles. Part 2 has puzzles that are much more challenging. Average as a whole, I think the puzzles are good. Plenty of clues are built into character remarks, particularly when they are getting close ---- but for players lulled by the lack of puzzles in the first half, the sudden appearance of a difficult one might catch them by surprise to the extent they do not realize looking for clues is something they should be doing.
The story was by far the best part of Act 1. But overall it too becomes a mixed bag. I will make an analogy.... consider a story told around a campfire. An interesting one, full of intrigue and plot twists. And then the scout master annouces that it is time for bed, so the story-teller has to conclude the tale in a big rush of resolution. It's not quite like the coming to a crashing halt, not can I really say it left plot threats untied. I don't know how to explain it, so I will try another analogy: Imagine a telling of the famous  Cinderalla story that is full of all the details we remember up until the time she enters the castle to dance with the prince. At which point hte narrator says "But she lost track of time and had to flee the castle but it was OK because she left a shoe behind so the Prince could find her again and marry her". Bletch. I will say, though, that the afterword viginettes shown during the ending credits were a nice touch.
So, how to give a yes/no rating to a good but flawed game? If you have read this far, I would recommend you play some adventure games from Daedalic Software, or King Art Games. If your answer is "I already did, should I play Broken Age as well?" I suppose my answer is Yes.

An interesting spin-off for the Fallout franchise that puts you in control of your very own vault. It's your job to build it, grow it, and keep the inhabitants happy. Things like crafting, collecting supplies, and sending your vault dwellers out on quests really capture the feel of the Fallout universe.
The free-to-play nature of it is handled incredibly well. You really can do everything and not spend any money. The microtransactions are barely noticeable. You can still feel like you are making progress while waiting on the timers.
Various updates have removed the need for almost constant attention the game required before. Now you can take some time off and not have to worry about your vault being in horrible shape when you return. They finally fixed it where you can pick up play it whenever you feel like rather than having your time with it being dominated by the game's needy nature.
It's a completely free-to-play spin-off that feels completely part of the Fallout universe. Building and managing your very own vault can be a blast. The pick up and play at your own leisure nature of it makes it worth a look for any Fallout fan. It's also worth a look for those who enjoy these kinds of building sims and don't want to feel like it's constantly shaking you down for money.

Heh, hard to begin. I'm a big time Lynch, Twilight Zone, Poe, Kafka and Lovecraft fan, not so much X-Files, so getting Virginia was an obvious choice. Probably high expectations ruined it in my case. I was thinking a long time to recommend this game or not and I'm aware some will dislike the review because of the red thumb. I really like deeper art than todays popular movies and games, so please don't take my review as a bull describing a flower. Anyway:
The best part for me was the music, which is obviously Twin Peaks inspired. I'm cool with the art style too, which blends nicely with the music. There are some pretty cool scenes, which are both emotional and I didn't see similar camera angles and situations in any other game, while there are plenty cliche moments too. The reason for my downvote is that this is all the game has to offer. It could be so much more. I suppose it's really not that easy to be Lynch as it seems. I'm actually fine that there ain't a single spoken word in the game, but then you need to be a badass director to evoke distinctive characters. Virginia manages to do it to some degree, but IMHO, not enough by far.  Lynch, Jarmusch, Coppola, some french directors can do it, but this simply isn't on that level and pretends to be. I don't want to be rude, but if you read still, I hope you understand my standpoint, so in a negative way, I could describe Virginia as a walking sim on rails without speech. But honestly this is so one-sided, it's not fair to the game. It makes you think "outside of the box", but unfortunately so hard, that it backfired for me. Maybe I'm just too stupid, but it has extreme changes in pace, which more confuse than excite. I think the writer should dance with the reader, not beat him. Not teach him to walk, but dance. Anyway, believe me, my review is more clear than the game :)
PS: save for me was non-existent. Not just save, but game settings too. It's short so you can play it in one sitting and also you can choose chapters to start from, so no big deal, but it's surely not a plus for the dev. Despite them recommending "cinematic" 30fps, I played it with 60. Had to set to 60 fps on every start of the game.
BTW The review almost took longer than the game :D

Alan Wake is a third-person atmospheric horror game about a not-quite middle-aged writer who wakes up from a car crash while on vacation in a small, bucolic mountain town by a lake and realizes he's lost a much-loved and highly vulnerable family member to an encroaching supernatural darkness spearheaded by a creepy old lady who OH MY GOD WAIT A MINUTE THIS IS SILENT HILL.
But it's Silent Hill in the best ways. Rather than copy the Bosch-by-way-of-Jacob's Ladder visual design of the original or the stupid plot beats that got retconned into later games in that series, Alan Wake takes the basic concept—throw a bunch of American horror tropes into a blender, hit 'Frappé', add just enough self-awareness to keep it from being too pretentious—and spins it off into a different story that wears its influences somehow even more firmly on its sleeve. There's plenty of Stephen King here—the guy gets namedropped in the opening seconds—but also some Twin Peaks, Twilight Zone, and even one extremely memorable sequence which probably was the brainchild of a drunken evening playing Left 4 Dead 2.
It's got a bit of Silent Hill in the not-so-great ways too—the controls and camera are not quite as clunky as the old 3D "tank" controls, but they're close. Sometimes you'll find yourself getting caught up on bits of scenery that didn't actually look like they'd be in the way, and your stamina is just low enough that running from enemies is rarely a viable option. Which is a bummer, because after a certain point it's just not all that much fun to fight off yet another trio of possessed lumberjacks who can hurl a neverending supply of axes pulled from I don't want to know where. Fortunately, upgrades come regularly enough that combat doesn't become too huge a chore for too long and by that point you're either caught up in the story or given up entirely.
As for the story, it's doing the Silent Hill this-doesn't-make-sense-but-actually-it-does-because-dream-logic thing, though it does it damned well. Revelations come at a comfortable pace, just quick enough to keep things moving...even if where things are moving to pretty much always involves sticking you in the woods at night.
So yeah, I recommend it. Don't know if I'd still recommend it had I paid full price, but fortunately for you Alan Wake's got enough years on it to merit deep cuts during the Winter and Summer sales. Go forth and snag.

When I first saw this, I thought it’d be a great Tower Defence with a Human Anatomy twist. It essentially is but it’s quickly comes to nothing more than that and here’s why:
Pros:
♦ No bugs that I’ve personally found (Great as everything seemingly works)
♦ Graphics and artwork are fitting for the game (Nothing special but fit for what the game offers)
♦ Sound is fitting (Again nothing spectacular but fitting)
♦ Can speed the game up to 4x (This is great s it makes the game less long and drawn out. However, it doesn’t speed it up enough see cons for more)
♦ Decent time waster (If you have nothing to do, this is great to pass the time. However, it’s not a game that can be idled or played for 5mins and then put down)
♦ Standard Tower Defence (If all you are after is a standard tower defence with nothing special or spectacular beyond the Human Anatomy artwork and graphics, then this is great)
♦ Great level designs, towers and enemies etc based on Human Anatomy (This is adds a great visual touch to the game, but doesn’t add much else to the gameplay)
♦ Strategy element is great (This is great as you have to have a certain strategy to beat levels on harder difficulties. However, strategy seems based on difficulty and there only seems to be one or two strategies that work for some difficulties - see cons for more)
♦ Can get your monies worth (I say this as I’ve played 8hours for $5 which is decent. However, you might get bored of the grindy, upgrade simulator and repetitiveness and not get your monies worth)
♦ Easy Achievements and has Trading Cards (Achievements are grindy but easy to get if you can be bothered)
♦ Level difficulty challenges are a great addition (Could be too hard though)
Cons:
♦ Slow and repetitive (Levels seem slow and very repetitive. This is because enemies hardly change during a level and you just fight the same handful repeatedly, towers are the same throughout the whole level and there seems to be too many waves for the round. Hence, a few waves into a level you’re sitting there wishing the level would end already)
♦ Feels like an upgrade simulator (This is because once you try to play the game on higher difficulties or progress through a few waves on any difficulty, it feels like you’re forever clicking to upgrade towers which is very slow and tedious as there is no fast way to upgrade them except by clicking on each tower individually numerous times)
♦ Strategy is based on difficulty (This is terrible because it seems as though there is one or two tower placements that work on harder difficulties and you spend numerous attempts just trying to figure out what placement is the best rather than finding a tower combo that works well together)
♦ Not many enemy types or tower upgrades (New units and tower types are added as you progress. However, they seem to cap early on and you seem left with the same 4 towers which you can only fully upgrade a few times in certain levels. This is annoying as you’ve explored all tower types before you’ve even finished the game and explored 90% of enemies before you’ve even finished the game)
♦ No way to tell before you start a level what enemies you will be facing (Some towers only affect certain enemies and there is no way to tell which tower affects what enemy and which enemy you will be facing in a wave until you face it. This is terrible as it makes planning towers early on almost impossible)
♦ Can get all achievements but the hero level achievement before you 100% the game (This is weird, as before you’ve beaten all levels on hard difficulty you can have 100% the game)
♦ Encyclopedia takes you to an external website to view towers, tricks and tips etc (This should be all incorporated into a menu within the game. There should be no outside website links loaded)
♦ Impossible to buy all champions without 100%ing the game and grinding (This is annoying because there is no replay value once you’ve 100%ed the game, so trying out the champions you haven’t unlocked is silly).
♦ Pill ratings per level make no sense (I can beat the level on easy and get three pills for that level. I would have thought to get 3 pills I would have had to have completed it on hard difficulty)
♦ Looks 100% like a mobile game that is poorly ported to PC (I say this as there is no pc options, graphics settings or anything to make it look like a pc game beyond the steam integrated features such as Trading Cards and Achievements)
♦ Doesn’t add anything new to the tower defence genre (It’s basically place a few towers, upgrade when you can and hope you’ve placed the towers in the right spot. Then you just must wait until the huge number of waves are finished. Needed to add a spin on the genre to make it stand out)
♦ No reason to replay (This is because once you beat all the levels on hard, if you can bother there is no reason to ever play the game again)
♦ No reason to play a level on any difficulty other than easy (I say this as unless you want coins or upgrade points early on there is no incentive to play on a harder difficulty. Plus, the harder difficulties are the same level just more waves and less lives and less money for towers. Also, there is an occasional tower restriction which doesn’t add much more. There is nothing that stands out that makes playing on a harder difficulty unique)
Overall, as there is nothing unique added to the Tower Defence genre beyond the Human Anatomy aspect and the fact the game feels like a grindy, long and drawn out upgrade simulator that you can only win harder difficulties by using a set strategy by the devs and not by finding a tower combo that works… I can’t recommend this game even for $5. However, if you like a basic mobile style Tower Defence that will give you some hours of play… then feel free to pick this up. However, it wasn’t for me and I can’t really recommend it for most.

I'm recommending this game, but guardedly so.
First, everything you've heard warning you away from the game is right.
It will make many of you motion sick. Turning the game's frame rate up to 60fps helps, but doesn't completely cure it for me. In many scenes there's a decidedly non-cartesian mapping of the mouse action. I experimented with turning my head in real life, and I think they were mimicking that. Perhaps this is for the VR implementation. Also, there's a lot of motion blur, and a lot of inertia. All of these combine to make the action feel very detached from your movements, which really contributes to the motion sickness factor and can make it frustrating to point at objects on the screen. On the up side, there is usually only between one and three objects in a given scene you *can* point at, and the cursor is very forgiving for it's definition of "pointing at".
It's very, very linear. I enjoyed playing it as a game, but I'm not convinced the people who have suggested that it would have been better as an animated movie are wrong.
Especially early in the game, but to some degree throughout, the game keeps relevant information from you through irritating tricks, usually consisting of suddenly jump-cutting to another vignette right when you get to or are about to get to see something you want to see. This is somewhat cinematic, but a bit frustrating for something in which you're supposed to be in control.
The game is short. (About two and a half hours for me, but I've seen reports of 90 minutes or one hour.)
The narrative is told in a highly symbolic fashion very reminiscent of David Lynch and is thus not trivial to follow. The ending may not be satisfying to many.
All of that out of the way, it was certainly very interesting. The art style was very unique and the music was amazing. There were a lot of good moments, and I found myself getting really caught up in the game at the end. And while I usually sell all my trading cards, I found myself keeping these and even collecting others, hoping to get the badge. So that's saying something.
I would recommend this mostly to people who are curious about game developers who are doing interesting things with the medium, or to big fans of Lynch. I would not recommend it to people who get very frustrated with extreme linearity, or who find not knowing precisely what's happening at any given moment or what's expected of them frustrating.

Alan Wake is one of those strange games that aren't great or horrible that is a bit like a chore to play. It's definitely not a bad game. The mechanics are good, the graphics are solid, the voice acting is passable. But do I recommend it? Meh, you could miss out on it and be just fine but if you are looking for a solid survival horror then it'll do the job until the next Dead Space or Resident Evil.
Oddly the story is both the highlight and detriment of the game. It is interesting and well told but sometimes comes off as a bit pretentious. There are a few loose ends and nothing is really explained too well in the DLC epilogue chapters. However I did like how the story tied into combat with light and darkness becoming literal obstacles and commodities along your journey.
Unfortunately combat does become repetitous and downright frustrating in several segments. Granted that's why it is Survival Horror and not an Action title. There were plenty of occassions though where enemies were a bit overwhelming. The worst part was dealing with levitating inanimate objects becoming possessed. There is almost no way to avoid incoming attacks leaving you retrying those areas plenty of times screaming "this is bulls***!".
Insofar at shock value goes, which is an important part of survival horror, there really wasn't too much of that. It wasn't overly violent and there weren't really many cringe worthy scenes. It reminded me of the movie Shadow Falls. Kind of like a horror movie censoring itself down to reach the young teen audience without their parents c***blocking them.
All in all it was still a satisfying experience but for not being an upper echelon game I could have enjoyed an experience half as long in the Alan Wake universe. If you have an itch for Survival Horror I'd suggest playing some of the gems you may have missed over the years like Condemned, Dead Space, Evil WIthin, Silen Hill, or any of the Resident Evils. If you played them all then by all means play this as a diversion until the next triple A title gets released.

I generally don't like action games, and I particularly hate shooters and bullet hells. Yet, I love this game. I have close to 300 hours played on it and I don't see myself getting bored anytime soon. I still get pumped when I start the game and get to the character selection screen. I don't know if I love that moment because of the music, or if I love the music because I associate it with that moment.
It matters not.
The premise is deceptively simple. There is a series of very short randomly generated levels populated with various enemies. You go through them until you die, which at first is not going to take more than a few minutes. Or a few seconds.
That's one of the game's three strongest points: player-based progression. When you start playing, the game appears impossibly difficult. But quickly, you become better. You live longer. You get further. And it seems like you never stop improving. After a hundred hours, after three hundred, you're running in the middle of hordes of enemies, destroying everything and never getting hit, in a way that you would have thought completely impossible when you started. I've never experienced anything like it, but it's quite amazing.
The second of the game's three strongest point is intensity. You're never wasting time, you're always in the middle of thick, rich gameplay. If you die, the Retry button is just one click away and you're immediately back in the action. Too many games waste our times with travel or grinding; this is pure action gameplay.
The third strongest point is replayability. There are twelve main characters, ten of which you unlock as you progress, and two special characters, all of which have their own Passive and Active abilities as well as unique mutation when they reach max level. There are a couple dozen mutations, and you're presented with four random ones to choose from every level that you gain on a run. There are dozens of weapons, of which you can hold two at a time. There are twelve crowns which modify gameplay, usually by giving a huge drawback for a significant advantage. Combined together, all these things create immense variety.
There are alternate levels and challenges to unlock an alternate appearance for each of the twelve characters. There's even a Hard Mode, which I managed to unlock after about a hundred hours, but in a process that didn't actually involve any grinding; it's unlocked by doing something that an experienced player could do in less than half an hour.
I'm not entirely sure how such a small, simple game could have produced such amazing results, but I'm willing to call it a masterpiece.

Solid Game. There's alot done well and alot left to be desired from what I have seen so far. Strange is the rating I am giving this one because well "Strange" is the most appropriate word for this title on multiple fronts.
Short Version...
Atmosphere and Innovation to the core X-Com mechanics highlight this experience. The suprise good-times driver for me was the story.
The core combat mechanics are servicable and enjoyable enough to get a slight plus one all bythemselves with extra points for trying different things. As a pure tactcial game I am still forming an opinion but overall I would say its a pretty fun take on the "cover and advance" aspects of X-Com.
Longer Version....
I enjoyed this story. On paper its a relatively straightforward plot from a narative prospective. I was pleased to find have some ability to change the course of the story through your choices and actions. Like most modern video games character development is lacking but to me it did not seem all that relevant to immersion or to me giving the storyline a big plus one. As with many tales of gunslinging revenge in the old west the romanticism and sheer kick-assery of the setting has no problem occupying center stage in this production. The depressing and grim nature of this particular tale had me thinking back to the horrifical brutal version of the West painted in Cormac McCarthy's novel Blood Meridian which is really more of an epic poem of brutal♥♥♥♥♥♥murder mayhem with touch of the supernatural and devilery thrown in for good measure.
The gameplay shakes down to tactical combat battles connected via a choice your own adventure style world map. Yes it's a strange as it sounds when you read that last sentence. To further twist up the bizare factor you are going to find that while there is a pretty solid central storyline its delivery is done through multiple view points across several scenarios with check points rather than save points. Still with me? Okay finally there is some core differences between the way the world map challenges you between these different scenarios that add in elements of resource managment/simulation type mechanics. Yeah so kinda strange.
The execution has been suprisingly decent in my playtime thus far. At least on the easy and medium difficulty settings much of the before mentioned game mechanics seem a bit underwhelming in their overall impact on the core of the game (tactical map battles in case you forgot).  The different meta game elements seem to shift just as you feel that your getting close to mastering and growing bored with it.
I would say the graphics are pretty solid Infinity Engine level production status. Which is to say miles behind the Triple AAA titles of the here and now. I enjoyed the comic book esque cut scenes and narration but the overall look of the game could stil use some polish. I found no issues with slowdown or memory leaks.
Will finish and add more to this review later....

I might give this game another try after bugs are ironed out and the game is polished or dare I say finished but as of right now this seems like a product that was rushed, released before it was ready just to make it out the door before the bigger tittles coming this season.

Take this from someone who hated Xcom (repetitive with a boring aesthetic)....Hard West is a great way to spend $15.
+Beautiful level art.
+Satisfying gun fights
+Nice polish on the game from what I can tell
+Some neat mechanics (such as building traits via a Poker Deck and gaining additional bonuses from actual Poker Hands)
+Nice variety of equipment and guns allowing you to vary your characters immensely
+Simple and reliable camera controls
Some of the sounds are canned sounds from other games which don't fit the Old West setting, but I can cope.  The campaign map is a bit useless and even your side missions rarely do much beyond changing the cost of items in shops (which you don't always need to use...).  The campaign map is also a good bit confusing on the first scenario.   The entire campaign map could be done away with and it would still be a fine game.
You get to enjoy 7+ scenarios each with a different cast of characters and play style.   It's got a nice dark undertone to the entire game and is overall a fun way to spend 5-10 hours.  It is ripe for multiplayer - but I don't believe that's in the cards.  It's system would work quite well.
Overall, you could spend $15 in a number of worse ways.  If you like turn-based games and Old West gunfights, pick it up.  You won't be disappointed.

Double Fine poses the question of what could adventure games have become if they were as popular now as they were back in the nineties, and they delivered what I consider one of the most memorable adventure games of recent years; while it comes short in comparison with adventure games of yore like Tales of Monkey Island and my personal favorite Grim Fandango, it still manages to communicate that sense of discovery of an unknown and charming world with mysteries, twists, puzzles, and of course a great sense of humor that adventure games are known for.
While the story does fall short in act II when compared to what act I promised, it still is a good tale of coming of age, the puzzles are challenging but fair, and while I needed no hints or guides to complete them that doesn't mean that newcomers to the formula will have difficulties on the later half of the game, nevertheless that's also part of the charm of adventure games and the feeling of genius when you finally complete that puzzle that has been stumping you for the past half hour is what I miss the most on modern adventure games.
The art style and animation are gorgeous, at each new scene I had to stop playing for a second and soak in all of it, and the places where the game goes are truly delightful, I've played other hand painted adventure games but none other comes close to the beauty of these environments.
If you have finished the game I'd recommend watching the documentary series of its making on youtube,
it's an amazing insight both into game development and the challenges the team faced while making the game which any aspiring game developer or game enthusiast should watch.
Broken Age is an amazing game that both adventure game veterans and newcomers should experience.

This review is coming from the experiences of someone who just grabbed a game suddenly and played it, start to finish, in one day.
Hotline Miami is a game for fast-paced aldrenaline junkies, basically. It will have you throw your life on the line again and again in hectic gunfights. Each level is basically a big maze, and you conquer that maze by learning the ins and outs of that level. Where can you stand without being shot? How far do these guys patrol? Can you run past these two guys without being hit? And then once you thoroughly learn the level, you piece together a plan, slowly. You follow that plan, making tiny adjustments and dealing with the unpredictability of the enemies until you eventually manage to beat them. It will require meticulous planning and a lot of trial and error.
Or... you just get really lucky, bust into a room, shank a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, pick up his gun, blow away two other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, then toss that gun at his black friend who just walked in on this party. Then you jump on that guy, smash his ♥♥♥♥ing head in, dive through the door, shoot two other guys with an M4 that was lying there, barely dodge a shot from that guy who you didn't notice, then lay him the ♥♥♥♥ out with some panic shots.
And before you know it you've just completed the whole level in a sudden flash of adrenaline-fueled panic.
The game's story is interesting enough. It had enough Boss battles and a good bit of interesting dialogue. The theme of the game is pretty cool, too. You're seeing the environment around you degrade slowly as you play through, and you can see the effects of what you're doing, which is incidentally, murdering everyone.
On the downside, the game is pretty short. I got 5 hours out of it, in total. Other than that, no glitches or anything, and I picked it up for 2 euro. Definitely worth it.

It took me a lot of stopping and starting to finish the first act of Broken Age. An interesting world with some fun moments, but overall a bit of a mediocre adventure game; one of the stories had pacing problems, and the other had serious structural and character motivation problems. Finally I managed to push through and was pleasantly surprised by the excellent ending to Act 1.
It was on the strength of that ending (and a kind of masochistic pig-headedness) that I played through Act 2, which is a complete DISASTER. The puzzles are obtuse and nonsensical in the worst tradition of bad adventure games. The mechanism of switching back and forth between story lines to gain information is ridiculous in a story where the two characters cannot communicate (What, are they telepathic?). There's an entire elaborate multi-stage puzzle sequence where your progress can be completely reset by doing things in the wrong order.
This wouldn't be so bad if we had a goal, or some sort of logical progression of steps to be following, but for much of the second act I honestly couldn't have explained to you what the characters were trying to accomplish or why what I was doing would in any way help. This culminates in a series of actions that every piece of information you have indicates will lead to your horrible and gruesome death, without actually gaining anything meaningful.
A pointless, stupid, and frustrating experience. If you haven't bought this game already, for god's sake DON'T.

I was one of the original Kickstarter backers for this game and as such my first time playing it was when only the first half of the game was available and it was in Beta. At the time I enjoyed the part of the story that I was shown, the writing, art and setting are all wonderful. However, I found it to be short, straightforward and all of the puzzles were overly simplistic.
Recently the second half of the game was released and the game had it's official release as a complete product. I played through the whole thing again and found that the first half of the game works so much better when seen as part of the whole rather than as a separate episode. All the puzzles from the first half of the game are the building blocks for puzzles later in the game and they gradually increase in complexity. The storyline as well really builds on everything from the first half in the second half and the whole thing comes together in a very worthwhile and impressive package.
Because of that, this game should never have been split into two parts. I understand that Double Fine did this so that they could create a larger game overall and generate funding, but at the same time, the experience of playing it as two separate acts took away from the overall experience for me.
That said I do highly recommend this game now that it is available as a complete product. Be warned the puzzles are very easy and overly simplistic in the beginning of the game, and the whole thing can likely be completed in 8 hours or less unless you run into any major snags. All the puzzles had fairly easy to understand solutions with only 2 or 3 instances where I really felt that the solution was too obtuse. In addition there was only one time that I had to look up the solution online (SPOILER the part where Shay has to simply let the snake attempt to strangle him until it falls off, how was I supposed to know I just had to stand there the whole time? SPOILER) and there was one instance where the solution is only shown by switching between the two characters which I found annoying.
I recommend this for fans of adventure games, and also those who can just appreciate the writing and art style that Double Fine brings to the table. If you don't like adventure games you might still find this accessible due to the simplicity of the puzzles and the engaging story. Otherwise, stay away.

Virginia will challenge you.  If you are not thinking while you play this game, you will end up lost and confused.  Even though I was paying as much attention as I could to every small detail, parts of this game still bemused me.
You play as an FBI agent in the 90's investigated the case of a missing boy in the suburbs of Virginia.  Unlike in, say, LA Noir, (one of my favorite games), you won't spend much time "looking for clues".  Nearly every scene in the game has some clear center of focus which will compel you to go up to it and click it.  For the most part, you are simply experiencing the story, with little control over what happens or how.  At times, the game will even take control directly away from you, either to turn your attention to something or even as drastic as an abrupt scene change as you walk.
The result of all this is a game that is incredibly cinematic.  I found myself at times very impressed by the composition of certain scenes.  The developers clearly put a lot of thought into the presentation of this game and it shows.
Oh, and there's no dialog.  Because of this, the game can only channel the story to the player in two ways: through the physical behavior of characters, the expressions on their faces (which are surprisingly emotive despite being composed of only several lines, like a cartoon), their actions and reactions; and also the music, which should leave you blown away.  The use of music in this game might be its greatest success.  As you begin walking towards the missing child's bedroom to see what you might find, the music swells, and it is enormous, terrifying, thrilling, and well performed by the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra.  Take away the music and this game would be incredibly boring.  But with the tremolo of the strings building anticipation, even a slow walk down a long hallway becomes filled with tension and dread.
Like its contemporaries Gone Home and Firewatch, Virginia frames the pervasive mystery with a potentially supernatural element.  I won't say anything else, for fear of spoilers, but this seems to be a new trope among first-person mystery exploration indie games.  I don't know if I like it or not; I'd rather the mystery be the mystery, without having to question whether aliens scooped someone up every time I feel like I'm about to crack the case.
A complaint I had that I imagine most other people have too is that occasionally you are presented with a document full of important information, but not given ample time to read it before control is pulled away from you to a new scene.  There is no inventory, no way to look at all the clues you've found so far.  If you want to ponder the mystery, you're best doing it by hitting pause and sitting at the pause menu, to ensure the game doesn't decide to fling you to the other side of town and twelve hours later.
One other complaint is that the chapters in the chapter select do not seem to "unlock" as you play; rather, they are all fully visible and possibly even playable all the time.  Because of this, going to chapter select could potentially give you spoilers, since the developers don't "hide" future chapters, and those chapters are shown as icons that give away where the story will take you at that point.  I had to squint at the chapter select screen to not accidentally see the locations of future chapters.
Will you enjoy Virginia?  If you are me, and you love games like Gone Home, Firewatch, etc, and you love a good mystery, I think yes, you will enjoy it.  Even more so, I think must play it, because at $10 this game is a steal for the rare experience it provides.  Virginia will pull you into a complicated world where every character has an ultior motive and no mystery is a simple as it seems, and it leaves those mysteries up to you to figure out on your own.  Be warned, though: the game will progress whether you figure these things out or not, so perhaps take some time to slow down and ponder what you've learned.
Having played the game through once there is still much I didn't catch.  I'll need to go back to see what else I can uncover.  Perhaps some of it I will never figure out, but I think that's okay.
I heavily recommend this game.  This is interactive storytelling at its finest, and if that's something you care about, please don't pass this up.
You will not be dissapointed.

This is my first review ever here on steam, and never has a game compelled me so much to review it as WL2, so here goes.
Short Review:  This is an unfinished game.  If we, as players, accept this very low bar of completion as OK, then we will reap the "rewards".
In-Depth Review: I think it's important to understand where this game is coming from before criticizing it.  Tons of Fallout fans were less-than-impressed when Fallout 3 came out and, despite being promised something other than a re-skinned Oblivion (now Skyrim) got just that.
As such, the hype was huge for a game from the original makers crowdfunded a true sequel with tried-and-tested Firaxis on board.  The target of 1 million was met and grew to 3 million dollars. The game won a GOTY award and has been well-received.
That was all I needed, so jumped in and was ready for just such an experience.
I did some reading and carefully crafted characters for the long journey ahead, nevermind thst there's very little in a tutorial to prep you.  I'm seasoned gamer, so go!
So I end up roaming the wastes and get random encounters.  Some I try, some I try to flee.  You get "caught", and then you're loaded into an instance.  The mobs are now romaing about in the instance, not chasing you, and you get to do these a lot unless you have one skill.  Same scenarios and maps.  Hmmm...is this GOTY material?
Then you get into your first quest to go to X place and do Y things.  Along the way, my noob party visited a much higher level area than they were fit for.  Hmmm...no warning?
Luckily, we left and didn'tengage our certain death.  We went on to the Ag Center.  I was woefully unprepared, but managed to survive most of it...until I found myself at an impass:  I had tried to crack a safe that has a critical keycard to enter one of the next areas, but I critically failed which essentially bricked the safe, which was the only place where I could get the keycard.
I went on having learned the critical rule of this game: you save about every 2 seconds and keep vast repositories of save lists.  Unfortunately, I learned this after i borked the safe with the keycard.  Not one to give up, I went on to other areas and did a boss fight where only 2 of my people had ammo left.  After about 20 tries, we got the guy without running out of meds for people he wasted.
Now, that's what happened in the game.  The combo of ridiculous bosses, minimal resources, and the CRUSHING fact that I might not get the keycard I needed nearly caused me to uninstall.
My reaction to this is now what you might expect, but it's what gets repeated ad nauseum on forums related to this game.  I took this as old school. You just have to deal with your decisions.  YEAH, and this makes everything more realistic, right?  So I left and had my NPC surgeon Rose desert us and picked up Angela Deth, who is great and all but nobody told me i'd need her, and we progressed...
But at the same time, the clunky camera and its limited zoom functions created this "very atmospheric" sense that I was lost.  I was...and just wanting one more level of zoomout as compared to the satellite view in my inventory.
And then you go into a scenario and place your characters just like you want them as you've done a thousand times by this point: in the right position but facing walls.
And this was the point of no return.  I just realized that, for all the "difficulty" you face,  the execution is just sucky.  I knew that, if enough people complained, patches would fix things,but, I thought to myself for the first time ever, "THIS is GOTY?"
I stopped blaming myself and started thinking "these are the problems that justify the existence of play-testers."  Did anyone playtest this game before release?  Not based on my experience, and forums suggest I'm not the only one who's had the same problems I've encountered.
AND AND, if you want to see this done right, X-COM does it to near perfection.
Bottom line: the game required a million dollar budget.  It got 3 million.  In turn, we got something that is still in beta. finished.
I don't blame players who are enjying this, but I'll never trust entities again which have chosen it as GOTY when it's not

Virginia is an interactive story with an arresting way of telling itself to you, pushing you along at a fair pace. Without dialogue, one expects to find great things in the animation of the characters, and how they might act, but often I felt at arms length from everyone, never quite understanding whether the protagonist (Anne Tarver) sympathized with anyone, or even whether your partner ever meant something to her.
The cinematic quality of this game is fantastic, the music, the mood lighting, the simple characters and the colours that lend the right sort of atmosphere. But it was when I quickly realized scenes were getting some heavy re-use, which is understandable for the sake of dream sequences - they became somewhat of a nuisance to go through. I honestly wanted more "world" to open up, and for the main plot to take you somewhere really interesting - but it does not, and that is probably the most disappointing part.
Many reviewers' have drawn connections to Twin Peaks (a series I adore), but the brief homages in this game are as close as you will get to a David Lynch style work. Too many, - bland - personalities abound in this game, and the repeat visitings of these people leaves much to be desired.
I will revisit Virginia soon just to see what things I missed, but I think upon my first play through I should have at least had the overwhelming sense of wanting to go back. For the reasons I have mentioned, it's hard to justify it. I recommend it for at least being a decent price and for being something a little different.

How could a game with this much effort and thought and love put into it still kind of suck? I've been eagerly watching the development of this game for quite a while now. Upon finally playing it, I am sad to report that it is far inferior to any of the recent (or classic) Fallout games. Just like Wasteland 1. They can't quite seem to hit on a winning formula.
You command a squad of desert rangers as they try to stop Very Bad Things from happening, mostly by killing all kinds of things in turn-based combat. Your rangers have absolutely no personality, and are combat units with a portrait. You can recruit other wastelanders to you cause, and they do have personalities, but for some reason the developers made the recruitable characters absolutely awful in terms of statistics. Managing your team of fighters is a chore instead of a joy. The interface is awkward and clunky, with strangely reversed controls. Typically, left click is "go there" and right click is "use/take/kill that", but this is reversed in Wasteland 2 with no option to change it.
It all comes down to a statistical analysis of the utility of various statistics and skills, with a larger dose of probability-based gameplay. It reminds me of business school, and is just about as fun. I literally had to make an Excel spreadsheet to keep track of who was going to learn which skills. The developers of Wasteland may have been groundbreaking and inspired the Fallout series... but they've pretty clearly shown why Fallout was a cult classic and Wasteland was quickly forgotten.

A richly detailed environment, in lightness and darkness, bring this game very much to life. Atmospheric surroundings and sound effects, embellished by excellent cut-scenes that help the narrative as the story unfolds.
The plot is fantastic yet grounded at the same time, riddled with clever what-ifs and many-layered implications of what it means to write creatively and what it is to truly push the boundaries between imagination and reality in this process.
The gameplay itself is pretty damn epic as well. Action remains fast-paced and challenging without being too frustrating, supplies such as ammo or batteries are plentiful enough to stop you ever running the risk of being completely defenceless while remaining sparse enough to keep you considering what to preserve and when, and there is a varying degree of weaponry and enemy strength and speed to keep it interesting.
One thing I really like about this game is that the game never gives you too much ammo, so you never really have that safe feeling when you are trudging through the woods. In other games you usually stack up on a lot of guns and ammo and end up being a one man army - not so in Alan Wake. Here, your character really is a frail writer with a flashlight and a tweed jacket, not a super soldier - your most powerful weapon is also the light. Without light, even the most potent gun cannot so much as even scratch the enemy.
