The Wizard's Lair is a roguelike game with simple graphics and gameplay. I've only gotten about halfway through the dungeon so far, but I have to say this is a little better than I expected.
Some other roguelikes on Steam I played were a little underwhelming. Randomness was so wide in its range of benefits it seemed like all chance instead strategy. Enemies were so basic that it was really repetitive, and some games even don't have any enemy movement, so they just sit there and wait for you to bump into them. Whether you attack or not seems more puzzle-like than roguelike, and not attacking is kind of boring because you can't do anything else. There are a number of ways to make roguelikes uninteresting.
But the Wizard's Lair is different. It doesn't have a huge number of enemies, but the ones it does have are at least up and moving around. After a while the levels are different. So far I've run into a labyrinth and a level that is all about teleporting around, and I imagine there has to be a few more. Not super thrilling (yet anyway), but something differnt to break up the monotony.
One thing I don't like is in its attempt to be more user friendly than a typical roguelike game with 30 or more keyboard commands it maybe went too far the other way. For example, a common situation is that your inventory is full and you want to eat a mushroom or ration that you ran across. There doesn't seem to be an eat option right away. So instead you move one step away, hit "?" for the special screen, hit space for the inventory, select something you want to temporarily drop, choose drop, move back to the food, hit space to pick it up, hit "?" and then inventory, select the food and hit eat, and then move back to the item you dropped and pick it back up. I really hope there's an easier way I'm just not getting, because that's kind of silly.
The graphics are kind of basic. They are retro-pixelly in a kind of a bland way instead of an artsy way. You know what I mean. But they work for what they are representing, anyway.
All in all this is a shortish basic roguelike that might be a fun diversion for a bit or to learn how the style of games work. It's not to the level of some other roguelikes and roguelike-inspired games on Steam, but then it's cheaper, and certainly a lot better than other games that are the same price or even slightly more expensive. Steam doesn't have a rating system with number of stars from really bad to meh to OK to good to great. It's either thumbs up or thumbs down. Thumbs up then, because it's more on that side than the other one.

Final update is out and I'm glad for the extra stability from it.
Nuclear Throne is immediate and challenging, with only a few mechanics which that have been fine-tuned to near-perfection. Every moment is high-stakes, as it takes 3 shots from the most standard enemy to put you down, and there's no invincibilty frames. There's only one instance of movement-impairment that's minor and avoidable, and the movement feels clean and responsive, making dodging feel good. Guns are mostly hit-or-miss, are strong as hell with really booming, chunky sound design, and make the moments when you mow down enemies really exciting. The mutations are varied and evenly-strong enough that you'll very rarely get a run that shafts you on your upgrades, and picking up a mutation that fits your current situation gives you an exciting power spike. It has an exceptionally enjoyable learning curve, and after the 20-30-however-many hours you take to beat it once, you're either gonna take a break right after because you need to breathe (nominate it for 'Mom's Spaghetti'), or you're gonna say,
"ok.
let's beat it again."
The occasional unfairness of runs is actually a  driving force behind the game; in my personal experience, when I get swarmed by heavy cops, I say, "Damn it, how was I supposed to deal with that? I don't have a long arms-melee!"
Then I jump right back in, because I am NOT taking that♥♥♥♥♥♥sitting down.
It's not for everyone; some will like Isaac better, some will like Gungeon better, but if you can keep up with Throne's fast pace and the ever-present challenge in every single stage, you'll love every second and be a King or Queen of the wasteland.
Tl;dr: It's immediately engaging and challenging, guns are fun to shoot, bullets are fun to dodge, mutations are fun to choose, and it's right on the fine line between challenging as hell and unfair.

"stop - think -proceed" Spintires is aiming on one of the archetypes of a "car" game. You control 5 different types of trucks in a remote area of Russia. While your objective is to transport log piles from point A to B, many different aspects are wrapped around this. Sounds easy?  at the moment there are 5 characteristic maps. Similarly to Warcraft the maps are cloaked in the beginning. You have to scout the place to discover the most suitable route for your transport.  The shortest track is not always the best. Think wisely about your fuel reservoir. Avoid deep mud and puddles. Some puddles are deeper than they seem. On some maps you start off with a vehicle that is not even suitable for your job - which means, you have to find those first. many trucks are scattered around deep in the woods. You need a suitable truck to get your vehicle out of the mud? You better invest 2 hours only to reach the heavy rescue truck.
The game has a Multiplayer (Coop). Now here, it really comes to life! I have spent 2 hours with some other dude. He asked me to help him out. after 15 minutes I have finally reached the location. Then it took another 4 minutes to take a suitable position to help him effectively. It is possible to tie your winch to the other players truck. He was stuck in a quite difficult position which demanded me to have some deep intuition to help him out effectively. For me this was the greatest moment seeing him slowly tilting back into an operational position. The multiplayer has sooo much potential! Sadly, once a lobby has been launched, it no longer seems to be possible to join a running game: which means: as soon as your teammates have left the game, you will be alone as the host. I really would like to see a dedicated server solution here, which allows hopping on and off.
There is a default and a hardcore mode in this game.  While you are allowed to reset your truck to the garage at any time, this wont be possible to do in hardcore mode. Furthermore it seems like if the differential lock is missing in the hardcore mode. I was playing the hardcore mode from the first minute and it is really bloody hard. I think that i traveled half the distance in the woods just by this damn winch!  Some guy said, Spintires is like the Dark Souls title in the vehicle game genre. No doubt, he is right at this point!

This game takes me back to my early days of gaming and first discovering Rogue-Likes (though I didn't know that name yet) by playing Fatal Labyrinth on the Sega Genesis (with annoying background music, so it could be worse!).  I fell in love with the formula of random dungeons with random items, random layouts, etc.  One playthrough you might get lucky on good items.  Or you might die after only a few floors.
There have been a lot of Rogue-likes over the years, and some people are picky about what aspects they like and don't like.     So let's take a look and see if this game fits your Rogue-like bill.
1.  Random floor layouts  (square rooms with corridors and sometimes dead ends)
2.  Fog of War (Everything is black except a small area around you.  The floor lights up as you walk and stays lit.)
3.  Need to find Food (as you take your steps through the dungeon floors your food level drops and you get hungry.  Find food items and eat them to regain your food level)
4.   HP replenishes automatically by walking (Yay!  But don't waste too much time getting your health back because you might get hungry!)
5.  Turn-Based (Nothing happens until you take a step, or you can skip a step if you need a monster to approach so you get first hit instead of it.  Monsters won't move until you move.  I don't know if using an item takes a move or not.)
6.  You can save your game and return later!  Very cool.
7.  Nice graphics for 2D pixel style game.
8.  Sounds effects, but no background music (so far)
9.  Permadeath?  I'm assuming, but have not died yet.
10.  Keyboard or Gamepad (I used keyboard, so don't know how good the gamepad controls are)
11.  ???  Something I missed or can't remember?  Let me know!
My verdict (so far):  I love the old-school look.  All the points above hit my buttons, so I'm very happy.  Looking forward to more playing and will update if I learn something interesting.
*** Update ***
There are traps on the ground.  Sometimes you can see the outline of them.  There is a spell scroll that will reveal them.  Ones I have encountered:  Damage traps (fire, etc.), Teleport Trap (moves you to random location on same floor, Healing Trap (it heals you!), and I think there was one that dropped me down a few floors.
Lots of different enemy types:  Undead (skeleton, lich); Fire (fire snake, cloaked fire guy); Ice (Blue Cloaked Guy--sorry I can't remember the name); Slimes; Minotaur; Rival Adventurers (loot their gear!); Frog; Thing with Eyeballs; and Dragons!  That's all I can remember of the top of my head.  I should really write this stuff down!
It seemed easy at first but I didn't make it to the bottom.  I ran out of food and died!  :-(   Save your food, people!
Oh, and limited Inventory.  You can you have 6 items, in addition to your weapon and armor.  That's it, just 6!  Decide wisely what to carry and what to leave.
Monster Room!   Just before I died I encountered a different sort of floor.  Just a small room filled with monsters, and tons of great loot in a room beyond.

I really enjoy roguelikes, so when I saw The Wizard's Lair I was hoping that the basic presentation meant that the developer(s) spent that time on gameplay, bringing new and fun elements to the genre. Unfortunately, the basic presentation honestly conveys what you get, shallow even by 1980's standards. While The Wizard's Lair has monsters, potions, armor, weapons, scrolls, and food there are no classes, abilities, or skills. Leveling up just increases your hitpoints as far as I can tell. You can fight in corridors to limit how many monsters can attack you at once, but beyond that there are no tactics. This is a game anyone could have written in a few weekends with an RPG generator.
For a basic roguelike get Dungeons of Dredmor instead - it is around the same price, relatively easy to get into, but still has depth and fun gameplay. Or for something deeper but also inexpensive, Tales of Maj'Eyal has a mixture of random and predetermined maps, quests, good graphics for a roguelike, lots of classes and skills, and a helpful online community.

Broken Age is an amazing point and click experience, reminescent of Steven Spielburg's The Dig in a light-hearted setting. The art stlye and some of its antics remind me of Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker,
The story touches on various enlightened understandings about life, and its quite meta; of itself and reality in general. There's quite a few gags and clever lines, and one in particular (a Terminator reference of all things) made me tear up and laugh at the same time.
It doesn't really go very far with the story, it doesn't aim to be the most riveting and jaw dropping storytelling experience ever. Still, its a perfect example of when the games medium does story telling well. Broken Age never goes overboard, but there's a lot to ponder about the philosophical meaning of different elements throughout. Its kind of light or deep as you want it to go, I think.
Its a little hard to review a game that's just a storyline with some secondary interactive elements without spoiling anything. I'll just say, the sound and voice acting are flawless throughout. The story is captivating as anything you'll find  in modern media. It has a good length. Its difficult to figure out what to do at a few parts, but its not ever bad enough to actually warrant using a game guide. The character swapping mechanic sees some token use to aid advancement, but I think over-use of that feature might make gameplay too novel.
If you like games like Monkey Island, The Dig, or just a good, mild storyline, I'd definitely recommend Broken Age.

After having played this game through twice, I think I can safely say that it, for the most part, does justice to classic adventure games. Though the puzzles (with some exceptions, but I will get to those in a second) are really very easy, the game itself is extremely enjoyable; this is mostly due to the fully realized characters, the fantastic setting (which does start to dry out with the second part), and great humor and conversation.
That said, the second part saw a pretty large detour from the first. It starts off on a relatively weak note, with astonishingly stupid plot twists (such as that of Shay's family) and long lists of tasks that the player has to do. Though a dedicated player will get past this section without pause, it provides very little motivation to keep going. In Vella's case, for instance, your first task (with the zero-gravity re-enabled) involves more timing than it does any intelligence. After this sort of "introduction" to Part 2, you are immediately hit with the aforementioned long lists of tasks. At this point, your primary goal in Part 2 is to wander the countryside and click on everything. You are stopped every now and again for a bout of puzzle-solving, but it feels very much like the puzzles are mixed throughout a game of wandering aimlessly. Even the puzzles of Part 2 are of varying quality. There are some that take legitimate thinking and reward you with a great deal of satisfaction, but there are others that involve screwing around with wires on the back of a robot (I am aware that the solution is hidden in the setting, but it was really very obscure). More than that, however, a number of the puzzles require you to get solutions from the other protagonist's story. This is irritating, but only because there is never any indication that this is the case. This can lead to some serious jumps in logic, as seen in many early adventure games.
The setting, on the other hand, is absolutely fantastic. I won't say much about the setting, because figuring out more about it is probably the thing Broken Age does best.

I'd like to give this a neutral review but since that's not an option, i'll give a slight recommendation.
first, i'd like to address the elephant in the room. this game was originally developed for tablet, which, as you should know, means that if you expect a real game, you're gonna be disappointed. if you want a real game that you can play for at least two to five hours without taking a break or getting bored, you may wanna take a look at Sheltered or something similar. generally, it's a good idea to stay away from f2p or tablet games if you want a real game. also, obviously, the controls are mediocre at best and annoying at worst, it really shows that it wasn't originally designed for pc.
ok, now that that's out of the way, let's get to the actual review part. the core gameplay mechanics seem pretty generic, as it can be expected from a f2p game. that's not really a bad thing though since it's basically a waiting game which means it is expected to deal with pretty basic mechanics. click on things to collect resources and items, click on people to let them level up, and so on. if you want to loose, you have to try very hard (if it's even possible to let everyone in your vault die, unless you play on survival), if you want to "win" you have to spend money or play for a very long time (what i mean by "winning" is having built everything that you want to build). nothing new.
the game will continue to run if you are logged out, and obviously while you're not online, you won't be able to collect anything. that is also not really bad though because after a short while, the resource consumption will be halted. so you will have a little less resources when you log back in but they won't be completely depleted.
generally, if you don't want to spend money on it, it seems to be a good idea to just log in every couple of hours, collect everything, send some people on quests, start a new weapon/armor production, maybe use speed-mode a couple of times to get a few caps and fill your resource-storage faster and once everything seems good, you can log out again. just don't forget to check your statistics-screen every once in a while, to make sure that your production per minute is still higher than your consumption per minute.
also, there are a couple bugs, crashes and other issues. if you decide to play this game, maybe you have already played some early access titles where the developers simply stopped to care and never fixed any bugs or anything? this game will remind you of that. there is absolutely no communication from the developer, certain bugs have been known for years but no one cared enough to fix them. after a simple look at the discussions you will also probably find that you shouldn't get too attatched to your vault and definitely shouldn't spend any money on it. almost every day i looked, there has been at least one thread on front page complaining about the game being unplayable due to crashes/freezes/etc or the save file being corrupted/disappeared. so it definitely is a bit of a gamble.
if everything works and you are lucky enough to not run into any game breaking bugs it can be fun but that is definitely not guaranteed. so if you like waiting games you can definitely give it a try but i would strongly suggest to not support the developer by buying anything in this game until they start to care a little bit more and fix bugs and other problems.

When Shadow of War was originally announced, I did a little fist pump, and smiled internally. What could be better than expanding the nemesis system in a setting which allows for more nuanced and varied organic narrative formation? As soon as pre-order option was available, I humbly offered over the pricey sum of a special edition, and settled to wait for release.
Apart from the special edition pricing issues, and these are not miniscule issues by any means, the game is exactly as one could hope for: open-ended, well-crafted expansion of the LotR lore with satisfying combo based battle mechanics.
The narratives and character portayals are more subtle than a gory orc-killing/raising/killing fest deserves, and widely read LotR fans can spot quite a few references to less known parts of the franchise. As one article summed it, Shadow of War is gory LotR fanfiction, and oh boy is it sweet fanfiction. The orcs have been expanded further, both as characters and their mechanics, and it becomes all too easy to form an emotional bond with your favourite captain only to have him stab you in the back at worse possible moment. Which is bloody marvelous.
Furthermore, with more complex orc hierarchy, now one has to know captains, their weaknesses, strengths, family relations (no I do not kid with this), and optimize decisionmaking. This makes this aspect of the game much more complex and interesting than the equivalent in Shadow of Mordor was.
The fighting mechanics have been expanded from Shadow of Mordor, with a focus on allowing different builds for Talion in order to enable as customisable gameplay experience as possible. However, it is clear that the different builds one can create using the revamped character menu have been geared towards online conquests.
Which brings me to the most mixed blessing of Shadow of War. The online elements. I would lie if I said I do not enjoy the grind and training of my army, and then charge fellow players strongholds, sometimes to glorious victory, and sometimes to embarrassing defeat. However, it is obvious that the online conquest mechanics are what drives microtransactions, and as enjoyable as conquests personally for me are, one has to question their necessity in this type of a game. Aware as I am of the past decade's trend of gluing online or multiplayer mode to every game in order to discourage reselling, it is not a development direction I support wholeheartedly.
What saves Shadow of War is the fact that the online elements are balanced enough for now. They are not mandatory, and as a person who has not spent one cent on loot boxes, the conquests feel doable enough. More work than with paying, but not impossible or insane. However quite understandably the grind aspect will not be fun for everyone, and the online conquests are not easily doable with non-optimized army.
Another factor that has undoubtedly alienated a few players are the day one DLCs, or special editions as they are called these days. As a gamer I am old enough to remember when this was not the industry standard, and the practice is a debatable one with modern triple A games, which tend to be pricy from get go. I feel that the extra elements covered by the special editions justify the extra price, but only just about. The developers and publishers have to walk a fine line in the future, as they have pushed the acceptable price/content ratio to the limit. Anyone more opposed to this practice, for you I suggest waiting until a seasonal sale cuts the price a bit.
All in all I recommend this game for everyone who enjoyed Shadow of Mordor. Shadow of War is a very good game, with story elements that appeal to certainpart of the LotR crowd, and organic expanded orc narrative generation system that should appeal to everyone else. Monolith has exceeded itself, again, with expanding the belowed universe of Tolkien, managing to create something new with it. While keeping the gameplay experience highly addictive and satisfying. This is no small feat.
However, the microtransactions together with high price tag and "special edition" content show that developers are giving in to the siren song og the worst practices of triple a games industry. As of now, I am a satisfied gamer; these elements are inoffensive in the game, but they are undoubtedly present.

Broken Age is an endearing game. It is the type of game you sit back and play after finishing a few high-stress matches of League or CSGO. It soothes you and takes you on a journey. I'm just going to get into the pros and cons though.
1) Light-hearted humor throughout.
2) Animation and art style are unique and easy to look at.
3) First half of the game's puzzles were easy but trained you for the difficulty of the second half's puzzles.
4) The main protagonists are both relatable and the characters in general are all fantastically depicted.
5) The two climactic points of the game are exciting and get you invested in the outcomes.
6) The voice acting in this game is absolutely phenomenal.
1) Some janky camera movements when walking across some screens.
2) The wiring puzzles in the second half of the game can be difficult since the first half didn't require you to switch                                               between characters to progress.
3) The story, overall was a little lacking in terms of fleshing out the universe and WHY things were the way they were.
4) It can be tedious moving throughout the sky colony and back to Shellmound village several times.
5) The last puzzle is agitating because if you mess up, the whole thing is reset and you must do it all over again. It felt more like trial and error than actually solving a puzzle with a solution and an answer.
Overall I'd give the game a 3.5/5 and would recommend it.

Civilization has been one of the main cornerstones of the 4X genre since its first entry in the 90s. I grew up playing tons of Civilization II until my brother got a copy of Civilization III for Christmas, and I've loved it ever since.
PROS:
+Grand strategy based on ruling an empire and balancing multiple facets including your militaristic, economic, industrial, scientific, and diplomatic agendas.
+Impressive number of Civilizations to play as (over 30), each with its own advantages and disadvantages.
+Despite the number of potential Civilizations, each plays with its own distinctive style.
+More peaceful options to win than spaceship-building.
+Numerous scenarios (or Conquests) including WWII in the Pacific, Sengoku-era Japan, Pre- and Post-Columbus America, and the Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire.
+Abnormally good soundtrack.
+Difficult to master, like many good strategy games.
+Introduces new game mechanics like war weariness, forced labor, and corruption.
+Included is a Scenario-maker, which is very comprehensive and allows for the addition of entirely-new civilizations, technologies, and maps.
+There's many of the popular fan-made maps and scenarios already installed with the game.
+Mods! (on CivFanatics)
CONS:
-Loses some of the characteristics form Civilization II (such as wonder movies, animated high councils, and "Our words are backed with NUCLEAR WEAPONS!"
-Doesn't run as well on modern machines. I've had game crashes on the Victory Screen, but I've heard of people not even being able to start the game.
-Tutorial hints hidden in the Preferences menu, so unless you've played Civilization II or IV, this one's pretty hard to learn. Other Civilizations (including this game's direct predacessor) automatically turned on the hints if played on the lowest difficulty, or had menus for learning the game.
Personally, it's my favorite of the grid-based Civilizations, and I always come back for more.

This is a tough one. As someone who loves Thirty Flights of Loving, Mulholland Drive and Gone Home it should have been very much for me, but it didn't quite sit right. I think the main reason is it felt like it had an aesthetic and inspiration, but no actual story to tell, and it feels obtuse for the sake of it. The jump cuts and blending of dreams and reality are great and an interesting way of doing the narrative, but it didn't give me enough to latch on to to want to unravel what it all meant or convince me there actually was a meaning at all. If you're drawn to it for the Lynch comparisons then chances are you'll be disappointed because the connections are superficial at best. It's also torn between wanting to be a fully scripted experience and making you a part of it. It so often wrestles the camera from you that you often don't realise you should be moving, and when you are given control you kind of wish you didn't have to bother because movement is a little tank like, and interactions are arbitrary mouse clicks. The environments tempt you to explore and feel like they will provide you with narrative hints, but rarely reward you for doing so. I also couldn't decide if the complete lack of dialogue was a stylistic choice, or a budget constraint, and whilst it was an interesting experiment, the lack of either strong characters or strong story left me a little cold. That said, I love that it's trying to do something fairly unique. I love that there are so many non-white characters in the game, and so many central female characters too. Continual shots of putting on lipstick and painted toe-nails feel like a bold statement of intent to redress some balance in video-game protagonist options. I also loved the Prague Philharmonic's phenomenal score that was both powerful and haunting and provided most of the tone and emotion for the game. So, we're back to the tough question of whether I recommend it or not. On one hand, I can think of at least five other "walking simulators" I'd rather recommend which have a greater impact and play better, but I am glad this exists, I'm glad it's trying some unique things, and I think other people could get a lot more out of it than I did. I think possible pretension and problems aside, it's still worth trying when the price suits you, because an experiment that misses the mark is still better than perfect mediocrity.

A richly detailed environment, in lightness and darkness, bring this game very much to life. Atmospheric surroundings and sound effects, embellished by excellent cut-scenes that help the narrative as the story unfolds.
The plot is fantastic yet grounded at the same time, riddled with clever what-ifs and many-layered implications of what it means to write creatively and what it is to truly push the boundaries between imagination and reality in this process.
The gameplay itself is pretty damn epic as well. Action remains fast-paced and challenging without being too frustrating, supplies such as ammo or batteries are plentiful enough to stop you ever running the risk of being completely defenceless while remaining sparse enough to keep you considering what to preserve and when, and there is a varying degree of weaponry and enemy strength and speed to keep it interesting.
One thing I really like about this game is that the game never gives you too much ammo, so you never really have that safe feeling when you are trudging through the woods. In other games you usually stack up on a lot of guns and ammo and end up being a one man army - not so in Alan Wake. Here, your character really is a frail writer with a flashlight and a tweed jacket, not a super soldier - your most powerful weapon is also the light. Without light, even the most potent gun cannot so much as even scratch the enemy.

Summary of why I do not recommed this.
==============================
(1). Old game engine. Game engine  seems to run on 2 of 8 available CPU threads. Low FPS (14-20) at 1080p in City areas even with a high spec gaming PC.
(2). Only supports Preview DX10 which is unfinished and gives rendering errors - my main issue is Road Lights which look like black 8 pointed Stars.

Details:
======
I just bought this on Sale on Steam.
I used to play MicroSoft Flight Simulator years ago ~ around end 2001 on an AMD Athlon 64 based PC.
I have some real world flying experience as a pilot (learning to fly a light aircraft, never completed the Pilot's Licence because I could not afford to complete the course at the time).
I wanted to find out how much Flight Simulators have improved today.
I had read reviews of Modern Flight Simulators available for PC today and this was recommended along with XPLANE-11.
I really cannot see why this was recommended as a Modern Flight Simulator at all.
It should be even cheaper than the sale price.  It is very outdated.
It does not seem to have improved that much in single player mode since Flight Simulator 2002 (end 2001) running on an AMD Athlon 64 based PC, in fact, I still have the PC and I feel could have just run this game on it instead.
Seriously this just looks so old and outdated in comparison to a real 2017 title.
I used to fly (pilot) for real out of one airport that is available on this game and It looks nothing much like the area, with very well known landmarks missing completely.
In some places you can see the main road with cars driving straight through buildings which are planted in the middle of the road. Ridiculous but it did give me a laugh I guess.
One other point, Steam is usually really easy to use for me.
I buy the game, I install the game, and generally I just run the game with no problem.
This thing took me about two hours and two install and verify attempts
just to get running because of a really stupid requirement.
You have to run Steam itself as Administrator before this game will run.
I normally do not write negative reviews, but I feel in this case there is nothing much really to say that is very positive at all if you look for a Modern Flight Simulator.
Some positive things I can think of:
(1). One thing I can think of is it it looks and flys like the game did many years ago, with admittedly higher resolution and some graphical improvement at playable framerates.
If you are into Retro Gaming and you do not have your old machine still running, and you have fond memories of playing Microsoft  Flight Simulator 2002 or later, then this game is for you.
However.
Regarding running the game with higher graphical settings.
I tested this game on a 1920x1080 resolution.
I have an i7-4770K (4 core 8 thread)  with Single R9 Nano FuryX active in this game review.
(I have Two R9 Nano FuryX's installed but have not tried to run the game in Crossfire yet).
Thats a reasonably high spec gaming machine, even for today.
The CPU is running at stable +16% OC and the R9 Nano FuryX's are running at +5% stable OC target on the GPU Clock, with Fan and Temp and Power Targets maxed out.
I am able to run the game with all visual settings maxed out and in that case it does look better than the game from end 2001. Even then though, things like water in harbors are completely static, no waves in the water etc.  In this case, even with a powerful Gaming CPU, GPU and running overclocked the Frame Rate drops to 14 FPS on a single monitor at 1920*1080p resolution. I wanted to run it on a Triple 1980*1080p Eyefinity Monitor Setup at the very least.
I need to check what is going on exactly, probably the game can only run on 1 core.
---> Checked.
i7-4770K = 4 CPU cores with 2 threads per core = 8 threads in total ( 8 Logical CPUs).
It looks like the FSX game launcher and background tasks max out 1 logical CPU (thread)  and the Game simulation itself max out two other logical CPU's (threads). The remaining 5 logical CPU's (threads) have some low level / uneven activity.
Some more  positive points to consider.
(2). The planes are very easy to fly using the mouse or keyboard mode, unlike the experience I had with XPLANE-11 demo in the past. It looks great but on previous Demo I just found it too hard to fly with the keyboard alone.
But this may be because SFX is like a cross between a simulator and an arcade game versus a XPLANE-11 which seems to be attempting more of a real simulator experince using a special Flight Controller.
More positive points I can think of about FSX.
(3). You can get some nice screenshots, provided you are high enough altitude so you dont see how simple the buildings on the ground look.
Perhaps I need to look at other features in FSX like a DLC pack, and MultiPlayer but I think I have been as fair as I can be in this feedback so far based on Single Player and Initial Install experience.
If you are into Retro Gamning and want to play Microsoft Flight Simulator from 2002 or later  then this is definitely for you. From that perspective it is nice that this game is still running and available on Steam. I think it is good that old games/code get preserved for future use.
If you look for a Modern Flight Simulator though, do yourself a favour and  buy something else.
This game seems to be pretty much MicroSoft Flight SimulatorX 2006 ported to Steam + new DLC with more planes / higher texture maps on DLC.
I have not asked for a refund from Steam yet as I am going to see if running the game with a Pair of R9 Fury X's in Crossfire or running it with an i7-4790K and a Pair of R9 Nano FuryX's will allow me to play at over 30FPS on Maxed out Graphics Settings at 1920*1080p.
---> Update. If you have a highend GPU like an R9 Nano (FuryX),  Crossfire will not help the FrameRate on FSX:SE.
(A). Crossfire will not turn on at all in DX9 Mode on FSX:SE.
(B). Crossfire will turn on in "Preview" DX10 Mode. Total CPU Utilisition jumps from 55% to 73%.
(C). On this game at least, turning on Crossfire make things worse in the toughest areas of the simulation where you need it.  I have lots of experience running Crossfire on this machine and on most modern titles that support Crossfire it runs well and will provide up good FPS Scaling increase.
The increase in CPU Utilisation turning Crossfire on is not unexpected.  However the problem is when you turn on Crossfire the Frame Rate will increase which will push up the load on the logical CPU's which are used to run the Game / Simulator. In FSX:SE only two logical CPUs run the simulator and they already run with very high utilization with Crossfire turned off. What I see when I turn Crossfire on is the additional loading due to  Crossfire processes is split off to the remaining 5 logical CPU, 1 logical CPU is already maxed out for the Game Loader and Settings interface at  around 90-100% utilisation. The remaining two Logical CPU Cores jump to 100% Utilization all the time. This results in CPU halting/CPU speedstep kicking in.
I want to look at the CPU Utilization Profile and see if I can get it running on Triple Eyefinity setup as well.
---> Update: Yes, Triple Eyefinity works fine, no Drop in FPS seen in this case with Crossfire off.
I can run it at 6016X1080p, but the FPS is in 14-20 range.
I think the reason I cannot increase the FPS is because the simulator engine seems to run on only two threads (Logical CPU's) with an additional thread for the Game Launcher/UI.
That 's it for this review for now.

Defend Your Life: TD is a tower defence (TD) game set inside the body of a patient on an operating table. You take control of the body's immune system to fight off waves of tapeworms, flu viruses, alcohol and other nasties. The game has the look of a 1970s educational cartoon. The graphics aren't actually bad. They're just a bit cringeworthy. However, there is a deliberate irony about the visual style and it's actually quite charming in some ways. For example, one of the hero units you can buy is based on the Incredible Hulk. As a TD game, it's quite well balanced and has the right mix to make it addictive fun. The main drawback I have found is the menu sits on the right hand side of the screen and obscures the place where the creeps exit, which can cause great frustration when you can't click where you want to.

I would recommend this game to anyone who is interested in driving big trucks through mud and off road. The game is a driving game but it almost plays like a puzzle game at times. Picking the right strategy for delivering your loads and taking the right path to the objective is fun and requires some thought.
The point of the game is essentially to deliver lumber. Sounds boring, but its more interesting than you'd think. It's also an exploration game and you have to explore areas to "uncloak" them. Keeping your trucks undamaged and fueled is also part of the game that adds to the fun and realism. You have to monitor your use of All Wheel Drive because using it uses more fuel and sometimes it will be very close on fuel and other times you will run out. The fun part is that you can fit another truck with a fuel tank and bring more fuel to the truck that ran out. Same with the damage. You can attach a utility unit to your truck and bring "repair points" to your truck if it gets damaged badly.
The 'roads' in the game are littered with difficult muddy sections to pass through and sometimes can be challenging and even a bit frustrating. Hardcore mode is cool because you can not rescue your truck if it's stuck or rolled over unless you pull it out or tip it upright with another truck (using the winch). This adds to the tension of passing through an uneven road and in very muddy areas. IF your truck with lumber in it tips, you will lose your load. It can be recovered with the crane attachment though. This is a bit frustrating as the placement of the logs in the truck is a bit finicky with the crane, but its a very nice addition to be able to recover lost loads if you accidently tip your truck. I'd recommend starting with casual mode until you get used to what each type of truck can handle.
The Bad:
-Wonky Controls
-Wonky camera
-Can't customize Xbox 360 Controller buttons
-Only 'true' objective is delivering lumber, but that can be quite challenging
-No wheel/pedal/shifter support (would be amazing with this.
-Lacks cockpit view
The Good:
-Fun for gear heads.
-Mud deformation is cool
-Good graphics
-Good physics
-Variety of vehicle attachments (though some are not too useful)
-Fuel consumption and damage adds to challenge (this is half the game)

Broken Age started out extremely strong. Act One was phenomenal in almost every aspect, however, I feel like Act Two kind of dropped the ball.
Graphics:
The graphics throughout the entire game were amazingly colorful and bright. Everything was pleasant to look at and really helped to bring the game to life.
Audio:
The voice actors did a decent job with bringing out whatever emotion they could from the script. The music was complimentary to what ever was going on in the scene at the time and also helped to add to the excitement.
Storyline:
The storyline throughout Act One was extremely well done. It gave an in depth sense of what was going on and why, and you knew exactly why you were doing the things you were. However, once you got into Act Two, the storyline almost seemed non existent. The puzzles became increasingly hard, almost to the point of wanting to give up, with very little clues to go on. For a good portion of the final Act, I spent a lot of time looking through walkthroughs just to be able to move on.
Even though I enjoyed this game for the most part, I have a hard time recommending this game, based on the fact that Act Two left too much to be desired. I have more questions at the end of Act Two, then I did when I started it. There are still too many loose ends that have not been tied up. The game itself had so much potential, and I think that is why there was so much disappointment at the end.

All right. I got this game from a friend sometime around 2012, I think. I played it for a bit but honestly, I had trouble getting into it. A lot had changed from Civilization II and I never really caught on to all the differences.
Picked it up during the Steam Black Friday sale on Thanksgiving. I gave it a whirl. At first, I had the same feelings I did last time I played all those years ago. It wasn't CivII, and the strategies that worked for me then were failing me now. It didn't help that there wasn't a tutorial or a manual of any kind, and the Civilopedia is not the most user-friendly interface, although it's critical to understanding all of the game mechanics the AI employs.
I played on Chieftain for a while, just trying to get a handle on the game mechanics, but now I'm bored of chieftain. Too easy. Once you learn and begin to understand the game mechanics, this is a pretty great game. That said, it's virtually impossible to win if you don't constantly expand and build one city after another. I mean, that is all you will do. Build and build and build. If you don't, the AI will and you'll lose. Pretty much the only way to win is to begin building a ton of cities in the early parts of the game.
I did like the implementation of cultural borders, and how borders clash against one another. The cultural conversion tool was also pretty cool, where cities could rebel and join your forces because they realized that their own culture was lifeless. So it's a pretty good game, and definitely worth the price for my 46 hours (and growing).
I do have to say, though, that a couple of the leader choices are really dumb. Mahatma Gandhi was not a leader of the Indian nation. Although he championed the move for India's independence, making him the face of India is weird, because he was a guru and not a general. And Jeanne d'Arc leading the French? She was a teenager and a peasant who, by her own confession, never even used her sword in combat. They could have chosen Charlemagne or Napoleon Bonaparte, but Joan! Kinda silly!

I'd like to give this a neutral review but since that's not an option, i'll give a slight recommendation.
first, i'd like to address the elephant in the room. this game was originally developed for tablet, which, as you should know, means that if you expect a real game, you're gonna be disappointed. if you want a real game that you can play for at least two to five hours without taking a break or getting bored, you may wanna take a look at Sheltered or something similar. generally, it's a good idea to stay away from f2p or tablet games if you want a real game. also, obviously, the controls are mediocre at best and annoying at worst, it really shows that it wasn't originally designed for pc.
ok, now that that's out of the way, let's get to the actual review part. the core gameplay mechanics seem pretty generic, as it can be expected from a f2p game. that's not really a bad thing though since it's basically a waiting game which means it is expected to deal with pretty basic mechanics. click on things to collect resources and items, click on people to let them level up, and so on. if you want to loose, you have to try very hard (if it's even possible to let everyone in your vault die, unless you play on survival), if you want to "win" you have to spend money or play for a very long time (what i mean by "winning" is having built everything that you want to build). nothing new.
the game will continue to run if you are logged out, and obviously while you're not online, you won't be able to collect anything. that is also not really bad though because after a short while, the resource consumption will be halted. so you will have a little less resources when you log back in but they won't be completely depleted.
generally, if you don't want to spend money on it, it seems to be a good idea to just log in every couple of hours, collect everything, send some people on quests, start a new weapon/armor production, maybe use speed-mode a couple of times to get a few caps and fill your resource-storage faster and once everything seems good, you can log out again. just don't forget to check your statistics-screen every once in a while, to make sure that your production per minute is still higher than your consumption per minute.
also, there are a couple bugs, crashes and other issues. if you decide to play this game, maybe you have already played some early access titles where the developers simply stopped to care and never fixed any bugs or anything? this game will remind you of that. there is absolutely no communication from the developer, certain bugs have been known for years but no one cared enough to fix them. after a simple look at the discussions you will also probably find that you shouldn't get too attatched to your vault and definitely shouldn't spend any money on it. almost every day i looked, there has been at least one thread on front page complaining about the game being unplayable due to crashes/freezes/etc or the save file being corrupted/disappeared. so it definitely is a bit of a gamble.
if everything works and you are lucky enough to not run into any game breaking bugs it can be fun but that is definitely not guaranteed. so if you like waiting games you can definitely give it a try but i would strongly suggest to not support the developer by buying anything in this game until they start to care a little bit more and fix bugs and other problems.

The barbarians have multiple AI options and can be absolutly brutal. Certain civilzations have certain traits which affect what actions trigger golden ages. You get to upgrade your palace in a way that actually changes the way it looks on the city screen. Also there is a city screen where you get a detailed overview of your city and all the wonders you built. As opposed to Civ 5's jam packed 3D model of your city.
Age helps, in a way, since with todays operating systems the turns are lightning fast, even with troop movement.
I know I have my nostagia blinders on, but I really like this game, despite whatever flaws I cannot see. I suspect that anyone who likes these kinds of games and doesn't mind the lack of 4k graphics, will definitely get their money's worth.

When Shadow of War was originally announced, I did a little fist pump, and smiled internally. What could be better than expanding the nemesis system in a setting which allows for more nuanced and varied organic narrative formation? As soon as pre-order option was available, I humbly offered over the pricey sum of a special edition, and settled to wait for release.
Apart from the special edition pricing issues, and these are not miniscule issues by any means, the game is exactly as one could hope for: open-ended, well-crafted expansion of the LotR lore with satisfying combo based battle mechanics.
The narratives and character portayals are more subtle than a gory orc-killing/raising/killing fest deserves, and widely read LotR fans can spot quite a few references to less known parts of the franchise. As one article summed it, Shadow of War is gory LotR fanfiction, and oh boy is it sweet fanfiction. The orcs have been expanded further, both as characters and their mechanics, and it becomes all too easy to form an emotional bond with your favourite captain only to have him stab you in the back at worse possible moment. Which is bloody marvelous.
Furthermore, with more complex orc hierarchy, now one has to know captains, their weaknesses, strengths, family relations (no I do not kid with this), and optimize decisionmaking. This makes this aspect of the game much more complex and interesting than the equivalent in Shadow of Mordor was.
The fighting mechanics have been expanded from Shadow of Mordor, with a focus on allowing different builds for Talion in order to enable as customisable gameplay experience as possible. However, it is clear that the different builds one can create using the revamped character menu have been geared towards online conquests.
Which brings me to the most mixed blessing of Shadow of War. The online elements. I would lie if I said I do not enjoy the grind and training of my army, and then charge fellow players strongholds, sometimes to glorious victory, and sometimes to embarrassing defeat. However, it is obvious that the online conquest mechanics are what drives microtransactions, and as enjoyable as conquests personally for me are, one has to question their necessity in this type of a game. Aware as I am of the past decade's trend of gluing online or multiplayer mode to every game in order to discourage reselling, it is not a development direction I support wholeheartedly.
What saves Shadow of War is the fact that the online elements are balanced enough for now. They are not mandatory, and as a person who has not spent one cent on loot boxes, the conquests feel doable enough. More work than with paying, but not impossible or insane. However quite understandably the grind aspect will not be fun for everyone, and the online conquests are not easily doable with non-optimized army.
Another factor that has undoubtedly alienated a few players are the day one DLCs, or special editions as they are called these days. As a gamer I am old enough to remember when this was not the industry standard, and the practice is a debatable one with modern triple A games, which tend to be pricy from get go. I feel that the extra elements covered by the special editions justify the extra price, but only just about. The developers and publishers have to walk a fine line in the future, as they have pushed the acceptable price/content ratio to the limit. Anyone more opposed to this practice, for you I suggest waiting until a seasonal sale cuts the price a bit.
All in all I recommend this game for everyone who enjoyed Shadow of Mordor. Shadow of War is a very good game, with story elements that appeal to certainpart of the LotR crowd, and organic expanded orc narrative generation system that should appeal to everyone else. Monolith has exceeded itself, again, with expanding the belowed universe of Tolkien, managing to create something new with it. While keeping the gameplay experience highly addictive and satisfying. This is no small feat.
However, the microtransactions together with high price tag and "special edition" content show that developers are giving in to the siren song og the worst practices of triple a games industry. As of now, I am a satisfied gamer; these elements are inoffensive in the game, but they are undoubtedly present.

Well now. This game is going to be controversial. I like it but a lot of people won't.
This is a game that defies expectations. It clearly owes more than a little to David Lynch (not just Twin Peaks). If anything, it's like an interactive film.  Sure, a lot of people will say 'This is not a game!' or hurl around walking simulator. But the devs always made that pretty clear. If that doesn't appeal to you - simply stay away, there's a lot of other games out there.
The game is absolutely beautiful visually and the music and audio is great. There is not a single spoken word in the game which strengthens it as far as I'm concerned but may be jarring for others. The writing is outstanding, one of the best I've seen in a short game. It really does a good job (better than most) in putting you in the shoes of the character you play.
Virgina is short and quite frankly somewhat railroady. If you're okay with that, great. Otherwise stay away.
In summary, if you like games where it's all story and the game revolves around the experience and narrative, not the mechanics this is a great one. If that's not your thing - just say away.

So, if you take the term 'CRPG' really seriously and enjoy getting in fights about how modern RPGs aren't 'real' RPGs, and you wish it were still the late 1990s, this is a great game for you and you don't need to read the rest of my review.
On the other hand, if you enjoy isometric party-based RPGs but also might like to see some progress from the last 15 years or so of gaming history, Wasteland 2 is kind of a letdown precisely because of how stubbornly it emulates the UI fiddliness of Fallout 1/2.  Get ready to remember which party member owns a shovel, switch to them, activate the shovel item, and wait while a progress bar fills up, every time you want to dig something up.  And this isn't just shovels, it's *every specialized skill*.  You're not realistically going to put together a party with more than one girl or guy who knows Safecracking or some other random♥♥♥♥♥♥ but the game will never let you just click on the safe and have the one Safecracker open it.
The maps suffer from a similar level of fiddliness.  You will have to memorize where in town that random questgiver is, or come back from a fetch quest to wander all over wondering where his shop is among a town of identical-looking dwellings.  No quest markers is fine, I don't think that the player should have telepathic knowledge of where stuff is ahead of time, but when you're looking to turn in quests (and the characters would already know where shopkeeper X is) it's just a hassle.  Isometric design also means that the level designers hide crates in places where you need to rotate the camera to find them ... which is fine, but after a while, it's not clever, it's just irritating to have to rotate the camera every time you enter a new room or potentially miss out on loot.
I could go on with examples of the weird sort of micromanagement that Wasteland 2 requires of the player (there are many more), but you get the point.
Bottom line, it feels like a game that came out in 2000, not 2014.  If you're fine with this, go ahead and get it (but you probably already did).  If you're not, and especially if you haven't played Fallout 1/2 to death, there's really no reason to play this instead of Fallout 1/2.

First and foremost - THIS IS NOT FALLOUT (first nor second)! Drill this to your head. Do not buy this game thinking it's Fallout. Do not PLAY this game thinking it's Fallout. Wasteland is one thing, Fallout is something completely different. Now lets begin.
Do you like post-apocalyptic lite CRPGs? If you do then this is something you should definately check out. Now when I say "lite" I do really mean it. This game feels, at times, extremely shallow and simplistic in everything from interactions with the environment, quests, combat and items. Everything is simplified. Yet this still is a good and enjoyable game and worth every penny you spend to buy it.
The closest comparison that I can make to this game is Fallout Tactics, which in my opinion was vastly underrated and received way too much flak than it deserved, and I still rate Fallout Tactics higher than this.
Character creation is based on the CLASSIC system (whereas Fallout uses SPECIAL) with just attributes and skills. No special perks or traits. You can customize your Rangers appearance, bio and so on but none of that affects your game in anyway.
Combat is single squad, turn-based and squared grid layout playing field. Nothing too fancy, straightforward and to the point. You have different guns, bombs and heavy weapons with some different fire modes and ability to try a headshot. The cover system is similiar to the new XCOM Enemy Unknown game with the icon showing cover positions.
Quests are typical (somewhat gliche'd) CRPG quests of fetch things, solve problems and make binary choices between factions.
Environment is a bit stoic. Things you can interact with can be highlighted with a press of a key and that's about it.
Game is full of easter eggs, dark humour and references. This was actually something that really started to annoy me. It feels like in every scene and place you visit is just riddled with them. I mean come on! Candy is nom noms but too much candy makes your stomach hurt.
As a whole Wasteland 2 is a good game. It's not fantastic or rebirth of CRPGs. It's just a good game. Just do not try to compare it to Fallout games. The only things these have in common are Fargo and the post-apocalyptic theme.

I purchased two copies, averaging $1.50 each. It was literally the best bang for my buck on Steam. Heck, I'd pay $30. The music alone makes it worth it, let alone the thrill of unlocking upgrades and facing new enemies. The graphics are beautiful, though frames drop when things get heated. The levels get slightly longer and harder as you progress. There are really no difficulty spikes when you rebeat unlocked levels for coins, which are used to permanently unlock perks. There are also diamonds you earn each level, which can buy single-use perks. Plus, you're given a few powers (like a bomb) with a downtime before re-use. The game actually warns you before playing a new level if you haven't unlocked enough perks. Unlike similar games, it will still let you play them if you dare.
This game requires you to use your head, which I love. Do you build several low-powered towers? Or a few high-powered ones? How many guard posts should you build, and where should you place them? When should you use your powers? And which one should you use? Do I have sufficient defense on the choke points?
This is my favorite single-player game on Steam, and I despise tower defense games. Ignore the negative reviews. This game is rated positively for a reason. It's a must-buy no matter your age; it even has educational value for youngsters. I will be spending a long time on this. Thank you, developers, for such an awesome, affordable game!

While periodically Virginia impresses with some of the best cinematic skill I've ever seen in video games, I was regularly bored and wanting more.
Towards the end, the plot matures and delivers some great character development, but then falls flat when everything tries to tie together. The ending could have cut at any point in the last few chapters and I would have felt no mroe or less satisfied.
I would compare this game in terms of gameplay to Thirty Flights of Loving (which is acknowledged in the credits as inspiration) and Dear Esther. I think both these games are stronger titles only because they are not long enough to get tiring.
Virginia is still an excellent title, but I fear with walking simulators, you need to be shorter and narratively clearer to really offer a great experience. I spent a lot of the game wishing this had dialogue and some gameplay, as the narrative and world was really excellently created and deserved exploring.

I honestly can't describe Paladins in a way that will make it seem good.
Most reason why people hate it, is because they think it's a Rip off of Overwatch. However, they share differences but the game itself feels like it looked to Overwatch for inspiration.
The key gimmic to each match is that you get to see the enemies Team Comp before the match starts, eliminating the chance of surpise. You are unable to, 1.) Leave the match (have to leave the game instead) 2.) Swap Champions 3.) Using ♥♥♥♥ing voice chat. They added a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ popup menu that barely works. Overwatch uses these, and they work hand in hand.
Another think that bugged me, is that you have to PAY to play different Champions... Why!?
I understand, it's a free-to-play game. Yet, so is something like TF2, but you don't stand with 1 of each class. You have all of them available for you.
Hero customisation sucks♥♥♥♥♥ You require gems for the really cool things, which, are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get. The animation for the emotes feel really sloppy, and they need some work.
Did I mention everyone has the 1 spray you can't change because they're all locked? My bad.
But in the end, I think they churn out more heroes instead of PROPERLY balancing them. With Overwatch, you get a new hero, say around every 4 Months or so. Yet, that works in the games favour, because devs and PC players are able to test the heroes, and for the rest of the cast, give feedback on what changes they want to see for a certain hero. Blizzard balance their game, if they see something used too much, or is found too OP, they'll be nerfed. Anything in Paladins, whether it be a new, or existing seems rushed. The designs look bad, the champions aren't balanced, the game will feel, at times unfair. (Pip, I'm looking at you).
There's also fewer maps than I was hoping for. Not much varaity in different landscapes. There's also not a good amount of different gamemodes. Both o the current game modes (excluding survival) are payload based. They couldn't of thought of something else to do. Just copy & paste the Payload code and use that.
You can argue, and say the games in Beta. But guess what, it's been in beta for a ♥♥♥♥ing year now. They still have so much ground to cover.
If you're looking for a fair, interesting free to play, go install TF2. Or, if you want to try out a more, fair & balanced game. Do yourself a favour and spend £30 - £45 on Overwatch. I don't recommend you touch Paladins.

Defend your life is a tower defense game which was inspired by Kingdom Rush.
Pros
- Unique setting. It’s not just a usual fantasy setting which is typical for TD games. You defend the human body from different viruses and bacteria. There aren’t many games in this setting, and this game is definitely the first one of this kind in TD genre.
- Although the game is a clone of Kingdom Rush, it has some new features. Magic tower has been replaced with a support tower. Each base tower can be upgraded into 2 different ones on level 1. Total number of towers is slightly higher than in KR. There are 3 skills instead of two.
- Game is simple to play
- There are game speed settings
Cons
- Although I found "Human Body" setting interesting, can anyone explain me what does Rocket Launcher do in my stomach? Why do bacteria wear iron helmets? I would advise to use antibiotics and vitamins instead of cannon towers. It would perfectly fit. The game looks like a lazily-done concept. My final impression about this story and setting is totally negative.
- This game was designed as free-to-play game for mobiles. There are consumable items which highly improve your defenses. Devs from KR cut these things when they ported the game to PC. But Alda Games decided to not waste their time and forced players to start the previous levels again and again to get "gems".
- Waves of each mission are short and always the same. It's pretty interesting to watch them during the first 2-3 missions. When you find out that the next levels have almost the same types of waves, you get bored.
The game is not bad. I think newcomers to TD genre would find "Defend your life" attractive. For these people I say wait for 60% discount and try it.
But I can't recommend this game for people like me who like to play innovative and interesting games enjoying every minute of the game.

This game combines excellent graphics, low-latency, frenetic FPS gameplay, great atmospheric scene-setting and engaging, strategic/team mechanics to make one of the best games I've ever played.
I've never screamed so loud into a mic before as an alien was bearing down upon my helpless, fragile, meatsack-looking marine body. When the teamplay and action is at its best, this game shines above others in its class. Imagine the fun, frenzied action of Team Fortress 2 fused with atmosphere of Doom and thrown into the mechanics of a 3X strategy game: THIS is NS2.
The only downside to this game, however, is absolutely ZERO interface with the devs for when (not if) bugs and problems arise. The community has done a great job of making this game feel alive, through the Workshop mods, through various user-created guides and through ardent communication strategies in game. The devs have done next to nothing, it seems, to foster this community further though. Which is a shame.

I really wanted to love this game. Really, I did. But instead, I'll likely finish this playthrough and never touch it again. Not bad, but not great.
I'll cut to the chase and say that the main problem is that the turn-based squad combat is missing a few CRITICAL elements to make it tactical. The key missing ingredient is an 'Overwatch' or 'Held Action' mechanic. This alone dumbs down combat significantly. Also conspicuously missing is an option to 'Defend' or 'Hunker Down.' It may not seem like a lot, but what these mean is that most of your squad's actions are... nothing. In XCOM (which admittedly set the bar high) every action is important. If you can't get a squad member into position they can usually do something that feels useful, even if that is Overwatching on the off chance an alien comes barging through. In Hard West there is just a lot of skipping actions, turn after turn, hoping that the enemy AI makes a mistake... because other than sitting in once place, there isn't anything else you can do to prepare for it.
That said, the atmosphere of the game is amazing. The storytelling is great, as is the ambience delivered by the music and graphic styles. The optional objectives really add to the immersion. They let me make choices to match a player's playstyle or to give notably different appriaches to missions. The interface is fairly intuitive, and even though a few mechanics are never explained, they're easy enough to figure out.
It is a shame that the core of the game (the turn based combat) is not as tactical or exciting as other games in the genre.
Overall:
-If you like 'weird west' settings, definitely get this game! Between the art and the narration, it feels like playing in a Deadlands campaign!
-If you like turn-based squad combat, meh, it's certainly not bad for the price, just don't expect an XCOM challenger.

SHORT REVIEW:
Average Game not worth $80. Buy it only for $30-$40
LONG REVIEW:
So, after beating the game completely (with all side missions and stuff) I can say that this game is worth buying only on discount or rent. Throught out the whole game the best part to keep you coming back is only the story (WHICH IS DRAGGED AS HELL) and right after you beat it you just dont feel like playing it anymore at all. I just realise how much I had to force myself to play it until the end. The game might and probably will fascinate you at first like it did to me, but later on it just gets SO ♥♥♥♥ING REPETETIVE to the point that you just sit in your chair bored as hell and trying to reach the end. The gameplay is very repetetive but the part that repeats itself (driving and combat) are made on a pretty good level which makes it possible to play this game. The story on the other hand in my opinion was pretty good but WAY WORSE than Mafia 2 story. From the beginning to the end you already know what is going to happen and its just simply disappointing. The ending isnt that great either they only made it a bit better by showing a little surprise and a throwback to the older games. In my opinion Vitos storyline in this game is better than the main one. So lets see the pros and cons of this game.
GAME SCORING:
Combat 10/10
Driving 8/10
Open World (Alive but nothing to do) 5/10
Story 6.5/10
Vito's Story (Very Short Since It's A Side Story) 9/10
Level of Repetitevness (Try hitting a wall a thousand times and make yourself think that you are doing something new every time) 10/10
Cinematics 10/10
Graphics 7/10
Atmosphere 8/10 (Good atmosphere but just isnt that Mafia one that I wanted when getting this game)
Soundtrack 9/10 (Just too short and gets repetetive often)
Boss Levels 8/10 (Again good levels but are just too predictive and simple (even on the highest difficulty))
OVERALL SCORE: 6.5/10

Spintires is a stuck-in-the-mud simulator much more than it has anything to do with a driving game/simulator. While it's fun for a few hours the game screams "unfinished" and has a distinct lack of actual content, and as such the $30 price tag is just absurd. While the destructable terrain and muddy roads provide an interesting and challenging concept in theory, the destructable part is also the game's biggest fault. As none of the vehicles you're provided are in any way suitable for driving in the soft mud that makes up 99% of the landscape, you end up getting stuck and tearing up the "roads" on your first trip, which means the "roads" can only be passed 2-3 times at the most before they're so ruined they're unpassable. It makes for a much more frustrating than entertaining experience.
Other than driving around to pull your truck out of the mud again and again and again, the game has basically nothing else to offer. Each map contains an objective to deliver wood, which in itself is a massive challenge as just reaching the lumber yard can be nearly impossible on most the maps without using the biggest truck you got to tow you in.
And literally, that covers the entirety of the game's content.
The game cannot be recommended unless on a heavily reduced discount (like 75% off), or until some major patching happens to turn it into an actual game with actual content worth paying for.

Broken Age is an old-school point-and-click adventure game funded through Kickstarter purely by nostalgia from fans that grew up with LucasArts games from the ‘90s along with Tim Schafer’s earlier works. For a very long time, Broken Age was Kickstarter’s poster-boy, all thanks to being the most funded project at the time. This meant that one small slip could potentially affect the way people perceive the risky-environment of Kickstarter projects in general. No wonder there was high pressure on Double Fine to deliver on their promises since they received almost $4 million in funding (which is almost nothing by today’s standards if it were funded by an actual publisher) in contrast to the $400,000 they were originally asking. The end result was split over two Acts, released approximately a year and half apart from each other.
With that said, what Double Fine delivered in the end is a wonderful adventure game with an interesting plot concept: a teenager by the name of Shay who is a prisoner in his own spaceship trying to escape from being babysit by computers he refers to “Mom” and “Dad”; and Vella, daughter of a family of bakers in a village who tries to oppose taking part in a traditional sacrifice to Mog Chathra, a creature known for devouring worlds. Two teenagers living in two different worlds, yet facing almost similar problems, eventually collide with one another. Although the story starts agonisingly slow, it eventually builds up momentum after two or so hours in and keeps you invested until the totally unexpected, nonetheless remarkable, plot twist near the end of the first act which makes up for any pacing issues encountered. I really dig the concept Broken Age is trying to follow here.
Additionally, compliments are to be given to the charming art-style. It is simply startling, albeit childish -- but that is its beauty, right? In fact, that is part of the story’s undertones. Sure, perhaps being an adult playing this might look silly, but from an artistic perspective it succeeds in capturing the aesthetics of a children’s storybook. It may not be what some people were expecting Broken Age to look like when the game was first pitched on Kickstarter, but I have no problems with it because Double Fine have done it very creatively. Likewise, while the humour might not be as memorable as in other comedy-oriented adventure games, Broken Age does not disappoint in this aspect either, all thanks to a couple of support characters such as the cutlery collective - the Spoon, the Fork and the Knife – whose dialogues and remarks never seize to be amusing. Throughout its duration, there are a handful of good chuckles to be had from time to time. Conceivably, I do not believe it was necessary for Double Fine to hire Hollywood actors as voice actors, but in the end they all did a solid job in most parts. Whilst there are minor moments where there might lack of emotion in the delivery of some of the lines, they do not break the immersion the game has to offer. And once again, Pete McConnell does a fantastic job on the soundtrack for this game, especially the three stellar tracks “The Lumberjack’s Cabin”, “Vella Wakes” and “Battle At Shellmound”.
If you read up to this point, then surely you may be wondering why I gave a negative review for something which, based on my comments above, sounds like an amazing point-and-click adventure game? Well, here is why, and it does actually break my heart to say it but:
Act 2 ruined it all.
Pretty much everything that is established in Act 1 is thrown out the window. The things we, as players, are to believe judging by how the story unravels in Act 1 simply do not materialise in the second half. In fact, the whole concept seems detached in places in Act 2. As far as the story is concerned, it becomes uninteresting and seems to go almost nowhere. Any new revelation either turns out predictable or unimpressive. And this may be due to a few major flaws which simply killed Act 2.
The most obvious crime committed here is the reuse of the same exact locations found in Act 1, with only Shay’s spaceship being “redecorated”. To me, one aspect of adventure games which sucks me in is the notion of exploration; finding new locations and meeting new interesting characters to advance the plot, aside from solving challenging puzzles. Desolately, that is not the case here. Simple as. In reality, what bothers me the most might not actually be the reuse of the same locations in the end, but rather all the fetching for items. In this part of the game, it did not click with me because it is a chore. But hold on a second, fetching for stuff has been in adventure games like this for decades? Yes, but the problem here is when you ultimately realise that most support characters are nothing more than “mechanical” characters. Paying close attention, almost none of them have any influence over nor take direct part in the story. They only exist there artificially for either Shay or Vella to retrieve a specific item from them to solve a certain puzzle. So this makes you stop investing time in caring for them, as characters. Also in regards to the puzzles, Act 1 is indeed a breeze for adventure veterans, so it is almost impossible to get stuck at any point – which in a way I do not think that is necessarily a bad thing at all. All puzzles, although pretty obvious, feel logical in Act 1. On the other hand, Act 2 bumps up the difficulty and takes some risks in being creative with some of the puzzles, but the end result is a mixed bag. Contrary to what other people say, I give Double Fine credit for the wiring puzzle in terms of creativity because it actually made you think (and no, it is not as hard as some people claim it to be – just time consuming). I only wish it was not as frequently used in the last quarter of the game and more intuitive, but stuff like the snake puzzle was badly implemented; waiting for a puzzle to solve itself? But yeah, most puzzles in Broken Age basically boil down to asking the right person for the right item and that is you more or less done. Sort of.
Comparing the two acts, it feels like Act 2 was either rushed or made up while they were going along (as in it was not planned out at the same time with Act 1), or both. The charm and humour are still intact in the second half, but everything in terms of plot, characters, concept and some puzzles took a major hit by some bad design choices. Plus, just when you think Act 2 would redeem itself by the end, Broken Age ends in an anticlimax which raises more questions than providing all the answers. Simply put, the writing is poor in Act 2, and it seems like poor management could have been another factor here.
In conclusion, Broken Age is a visually beautiful and well-crafted game where all the passion was clearly injected a lot more in the first act, but all its potential is completely ruined by its second act plagued by poor writing and some bad design choices which reduces it to no more than an adequate adventure game at best. Broken Age could have been the next big thing in this genre, and Act 1 is a valid gauge, but when modern adventure games like The Book of Unwritten Tales or even the more retro-y Blackwell series (as a whole) exist and provide a (subjectively) better and more fleshed out experience, then you know that something went wrong at some point in your game. Broken Age is still worth at least one shot thanks to its promising Act 1, so long as you lower your expectations in the next act. If so, then this still is a good starter for anyone new who wants to delve into point-and-click adventure games. Otherwise, for old adventure fanatics, I cannot really recommend it; easily skippable thanks to Act 2. To be honest, I could have also easily given this a neutral review if there were such a button on Steam.
I am still looking forward to Double Fine’s next project, but what a bummer coming from Tim Schafer.

As other reviews have stated, there are optional micro transactions.  Here's a quick summary of it:
There's an in-game market, in which you can buy different types of loot crates containing gear or orcs, which are used to defend or attack cassles.  You can buy golden loot crates or silver ones.  The golden loot crates are purchaseable using gold, whiile the silver ones are purchased using Mirian (silver currency). The loot/orcs obtained through the golden crates are better than the silver crates.  However, the stuff obtained through silver loot crates is still good.  I have not spent any real life money to purchase loot crates and  there really is no need.  In my opinion, the reviews complaining about micro-transactions in this game are way overblown.  Don't let the option of microtransactions stop you from playing this game.
