As a long time fan of Shadow of Mordor, I still can't recommend this game.
The first game perfected the feel of combat and this one takes a major step backwards.  Insta-kill counter-attacks sounds great, but you lose all of the power from your attack buttons and the fastest way to kill things now is to let them hit you.  Instead of rhythm based combat now it's a waiting game.
This minimizes executions and makes combat feel grindy.  Instead of constant zooms and slow-mos into the act of cleaving an orc in half, instead from far away you see several orc gettings stabbed while attacking you and then disappear.  It never feels like you're earning the kills.  More like you're waiting for flies to land on your arm so you can smack them.
The use of orcs in your sieges, bodyguards and castle defense is actually pretty neat.  There's not really any reason for them other than to justify the crate system and microtransactions to fill your supply of orc captains I guess.
But honestly, this was the game decision that made the most sense to me.  It's whimsical and involves murdering hoards of orcs.
If a little bit is good, more must be better!  The idea seems clear.  In practice it just introduces a lot of grind.  Go to the new area and now you need to figure out who all the orcs are again because they're unknown.  And you need to find all of the towers and artefacts again.
There's never really any reason to backtrack to a different area unless you're deciding to defend a castle.  All the areas are essentially identical.
What made Shadow of Mordor fun wasn't the number of towers in the game, it was the fact that you could be separated from the towers and murdering hords of orcs.  Now it feels like you're supposed to run past hords of orcs so you can unlock your towers and get to the next area.  So you notice the scenery even less than before.
The idea of giving players unique playstyles is great.  The idea of letting you customize the perks on that skill tree and change your playstyle is also great.
But that's not what the skill tree actually introduces.
The problem is that almost all of the perks have a clearly overpowered option.  For instance, either gaining bonus combos on counterattacks, or the counterattack straight up kills orcs.  Not a decision anyone is going to consider very long.
After paying for a game, it's tedious that these exist at all.
However the purchases are so unnecessary that I don't understand how people are getting upset over it.
Sure, you could pay a few bucks and get 3 orcs.  But you could also spend 10 minutes playing and get 3 orcs, so there's not a lot that you're going to miss out on.
Great ideas.  Good direction.  Poor execution.
If you want to buy this game, just go replay Shadow of Mordor instead.

This review it's a tough one...
First of all, is it a bad game?
Is it a game for everyone? Still:
For who doesn't want to read the whole review, here's the nutshell: you know Dear Easter, right? Well, it's the same deep, insightful narrative (
). It's the same "open-for-thoughts" ending. (
)
Think you gonna like it? Fine, buy it. You don't like Dear Easter-like games? Avoid this game like the plague.
Now for Virginia: this game it's a movie, quite literally and in a very good way. This games shines of originality, I've personally never before witnessed to a narration presented this way. Does it work? Yes, the developers made a really got job. You are an observer, your interactions with the world are very, very, limited. But, at the same time, you don't feel most of the time that you're basically, constantly, on rails. It's not diffrent from you sitting in a movie theatre watching a movie. You know you can't change the movie, it is what is it is, you just can't change it. You just "
" it, and get feelings, thoughts, insights etc. etc. depending what you saw in it. Virginia it's the same thing.
Now, this game it's full, seriously,
of symbolism. Baudelaire would be impressed.
When you pass the hour, you realize that everything you saw means something, and that probably everything you "witnessed" it's not exactly how it presented itself. You have to
, you have to
how things really are. So don't worry if you'll be like: "What the ♥♥♥♥ am I watching?" for most of the time.
Problem is, with this metod of exposure of the plot, it's really,
easy to see more of what it really is. I read some reviews and discussions on the Hub. Some say that you should take this game as it is. Someother says that this game, very deeply, even inspects the fabric of society itself.
Imagine that you're in literature class: "The poet wrote that the curtain was blue because he was depressed and the curtain was the symbol of his depression, that prevented him to see the sun outside."
While it can also, with equal possibility, be: "The curtain was blue because the curtain was blue, period."
Imagine also, as another example, that you are in a museum. You stand before a painting observing it. You can hear the guy next to you marveling about how that picture it's so deep, so full of ideas, concepts, thoughts, coclusions etc. etc. while you stand over there like "Meh, it's just a woman walking her dog on a country road". Virginia can also be like that.
The ending is very open. This, in my opinion, cements my belief: you should draw your own conclusion yourself. If this was the objective of the developers, well, standing ovation to them because they nailed it. If not... Probably I didn't see their vision the way they wanted.
It's either one of this two:
The writer(s) should get thrown in a mental health hospital.
That was a powerful, deep, insightful experience that I can't wait to dig up, playing this game over and over again to get all the tiny clues and symbolisms.
Belive me when I say that there's
middle ground between these two options.
I won't spoil the plot in any way, that way you can experience it the best. Again, I don't know if it was intencional, from the developers, to make this game misterious and thoughtful. If it was congratulations, you made a fine A work. But, at the same time, it's very easy to just "throw" stuff to let people rack their own brain over them while they really mean... Nothing.
This is the biggest fear: it all means nothing. Devs simply used those overly misterious messages, this constant symbolis, just because... Well, they had nothing to tell, so they hidden behind a thick fabric of brain food just to let people run in circle without having a single clue of what "
"
See? It's a coin with two faces, if you want to buy it I deeply suggest you to at least acknowledge both.
Overall it's a great "interactive movie" which springs of originality. Of particular remark it's the absolutely astounding soundtrack, you'll be blown away by how well it fits in most scenes.
So... Are you ready to flip the coin?

The game "travel" system is like mount and blade where you take your group on a journey through the wastelands of arizona trying to do all the nobel stuff that rangers do. The problem is that you have to avoid radiation and check your water levels so you dont die of thirst or radiation poisoning. while that may seem easy it can be pretty annoying to have the shortest route blocked by radiation and to take a detour means that you have to waste all your water and you end up with a dehydrated and tired group walking into an encounter. Combat is much like certain classic games, your characters initiative skill determines what order your turn is in, and works as a top down turn-based rpg. all of your actions require Action Points so it's important to conserve them, any excess points will be carried over to the next mission.

The Setting alone is great (Why aren't there more western games?) Hard West has this really cool mixture of western and horror. If you've ever played the old-school RPG "Deadlands" or have read Stephen King's "The Dark Tower" series, than you'll feel right at home.

If you're in the mood to test your patience, then this is the game for you. Spintires offers a welcome relief to take time with the game and enjoy an impressive environment along with simple objectives. However, in order for simplicity to be enjoyable for a prolongued period of time, the mechanics upon which it is based must 1) make intuitive sense and 2) WORK. What destroyed this game for me was the physics engine, particularly as it related to the mud mechanics. While at first their pseudo-liquid effects and malleable terrain are an awesome concept, I found that driving through the same section of mud more than once resulted in my commercial-size 6-wheel truck being submerged more than half deep. Now, I can understand that mud is a problem, but at this point I'm drilling for oil simply by driving a vehicle.
The core challenge to completing objectives in Spintires seems based on navigation and not getting stuck; and the winch mechanic helps profoundly with the latter. Unfortunately, I found myself using it constantly, which didn't just slow down gameplay, it just starts getting in the way of it. Without exaggeration, I found driving under lakes to be easier than traversing muddy roads. This could be a much better game, but the mud physics are unrealistic beyond the point of reason. It transformed what was a slow-paced, relaxing game into a trollfest.
The physics engine also has some interesting quirks in regards to gravity, where I can roll a vehicle down a steep slope into a gulch and suffer no damage, but hitting a slight dip on a road takes out one quarter of the same vehicle's health. An Xcom style turn based strategy game, set in a supernatural western world, with a heavy focus on narative.
_Cool, interesting setting.

You bet your♥♥♥♥♥ Billy. It's fun and unique, and stands on its own strength. I mean, I put down Fallout 4 to play this. Enough said.
Now for more details...
A turn based shootout sim focused on cover and positioning. You take cover and carefully plan your next move, while taking every pot shot at the enemies you can. Combat is very familiar here: You move, try to flank your enemies, shoot, move, reload, use abilities, etc. It's super competent, and fun. Not to say there's nothing new here, but we'll cover that more below. Hard West trades in XCom's base building and research for a choose-your-own-adventure naration between combat missions. It feels more like an RPG with meaningful choices and an emphasis on story-telling. There's also a skill system that feels a lot like the perk system in older Fallout games and give your characters a lot of uniqueness.
Characters have luck, a visual representation of their survivability. A shot that might look like a hit could miss if your character's luck is high enough. As good thing happens, though, their luck will start to drain, putting a more literal meaning on the phrase "out of luck." It's really cool, fits with the Western setting and is an interesting mechanic. The game's unique supernatural edge also makes gameplay more interesting. For example, one of the skills you could pick up gives you the ability to canibalize corpses to regain health. It also gives you some oportunity to fight demons and cultists alongside your standard bandits and cowboys.

I really wanted to like this game. I reserved judgement until I'd seen the whole thing, despite the protracted release, but the end result is so mediocre.
Positives:
+ Charming art style.
+ Shay's story arc on the Bossa Nova was pretty fun.
+ The spoon would've been a fitting character in any classic adventure game.
+ I appreciate that they at least tried to put more puzzles in the second act.
Negatives:
- The storyline falls apart in the second act. It feels so rushed, poorly thought through, and completely detached from the mood of the first act. It seems like the ending was written and re-written well after the first act rather than as one continuous story. Disappointing.
- I realize that not every adventure protagonist can be Guybrush, but Vella is a thoroughly uninteresting character. She's too bland to even be unlikeable. Given what she faces in the story, I can't understand why they directed her voice actress to sound like she's on a high dose of Xanax.
- The dialog trees feel tired and rarely capture the charm of Schafer's previous efforts.
- There's little enjoyment to be found in exploration, and that's the whole point of this genre.

As a huge Double Fine and Lucasarts fan I backed this game at one of the higher tiers, bought more merch along the way to support the extended development, and quite enjoyed Act 1.
That said, now that the full game is here, I can't really recommend Broken Age, and I'm pretty disappointed with the game itself.
I think the game suffers from a lack of a single cohesive world, two main characters that have no relationship, and what turns out to be a pretty ridiculous and silly plot (which would be fine in a comedy adventure, except it doesn't pay off the expectations that are built in the early parts of the game, i.e. it's a total let down). Many of the characters don't seem to have any purpose other than to be an artificial road block for puzzle business in the story line, and only a couple of characters I found to be memorable (often the characters that had the least screen time unfortunately).
The second half of the game also spends the most of its time recycling the same environments and characters for the sake of some pretty tiresome puzzles. The timing puzzles are particularly irritating and don't communicate well visually. I worked through most of the second act without needing any hints, but eventually I hit a point where I just wanted to be done with the game and so I read the solutions. No regrets there.
I really like the art in the game, but I think a different, more traditional adventure game art style may have helped get the game done sooner, and I would have rather played a game with worse art, that felt more polished, with more environments, better developed characters and more refined puzzles, than this game, which feels like made a lot of compromises simple because it was so damn time consuming to paint and animate.
Finally though, I have to say that I don't feel ripped off and I still hope Double Fine can come back from the damage that Kickstarter and Early Access have done to their reputation in the past year or so. The documentary is great (particularly the first 10 or so episodes before development started getting into trouble) and was worth the price of entry alone, and it's clear that the people at Double Fine care a lot about what they do, but this project had  some fundamental problems right out of the gates and the result is a game that I can't put up alongside classics like DOTT or Full Throttle.

As other reviews have stated, there are optional micro transactions.  Here's a quick summary of it:
There's an in-game market, in which you can buy different types of loot crates containing gear or orcs, which are used to defend or attack cassles.  You can buy golden loot crates or silver ones.  The golden loot crates are purchaseable using gold, whiile the silver ones are purchased using Mirian (silver currency).  Gold is purchased using real life money (but you can get a little bit from completion of a quest), while Mirian is in-game currency obtained through playing the game (quest rewards, selling old gear).
The loot/orcs obtained through the golden crates are better than the silver crates.  However, the stuff obtained through silver loot crates is still good.  I have not spent any real life money to purchase loot crates and  there really is no need.  In my opinion, the reviews complaining about micro-transactions in this game are way overblown.  Don't let the option of microtransactions stop you from playing this game.

As a long time fan of Shadow of Mordor, I still can't recommend this game.
The first game perfected the feel of combat and this one takes a major step backwards.  Insta-kill counter-attacks sounds great, but you lose all of the power from your attack buttons and the fastest way to kill things now is to let them hit you.  Instead of rhythm based combat now it's a waiting game.
This minimizes executions and makes combat feel grindy.  Instead of constant zooms and slow-mos into the act of cleaving an orc in half, instead from far away you see several orc gettings stabbed while attacking you and then disappear.  It never feels like you're earning the kills.  More like you're waiting for flies to land on your arm so you can smack them.
The use of orcs in your sieges, bodyguards and castle defense is actually pretty neat.  There's not really any reason for them other than to justify the crate system and microtransactions to fill your supply of orc captains I guess.
But honestly, this was the game decision that made the most sense to me.  It's whimsical and involves murdering hoards of orcs.
If a little bit is good, more must be better!  The idea seems clear.  In practice it just introduces a lot of grind.  Go to the new area and now you need to figure out who all the orcs are again because they're unknown.  And you need to find all of the towers and artefacts again.
There's never really any reason to backtrack to a different area unless you're deciding to defend a castle.  All the areas are essentially identical.
What made Shadow of Mordor fun wasn't the number of towers in the game, it was the fact that you could be separated from the towers and murdering hords of orcs.  Now it feels like you're supposed to run past hords of orcs so you can unlock your towers and get to the next area.  So you notice the scenery even less than before.
The idea of giving players unique playstyles is great.  The idea of letting you customize the perks on that skill tree and change your playstyle is also great.
But that's not what the skill tree actually introduces.
The problem is that almost all of the perks have a clearly overpowered option.  For instance, either gaining bonus combos on counterattacks, or the counterattack straight up kills orcs.  Not a decision anyone is going to consider very long.
After paying for a game, it's tedious that these exist at all.
However the purchases are so unnecessary that I don't understand how people are getting upset over it.
Sure, you could pay a few bucks and get 3 orcs.  But you could also spend 10 minutes playing and get 3 orcs, so there's not a lot that you're going to miss out on.
Great ideas.  Good direction.  Poor execution.
If you want to buy this game, just go replay Shadow of Mordor instead.

Sorry, I'd love to recommend this game, but it just didn't do it for me.
I have nothing against mostly narrative 'walkie' experiences - I loved 'Dear Esther' which was like a haunting eulogy/poem, and liked 'Everybody's Gone To The Rapture' with it's small town dramas set against an apocalyptic backdrop. 'Gone Home' was nice too with the house revealing bits and pieces of the characters' past.
I think the difference here is that there's absolutely no dialogue, text, ANYTHING except animation and music. So it's all left up to your imagination as to what's going on. The problem for me was that the storytelling just wasn't strong or interesting enough to grab me at any point, even though the music kept trying to convince me that I was taking part in 'epic' scenes. When the 'revelations' come at the end, they make little sense, emotionally or intellectually even if you've been following all the 'clues' along the way.
I've heard some comparisons to 'Twin Peaks' but other than an obvious homage scene in a roadside bar with a sound-alike tune playing, it reminded me more of 'The X Files'. The music especially was very very reminiscent of 'The X Files'. Imagine an episode of 'The X Files' without dialogue. In first person. That jump cuts around. And you're not sure what's present/past/future/hallucinations. Which is the major issue here... other than some basic plot, I was never quite sure what's going on, why, or what meaning it had in the grander scheme of things... so I never got caught up in it.
It sort of feels like it's going to be playing a detective game... but you don't do any detecting or figure anything out. You just sort of click through scene after scene. If you do happen to walk around... you can occasionally pick up a flower or a feather, which at the beginning you assume there must be some meaning or point to, but the meaning never really comes...
Overall the experience was a little too willfully vague and arty for my tastes and left me cold. Points for a nice art style, lighting etc. While the music was well orchestrated, again it felt a little heavy handed without knowing exactly what was going on.
Even for ~$10... it's hard to recommend this game. Emotionally it didn't grab me. Intellectually it was too vague for me to feel like I was figuring anything out. Mechanically there's really nothing to do other than scan for the next hotspot. Narratively the story is pretty slight and doesn't hold much weight because you're perpetually waiting for clarity which never comes.
Advice for their next game? Steer a little less on the obscure side, just a little, if you want your players to be able to get wrapped up in the tale you're telling.

I have played Hotline Miami for 39 hours and have 100% on the game. Ive have never in my gaming life 100% a game because it just didn't appeal to me, the games never offered me anything in return for 100%ing the it. However Hotline Miami did, not by giving me a item in game or any sort of unlockable but answers to the questions i was asking myself while playing the game. When I found every puzzle piece and got one answer to my many questions i went ahead and got an A+ on every level becasue maybe just maybe the game will give me more answers. I have never played a game with such a well built game world that had me actively searching for game lore.
But what is Hotline Miami? Hotline Miami is a fast-paced, bloody mayhem, murder simulator as i like to call it where you start each level by choosing a mask to wear that will give a slight advantage that will help you and then you walk into the building and either shoot, stab, or smash every living thing in sight. The game promotes and even rewards killing your enemies in the most violent way for example you get lets say 100 points for just shooting some one but 1000 or so for smashing them in the face with a door then sticking a brick in their mouths and stomping on it. More points equals more weapons and more weapons means more ways to earn points which in turn leads to more weapons which goes on until you unlock all weapons.
Now what is the story of Hotline Miami? Well the game has a very odd and unique way of story telling but you the player are receiving strange phone calls urging you to kill everyone in a certain place so of course you go and do it, from here the plot thickens however i cant go much further then this due to spoilers, and I highly recomend you stay from spoilers of this game, ruins the whole thing.
Now one last thing I want to mention is that this game has an amazing soundtrack and deserves more credit then it gets for its soundtrack.
I would highley recomend this game to anyone with the stomach to handle it. Everything about this game is good the only complaint I have is that it sometimes just crashes to desktop but that may be a thing with windows 8 so I cant really blame the game.

Binding of Isaac is top-down roguelike shooter; and boy is it tough!
You start out with nothing to defend yourself besides your tears, in a randomly generating basement of horrors. The bosses, levels, rooms and powerups are different every time you play; and with death being permanent you will get to re-roll often!
Due to it's random nature, entering a room can either reward you with some great powerups, or really ruin your day if it's full of enemies! There is a very addictive element at play that makes you want to try again right after you die, to see if you might make it just a little father this time.
Fully randomized games like this can lead to frustrating or hopeless playthroughs depending on luck, but being that this is by design it's hard to fault the game for this. If you have this game in your library from a recent bundle, give it a go!

After pre-paying this game through a steam sale for $10 and waiting for the second half to complete the game, I can safely say that Broken Age is not worth buying.
Story: Act 1 presented a clear theme of defiance since the protagonists of the story yearning to break free from their own culture respectively and tackle a conflict in their own respective worlds. Act 2, on the other hand, tries its best to answer the players' speculations (or guesses about the lore of the game) from Act 1 but only to end up with more head scratching and confusion that makes you want to say "How does this makes sense?" or just "What?". I'm not going to spoil the ending but the second half's story just feels like it's just wasting your time but the game is obligated to finish the writing.
Gameplay: In Act 1, most of the time, it was a breeze to solve through the puzzles. In Act 2, on the other hand, Double Fine did take the feedback of past players (who played act 1) for more difficult puzzles and made it happen, which I ended up pulling out a guide frequently because I encountered some puzzles that required you to just WAIT and one that you have to fix something with broken wires eats up an hour of the game because there's not much explanation on how this puzzle works which leaves me much frustration for every time the proposed solution doesn't work. I will never understand why hard puzzles complement well with a great story (not this game at least).
Art: The only good aspect of this game, I praised the art design because it's like an interactive children's storybook adventure and now I won't be able to play this game again with my little brothers and sisters due to how the second act ruined the overall story of the game.
Overall: I gave this game a 5/10, I was going to give a 6/10 for its art and some humor but I couldn't, because this is the first video game from kickstarter that achieved publisher-like funding that everyone hoped for AAA quality, and now, here we are, getting a game that ended up mediocre.
Sadly I love playing Psychonauts, and I'm even more sad to say that I'm disappointed in Tim Schafer not able to deliver the game's promise. No matters what others say about cutting him some slack or that we're all too hard on him and his company, this game was funded "$3.3. million + requested additional funding", there's no excuses for delivering a mediocre game.
Again, I can't recommend this point-n-click adventure game. You're better off spending to other interesting games that are worth your time.

As other reviews have stated, there are optional micro transactions.  Here's a quick summary of it:
There's an in-game market, in which you can buy different types of loot crates containing gear or orcs, which are used to defend or attack cassles.  You can buy golden loot crates or silver ones.  The golden loot crates are purchaseable using gold, whiile the silver ones are purchased using Mirian (silver currency).  Gold is purchased using real life money (but you can get a little bit from completion of a quest), while Mirian is in-game currency obtained through playing the game (quest rewards, selling old gear).
The loot/orcs obtained through the golden crates are better than the silver crates.  However, the stuff obtained through silver loot crates is still good.  I have not spent any real life money to purchase loot crates and  there really is no need.  In my opinion, the reviews complaining about micro-transactions in this game are way overblown.  Don't let the option of microtransactions stop you from playing this game.

Six hours in....
It's a good thing this game is free, because Fallout Shelter is the very definition of a grind: inconsequential clicking and long waits with the sole purpose of making small numbers grow into bigger ones.
There is actually very little to do. If it wasn't necessary to click on your vault dwellers when they level up or give birth, or click on rooms to collect resources, the game would probably play itself just fine. Raider attacks and radroach infestations are a joke, as your dwellers will easily overcome them without your input. You can equip them with weapons, outfits and pets to make them more effective, but they don't seem to matter much. Their attributes (the SPECIAL stats that Fallout fans will be very familiar with) seem to dictate how well they do certain jobs, and their level seems to have a major influence on survivability; however, despite the wealth of tips that pop up, it's unclear exactly why or in what way these things matter. Is a vault dweller with high Perception better with a pistol than a vault dweller with low Perception? Fallout lore would say yes, but in Fallout Shelter it doesn't seem to make much difference.
You can send your people into the Wasteland to explore, where they randomly gain XP, caps and items as well as slowly have their health whittled down by enemies. They can be recalled at any time; the longer they are out, however, the longer it takes for them to return, meaning even more waiting. Once you have the Overseer's Office room, you can also send groups on quests that consistently turn up much, much better loot but again have irritatingly long travel times to and from the destination. The gameplay when they get there is a huge disappointment; click on a room to explore, click on an object to loot it, wait as combat happens automatically, click on the End Quest button when it's all over. Again, with a little automation, this rather boring questing could take care of itself while the player concentrated on more interesting activities - of which, sadly, there are none to speak of.
It occured to me at about this point (right before I decided FS wasn't worth any more of my time) that Bethesda missed a golden opportunity with this game. The Vaults in Fallout were each the site of some kind of social experiment. Why on earth did this not carry over to Fallout Shelter? Couldn't we have built the Overseer's Office and then, having built the foundation of a stable Vault, been randomly assigned some crazy end goal to give the player a purpose?
Ultimately, though, that purpose is to send Bethesda a steady trickle of your hard-earned cash via microtransactions. The wait times can be skipped or shortened with Nuka-Cola, and random loot boxes - with caps, vault dwellers, pets, weapons, outfits and crafting materials inside - can help expand on your collection of practically useless equipment, and both can be bought from the store. However, it's just money tossed on the fire to push you more quickly to an endgame that may or may not exist.
Then there are the little things that make the game....less like a game. For instance, your Vault Dwellers will level up over time, but they stop gaining XP until you click on them to acknowledge that fact. Unless you buy the feature from the store to get around that. Which, if I'm reading this right, means that you can pay Bethesda to remove activities from a game that's pretty anaemic when it comes to gameplay already. I mean, I can see the point (money), but I can't see why Bethesda don't even try to hide it.
I think we're hitting microtransaction critical mass these days, in which gamers are so accustomed to pointless cash purposes that devs don't care whether we notice them fleecing us or not. That probably describes Fallout Shelter in a nutshell, so let's get this review over with.
Summary: A freemium game with the life and soul of Fallout sucked out of it and a microtransaction system that will make you weep with it's pointlessness. There may be some goal worth working towards later in the game, but after six hours I've seen no evidence of it and have lost all motivation to keep looking. It gets a point for the Fallout aesthetic, but everything else falls flat. Watch paint dry instead - at least you won't be tempted to pay someone to accelerate the process.
1/10, a complete waste of time.

As a long time fan of Shadow of Mordor, I still can't recommend this game.
The first game perfected the feel of combat and this one takes a major step backwards.  Insta-kill counter-attacks sounds great, but you lose all of the power from your attack buttons and the fastest way to kill things now is to let them hit you.  Instead of rhythm based combat now it's a waiting game.
This minimizes executions and makes combat feel grindy.  Instead of constant zooms and slow-mos into the act of cleaving an orc in half, instead from far away you see several orc gettings stabbed while attacking you and then disappear.  It never feels like you're earning the kills.  More like you're waiting for flies to land on your arm so you can smack them.
The use of orcs in your sieges, bodyguards and castle defense is actually pretty neat.  There's not really any reason for them other than to justify the crate system and microtransactions to fill your supply of orc captains I guess.
But honestly, this was the game decision that made the most sense to me.  It's whimsical and involves murdering hoards of orcs.
If a little bit is good, more must be better!  The idea seems clear.  In practice it just introduces a lot of grind.  Go to the new area and now you need to figure out who all the orcs are again because they're unknown.  And you need to find all of the towers and artefacts again.
There's never really any reason to backtrack to a different area unless you're deciding to defend a castle.  All the areas are essentially identical.
What made Shadow of Mordor fun wasn't the number of towers in the game, it was the fact that you could be separated from the towers and murdering hords of orcs.  Now it feels like you're supposed to run past hords of orcs so you can unlock your towers and get to the next area.  So you notice the scenery even less than before.
The idea of giving players unique playstyles is great.  The idea of letting you customize the perks on that skill tree and change your playstyle is also great.
But that's not what the skill tree actually introduces.
The problem is that almost all of the perks have a clearly overpowered option.  For instance, either gaining bonus combos on counterattacks, or the counterattack straight up kills orcs.  Not a decision anyone is going to consider very long.
After paying for a game, it's tedious that these exist at all.
However the purchases are so unnecessary that I don't understand how people are getting upset over it.
Sure, you could pay a few bucks and get 3 orcs.  But you could also spend 10 minutes playing and get 3 orcs, so there's not a lot that you're going to miss out on.
Great ideas.  Good direction.  Poor execution.
If you want to buy this game, just go replay Shadow of Mordor instead.

Great story, great setup, awesome music and atmosphere. It feels like reading a good book.
You take the role of a writer having creative block. There's good character development of the protagonist, his wife and friends, people that he meets and the "dark essence" thing that he encounters.
The game revolves around the battle between light and darkness, so flashlights, flares and other efficient light sources are your only defences against the all-consuming evil.
There are enemies to fight, but you can only harm them in the light (also the aim needs some getting used to because of the awkward camera view). This makes the combat system more interesting and challenging.
The story itself is presented in chapters, told through cinematics and snippets of text/audio here and there. There's plenty of stuff to discover and the game invokes enough curiosity to go exploring now and then.
The horror element is soft, very good for people with little or no experience with horror games. It starts off a bit sharp, setting the mood, but there's good balance between "everything is fine" and "run for your life". It's more of a thriller really.
Voice acting, music, cinematics, graphics and game mechanics are all top-notch. Get this game if you like a good story.

I have to re-write my review after the game, with all of its promised DLC delivered and completed.  I have been a gamer for over 30 years, and I am very picky about what I play now that I'm in my 40's.
First off, I want to say that I enjoyed, and would recommend Mafia 3.  Let's get that out of the way.  The story is excellent, the immersion is good, and the flavor of the place is what keeps me coming back just to raise a bit of hell here and there.  I have done just about all there is to do in the game, and I'm basically out of bad guys to kill, and things to blow up.
The best feature of any game that can be made is to give an excuse or a reason for someone to keep playing.  This is why I think a game like this with a noticeable affect on the entire game world is necessary.  The story is fantastic.  All of the DLC is quite good, and their stories are very good.  I can't fault it, really, but the game does have serious issues with physics, and it's buggy.
The "Herbalism" bit has errors in it that are very frustrating, and cascade, and cause me to re-do and throw away strains that have taken me HOURS to put together.  I find this to be inexcusable.  I have mentioned this bug on the forums, and there's been no response to it.  I feel rather disenfranchised because of that.
The street conversations and commentary get redundant after a while.  It's totally possible to add more conversation, and this should have been done.
The combat is repetitive.  It's fun, but it's repetitive.
The feeling that you're doing something in the world or having an impact needs to be reinforced more than just a radio report or an angry reply to a talk radio show.  I was awestruck when I first played the game, and heard "The Hollow Speaks" while I was on a boat in the Bayou.  It was epic.  Much of the quality of the actual gameplay is a bit superficial, and in the 17th year of the 21st century, added depth is not too much to ask.  In Mafia II there were elements of the game superior to Mafia III, and it's a shame that this is the case.  I love playing a black antihero, and getting an education on how things were in the South in 1968.  I think it's brilliantly done, but there needs to be more depth.
I'll give examples:
1.)  As your wealth and reputation bolsters, word on the street WILL get you more respect among some, as well as make you a target for others.  This should be a constant throughout the game.
2.)  While you cultivate marijuana and name your products and have them dispensed, you should overhear people saying things like, "You 'aint lived 'til you tried some Bayou Bliss!"  (Or whatever the name of the stuff is you make)
3.)  If you cannot do a side mission anymore to increase the earn of an underboss, the mission shouldn't even be available anymore.  It shows lack of polish.
4.)  The Artificial Intelligence is a bit laughable at points.  Whether it's the public, or enemy players you're fighting.  Too often I see people DIVING right in front of me while I drive, and I cannot avoid them.  They wind up dead, and some witness goes screaming to the telephone to drop a dime on me.
5.)  Walk/run should be TOGGLED.  It was toggled at first, and these people removed it.  Don't know why they did that, and I'm not impressed with that.
6.)  There should be options for buying property and donating to renovating neighborhoods.  Paying off politicians, and influencing decisions made by elected officials in the city.  Working/playing the game to build things up and have something visual to show for it all would keep people playing, and eager to recommend the game to others.  This game was released incomplete, and people like myself paid a high premium for the seaso pass, and I was left wanting more, which in a game like this isn't really a bad thing.
I've gotten my money's worth of enjoyment and time played in the game, and I'd recommend it with enthusiasm, but I don't feel like the developers much care about what the gamers want with this title, and I don't want to see the Mafia franchise fail.  There's still potential to make the game far better than it is, and I hope these new devs do something with it.

Alright well I'll start by saying that I've now played through the storyline once and have completed the entire game and am starting my second run. I was a fanatic of Mafia II, putting well over 1000 hours into the game, so I have an emotional attachment to the series, so the way I graded the game was considering the fact that I held it to a premium standard.
Pros:
-Fantastic storyline (As expected)
-Very long storyline, plenty of hours of singleplayer fun
-Great character progression
-That wonderful Mafia soundtrack in relation to the time-period
-Incredibly fun driving (In Simulation mode)
-Beautiful cinematics, both graphically and in relation to the storyline
-Increased functionality when it comes to running the mob
-Several ties to Mafia II (Which is really great for a Mafia series fanatic such as myself)
-Very historically accurate
-Immersive feel to the game altogether
-Decent replayability
-Large map
Cons:
-Graphics are not too much of an upgrade from Mafia II
-Definitely less of a Mafia feel to the game, more of a gang
-Tasks seem repetitive: Destroy this, kill him, steal that
-No buying cars/switching your outfit
-Much less free roaming options: No going to restaurants, buying hot dogs, getting your shoes shined, etc.
All in all, I really do enjoy the game. I love the new functionality when it comes to running the mob, however I wish it would have been more of a 1940-50's style Italian Mafia, rather than this new era ghetto gang, no offense. The music is awesome as expected, the storyline is great and I love all the Mafia II references, some of which will really catch you by surprise.
To conclude: Would I recommend paying $60 for this game?  For anyone who enjoys the Mafia series, or the Mafia in general, absolutely. This is a great addition to the collection. For someone looking for a 1960's GTA, maybe this isn't the game for you. This game has plenty of potential if you give it the chance.

It's bad. It's really bad. You want to like it, but it's just bad.
The narrative is trope and cliche with flashes of "oh that's neat." The visuals are garbage with a miser's pinch of "oh that's pretty." The action is mediocre with one redeeming quality, the guys die in agony when you kill them. No moral dillemas to speak of, no real consequences to your choices beyond angering your NPC buddies (only one of whom I found even remotely likeable.)
There are 3 missions: kill, interrogate, destroy. But really there may only be one kind, kill and then when you're done killing do the other thing. They don't even let you accidentally kill the guys you're supposed to interrogate. They go to one knee after being shotgun blasted in the face 6 times so Lincoln can stab them to death after. Like if you NEED to have this interrogation mechanic in there, at least make it a mechanic and not just a "press b to win."
THe combat had the potential to be glorious, but there's not much reason to buy guns as the bad guys all carry whatever you'd want and Lincoln doesn't carry much ammo so you always do the drop and swap in longer fights, and the finishers are brutal until you've seen all the animations. There are about 3 on the rails finishers per weapon type. Once you've played for 4 hours, you've seen them all. After that, it's generic over the shoulder try stealth and then blow everyone up cause you got caught.
And let's talk about the stealth actually- 1) there's no benefit to using it. You don't get anything but the odd satisfaction of "no one saw me, a 6 foot 4 bodybuilder, creep through this warehouse in the middle of the work day" if you do a mission all stealth. 2.) Civillians don't give you way either. 3.) You can get through a mission without shooting anyone because the line of sight for enemies is about 15 inches as far as I can tell. It's just... cheaply implemented. It feels like the stealth mechanic is just there so they can say "and you can approach missions in a variety of ways." Variety does not equal 2. And both ways are boring.
Driving is not fun. Won't say much about it.
Map is small, which I can almost forgive because there a lot of enterable buildings and the assets are good looking. But still, there's a bit of copy and paste throughout.
Just... don't buy it. Seriously. Above all else it's a bad PC port. I won't even say wait for GOTY or expansions, because at its core it's a mediocre hunk of crap.

Got this game as an impulse buy today after reading the description on the Store Page, and because the game art is reminiscent of "Guacamelee!"
The most important thing you need to know is that this game doesn't have AI opponents to fill the gaping friendless hole in your soul. Note the lack of a "Single Player" tag in the game's description, that's painfully accurate. The game is fun, but in order to enjoy it you need to have real flesh-and-blood friends (local or online), or at least sarcastic siblings who will humour you and your weirdo review-writing habit.
Without another person to play with, your foot will have to play the unenviable role of "Punching Bag #2" by occasionally tapping the Jump and Fire buttons.
The controls are simple enough that you lonely nimble-toed gamers out there could very well play effectively with yourselves with a rolling fat-toe-pinky-toe technique. There's Jump, Shoot, and Move, and that's all you need to enjoy this game.
No? That's right, you also need friends. Hey, look at that, you ARE paying attention!
With a controller, you move around with a Stick or D-Pad, Shoot in any direction by tilting the other Stick, and Jump with the Trigger buttons. Contrary to what the shrieking young man in the Game Description video says, the controls are fine. If your brain can't adapt to using Trigger as Jump in a game with only 2 action buttons, then you have bigger problems than not having any friends to play with.
(He does have friends though, and I'm very jealous.)
Keyboard controls are familiar; Aim with the Mouse, Shoot with LMB, Move with WASD, Jump with Space or RMB.
Every player starts a match with a basic trusty revolver. It fires continually as long as the Aim Stick is tilted, and reloads round-by-round whenever you stop blasting the hell out of your imaginary friend's digital corpse. Lots of weapons randomly appear as power-ups that give you a cool new deadly thing to fling around, while its ammo lasts. There are bows, knives, boomerangs, some kind of rocket fist, sonic pulse weapons, vengeful spirit skulls, you know, the usual. They're all useful, none of them make you feel bad you went for the bottle-bombs instead of the throwing axe, especially because any weapon will OHKO a player.
There are currently 5 Stages to fight in, and they all look great. One of them even has destructible, regenerating platforms for more mayhem.
A quirk I noticed is that I couldn't jump down through platforms, but I could jump up through them. Also, some weapons aren't stopped by the environment. For example, the Boomerang corkscrews freely through the map until it wangs someone in the neck or disappears on its own. There are absolutely no safe zones or cover from the starting Revolver, it passes through everything. Things like Dynamite and Knives do bounce off the floor and walls.
To wrap this up, $4.00 gives us a solid framework on which the Developers say they will continue to build on, giving us more content in the future.
And to unwrap this, with so many games like this popping up, they need every bit of help they can get. Currently it's almost impossible to find an online match, even after switching through all the available servers. And while that's not a problem for you hoity-toity types, with your local friends and families all sharing in the lead-slinging fun, us rebel loners with sweet♥♥♥♥♥'90s action mullets are left out.
The developers said there are no plans at this time to add AI opponents. Bummer.
So, why am I still recommending this game even though I'll probably never play it again? Because the world doesn't revolve around me or what I want or what I think is best. The developers made a game intended to be played with friends, and that's exactly what it is. It excels at that.
Good job, Devs, I'm looking forward to that future content, if not for AI players then for more of the colorful yet haunting stage art.

TL;DR version
Pros:
- Very cheap price tag
- Easy to learn
- Fun party game to play with friends
- Has a sense of humor
- Good selection of characters
- Good amount of guns/powerups
- Supports Local Multiplayer
- Controller support
- Wilhelm scream
Cons:
- No Ai/Bots
- Small playerbase so it's hard to find a match online
- Not very Mouse&Keyboard friendly (at least navigating the menu)
- Small amount of maps
- Spawning needs tweaking
Long version
This game is actually quite fun but its biggest drawback is the lack of AI/bots. This is crucial due to the small playerbase which means finding other people online to play with is almost impossible at the moment. THAT SAID, there is local multiplayer so you can play with up to 3 of your friends on your computer. The game is also quite cheap so convincing a few friends to buy it so that you can play with each other online shouldn't be too hard.
As for the game itself, you have 4 different game modes and 5 maps to play on for now. The game modes are Loot, Deathmatch, Capture the Flag and Banditos. In Loot you try to collect as many bags of loot as you can while trying to take out your enemies to make them lose money. As for Banditos, you have hold onto a golden monkey idol to earn time/points. The person who held it the most/longest by the end of the round wins. The different game modes add some nice variety but I have only played them against one other person so I'm not sure how balanced they are with a full group of 4.
The maps themselves are interesting but I feel like some would get really chaotic with 4 players due to the small size. When I say small size, I don't necessarily mean that the maps themselves are small, but that you have to take into account that you're shooting projectiles that travel a good distance and are able to go through most of the floors and platforms.  Also, spawning next to an enemy is somewhat common so that's something they'll have to tweak. The player who respawns after getting killed has spawn protection so if they spawn right next to you then you're most likely going to die.
There are 19 characters to choose from which vary from classic western to unique characters like Cheese Wedge which is literally a cheese wedge with a cowboy outfit. This means you can try to have a classic showdown or a goofy battle depending on what your tastes are. Either way, someone's getting shot ;)
You can tweak the Match settings (amount of rounds/length), Powerup and Weapon settings before selecting a game mode. This is handy for those who find the default round length too short or want to change the default weapon, etc. As for the weapons/powerups, they certainly spice things up during the matches and can change the tide of the battle if you pick up the right one. They do spawn on random parts of the map so you gotta be lucky that it spawns close and that it's the weapon you want to use. Each weapon is unique and, depending on your preference, can be either good or bad.
In conclusion, it's certainly worth a buy if you have a least one other person to play it with. If you're unsure that you'll have someone else to play the game with then avoid it and wait to see if either the devs decide to add bots to the game or the game's playerbase increases.

I have no regrets backing this game. It's a charming adventure game with an interesting story, engaging characters, and clever dialogue. Everything I wanted out of a Tim Schaefer game. It took longer than promised, but if you watch their documentary, you'd learn why.
Honestly, my one complaint are the puzzles in the second half of the game. People complained that the first half's puzzles are easy. And to be fair, they are for the most part. The second half, however, has some incredibly frustrating, unintuitive puzzles that make you want to pull your hair out. Without giving anything away, these are the pipe, knot, and wire puzzles. Most especially the wire puzzle, which comprises most of the final puzzles in the game. These especially require pen and paper beside you to write down diagrams and guides. It's the only way to complete them without having to go back and forth too much.
Still, despite those frustrations, I greatly enjoyed the game. It's a satisfying game that any adventure game fan will enjoy.  It's no Grim Fandango or Monkey Island, but it's still a perfectly good adventure game. I honestly don't think it's worth the full asking price, but it's certainly worth it if you can nab it on a 50% (or lower) sale.

I played Shadow of Mordor many hours and in my opinion this Game is a great improvement of the previous Game.
Gameplay: There are still some little Clunky things in the movement but most of it got improved very good, for example that you can sprint without looking for stones on the ground that give you Elven Sprint. Alot of the Combat animations are the same but it feels more fluent than in the Shadow of Mordor.
- Now we have big Fortresses to  attack or defend against invading Orc armies.
Orcs: There are more different, Intimidating, funny,  Orcs around and now we have combat trolls called Olog-Hai. There are more ways to interact or meddle with them, like letting them fight against other Orcs in the Fight Pits to increase their level or, if they are defeated just take the Orc that killed yours into your Army!
- After you gained the Dominate skill in Shadow of Mordor, the game turned into an easy runthrough, now you have Orcs that can resist getting dominated and there are orcs that give you a real challange.
It felt really good to defeat them after they killed me a couple of times.
Story: The Story feels way better than in Shadow of Mordor and gives alot of memorable Scenes, there nearly was nothing like that in Shadow of Mordor's Story.
Online Mode:  You can do two kinds of online missions:
Vendetta: Avenge your Friends or other Players who got killed by a nasty Orc to get rewards, a sick looking legendary Set for example.
Online Fortress Siege:  You can attack the fortress of your Friends or other Players to get Ranked up and get nice rewards, it gives you a good challange and you can see what orcs fellow Players choose to recruit.
Only downside is that if you attack a fortress your attacking captains CAN DIE, so choose your forces with care.
You can even attack your own fortress to test your defenses!
The Endgame: It's grindy and repetitive, i still had fun doing the "Shadow Wars Act"
Lootboxes: You don't really need to use that option to finish the game completely.
- The Silver Boxes are quite nice because you can get some different Orcs and Bonus abilities for them and they cost Currency you easly get ingame by killing orcs or doing missions.

I'm a big tower defense fan and I think have played most of them (including a majority of the wc3 TD's), and I'm also a sucker for hunting achievments to 100%. (Just for you to know how much your views aligns with mine). Steam says I spent 70 hours on this, but I think half of that is probably closer to the truth.
"Defend Your Life" is a "kingdom rush" clone (which I believe set the precendent with "guardhouse"-towers spawning blocker-units).
The artstyle is consistent and good enough for any TD as far as I'm conserned. It has a fairly original theme and sticks to it.
The gameplay has a few ideas you seldom see in TDs: Like two monster-types that combine into a stronger if you fail in preventing them from meeting up. Or the map with a destroyable bridge to change monsters' path. Or the oxygen-fans (income) that are boostable by your other towers.  Nice but not exactly revolutionary - nothing game changing.
The amount of towers in your arsenal is sparse at best.
The progression feels very standard but there has clearly been an effort to make a few maps specificly target certain talents. It's a good thought - talents should be situational in TD's to make the strategic choices interesting. BUT it fails short because the talents are too dull and the choices are too stupid: "On this map you can only use power ups" or "On this map you'll only see one monster type the first 20 waves and then it changes" (Yeah, there is actually a pop-up message telling you just that as the map begins).
The biggest issue this game has is the hero-control. It's clearly made for phones/tablets. It feels like it has been copied from similar games. Actually I'm sure it has been copied. It's WAY too familiar and I wouldn't be surprised if I learned the control scheme is coming directly from the unity asset store, perhaps some TD kit?  The problems with moving your hero (or not moving your hero) depending on if you click on pathable or non-pathable ground. The notion that deselecting your hero after moving him once. The way your hero approaches monsters, ignoring any and all pathing while the monster stops to wait. It's all way too familiar, and it's not good!
On later levels a big chunk of the gameplay depend on you targeting specific monsters, and the controls being so inprecise can be infuriating.
There are however decent keyboard shortcuts in this game which I applaud the devs for! (In worse TD's It's the face palm moment when a mobile port TD hasn't even bothered to include keyboard shortcuts)
I also really appreciate the difficulty of the last (say 5 or so) levels in the game.
You can't avoid any of the achievments as go through the game, which makes them bland and superfluous. (I got the last achievment "Level up your hero to level 50" at level 48, How now that is possible?)
So to sum things up:  A somewhat generic TD with a fresh layer of paint on top. Poor controls. But it's still better than your average TD and gives you a decent spin for your money. I'd say give it a go if you don't hate TD's and the price is around $5 or less.

I've put sixty hours in both Shadow of Mordor and Shadow of War, collected all there was to collect in the former, and almost with Shadow of War; and cleared up to Stage 3 of the Shadow Wars in Shadow of War-- and overall, I'd say Shadow of War was an amazing game... Through the first three acts. I didn't run into all that *many* bugs, and what bugs I did see weren't the most game-affecting of what I found; but my biggest gripe with SoW is Act 4: The Shadow Wars.
As prior said, I'm in Stage 3; and frankly, that's probably exactly where I'm staying. When I got this game, I was under the impression from journalist reviews that the presence of microtransactions wasn't onerous in the slightest, that they were wholly unnecessary, and the game could be beaten without them.
I no longer believe this.
Over the first two stages of the Shadow Wars, I have lost-- counted-- a full 27 captains to the one method of leveling your orcs up in this game: The Fight Pits. Out of those 27 losses, 18 of which happened in Nurnen, 6 of them were both higher leveled than their foe and at least had a soft counter ($enemy_captain is damaged heavily by $element) and 8 of them were close in level, but had a hard counter(Terror of various elements, Beast Fodder, Soft Target, etc). The AI for these fights is garbage, you can't do anything to help your orcs when they're in a bad situation, and the only recourse you have for losing an orc is recruiting the one who killed him at the end... Which wouldn't be that bad a thing if they didn't succumb to the exact same problem as all the other captains I've watched die now.
This just straight up isn't fun. At all. I don't have the tolerance to grind an RNG screensaver for hundreds of hours just to get a cutscene that isn't even all that worth the time that I could see wasting on the Shadow Wars if I had more spoons for tedious content.
Overall, I can recommend this game for the first three acts, but that's about the point where the game runs out of gas. We'll see if the DLC campaigns are worth a reinstall.

TLDR: This game is not MAFIA 3 I wanted, but it is still very fun to play! (If you can run it)
Long Story:
-Technicals..
First of all, 30 fps really worsened my the first impression. However, with patch out I gave it another shot and realized its actually very fun! At 1440p with 4790k and 1070 OC it runs 45-60, which is OK. On 1080 it runs smoothly at 60fps. I think many people who are expecting optimized experience need not apply. It takes about 2.5 VRAM, but textures is not the strongest point here. IMHO, I think the developers followed 'Witcher 3' path where shaders were more of a focus rather than large textures. I have to say, each persons' preferences are different, but I love what Hanger did with lightning effects. Warning, AA makes it look very blurry, so turn it down! The sunrise\sundown\rain colors and reflections are pure beauty! As a package, the game looks quite good.
-Story
Well, without spoiling much, you are playing as Lincoln Clay who is out to destroy Sal Marcano's Mafia in New Bordeaux. He is not an Italian, nor part of another Mafia. He is just there for the act of vengence. There is not much of a climbing the Mafia ladder, just kill, clear territory, and kill some more. The story is bretty good, but it is not Mafia story, or I guess not what I would liked it to be. However, it is still enjoyable as hell.
-Is it fun? 'Gameplay'
Yeah, I would say it is loads of fun. The shooting is the most satisfying I have ever experienced. Melee attacks are freaking awesome. Punching, shooting, music, and voicing sound amazing. There are also many small details in this game that makes it so immersive. The missions can get representative at times if your only goal is to go trough all of them as fast as humanly possible, but they are followed with some good story pieces that makes it worth the trouble.
I rate 'Big Black Boy's Vengance Story'  3 letter K's and a big Thumbs Up!

Overall, I love this game. I would love to say it's really great, but it's got some pretty glaring flaws. I'm running everything on its highest possible setting and the graphics are still pretty dated- arguably on the same level as Mafia II.
While the graphics hold it back (and seriously, they do- the foliage looks like a game from 2005) the rest of the game is pretty sound. The voice acting is good in my opinion, and the soundtrack is pretty good as well. The vintage theme of the game is what really gets me. When playing Mafia II, one was acutely aware that it was a fictionalized game rather than a pure historical look- however, although almost eveything in this game is fictionalized (locations, restaurants, auto brands, etc.) it does feel like one is stepping back in time. The theme really does feel like 1968, rather than a GTA game with a 1950's skin on it.
The gameplay itself is good. Not great, but good. What's really interesting is that there are some actual Playboy articles scanned into the game- so yes, you can now read Playboy for the articles. There are, however, some downsides. Cover and stealth sometimes feels pretty clunky, and the shops seem to serve little to no purpose which is pretty disappointing considering there are so many of them.
Overall, I bought this game because I was excited to find an open world game set in 1968, and I liked Mafia II enoguh taht I was roped into buying the sequal. Thus far, it's been pretty impressive, but there are some fundamental issues with the game, primarily the poor graphics quality. The obnoxious 30FPS cap has been removed, so thankfully that's not a problem anymore. Overall, I would say it might be woth it at 59.99, but if it goes on sale in the future, it is definitely worth a sale price.

NOW ONTO THE REVIEW.
graphics, sound & artstyle
- Sombrero has a very rustic yet coming of age look that almost hypnotizes you. Whether on regular or "Grandpa's TV Mode" this game seems, sounds and looks like it was one of yester-years greatest couch multiplayer games. I am absolutely enamored by the look of it and every character plays to the feel of the whole game and really brings the experience to another level.
gameplay:
- 1-4 player multiplayer game. gameplay is simple to grasp. (With control pad) You move around with the left joystick, jump with the triggers and shoot in the direction you want with the right joystick. There are four game modes, each with very distinct feels to them.
Loot, puts players up against each other in a time limit setting to gather the most money or "loot" they can. Each kill takes money away from other players and certain pickups could mean all the difference in a game. Every penny counts till the last second. (There were a couple of games that were won in the last few seconds by less that $10!)
Deathmatch, simple and straight-forward. First to get to a certain amount of kills wins and with one hit kills being a main focus of the game, it's always up in the air on who may win.
Capture the Flag, here there are no teams, the only objective is to get as many flags back to your own base before the time runs out. What makes it fun and difficult is the sporadic spawns. You can have made a run and killed a player protecting their base, run back with their flag to your own base only for them to spawn in your base. It's frustrating at times, but definitely an equalizer!
Banditos, probably in my opinion the best game mode. You fight for control of a talisman and the person that holds it for the longest time after an allotted time, wins the game.
Whats the price?
- The retail price for this is $14.99 USD.
How many hours estimated?
- I can see myself playing the game for well over 20+ hours. With local and online multiplayer game modes, this is the type of game I love to just pickup and play for an hour or two at times.
Pros/Cons
- Pros:
'aesthetically beautiful
'great sound
'easy controllers
'online multiplayer
'4 very distinct game modes
'plethora of characters to choose from
'short matches
'extremely fun
-Cons
'online community is small; wait time is long
'no bots
Buy it, Wait for it to go on sale, Don't.
-As noted earlier, the game is $14.99 USD and at it's current state, I really have no complaints other than perhaps with Bots, it could be a lot of fun when your friends just cant come over. Also- at times with all the chaos happening I would lose my concentration and forget where I am. But, I had a ton of fun with this game and I was just immersed in the world of Sombrero. Santa Muerte, Rojo Caliente, Senor Padre, i felt compelled to go back and play with every character I possibly could. I would absolutely recommend it to anyone who loves Indie Multiplayer games, Spaghetti Westerns or fast paced action. BUY IT NOW.

There are games that get pumped up with so much hype whipping people into a frenzy, parting with their hard earned cash, only to then leave the gamer wishing they had not wasted their money, and then there are games that truly deserve the hype and actually end up exceeding the gamers expectations. Bioshock without any shadow of a doubt is in the class that should DEMAND you play the game. This game has the ability to suck you in, leaves you marvelling at just how much there is to do and the fun you can have doing it and… well… quite frankly for the last four days certainly left me with severe lack of sleep as I just could not put the game down. In short this game rocks and must be played!
Bioshock the latest first person shooter from 2K Games and considered “spiritually” to be the successor to their previous System Shock 2 title, is set in 1960 starting with our hero Jack surviving a plane crash in the ocean and making his way in a bathysphere (mini submarine) travels to the underwater City that is Rapture. On his journey in the bathysphere Jack is painted a picture by a man named Ryan that Rapture is a beautiful and wonderful place to live, only to leave Jack bearing witness to a completely different picture arriving at Rapture and to a City that looks to be in ruin and with Jack quickly being attacked by a rather grim looking creature that is a Splicer. Armed with a two-way radio Jack is befriended by Atlas and starts his journey through Rapture for what will become the fight of his life. Welcome to Rapture, this is Bioshock and make sure you have a good stock of clean pants, because you are in for one Hell of a ride.
Control wise Bioshock is played from the first person perspective and the buttons are mapped very neatly. Your right shoulder button cycles through all your collected weapons with the right trigger controller the fire on each weapon. Holding the RB button brings up all your weapons and makes it a lot easier to quickly change to any weapon when the heat is on. The left shoulder button cycles through all your available plasmids (more on that later) with the left trigger activating your chosen plasmid. Again holding the LB button brings up all of your active plasmid choices and lets you switch quickly when needed. That leaves the face buttons to be assigned to the likes of using a med kit, reloading a weapon or topping up on your plasmid eve, interacting with objects and jumping. Finally the thumbsticks are then left to control movement and panning the camera and clicking in the thumbsticks will activate crouching (left) and also zoom control (right) if a weapon allows it.
The first thing you will notice in Bioshock apart from the fact you are deep underwater is that your surroundings are rather dark and as a hint for the people that have yet to play the game, before you even start playing you are asked to agree the lighting levels and if you feel the need, then whack it up slightly to help you… That said I never touched any settings as the mood is perfect and fitting for a destroyed city and getting leapt on by a Splicer out of the darkness is all part of the fun really.
Now while I leap into the gameplay aspect I don’t want to give too much of the game away as the plot has more twists and turns than a roller coaster so I will leave the gameplay to what you have in front of you rather than what you are doing for who and who said what. But in saying that, and just to get the ball rolling… you have arrived in Rapture with Atlas talking you through where you need to go and with Ryan the creator of Rapture watching you on the CCTV system and seeming to think you are CIA or KGB decides to set his army of Splicers and bots on you… “Well nobody ever said life was easy – eh”.
Surviving in Rapture will come down to a few things. Firstly there will be the choice of weapons from wrench through to pistol ending in a rather awesome flamethrower. The neat touch here is that these weapons seem to have been created after the city was in ruins with people fighting to survive so have a rather home feel DIY look to them bolted together with empty tins and what not rather than being all futuristic (well after all this is 1960). You will find weapons scattered throughout Rapture but your best bet is to look to prise them from the dead hands of a Splicer you just killed. You will also find two types of vending machines throughout every level of Rapture that will allow you to keep topping up on your supplies of ammo should you be running low – that said ammo can also be collected from fallen enemies and you should never struggle to be without. You will also later in the game have the ability to create your own ammo from bits and pieces you find scattered throughout Rapture with the U-Invent machines and you will also find weapon upgrade machines that can only be used once, but will change how your weapon operates improving it in certain categories.
Your second piece of survival comes down to plasmids, and plasmids genetically modify your bodies’ structure allowing you to attack people in a whole new way. These plasmids include being able to shock someone, stunning them so you can move in for the kill, freezing someone allowing you to explode them into shards of ice and through to setting people on fire to name a few. Plasmids can be found throughout Rapture but later in the game pretty much becomes purchased with ADAM (will cover that little bit later). Just like you have a Health bar, you also have an Eve bar, and it is Eve that is the substance needed to sustain your use of plasmids. Top ups to Eve can be found in syringe form throughout Rapture or again by purchase from a vending machine/finding the syringes on dead bodies. Without doubt plasmids make the game what it is and are damn fun to use, and you will end up on the look out for bigger and better plasmids so you can experiment over and over again with new and stronger attacks. Having a Splicer run at you only for you to freeze them, whip out your shogun to watch them explode into tiny shards of ice never stopped being funny, amazing to see in action and damn cool to do. Aside from plasmids you also find and can purchase tonics, which are designed to enhance you in a number of ways from both physical attributes to mental. These cover the likes of being able to disappear if you stand still, through to being able to move faster all the way through to being able to hack objects easier. Tonics are not to be confused with plasmids, which in effect are weapons… tonics are there to make your life a bit easier but are not physical weapons you can see in action – just think of them as enhanced abilities.
I referred to ADAM which essentially is the substance needed to enhance your abilities but gathering ADAM in itself presents you a constant two prong problem. Little girls in the game which are referred to as ‘Little Sisters’ carry ADAM in their body, but your first problem is finding them with your second problem is having to get past their personal body guards that are the ‘Big Daddies’. Big Daddies are genetically modified and walk around in huge diving suits and carry enough armour and weaponry to scare the living daylights out of anyone. To get the ADAM you have to defeat the Big Daddy and then should you manage to do that the game then switches you to a moral choice to make in order to obtain your prize. When you move up to a Little Sister that has just lost her body guard by your hand you are given two choices. Harvest the ADAM which will give you the max amount but basically means killing the child, or rescue the girl which gives you less ADAM but with another character in the game (no spoilers as to who) promising you future rewards for having done so. Your moral choices will also ultimately give you two distinctive endings to the game… I was the good guy and rescued them all, so I am yet to see my evil side ending, but having seen pieces wrote on it

Granted I haven't played the original Witcher due to the combat system in it, Witcher 2 is a lot better than its predecessor. The continuation of "multiple" paths in the story line to effect the overall outcome continues and with the well expected conclusion of the trilogy coming out soon, it's even funner now to replay through it again and relive the adventure.
The storyline is intriguing and while some actions are locked in place, the overall feeling that you can change the environment is there. Most of the characters have advanced back storys that help add to them to make them feel more than just a single random person throwing quests at you and you don't have to kill the trolls!
The combat style supports a miriad of different techniques such as support caster builds, ranged assassin builds, stealth attacks, straight out melee sluggers, and of course the balanced approach for all skill sets. The only thing really missing is the fact you still cannot use a dedicated ranged weapon such as a crossbow or longbow. While I am a fan of swordsmanship, there have been times when having a crossbow would of been a godsend.
The gameplay mechanics are smooth and 99% of the time, balanced and fair. It's rare that I find a glitched area or a zone that results in a reset as in some games such as Fallout where you can get stuck on a cliff or stuck in mid-air while jumping. Visual appearances are, even on lower settings very eye-catching and the developers did a very good job in making sure that the game looks as good as it plays.
Overall score: 8/10
+ Good storyline and solid character builds
+ Balanced combat styles that are both unique and worth using
+ You can actually for the most part, stealth through the game if you really want a challenge
+ Both routes can be set to a good or bad ending instead of fixed
- Combat can be unforgiving when barrel rolling
Definetly would recommend this game to anyone who has played and enjoyed Skyrim, Assassins Creed, previous Witcher title, Tomb Raider, Fallout. Worth the time it takes to play and definetly worth playing through four times (both good endings, and both bad endings)

Mechanics on the other hand is an completely different story, new varients of enemies, captain classes with indvidual strengths to change your approach to battle (Yes these changes of strategy are minuscule, while environment is still OP as hell, it's the variation of the experience which is the positive thing).
