Not only does it make the thing you're killing more interesting, it also is an immersive element.
Exploration now uses the similar system of Witcher III: The Wild Hunt, in which you have main quests, side quests (from this game's perspective and points of interest within multiple sections of maps. While the previous installment has this, the new one has more than double the amount of sectioned maps, slightly smaller, but overall covering way more surface area.
Gear has now become more advanced and customizable. An leveling system is used according to crates on the market, enemy leveling and level scaling. Challenges have been added to rare, epic and legendary gear, which once complete, allows the player to upgrade their gear to the predestinated level stated in the information section. Gear can also be upgraded with gems, which provides bonuses, which alter depending on two things; the type of gem and the type of loot it is being fused into. Gems also have an progression system which amplifies the effect.
With the gaming industry going to♥♥♥♥♥♥ microtranscations within an single player RPG is one symptom of that. I will try to be as least self-rightous as I possibly can be in this next paragragh. Only someone who either likes to waste money or who has an incredibly shallow understanding for this game systematically speaking, would buy any of these microtranscations. If you like to spend time doing captain missions and doing everything on the map, you're going to level significantly faster than those who don't, even if you don't -- main quests provide a lot of XP.
From an theoretical and realistic persective (I haven't bought any microtranscations), if bought two gold loot crates, granted you'll get very good loot, with exceptional qualities, 10 ish hours later you'll more than likely come accross better gear. Which then comes to my other point, there is an painfully obvious reason why they'd add XP boosts, because the loot system is specifcally designed to work like that so you keep buying crates.
One good thing that is good about this microtranscation system, it's completely optional. It won't effect your gameplay in the slightest if you don't invest. If you wan't to buy them, go ahead but just remember you're endorsing something which is ruining the industry.
I found that the story is more interesting than the previous games, especially when there is more characters and lore from the books directly involved. To some respects there can be small twists, which peak interests but aren't experience changing. I will keep this section short but as an concluion the story definately feels a lot more "Middle-earth" than the last game.
To conclude this review, I must say that if you did enjoy Shadow of Mordor, you definately will enjoy this game, especially with the more immersive and advanced mechanics that have been added. At full price, totaling at 45 GBP, price for content ratio is good, however because of the repetitive nature, everyone will have an different tolerance to this. If you have assurance that you'll enjoy the game and get your moneys worth, i'd recommend this to you.

First of all let me say that I am biased to anything with good music, and the orchestral language utilized by Virginia is nothing short of spectacular. The sheer breadth of the music is astonishing, it moves smoothly from touching to curious, to excitement, to shock… In fact, it is what I find to be the central piece in navigating through the somewhat chaotic narrative structure. It holds the central theme of each segment and paves the way for the movement ahead. For me, the music brought alive the story, especially when there is no speech to be found, it fills the void with something truly sublime.
Virginia is a courageous experiment, it is heavy-handed and linear, but compact and elegant. This is my personal preference, but I found a remarkable sensitivity from the creators of this game. Given the fractured structure and many surprising narrative jumps, I found myself swaying on the thin line between maddening frustration and curiosity. It somehow managed provide a solid footing while constantly knocking you off balance. Aside from the array of 1990s TV references, the skill and attention needed in crafting this story demands my applause.
It is very difficult to speak to the pros and cons for this game, if you can call it one. It is a mosaic of moving pieces, only to be vaguely made-out from afar. This is an entirely different animal. It is also the product of many rather interesting choices, for one, why make a video game if there is pretty much no interactivity? Really, what is the point of a game if you can get just as much out of it by watching someone else play? Player freedom seems to have been redirected to pointless movements such as looking at trees and flowers and bird feathers. Yet it provided a strange level of depth to this intricately crafted story, but maybe it is just my post hoc justification. No, I don't think they are commenting on the metaphysics of choice and folly of free-will. It seemed to me to be fundamentally artistic, meant for expression under the suspension of disbelief, not persuasion, and most definitely not meant for entertainment.
My struggle with this work is that I found no catharsis or insight at the end, I really thought it was coming. To be frank, it made no sense to me. Its significance wholly capsulated in its own world, safely removed from the player. The compound of overlapping motifs and symbolisms was not granted the time nor the space to fuse and yield meaning. It is as if they piled up a bunch of fireworks for the finale, but just as it’s about to go off, instead you are handed a piece of paper which reads, “oh, and then the fireworks went off.” Bloody infuriating.
The immediate experience of Virginia is incomplete, the whole thing has the feel of a phenomenological experiment for a post-modern art study. But despite its faults, I found myself very much enjoying the artistry, the craftsmanship, and above all, the masterful music of Virginia. One last point, I feel this game deserves to be put into VR, it would mitigate much of the interactivity issue.

I got to play this game for a bit on a friend's ipad back when it was first released and i was pretty intrigued. I really liked the idea of running my own vault and I'm glad i finally get the chance to try it again. It's changed a fair amount since I first played and I like the pets, robots, and quests that you can use to help level up your dwellers and make more caps. It's a much more engaging game than it used to be. It's still a waiting game, for sure, but I find that there's a lot more to do than just collect resources and caps and wait-over and over. The quests and locations let you pretty directly control your dwellers while exploring locations. There are plenty of quests with a decent amount of story to them and I like that they give you dialogue options and bring the charm and fun of Fallout's world and lore to this style of game. I like that you can get robots now that will collect your resources while you're away. Being able to find, scrap, or use the junk and salvage from the wasteland to make outfits and weapons for your dwellers. I don't see any features for trading supplies with other vaults or friendly settlements, but I hope a feature like that gets added as it would give even more moneymaking options and give more uses for the junk, weapons, and outfits you find. Being able to buy weapons, outfits, pets, robots, and the like from other settlements would take this game over the top. And it's already such a good game already. I like that you can train all of your dwellers in all of their special stats to help them be more efficient at their various jobs. Plus pretty much every dweller can mate with any other dweller (so long as they're not related). It makes increasing your population fairly easy. You can just use a few males and get all the women pregnant and have new babies and adults every hour or so if you time it right and have enough resrouces stockpiled. Utilizing your dwellers' SPECIAL stats becomes more and more important as the vault expands, it seems.
In all, I would recommend this if you are looking for a nice casual game to play. It's not the best if you're looking to be fully engaged for a whole day, but none of these kinds of game really are. It's why they're usually free to play like this one is.
(Also, it gets annoying trying to control your dwellers manually with the mouse. It is very obviously designed for touch screen controls and it gets frustrating during infestions and raider attacks to control your tiny dwellers as they are frantically running all around getting killed. Pregnant women won't engage in combat either, so make sure you space them out in case of an animal or raider attack as they are useless in combat but sometimes seem to get stuck in a room during a crisis and take up a slot in the room that forces you to manually remove them so you can manually move someone else in there to help out with whatever the situation is.)
Edit: the deathclaw attacks and radscorpion attacks are getting more and more tediious the higher level my dwellers reach. each one nearly wipes out out my stockpile of resources and all my stimpaks and radaway. why are they so overpowered? this is insane. since i wrote my reeview i've noticed i'm spending all my time dreading the next deathclaw or radscorpion attack as i know they'll deplete everything i have. why is it setup this way? this is not fun.
Edit: changed my review to a negative one as i can no longer enjoy/really play the game. every time i come back, i have 10 seconds or so before i get stuck with yet another deathclaw attack. my resources are gone and my vault is in shambles because of these relentless attacks. i'm not even playing anymore-i'm just trying to survive deathclaw attacks. what did you do to this game, bethesda? is this intentional? because i have no idea how you rationalize deathclaws busting down a door designed to withstand a nuclear blast. not only can they not do that, but there's no reason for them to. i am fine with all the other aspects of this game-the raider attacks, the radscorpion, radroach, and mole rat outbreaks. but these deathclaws are too much-it's literally unplayable as you can't rush rooms, build rooms, breed dwellers, or do pretty much anything until the deathclaw attack is over. so glad i didn't waste money on this. please fix this so i can play the game-because it really was fun until that got out of hand.

I went into Virginia really wanting to like it. I like Twin Peaks, I like Fargo, and I liked the little letter from the developers in the main menu that made the game feel more personal and "indie". I tried to force myself to enjoy it, but by around the halfway point I realized that it was never going to start getting fun.
First off, if you're sensitive to low FOV you should just stop reading now because this game will be a headache-inducing vomit comet because of how low it goes, combined with the game's insistence that you play it at 30 FPS (though it does allow you to break that limit if you choose to). But beyond that, there's not much to say about the gameplay because it's not even really a walking simulator because that would mean you were able to walk through most of it. About half of the game is just being sat in one place and having no controls except looking around and occasionally clicking on a thing or two, and you get so used to it that when you finally get to a point where you're actually expected to walk around it sometimes takes a few moments to realize that you aren't chained in place anymore.
The game makes itself out to be some sort of mystery game in the description, but you don't do any actual mystery solving, or really much of anything except walking and then getting abruptly carted off to the next setpiece before you can figure out what's going on. They bring up Fargo and Twin Peaks as inspirations, but a significant part of why those series are so beloved is because of the characters, and more importantly, their writing and dialogue. So of naturally when making Virginia, the obvious choice was to make a game completely devoid of any dialogue at all. The actual small-town mystery takes up about a third of the 2 hours it'll probably take you to finish it, and the rest of that is a jumbled series of is-it-a-dream-or-not-ooooooh sequences that seem to just serve to make the game seem deeper and more arbitrarily confusing.
I really wanted to like this game, but it's just not very good. Even for a "walking simulator" type game there's just not enough substance for me to really recommend it to anyone. It's like Gravity Bone (or Thirty Flights of Loving more specifically, but I thought TFoL was worse than Gravity Bone) except several times longer and several times less interesting. But at least the soundtrack was good. As a hot tip if you do buy the game, be sure to turn on the subtitles. There's no dialogue, so everything is just [sips coffee] or [unusual noises abruptly stop] and it's kind of hilarious, which gives you at least some entertainment.

All in all, this is a good game and I highly recommend it.

I have over a 100+ hours on this on my Ipad. Here's a full review, including the "late game" experience.
In short: Cute little game that has its flaws, but is fun if you are patient and can adapt to its special way of doing things. However it's a bit of an odd package, because it doesn't fit either the "hands off, mining while I am away" nor the "active game, give me things to do and micromanage" mold. It's somewhere in between and most problems come from that aspect.
PROS
- Fallout universe, experience what it can be like to be an overseer and managing your own vault
- Great design, simple yet efficient and fitting the universe and graphic design set by the other fallout games
- Relaxing! It's not about stress or micro management, it's about patience, resource accumulation, and seeing your vault grow.
- Once your vault grows a bit and you have around 80-100+ dweller, things are more fun. You will have a lot of explorers (max is 25 on ipad, not sure if there is a limit on PC) who will find stuff for you. You will have multiple crafting rooms to make weapons, outfits, themes, etc. You will train your dwellers and make them better. You will also be running up to 3 quests at the same time (sending dwellers out for specific tasks that have micro stories and better outcomes than exploration)
- A good way to start your day, check on your dwellers in bed while you are waking up a bit, and then check on them again in bed before sleep. Twice a way is enough to keep this game going.
CONS
- Resources don't accumulate while you are offline, except for your explorers finding stuff (which might be enough)
- Forces you to do some stuff you don't want to do, misplaced micromanagement. For instance, each time someone levels up, you have to click him to acknowledge it or else he will stop getting experience.
- Same thing with training dwellers, if you put someone on strength training, you have to be there to approve each of his level up or else they will gain 1 stat then stop and wait for you... for this reason you can't just leave a dweller in a strength training room for a couple of weeks then come back and find him with maximum strength... you have to validate each level up. It's annoying but not game breaking, since this is the kind of game that requires you to check on it a couple of times per day at least, else don't bother playing.
- Very slow start. It pickups mid to late game and has more things for you to do when you get 100+ dwellers, but when you start it is very boring to watch resources accumulate. The early game needs more gameplay to make it more interesting. My advice is to NOT play this game actively at the start. Make babies, leave, check a few hours later to check on kids, then leave again and come back to see those new adults and put them to work. Don't play it too actively at the start because you will get bored.
REVIEW
This game is about having a relaxing time building your vault and accumulating loot. It starts off slow with only half a dozen dwellers and everything yet to be built. You start producing food, water, and power, and focusing on growing the number of dwellers, either through attracting some from the wilds (building a radio station, which attracts dwellers but also attacks from raiders and other monsters), or through mating your dwellers and making babies.
Midgame as the number of dwellers grow, you unlock more buildings and more possibilities for gameplay. This includes the "overseer office" that lets you start quests, which are like little adventures in the wild that you micromanage. Training rooms so you can enhance the SPECIAL attributes of all your dwellers and make them better at their jobs. Production rooms to make stimpacks (healing) and radaway, and also rooms that let you make weapons, outfits and armors, themes (different designs for your rooms inspired by the institute, rail road, minute men, etc.), and better production rooms such as more powerful power / water / food production facilities. There is also the barbershop that will let you customize the look of every dweller, chancing their hair, face features, and accessories.
You will surely also chase the steam achievements obviously, and it is fairly possible to get them all by late game.
The late game is mostly about getting your dwellers perfected with great stats, running 3 different teams on the quests to try to finish as many quest chains as possible for the rewards, perfecting your vault layout (at that point you will have used every available space and have to think more about what you want to keep and delete), and finally a bit of roleplay as you give your dwellers specific names and customized looks inspired by your favorite characters, and finally sending them very far into the wild to get better loot (the farther they go the better loot they find, every SPECIAL stat gives them an edge, also their weapons, outfits, and quantity of stimpacks and radaways). At this stage in the game, you are mostly a collector, trying to get every recipe and blueprint, making guns and outfits, and just enjoying having a great fully functional vault and pushing it to perfection.
MICRO TRANSACTION, PAY TO WIN OR NOT?
It is not. I played on my Ipad without spending anything, and i eventually gotten all the things that you can purchase with money. I got the legendary dwellers, i got the legendary weapons and outfits, i got all the caps i need and more, and my explorers regularly bring nuka cola (it lets you speed up things like travel time or train time) if i am actively playing to collect them, and i even got enough Mr Handy (they collect the resources from dwellers for you so you don't have to click them), and i even got a lot of pets from exploration. No need to spend anything! If you spend it will be because you want to advance faster or be more comfortable, which is your decision to make.
That being said, here's some advice if you want to spend your money and what is the best way to do so :
1. If you buy something, start with Mr Handy... it will reduce the micro management and let you focus on other things
2. The starter pack is nice ONLY because it gives you a pet that lets you return faster (4 times faster which is quite a lot, most pets you will find will give you 1.25x speed to 2x speed, a 4x times speed boost is very rare and valuable) from exploration and missions, the Mr Handy is also nice.
3. Avoid the lunch boxes, they guarantee a rare but is often a rare salvage and rarely a weapon or outfit, meaning it is often a waste of money (crafting a legendary weapon takes about 9 legendary salvage, so even in the off chance you get one legendary salvage from a box it is quite insignificant). You will get lunch boxes from quests and active exploration, and it is too much hit and miss to be worth the money.
4. Pets are rare enough and powerful enough that they might be worth buying, but again not necessary. Some of the most valuable ones are travel time, damage resistance, added damage, and crafting time reduction.
5. Nuka cola speeds up things, especially travel times to quests. But the issue is, you'd need a lot of it and it can be very expensive (1 nuka cola saves you about 2 hours of wait time). I would not bother, just practice patience as you will be playing this game over weeks and months, and speeding a few hours or even days at a time is a very tiny advantage over the long run.

Paladins is easily my current favorite game. Getting right to the first point everyone makes, you could draw a clear line between characters in Paladins and Overwatch (and even League of Legends). But visually is about where the similarities end. The abilities of the characters and how the games play are quite different.
+ Free-to-play.
+ Active player base.
+ Active development team that listens.
+ Frequent updates.
+ Many diverse and unique characters that suit many play styles.
+ Card system to adjust and build to your play style.
+ Play to unlock items and get in-game currency (spending real money is not necessary).
+ Sweet horsey mounts.
+ For a game in beta, there's a refreshing lack of bugs and glitches.
+ Relatively low system requirements needed to run the game.
- Too many different in-game currencies (3).
- In-game currency (crystals) are way too expensive (real money) for how little you get when compared to how many crystals it takes to unlock certain things.
- Lack of levels. You'll play the same maps over and over.
~ No changing characters once the match has started. Choose wisely. Build a balanced team.
~ Many have recently argued the game is pay-to-win. I do
share this opinion.
~ Some characters are OP/need nerfing. However, cards and play style can "work around" most. And future updates generally level things out.
~ Some long queue times. Not too often, but I have sat in queue for 5+ min on more than a few occasions.
~ Some updates are "two steps forward, one step back."
~ Server downtime. It's beta. It happens. But it happens enough to be worth noting - mainly around events, unfortunately.
I'm sure I've overlooked or forgotten to mention some things. That said, this game is tons of fun, and I would absolutely recommend it to any of my friends. For a free-to-play game in beta, it wins my vote over many other established, polished, and more refined games.

I really wish Steam reviews had a 'mixed' button....
Ok. Broken Age is... mostly solid, as a fun quirky throwback to old style adventure games. Nice art, ok Voice Acting, some fairly decent puzzles. It's short in theory, but your first playthrough should take a fair bit of time as you explore the world and try to work out the logic behind some of the puzzles. If you're into classic point and click adventure games, I do have to recommend this.
However, Act 2 was ultimately somewhat disappointing to me, for a few reasons. The story's resolution, whilst there, is cut somewhat short and a few key plot points are left either unresolved, or barely touched upon. Alongside that however, is a completely illogical final sequence, where the player's end goal is not clearly explained to them, the puzzle requirements are irritating and time consuming rather than rewarding intellect, and where the plot closes out without a resolution on the underlying conflict.
It has its virtues. I recommend investigating it if you're curious. But ultimately, the game did not justify the hype, or the Kickstarter. It will be remembered for kicking off the indie kickstarter boom more than as a game in its own right. Which I feel is a shame given the talent that act one displayed. Double Fine needed a stronger brief with this game, and I feel that ultimately they wavered and improvised the end.

Natural Selection (2) is a great blend of FPS and RTS action. Also called a mix of Counter-Strike and Starcraft, the game features two asymmetrical teams (the aliens or 'Kharaa' and marines or 'Frontiersmen') who fight for control of the playing field.
Marines can use weapons to shoot the creepy crawlers, but the aliens with their messy spores, big teeth, slime and scythes can shred marines to bits when given the opportunity.
Each team is led by a Commander who sits (relatively) safely in either a Command Station or Hive. The Commander has to lead his/her team to victory by giving instructions and orders, and by building and expanding a base.
When every Command Station or Hive has been destroyed, the team who owned those structures will lose.
This is a game that you cannot afford to miss, wether you like Alien-inspired themed games, shooting aliens or biting marines or like to give orders and work as a team.
--------------------------
More information...
-=Gameplay=-
Q: How is it played?
A: The main objective in regular NS2 gameplay is to destroy all command stations or hives, depending on which team you're fighting.
Joining a server will spawn you in a waiting room of sorts, where you will find portals that, when walked through, assign you to a team. The choices are aliens, marines, random or spectator.
Joining and leaving a team can happen at any time during the game. When both teams have a commander (any player who approaches the command station/hive and activates it) the game starts. Other players spawn in the same room while the commander gets an RTS-style overview of the game. Soldiers have to move out to build or defend constructions and take down enemy buildings.
Players are free to choose their own path, but have the best chance of success when following orders from a smart commander. The commander places buildings, researches upgrades and keeps lays out a battle plan on the go. The soldiers have to conquer territory and alternate between attacking to take over and defending their own rooms. Alien buildings grow slowly on their own, marine buildings materialise as transparent 3D blueprints and have to be built by the marines in the field.
The currency of the game is simply referred to as resources (res). These are acquired automatically, slowly over time. Every player receives personal resources (p res) and the commander can spend team resources (t res). Players can spend p res to buy weapons and equipment or to change into more powerful life-forms and upgrade those. The commander uses t res to purchase and place (blueprints of) structures and to research upgrades as well as providing field support for his troops. Both teams must build extractors/harvesters to increase the resource income. The more resources you acquire, the quicker you can acquire upgrades and better equipment or life-forms. As your team becomes stronger, you'll more easily push the enemy team out of rooms and eventually back into their last base. Destroying their only remaining command station or hive wins you the game.
-=Graphics, sound, experience=-
NS2 is a decent looking game. There's been a lot of improvement since the first game. With the infestation that spreads from alien structures to the textures of alien life-forms, marine exo-suits and the scenery in maps, there's enough to look at. But you'll be too busy hunting down your opponents to actually take it all in anyway!
The sound is also good, but don't expect a lot of music. It's all about sound effects to help you locate your enemies, or at the very least be aware of their presence. Listening to music is not really recommended while playing, as long as you're playing a marine or an alien without the special detection upgrade. Footsteps and the sound of claws on metal serve to give away the enemy's position. The marines have taunts and the aliens can growl a bit, there's not much to that, but there's plenty of interesting sounds for all the abilities and weapons.
-=Technical, controls, etc.=-
May be a little heavy for some machines. Many players resort to turning graphics down to keep framerate up. It's not terrible, but can be a problem when there's a lot of players fighting in a small space with lots of particles being thrown around. The controls are easy and fairly intuitive. As they say, less is more, and NS2 agrees. At least in the controls of players out on the field. Commanders don't have that much more, but to be quick and effective they have to remember quite a few shortcuts.
Pro's:
-It doesn't take long to learn how to play (as a player in the field)
-The game is well balanced
-The game works with upgrades but there's no real RPG elements involved, anyone can jump into any game and contribute right away
-A match that's going nowhere can be ended early by having either team vote to concede with a majority of players, other methods include voting to restart or having most/all teammates go to the ready room (leaving the team), often ending the match
Cons:
-Playing commander is far from easy. It takes time to learn and become good at, and games often take a long time to start because nobody wants to take up that position.
-Experienced players tend to stack up in teams, making it hard or impossible to win for a team of average "pub" players (this is not a game flaw, but it's something you'll often face when playing it, and as this is a multiplayer-only game, it's relevant)

Alan Wake is not quite a horror game, but more of an adventure game.
You control Alan Wake, a novelist, who went on vacation with his wife because he had writer's block and could not complete his book,"Departed." While on this vacation, Alan's wife goes missing. During his search, he experiences events from "Departed." Though he has written the book, he has no memory of writing it. The narrative of the game is compelling and makes you want to complete the story to see what happens.
The game is structured in an episodic format. There are 6 episodes, excluding the DLC. The DLC shows 2 additional episodes. Each episode takes about an hour and a half to 2 hours to beat. This will give you roughly 11 hours of game play. If you choose to get all the different collectible and achievements this will take much longer.
The game wants to present itself as a psychological survival horror game, but falls short in the psychological and horror areas. The game lacks an open narrative and decisions that are  necessary for a psychological game to be tailored to the individual playing it. The horror aspect of the game is also quite lacking, as all the enemies are very similar and the same methods are applied to defeat them all. The enemies are cloaked in darkness and are invincible. To defeat them, you need to shine your light on them and fire your revolver at them to damage them. The first few times you encounter these shadowy figures, they are a little unsettling, but as you encounter them more often they loss the creep-factor.
The combat in this game is quite repetitive. You shine the enemies with your flashlight and fire your revolver. The combat is easy to pick up and play, but doesn't really change to scale with the player or the difficulty. The most difficult sections are when you are faced with multiple enemies at once, or if you are low on ammunition. This combat format fits the game well, but doesnt make you feel like you are the character.
The collectibles are interesting, as there are multiple kinds of collectibles in the game. My personal favorite collectibles were the Manuscript pages. These pages tell the story of Alan's next book that was not finished due to writer's block. I found these insightful as they may explain different sections of the game and tell a separate story to that of our protagonist. If you wanted to collect all of the pages you need to play on Nightmare mode, as some of the pages can only be found during this mode.
Overall, the game feels like an adventure game. It handles very well and is a joy to play. The story is interesting and tells more than just the main character's story. The collectibles are challenging, but not impossible to obtain. I would suggest this game to someone looking for a great story, but not for someone looking for a challenge.

You've just spent the last hour fighting slogging through the deep mud trying to get your last load of logs to the drop point.  Your almost there and it is going really smooth but then you start to see the rear trailer tires sink. The trail here is getting really bad from the multiple runs you have already made.  You've always made it before, why should this time be any different?.  The trailer starts to lean heavily to one side.  If you stop you will probably get stuck. There are no trees near by to winch from and getting stuck means going back for the other truck to pull you out and will mean at least another 30 minutes lost and it is getting dark.   The trailer is creaking and moaning under the stress.  You are so close, only a couple hundred meters out. You hammer the accelerator and the rig groans through the mud but then the whole rig starts to sink in deeper and deeper.  You might be able to stop and reverse out but it may already be to late as the truck grinds to a halt stuck in the mud.  The tires are spinning trying to grab onto anything solid but it is of no use.  Your stuck.  Going to have to get a rescue vehicle now.
Spintires is not for the faint of heart.  It is tedious, long, and downright frustrating at times.  But when you are driving the big MAZ 537 through the deep mud making huge ruts with a load of long logs and you see the beast pull through into the drop off point it is even more rewarding.  It won’t give you a bunch of money to spend on upgrades or unlock some super high tech vehicle.  It is it’s own reward. It is that good feeling you get when you know you conquered the terrain and did not succumb to all the hazards of it.  It is about taking on what seem to be insurmountable odds and still beating them.  Its about having fun and seeing how bad you really can bury your truck and then figuring how to get it out.
Spintires has two game modes.  Casual and hardcore. Casual is much more forgiving and great for beginners.  You can instantly rescue any vehicle back to the shop, have lower fuel burn, and can lock the differential on the fly in automatic on the transmission.  In hardcore more, there are no magic vehicle rescues.  If you want your truck back, you will have to get it yourself.  You still have an automatic transmission but if you really want to get there you better learn the manual one fast and start figuring out how you will get fuel to your truck out in the middle of nowhere. And there is no magic little red line to follow from your planned route on the map.  Hopefully you know the terrain by now.
Spintires is a completely open world.  There is no one route to get there. Its about planning and knowing the risks.  Take the beaten, torn up roads, or make your own trails to cut time and find virgin ground to trample on?  The trees on the map look really thick but if you could squeeze through there is a paved road right on the other side.   Routes that seamed impossible at first because they were so difficult and at times seemed impossible to scout sometimes become your best avenues of travel.   There is a learning curve but there are numerous guides to help you get started.  Learning the maps and the vehicle characteristics is just trial and error at times. Expect a few hours on each map just learning the general layout. There are some guide maps that tell you where things are, but they won't tell you how bad the mud is, or where the hills are, or how deep the water is.  The in game camera is not the greatest but it is not bad as most say and is very manageable if you play on a game pad.
This game is a ton of fun if you have some patience and can laugh when you see your truck disappear into the water depths knowing you drove it there.  And then can laugh again when you get your second truck struck while trying to pull the first one out. This is not a game about driving fast.  It is about crawling through the mud.
I highly recommend this game.  If you like hard core, off road, real life simulations, you can't do better than this. With its real time terrain deformation, you can watch as a new trail will start to deteriorate into a slop pit as you drive on it again and again leaving huge ruts that will still be there when you come through again.

Took the plunge and was not disappointed! This is pretty much the best true off-road simulator you'll find but bear in mind its NOT A RACING GAME. Speed is not the name of the game here but rather realistic navigation of a deep Russian forest! You've got mud, pools/streams/rivers/oceans of water, steep inclines, dried out riverbeds, dense forests, sharp switchbacks up a mountain side... a good variety of terrain.
The game is incredibly simple in its objectives but its just plain fun to set out on a new map and find the best routes to load up and then deliver loads of lumber. Yes, thats the current way to "beat" the maps - you need to load lumber either with a crane or by going to specific lumber yards and loading up on short, medium or long logs and then hauling them across the map to drop points.
AND THE PHYSICS! Damn, best mud and water physics I've seen for a driving game. Your tires will dig massive ruts, water has realistic currents and will flow even between your tires... its amazing. Where there was once a pristine trail could become a muddy hell at the end of the map after you've hauled heavy loads through it.
As for the vehicles you've got an assortment of Russian trucks such as an old dually, a recon jeep and then you can even get up to massive 8x8 rolling fortresses that can only be stopped by the worst mud pits imaginable. Speaking of that recon jeep, each map starts out cloaked in black swirls/clouds that prevent you from seeing all the map right away. The cloaks can be removed simply by moving near them but they are often hidden away in deep forest/rough terrain and its pretty fun to scout out the unkown with your trusty jeep and reveal the map!

The game is medicore.  It's just a plain and simple game. I've played Mafia 1, 2, 3.  Played all of the games to death (Collectiables, etc).  Why didn't they re-add FreeRoam Extreme or anything.  Continue or New Game; only options clickable at main menu.  It seems like a downgrade to me coming from Mafia 2 to say the least.  The combat is average, death animations are meh (~3 for every gun/melee), driving is like Watch Dogs/Godfather and car damage is...no.  Reminds me of Godfather 2 car damage and combat with a mixture of Saints Row 3 HUD from console days.
The sky is choppy and pixelated, no option for draw distance - can't turn off Ambient Occlusion.  When Lincoln Clay gets hit by a driving car, he doesn't fall to the ground, rag doll doesn't take place: stationary standing still and says "UGH." You just got hit by a car, fall to the floor or do some kind of animation. Not just UGH.  Magic ability to be able to jump from a moving car at 90mph and roll to a safe standing pose with no damage being dealt.  Didn't know was part of the Marvels squad.  Fascinating.  So much arcade present.  We didn't ask for Joe's Adventures (M2), and yet you released it with a DLC cost.  I watched and responded to people on the 2K forums, asking why you're adding point systems into the game.  This isn't an arcade game, Mafia1 wasn't an arcade point game.  It was story driven with cutscenes I will always remember.  Do not do the same for Mafia3 as you did for the Mafia2 DLC.
Feel like I'm at the Coin Arcades back in the 1990's looking for quarters to play House of the Dead. The half cutscenes (when talking to NPC/non important people) just look blurry and terribly scripted.  Really just appears they put the game together too quickly.  Nothing flows or feels like you want to come back to the game; nothing drags you back wanting to play more.  Has very nice movie cutscenes, and that's about it.  Mafia3 holds your hand through everything - telling you where to go from driving to an objective, pop ups during missions literally explaining what you have to do, to icons being on the car door.  Icons everywhere, icons on everything, icons ICONS ICOONS.  Where's the adventure? Where's the sense of mystery? Playing on Hard difficulty, they could have made the game HARDER and get rid of all the icons and additional help with this difficulty selected.
Majority of "missions" are go to point A, rough up X guy, go back and talk to guy C afterwards.  It's a blast.  The games' world isn't feeling alive. I feel like an 8 year old being taught how to play video games for the first time.  Rain doesn't splash off cars, water looks meh, no first person option or change 3rd person view height.  Character has the stamina of a 100 year old that has some how survived after 3 packs of smokes a day (get more stamina through certain underboss perks, which is also dumb).
Cops. Not doing their job.  What else is new though.  Aren't pulling people over or getting into gun fights with NPCs.  How unrealistic.  Cops billy-clubbing everyone back in that day without question.  Billy-club now, question maybe later; maybe not.  Ontop of that, enemy AI is plain horrific.. Did they copy paste from Mafia1 AI? Probably the only thing they took out of M1.  All the player has to do is crouch stealth through all the missions.  No NPC will notice you if you stealth kill - so easy.  When you get the silenced handgun you can literally crouch and 1 tap every enemy without difficulty.  I've hi-jacked a car in front of a patroling cop (walking on sidewalk), speed, fly through red lights, just about anything illegal in front of a cop; nothing happens.  For some reason a little blue cursor looking thing pops up every time I pass a cop, but what's it for? Who knows.  I'm not wanted and I just commited at least 10 moving violations/felonies.
Enemy AI/Hitman will shoot at me outside of a mission, and cop does nothing on the street.  Everything that M1/M2 had to offer, is no longer valid.  You can't fix your cars up at the shop, put superchargers on them (Mafia2), store them (no house just compounds with nothing to do), no weapon customization, no era changing buildings or rooms (M2), get pulled over for speeding; nothing.  I don't really know why they took so much content out of this game. What made Mafia, Mafia; is not there.
I'll always remember moments from Mafia1/Mafia2 story; Mafia3 not so much memorable.  Chasing after Frank in M1, Hotel bomb plant in M2, M3 is just meh.

This game has fallen into the micro transaction market with the loot crate system with a whole Act of the game that seems there just so you buy the loot crates to get top quality orcs. Hopefully not many people bought them; if everyone boycotts this system they won't try it again.
There are bountiful glitches that make the game whack af. Sometimes when you zoom on an orc from far away the camera will zoom into its head and start shuttering around the inside. There's also problems with the parkour system. SO MANY TIMES you'll be trying to go onto a certain level of a structure but Talion will reach for the roof instead of the platform and keep climbing. It's incredibly annoying, and occurs all throughout the game.

The skill system is massive, but could have some improvements that would make the game a little more streamline such as a skill line around maximum health, focus, wrath and might that are hard to get (e.g. needing level 53+) so they regenerate faster over time, or increase the base amount etc.

I got to play this game for a bit on a friend's ipad back when it was first released and i was pretty intrigued. It's a much more engaging game than it used to be. It's still a waiting game, for sure, but I find that there's a lot more to do than just collect resources and caps and wait-over and over. The quests and locations let you pretty directly control your dwellers while exploring locations. There are plenty of quests with a decent amount of story to them and I like that they give you dialogue options and bring the charm and fun of Fallout's world and lore to this style of game. I like that you can get robots now that will collect your resources while you're away. Being able to find, scrap, or use the junk and salvage from the wasteland to make outfits and weapons for your dwellers. I don't see any features for trading supplies with other vaults or friendly settlements, but I hope a feature like that gets added as it would give even more moneymaking options and give more uses for the junk, weapons, and outfits you find. Being able to buy weapons, outfits, pets, robots, and the like from other settlements would take this game over the top. And it's already such a good game already. I like that you can train all of your dwellers in all of their special stats to help them be more efficient at their various jobs. Utilizing your dwellers' SPECIAL stats becomes more and more important as the vault expands, it seems.

Edit: changed my review to a negative one as i can no longer enjoy/really play the game. every time i come back, i have 10 seconds or so before i get stuck with yet another deathclaw attack. my resources are gone and my vault is in shambles because of these relentless attacks. i'm not even playing anymore-i'm just trying to survive deathclaw attacks. what did you do to this game, bethesda? is this intentional? because i have no idea how you rationalize deathclaws busting down a door designed to withstand a nuclear blast. not only can they not do that, but there's no reason for them to. i am fine with all the other aspects of this game-the raider attacks, the radscorpion, radroach, and mole rat outbreaks. but these deathclaws are too much-it's literally unplayable as you can't rush rooms, build rooms, breed dwellers, or do pretty much anything until the deathclaw attack is over. so glad i didn't waste money on this. please fix this so i can play the game-because it really was fun until that got out of hand.

I have over a 100+ hours on this on my Ipad. Here's a full review, including the "late game" experience.
In short: Cute little game that has its flaws, but is fun if you are patient and can adapt to its special way of doing things. However it's a bit of an odd package, because it doesn't fit either the "hands off, mining while I am away" nor the "active game, give me things to do and micromanage" mold. It's somewhere in between and most problems come from that aspect.
PROS
- Fallout universe, experience what it can be like to be an overseer and managing your own vault
- Great design, simple yet efficient and fitting the universe and graphic design set by the other fallout games
- Relaxing! It's not about stress or micro management, it's about patience, resource accumulation, and seeing your vault grow.
- Once your vault grows a bit and you have around 80-100+ dweller, things are more fun. You will have a lot of explorers (max is 25 on ipad, not sure if there is a limit on PC) who will find stuff for you. You will have multiple crafting rooms to make weapons, outfits, themes, etc. You will train your dwellers and make them better. You will also be running up to 3 quests at the same time (sending dwellers out for specific tasks that have micro stories and better outcomes than exploration)
- A good way to start your day, check on your dwellers in bed while you are waking up a bit, and then check on them again in bed before sleep. Twice a way is enough to keep this game going.
CONS
- Resources don't accumulate while you are offline, except for your explorers finding stuff (which might be enough)
- Forces you to do some stuff you don't want to do, misplaced micromanagement. For instance, each time someone levels up, you have to click him to acknowledge it or else he will stop getting experience.
- Same thing with training dwellers, if you put someone on strength training, you have to be there to approve each of his level up or else they will gain 1 stat then stop and wait for you... for this reason you can't just leave a dweller in a strength training room for a couple of weeks then come back and find him with maximum strength... you have to validate each level up. It's annoying but not game breaking, since this is the kind of game that requires you to check on it a couple of times per day at least, else don't bother playing.
- Very slow start. It pickups mid to late game and has more things for you to do when you get 100+ dwellers, but when you start it is very boring to watch resources accumulate. The early game needs more gameplay to make it more interesting. My advice is to NOT play this game actively at the start. Make babies, leave, check a few hours later to check on kids, then leave again and come back to see those new adults and put them to work. Don't play it too actively at the start because you will get bored.
REVIEW
This game is about having a relaxing time building your vault and accumulating loot. It starts off slow with only half a dozen dwellers and everything yet to be built. You start producing food, water, and power, and focusing on growing the number of dwellers, either through attracting some from the wilds (building a radio station, which attracts dwellers but also attacks from raiders and other monsters), or through mating your dwellers and making babies.
Midgame as the number of dwellers grow, you unlock more buildings and more possibilities for gameplay. This includes the "overseer office" that lets you start quests, which are like little adventures in the wild that you micromanage. Training rooms so you can enhance the SPECIAL attributes of all your dwellers and make them better at their jobs. Production rooms to make stimpacks (healing) and radaway, and also rooms that let you make weapons, outfits and armors, themes (different designs for your rooms inspired by the institute, rail road, minute men, etc.), and better production rooms such as more powerful power / water / food production facilities. There is also the barbershop that will let you customize the look of every dweller, chancing their hair, face features, and accessories.
You will surely also chase the steam achievements obviously, and it is fairly possible to get them all by late game.
The late game is mostly about getting your dwellers perfected with great stats, running 3 different teams on the quests to try to finish as many quest chains as possible for the rewards, perfecting your vault layout (at that point you will have used every available space and have to think more about what you want to keep and delete), and finally a bit of roleplay as you give your dwellers specific names and customized looks inspired by your favorite characters, and finally sending them very far into the wild to get better loot (the farther they go the better loot they find, every SPECIAL stat gives them an edge, also their weapons, outfits, and quantity of stimpacks and radaways). At this stage in the game, you are mostly a collector, trying to get every recipe and blueprint, making guns and outfits, and just enjoying having a great fully functional vault and pushing it to perfection.
MICRO TRANSACTION, PAY TO WIN OR NOT?
It is not. I played on my Ipad without spending anything, and i eventually gotten all the things that you can purchase with money. I got the legendary dwellers, i got the legendary weapons and outfits, i got all the caps i need and more, and my explorers regularly bring nuka cola (it lets you speed up things like travel time or train time) if i am actively playing to collect them, and i even got enough Mr Handy (they collect the resources from dwellers for you so you don't have to click them), and i even got a lot of pets from exploration. No need to spend anything! If you spend it will be because you want to advance faster or be more comfortable, which is your decision to make.
That being said, here's some advice if you want to spend your money and what is the best way to do so :
1. If you buy something, start with Mr Handy... it will reduce the micro management and let you focus on other things
2. The starter pack is nice ONLY because it gives you a pet that lets you return faster (4 times faster which is quite a lot, most pets you will find will give you 1.25x speed to 2x speed, a 4x times speed boost is very rare and valuable) from exploration and missions, the Mr Handy is also nice.
3. Avoid the lunch boxes, they guarantee a rare but is often a rare salvage and rarely a weapon or outfit, meaning it is often a waste of money (crafting a legendary weapon takes about 9 legendary salvage, so even in the off chance you get one legendary salvage from a box it is quite insignificant). You will get lunch boxes from quests and active exploration, and it is too much hit and miss to be worth the money.
4. Pets are rare enough and powerful enough that they might be worth buying, but again not necessary. Some of the most valuable ones are travel time, damage resistance, added damage, and crafting time reduction.
5. Nuka cola speeds up things, especially travel times to quests. But the issue is, you'd need a lot of it and it can be very expensive (1 nuka cola saves you about 2 hours of wait time). I would not bother, just practice patience as you will be playing this game over weeks and months, and speeding a few hours or even days at a time is a very tiny advantage over the long run.

What a game! Alan Wake plays like Stephen King meets Max Payne, meets Twin Peaks and The Twilight Zone, meets a mix of zombie and vampire movies!
Remedy did it again, the game felt quite like Max Payne did, while at the same time managing to set its own distinctive path.
The atmosphere, story and graphics were awesome, like a good Stephen King horror book/movie should be. The creators made it so the game plays in episodic segments, much like a TV series and the inspirations they got from said movies, tv shows and books are noticeable throughout all its length.
I personally found it to be much more than a horror story though, it also has the classic struggle of a man to save his loved one, but even more than that, it's a metaphor for a man who tries to overcome his fears and problems and in the end manages to "return". I won't spoiler you the rest, play the game till the last dlc to understand!
Despite all that, the comedy element, numerous references and witty lines which defined Max Payne are present here too, Remedy made sure of that. Especially Alan Wake's best buddy, Barry provides great comedy relief feeling and lines!
The soundtrack was equally awesome, from its haunting pieces to fitting works of various artists, with band Poets of the Fall being in the spotlight with 3 songs. The band had also worked on the second Max Payne game.
My only complaints here were the gameplay and the checkpoints system.
The gameplay manages to catch your attention at first with its innovative style, but gets repetitive and annoying pretty fast and unfortunately it doesn't improve much later in the game. Max Payne had a similar issue, however, being a more fast paced game, it didn't stand out that much.
As for the checkpoints system, I wished there were more in some spots, as losing in said points and starting all over was quite infuriating.
Hopefully they will fix these issues in the game's true sequel, which, due to poor sales performance, seems like will never see the light of the day, but I do believe will eventually manage to come through and shine light in the darkness!
Until then, if you are a fan of all the above, wake up and play Alan Wake!

Natural Selection (2) is a great blend of FPS and RTS action. Also called a mix of Counter-Strike and Starcraft, the game features two asymmetrical teams (the aliens or 'Kharaa' and marines or 'Frontiersmen') who fight for control of the playing field.
Marines can use weapons to shoot the creepy crawlers, but the aliens with their messy spores, big teeth, slime and scythes can shred marines to bits when given the opportunity.
Each team is led by a Commander who sits (relatively) safely in either a Command Station or Hive. The Commander has to lead his/her team to victory by giving instructions and orders, and by building and expanding a base.
When every Command Station or Hive has been destroyed, the team who owned those structures will lose.
This is a game that you cannot afford to miss, wether you like Alien-inspired themed games, shooting aliens or biting marines or like to give orders and work as a team.
--------------------------
More information...
-=Gameplay=-
Q: How is it played?
A: The main objective in regular NS2 gameplay is to destroy all command stations or hives, depending on which team you're fighting.
Joining a server will spawn you in a waiting room of sorts, where you will find portals that, when walked through, assign you to a team. The choices are aliens, marines, random or spectator.
Joining and leaving a team can happen at any time during the game. When both teams have a commander (any player who approaches the command station/hive and activates it) the game starts. Other players spawn in the same room while the commander gets an RTS-style overview of the game. Soldiers have to move out to build or defend constructions and take down enemy buildings.
Players are free to choose their own path, but have the best chance of success when following orders from a smart commander. The commander places buildings, researches upgrades and keeps lays out a battle plan on the go. The soldiers have to conquer territory and alternate between attacking to take over and defending their own rooms. Alien buildings grow slowly on their own, marine buildings materialise as transparent 3D blueprints and have to be built by the marines in the field.
The currency of the game is simply referred to as resources (res). These are acquired automatically, slowly over time. Every player receives personal resources (p res) and the commander can spend team resources (t res). Players can spend p res to buy weapons and equipment or to change into more powerful life-forms and upgrade those. The commander uses t res to purchase and place (blueprints of) structures and to research upgrades as well as providing field support for his troops. Both teams must build extractors/harvesters to increase the resource income. The more resources you acquire, the quicker you can acquire upgrades and better equipment or life-forms. As your team becomes stronger, you'll more easily push the enemy team out of rooms and eventually back into their last base. Destroying their only remaining command station or hive wins you the game.
-=Graphics, sound, experience=-
NS2 is a decent looking game. There's been a lot of improvement since the first game. With the infestation that spreads from alien structures to the textures of alien life-forms, marine exo-suits and the scenery in maps, there's enough to look at. But you'll be too busy hunting down your opponents to actually take it all in anyway!
The sound is also good, but don't expect a lot of music. It's all about sound effects to help you locate your enemies, or at the very least be aware of their presence. Listening to music is not really recommended while playing, as long as you're playing a marine or an alien without the special detection upgrade. Footsteps and the sound of claws on metal serve to give away the enemy's position. The marines have taunts and the aliens can growl a bit, there's not much to that, but there's plenty of interesting sounds for all the abilities and weapons.
-=Technical, controls, etc.=-
May be a little heavy for some machines. Many players resort to turning graphics down to keep framerate up. It's not terrible, but can be a problem when there's a lot of players fighting in a small space with lots of particles being thrown around. The controls are easy and fairly intuitive. As they say, less is more, and NS2 agrees. At least in the controls of players out on the field. Commanders don't have that much more, but to be quick and effective they have to remember quite a few shortcuts.
Pro's:
-It doesn't take long to learn how to play (as a player in the field)
-The game is well balanced
-The game works with upgrades but there's no real RPG elements involved, anyone can jump into any game and contribute right away
-A match that's going nowhere can be ended early by having either team vote to concede with a majority of players, other methods include voting to restart or having most/all teammates go to the ready room (leaving the team), often ending the match
Cons:
-Playing commander is far from easy. It takes time to learn and become good at, and games often take a long time to start because nobody wants to take up that position.
-Experienced players tend to stack up in teams, making it hard or impossible to win for a team of average "pub" players (this is not a game flaw, but it's something you'll often face when playing it, and as this is a multiplayer-only game, it's relevant)

8/10: A nicely stylized point-and-click adventure about a boy and a girl from two different lifestyles realizing they aren't as worlds apart as it seemed. Nothing says "evil" like social Darwinism!
Broken Age is Tim Schafer's Kickstarter success, a point-and-click experience that allows the player to switch between two young protagonists. Vella from Sugarbunting is a plucky young girl who has been chosen for The Maiden's Feast, which is a ritualized virgin sacrifice to a monster named Mog Chothra that supposedly keeps the creature from raining destruction down on the town. Shae, a young dude, is trapped in a juvenile routine on a spaceship at the overprotective behest of MOM, and yearns for anything resembling real adventure.
Needless to say, Vella doesn't take her impending sacrifice lying down, and Shae goes out of his way to find some real action. Without getting too far into spoiler territory, this derails the long-standing ritual and reveals that both of their roles served a far different purpose than they originally believed, and that those responsible for their respective scenarios are the true antagonist(s).
All of this is experienced in the typical point-and-click fashion as you wander about, picking up various objects and discerning how exactly they can help you overcome your current roadblock. Sometimes the answer is obvious, occasionally it's unclear, and in some cases you have to switch between the characters to find the solutions you need, but the game rarely leaves the player grasping at straws for the solution, especially since making mistakes will at times reveal a hint for figuring out the right move.

My impressions at length, if you're not sure why I reached this conclusion:
Also, your steam playtime counts the time the game spent paused while alt-tabbing. I have in fact played through the game once, and it took about 7 hours of actual playtime.
Part 1 was a nostalgic, traditional (charming) point and click adventure. Part 2 is very much not.
The puzzles in part 1 were very much typical, nostalgic point-and-click adventure puzzles that could be solved by talking to everyone and clicking on everything. They were mostly logical, congruent with their setting, and solvable by understanding how the locale in which they are found works. The puzzles in part 2 are "puzzle game" puzzles for the sake of puzzles (does puzzle look like a word anymore?), in the tradition of Myst or (a better example) Puzzle Agent 2. They are arbitrary, have little to do with their surroundings, and interchangeable.
The thing is - no one at Double Fine ever designed a "puzzle game" before and (consequently?) they are really really terrible at it. In (say) Puzzle Agent, you solve a puzzle by figuring it out logically (mathematically, whatever). In Broken Age act 2, you solve a puzzle by following instructions. The only difficulty you're facing is the fact that the instructions were written by a drooling retard, and you have to write them out and puzzle the meaning from the gibbering.
(Also - almost everything in act 2 is also recycled from act 1, and the conclusion to the story makes absolutely no freaking sense.)
I rather enjoyed the first act, though it was over in 2 hours or so (fairly complete exploration with no walkthrough). Act 2 had very little joy, and was mostly frustratingly obtuse. I would not recommend you purchase it. In fact, I really should have youtubed a playthrough of act 2 after completing act 1, even though I already had the game.

I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. It's gorgeous, it has a nice story beginning to end, the characters are likeable, and the music and voice acting is excellent.
I'm pretty okay at adventure games, but not the best. I've played quite some (among my favourite are Day of the Tentacle, Sam & Max Hit the Road, Machinarium and Book of Unwritten Tales), and I'm familiar with the general way of how adventure game puzzles are structured. The puzzles ranged from simple to challenging, but I never found them dull or illogical. I reached for a walkthrough once, and when I read the solution to that puzzle, I immediately realized where I had forgotten to connect the dots. I had disregarded some comment by one of the characters as irrelevant and forgotten about it, but it turned out to be relevant after all.  That's something that happens to me a lot more in adventure games, and I'm fine with that. Never have I thought "Well how was I supposed to come up with that?". As is common in adventure games, sometimes you do think "Why can't I just solve it this way? That would be way easier!" or "Surely that other character has the necessary qualifications to solve this issue for me". But obviously, if it were way easier, or you would let someone else fix things for you, you wouldn't have a puzzle to solve, now would you? :).
There are some puzzles where Vella or Shay will give a hint when you do it wrong a few times. Sometimes I thought they were a bit soon with that, I would have preferred to muddle along a bit more without any hints.
The characters often have funny things to say, and I've laughed out loud on many occasions. I have properly enjoyed myself playing the game, and I found the end satisfying. Sometimes a game is very nice while you play, but they botch up something at the end that leaves you unsatisfied even though you enjoyed it right up to the end. Luckily, this is not the case here. Oh, on that subject: the pictures surrounding the ending credits give a sort of epilogue to the story, so even if you usually click through the credits, you might not want to do that for this game.
It runs fine on my Linux machine, which is nice, because I only boot Windows for games that don't run or don't run well natively on Linux. But I could use my preferred OS just fine.
I could only find one problem with the game, related to clicking on objects in a scene. It turns out I need a lot of explanation to make clear what the problem is; so here goes.
When you try to use an object from your inventory on an object in the scene, the object in the scene is highlighted. However, when you simply hover your cursor on an object in the scene, it's not highlighted. The cursor does indicate you can click, but the thing you're clicking on is not indicated. This can get confusing when you're trying to determine if something is clickable or not; whether it's background or a usable object. Say there's a person in the scene, and a space ship control panel next to that person. When I hover over the control panel, the cursor indicates I can click. But when I click, it becomes clear I've chosen to interact with the person. This can be confusing: is it indeed the case I can't click the control panel, or was I clicking too close to the person? After several clicks which initiate talking to the person, I'm concluding the control panel is part of the background scene. This can be annoying, because knowing what you can interact with is very important in a point-and-click adventure. Note that there is no pixel hunting in this game; it's not as bad as that. Everything you can interact with has a decent size, it's just that not everything that has a decent size can be interacted with :).

When I bought a game written by the great Tim Schafer, creator of legendary game Psychonauts among other things, I really wasn't expecting to be let down by just about EVERYTHING the game had to offer. An pair of two intriguing stories running parallel to each other suddenly shift into a single story that loses all intrigue by the end of it. The plot, which seems to have so much potential at the start, becomes so incredibly uninteresting by the end that I only felt obliged to finish the game because I'd spent money on it.
The main characters are bland, unintelligent, and seem to have very little interest in anything happening around them, even when possibly faced with their own demise. The settings, while interesting, are small and will only hold your interest long enough for you to realize how little world-building Double Fine has done with the world they created, and will leave you wishing they put some actual effort into them. And the gameplay: It's a point and click adventure game, so what little gameplay it has can only be based on the puzzles. Almost all of them are too easy, being tasks that a 5-year-old could figure out, or they're so obscure that you'll either need a walkthrough or a bottem-less well of patience as you click on every interactable thing in the game in every possible order, searching in vain for the thread of logic the developers were operating on.
To top it all off, the game ends with our two protagonists finally meeting after an entire game being seperated. What happens then? Nothing. They see each other, say nothing to each other, and the credits roll. No real resolution is reached either, as the antagonists (who were introduced very late on, I might add) were neither truly defeated, nor were they even properly explained beyond some very forced exposition.
Do yourself a favor, do NOT buy Broken Age. Save your money, spend it on a better game like Psychonauts. That way you can see that Tim Schafer actually had some talent at one point in time before it suddenly faded and he started putting out garbage like this.
(PS: The only saving grace this game has a a few key side characters, the majority of which are SILVERWARE. Seriously.)

One of the biggest Kickstarter projects ever, developed by legendary Tim Shafer is sadly, one of the biggest gaming let downs I experienced in recent years.
While Act1 of this P&C adventure was fun, enjoyable, nostalgic ride with balanced difficulty and amazing story potential, Act2 feels rushed and unfinished. As Vella and Shay you revisit same exact locations as in part one, to do some of the most annoying puzzles I had the displeasure of solving. That was a throwback to "good old days" I did not expect.
What caught me by surprise is how all character development from Act1 was seemingly replaced by almost nothing at all. Have you ever wondered how Vella's rebellion against decades-old traditions will resolve? How will her family and whole community of Sugar Bunting will react once she returns? Perhaps you wanted to know if Shay will manage to break free from his patronising prison? Being so used to infantile challenges how will he cope with harsh reality? Well, you certainly won't get the satisfying answers here. Broken Age just suddenly stops being a game that explores the themes of adolescence in unusual situations and complexities of being a teenager and becomes convoluted mess that pulls out plot points from nowhere.
Can't recommend at this price. Not a bad game, but very disappointing one.

Spintires is based on a seemingly simple idea, but has surprisingly much depth. The basic premise is that for each map, you need to haul a specified amount of timber from one location to another. To achieve this goal, you start out with one or more trucks and/or a Russian 4x4 jeep, the UAZ (in-game designation: A-469). To make things more challenging, most of the map is concealed by so-called "cloaking" spots. To unlock these, you need to drive up to the center of the cloaking spot. This is where the planning starts: do you start out by removing cloaks or do you start working towards the objective? Or perhaps you start looking for other vehicles that are located on the map and can be unlocked by driving up to them.
On Casual mode, it only takes a click to go back to the garage if you get irretrievably stuck, or if you tip over. On Hardcore mode, you have to salvage your vehicles. In addition, you have to make sure you don't run out of fuel. Consequently, you can either hone your driving skills or plan ahead by unlocking all the trucks on the map and then using them to support each other. All trucks have their own strengths and weaknesses. In addition, you can choose if you want to haul a heavier load, using a trailer, which is more difficult but will require fewer trips back and forth. When you get into a tricky situation, the physics engine allows you to get quite creative, using multiple vehicles, winches and cranes to remedy the situation.
I found Spintires to be much more engrossing than I had expected. More than once have I lost track of time playing it, always an indication of a good game. The slow and careful work required to move heavy vehicles across difficult terrain brings back memories from my army days, when I served in an engineer company. The scenery is beautiful, and along with the ambient sounds it truly conveys a feeling of isolation and wilderness. The only downside is that the camera is not always easy to use, but with a bit of practice that becomes a marginal problem. I strongly recommend this game to anyone who appreciates a game that skillfully combines patience, planning and logistics with driving.

Virginia is basically a 2-3 hour long cutscene where you have control of your character, but no real agency (though there are a few optional and actually tricky puzzles to do for the achievements that involve you sort of reading the achievement descriptions and trying to figure them out, many span over multiple chapters even). There is no choices, the story is linear, and you in the end have to do what the game wants you to do to progress. While it's narrative-based, the game doesn't have a line of dialogue in it, the characters don't even make any sounds at all. No grunts or breathing sounds either.
So why is it being so well received? Simple, it is an engaging experience that makes use of what only very few film directors figured out, let alone game developers. The game manages to be touching, emotional, and have deeper characters than most games without a single spoken word, the music is phenomenal (performed by an orchestra), but with fantastic direction for a game as the music sort of moves and changes with your own actions, it does it so well the transitions feel natural and always fit what's going on, even if you take your time to get to the next point and continually lead well into each other and add so much to each scene. And the scenes themselves are engaging, I won't spoil it, but the game has some fantastic art direction, and builds up a multi-layered mystery with great environmental and detail story-telling full of repeating imagery, breath-taking scenes, and pulls from surrealist works of the likes of David Lynch not for mood, but the idea of deeper meanings and various connections you can make as you play of how everything connects and comes together.
It won't strike with everyone, but those who find the appeal of the game may find themselves engrossed in it, and it definitely sticks with you past the ending. Also been reading a lot of people who finished and immediately went back to play through it again, it is a game with a lot to appreciate on a second playthrough, and is interesting to talk about theories, thoughts, and observations with others.
There is a lot more to be said, but going deeper would spoil things. If this sounds like something you'd enjoy, I recommend it. And it is worth playing, letting yourself explore and become immersed in the world of Virginia is quite an experience, and one I don't regret a moment for delving into.
