I am little late to the game but I had to post how EXTREMELY pleased I am with the Steam version of FSX. Dovetail really did a good job working out all of the kinks. I have been trying to run the FSX boxed version since it was released. Bought more powerful computers and still have never been able to run FSX successfully. And successfully means flying a whole route from gate to gate without crash. Ive always foind myself tweaking the settings and searching the internet to figure our how to get it right... Because surely Microsoft wouldnt release a product that only works on some systems right?! Well i never got it to work. I have been flying on FS9 instead which is VERY stable. The problem? None of the latest and greatest addons are compaitable with FS9. Grrr
Enters FSX-SE
I have done several long distance flights this past week without one crash or hang up and frame rates are awesome. All of MY addons are compatable. I have several payware airports and payware planes, all work without a problem. If you are still having issues with your boxed version of FSX or find yourself constantly tweaking the settings to get somewhat optimal flying performance then you should give Steam version a go. Hello my fellow steamers, hope your having a lovely day looking at and buying games. I know that ya'll probabably want wasteland 2 as well (no♥♥♥♥♥♥right), well let me lay down the game for you in a very frank manner. The game Barely makes it on my recommendation list; here are my reasons.
The Positives.
1.WORLD: The world and lore is very well wrighten and thought out. The world itself feels very much so like a post apocolyptic society where the weak die and the strong survive. You, being the Desert Rangers with a lush backstory of your own, are essentialy the East Coast Brotherhood of Steel gardians of Arizona. You are the good guy (or not depending on how you want to go about things) and your job is to address the many grievances that plauge the good people of the Arizona dessert with the utmost "care and consideration".
2.RADIO: THE RADIO ITSELF IS ♥♥♥♥ING BRILLIANT. So much character in those radio broadcast, it makes  commenters in real life sound like a highschool math teacher on retilin.
3.INVENTORY SYSTEM: Unlike Divinity: Original Sin, the inventory system in this game and the grouping with party members is not nearly as tedious and annoying and bares a HUGE shout out. In these kinds of game, tediousness is a very real problem that they suffer from and thankfully (for the most part) Wasteland 2 dosen't.
The Cons
1.COMBAT: Sadly, the Combat is no where near the level that the wrighting is. The combat is not bad, however it is a bare minumum. Its no where near the level of Xcom:enemy unknown, hell its no where near the level of Divinity: Original Sin. Think of it like this, take away everything that makes Xcom's combat fun; the abilities and personalization of every shot and leave it with only a cover system and a Headshot special ability which everyone has and nobody earns.
2.CUSTOMIZATION: The "customization"  in this game is so dated and bland that its worth mentioning. All it is is a stat system where you allocate your points into different skills and attributes and thats it. You can also have your Rangers wear different clothes but that is a minimul form of customization as far as I'm concerned.
3.TEDIOUSNESS WITH LOOTING: Many people think this is a miner gripe but trust me, its not. The number of times that a person has to select a party member to lockpick a box or disarm a trap is WAY, WAY to much. Like I said, the game, for the most part, dose not suffer from tediousness. the only other part that does suffer is that, later on in the game, a couple of my weaker party members are easily over incumbered and thats because they are either the weaker members of the group or they carry assault rifles (in my case its a mix of both) and, well, theres a reasen why they have a distribute button.
4.ENEMY CHARACTER: The enemies in this game are very boring. Some are humorous (giant honey badgers are cute, until you find out that their one of the toughest enemies in the game) but a LOT of them are SO, SO boring. none of them are unique in anyway save for a couple here and their, and most of them are essentially reskins of your rangers (even the animals) and that is just absolutely depressing. Granted, the giant toads can tounge lash your weapons away and you can get crabs from junkies but most really are just shoot, dodge, and grunt.
5.GRAPHICS: GRAPHICS ARE AN ABSOLUTE DISCRAISE TO THIS GAME! Really, they are. For me, graphics are far from everything and I can get by but most people will and have looked at a screen shot and have said and I quote from the little thought bubble over their head "Nah, man. nah. this game is a ♥♥♥♥ing eyesore". look man, when my own feacies has a better face then most of the character models, you know that its pretty bad.
6.WEAPON MODS: Weapon mods go hand in hand with customization so I won't say much, all I'll say is that they lack character; nothing special, just state boost which bugs me and speaking of bugs.
7. BUGS: I have only once ran into a bug that broke my game. During a fight, when I tried to move around in the world, things got weird. The land itself would stay in place but the shadows would act like i was moving the camera. I hope Enxile takes care of that, im shure they will because of updates. right, Look guys, I dont know about you but me, frankly, I'm getting really tired of DMs releasing a product knowing full well that their are bugs in it and trust me, their are more bugs. To me, that should not be an excuse for a game to release in a "dirty' state esspecially when Enxile held this game back so many times to help make it "perfect".
8. COMPANIONS: Put it simply, almost complete lack of interaction.Think along the lines of Mass Effect or Dragon Age in that they talk while ya'll walk but other then that, can't really talk to them unless recruiting them to be a companion. No special, awesome quest exist (they do but only on a subpar level like helping schmo sniff out his stash of liquor is one and thats it; they could have had a hobo ambush at the very least, common guys.) nor any real upgrades for your companions save for the usual level ups or any useful, companion specific items save for Ace's Wrench.
Final Conclusion: WOW, what a list; almost seems like I absolutly dispise this game, dosent it? This game has a LOT of flaws, a lot of mechanics are underdeveloped. In all honesty, it feels like the game is primative; old in many respects and feels like it was made before any of these new ideas of in-depth Companion interactions where made or some really meaty Costumizations like synthethic augumentations or mutations where ever even thought of. Hell, the graphics makes it look like it was made in 2001. So why do i give this game a thumbs up? Very rarely do I find a game nowadays that really has character and this game has it in spades.
The world truelly has a personality all of its own, hell, to me Enxile did a really good job in making this world feel real. The Radio broadcast are absolutely commendable, the characters you talk to are all unique and how they emplemented key events of the 1st wasteland into the new one was very colorful and unexpecting.The world truelly does feel like its alive in many aspects and its hard to find that in a lot of games nowadays.
Simply put, if your a person who really likes a world with character and heart and dont mind the outdated mechanics then this is the game for you, if not well keep this in mind before you bash the game. Mr. Fargo develped this game for people like him who grew up in the time when games where still a very nerd only thing and this game pays tribute to those days. I can bash the game on its primative nature all I wont but at the end of the day, he and his team made it that way and they made it that way on purpose, or at least I assume so, and I can respect a person for doing something like that; something that was more from the heart then for the wallet for once in this industry. And with that being sayed, I believe he was sucessful in achieveing those old memories for him and the rest of the "Old Timers".
P.S. I've stated my peace on the subject and hope that Mr.Fargo and the rest of EnXile realise this because at the end of the day, these guys have got to kick it up a notch to survive. So, without further ado, heres hoping these boys can take what I've sayed, empliment it into Plain Scape: Tides of Numenera, and hit that ball way out of the ♥♥♥♥ing ball park and right into those publishers mouths! Lord knows those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s need their asses wipped and guys like Fargo are just the types to do it.

The most amazing adventure game I have ever played. And it even features time-travel in a very special way that feels natural and almost believable!
What is (for me) the most surprising in this game is that:
The whole environment and characters, items, technology... everything feels pretty normal and natural !!
There are tons of thrilling emotions and moments of surprise / realization in the story!
1. The Story!!! I have no words for this level of perfection............ *GODLIKE* !
- The psychology of characters - every thinkable typical type of character is there. All dialogues, backstories...
- All is Perfect in every tiniest detail! It is truly *unbelievable* how detailed this adventure experience is.
2. Graphics is looking good and pretty and has a really original "overtone" or atmosphere - a mix just between realistic 3D and surrealistic-3D-cartoon, that leaves some space for fantasy - just like the visuals in game "Dear Esther".
- and there are those especially *beautiful* and slightly dynamic (moving) drawing-like quest markers... which somehow seemlessly blend into the 3D scene! :O
3. Music - absolutely perfect atmospheric music, accenting and *enhancing* the story.
4. Sounds - really good and perfectly accenting the story.
5. Controls - the control by mouse is a bit contra-intuitive at first. Takes forever before You realize that You need to *click+drag* from the center towards the drawn-font option what to do. By the time I realized how to control this game with mouse,  I already have gotten an XBox360 Controller for Windows and I have finished the game. :-)

This game is quite honestly tough to rate as it will make you feel conflicted. Nonetheless, here is my take on this game.
Please note that some positives also pave the way to a negative that you will see below.
Positives
- Increased map size. Now divided into regions. Each is about the size of one of the two sections in SOM.
- New abilities. From leaping off your enemies, chaining stealth kills, and even chaining shadow strike kills. There are more but I am trying to keep this review spoiler clean.
- New missions for followers(From hunting catagors, graug, to even raiding captains supplies).
- Story, the missions were engaging and kept me playing. The game's cutscenes were well done in my opinion.
- Combat has been improved, however it does take getting use to and has negatives.
- Some abilities will consume focus instead of your arrows(elf-shot). You can increase your amount of focus by equipping better gear.
Cons
- Abilities, while listed as a positive because it brings something new to the table, the way in which it was done makes you scratch your head and questions what was going through the developers heads. There are core abilities and then modifiers for said abilities. Ex. Shadow strike is a base abilitiy with three modifiers. But, and here is the negitive, you can either choose one of those three options, two off my head are, chaining your attacks to other enemies near you, or being able to target an enemy and dominate them instantly. In addition if you want to dominate basic enemies you must have that modifier enabled. Due to this change it feels as though you have to miss out on certain play styles as what was once basic, is now something you have to choose to have because instead of dominating basic enemies you can have it to where it would replenish your arrows( or elf- shot). Not using this will cause you quite often to have no arrows to use on a captain that can only be damaged by range or stealth... in a fortress.
- Repetitive enemies. One new type of enemy is introduced... that's it. Ologs. Bigger and attacks cannot be countered. Enemies often look the same despite cosmetics on their appearance having variety. You will feel as though you are fighting the same enemy over and over again. The nemesis engine attempts to solve this problem with adding personalities. While it does add depth to the combat system with captains able to adapt to your moves if used to much, you still see personalities being repeated, though there are a greater amount of them.
- Travel. By travel, I mean being able to get around. Talion's basic run speed is extremely slow. Feels as though you are simply crawling and the fast travel points are often far from your destination/follower mission.
- Story. Multiple times I could tell what was going to happen long before it did.
- Missions for your followers can be repetitive. When attempting to level up one follower, I ended up doing 3-4 of the same mission in a row while also having to travel back and forth across the map to them, becoming quite tedious.
- Micro-transactions. While I did not experience too invasive ads, I did not do any multiplayer sieges. However, the game is priced at $60 USD, micro-transactions are priced at 100 maximum for an amount of 10k gold with 2k bonus. Cost of some of the items is 860 gold for a bundle of three chests. woohoo. I did not spend any money and instead used the currency that is available to be earned in-game for completing the story and optional objectives.
This game feels more like a study of what we gamers will accept as a new normal. If you feel as though you must get this game, do not encourage further additions of Micro-transactions in games by using them and spending more money. I cannot recommend this game.

Here's what I think of this game, I'll compare it to Civ 5 since most people consider that to be the best Civ game.
Music: Both Civ 5 and Civ III have fantastic soundtracks as with pretty much all Civ games. CIV 5's soundtrack is better, but that doesn't mean this soundtrack isn't worth listening to.
Diplomacy: The diplomacy here in Civ III, in my opinion is better. You can trade maps technologies, change how agressive the AI is. The AI does get quite a bit agressive once you get to medium agressiveness although.
Scenarios: The scenarios here in Civ III are quite interesting. We have Rise of Rome, Fall of Rome, Napoleanic Europe, WW2 in the pacific, etc. I honestly can't choose between Civ 5 and 3 in terms of which had better scenarios.
War: And here is where we start to see the flaws of Civ III. There are certain units made for attacking, defending, and seige units. The seige units must be protected otherwise they will be either captured or destroyed immediately, and the attacking units are vulnerable to counterattack. Defending units ensure your cities are protected and your attacking armies. This part of war, I liked, It made sure I don't just build completely one type of unit.
Cities are instantly captured if there is no unit inside. I wasn't as fond of this as the unit diversity, but it was tolerable at least.
But then their's the battle system. It's luck based, which I have a burning hatred for. I could attack a spearman one time with an archer and not take any damage, while another time, a defending spearmen exactly the same as the other one could take out my archer, without taking any damage. How does that make any sense? I get it it's an old game an all, but come on.
Also the AI seem way too powerful. I met Scandinavia on turn 2 and it already said his forces outnumbered mine.
CIv 5 definetly, has better war mechanics.
Barbarian encampment and ruins/friendly encampments: Whether you love 'em or hat 'em these guys are around, some encampment are friendly and will give you something like gold or a settler to give you a huge early game boost. and of course the hostile. You can make the hostile encampments non existant, sedentary, normal, roaming or raging. Since there is more option than Civ 5, I'd say these are slightly better.
Civilization balance: Civilization 5 isn't exactly balanced, (Babylon is much better, is pretty much better every aspect compared to let's say the Iroqouis). Civ's are more balanced here. Each Civ have a unique unit, 2 free technologies and 2 bonus'. Military bonus' allow you to build stronger armies faster, science allows you to build science buildings faster, religious allows you to build cultural building faster, etc. In my opinion the two best are science and religious (Which Babylon ironically has both XD). Besides that Civ's are quite balanced besides early game Unique units (I'm looking at you bowmen)
Victory types: Time victory is always on here, which I don't like (although you can push back the counter for time victory to kick in) cultural victoy revolves around how much culture you can get in either one city or your entire empire, dominatuion requires you to own at certain percentage of the world's population or land area, conquest is to eliminate all rival civilizations., wonder is to build a certain amount of wonders, diplomatic is to get people to vote for you once the UN is built, and space race to leave this filthy planet. All good, although most of the time you will win by either cultural or time.
Graphic: I don't really care for graphics much, but the graphic here are at best, pleasing to the eye and at worst, tolerable.
Conclusion: CIV 5 is obviously better, but Civ 3 is extremely enjoyable also, I have many hours into this, and many more will be put into playing this. I know the flaws I listed here aren't going to be changed unless everyone at Firaxis gets high. I haven't seen any bugs, just a great game.

So my first few hours of experience goes as follows:
"I started a couple of practice matches to get the hang of the game.
First practice match was AFL Women's team Melbourne Demons VS  the Under 18s team NT Thunder, in which the women won comfortably over the kids.
After only two matches I felt I was getting the hang of the controls, so I started a career mode. I created my character, a 28 year old 5'7" Right Half Forward playing with Gippsland Power in the Under 18s TAC cup.
A few games in, and everything was feeling too easy, the controls were getting pretty intuitive. Bump up to medium difficulty, and that seems to be decent, yet still easy enough to learn for now.
Eventually, we win the Cup, my character wins Goal Kick, Best & Fairest and the Morrish Medal. A 28 year old kicking♥♥♥♥♥against under 18s.
Being impressed by my character's ability to beat kids, Greater Western Sydney offer me a 1 year contract which I accept.
I play my first game in the big league. I notice that everything is much faster, running, kicking movement, everything has turned up to 11!
Regardless, I gather 20 disposals and kick 5 goals."
All in all, so far AFL Evolution is streets ahead of any previous AFL game, a lot of new features have been added and gameplay has improved.
Is this as polished a NBA 2k or FIFA? No. There is definely things that could be improved on, but I think considering the budget and experience those two franchises have compared to AFL Evolution, this is a decent crack at creating a decent game for our great National sport.
Do I recommend? For AFL fans, yes. This improved upon everything AFL Live had, and adds so much more.
For non-AFL fans, it's hard to recommend this for it's full price, when there's more polished games for cheaper.
I bought it because I love AFL, and want to support the developers and hope their next iteration is even better.

I enjoyed Alan Wake. I'd say the game is softcore horror shooter. I liked the world that was created, it did feel quite big, even if you are forced to stay on somewhat narrow paths at times.
The good:
World. The backdrop or rendering distance looks great. No time really spent in loading screens. Does look like a real place to me.
The Atmosphere. There's fog, there's darkness, there's hope in the distant lights. I think the atmosphere in the dark forest is what carries this game for the most part.
Level design. Quite straightforward, but still there's always something to explore; a hidden path, a hut with supplies. If I was to replay the game I'd explore the levels a bit more thoroughly, there's a lot of stuff I missed for sure. Casual puzzles can also be found, never too much trouble, but still nice change of pace.
Technical Performance. Runs solid 60 FPS, or more, even on a weaker machine I'd think. Certainly not a horrible port. Controls were also very good with KB+mouse.
The things to improve:
Facial animations or animations in general. I don't really remember how this game compares to the stuff released at that time, but the facial animations were pretty bad. It's not really something that takes that much away from the enjoyment for the game, but characters could feel more alive for sure.
Combat. The basics are okay with me. You need light, you need weapons. I think I would have just wanted to see a bit more interaction with the world with this. You can't make any sort of traps, there's the occasional gas tank that blows up, but even those weren't exactly useful or needed. I wish there were more powerful combat solutions offered in the level design, like collapsing stuff or dropping something etc.
Driving parts. Pretty boring. I guess you don't have to use car if you don't want to, but that would be pretty hard I think. At least the car can drift :D
Story. I think it's silly to say it would be just bad. It wasn't. Just not my favorite one ever. There's just too many questions left after completing the game. The answers I got weren't really that fulfilling.
Horror aspect. I think they could have made this game 10 times more scarier, by just giving the play way less info about what's going on. Now almost everytime there's enemy spawning they really let you know. There's a real lack of true ambushes or jump scares, they exist, but only a few times really.
Texture work. I think everything or most stuff is directly ported from xbox360. There's some pretty bad textures in this game at times.
Overall I'd give this game 7/10. Quite entertaining, I enjoyed most parts, even if this game should have been way scarier.  I think Remedy was aiming for more sense of desperation and bigger worlds where you could maybe even get lost or something, but since the game was in development hell I guess, they had to release something and went with more traditional linear scripted shooter. At least the pacing stayed good and things never really get boring.

Wasteland 2 does many things right but also many things wrong. The biggest problem I have with the game is that it is too long. If they cut out a little bit here and there I woudlnt loose motivation to play this, but after 30h, which is a lot, it kinda got dull.
Another big problem is that if you want to open a safe for example with safe-cracking and you have 50% chance of opening it, you can just save the game before opening it and then keep loading the save file and try to open it. Of course you can decide not to abuse this, but the game itself could prevent this easily.
But I had a good time with Wasteland 2. I didnt finish it, but thats okay. I really like the combat system which seems simple at first but is really enjoyable in my opinion unlike games like Shadowrun Returns. What I like the most is that you dont have just 2 moves for every character but every character has different amount of action points and every action the character can do costs different amount of AP and every weapon has also a different AP cost. This is a very flexible way of balancing the game and it works.
I also like the visual feedback when you overkill an enemy he just explodes or his arms go off or something. The graphics of the game are bad though which wouldnt be that big of a problem if it had a distinct art style but its just dull graphics from early 2000s.
The quests are really well designed and feel relevant and the characters you meet are also not bad. However I had some bugs here and there which prevented some quests from getting completed, but those bugs might be fixed now.
What is a bad design decision in my opinion is perma-death. When one of your characters die, he is dead forever. The thing is having 1 more or 1 less character in your party makes a HUGE difference, so every time one of your characters die you are pretty much screwed and you have to reload a previous save game. Only place this would make sense is when people who can join your party can die, but when one of your primary characters die it should be game over.
And I also dont like how you can make people join your party because as I said it makes a very HUGE difference how many people are in your party, so depending on how you skilled your characters and how many people you find or miss the game is either extremely easy or unfair. In my opinion the game should stick to a 4 character limit and balance the game with that in mind and give you a game over when 1 character dies. What they could do is increase the limit at certain parts of the game and offer you an additional party member or so. It isnt balanced well currently though.

Here's what I think of this game, I'll compare it to Civ 5 since most people consider that to be the best Civ game.
Music: Both Civ 5 and Civ III have fantastic soundtracks as with pretty much all Civ games. CIV 5's soundtrack is better, but that doesn't mean this soundtrack isn't worth listening to.
Diplomacy: The diplomacy here in Civ III, in my opinion is better. You can trade maps technologies, change how agressive the AI is. The AI does get quite a bit agressive once you get to medium agressiveness although.
Scenarios: The scenarios here in Civ III are quite interesting. We have Rise of Rome, Fall of Rome, Napoleanic Europe, WW2 in the pacific, etc. I honestly can't choose between Civ 5 and 3 in terms of which had better scenarios.
War: And here is where we start to see the flaws of Civ III. There are certain units made for attacking, defending, and seige units. The seige units must be protected otherwise they will be either captured or destroyed immediately, and the attacking units are vulnerable to counterattack. Defending units ensure your cities are protected and your attacking armies. This part of war, I liked, It made sure I don't just build completely one type of unit.
Cities are instantly captured if there is no unit inside. I wasn't as fond of this as the unit diversity, but it was tolerable at least.
But then their's the battle system. It's luck based, which I have a burning hatred for. I could attack a spearman one time with an archer and not take any damage, while another time, a defending spearmen exactly the same as the other one could take out my archer, without taking any damage. How does that make any sense? I get it it's an old game an all, but come on.
Also the AI seem way too powerful. I met Scandinavia on turn 2 and it already said his forces outnumbered mine.
CIv 5 definetly, has better war mechanics.
Barbarian encampment and ruins/friendly encampments: Whether you love 'em or hat 'em these guys are around, some encampment are friendly and will give you something like gold or a settler to give you a huge early game boost. and of course the hostile. You can make the hostile encampments non existant, sedentary, normal, roaming or raging. Since there is more option than Civ 5, I'd say these are slightly better.
Civilization balance: Civilization 5 isn't exactly balanced, (Babylon is much better, is pretty much better every aspect compared to let's say the Iroqouis). Civ's are more balanced here. Each Civ have a unique unit, 2 free technologies and 2 bonus'. Military bonus' allow you to build stronger armies faster, science allows you to build science buildings faster, religious allows you to build cultural building faster, etc. In my opinion the two best are science and religious (Which Babylon ironically has both XD). Besides that Civ's are quite balanced besides early game Unique units (I'm looking at you bowmen)
Victory types: Time victory is always on here, which I don't like (although you can push back the counter for time victory to kick in) cultural victoy revolves around how much culture you can get in either one city or your entire empire, dominatuion requires you to own at certain percentage of the world's population or land area, conquest is to eliminate all rival civilizations., wonder is to build a certain amount of wonders, diplomatic is to get people to vote for you once the UN is built, and space race to leave this filthy planet. All good, although most of the time you will win by either cultural or time.
Graphic: I don't really care for graphics much, but the graphic here are at best, pleasing to the eye and at worst, tolerable.
Conclusion: CIV 5 is obviously better, but Civ 3 is extremely enjoyable also, I have many hours into this, and many more will be put into playing this. I know the flaws I listed here aren't going to be changed unless everyone at Firaxis gets high. I haven't seen any bugs, just a great game.

A fun but ultimately unworthy sequel to the first. There are a litany of irritating design choices which mean the game has ultimately gone backwards. Whilst the lighting in the first was criticised for being dark it had mood, now all the lighting appears flat and all the colours, textures and characters are much more crayon esque without any of the depth of detail lighting gave the first. The combat has also regressed rather than improved. The sword strikes now feel lighter, the movement is more awkward and less fluid, hit detection isn't as solid and striking enemies no longer feels as impactful as before.
Then, in an effort to make the game more varied, there are the multiple side missions, quests and collectibles. These are shoddily done and add very little to the story, often distracting from it. There seem to be inumerable collectibles everywhere and you can simply run between them, largely ignoring the orcs and collect at your whim. These are often long, pointless challenges to reconstruct memory fragments or collect bits of lore.
There's fun to be had here, the combat is still enjoyable but not as slick as the first, and whilst Talion remains an annoying alpha male everyman with a boring monologue tone, some of the side characters and enemy characters are interesting. Can't help but feel the game's one big feature, the nemsis system, would be better used on a more polished title that actually built on the first rather than letting the quality slip. Fun, but do not pay full price.

"Hotline Miami."
A review by Richard Valkinsenn.
"I've never seen brains like that before, man."
"Brutal" is the word for Hotline Miami. Both in terms of violence and even gameplay. And it shows no mercy in both regards. Sporting a memorable retro style in both it's pixellated visuals and top-down gameplay--for better or worse--Hotline Miami serves as a glorious, albeit very frustrating, throwback to classic top-down 1990s games. The game also features a brilliant and unforgettable synth-pop soundtrack, along with an interesting narrative about an unnamed protagonist who receives phone messages cryptically instructing him to head to various locales around Miami. Usually under the guise of business transactions, these messages end up initiating nothing short of a slaughter once the protagonist, nicknamed "Jacket," reaches his destination. From there, many more killing sprees follow, along with a twisting, winding story packed with revelations the player may or may not be ready for.
But, to be honest, while Hotline Miami is an excellent game with an excellent story and soundtrack, it isn't without faults, and these faults generally lie with the gameplay. The game is brutally difficult, and it isn't helped by the awkward and rather clunky control system that directly ties the crosshair to the player's movements instead of the other way around. In essense, you move, and the crosshair awkwardly moves with you, potentially removing it from an advancing enemy. And enemies in Hotline Miami will suicidally rush your position and kill you in one hit, no matter how many of their friends you've killed so far. What makes all of this worse is the fact that, given the game's pixellated aesthetic, the crosshair is actually remarkably easy to lose in the game's environments, making it pretty hard to pick out in the midst of the carnage that the player can inflict.
However, even with these gripes, Hotline Miami is still an enjoyable game that is definitely not worth missing and absolutely worth picking up.
Final Verdict:
I liked it.
Until next time, this is Richard,
Signing off.
P.S. Point of note: though it doesn't feature vehicular gameplay, it DOES look a lot like Grand Theft Auto: Classic.

Act I is a somewhat decent (albiet very simple) point and click adventure game. However it only really peaks in intrigue right before the second part of the game begins, which has just finally released.
Unfortunately... Act II takes a massive dive in quality. The story fires tons of bizarre new information at you off the bat. 95% of the new story could have cut to focus on making a better, more coherent story. The themes Act I was building are suddenly gone, with the game awash in non-sequitor new plot points for no reason.
The gameplay also took a frustrating downturn. People complained it wasn't hard enough or complex enough in terms of puzzles before. So they added lots of backtracking where you do nothing but click on the edge of screens over and over and over and over and over. Other than that "harder" is only a matter of trying every inventory item on everything, pretty much. If that's the extent of their retooling... unfortunately this game would have been much better served to suffer critcisms of being too easy.
It's a bit of a wonder they didn't test any on or get feedback from the backer community... as people would have told them these things before release was said and done.
At any rate, now that the story of this Kickstarter project is concluded, and for me it turned out to be a miss.

Full Disclosure: I am a backer of Broken Age on Kickstarter. You can find me in the credits listed under backers as 'Samuel "Iron Curtain" Abram'. I will try to be as spoiler-free as possible when reviewing the game. I'll start with the bad first:
CONS:
1. Plotwise, after setting us up in Act 1, Act 2 answered some questions but also raised others in their stead, even after going to every room and exhausting every dialogue option. It felt like there should be an act 3 but that's not happening unfortunately.
2. The final sequence was extremely underwhelming and anti-climactic, as was the ending. When I wanted an epilogue, I was given it, but only in a form of a WALL-E-style credits montage rather than actually watching a cutscene or discovering through gameplay, which I would prefer.
PROS:
1. Absolutely gorgeous artwork. Gorgeous Art Style. Not to mention original and inspired. I give it two thumbs way up!
2. Puzzles made sense and were logical. They were easy in Act 1 and got harder in Act 2 but I was still able to solve them all without a walkthrough (with only one exception). This is in contrast to Grim Fandango, wherein I had to consult a walkthrough frequently and when I found the solution, I thought "That's insane! I never would have thought of that!".
3. Characters are interesting and well-fleshed out. I actually care about everybody other than the two main protagonists!
4. Dialogue is funny and full of Schafer's trademark wit.
FINAL SCORE: 8.25 out of 10. BUY THIS GAME!

Having only briefly played it's predecessor, my main fear was that the combat system was going to be atrocious again. Nothing is less true.
Immersion is magnificent, and I enjoyed exploring the three areas.
The combat system is very satisfactory and not too difficult to comprehend and use.
You have a hard and a soft attack, and can block. But these three elements need to be timed and practised well enough, because button-mashing won't save you here.
If you do not pay attention, even a single swordsman foe can bring you down from 100% health. Gerald's skill is on par with yours, so be sure to pick a proper difficulty.
Magic is, like the lore correcly depicts for Witchers, both a combat aid to support your swordsmanship, as well as a tool. Throughout the game, all five spells serve their own purpose.
Choices ripple through the game, although some weigh heavier than others.
You won't feel the expectation to change the course of the story, but you still feel the result.
Must-have for RPG fans.

The Witcher 2 is an exemplarary sequel that manages to build upon the strengths of the Witcher 1, namely it's combat mechanics and plot twists, while addressing and improving on it's predecessor's flaws . An outstanding Role Playing Game, no two replays of this game will ever be the same. In the Witcher 2, you are thrust into the character of Geralt of Rivia, famed monster slayer and unintended savior of a king, where you must make the decisions that alter the fates of not only the protagonist but the world and its many characters about him. Its a compelling narrative about maintaining neutrality in a world that is morally ambiguous and deceptive. You will feel the sting of unintended consequences, and with a variety of supporting characters, all whose lives and motivations you will come to understand, decisions in this game are not made lightly . Aside from its storyline, the actual mechanics of the gameplay are superbly executed. Combat is visceral and tactical. Magic, Alchemy, and swordplay are your means of defeating your enemies, and the Witcher 2 introduces a menagerie containing all sorts of monsters, both fantastically gargantuan & sometimes human, whose strengths/weaknesses must be taken into account, especially on the hardest of difficulties. In the end, the Witcher 2 is a satisfying video game with a storyline that leaves it's impression upon you because of it's relation to your impact as Geralt. I'm optimistic about this franchise and look forward to future sequels.

I only picked up this game when it was on sale for like $4 and took a year or so before I actually got around to playing it.
I'm sorry I didn't find out about this game when I came out and that I took so long to play it after buying it, because it's amazing.
First of all, it's heavily influenced by a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥that I like, mostly Stephen King, and Twin Peaks. Particularly Stephen King, although other literary references are dropped here and there.
The main plot is that you are a deeply troubled writer on vacation with your wife in a quaint mountain town. Pretty quickly you realize that things are going on in this town that are quite strange, the supernatural is afoot, and pretty quickly your wife disappears and you are on the run for your life from the dark, spectral inhabitants of the town. 2SPOOPY4ME!
But seriously though, although some of the plot points are a bit cheesy, the core of the story is very good. You spend the whole game fighting dark creatures while traveling through the town, and the whole time, you question whether or not what you're experiencing is "real" or Alan Wake descending into insanity. It's a theme the game comes back to quite a bit, which is also indicative of the Stephen King influence.
And in the end *SPOILER*after all this questing to retrieve your stolen wife, you end up having to sacrifice yourself to do so, by trapping yourself in the dark world in which she was being held. It ends the game on a really good note in my opinion, because it shows the dedication of Alan Wake's character, and allows him more character building in the American Nightmare storyline and the extra chapters. *END SPOILER*

Originally, I wrote a positive review for this game, but I've come to realize that that was a mistake.
There is a fine line between a game being hard, a game being brutal, and a game being flawed.
This game flies way off the handle of being brutal that, once you know what you're doing, this game is pure torture.
Many people will say that this review is just coming from somebody who can't handle a hard game, or someone who just needs to get good. But, that's just the problem; you can only get so "good" at Nuclear Throne.
Every enemy moves at complete random; you can memorize what they do to attack, and the patterns for the few attacks in the game that aren't just a mindless spray of bullets, but almost every single enemy in the game moves, and attacks, at complete random. There's only so much skill that can come into play.
I'm so tired of torturing myself trying to get everything in this game. It's absolute torture. Name any other game known for its difficulty, it pales in comparison. Getting Over It? A ♥♥♥♥ing cakewalk. Isaac? I've 1,000,000,000%ed it, I beat Mega Satan with The Lost before The Lost was buffed, I'm no stranger to masochism. But this game goes beyond that; to its core, it is a flawed game. The developers don't care, they've never cared. Look at Lil' Hunter, the boss that makes most casual players want to quit the game entirely; it was bad before, but they kept buffing him and buffing him, despite spawning in the most crowded and awkwardly generated level where you pretty much get zero cover while he constantly flies on top of you. The Throne forces you to destroy massive explosive generators within seconds while also dodging showers of bullets if you don't want to just get what is essentially a game over. The Captain is a ♥♥♥♥ing joke. I honestly doubt the developers even play tested her, it feels like a boss that you're not meant to be capable of winning. Sure, these make the game harder, but they're not challenging. They're just torture. The poorly made, inconsistant hitboxes, the enemies which ignore all knockback and WILL kill you if they feel like it, the randomly generated levels which half of the time put you in an inescapable line of fire from dozens of enemies in multiple directions, the inpercise controls, the developer's inability to make a game run in 60 Frames per second because it's allegedly more aesthetically pleasing, and, really, Vlambeer's general incompetence as a whole.
Originally, I decided that I'd recommend this game because it's a challenging experience, but I can honestly say I would not recommend this game to anyone. Even if you enjoy brutally difficult games, this game will haunt you. You want to get better at it, but you can't. It's like saying you're good at gambling; the only winning move is not to play.

"Hotline Miami."
A review by Richard Valkinsenn.
"I've never seen brains like that before, man."
"Brutal" is the word for Hotline Miami. Both in terms of violence and even gameplay. And it shows no mercy in both regards. Sporting a memorable retro style in both it's pixellated visuals and top-down gameplay--for better or worse--Hotline Miami serves as a glorious, albeit very frustrating, throwback to classic top-down 1990s games. The game also features a brilliant and unforgettable synth-pop soundtrack, along with an interesting narrative about an unnamed protagonist who receives phone messages cryptically instructing him to head to various locales around Miami. Usually under the guise of business transactions, these messages end up initiating nothing short of a slaughter once the protagonist, nicknamed "Jacket," reaches his destination. From there, many more killing sprees follow, along with a twisting, winding story packed with revelations the player may or may not be ready for.
But, to be honest, while Hotline Miami is an excellent game with an excellent story and soundtrack, it isn't without faults, and these faults generally lie with the gameplay. The game is brutally difficult, and it isn't helped by the awkward and rather clunky control system that directly ties the crosshair to the player's movements instead of the other way around. In essense, you move, and the crosshair awkwardly moves with you, potentially removing it from an advancing enemy. And enemies in Hotline Miami will suicidally rush your position and kill you in one hit, no matter how many of their friends you've killed so far. What makes all of this worse is the fact that, given the game's pixellated aesthetic, the crosshair is actually remarkably easy to lose in the game's environments, making it pretty hard to pick out in the midst of the carnage that the player can inflict.
However, even with these gripes, Hotline Miami is still an enjoyable game that is definitely not worth missing and absolutely worth picking up.
Final Verdict:
I liked it.
Until next time, this is Richard,
Signing off.
P.S. Point of note: though it doesn't feature vehicular gameplay, it DOES look a lot like Grand Theft Auto: Classic.

(Discalimer: yes, this review was indeed a result of the band wagon, however, I have plenty of hours enjoying the game and still hadn't writen a review!)
Kerbal Space Program is a highly moddable singleplayer sandbox space flight simulator where you can use a large selection of parts and place them together in almost any maner of way. It isn't hard to make things that fly in KSP. It, however, does require some attention in aerodynamics, weight distribution, fuel ecconomy, orbital paterns, etc. to make them fly to the Mun.
I was not the most enlightened about the majority of these criteria, but nonetheless KSP is a decent platform to learn. When I started, I was just tossing rockets straight up into space like there was no tomarrow (but there was thanks to a sandbox mode). I first learned escape velocity, then how to intercept another planet (with help of a built in flight path calculator that just requires pulling on a a few nodes, pointing, and shooting. I then learned how to land on the mun, and soon later, how to send a rescue pod to the Mun. I then learned how to orbit the Mun.
The game is also quite open to what one can do in it;
Stick a small just inside a rocket? Done.
Stick a small rocket on a plane? Done.
Pilot a jet-powered submarine dozens of kilometers across the ocean? Done.
Shoot an ASROC at it? From a mobile launching vehical in the Admin Building parking lot? Done.
Another thing I admire about KSP is the small amount of computer resources that it requires to run. It'll work if your RAM only consists of a single 4 gigabyte stick. I know that because I used KSP to test each of my only two 4-gig sticks.
Last thing (for the band wagon!), the game is highly moddable. You can tweak the stats of an engine just by retyping it in notepad. I can't recommend this game.
Act 1 is short, fun, and whimsical. Its puzzles are easy, which allows you to explore the beautiful environments and meet all of the interesting characters without too many barriers in your way.
Act 2, on the other hand, is just a frustrating mess. The entire act merely retreads the areas visted in Act 1, which removes the element of exploration that makes act 1 interesting. Worse yet, a lot of the puzzles are just ridiculous. Obvious solutions never work, and the actual solutions often make no sense in terms of why they would work or why the characters would try them. I've spent hours going through the levels clicking everything and trying to use my items on every object, and this is a common trend among players. For some puzzles, you have to go to the other character's perspective in order to find the solution, but the game never tells you when this is required, and it goes counter to everything you've done in act 1, so you might go through entire levels looking for answers that aren't there.
After Double Fine spent over a year developing act 2, it's such a disappointment to see recycled environments and puzzles that are just badly designed and badly thought out. Perhaps those problems might be more forgivable if the quality of the story made up for it, but it doesn't. Despite the brilliant setup in act 1, neither of the two main characters undergo much if any character development in act 2. Instead, we're treated to a bad science fiction plot which tries to explain the superficial elements of the world, and yet still leaves many questions unanswered in the cliffhanger ending. The villains expose themselves as something out of a children's cartoon, and some of the dramatic reveals only make sense if you don't think too deeply about act 1.
This game is a huge disappointment to me, and thinking about it still leaves a bitter taste in my mouth. If you want to see the interesting environments and the story that could have been, watch act 1 on youtube. If you must, watch act 2 on youtube as well. The game itself is absolutely not worth playing.

Well, I have good news and I have bad news.
The good news is that Act 1, if you've already played it, is visually stunning, very charming with a lovely soundtrack, very nostalgic and ends with a twist that had me on the edge of my seat for more than a year, waiting for the resolution.
The bad news is that Act 2 is here to ruin that.
Act 2 fails to live up to the hype. The puzzles are irritatingly convoluted and in no way advance the story, there are no new environments to speak of (only two or three new screens per character), and the ominously sinister undercurrent behind Operation Dandelion and the Maiden's Feast hinted at throughout Act 1 collapses into nothingness almost immediately. Shay and Vella learn nothing, they do not grow, and the entire backstory, the entire reason for the plot, is dumped in a few lines of dialogue in a completely missable conversation. At the risk of spoilers, we have the opportunity to infiltrate the enemy base and learn these things first hand for ourself, to engage the people beyond the plague dam and see how their society parallels that of Sugar Bunting/Meriloft/Shellmound, but that chance is missed, as we remain stranded on the Little Tykes space ship at the risk of... what? Rendering a new environment? Writing a few more characters?
This game was so profoundly disapointing, it's haunting me a full 24 hours after finishing it. I have so much respect for DF and Tim's work, even the things I'm not the target audience for (Hey, I even played Once Upon a Monster with some family and found the unique DF flavor charming and nostalgic). I'm not here to demand to know where all the money went (we know where it went, its not a mystery) or ask why it took so long (I'd be happy if it had taken longer to be honest. This felt like a rushed and unloved project.) But there are games made for the simple love of it, with a team of one or two people in their off hours from their day jobs, in RPG maker or similar programs that have significantly more depth than this. Money does not equal a good game. Without a solid story, Broken Age is...well. Broken.
CONSIDER BUYING INSTEAD: Hatoful Boyfriend. NO WAIT come back, I'm serious! The original build of Hatoful Boyfriend was made with royalty-free music and stock graphic assets suplimented by photos taken by the creator herself and it still has a rich, unique cast of characters and tells the story of a truly chilling murder mystery. Its an emotional roller coaster disguised as an otome parody, and a perfect example of a great game made without a big budget.
Maybe Broken Age could have been better if it had been forced to work with a humbler budget. Who knows.
Bottom line: pass and maybe go play Psychonauts again. It's still amazing.

Alan Wake tells the thrilling story of a writer suffering from writer's block who has travelled to the small town of Bright Falls with his wife to get away from the pressures of being a best selling author. However shortly after arriving in the mysterious town his wife goes missing under unusual circumstances as a seemingly supernatural presence haunts his every move.
The story unfolds over 6  (+2 DLC) episodes each opening with their own 'previously on' segment and credits sequence accompanied by some pretty good episode appropriate music. The pacing of each episode does a great job of slowly building intrigue about the mystery of what is going on in this Twin Peaks-esque town and propelling you forward into what's to come. There are mellow, slower moments in which you interact with the town's quirky characters and history as well as tense, fear inducing moments in which you battle against people possessed by the darkness which hunts you down.
The majority of the game has you battling the dark presence with just a flashlight and a small array of guns, flares and flashbang grenades. You use the flashlight and flares to deteroiate the shield of darkness covering the enemies, followed by using your guns to finish the job. This sequence is repeated ad nauseam. At first, this makes every combat encounter meaningful and frantically tense and goes a long way towards making the Dark Presence feel like something you have no hope of fighting against in the grand scheme of things.
Although this feeling doesn't last long as the lack of enemy variety and weapon selection causes things to drag towards the latter half of the game and the game does little to add variety to the combat encounters other than throwing more enemies at you. As I became more invested in seeing how the artfully told story unfolds, I became less interested in foraging for supplies and engaging in the combat and simply attempted to run past all of the enemies as it became more and more frustrating to deal with the barrage of seemingly never ending enemies.
The game is also littered with collectibles; There are coffee thermoses, another homage to Bright Falls inspiration Twin Peaks; An in game FMV TV show entitled 'Night Springs', which is very heavily inspired by episodes of The Twilight Zone; Radio's which provide insight into the town and it's inhabitants through nocturnal radio host Pat Maine and Prophetic manuscript pages written by Alan Wake which foreshadow events that transpire throughout the game, each one fully narrated by the protagonist.
The abundance of collectibles combined with the games fairly large environments make you want to explore every nook and cranny to uncover as much of the narrative content there is to see but in doing so you'll find yourself engaging in more and more of the quickly tiring combat as the longer you find yourself in the darkness, the more opponents you'll find yourself fighting against which seems completely antithetical to itself. I often found myself battling the compulsive urge to find everything with the desire to engage in as little of the combat as possible.
Despite these shortcomings, I found the intrigue and mystique of the story was more than enough to hook me and keep me playing and interested. Each episode ends in a way that propels you forward and the authorial nature of the protaganist, who frequently shares his often hammy thoughts through voiceover narration, will get you invested in the characters and in discovering what's going on and leave you wanting for more when it reaches the final credits.

Xbox 360 owners didn't really realize what they had with this insane and criminally underrated game, and the fact that this game nearly put Remedy out of business is absurd.  That is, until a high-quality PC port came out and sold by the craploads.  I'll go ahead and get my one complaint with this game out of the way: faceposing.  It's not great, probably since the game was in development hell for almost 10 years and had some ancient tech in there.
It's a great game with some serious atmosphere and confusing special effects that really get to you while playing.  Watching the forest start blurring out and darkening all around you is one hell of an effect that never ceases to screw with you, and the combat itself holds up throughout the whole game.  Combining that with variety and crazy survival scenarios, it leaves very little to complain about for its 15 hour campaign.
It also packs a near-flawless narrative and a unique setting very reminiscent of Stephen King and The Twilight Zone.  I have very few criticisms with the overall storytelling, because there's simply nothing to complain about.  It felt perfectly paced, it blended with the gameplay well, and the level design didn't stop the flow of the story-- in fact, I played the entire game with the HUD off and rarely got stuck (though I did end up wandering off-track in a few places).
Oh, and did I mention it's a great port?  It's a great port.  It's very well optimized, and though it takes a somewhat recent card to get working due to some of the special effects and forced MSAA, it's fairly easy to maintain a constant 60 FPS with a decent CPU and decent-er GPU.
Do I recommend it?  Absolutely.  The full price of $15 is fairly small, and it goes on sale all the time.

I've played many games this year.
I battled villains, I drove cars, planes, boats. I zerg-rushed countless bases and ground my way to better stats and gear. But none of this matters, because I also played Spintires.
SpinTires is relaxing, mentally challenging, it satisfies my inner 5-year-old. It is so simple, yet so complex. Why is it so good? Is it the near absence of constraint? The absolute, total freedom? Is it the jaw-dropping physics or the lush visuals? Is it the way it shows you how "stupidly slow" can be "ridiculously entertaining"? Is it the way every playthrough actually feels like an amazing, mechanized adventure in the forest, without any writer ever having anything to do with it? Is it its charming, ingenuous elegance? Is it how it creates new puzzles, new challenges, new stories, out of the most mundane mishaps?
It's all this, and then some. SpinTires is the ultimate demonstration that emergent gameplay is the best kind there is. And that, in my book, is what makes SpinTires GOTY 2014.

-Engaging boss fights that require some skill or planning to take on

Cons

-Can be easily frustrating on certain levels

This game had a surprising impact on me.  I initially downloaded the first episode when it went free, due to all the praise and accolades it received, back in Summer 2016.  It sat on my hard drive without another thought until January 2017.   I had bought the rest of the episodes on a whim during the winter sale and decided to finally give it a go.  The first episode came off as a sort of high school teen drama with the usual tropes.  I was not sure I wanted to continue, especially since the player experiences these things from the perspective of a teenage girl.  While I have nothing against female protagonists, assuming the role of Max Caulfield as an adult male was sort of weird for me.  I pressed on and eventually decided things were getting interesting.  The addition of the supernatual elements helped me become engrossed with the story and I was even hooked on the drama.
There are a lot of complaints that this game is boring, or the teen drama was unnecessary, but I feel it is more a matter of likes and dislikes.  The school setting is definitely not for everyone; even I was skeptical, at first.  By Episode 2, the focus is shifted less on the student life, and more of the intricacies of the story.  If you are a Call of Duty junky that requires combat action and excitement at every turn, then this game is obviously not for you.  That does not make this a bad game.  Within the story driven adventure genre, this one deserves a spot in the top 10.  This is one of the only video games to have ever invoked a genuine emotional response in me, and to me that is incredible in an age where games are a dime a dozen and so cookie cutter.

In the game Life is Strange, the player plays the character Max Caulfield, an eighteen-year-old photography student. After her witnessing her childhood friend Chloe get shot, she discovers she has the power to wind back time, and she uses her power to solve the mystery about a girl that disappeared from her school.
The story line of this game is compelling. Since the game is heavily based on the choices the player makes, it makes each playthrough unique, especially if the player goes back and changes different elements in the game, from deciding whether to water the plant in Max’s room to choosing who to blame for the disappearance of the missing girl. It is also interesting that the player can choose different paths within the story and see some of the dialogue, but each choice has its own specialized storyline and dialogue. At the end of each chapter in the game, it shows all of the choices the player made within the chapter, and compares it to the decisions other players have chosen. This feature is intriguing since it compares every choice players have chosen, and it allows the player to see how they stack up with the rest of the Life is Strange community. Compared to other games that are heavily based on choice, such as the Fallout series, this game makes the player feel as though their decisions really matter, and it presents an interesting moral dilemma with each choice, allowing the player to go back in time and hear both morals and make a choice.
The actual gameplay of Life is Strange is weird, but I think it works for the particular story. While it is not high action, the game is set in a small town, often times at Max’s high school, there is not a lot of need for too much action. Rather, the gameplay relies on the player choosing from different moral dilemmas. Once a choice is made in the game and the player is no longer able to change their path, the game creates a unique story with different outcomes for each choice. In moments like when Max and Chloe are about to be attacked by a drug dealer, Josh, dog, the player has the option to throw the bone in the parking lot or in the street. If the player throws it in the street the dog gets hit and Josh becomes an enemy, but if the player throws it in the parking lot then the player risks being attacked again, but they are on better terms with Josh. This gives the player enough action to remain entertained, but since Max can go back in time, they can ponder the different choices and choose the one they want to play with. But most of the choices have consequences later on in the game, and that drives the player to keep playing in order to see how their choices impacted the game.
Overall Life is Strange is not a very difficult game to physically play. Since the main character can never truly die, there is not that threat to make the game hard. Since Max can also travel back in time, anytime a character is close to dying the player can rewind time and not allow the character to die. This makes the game not interesting for the player who wants a major challenge, like in The Last of Us. But, Life is Strange covers very heavy and mature topics that may be challenging for the player to deal with, like the part where Max has to try to save her friend, Kate, from jumping off of a tall school building, or when Max can choose to warn Victoria about a potential kidnapping, it makes the player think hard about their choices and how they affect both the characters in the game and the player in their real lives.
This game in particular is unique since the player can replay this game multiple times and still have the same amount of enjoyment they got from the first time they played. The player can go back through the game over and over again, choosing different paths and different choices to see how their actions change the story line. A player could even make one big change in the game and keep everything else the same, and the rest of the game would change drastically, so there are so many possibilities that players would have a hard time trying every story line.
One thing I did not care for in Life is Strange is how the game was released. Since each chapter is a separate file, it was a bit annoying to download each chapter taking several hours before I could play it. I can see how this game strategy could pull people into the game, making them crave more, but it was also a bit strange for a game, and it made the game feel more like a television show. This made the game seem a little distant from everyday life since the events in the game happen within a very short time period, but with it spread out over the course of several months that connection was lost.
Overall Life is Strange is an amazing game. I really enjoyed every minute I played of it, and can hardly wait to replay through it to see how the story ends up changing. This game is by far one of my favorite games, and there should be more games like it in the future.

You're running through the forest- gasping for air, a revolver in your left hand, flashlight in the right,  low on ammunition and batteries, with enemies behind you, too many- swarming, coming closer. You won't get far.
You narrowly dodge an axe swing, only to have to keep running- not being able to stop and catch your breath-
Then you see it.
Your safe haven. The one true friend in this cold, desolate and horrifying region.
The one thing that can save you from the monsters that chase behind you.
You step in- into the light. You catch your breath, and look up at the lamp above you, sighing. Knowing you cannot stay inside this heaven.
You keep going.. until it's over. Until the light comes. And your story continues. Until it cannot continue anymore. You're on a crazy rollercoaster, with many twists, turns, and drops. But eventually it ends. It all ends, and the light consumes the dark. Contrast.
Alan wake is definitely an intriguing game- concepts I haven't seen much of, though I've been told by one friend the light/darkness system is reminiscent of ''Alone in the Dark.''
The combat system is like this- you have a flashlight which destroys the darkness surrounding the ''Taken.'' The monsters in this game. You are then able to shoot them, after first destroying this games concept of a shield.
The weapons in this game are powerful- enough to take out the enemies, sure. However, sometimes you get (no pun intended) taken over by the enemy. And your only choice is to run into the light. Your choice of weapons in this game are as followed as found during the storyline: Revolver, Shotgun, Pump Action Shotgun, Hunting Rifle, Flare gun.
My preference for using these weapons were this- if I had to take care of the Flankers, (the ones with a sickle, or axe, that attack rapidly) I'd use the Revolver primarily, considering, if you shine the flashlight on them and then shoot them with the Revolver they usually die with one bullet. For the Common Taken, if I got overrun I'd use a flare and drop it to give myself room, and shoot them with the shotgun. But the revolver still was my primary.
For the Tele-taken, (the ones that teleport) I would stand, and wait for them to lunge towards me, quickly turn to them, and shine the flashlight on them until their darkness was gone, and then shotgun blast them.
For the Assault Taken, (the ones with the chainsaws) I would either run, use a flashbang to help lower their shield then take them out, or flares. The Ravens that attack, I would just shoot the swarm with flares, and they would dissipate, but you also can use the various flashlights throughout the game to take them.
This game also has Poltergeists, which I recommend running from because they have the ability to throw objects at you- whether it be a tree, a car, or anything of the sorts. But if you want to stay on the offensive, use the flares to give you some room, and shine the light on the objects and they will disappear. There is also liquid Taken, which looks like black goo, and if you step it, it instantly takes damage. Shine your flashlight on it, and they'll be gone. Just look out, however for it. At one point when in the forest, there are also bear traps, and if you're not careful your own book will become your demise.
There's many different flashlights in this game- and the better the flashlight, the more you'll have to be careful about how many batteries you use. Along with ammunition, you should do your best to conserve. However, the good thing is that ammunition and batteries and all of those commodities aren't scarce- but in the heat of combat, you DO NOT want to run out of resources.
The storyline goes like this- you are Alan Wake. Horror novelist. You haven't been able to write a book in 2 years because of writer's block. Your  friend, and agent Barry Wheeler has suggested you take a vacation to clear your mind. And your wife Alice has arranged for it. You're going to Washington State, into the town of Brightfalls. You arrive at the cabin, and your wife tells you that she arranged for the trip to try and help you get over your inability to write. You storm out, and then look back at your cabin to see that your wife is being taken into the lake by a mysterious force- in this game, your main objective is to save your wife, rewrite the story, and defend your friends and yourself against 'The Darkness.' (I'm not spoiling anything, that's the main few points though.) You'll travel through the mountains, near the lake, over logs on a river, into desolate and empty towns filled with darkness waiting for you, a gas station- many MANY locales all in this one region.
The storyline is beautifully written in my opinion- it's sublime, the pacing is good- you do sometimes get the feeling of Deja Vu when the game does something over- or you see something play out in a different way. There are lots of twists, and honestly, a lot of it is nonsensical, however, it is poetic, the dialogue is well written and funny- there are light tones with the characters speaking, such as your Agent Barry joking around, to help contrast the threat you're up against. There are dark parts of the dialogue, bright, and humorous, it's very diverse, in a well thought out and intriguing way that makes you keep coming back for more.
There also are manuscripts you'll find yourself collecting throughout the storyline- they're enjoyable to collect, because they tell you how a character feels, what comes next, or valuable storyline information, and Alan's thoughts. Keep in mind, all of the manuscripts in this game are read by the character of Alan Wake.
The soundtrack to this game is beautifully- fitting, and haunting in certain parts of the storyline. Definitely one of my favorite soundtracks for a game. At one point, you also have a song incorporated into the game by a record player, that tells you a certain thing you have to do. The graphics to this game also looked very pretty, and serene and induced shivers at some points in it. Having it foggy- and a tele-taken teleporting around you and you can't see where they are is definitely a thrilling and slightly chilling experience. The facial animations are lacking in certain spots, such as Alan's eyebrows. But, I thought overall the graphics did this game well. I felt the atmosphere, felt like I lived it, and it made the game that much more successful for me.
The negative I can think of- is that over the time I spent beating this game, the combat gets very repetitive, and the running sequences and certain assault sections. I had to take breaks to get through it, albeit short breaks.
Also, because of the dark and light and the various shadows, I found, if you over play it like I did, you can actually get a headache. However, that's probably just me. Another negative is that I thought that there isn't much characterization- from the start to beginning, I didn't think Alan grew too much as a character. And pretty much every character seemed stagnant.
That isn't to say this game isn't beautifully haunting, with it's atmosphere, storyline and twists and turns. This game is great, and one of my favorites as of right now. If you're looking for a storyline driven game, with Stephen King esque horror elements, go for it. The combat can be repetitive, but it is fun nonetheless. The characters are good, the different enviroments are diverse, and eerie, and at the same time beautiful.
Overall an enjoyable experience, I'd definitely buy it again. Over and out.

Just saying the name 'Remedy Games' already has me frothing at the mouth and tingling around the naughty bits with excitement, so if you came here searching for an unbiased, fair outlook on this game, NEXT!! I played the Max Payne series many times and upon each romp through Sam Lake's brilliant story telling prowess I feel a potent mixture of depressed and absolute contentment by the time I see his name in the end-credits. You know, like the feeling when consuming your third batch of questioneably grown mushrooms at an earthdance festival? These games have a way of tugging at my sensitive side while simultaneously scratching my action-craving itch in a way that no other AAA title can quite pull off today.
So what then to make of Mr. Wake and his X-Files/Stephen Kingish embarkment through the mysty woods of Bright Falls. Well Sam Lake definitely delivered. Except for the game's ending however, which instantly had me yelling "Hey Siri search Alan Wake ending explained #WTF!!."I mean I get that developers and writers often leave certain aspects of a game's conclusion somewhat open ended for potential future monemaking eff... I mean sequels, but then 1) this does NOT give the the writer permission to end the game in a unsatisfying way and 2) there actually has to BE a sequel in the not to distant future. At the time of writing, four years after the game's pc release, no sequel has been announced.
Nonetheless, this game is spectacular in terms of creating atmostphere and sending enemies towards you that are genuinely scary and intimidating (without the stereotypical jump scares). It is also very clear that the developers put a lot of effort into the games overall look and feel, even when Alan Wake is just moving around different areas between combat. The latter is somewhat dumbed down and repetitave at times, but somehow still fulfilling as you experiment with different weapons and techniques.
Overall, this game would make an excellent addition to any collection, as it is a testament to how atmosphere can play an unnmatched role with regards to how we consume a game's story. There are certainly a few sections that will annoy even the most hardy of Sam Lake's fan's (such as myself), but an unfolding of Wake's nightmare in the forsaken town of Bright Falls, which is aided by a superb sountrack, will leave every player wanting more after the game is over. Play it.

I really, really wanted to like this game. But I really just can't like it. Alan Wake I think is trying to be a survival horror game. The basics of the game are that enemies are protected by darkness, and cannot be hurt while they're protected by it. The way to remove the darkness is by shining your flashlight on them for 10-20 seconds until the darkness is removed in which then you put them in the face with bullets. I just saved you 14 hours of gameplay. I think on paper this idea is actually really interesting. But when put to practice it is not fun. The act of fighting enemies instantly becomes a chore because I just have to stare at them for ♥♥♥♥ing 30 seconds before I can even start to hurt them. Staring at enemies is not fun. Let's talk about the enemies for a second. They are humans with dark blueish skin. They are the least scary enemies anyone could ever have thought of. There are really only 3 or 4 types of enemies in the game. The regular ones that take 1-3 bullets to kill and 10-15 seconds of the flashlight, the big enemies that take 3-6 bullets and 30-45 seconds of the flashlight, and the faster enemies who aren't ♥♥♥♥ing matter at all because they just teleport everywhere but never actually came near me once. There are also inanimate objects like barrels that become possessed and throw themselves at you. You just stare at them with your flashlight for 30-50 seconds and they go away too. Let's also mention that fact that these enemies are not scary also because you have so much ♥♥♥♥ing ammo all the time. The game regularly rewards you with ammo for guns, and batteries for your flashlight. So often that I have been almost always maxed out on both of those things. The game also regularly rewards you with GRENADES. Listen these "big" "scary" enemies are not so scary when I have a stockpile of grenades that I can chuck at them. The game also goes into slow motion and zooms out a lot every time enemies spawn around you, and before they even spawn there is a sort of liquid effect applies to your screen in order to telegraph that enemies are coming. So this means that you are never surprised by enemies because the game holds your ♥♥♥♥ing hand through every encounter. I think all of this is the core problem of the game. I feel like Alan Wake wants to be a survival horror game, but it fails miserably because the player never feels vulnerable, or weak. The player is never surprised, the player is never low on ammo or munitions, the player always knows what to expect because there are so few enemy types, the enemies don't even look scary. This sucks any sort of hope that the game could be scary. So really what we're left with is a third person shooter that is boring as hell because of so few guns and enemy types, not to mention that I played on the hardest difficulty, and the game was still easy as hell with laughable bosses. As far as the story goes, it's... interesting. The story is certainly original, but the characters are bland as hell and very stereotypical. The game is insanely predictable and it's "plot twists" aren't really "twists" but more like "plot bends". Oh, and lets talk about the graphics of this game that apparently everyone but me seems to like. The in game graphic are fine. A bit low resolution, but this is an old game so I can let it slide. What I cannot let slide is the ♥♥♥♥ing cutscenes. WTF is that♥♥♥♥♥♥?!? It's vomit inducing, it's super low detail and looks WAY worse than the ingame engine. Like I said I really wanted to like his game. But it just feels sloppy to me. I feel like it had so much potential, and I could easily see this game being good if a significant amount of changes to the gameplay were made. But the game just feels so short. Though I think its worse downfall is its price. 30 dollars for a game that came out in 2012? That is absurd! and there are many other much better games to spend $30 on. Please don't buy this game there are much better ones out there that deserve your money.
