I went into Alan Wake without a whole lot of information.  I'd pretty much heard it was good, and I'd heard that you have to shine a flashlight on enemies to make them vulnerable, but otherwise was going in without much info.  For a horror game, I have to say I was pleasently surprised.  Alan Wake manages to build tension without relying on jump scares, the flashlight-and-gun mechanics work very well and make sense in the context of the game, the pacing is perfectly done.  Presented in an episodic fashion, the game allows itself to build to cliffhangers at just the right times.  The music score is well-done and adds to the experience in the same way the best horror soundtracks do, and the licensed music is well-suited to the times when it is used.  Though the game indicated my computer did not meet the requirements (which it absolutely did), I had no problems, graphical or otherwise.
The one thing that stands out as a possible negative to me, though I ended up finding quite humourous by the end, was product placement.  In the first couple hours of the game, there are subtle placements for Lincoln automobiles, Ford Sync (by Microsoft) and Energizer batteries.  Later on, there are television ads for Ford Mustang and Verizon, and billboards for both Verizon and Energizer.
All in all, though, Alan Wake succeeds as a horror game that has some original ideas, great graphics, excellent music, voice acting and casting, and doesn't rely too heavily on the tired old tropes of most horror games.
Also, kudos to Remedy for getting the Oh Deer Diner to so closely resemble the Twede's Cafe in North Bend, Oregon, home of cherry pie and a damn fine cup of coffee.  I'd visited there on a trip shortly before beginning Alan Wake, and definitely had to do a double-take!

Have a non-combat leader with Attributes 2-1-2-2-1-10-10 (trust me, this will make sense). Then one sniper and two Assault Rifle with 2-1-8-4-8-4-1-1. You get one Attribute point every ten levels. Give the leader strength for HP and carry weight and give the troops Awareness then Speed for a mighty 19 Combat Initiative.
You can ignore Alarm Disarming, Mechanical Repair and Brute Force (if you carry explosives).
The flashing inventory items are useful somewhere, try to hold off selling them.

Whilst the lighting in the first was criticised for being dark it had mood, now all the lighting appears flat and all the colours, textures and characters are much more crayon esque without any of the depth of detail lighting gave the first. The combat has also regressed rather than improved. The sword strikes now feel lighter, the movement is more awkward and less fluid, hit detection isn't as solid and striking enemies no longer feels as impactful as before.
Then, in an effort to make the game more varied, there are the multiple side missions, quests and collectibles. These are shoddily done and add very little to the story, often distracting from it. There seem to be inumerable collectibles everywhere and you can simply run between them, largely ignoring the orcs and collect at your whim. These are often long, pointless challenges to reconstruct memory fragments or collect bits of lore.
There's fun to be had here, the combat is still enjoyable but not as slick as the first, and whilst Talion remains an annoying alpha male everyman with a boring monologue tone, some of the side characters and enemy characters are interesting. Can't help but feel the game's one big feature, the nemsis system, would be better used on a more polished title that actually built on the first rather than letting the quality slip. Fun, but do not pay full price.

I really wanted to recommend this game, but for what you get for $60 it's just not worth it. Since I love to pretend I'm a competent game reviewer and stroking my ego though, this is going to be a long as ♥♥♥♥ review.
The story is garbage. I know, it's probably not a game that's trying to have an interesting story, but I couldn't stop yawning through half of it. There was one side-quest that was actually entertaing, the one about the necromancer orc raising the dead, but that was because it had different gameplay mechanics, with everything else being the same and a drag. The "twists" for the main story are predictable, and the first ending is ruined by terrible pacing. For a sequel of a game that had a partly interesting revenge storyline, I had expected more, but was sorely disappointed, especially with the ending setting up for a good final confrontation that poor Talion never gets.
A lot of reviews mainly focus on the micro-transactions, and to touch lightly on that subject, it's stupid that they exist, but you can get through all of the single-player content without purchasing a single thing.
The loot system in this game is absolutely atrocious, and I think it's because of those dank lootboxes. All of the orc captains have three ranks, regular, epic, and legendary. Depending on what rank they are will dictate the loot that you get for killing them. However, the game almost never spawns a legendary orc unless you rip it out of its desperate claws (see Guides section for most popular guide "How to farm legendaries"), and of course the legendary orcs drop the best loot. There's no reason to touch any of the other weapons and armor besides legendary, as they are all significantly weaker then even an underleveled legendary. Don't worry though, because for the low low price of $4.99 you can purchase a super lootbox with 1 guaranteed legendary orc/equipment. Give me a ♥♥♥♥ing break.
The saving grace for this game is that it didn't completely ruin Shadow of Mordor's gameplay. It's more of the same, and admittedly I had no serious complaints with movement, although it's frustrating that there's so few obstacles to jump over to trigger the super speed more that speeds the game up. Combat is still as strike spamming as it's predecessor, but Talion gets some upgrades that make combat more varied, or at least at the beginning anyways. If you haven't played through SoM recently then it'll definitely be fun to play through the first hours of this game, as the first area is where the game really shines (because that's prior to when you can recruit orcs, and that's coincidentally the main use of lootboxes). I swear, the gameplay was amazing before you unlock the second area, as every Nemesis mission you take on   always has some crazy hijinks that happen. For me, I'd always get ambushed by one orc, then another orc called "Dush the Survivor" would show up bragging about how he cheated death once again, and it was a fun fight. I had to use all the abilities and the environment to survive.
Then the game opens up, and you can start recruiting orcs, and the gameplay grinds to a stop. Orcs stop ambushing you, and because an orc cheating death has a chance to make them legendary and therefore allow you to circumvent the lootboxes it suddenly stops happening as frequently, and encounters become 1 on 1s, where Talion will always win.
Sieging castles is somewhat fun, yet I'm still disappointed. Looking at the "alpha gameplay", the first trailer on the Steam page, which was playing whilst I wasted my time being pretentious in this review, I see a clearly different system of sieging that would have been way more interesting. There, it shows Talion capturing the gate to allow his orcs to enter into the keep. This never happens in the full game. In the actual game, you have 3 slots by default that you can slot your orc captains in to. Once slotted, they can purchase one of three upgrades, that aren't even specific to the unit type. Choosing a "Poisonous" orc over a "Cursed" orc changes nothing, you can still pick the poison siege beasts or the cursed siege beasts. There's no point to recruiting certain orcs over others, as they all accomplish the same tasks given to them.
Therefore, recruiting orcs is no longer a game of chasing down the strongest ones, and instead working on a first come first serve basis, effectively removing any effort from recruitment. All they had to do was lock certain upgrades off for only certain orcs, but they couldn't even do that. Warner Bros. would rather save locking off stuff for actual content behind an expansion pass. After recruiting your motley crew of orc pals, you have the option to do even more damage and try to take down the warchiefs that control the upgrades for the castle. You can even place spies within the ranks, which when you finally lure the warchief out will betray them and make it rather exciting. The first couple times, at least. After that, it's just more of the same "I'm doing this for the Bright Lord!" and then sliding across the screen to stab the warchief in the back.
Defending castles is another story entirely. There's absolutely no strategy to it. It's just killing off orc captains like you would the rest of the game. Enemy orcs don't do any surprise tactics, they don't install spies in your castle, they just show up, breach a wall, then start teleporting to where-ever they want. Defense then devolves into running to each capture point resurrecting your dumb followers who can't do anything on their own, and trying to hunt down the one legendary orc the game was kind enough to grace you with during the siege.
And that's when the rest of the flaws of the game become significantly more apparent. The Nemesis system goes completely unused. Save for the random "blood-brother revenge" that happens occasionally, the orcs barely interact with one another. They do raids against each other but nothing comes from it except for one maybe dying and the other getting an increased level. As mentioned previously, you stop getting ambushed as frequently. The only encounter I had that was interesting was there was one time I was saved by a random orc during a last chance called "The Mysterious Stranger". The thing was is that I wanted to recruit the orc he killed, so now I wanted to hunt down this stranger and kill him. He didn't exist on any of the maps, which leads me to believe that he's just a joke character that has a rare chance to show up. This only happened one time, the rest of my playthrough I never saw him again. The dude just showed up to ♥♥♥♥ up my plans and then bailed, thanks Monolith.
There's absolutely at most 20 personalities the orcs can have in the game, and you will cycle through them quickly. I've heard 5 different orcs give the same stupid unskippable speech about how they foresaw this day coming. A game that knew it was going to be having orcs running up to you should have put more effort into diversifying them, but it's not like that. Then, there's 3 missions the orcs can do against each other, they have 3 missions they can do to "prove" themself, and then there's 1 type of vendetta mission. That's not even double digit missions, yet they expect this to last the entire playthrough. Like I said, the ambushes stop happening after the first area, where before a third orc could show up to a 1 on 1, but after the first area you're lucky if even you show up, as you won't really feel bothered to take on any of the orcs once you have the 4 you need for your assault of the fort, and since none are going to be legendary, the loot is worthless as well.
So there, that's my review. I probably spent more time on this♥♥♥♥♥♥then Monolith spent balancing the loot system, but whatever. More potential wasted, on to the next AAA game with broken promises.

Easily the best RPG game I have ever played. There are several reasons for why this is true.
1. Decisions & Consequences: In Witcher 2, decisions are not an easily-decided; even when it appears that they might be, the consequences may be more than what you believed them to be. Perhaps the best aspect of the "roleplay" part of this game, is that it does not contain the all-too common dichotomy of a "Black & White", Bioware-esque system. It's all shades of grey from here on out.
2. Delayed Consequences: The decisions you've made throughout your journey tend to take a while to come to fruition, and when they do, they tend to pop up unexpectadly later on in the game.
3. Realism: For a universe that deals heavily with magic, this is a game that also deals heavily in trying to bring the player to a world of realism, whether it concerns the absolutely stunning graphics, to how Geralt wields his swords in a way that was true to medieval swordsmen; none of that Hollywood hack & slashing here

Orion: Prelude. Where do I start with this game?
Orion: Prelude is an extremely fun experience, especially with friends. Having bought it in the early-ish stages of Orion: Dino Horde (what it was formerly called). I can say this along with everyone else: This game has improved loads since its initial release.
Let's start with the gameplay. Orion: Prelude feels alot like other wave-based survival games, but with dinosaurs. Pretty self explanatory. (There are also PvP gamemodes, but I haven't played them, I just bought this game for the co-op). However, the variety of maps and settings keep this game fresh, especially the fully customizable "prehistoric" difficulty setting. The open world game mode (conquest) is great, and I still haven't fully explored the open world maps.
The visuals, simply put, are good. It's no Crysis 3, but everything looks really nice. The tasteful lighting and particle effects add to the atmosphere and overall feel of Orion: Prelude. However, the environments and such sometimes clash with the player models (the player models being the ones doing most of the clashing), making the game's graphics look imbalanced at times. Some of the animations are slightly mistimed. None of these are major issues though, and don't really affect the feel of Orion: Prelude. For the price, you just can't get visuals this good.
The soundtrack is excellent. My only complaint in this department is sometimes a song won't play all the way through before switching to another song, and the song-changing seems unrelated to what you are doing in the game.
Orion: Prelude is a great game. It's not without flaws, but I can definitely recommend it. For the price, this is probably the best game you can buy on Steam.

I thoroughly enjoyed Act 1 and was really excited for Act 2 to be released- I must have checked at least weekly to see when it was coming out. I can't really say much here that you won't find in other reviews. Clearly there are a lot of feelings about the politics of development that resonate through a lot of people's reviews here. I can't say I was really affected by that. But I can share some of my feelings about my experience of the game as a puzzle adventure, and that'll be that.
I won't get into any details really but just say that Act 2 had certain puzzles that made me feel like I was having a joke played on me. Certain puzzles require a few steps to set up and when you get the final piece incorrect, everything unravels and you have to start over. That's to be expected in a videogame of course (I remember saving a game at a point in King's Quest 6 where I literally had to restart the entire adventure because I had missed an item along the way), and I'm no stranger to having my house of cards crash down around me.
But in this game I couldn't forgive the break of immersion that followed in those times, and that mostly had to do with the voiceovers and cutscenes. I really struggled with the choice to either 1) listen to the same phrases and watch the same cutscenes for the 5th or 6th time, or 2) skip quickly through the cutscenes and break myself out of the beautiful strange world I was in, while still being offput by the tedium that sometimes developed.
I'll just end with this- I sort of wish they had never released Act 2, and instead of feeling disappointed with the complete project, I could have loved the world of Act 1 and agonized over how great Act 2 would have been if they had only been able to release it. So with a heavy heart I can't say I would recommend this game, but if you can get it half price just play Act 1 and revel in the blissful ignorance of the rest of the game.

One of the best. Freaking. Games. I have ever. Played. One second you're a marine, building things for your commander and shooting (Cute) aliens. The next, you're in a giant exo dissolving (Still, cute) massive aliens called Onos (Oni for plural?). The next you're laughing as you play an alien, eating the faces of marines (And being cute as you do so). Finally, you evolve into another version of the aliens, and laugh as you (Cutely) Annihilate the last thing standing between you and humanity. Yeah, it's a really good game. I like how aliens can evolve to different classes; They can stay as the cannonfodder that is a skulk, they can turn into a (OMG CUTE) gorge support class, they can turn into a more DPS based support class that is the lerk, who can poison enemies, attack from a distance, and, when upgraded, release a choking cloud of green gases (I think it's just farting) that does DoT. However, with even more resources, you can become a teleporting assassin class called the fade, and simply destroy enemy outposts. Finally, and most expensively, you can become an ONOS and just SMUSH everything in your way! All transactions are in game and using in-game currency called resources (Which reset each round). It's a perfect balance of melee and ranged combat, and you will love it too. :)

Concept: your mom, believing that she is hearing the voice of God, is trying to kill you. You jump into the basement where more stuff wants to kill you.
Gameplay: it's a topdown, roguelike run-like-hell shooter where randomness really plays a factor as you get used to the game. It lags a LOT in intense environments and is still a bit buggy(just as if it'd been ported right from NG!) but has very simple and useful controls. The dungeon generation is not lacking and, with the DLC, there is a lot of diversity in what you can encounter.
Graphics: the graphics are a bit lazy, even if the hasty thicklinedness is supposed to be part of the style. I mean, Isaac could at LEAST have a two-frame idle animation.
Audio: the music's pretty good and, surprisingly enough, the sound effects are alright.
Difficulty: fairly difficult, and not just because of randomness. Mastering the art of directing your shots at noncardinal angles is something that helps a lot.
Synopsis: expect to drain a lot of hours with this. $5 is a ♥♥♥♥ing steal. $3 for the DLC isn't bad either.

The camera controls were so sensitive that I had to set them to zero just to move my camera in a normal way that allowed me to see what I was doing and not crash into everything immediately.
Graphics are alright (facial/character animations are awful as hell, though; at one point, Alan blinked, and I was mortified at the rendering of his eyelashes, which seemed to cut straight through his eyelids). Story is meh. I like the concept of "defeating enemies with life" but it gets ruined when you add guns it. I thought the game was more of a "use a flashlight to kill enemies", not, "use a flashlight so you
kill enemies", which really ruined the gameplay. Speaking of that, the gameplay is awful. It's nearly impossible to fight the way the game wants you to. Facing off against more than two enemies means you'll get swarmed from every side and pelted with projectiles. Aiming is wonky; still not entirely sure how to do it properly. I find both Alan and Alice irritating, especially because Alan feels the need to enact "tell, not show" for everything, including things that I can clearly see. Alan is extremely rude to people for no reason, and he's a huge crybaby about doing his work. Alice is frustrating to listen to and completely helpless. Maybe it would have been interesting is Alice was just slightly more dimensional than her one character trait (fear of the dark, aka "how can we shove as many light/dark themes into this game as we can in a way that is absolutely not subtle at all").
Also, I have a particular bone to pick with the people who made the wood textures. Making all the wood extremely dark was a bad idea. In the beginning, when you have to turn on the generator in the cabin, you have to go into a shed off to the side. I couldn't find the door inside because all of the wood was so dark that you couldn't tell a part of the wall from the door. I spent seven minutes trying to jump into the window to get inside (at one point, I thought it actually worked because it showed Alan's climbing animation, when I thought meant that I was doing the right thing).
It's interesting and a bit gimmicky, which is usually my thing, but gameplay is just so awful that I can't bear through it to get the story. If this kind of stuff interests you, go for it. For me, it's just not my style. The story is alright from what I saw, but others say that the ending is terrible, so take that with a grain of salt.

I can't say how much I recommend this game. This game is literally the reason I got into gaming (I saw the NPR piece about it and I knew I had to get my hands on something that lovely).
Story:
The first half is fantastic story. In the documentary they pointed out that things really kick up once Merrick shows up and that's definitely true. You don't really know what is going on or who to trust. Then you have the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half.
The big mysteries in the first half are pretty quickly filled in within the second half but personally I loved the ways they were revealed (for one my husband was watching over my shoulder and exclaimed in surprise) and that the focus of the game was then executing specific tasks, rather than hunting for clues.
I also really liked the ending; it reminded me strongly of the ending of Transistor with it's understated approach and use of the credits.
Overall the story was just suspenseful/unnerving enough without being something I wouldn't recommend to younger players and fantastically winsome and memorable.
Character Balance/Development:
In the first half Vella's world is more flat than Shay's. She's less clearly motivated and the objects she carries don't result in really any clever dialogue at all (as far as clicking on them in inventory, offering them to everyone, etc). Shay's world on the other hand was amazingly rich. The spoon and knife I didn't really discover until my second play through and they alone make his entire world more charming.
In the second half that's much more balanced. While Shay still has more interesting tasks since he isn't trapped as much in one locale, Vella picks up the knife and a fork and some new characters show up in her locale (along with an old one I was really hoping we hadn't seen the end of!) that give her more engagement. Shay has more of the "I don't think we can use that that way" lines in the second half.
Shay is in my opinion more rounded and makes more sense than Vella. We don't get a good sense of Vella without really digging into one or two lines; otherwise she comes off as needlessly and oddly intense. But they are both very winning and you feel a vested interest in them.
One thing character wise that bugged me in the second half was the fact that one character stands around on a beach and you can't really talk to him. His big issue is pretty easily solved and then he's just there for most of the game. If you try to talk to him you get the auto "Never mind!" line and have to walk away. That seemed really pointless.
Puzzles:
They are definitely uneven but not unduly so. The first half of the game they are realizing things are not as they seem. The second half they are trying to cope with certain big revelations and new realities. It makes sense that other things are suddenly harder as well.
I have NO idea why people hate the second half so much. The puzzles are clever but not so obscure that you would never get them (I found the knot puzzle easy while I would miss certain more obvious items, like how to get the shell). Most of the time if one side got old I would switch and play the other and suddenly things would make sense to me. So I felt like it played very smoothly. You need to diagram some things out but please, that's point and click standard. If you don't see that as the sign of a good game then don't play point and click.
I also didn't understand the claims some have made about not having a hint system. When your character tells you "Maybe I should look for X" how is that NOT a hint? Same with your character asking another repeatedly if thing X will cause reaction Y.
I like all others would have liked more new territory, but again, that's point and click standard to have one environment you really scrub over again and again. If it had all been released at once it would have been less striking.
I know there's more I could say here but these were the reasons I got into the game and these are the only things that really matter to me. It's a gorgeous game that is incredibly addicting and charming. If this appeals to you at all, buy it! It's well worth every cent!

The first act of Broken Age is very amazing. A AAA level quality of animation, funny jokes, amazing voice acting, and the most important aspect, the Story, was full of explorations, mysteries, and imagination. You'll keep wondering what happen, why it happen, and what will happen.
The second act however, is not as good as the first act. IMO, it's just lazy. You'll just re-exploring the places that you have explored in Act I, and for an adventure game, re-exploring is not fun. Though it still have the same quality of animation, jokes, and voice acting. The story is also a bit lacking, the great thing about act I, is that it makes player keep asking question throughout the game. Unfortunately, in Act II, the important mysteries already solved in the beginning of the game, and the remaining mysteries are remain unsolved until the end.
But still, with all the disappointing elements in Act II, Broken Age is still an amazing game. The animation, jokes, and storytelling are something that should not be missed. Just think of it as a great game and it's not-so-good sequel compiled as one.

This is a free to play mobile game so obviously if you have a cell phone you can just download the free full version and see if you really like it.  The $4.00 is really just to bypass micro transactions in the game which are.... not really all that necessary.  I finished the game on all difficulties in a single playthrough with relative ease.  People who don't play tower defense games may struggle a bit, but in terms of difficulty, it's not so bad.  But when I went to the mobile version I noticed that it was actually mildly more difficult because of awkward touch controls.
The game does import some of the awkward touch mechanics from mobile.  Unfortunately playing it on an actual touch screen like mine just doesn't really work all that well.  Instead you use a mouse and deal with input lag.
The most unusual choice was to release it on PC with all of the crucial buttons being at the bottom right of the screen.  Steam users know this as the default location for announcements for achievements and friends to appear.  It's always fun when you're playing and all of your abilities are covered up by achievement spam.
Honestly it's probably not even worth $4.00.  There are better tower defenses on Steam, Speedrunners 2 was also a mobile port but it's far better.  Get that one instead.
Edit: They developers for the game added some "PC friendly features."  They added 1080P... sort of.  Instead of having native 1080P they just added black on the sides of the screens... looks like a square still.  Thankfully it's now playable on PC which is still an improvement.  It still suffers from a lot of the mobile issues.  You are forced to use the micro transactions store to progress.  The micro transactions don't cost money, but it is a currency that will eventually run out.

Boy oh boy. This game is really a game I have never experienced before, it isn’t a game I can simply put in a box as a “top-down shooter” or  “Indie game”, it really is an experience that a player can’t get anywhere else. The game is based in 1980s Miami (hence Hotline Miami), you play jacket, a character heavily fogged by mystery. What is known is that you keep getting cryptic calls, calls that lead you somehow to a murdering spree of Russian mob members, the homeless, and the police. The story throughout the game is fragmented and mysterious, breaking at parts, morphing into alternate realities at others (basically one giant mind f**k). The story although vague is really interesting, the vagueness is intriguing. Like looking into the mind of a madman (in a good way, if that is a good way). The gameplay is pretty brutal at start, the enemies can one shot u from miles away, the bosses are fast and unforgiving and the level only checkpoints at the different stories of a building, so you could be on a complete spree on the first level then the last guard gets a lucky shot, you start at the very start of the f**king door ;-; . Accompanying the brutality of the game and your rage is a phenomenal soundtrack, I mean honestly this game's soundtrack was one of the best I had ever experienced EVER. It gives you a gritty feeling yet keeps you intrigued, giving that really nice vibe that I love. The games overall art isn’t bad either, some animations, though, kind of trump me but those won’t subtract to the game, they just confuse me a little. OVERALL: the game is really a game I recommend to anyone who is interested. Honestly, it was worth my money and my time and I would easily say I would play it again, and again, and again. . . f**king dogs

This was the year of the RPG and this was one I was really looking forward to. A strong pitch which felt like it laid out realistic goals, along with a spokesman who was hitting all the right notes. Yet what they delivered was so very bland. A combat heavy game with an incredibly shallow TBS component, one where it felt you did little more than maximise your damage each turn and terrain had little to no impact. Compared to Shadowrun Returns/Dragonfall, which had built their entire editor around creating good combat layouts, this was weaksauce.
More than that though, the characters and story were dull. You have a team of nobodies, which would be fine if you had a strong combat system to back it up. The personalities you do collect are at a Baldur's Gate 1 level, and less memorable than those. Not one of the NPCs, party or otherwise, stands out.
It just all came together to form a rather dull experience, and after a while I found I just sort of stopped playing. I couldn't find anything to motivate me to push on. That the primary mystery is spoiled during a joke death scene was just the icing on the cake.
It leaves me worried for Torment.

I've put in over 547 hours (on record... Playing backups doesn't count toward Steam's total play time). What can I say? Well, I've become so obsessed with this game that I'm building a Kerbal Control/Instrument panel into my desk, with real toggle switches, joysticks, dials, analog meters, digital readouts, a tape meter, and even a WORKING NAVBALL (salvaged from an Israeli F-4 Phantom flight simulator)... All this because I LOVE this game with a passion!
I also am afraid for this game's future... I keep NUMEROUS backups of this (currently) DRM free game, along with all the NUMEROUS mods I use, all the way back to the first version i played, which was 0.25. KSP is my MOST MODDED game... I have Minecraft... and KSP is more heavily modded than it... Let that sink in. Mods like MechJeb, TweakScale, GPOFuelPump, and Kerbal Alarm Clock are essential tools. Chatterer and other visual and audio mods improve the game's asthetic appeal... And now Take-Two, one of the most modding UNFRIENDLY companies out there have purchased Kerbal Space Program... This news is MORTIFYING to me! When I first read it... I nearly teared up... I could hardly breath...
I hate Take-Two with a passion, and don't want to give them a single penny of my money... This game is worth it, SO worth it... but if you are going to buy it, buy it NOW, and BACK IT UP. It's DRM free, and not dependent on Steam to launch. That means if Take-Two kills mods for it in future versions, you can version lock on the current version and keep modding. The day Take-Two kills KSP mods, is the day I never update KSP again, abandon all new developments as nothing more than dead end failures to not download, and switch my rating to negative.

I write this with a very heavy heart..
Let me give you a round-down of the game.
First 20 hours or so - Your normal narative, nemesis system, taking control of fortresses. What you'd basicly expect.
And the sidequests are an absolute blast to go through.
20 to 30 hours in - You get to what you assume is the final episode of the game. It all boils down to this fight of epic proportions. And it feels good knowing that you've reached the point of no return (the game actually tells you that),
30 to 35 hours - the narative gets completely turned over! Really, just, wow! What an amazing work on the storyline, and thinking that I was getting to the end, seeing such twists and turns in the story, which I thought to be quite avarage with good points here and there, really got me excited to see what the devolopers had in store for me.
35+ hours - it's just complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ The twists in the narative only serve the purpose of making the game longer. The whole point is to recapture or defend fortresses that you already own, and almost nothing changes - although, given the storyline, you expected EVERYTHING to change!
Might as well call this game: Middle-earth: Micro-transactions of war, 'cause that's exectly what it is.
A game that brings you to the edge of madness, only to make you truly consider giving some money in exchange for a decent closure and an easier experience.
And given the first game, which was a blast and a welcome surprise - it really makes me sad.

Mad max, wasn't perfect though, but, sadly, I would rate it higher that Shadow of War.
The mechanics of Shadow of War is Warner Brothers best to date.  The combat is fun, dynamic, satisfying, and the difficulty balance is much better.
However, the biggest flaw to this game is it's arguably it's greatest strength. The Nemesis system.
The Nemesis system, though, groundbreakingly brilliant and innovative in Shadow of War, I found essentially made the game progression pointless.
There was also no real linear game progression, no real story driven narrative, that drew you in, keept you wanting more, or made you feel like you were actually acheiving something.
This made the game, for me, a rather pointless excercise. A repetative, boring, and ultimately empty experience long term.
It's saving grace however, was the brilliant loot system. Also not perfect, it, made setting up that perfect takedown so satisfying, challenging, and rewarding when that loot finally dropped.
However, that is completely gone in Shadow of War.
Instead, it is replaced, with, a useless, confusing loot grind, and what appears to be, a pay to win system.
Again, there is no real linear progression to the storyline. I'm actually wondering if my game is glitched somehow, it's that bad.
And, what's worse, the repetative, boring, and ultimately empty grind through the two areas of Shadow of Mordor, is now replaced, with a world sized, much longer, and even more pointless one.
With the release of each of the DLC's for Shadow of Mordor, you could feel the game getting better, the mechanics being refined, the experience improving.
Coupled with the very enjoyable Mad Max to tide me over, I had such high hopes for Shadow of War.
Sadly, those hopes have been dashed.
Yes, the mechanics are better, more polished, and hunting Uruk, and being hunted by Uruk is still fun, but, it's not what I would call an improvement over the original.
It's a pretty much, a boring, repetative, pay to win annoyance, than anything else.
It really is a shame, this could have been one of the greatest games of all time.
I guess, I'll have to wait for Mad Max 2 to see if Warner Brothers can turn this around, and get back to what Shadow of War really should have been.

This game is complicated, difficult, frustrating, and oh my goodness so much fun. I think this is probably *the* gold standard for turn-based strategy games, even now, all these years later. I've tried later iterations of the Civ franchise, but /// is still my favourite. The 2D graphics are clear and very pretty. The mechanics are incredibly detailed and complicated, but also fit nicely together into a unified whole. The gameplay is fun, and the game always gives you plenty of different things to do -- without making you feel overwhelmed (well, at least once you get used to the basics). The interface gives you access to tons of information and lots and lots of options without ever feeling cluttered; in fact, on most of the screens you'll be seeing, the UI feels slick and very attractive, while still remaining effective. The game even has a lovely sense of humour -- the "you say you want a revolution?" bit always makes me smile. :)
In short, this is one of the very best computer games I've ever played, in any genre, and definitely the best strategy game. At this ridiculously low price, which includes all of the game's various expansions (including internet multiplayer, which still works very nicely and will lead to lots of fun and/or horribly frustrating gameplay time with friends), there is no reason not to snap it up.

8-Bit Invaders: a game that I so desperately wanted to like, yet can’t find myself playing for anything longer than a few hours. Understand that if I had the option to go for a mixed rating then I would, but as it stands I do believe it’s worth a purchase. Invaders is the third, and last, game in the 8-Bit series, precursed by 8-Bit Hordes and 8-Bit Armies, and keeps the formula almost exactly the same from both previous games. This means there’s no story whatsoever, besides a brief paragraph on the campaign screen giving some context to your mission, which is an extremely bold move for any game to make. I’m not entirely sure a decent story could even have been made here, and am even less sure as to whether or not it’s better without one, but it does kinda feel lazy that they didn’t even try and just went with a campaign of skirmish matches. The problem with having no story and focusing exclusively on gameplay is that you have to make sure that your gameplay is top-notch to make up for the complete lack of narrative. This is something 8-Bit Invaders tries to do, but ultimately I’d say that it fails because of just how average everything is. That’s not saying anything negative necessarily, it’s a solid RTS and clearly quite well made, but it’s still the exact same game as the rest of the 8-Bit series. As I mentioned before I can’t really keep myself playing this game for more than a few missions, and I think the reason for that is just how much of a slog it is, doing the same things repeatedly each mission only to finally win and have to do it all again in the next one. I have no problem with a game that takes something already done before and solidifies it with extremely well-crafted gameplay, look at Company of Heroes and you’ll see a perfect example of that. I do however have a problem when a game simply copies its previous iterations and pastes them back into the Steam store, each as a full priced release instead of the DLC they should have been. That’s really what this comes down to: 8-Bit Invaders would have been a nice expansion to 8-Bit Armies, but I’m extremely conflicted as to whether or not it has enough to stand on its own as a $15 release.
Now for some more detail. 8-Bit Invaders is an RTS, so that means you’re going to be commanding a host of units in your attempt to bring the opposing faction ruin and annihilation. It’s important in an RTS game that every unit has both a viable role and a certain uniqueness, and this is where Invaders falls off. I can’t overstate how much I love the unit design visually, with appealing pixely robotic war machines and aliens, but I also can’t overstate how boring most of the unit roster is. Generally, the units are enjoyable to look at, but significantly less enjoyable to actually use. There’s a handful of exceptions to this rule, but since most of them are heavy end-game units you aren’t even going to be able to deploy them most of the time. This is a huge bummer since a lot of these endgame units are actually fascinating, like giant slug robots or huge UFO motherships. I think that how cool the units are is somewhat irrelevant when you consider that you more than likely are never going to be able to use them, since there’s no reason to. That’s what hits me the hardest when it comes to 8-Bit Invaders: a lot of the stuff in this game looks so extraordinarily fun to use and just beautifully designed, but is completely useless because instead of producing super-units you’d be better off just building a massive ball of expendable ones. While these units are definitely unique, they aren’t unique enough for me to want to handicap myself by trying to build them and they certainly aren’t unique enough to make up for the lack of general strategy and tactics. While I enjoy 8-Bit Invaders, I feel that if there is enough content here to warrant a purchase, it’s just barely; most of the missions are the exact same and the uniquely 8-Bit aesthetic wears off pretty quick after you realize that, even for 15 bucks, there really isn’t much here.
8-Bit Invaders has me asking the question “Are well-crafted graphics enough to make up for laughably monotonous gameplay?” to which I find myself just about always answering no.

At the foundation, NS2 offers a very tight controlling shooter where the movement and feel of the action is perfectly responsive. The feeback from firing and landing hits is so crisp, you wish that other games could pull this off. In this regard, NS2 is already ahead of the competition along with the likes of Half-Life, Team Fortress 2, and etc... But on top of the already rare achievement, NS also offers something special: the real time strategy element.
There are two teams in NS2, the marines and the aliens, each side led by a "commander" who plays the game in a top down strategy fashion. Securing more resources than the other team provides an advantage in the form of better weapons and technology for the marines and higher evolutions and abilities for the aliens. But there are a set number of resource points on the map. Very quickly, the game becomes a struggle for control of space and strategic positioning. Objectives form organically as each team attempts to coordinate strikes into each others' weak points while also responding to advances made by the other. It makes objective based modes in most games seem inadequate.
There definately is a learning curve as players must throw away their lone-gun playstyles other shooters have ingrained. You must watch each others' backs and use small group tactics. When alien, shadows on walls and ceilings are your friend... and always hunt in packs. Games are usually won by the better coordinated, so strive to be so. Learn to listen, check your map often, and ask for tips. I can't recommend this game enough.

What a bargin! I got this game for 1 EUR and it is a really nice TD.
I'm not crazy with the health concept that provides the 'story' for this game, but from a gameplay perspective it is really good. There is nothing new, but it is solid TD with loads of towers, many different type enemies, and a nice set of levels. You replay each level for new challenges - don't let the titles Easy, Middle, Hard fool you - each is a new 'campaign'. You have a hero, and can buy different types. Their skill increases as you play.
In general, this game is a casual Kingdom Rush lite.
It has really good tutorials and there are videos for each level if you fail, which makes this game an execellent 'TD starter' casual game for people who wants to try TD.
And it is a casual TD - there are no advanced concepts, developments, or a multitude of levels - but it is casual fun and incredible good value for the money.

Colossally overrated.
-Most skills are just keys to open up different kinds of boxes
-The game is a tunnel with only one way forward. You need all the skills to open all the boxes along the way, and that's it.
-Sometimes, but not often enough to matter much, the tunnel branches for a moment before it merges again.
-Characters are simplified and have personalities as thin as cardboard. You'll find more character depth in most FPS titles than this.
-The animations are unfinished and lazy.
-Combat looks and feels as real and visceral as your average MMO title.
-There's a lot of dialogue, but very little of it is meaningful in any way. You just click through it all and move forward in the tunnel.
-In fallout 2, playing a character with vastly differing stats changed the entire game experience and modified the plot. Here it changes your action point amounts and HP.
In short: This is not the worst game out there, but if you want to play your next fallout 2, keep waiting. It isn't here.

I write this with a very heavy heart..
Let me give you a round-down of the game.
First 20 hours or so - Your normal narative, nemesis system, taking control of fortresses. What you'd basicly expect.
And the sidequests are an absolute blast to go through.
20 to 30 hours in - You get to what you assume is the final episode of the game. It all boils down to this fight of epic proportions. And it feels good knowing that you've reached the point of no return (the game actually tells you that),
30 to 35 hours - the narative gets completely turned over! Really, just, wow! What an amazing work on the storyline, and thinking that I was getting to the end, seeing such twists and turns in the story, which I thought to be quite avarage with good points here and there, really got me excited to see what the devolopers had in store for me.
35+ hours - it's just complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ The twists in the narative only serve the purpose of making the game longer. The whole point is to recapture or defend fortresses that you already own, and almost nothing changes - although, given the storyline, you expected EVERYTHING to change!
Might as well call this game: Middle-earth: Micro-transactions of war, 'cause that's exectly what it is.
A game that brings you to the edge of madness, only to make you truly consider giving some money in exchange for a decent closure and an easier experience.
And given the first game, which was a blast and a welcome surprise - it really makes me sad.

A dissapointing, missed opportunity.
There is much good about Shadow of War, but, also, some pretty giant flaws.
The combat, stealth, and sheer fun, of being the unseen hunter, stalking, and being stalked by, Uruk in Mordor is back, with greater polish, mechanics, and a far more expansive world, but, the flaws of it's prequal, Shadow of Mordor are also back, and they've been magnified.
I had great hopes, when I played Mad Max while waiting for Shadow of War. The semi-familiar areas, boss zones, area progression, and a great blend of stealth, ranged play, and hand to hand combat was there, and it seemed like Warner Brothers were refining their, world leading imho, game design, to an even higher form.
Mad max, wasn't perfect though, but, sadly, I would rate it higher that Shadow of War.
The mechanics of Shadow of War is Warner Brothers best to date.  The combat is fun, dynamic, satisfying, and the difficulty balance is much better.
However, the biggest flaw to this game is it's arguably it's greatest strength. The Nemesis system.
The Nemesis system, though, groundbreakingly brilliant and innovative in Shadow of War, I found essentially made the game progression pointless.
There was also no real linear game progression, no real story driven narrative, that drew you in, keept you wanting more, or made you feel like you were actually acheiving something.
This made the game, for me, a rather pointless excercise. A repetative, boring, and ultimately empty experience long term.
It's saving grace however, was the brilliant loot system. Also not perfect, it, made setting up that perfect takedown so satisfying, challenging, and rewarding when that loot finally dropped.
However, that is completely gone in Shadow of War.
Instead, it is replaced, with, a useless, confusing loot grind, and what appears to be, a pay to win system.
Again, there is no real linear progression to the storyline. I'm actually wondering if my game is glitched somehow, it's that bad.
And, what's worse, the repetative, boring, and ultimately empty grind through the two areas of Shadow of Mordor, is now replaced, with a world sized, much longer, and even more pointless one.
With the release of each of the DLC's for Shadow of Mordor, you could feel the game getting better, the mechanics being refined, the experience improving.
Coupled with the very enjoyable Mad Max to tide me over, I had such high hopes for Shadow of War.
Sadly, those hopes have been dashed.
Yes, the mechanics are better, more polished, and hunting Uruk, and being hunted by Uruk is still fun, but, it's not what I would call an improvement over the original.
It's a pretty much, a boring, repetative, pay to win annoyance, than anything else.
It really is a shame, this could have been one of the greatest games of all time.
I guess, I'll have to wait for Mad Max 2 to see if Warner Brothers can turn this around, and get back to what Shadow of War really should have been.
Overall: 6/10
Certainly not worth the $100 gold edition, that I so happily pre-paid for.

The series ended here, as far as I'm concerned. Now, Civ 4 was a good game, and while the less that is said about Civ 5 the better (if you ask me), in my mind Civ 3 was the epitome of the Sid Meier vision for the series and the greatest achievement of aesthetics, style, pacing and general gameplay - as far as Civ gameplay could go.
I think this has a lot to do with the predecessors. Civilization: Call to Power was an epic computer game, surpassing and extremely entertaining. Alpha Centauri was of course one of the very greatest titles the genre has ever seen, encorporating gameplay additions and features - so much recorded voice acting~ - that still feel fresh and ingenious to this day. It was into this setting of established 2D, top down turn based strategy excellence that Civ 3 had to plonk, and what a plonk it was.
How did it work so well? Well it was the way the game juxtaposed itself against it's lineage as much as the way it reproduced and refined it that really rung true with me. Civilzation 3 was all about resolution, refinement, aesthetics and staid excellence. The pacific colours, the fantastic drawn visions of your cities, the subtly faux-3D border markers, the movements of the characters, sounds and the pacing of the game were all just totally lovely touches that made this experience feel high quality and timeless.
Playing it today reveals a game that is completely succesful as a final installment in a series, even though the series itself continued on into the age of 3D. There are flaws of course - in end game especially the dominated maps completely cede any kind of influence over gameplay to your railways, aircraft and ICBMs, the voice acting of Alpha Centauri would have been really great here (it was used for Civ 4, famously, with Leonard Nimoy granting that game degrees of cultural magic that few computer games enjoy) and one could say that consequently the gameplay gets a bit stale towards the later stages of a long game, but it is what happens in the interim - especially the first three quarters of the span of civilization you navigate - that is a really wonderful experience, worth any price.

Broken Age is a game of two halves thanks to how development went and it really feels like it, as they completely changed how the game was from one act to another. Act 1 is all about setting up the story with a few puzzles here and there but nothing that will get in the way of enjoying the experience. Then you get to Act 2 and it feels like you're hitting a wall with puzzle after puzzle that will make you go back and forth, the game never makes it that apparent what you can or can't interact with either so sometimes you may need to pickle hunt. It can be frustrating and unintuitive as sometimes you will have to find something using one character to use with the other as if their minds are telepathically linked.
It is unfortunate as the game did have a lot of promise in Act 1 with interesting characters, a story set up to make you wonder what is going on with this world, decent voice acting and writing but by the end because of the frustration I felt, act 2's story didn't save it and felt almost trapped behind the puzzles, the ending wasn't very satisfying either so I left the game feeling dejected.
I cannot recommend this game, if you are all about the puzzles then you may well enjoy this but then you'd probably feel that act 1 was too easy and possibly boring for you. If you're more interesting in story, characters and the world then you could just end up feeling like I did.

Some of the most fun I've had with a game in recent times. Vlambeer have basically set a personal rogue-like and top down shooter foundation for me to judge any future games of the genre upon. At the point of the game where you're looping at least twice, the screen becomes such a cluster to the point where the player has to rely on either good spawns/mutations to guarantee safety or absolutely cheese through the bullet hell with good ranged melee weapons. The other complaint would have to be the unavoidable frustration when going for particular Crowns, golden weapons or other side challenges due to the inevitability of occassional failure. The positives certainly outweigh the negatives for this game though.

I suppose I'll start this review off by saying I really didn't want to reccommend this game, but because I "sort of enjoyed it enough to play it twice I guess", then I shall. It's an impressive game, but this is going to be a very critical review. I find people get more out of a review if it states somethings faults rather than its values, so that is what I will do here.
In this game you play as Alan Wake, an acclaimed but troubled writer who hasn't written a word in years, who is brought to the remote town of Bright Falls by his wife in the hope that he can find some inspiration for writing. This all goes disastrously wrong and results in Alan trying to save his wife from a dark evil presence. (hoorah)
The story is clearly the winning point of the game, I mean it's kinda hard to avoid when your main character is a writer. Theres little bumps and bits that spark a lot of questions along the way, but it's always interesting enough to keep your fullest attention and wanting to find out whats next.
The problem with this game is the lack of balance between the excitement of the story compared with the gameplay. The majority of the game pans out like this-
1. Oh look its a really cool story, I want to know more
2. Oh dear...looks like I have to walk around a forest for an hour shooting things until I'm given the next part of the story.
3. Wash rinse repeat
I would have no problem with this method, a lot of games do it well. But this game just butchers it.
The gameplay consists of shining a light at enemies, and shooting them. It's an interesting concept, but becomes boring after a while, and by the time midgame comes you're only shooting things to find out what happens next. It becomes a chore, and just no fun. It's as if a writer who knew nothing about videogames wanted to make a videogame, that's the kind of vibe I get from this.
Another note I have to make about this game is the difficulty. When you load the game, you're given the options of easy, normal and nightmare. Wanting to play the game as it should be, I play on normal for two playthroughs. I didn't find it difficult, I found it frustrating. Deaths were always unfair, you were punished for exploring, and in the early game ammo was often non existent in certain areas of a level. Combine this with the fact that this is a story driven game, it doesn't pile up to much fun. After my troubles, I looked online to see if others had similar problems as me and I came across something that triggered a facepalm.
The difficulty levels on consoles and pc are labeled differently. On the console, the difficulties are labeled normal, hard, and nightmare, where as on the pc they are labeled easy, normal, and nightmare respectively. Keep in mind that they are the same difficulty, simply labeled different. This means that when I was playing what I thought was normal mode, it was actually set to hard. I even got the "complete in hard mode" achievement on steam. Whether this was deliberate or a mistake, either way it should be made more clear to anyone playing the game. Still, for a hard mode it wasn't fun, it was just frustrating. I'd hate to think what nightmare would be like.
Like I said at the top of this review, this is a good game, but I was going to critical, and I have been. It runs amazing, it looks amazing, it has an amazing story, let down by less than amazing gameplay and truly faulty mechanics.
This game is constantly on sale for 90% off, that's 2.99 euros. When that time comes, buy it if you so wish. If not, leave it.

I kinda loved this game. Given that now, if you come to this game, you might know it's history, you might know the negative reation behind the time and money it took to make it, or, and this bit would be wonderful- You could have no idea at all. The people with an idea, or any involvement in funding the kickstarter, might have a bitterness attached to some proceedings, but they're too blinded to see the truth. The people with no idea? You may well be in for a very awesome treat.
One thing people don't get about kickstarter is that you ask for what the minimum amount you need is. If you got 100% funding, would it be able to be the game you want to make, completely? No, but you'd be able to have the story told. You might have to have less staff, it might take longer, the graphics probably wouldn't be as good, the story wouldn't be as long, and you might have to trim the number of locations down.
In an ideal world, you'd ask for 3 million, you'd get 3 million, and the game would be exactly what you wanted it to be. However, people see that it got so much more than it was asking for and were thinking 'great, it'll be here sooner, be graphically superior, and with the ability to pay so many staff and so much electricty costs, they'll be done in no time!' Only that's not how it works.
3 Years ago we got a glimpse of a game, and now it's complete. you ask any game creators out there, and that is an a-typical story, only we got a glimpse sooner than most of them would give, because that's how they needed to get their funding. I think, if people expanded their thinking on that, there might not have been so much anger towards this game.
On the game, however, it is a funny, engaging game, filled with everything I've come to expect from Double Fine and point-n-click games. I recommended it to anyone who fits into that venn diagram!

This is my first experience with a mobile-themed game. After sinking $65 in and having nothing to show for it, the only conclusion I can draw is that the mobile gaming market is a scheme to devalue the returns on microtransactions over time.
This game starts you off in a small vault of digestable scale. You're having fun figuring out how to make it "just work." Stick the guy they give you in a restaurant or a power plant and before you know it you're king of the castle. Everything is coming together quickly until you realize that you have to maintain any growth by backtracking to grow and staff these resource centers. That's alright, you can sit back and click on mysterious stranger to earn the caps and upgrade your plant. Wait, you have to upgrade it again if you want to leave basics? Well that next upgrade is expensive, so you'll try out this quest. After a 3 hour timer?!
3 hours later and you're ready to enter the dungeon. Finally, this feels like a Fallout game! For a brief moment, you battle rad-creatures and raiders to earn some decent rewards. You now have enough caps and materials to get caught up. That is, after a 3-hour trek back. You dump your reward into whatever resource room allows you to expand, but now you don't have the caps to expand. This is precisely the moment when the impatience sets in and you become desperate to believe you are playing a game. You buy that big, glowing starter pack that pops up when the game predicts it has you hooked. And what a return you get on that $5.
A Mr. Handy to put out fires or collect resources. Isn't that lovely to have a passive, invincible wasteland roamer collecting caps for you?
A pet. Who doesn't like adding some flair to their lemmings, especially when they have passive bonuses themselves?
A bunch of resources... Enough to build the first tier of your next room without having to wait and wait and wait.
A good number of quantum colas? Now I can get this show on the road!
A legendary dweller?! ALISTAIR TENPENNY?! NOW you're excited. An established, beloved Fallout character is now under your command. Oh, the adventures you'll have! From Knob Creek to Hodgenville you'll roam.
You send your Mr. Handy into the wastes and after 3 days he has 1400 caps. Not much of a return, so you call him back and keep him on fire duty. As fires break out, he rushes to treat them and suffers damage quickly. Can't seem to heal him either. This robot has a death wish. Eventually some raiders come in and Mr. Handy decides to take them on himself. He rushes in and dies almost immediately. There is an option to revive him for 2000 caps. It costs more to revive this thing than it gathered from the wasteland! So you forget about it and move on, acknowledging that you paid for this drain on resources.
Your pet is cute, but its effect is unnoticeable. -7% crafting time or something. Well, there's nothing worth crafting unless you're ready to wait a year to get 80000 caps.
With the fast resources you earned and the quests you blazed through with quantum, you build more stuff. The quests are broken down into as many as 15 pieces to force you to choose between buying quantum and waiting 20 hours up to 30 times before they're truly done. Those wait times are increasing, and so are the prices for rooms. The currency in this single-player game is inflating to prevent you from achieving growth without investing in Todd Howard's next sports car.
Even if the resource game is rigged, you still have Tenpenny. Good ol' Tenpenny. Until you realize he has none of the personality that made him prejudiced, petty, but ultimately memorable. He's the same as your other dwellers; The only difference is that he has a couple of equipped items that can be unequipped and added to another character to turn THEM into Tenpenny. These empty "legendary dwellers" are the main attraction, and 20 out of 23 are from Fallout 3. The other 3 are followers from Fallout 4. Bethesda is as likely to acknowledge New Vegas as Vince McMahon would be to induct Chris Benoit into the WWE Hall of Fame.
As a closing statement, I'd like to point out that Bethesda knows how hard they're ripping you off because there's an option to buy $99.99 worth of quantum. That's $40 more than Fallout 4 was and that was most definitely a game. This is not a game.

I would recommend this game at the discounted price of $1, and maybe at the normal $5. Although I wouldn't consider myself a veteran of TD games, I have played a few, and nothing about this game really stands out to me. It's cute, charming, good for a few hours of fun; but it wasn't anything that I couldn't walk away from, and now that I've stopped playing it, I don't really have any wish to continue.
I bought it primarily because I thought a TD game based off of the human immune system would be really cool. I was expecting a game where I could control all sorts of white blood cells to kill foreign viruses and bacteria. However, the game really doesn't follow this theme very well. For starters, your arsenal towers consist of the tesla (which is literally a metallic tower with an orb that fires electrical pulses), the cannon (again, literally a cannon resembling a tank or a machine gun), and the bomber (which fires literal cannon balls). Now, the cannon balls do visible damage to your body on the map, but this doesn't affect the game whatsoever. It's just an aesthetic effect. I think that's a real shame; it wouldn't have been very difficult to incorporate some kind of health meter for the body. When our immune systems fend off invading microbes, we do damage to our own cells as well, and that can lead to a lot of problems. So it wouldn't be inaccurate at all to impose on players the need to balance killing the infecting virus and bacteria without doing too much damage to the body. The currency in the game is oxygen, which is generated by a windmill. And there is a vitamin factory (which provides a boost to your melee towers), but it looks like some tower you'd see in a space station or some alien colony. You can even employ a hero such as the Hulk or a Lumberjack to run around inside your blood vessels.
The worst part of it is that the enemies are all legitimate viruses and bacteria, and the path they're traveling through is the blood vessels. So the overall effect is that you're inside your body, there are viruses and bacteria circulating through your system, and you're blowing them up with machine guns. And let's not forget the Lumberjack--inside your blood vessel--sawing his way through everything. There is such an odd disynchrony between the towers and the enemies, and it makes no sense. It just doesn't work at all. If you're thinking of buying this game because you, too, are allured by the whole human physiology aspect, prepare to be disappointed.
I believe that there are 17 levels in total, in different areas of the human body (lungs, stomach, kidneys, intestines, etc). I've already played through 7 or 8, and I'm still not fully done the tutorial, i.e. there are still features and upgrades I have yet to unlock. This should also speak for the length of the game (my playtime of 2.2 hours is accurate). The background art is well drawn, and does reflect the different parts of the body well; but the different maps are all very similar and I stopped paying attention to them at about the third or fourth level. The soundtrack is unremarkable, and I can remember nothing I want to say about it. The selection of towers is pitiful (I've already described every unit you can build in the game except one). And one thing that really annoyed me is that the level limitations don't change regardless of your difficulty setting. So, level one, easy: you obviously don't have all your towers or upgrades. That's fine. But once you advance in the game and go back to play level one on medium or hard, you still have only the same towers and upgrades as you did in the easy setting. Nothing you unlocked later on in the game is available to you. This greatly annoyed me, and makes it very difficult to win the more advanced levels. Again, I will say that I'm no TD veteran, so perhaps this would pose no challenge to you; but I do believe that players should have access to everything they've unlocked through their progress. For me, at least, it destroys replayability.
This game also has Steam pop ups for achievement progression. Not only that, but there are progression notifications for several achievements at once. So once you kill 100 viruses, expect a pop up that tells you you are 100/1000 to earning the first achievement, 100/2000 to earning the second, and 100/4000 to earning the third. The notifications convienently block access to some very important buttons, and if you get more than three at once, the entire game screen blacks out until the pop ups disappear. I don't feel like disabling my achievement notifications for one game. Devs, please fix this.
I can't speak for how well the game runs. I have a brand new 2015 laptop, so if I can't run a game like this, I don't expect that anyone would be able to. And, then again, considering how basic this game is, there really shouldn't be performance issues.
As I said in the beginning, I do recommend it if you can get it on sale. It's certainly not a polished game, but it's still a functional TD at heart once you get past all the inconsistencies and how generic it is. If you're looking for a break from other games, give this a try.

This game is full of atmosphere and immerses you in a post apocalyptic world. It is a wasteland full of freaks, gangs, megalomaniacs, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and weridos. There's also some good homely folk trying to make their way and of course there are the desert rangers - those who still believe justice has a place in a world that is hanging together by a thread.
The gameplay itself is great. The turn based combat system works well and the interface is natural and intuitive. There is a plethora of skills and attributes to explore, which lead to very different game outcomes. I suspect most of them haven't been 'discovered' or explored properly since most team build focus on straight up combat. The point is, there is scope for experimentation.
Combat is fun and satisfying although it could have been more 'technical' and tactical. Gamers who enjoyed Fallout Tactics (myself included) generally agree FT has the better combat. That said, Wasteland 2 is much more adventure based, which is where it particularly shines.
This game isn't for eveyone though. If you're not into RPGs, don't care for reading text, or prefer linear action games then you probably won't like this. Your  initial team development requires a fair bit of thought and care and can be the difference between a smooth game and a frustrating one.  For seasoned RPG players I absolutely recommend it. For beginner RPG players I'd suggest play on the lower difficulty settings and consult the forums for party creation tips.  If you are a fan of the fallout series then you'll feel right at home. If you played and loved the original Wasteland game 25 years ago then I don't need to say anything else except "Get it". Congratulations Echo One!

(Disclosure: I was an early backer, and patiently waited through the delays and whatnot because these things take time and that's fine by me, so this review - I hope - isn't based on the Kickstarter campaign or the game delivery, just the content and gameplay).
I wish I could recommend this game but I really can't at this point. Act 1 was fairly well executed, if simple and relatively short, and it set up a lot of potentially interesting events in Act 2. The overall idea of two playable characters in parallel but interconnected story lines is interesting as well, as is the world they occupy.
It's not a "classic" point and click. It's a more modern take on the genre - high quality art, more snazz, quality audio and voice acting - and clearly shows where the money raised has been spent.
Sadly, there are some minor gameplay issues and major plot and puzzle issues that make playing through the game difficult once you get into the 2nd Act.

- You can't skip through lines of dialogue like in most adventure games today; you can only skip the entire "cut scene," which is a pain when the puzzles are designed with some repetition necessary (e.g. trial and error)
- Primordia for example, had a map system to help you quickly navigate the various areas of the game that you'd already been to; Broken Age lacked this

That's ridiculous, and I've played the Monkey Island games. The result is that the player gets frustrated, sucked out of an already problematic story, and left to engage in trial and error puzzles that are situationally unrealistic.
Doublefine have done a reasonably good job here, but have created a form of storybook point and click adventure game with a thin and curtailed moral/philosophical veneer, a plot with holes that become increasingly difficult to ignore, an ending that screams budget/time constraints and a sense that this game could have been a lot to a few rather than a little to many.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and the second act in particular.
The story is the center in Broken Age, and it is quite charming with a sinister touch that makes it more appealing to me. While it might seem like a story for children, the tone is more serious than some of the old Lucas Arts games (MI, DOTT), underneath the bright colorful appearance. The dialog writing is great for the most part, and many of the characters feel real and memorable.

Having now played both Act 1 and Act 2, I feel the need to completely edit and amend my earlier review:
This is an interesting concept for a game. You start out with the option to choose between two characters, and you can jump back and forth between their separate stories at will.
The hand-painted character designs, locations, and background art are completely unique and absolutely beautiful.  I would recommend playing through for the visuals alone. I also really dig the musical score and the voice acting. In general, the production values are incredibly high.
For the most part, the puzzles in Act 1 are easy.  If I was stumped it was either because I was over-analyzing the situation, or it was because I failed to pick up an item earlier in the game and needed to backtrack.
In Act 2, many of the puzzles are still intuitive, but there are some that are more complicated or frustrating than they need to be, and there are others that require information and clues found in the other character's storyline. You will *need* to switch back and forth between playing as Shay and playing as Vella at regular intervals, and you will need to pay careful attention to every item description, detail shot, and offhand dialogue comment.
Throughout the game there is a fair bit of comedy, more so in Shay's story than Vella's.  Make sure to talk to everyone, examine everything, and to use each object with every other object/person in order to get all the flavour dialogue.  The spoon and knife are particularly amusing.
I had initially disliked the plot of Act 1 because it felt very misogynistic, and even now I am still slightly bothered by Vella's story. I think what the writers were going for was to show current women's struggles (limited options, needing to prove their inherent worth to the world, needing to sometimes be overly-aggressive to make their voices heard, having a cultural obligation to put the needs of others above their own, etc.) within the context of a familiar sci-fi/fantasy plot device (virgin sacrifice).
Unfortunately, the way the writing was handled made it seem like just another case of lazy violence against women, and made her and everyone else around her look petty and cruel. I think they could have explored the same issues in a less offensive manner and been more successful; however, after playing through the entire Meriloft section in Act 2, I have restored faith that the intentions of Act 1 were indeed positive, even if the execution was flawed.
Shay's story, on the other hand, is wryly humorous, immediately relatable, and culturally relevant. We understand over-protective helicopter parents, we commiserate with his teenage desire to be grown up and take risks, and we are sympathetic to his need to take on responsibility and do something important and heroic with his life.
The issue is that juxtaposed against one another, the stories of Act 1, at least on the surface, come across as "white boy who feels entitled to more control" vs. "female PoC who just wants the right to live," rather than "kids who want autonomy," whether that's what the writers intended or not, and it at once both highlights and re-enforces cultural inequalities.
Act 2 does a better overall job with the writing; the main characters are more well-rounded and developed, the side characters are deeper, there is a greater sense of balance and equality, the plot hook is more compelling, and within the first five minutes they threw some major twists in I wasn't anticipating.
At the same time, they also introduced plot holes you can drive a bus through, and they don't answer any of the meaningful questions they raise. I expected with the amount of time and resources at their disposal they could have created a coherent well-thought-out conclusion, but it felt rushed, unsatisfying, and nonsensical.
Act 2 also gets mixed marks in other categories:
I liked that Vella and Shay get to learn about each other's backgrounds, but for the most part you spend your time backtracking through the same exact screens you saw in Act 1. (Navigating around each location can be a bit of a slog, but double-clicking will expedite your characters' movements.)
Also, while I like the idea of achievements, it took some of the joy out of playing when I saw they were for things like "do this really long and onerous sequence in one shot" or "pick the right answer on the first try instead of exploring the other dialogue options" or "speed run this not-very-fun game in an hour." Those kinds of achievements don't lend themselves to an adventure game.
I'm not sure what to rate the complete game, honestly. As a point-and-click puzzle-adventure, it's adequate, with a couple of frustrating puzzles overshadowing the otherwise decent gameplay. As an art piece, it's production values, acting, and music are beautiful. As a story, many of the individual concepts and characters are great, but the overarching plot is full of holes and uses a passe trope for its macguffin, and it also dodges answering any of the meaty questions it raises. As a piece of social commentary, it sends mixed signals. As a comedy, it has several moments of brilliance and a few cringe-worthy duds. As a game that crowd-sourced more than 8x the needed funds and then took 3 years to complete, I was hoping for better. I guess that now leaves it somewhere in the 5.5-6/10 range. I would not pay the full $25 for it.

Let's get the bad out out the way first.
- Standard "go kill this guy, steal that thing" Open world game play. If you want a game to turn the genre on it's head this is not it.
- Day one it was locked at 30fps. (This is now fixed by 2k and you can run as many FPS as your potato can handle.) Visuals are not "next gen". They are serviceable. They don't burn my eyes out of my skull with ugly. But you can't help thinking. "GTA V" looks soooooo much better.
There is also this weird washout orange color pallet that looks like a bad Jerry Bruckheimer movie. Luckly we are all in the PC Master Race here and there is already a Sweet FX shader that can change this if you like.
Now let's get to the good and downright GREAT.
If you are a person that values storytelling over gameplay then Mafia 3 is your game. This is the best damn story in any medium I have been engaged in since.... Deus Ex 1.
-Voice acting. A+++++++++
-Cutscene rendering A+++++++++
-Script A+++++++++
-Setting A++++++++
I live in New Orleans and 2k has competely nailed the setting. I don't know why more video games are not set in the city. It's such a diverse and dirty playground to explore.
TL;DR If you want  amazing, game of the year quality storytelling and don't mind plodding through serviceable open world gameplay to get it then MAFIA 3 is your game.
But if you're looking for GTA V's level of open world freedom and distraction from the main game then just fire GTA back up.
