The PC port of the idle/exploration/simulation fusion Fallout Shelter is a near ideal version of the mobile game, incorporating all the mobile game's expansions while adding a few other improvements of its own.  It fixes two of the biggest problems of the mobile version:
1)  On mobile, you are effectively unable to control the camera.  On PC, WASD+Q/E control the camera and make it simple to get to exactly where you're going, rather than having to edge your phone's touchscreen to get it to the right point.
2)  On mobile, you quickly have nowhere to go.  On PC, in addition to the Quest system, which you unlock shortly after you've got your vault self-sufficient, you have several rooms that allow you to craft items directly, which you unlock shortly after you've got your Quests underway, and at ratios that are more forgiving than the microtransaction-heavy mobile port.
Curiously, this makes microtransactions even less attractive than usual - the same junk system that lets you craft gear also competes for storage space with your initial bequeathed weapons and armor, so microtransaction purchases could go to waste.  Acting against this, the creators added a new microtransaction currency, Quantum...  but there's more than enough free quantum from quests, daily quests, weekly quests, and randomly available from challenges, the Mysterious Stranger, and the wasteland.
There are some bugs - but largely ones that also existed on mobile (such as trying to drag characters from one room to another needing to hit an unlabelled 'drag zone' to complete).  But few are really troublesome.
In short, this is the definitive version of Fallout Shelter.  Get this if you're looking for an idle game that offers you more in-depth challenges than "buy the next upgrade" when you start it up.

I tend to think of
as a case study in why cliches become cliches: they work.
tries to be unique and original, but the unfortunate result is a mess.  Both the story and the gameplay are unengaging, leaving us with the worst of both worlds.
The story in
is about a military coup and the counter-revolution in a fictional Latin American country in the 70s.  That's an interesting setting.  But then the decision was made to tell the story from the point of view of an outsider who has only limited involvement in the plot.  What little Angela does occurs off-screen; all we see is the same apartment day after day, so most events are told rather than shown.  Then there's a romantic subplot between Angela and another character that we never see or talk to; I think even in-story, they never actually meet till the end.  This all serves to make the narrative feel distant and artificial.
The gameplay can be described as a first-person clean-em-up; each in-game day you have a list of tasks and a short period of time to do them in.  Perhaps not the most exciting possibility, but it could offer some amusement.  Except that there are no consequences for not doing the tasks.  What is particularly damning is that since you are paid to be a cleaner, there's actually an in-universe reason why failing would have a cost.  By ignoring it, both immersion and any sense of a challenge are lost.
It's a shame, as there are some original ideas here.  If there had been some reason to actually do the cleaning tasks, and your actions could have more of an effect on the direction of the story, this could have been enjoyable.  Not for everyone, but at least worthwhile.  As it is, I can't recommend
.  Even if you like the atmospheric narrative/walking simulator genre, there are much better ones out there than this.

The game description does a good job of telling you what it is about, and other reviews as well, so I won't go into that. I'll just talk about why I liked the game.
Because I actually really like this game, and honestly have some trouble understanding some (most?) of the vitriol it has received.
The mechanics are extremely simple, and they serve well the way you get immersed in the story: through your own interpretations and actions. The immersion I mean here is not the one conveyed by narrative information - you get that quite directly and in a pretty linear way. No, the immersion really comes from the multiple possibilities you have to get involved with every detail of the game. Your choice of doing the chores in a certain way (or of not doing them at all), the interpretation of the paintings and the statues, the simple pleasure of looking at the gorgeous appartment... all this goes a long way, and as the game progresses you'll see your relation to these objects and choices be recalled.
Obviously, not everything is perfect: the character's walking animation is sometimes a bit weird (and in one occasion you can see the reflection of the back of your own head), the politics and philosophy are sometimes a bit simplified, and the relationship between the protagonist and the appartment owner can evolve in a bit of a contrived way, depending on your choices. But this all remains completely acceptable overall.
One point I absolutely have to praise the game for is the music: it is *really* good, quite varied, and goes very well with the whole ambience. Special points for the attention to detail in the sound design: wearing headphones in-game changes the stereo image of the music. Simple and completely brilliant idea.
So if you like exploring a nice appartment while History unfolds just beyond your reach but still affects you strongly, and if you like to take your time in a game, and if you like nice visuals and very nice music, Sunset is definitely for you.

The fact that you play as a black female maid is an essential part of the character of the game, not simple trolling (but would that be so bad?) - yes, Sunset is political, but that's also part of the point. The game is encouraging you to put yourself in this woman's very specific shoes, and it's asking - what would you do in this situation? I think that's truly unusual among games, and even among "walking simulators". Although I should note that Sunset is more of a game than other games in this genre. You have time limits, you have goals. It's incontestibly a game, using game mechanics to encourage you to get in the head of a character. Sunset should be celebrated for pushing the envelope.

Civ III is an apogee of the former "Civilization" games focus. Why play it now, when Civ V is tuned, fixed, updated so many times - and even price looks fine for almost every pocket? Well, it's all for that focus I'm talking about.
First three of Civilization games were taking the player back at the dawn of the known history - and to help to notice the flow of time, there was some borderlines across that mighty river of the so-called "4th dimension". Starting with the Civ IV this process of moving through timeline were "smoothed", to the point where player gliding from the start to the end of the game without any noticable delay. I'm not saying that's bad - I like Civ V myself - but sometimes you don't want simple transfer from A to B, from the stone to electric age - you want to see cornerstones of each specific era. And with that - Civ III is giving you the better experience.
All that I said in the previous passage, is arguable, of course. But here is another trait of Civ III which was intentionally cutted off (in favor of balance, of course): the size of armies and all warfare business.
With all complexity of the game mechanics in the Civ V, armed conquests there looking as they performed by 10-20 people at best. In Civ III, we have totally another scale. So, when I want to win a game of Civilization by assault strategy, I start Civ III.
The third volume of Civilization is dated, but still deep, still challenging, still holding the billion of possibilities to build your Nation. Make Your Way. So I'll mark the game as 9/10 - not ideal, but so much enjoyable.

I've played through the whole game, and I must say that story-wise this may be the best game I've ever played. I got very hooked (although the auto-save-only function did help with staying with the game, since I couldn't stop anywhere) during the first episode and got the rest for 5 euros on a sale, but after finishing the game, I think this is worth the full price.
As a writer, I am very jealous of the writers of this story for what they have achieved at doing, because the story's fantastic - well, that word doesn't really do it justice, but you get it, don't you? I'd love to be able to do a story as good as this. Even the nastiest characters have something good in them (well, I'm not that sure about one... but let's exclude that character) and no character is simply good/bad/something, they have depth and different sides. They feel realer. And while Chloe's selfishness and times of not listening and being a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥aren't things I like about a character, her good sides made me love her with her flaws which do fit her character. And heck, she stands out! And not just that; her interaction with Max, as they bond again after being separated for five years, is something I utterly love. Via those moments I got attached to both her and Max.
Another thing is that the story messed me up many times with its plot twists which came completely out of the blue. I'd be lying if I said they didn't leave me swearing for some time in shock. One thing that also surprised me was that suddenly the game got so emotional that it made me cry multiple times, something I think no game has ever done. Or maybe I was just so hooked in it that I didn't notice the onion-cutting ninjas that visited either to mess with my playing or because the game spawned them there XD And I must say that some choices are very difficult.
Anyways, while it can be hard to get the right object to be picked, it's playable with keyboard and mouse, although it can be easier to pick the action for objects with the buttons of a controller rather than dragging your mouse to the one you want. But otherwise it's very good.
Pros:
+Amazing story that will get you hooked for hours starting from the very first episode
+Fantastic characters with depth
+Effective plot twists
+Your actions have real effects on the world around you
+The time rewinding power is cool and it has its limits and cost; it's not infinite, which is a nice add, since the story is set into this world while everything is fictive
+The gameplay is smooth
Cons:
-It can be a bit difficult to focus on the right object
-Picking the action you want is a bit harder on a mouse than a controller, but it's still very doable
-The game does only auto-saves, so it's hard to get a moment to stop playing without losing progress
-Because of not being able to save whenever you want, it takes a lot of time to play at once (and it gets even worse if you get so hooked that you can't stop until the end of the episode)
-A problem of story-driven games: While the plot twists are effective on the first playthrough, they won't work that well on following ones since you already know what's gonna happen (unless you are lucky enough to forget them very well), so replayability is not that good
Tl;dr: A fantastic story and characters I'd love to be able to write myself. It hooks you, then messes you up with unexpected twists and onion-cutting ninjas. I totally recommend to anyone who likes story-driven games and those who like games in which your choices matter. It's absolutely worth the full price.

Different and a very interesting take on a truck simulation. Your goal is to haul lumber with a soviet era vehicles at a muddy backroads of syberia. Your trucks tend to get stuck and you have winch them with other vehicles or use the winch on a tree. When you discover a new vehicle it may be broken or out of gas, on that case you have to use a specific add-on on some of your truck and drive to it to repair or refuel it. But when using a fuel truck, you have to find a place to fill it up first. You can also get lumber from outside of the already pointed areas but in that case you have to use the crane.You can also use crane to rescue logs when your truck tips over. All this extends to suprisingly deep experience and the hours i have spent in the game speaks for it self. And there is more to come, i have only nearly finished all maps and objectives on casual (as casual you dont have to save your trucks by other trucks, you can instantly save them to garage).
But there are some problems (some that will, some that might be repaired):
- Camera is bad, it does not bother while driving but while using crane it is painful, it is really hard to get decent view and it makes using crane frustrating.
- No behind the wheel camera, belongs to a simulation on my opinion.
- No wheel support, same as above.
- Bugs that are gamebreakers but only if you play in a hardcore mode (wheels get stuck under the map, anchors get stuck under the map, thus making the truck impossible to rescue in harcore mode).
I could go more into detail but i think here you have the most important information, with the sceenshots you should get a good picture of the game visuals, screens are very honest. Totally worth the full price for me, for some who would like to play only in hardcore mode it could be too much, because some of the bugs.

The game is really fun and has improved over it's predecessor!
Prolly the best thing about the game was and remains the Nemesis system (the orc hierarchy of captains, warchiefs and overlords), which can chalenge each other and can also be dominated to do your bidding (attempt to kill other captains, infiltrate them as spies)
Combat system is very similar with the one in Batman games (Arkham City/Arkham Knight) and is relatively easy (at least on normal mode). Main story quests are also pretty easy on normal difficulty. Basically the only thing that brought some difficulty to my play-through were captains with supper annoying trait combos (like guys with shields -can't be attacked from the front- which also can't be jumped over with and who don't really have any weaknesses which can be exploited). But fights against those captains made it all better when after a hard fight I could dominate them and add them to my ranks.
The game also has some (a lot) of flaws:
-lots and lots and lots of cut scenes that you can't skip, from every orc captain that you meet, every damn time!!!
-many missions (not story quests) where you actually take more time getting there than you spend doing the mission
-micro transactions in a single player game which costs a premium price!! while these are totally optional, the last part of the game, which continues after the main story ends, and is supposed to reveal the "true ending" becomes extremely grindy and repetitive. I think they made this part of the game so hard to grind with the purpose of determining people to buy some lootboxes and make things less frustrating
-fights become really chaotic some times, because in crowded fights it gets pretty hard to hit the target that you want to hit, or perform the moves that you want (like you want to doge and end up jumping over an enemy that is immune to jumps over him)
-and there are more but I think those are enough

Broken Age is a beautiful game, and it's first Act is a wonderful introduction to the old-school adventure genre for a new generation. The story is intriguing, and the puzzles intuitive and fun ... in Act 1.
Unfortunatley, everything seems to start falling apart in Act 2. Massive plot holes are introduced to the story, and the puzzles become convoluted and frustrating. I can't imagine ever solving the final puzzle without consulting a guide - something I never had to do in Act 1, or for any other part of Act 2. But the puzzles in Act 2 are everything that was wrong with adventure games in the 1990s. Double-fine paid too much attention to the hardcore player's feedback about Act 1's puzzles being easy and ramped up difficulty (i.e. moon logic) enough to kill the enjoyment for all the other players in Act 2.
The characters and world are still engaging, but everything else in Act 2 is a massive let down compared to the first Act of the game.
I tenatively recommend the game if you can catch it on sale, just because Act 1 is so flawless and enjoyable, but Double-Fine dropped so many balls with Act 2 that it is a tragedy.

If you come into this game expecting gameplay choices like you do in Fallout, prepare to be disappointed. Keeping in mind that this was originally a mobile game (a medium that traditionally lacks the ability to dive into lore), there’s very little to learn about the world of Fallout. Interactions with outside characters are thrown in amongst hours of tedium and impacts on the world are longlasting. This game will leave you wondering, “why the hell do I care about this Vault again?” Also there’s no end-goal, so you’re just grinding for the sake of grinding.
Starting from a mobile game and porting to PC, there was so much opportunity to improve on the basic formula. Many of the menus are *very* clunky and leave you clicking in and out. My biggest grievance — the bigger your vault gets, the more you have to scroll out to manage your dwellers at the macro level. Unfortunately, the hitbox or clickable area for almost all clickable objects in the game might not line up with the sprite. If you’re anything like me, you’ll end up having a lot of wasted clicks that pile up as minor annoyances into a gargantuan garbage heap. A big improvement would have been menus or buttons for auto-assigning dwellers. Actually, no, my BIGGEST grievance is when your vault gets attacked: you can only assign 2 dwellers to guard the door, and the invaders will run right past them! The rest of your dwellers just walk along or twiddle their thumbs while the vault is being torn to♥♥♥♥♥♥ And you can’t get dwellers, even the ones assigned to the entrance, to follow the invaders around! (Also, during the duration of that event, you cannot let in new dwellers or get your old ones back from the wasteland. Very irritating.)
It did start as a mobile game, and in keeping with the medium, the style is cartoon-like and keeps with the quintessential spirit of Fallout with all of its anachronisms and art influences. It can be difficult to differentiate dwellers unless you assign standard outfits (which will take a long time to collect) to specific rooms. Ex., all of the dwellers working in the hospital wearing labcoats, dwellers working out wearing fatigues, etc. As a result of many-generational breeding in my vault, almost everyone has dark skin and dark hair. They are *very* difficult to tell apart and due to the menu system sucking, it leads to a lot of confusion. The graphics aren’t great, but I suppose they could be worse.
I don’t actually remember music playing during the game except small cues when I accomplished something. Could be a bug, I suppose. The jazzy, classic soundtrack of Fallout 3 and 4? Forget it; you’re not getting any of that here. Also, points off for having blaring alarms while your vault is being attacked. It’s annoying after the first two minutes, and you will be hearing it a lot over the course of the game.
I haven’t completed this game. While I do have all of the rooms unlocked and built, I find the progression to be very empty. It’s not rewarding and a lot of mechanics that should have been addictive fall flat because of the aforementioned awful menu system. There’s a lot of micromanaging involved and with 100+ dwellers, it just becomes a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
I enjoyed this game for the first hour that I played it, and kept playing out of a love for Bethesda. This isn’t a good Fallout game and it isn’t a good mobile game either. Also, though my computer is a bit outdated (I have a GTX 260 in my box), I figured a mobile game should run very quickly. Not true; there are still decently long loading screens when exploring the wasteland and making changes to the vault. I would expect a game with such simplistic graphics, programming, and mechanics to run much faster, even on old machine.
In the short-term, you might enjoy this game, but in the long-term, you will probably experience frustrations with the menus, hitboxes/clickable areas, and loading times. If you want to support Bethesda, put money into one of their games that has more than an hour of play in it.

For starters, there's only one class out of the 3 you are offered that is actually worth anything, and that is the Assault class (the guy with the jetpack). The other ones have a cloaking mode and a healing gun, but they aren't worth giving up the ability to NOT DIE when you are picked up by a pterodactyl, stop yourself from being mobbed or casually fly around the triceratops that you are pumping full of lead.
There are a bunch of purchaseable guns on offer when you finish a wave, but most of them are either too weak or have horrible accuracy/recoil, so expect to use the same guns on every match. Or you could drive around in a warthog-ish buggy and have some guy man the turret (or man it yourself) to become almost invincible to the dinosaurs.
There are some things that Dino Horde does right, though. It mixes it up by having you defend generators, fight boss dinosaurs, and move around to different bases, which breaks up the monotony quite a bit, and it is rather satisfying once you get a hold of one of those badass turrets, admittedly.
I feel a bit bad for bashing an indie game, and honestly, if you're the forgiving sort, you may get a good amount of fun out of this game, but there are better games you can play about surviving waves of enemies. There are better games about blowing dinosaurs up. There are none to my knowledge about surviving waves of dinosaurs, though, so if you have a fixation for surviving a horde of prehistoric reptiles (perhaps it's the only way you can get it up, i'm not judging you :-D) then pick it up in a sale or something.

I'm going to put aside the games CURRENT 30fps lock and lack of SLI support (as someone running 2 GTX 1080's it's really frustrating to see a AAA game locked at 30 and no SLI support), even though it screams "I'm another shoddy PC port." Even though this also happened during my gameplay:
So with the potential PC conflicts aside lets juts look at two massive issues I see with the game itself.
Graphics:
Very muddy textures. If you spotted Angry Joe's rant where he used the sky as an example  and litterally compared the sky in this game to the sky in Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. It's pretty sad to see how lazy development got here. Some of the tree's and vegitation does look decent though, as a plus. Missions and game design:
Yesterday I tracked down a collectable Playboy in an area. It was inside warehouse on the second floor. There where some stairs leading on the outside going straight to it. I've played 10 hours worth so far, the last couple hours with the patch update unlocking the framerate.
Pros:
- Well-developed, compelling story, presented effectively in a sort of documentary-style format
- Great voice acting
- Feels like a large open world
- Nice pastiche recreation of New Orleans
- After a little time, the K+M controls feel pretty good (especially after remapping a few of the actions)
- Driving feels pretty well controlled
- Graphics aren't nearly as bad as some people would have you believe
- Brutal takedowns and stealth kills continue to feel satisfying
Cons:
- Could be better optimized: on my i7-4790K + EVGA GTX 1080 FTW at 2560x1440 with unlimited framerate, I get anywhere from 40-80 fps. Nothing about this game visually seems to indicate that it should require as much muscle from the hardware as it seems to need.
- Occasional visual glitches. Nothing game-breaking for me though.
- No quick save or manual save
- The AI is pretty stupid (although that also allows for mostly effective stealth approaches)
- While the world feels large, most buildings are simply facades, making the world feel empty
Other Thoughts:
For me, this plays similar to GTA V but with a main anti-hero character whose motivation is far weightier. So in that sense, I actually prefer this to GTA V personally (I know that puts me in the minority). While some PC gaming snobs are turning their noses up at visual glitches and the fact that the game didn't launch with some display options that should be a no-brainer these days, I've been enjoying the heck out of this game so far. Complaints about repetitive missions aren't necessarily wrong, but I've rarely played an open-world game where missions weren't repetitive.
I definitely recommend this game if you're willing to overlook some minor glitches and competent gameplay for a fantastic story in an artistically well-designed open world.

Now that I've had more of a chance to spend time playing this game I wanted to write a proper review which will be more helpful to people considering getting this game.
Mafia 3 has a really good feel to it, and is engaging enough that I can play for long periods of time without even realising it - something which I have been finding very hard to do with games recently. The gameplay style is simmilar to that of red faction gorilla and mad max where you have to complete challenges to take over teritories, but the story which goes on behind it and the mechanics which tie it together are excelent.
The cover based combat is simmilar to that of the last game and gta 4 and 5, although this time stealth is a very powerful tool as well. If you have played games like Hitman then you should turn the difficulty up to the hardest setting.
The time period feels really authentic and truely feels like a Mafia game. There are a lot of references to current events in the 1960's and the radio and dialogue all fit. I think the writers did an excelent job and put a lof of time into crafting it all because it feels really seamless.
My one problem with this game is the driving  (There are two modes but they both feel arcade). This game is set in 68, and has a lot of cars which people would have been driving at the time, but unfortunately this is where the whole imersion breaks for me. The cars all feel like large gocarts and there are lots of moments throughout the game where I have had to switch my brain off because a great lumbering 2 tonne 60's sedan has done a hairpin turn at 45mph, with no body roll. I love this game but a lot of the time I'm thinking, "well, that's not really how cars handle".
I still have a lot to do in this game. I am very excited to see what comes next, and replayaility might be on the cards. Hopefully this will give you a good idea of what you are getting into, and I hope you can enjoy this game as much as I have.

This game quickly became one of m favorites as I played it for the fiers ttime. I understand why it may not have been everyone's cup of tea. The developers took several risks, not the lesat of which is choosing a protagonist with whom many gamers may not readily identify, and making hers the only character players see and hear from during the game.
Then there is the setting of the game. While the story takes place in the capitol city of a country in the midst of a military coup, the game takes place in one apartment which, though in the city, seems far removed from the drama and danger of the fight between the military coup and the rebellion. The explosions and gunfire are seen and heard through the windows of the apartment. Only rarely does the external politcal struggle and guerilla warfar invade the aparment, and then the player, though the protagonist, onlly sees and experiences the aftermath.
Iin fact, the two main characters -- the protagonist and the owner of hte penthouse she his hired to clean once a week, just for one hour before sunset -- aren't even major players in the political intrigue and warfare. Of the two, the protagonist is the farthest remoived from the action. Her involvement is limited to choices that influence of assist her employer and/or her brother -- who is a leader of the rebellion, and the other unseen and virtually unheard major player in the rebellion.
The developers set themselves up with several significant challenges, which forced them to make choices that would have the effect of severly limiting the games audiende, but managed to produce a compelling game that still haunts me after playing it through just once. Initially, the protagonist seems almost to enigmatic to engage players, but her voice grows stronger and her character clearer as the game progresses, influenced by the player's choices, much as the story line itself.
The developers risked the game being monotonous by essentially limiting the story to once character's view and voice, and then only in one place.
Gameplay is essentially a series of apartment visits, punctuated by tasks that are by their nature mundane, even when they influence the direction of the story. The only changes are the external state of the city and the fighting, and the internal state of the relationship between the protagonist and her employer. Those changes are reflected in changes to the apartment that are mostly subtle from one visit to the next, and only become more dramatic as the story draws to its end. While its ending drags a bit (at least the one ending I played), the story is made no less compelling for all its subtlety.
Perhaps this games fails to satisfy some because it straddles the line between classic game and interactive fiction. The apparent focus on the latter may have led to game mechanics that frustrated some players The developers certainly took a risks that would limit its appeal. But where Sunset succesdes it does so preciselly because of those risks.

I am a fallout fan, and I love management games, (such as city skylines and Basement) although, this game is a boring clicking and gathering game. You can send your people on quests and that's pretty much it, but all you do is just click and gather. With most management games, there are challenges, such as using your BRAIN to solve issues rather than spamming the rush button, logging off, and checking your base next weekend.
A person in the comments pointed out that this game is meant to be played in increments. It wouldn't be as good of a game, wouldn't it?
In conclusion, if you're into clicking simple management games, I would recommend you play this one occasionally. But I cannot recommend this game to people who want to play more "complex" management games, because simply, you will get very bored :/

if you're looking for a TD fix at a cheap price.
At the moment, when I write this review, it's 80% off.
Otherwise, there's nothing new compared to others in the swathe of TD games on Steam.
If you're looking for something new in terms of mechanics, look elsewhere.
The graphics isn't something to write home about; obvious mobile port is obvious.
The assets are well-drawn, detracting this game from the rest of the run-of-the-mill TD games.
Kinda reminds me of Worms.
It's based on Unity, with the usual Unity launcher and a maximum resolution of...1024x768?
I'm guessing the supported resolutions depend on the max vertical resolution of your display/monitor, which mine is 1366x768 since I'm on a laptop.
It does, however, seem to support multi-display, as in you can decide on which monitor you'd want this game to be displayed in via the Unity launcher.
There are (limited) global upgrades that affects towers' attack & range, tower sell value, specials' effectiveness, and in-level currency-related like how many starting oxygen per level or how much you get per mob kill.
These upgrades are bought using 'tablets', which you can get from finishing a level.
Each level holds a maximum of 7 tablets, which is divided to 3 at Easy, 2 at Medium, and 2 at Hard.
The tablets are finite, but you can easily 'sell' upgrades if you want to put the tablets into other upgrades that you want more.
The specials?
It basically breaks down to the basic three.
A bomb (AoE nuke), electric shock (global nuke), and adrenaline (AoE tower buff).
Yes, that's it.
Specials have infinite usage, though...limited only by their cooldowns.
The in-level currency is oxygen, and the in-game one is crystal.
Oxygen is what you use in a level to build towers.
Crystal is, I'm just guessing here, effectively what you'd buy with real money in the mobile version.
Crystals are used to buy boosters, which either adds oxygen, adds life, adds an extra of your strongest unit, resets all specials' cooldown, and global adrenaline.
Yep, typical freemium boosters.
The Encyclopedia is probably the most dodgy part of the game.
The Enemy details is in-game, but when you click for Tower details, the game opens up your browser to load the related webpage on the game's website.
Tips & Tricks is no different from Tower details.
Others is basically other games made by the game studio, and yes, acts the same way as Tower details.
Keep in mind that this game is a 430-ish MB download and 660-ish MB installed, so I don't really get the technical reason as for why they couldn't just cram everything locally in the Encyclopedia.
My conclusion?

For such a cheap price at  release i.e. 80% off the usual £3.99, I had more fun playing  this Tower Defense  (TD) game  than I've had playing  a lot of games I've paid 20 times as much for.   Defend Your Life is  a  typical TD game with the usual  tower purchases, for example  upgradeable cannons and   tesla towers,  as well as other towers that  slow units down or toss grenades, plus there are special towers such as  those that give you extra oxygen.  Oxygen is the currency in game  which  allows you to purchase  more towers and  upgrades, plus  at the end of each  level you are awarded  tablets and  diamonds, both of which can be spent  either on  upgrading your tower  defenses or on special  upgrades that can only be used once to  top up  other  defenses that  usually take time to recover such as the electric shock , bomb or adrenaline.
The theme of this  TD game is  biological, with a human body  being attacked by viruses.  Each level gradually takes you further into the body.   You can set the speed up to four times the normal speed  and/or  select from three different difficulties.  Even at full price  I think Defend Your Life is  a bargain.   I reckon most  TD fans    will enjoy this game and it's also an  excellent  introduction   for those new to the genre. The easy mode is relatively easy to beat.  I played   through several levels  with no losses. The harder levels  give less currency to buy the various upgrades and   the speed of  the viruses  are increased, plus you get less oxygen currency to start with.
With 22 different enenies,  all with different strengths and weaknesses, for example the flu virus  divides into two weaker flu viruses  when it  is  killed  and the Nicotinic unit disappears when  first hit and is immune from attack while invisible, at least from the tower defenses. You can still damage  these with bombs and electric shocks.
There's a tips and tricks section as well as an encyclopedia that  gives you  information  about each building, for example  the Tesla tower  does more damage  for each shot  than any other  tower, but takes a longer  time to recharge.  There are some nice little touches like the defensive towers that  when activated  create little  beings that    don't do actual damage, but block the path of incoming  viruses.  When damaged they  recover  fairly quickly. If destroyed   new ones will replace them before the next wave.  You can  start  the next wave early by clicking on the warning symbol that pops up near the place where the viruses  first appear. The quicker you do this, the more oxygen is added to your total, giving you more currency to  buy or upgrade towers.
The 20 achievements  for this game are  relatively easy to attain, so long as you can survive the waves of viruses.  You can see a video of game play

Sunset presents itself as a narrative-based experimental videogame, an experience constructed from its character, exploration, interaction and time management.
It's neither of those things.
The narrative, which reads like Cold War fan fiction written by someone who skimmed through a Che Guevara biography once, runs along the game almost unconnected of the actual gameplay or your actions. The themes and conflicts are unsubtly spelled out for you, in what feels less like fiction and more like low-tier political propaganda. The dissonance between the "importance" of the plot and the little influence you have as a character is never resolved, all wrapped up by a pretentious, cliched non-ending for a story that never went anywhere or said anything as important as the game takes itself to be.
The main protagonist seems less like a character and more like a megaphone for the developers to spout their views from, having little to no agency in the plot besides pointless busywork, which the developers would like you to think are important choices. A ridiculous concept considering there's a literal war happening outside the walls of the room you're locked in. The themes are constructed with zero respect for the historical context of the events, culture, symbols and conflicts referenced, with no nuances or decision given to the player of what to think or interpret. It's narrative hand-holding pretending to be educational.
The gameplay itself, which scraps the bottom of what could be considered a videogame to begin with, is an example of what Tale of Tales considers to be "experimental game design": that is, to remove those essential elements from which videogames are constructed, rather than reconsider or expand on them, leaving a game that seems built as the equivalent of removing the wheels and motor of a car and pretending this is "an advancement in automobile technology."
It runs horribly in most computers, and seems completely buggy: the first time I ran it, the 'activities' didn't load into the game's engine, leaving a barren level with nothing in there to do, making me think that I was actually playing the game wrong. An hour later, I realized that it was the game being shoddily made. The solution to the bug? Run the game again and hope that it works the next time. And that's on top of the ridiculously bad performance and cheap "Photoshop for Dummies" GUI.
And even when I could "play the game", I discovered that the game's 'activities' were nothing but button prompts, followed by title cards informing me that I had done the activity, which puts this game below the definition of an actual simulator, into what can only be considered to be a text adventure with a low-effort level rendered on top. THIS GAME IS JUST NOT FUN. There's no progression, nothing to learn, no skills to apply, no puzzles to solve, and even ignoring the gameplay, it's also not fun on a narrative level. There's just nothing compelling going on here.
So, considering the game's text is incompetent, the gameplay cheap and pointless, and that the title might not even work when you run it, I think Sunset can only be regarded as trash not worth any asking price, and an insult to the craft of videogame making AND gaming audiences everywhere.

Another 8-Bit blah. The best thing about this one? Yeah, you guessed it, the soundtrack by Frank Kle♥♥♥♥♥!
To be fair, they did at least try.
New features:
- Harvesters stay at resource node and continuously mine instead of travelling back and forth for both new factions.
- Some gimmicky units and faction differences
- Titan units
There are 2 new factions, the Marins and the Cranioids. The Marines field pretty much exclusively mechanised units. Even their infantry is mechanized. The theme here is pretty good and cohesive for once. The tech tree on the other hand is really weird. Why do I need a barracks to build anti air turrets, but a tech lab or whatever to build ground defenses (which are slow firing aoe pulse towers with laughable range)? I mostly just skipped the barracks later on alltogether, because the units produced from there are just pointless in big fights. The only real highlight here is a unit they copied from SC2 (the Reaper only with a melee attack), which can jump up and down cliffs, just like its better pendant. They are useless in fights, however, due to their ridiculously low HP, so you either just use them once in the campaign when you're forced to, or maybe to sneak into the enemy base and destroy a key building, which you will most likely also just do in the campaign to suicide win (yes, that's still a thing...no matter how many thousand units are bearing down on your already destroyed base, you still win by just eliminating some key buildings...sigh).
Marines also get some air units you will hardly ever use and a big Titan unit that for some reason doesn't attack if units are too close or too far away, even if you give it a move command and even though it can move and attack at the same time. Theoretically a melee unit could kill that Titan without it ever trying to fight back...sigh. Marines are also perhaps the most overpowered faction in the 8-Bit universe so far. Why? Half their HP on buildings and units are self regenerating shields! Especially in small skirmishes with good micro you should always be able to beat an opponent with the same amount of units (or even more and better units). Unless you one shot one of these units they'll just rejoin the fray a few seconds later with almost fully recovered shields. Add to that flying repair units that can thus only be targeted by ground to air units and you have an almost unbeatable army, unless the enemy gets 5 times the number of units to throw at you (in the campaign this happens on almost every one of the later maps). Buildings once again need power by the way, so this is the 3rd faction that builds generators.
In contrast the Cranioids are a menagerie of all silly alien beasts you can think of: small green martians, alien xenomorphs (complete with acidic blood that will constant damage all enemy units standing in the pool after a unit is destroyed, which can easily mean they take massive amounts of damage, as everything just clumps up again), War of the Worlds striders, UFOs, bugs and a giant Titan beast reminiscent of a big Ape-Lizard that can wipe out whole armies if you don't pay attention for one second (lingering AOE damage field). This faction once again uses farms and food supply like the Hordes factions. They behave like every other faction in that their units don't auto-regen and have no shields. Run of the mill. Boring in the end. Their healer unit is a giant flying saucer with an aoe heal.
The campaign is once again completely uninspired, but to up the difficulty the game just likes to throw hundreds of enemy units at you at every turn. That is not difficulty, it's simply boring and frustrating to get swarmed after 3 minutes by a vast horde of enemy units for the next 5 minutes, after which there is a brief lull of 1 minute before everything gets repeated. Buy it for potential MP only.

8-Bit Invaders is the third game in Petroglyph's series of 8-Bit RTS (real time strategy) titles. If you missed the last two games, those were 8-Bit Armies and 8-Bit Hordes respectively, with each taking a different sort of spin on the classic gameplay found in some of the more popular RTS titles out there (hey, can you tell which one is like Command & Conquer and which one is like Warcraft?). Honestly though, the 8-Bit RTS games play like Command & Conquer more than anything, which makes sense - some of Petroglyph's staff are old Westwood Studios veterans. If you're not familiar with that series, it essentially boils down to building the biggest, baddest, and coolest army out there in order to smash your opponents. 8-Bit Armies was aesthetically similar to C&C, 8-Bit Hordes was graphically more similar to fantasy RTS games like the Warcraft series, and of course, 8-Bit Invaders tackles the sci-fi side of things with a look somewhere between
, the Alien series of films, and Starcraft. It's nothing massively different for RTS fans, but I think that this is perhaps the best game yet in the 8-Bit RTS series.
8-Bit Invaders features a few different modes for you to mess around in: 2 different five to ten hour long campaigns, a typical skirmish mode, cross-game multiplayer (between Armies, Hordes, Invaders, and the free multiplayer-only "Arena" client), a co-op campaign, and perhaps the most noteworthy new addition to the series, the Metaverse mode.
The campaign mode is pretty fun and definitely fairly challenging. As someone who's only played a few RTS games, I had a rough time with some of the missions while breezing past others. In particular, some of the missions mixed up the gameplay in ways that threw me off guard, like a stealth mission involving only melee units (against mostly buildings thankfully) or a mission with only aircraft. Of course, there's also the typical RTS missions with such riveting objectives as "smash the enemy", "smash the enemy in 10 minutes", or even the incredibly unique "defend your base for 15 minutes". I'm being a little facetious of course - the game actually has a surprising amount of depth to its campaign mode. There's multiple difficulties, stuff to unlock, side objectives for each mission that permanently reward the player with extra starting units or buildings in every mission, and even a cute (and powerful) little penguin hidden in a box somewhere on every mission. Oh, did I also mention that there's not one, but
campaigns? The only significant downside to the campaign mode is that there's no cutscenes or a real story of any sort - instead, there's a brief text box before each mission explaining why you're fighting. It would've been nice to have more of a substantial overarching narrative, but it's understandable why one wasn't really included - most of the production costs went into creating a solid game, which is totally fine.
In terms of the other modes, skirmish is exactly what you'd expect: pick a faction (including any from the other 8-Bit RTS games if you own them), and duke it out with an A.I. opponent, or multiple, if you'd prefer. There's a decent number of options available to you, including the opportunity to use custom player-made maps.
8-Bit Invaders has a pretty fun multiplayer mode as well, which is to be expected of most RTS games at this point. It lets you play as not just the two factions this game presents (the Marines and the Craniods), but also the ones in the other 8-Bit RTS games if you also own them. I think it's honestly fine if you don't though, because I was able to hold my own against four human opponents for a while as the Marines after my teammates had all died, so the factions they give you in Invaders are pretty solid overall.
The game also features a co-op campaign that's pretty decent. I really enjoy when RTS games let you play together with others, and this game's co-op mode was no exception. Me and a buddy had a pretty fun time doing missions together, some of which were pretty challenging. I have to give props to the developers for one map in particular that was similar to the melee-only stealth mission in the Marines campaign. My friend and I really struggled with getting all 3 stars on that map and we had to work together and plan things out pretty well to succeed, so it was definitely a fun map to play.
What might be the biggest addition to the series as a whole though (especially since they ported it back to the other two games) is the inclusion of the new "Metaverse" mode. Similar modes have been in other RTS games so it's not massively unique, but it's certainly a very refreshing and welcome addition to the 8-Bit RTS franchise. Essentially, the mode is what it sounds like - you have a world map of tiles and your goal is to conquer your enemy's home base and/or every tile on the map, depending on what setting you picked. Like most modes, you can build units and buildings, but in this mode you also can research new buildings/units using resources you get from conquering new tiles. To conquer tiles, you have to attack them with your army, which means you either physically fight the battle out yourself or you can auto-resolve it if you think your forces are large enough. The Metaverse is pretty challenging on higher difficulties and it can be pretty heavy on micro-managing regardless, but it's definitely a lot of fun.
Aesthetically, the game takes a lot of inspiration from other 8-bit/pixel games, but more significantly in my opinion, it looks most similar to other "voxel" games out there (like Minecraft, Trove, or Ace of Spades, just to name a few) - that is, the game employs uses 3D graphics to emulate a retro look, and in my opinion it looks pretty nice. It's kind of the whole graphical gimmick of the series, so if you're into the game's look, it should definitely deliver on your expectations.
The 8-Bit RTS games have always had some pretty kickass music, courtesy of the same composer as the Command & Conquer series, Frank Klepacki. This game's soundtrack does sound super similar to 8-Bit Armies', but regardless, I think Klepacki's tunes still capture that mix of action-packed battles and strategic thinking pretty well.
Overall, I was really pleased during my time with 8-Bit Invaders. It felt like it took all the things that 8-Bit Armies did well and expanded upon them. It's a great title for both newcomers and veterans of the RTS genre.

As a little background, I have played all previous games in the 8-Bit [Armies] franchise. The first game wasn’t all that remarkable with both factions looking identical other than their paint colour. Then the Guardian’s Campaign DLC was released. This made a whole new faction with a whole new playstyle turning 8-Bit Armies into a really nice retro-RTS game from the previous slightly dull game it had been. Next 8-Bit Hordes launched which was in stark difference from the original game. In my opinion, it was far superior in almost every way with both factions looking and playing completely different from each other and the graphics being overhauled. Now with 8-Bit Invaders! it feels like more of a successor to 8-Bit Hordes than the original 8-Bit Armies.
If you have never played any of the previous games, it is basically a true to form classical Real Time Strategy game. You build your bases and units and try to destroy your enemies as you complete your objectives. Which units and buildings you construct and when is completely up to you.
As with 8-Bit Hordes, there are two factions for you to play as, each having its own campaign. There are the Marines, which is your typical futuristic human army full of power-armored soldiers and mechanized vehicles. The other faction are the Aliens, which have a striking resemblance to the Martians from Mars Attacks! They tend to favour the energy weapons so you are treated to ray gun sound effects rather than the standard ballistic sound effects of the Marines. The vehicles and infantry of the two factions are completely different, which is really a step up from how it was in the original 8-Bit Armies.
The campaigns here are basically the same as they were in all of the previous 8-Bit Army games. Mostly the same pros and cons exist in this game as they did in the previous ones. The timer element is back in this game; however, it isn’t as prominent as it was in 8-Bit Hordes or the other previous ones. You are still pitted against the clock on some missions if you want to complete the Gold objective, but it isn’t in every mission. This means you don’t have to rush quite as much as you may have had to in previous entries in the series. If you go back and replay a level once you completed all the objectives, you can enjoy it far more. You are able to explore the map, find the hidden boxes, and enjoy the detailed units and scenery. The fact that completing bonus objectives gives you permanent rewards is something that I have enjoyed about this series. Having the unlocked extra starting resources/units/buildings retroactively added to all previous missions can really help you out come later on in the game. In fact, the game even suggests if you are having too much trouble with a bonus objective that you should wait and come back once you unlock more stuff as it will help make the challenge that much easier.
Graphically, the game is an improvement over the earlier games. It still has the blocky charm of the previous games but the units appear far more detailed now. Much like as in 8-Bit Hordes, the units are also far more diverse than they were in the previous 8-Bit Armies. The Aliens and their vehicles all look like something you would find in a science fiction B-movie with the tri-pod walkers, floating brains, acid-spewing dogs and UFOs making up just part of their repertoire. Each of the units is quite well detailed considering this is meant as a retro styled game. The Marines had the standard human in a battle suit for their infantry and had mechanical units reminiscent to the MechWarrior or Battletech series supporting them.
As with the previous games in the series, you still can’t rotate the buildings, which takes away a certain charm from the base building elements, but I can overlook that. Other than sometimes making a building fit into a spot it wouldn’t have otherwise fit, rotation serves an almost pure cosmetic function anyway. Also like the previous games, you still need to spam additional copies of buildings to speed up production which can really clutter your base, but also saves you from losing valuable production capabilities if the enemy breaches your base. This is perfectly fine but it would be nice if you could just add to an existing building to enhance its output too.
If you have already beaten the campaign or have reached a mission that has you stumped, you can always play a skirmish map or play the meta-verse game. Skirmish Map is simply you picking a map you want to play on and the faction you want to play as and go to it. There are no special mission conditions, just good old fashioned kill the enemy. The Meta-verse is far more interesting though. In the Meta-verse, you are set on a grid where each tile represents a battle/base location. At a friendly base, you can construct up to three buildings, and produce units until you reach the unit cap for the tile. You use these units to capture adjacent territories. The object here is to either capture every tile, or capture the enemy headquarters depending on which mode you opted for in the start. It adds a fun twist to the game because you will be playing on maps and encountering factions from the previous games. There is something satisfying about sending my squad of Aliens against the Horde of Orcs. When moving on the offensive, depending on how strong your force is and how heavy the enemy resistance is, you can choose to either fight the battle on a standard battlefield, building your base and training units to wipe the enemy out, or you can choose to auto-battle and let the computer battle it out for you. Auto-battle is a bit luck of the draw though, as I have won an auto battle when I only had a 26% chance of victory and lost a battle when I had an 84% chance of victory.
There is even an online co-op or versus mode available for you to play in as well. Unfortunately, during the time that I spent with the game prior to writing this, I was unable to find a co-op match to play. It could just be the time of day when I was trying or it could be the fact that people are not willing to wait around long to see if a lobby opens up. Most likely the best way to play a co-op match is to find some friends with the game and set up your own lobby. As for the online skirmishes, I did manage to play a few of those. The neat thing about those is the fact it lets you cross-play with people playing other games in the 8-Bit [Armies] franchise. There were never that many games available in the lobby, but that was okay, generally it didn’t take long to get a match going and I never particularly cared which map we were going to play on.
Overall, 8-Bit Invaders! is a welcome entry in the 8-Bit [Armies] franchise. It and 8-Bit Hordes are the best of the series in my opinion, although I’d still recommend picking up the original with its DLC as well as it is quite reminiscent of the old Command and Conquer games prior to franchise killing C&C4. The missions in all of the games are basically the same, so if you are looking for something completely different, you won’t find it in the main campaign, but really, how many variations of gameplay can a traditional Real-Time Strategy game offer? It’s the new factions that are the real selling point of 8-Bit Invaders!, with the Alien race being my favourite in the entire series. The story elements, which are displayed as a brief text box prior to the mission sets the reason why you are doing what you are doing. They do not really feel like they are driving any kind of overarching story but are more just there for atmosphere. Overall, if you liked the previous games, especially 8-Bit Hordes, then you will most certainly like 8-Bit Invaders! With the addition of its new meta-game mode, 8-Bit Invaders! is likely the best game of the series to pick up if you only plan to get one of them.

Broken Age is absolutley FANTASTIC.  Its so good in fact that I would rank it as my second favorite thing Tim Schafer has ever done behind Psychonauts, THAT is no small feat.  It has all the hallmarks of Schafer's greatest works: amazing cast of characters, perfect exceptional voice acting, challenging and hilarious puzzles/gameplay, excellent Peter McConnell soundtrack, incredibly written script, its all here and its awesome.  The real star of the show, though, is its story; the story here may be simple but its one of the best and most original plots I've EVER heard in a video game, built around 2 seperate plot threads that seem completely unrelated until a few plot twists mid-way through.  This two-story structure also plays into the gameplay, where you switch between the two main characters in order to complete the grander whole of the game.  There are also a few streamlined features that help speed up some traditions of the point-and-click genre that have long needed an overhaul.
That said, as is the case with ALL point-and-click adventures, it has a few niggling problems.  For the record any PAC game that has time-based puzzles never fails to frustrate me; there are times where you will be on the correct train of thought for solving a problem, but still fail because you didnt click in the right timing.  This doesnt sound like a big deal, but when you do fail this can cause you to try seeking other ways of completing the puzzle and waste a ton of time in the process.  There are other logic issues with some of the puzzles, but overall I think the difficulty was perfect for this genre, and overall I only needed to get help under 10 times in a lengthy adventure.
All in all if you are a fan of Double Fine, Schafer, or a point-and-click fan in general you absolutely MUST play Broken Age.

NS2 is a complex FPS/RTS hybrid game.
Those coming from any other FPS games will find marines comfortable to play as they are at the very least, familiar due to being so similar to so many FPS games out there.
Those coming from RTS games will enjoy being in the commander chair/hive, I recommend at least going through the tutorials for these regardless of how familiar you are to other RTS games, just to get to grips with what each team has to offer and how to do the basics for those teams... other than that, both teams play for the most part like 90% of RTS games.
Playing Aliens is different. Even people familiar with playing games like the old AVP games will find aliens in NS2 to be unusual.
They are complex to learn, have a high skill ceiling and in my opinion are the reason NS2 stands out from every other competitive game available.
Aliens make this game fun, the variety in styles of play and abilities that each lifeform can do make for interesting and engaging gameplay.
The community of NS2 is for the most part accepting of newcomers, helpful and friendly, just make sure, if you're new, TELL PEOPLE that you're new and ask BEFORE you jump into the hive/chair to command... some people can be quite vocal about "rookie commanders".
As with most competitive games, there are some "toxic" players, but surprisingly, the majority of them will help you out and try to teach you what they know about the game if you tell them you're relatively new and want to learn.
All in all I would recommend this game whole heartedly... it can be hard, it can be frustrating, but with over 3k hours playing, i'm still loving playing and have no intention of stopping any time soon.

Don't believe the naysayers, this is an excellent, fully voiced and animated AAA adventure with a special sense of humor that lasted me 14 hours.
Like Peter Molyneux's "Godus", Tim Schafer's "Broken Age" gets dissed by a lot fo fans who supported it on Kickstarter. As with Godus, I set out with the expectation to find out if its detractors are right, or if the game is being unjustly treated. I didn't like Godus, but Broken Age delivers all that I want. Note that I never played the unfinished game.
All puzzles are logical and have the clues needed to solve them available at all times, though they can be difficult to find or to figure out. Perservere! I got stuck 3 times and in hindsight wish I had perservered, I was never far from making the final connection that would have let me figure it out myself. It definitely has that old-school adventure feeling.

Don't buy unless you're keen on a really risky investment. Love how straight forward it could be. It's frustrating however to see bugs springing up left and right. Basic commands cease to work over time, frame drops (like come on, it's not even graphic intensive) and a litter of glitches that break immersion. Unplayable for longer than 30 minutes tops. Just to list them;
-Very first play attempt and I got confused as to where my CO was. After a bit of looking around it dawned on me what had happened. The shuttle he arrived on in the tutorial was still bound to recall even though it had de-spawned. In my spamming of commands I believe I had somehow managed to recall to a ship that didn't exist which is why when I double clicked his icon the camera panned to the empty space where the shuttle had been.
-Throughout the game I found myself repeat clicking, constantly re-issuing commands and click spamming just to get others to even register. This wasn't broodwar level lagging however, this took command lag to the next level. First I had to click what I wanted, had to wait for my character to get there, find out it was bugged, then had to walk away in order to un-qeue the order and then try again,
-To illustrate just how poor the UI is, you don't actually click on the overlay, you have to find the tile amidst the clutter of overlapping textures that are in the way to select the item you want. This resulted quite often in random civilians being attacked accidentally, brawls ensuing, and crew being evacuated to de-agro the AI. The flip side problem with this is other objects ARE accessible simply by clicking their overlay, This becomes frustrating as you realise there will never be a way to move your torpedos out from behind your nuclear reactor if you start with the blue ship.
- At one point I ran out of food and so naturally I bought more. But the game failed to register that the box of food was even an interactable object so my crew proceeded to starve around the completely full box of food. (kinda morbid)
-There are no hot keys or auto-fire capabilities for weapons stations. This makes combat fairly harrowing as you go from issuing commands to go back down to manually ordering your weapons to fire. And in engagements where you're outnumbered with allied ships taking fire, it becomes a management nightmare. At the very least I should be able to issue fire commands at the press of a key, not trudge the the exasperating struggle of managing my apm between in map actions and toolbar effects.

Act I was very good. I loved the visuals, the music, the voice acting and the characters. I really enjoyed how the game was an allegory for growing up, while also being a fantasy-scifi-mystery at the same time.
However it became immediately obvious that greed had poisoned the production of the game. Even with all the excess budget they still managed to run out and, after a hiatus of a year, release a poor conclusion to the game.
Act II got absolutely everything except for the visuals and voice acting so wrong. All of the themes and mysteries of the first game were given nonsensical explanations or barely explained at all. The ultimate conclusion of the story is relegated to a series of silhouettes in the background of the credits. The puzzles were not fun to solve, and are never explained.
All in all, it was a very promising game that failed to deliver anything other than disappointment. I just hope that in the future, we can forget about this tragedy and remember games such as Pillars of Eternity and Divinity: Original Sin as the shining examples of what crowdfunding can do.

This game has lots of very interesting and unique ideas that completely fail to come together.
I love the idea of a Gone Home-style game where you learn about a character's personality through their living space, and making the protaganist a housekeeper provides a great justification for this and adds the potential for a bit more gameplay that what walking simulators normally have. The idea of watching a major revolution as a complete outsider who wants nothing to do with either side is also very interesting.
Unfortunately, this game plays and runs terribly and fails to deliver a great story. Every day you have one "hour" to clean Ortega's apartment and do whatever tasks he has set out for you. You can do most tasks in two different ways, and choosing one will influence your relationship with Ortega. Instead of letting you choose between the two items on the same screen, you can only see one option at a time and will often have to awkwardly walk around whatever object you're trying to interact with to find the correct angle to trigger whichever option you want. When you do manage to succesfully interact with something, you are rewarded by the screen fading out and a seemingly somewhat arbitrary amount of in-game time passing. This process gets boring quickly, especially in later days when Ortega gives you fewer new tasks. It's also important to note that the game runs inexcuseably badly even though it has very simplistic (albeit pretty) graphics.
I also did not get invested in the characters and larger plot of the game. One of the biggest issues is that you are supposed to learn about your character through her journaling, but journaling is only triggered when you sit down, and then you have to watch her journal painfully slowly as that day's hour slips away. It's frequently literally impossible to complete all the day's tasks and also get the full journal entry. Your interactions with Ortega often feel very flat and limited and you are never really given much of a reason to care about the revolution.
This game takes lot of fantastic ideas and handles them all terribly. It's very disappointing and incredibly overpriced.

A really immersive, touching and atmospheric little game. The gameplay is all about subtelty and exploring the environment, very much "show not tell" for a lot of the narrative. Of course, if that's not your thing, you won't like it; maybe that's why there are so many (undeserved, in my opinion) negative reviews?
The game starts deceptively simple - you make your way to a high-ranking official's flat every afternoon, and have to complete a to-do list around house chores. Thing is, after a few days, you start noticing that you can complete the tasks in a couple of different ways every time, and that by exploring and looking at the right things you can start building a slow relationship with the flat owner. Your choices *will* affect the game, sometimes in unpredictable ways, and it's fascinating to see the characters develop through the choices they make. The story is also highly personal and although the every day actions are pretty trivial, there's a real sense of sadness, anger or even danger at various key points. That was a really nice surprise.
Graphics-wise the game has a very 1970s feel and palette obviously, again maybe not to everyone's taste (I personally really hate everything 70s!), but really well designed and elegant. It also makes a lot of cultural references to 20th century art/literature/music, which is quite interesting.
It ran perfectly on my 2yo mid-range gaming PC, so no issues there. Controls were very simple, could have done with a little more explanation (for the alternate choices for example), but definitely not a deal-breaker.
Tl;dr: try it, and like me you may get a really nice surprise. :-)

1- GENERAL
Paladins is a free to play team based FPS. As all of those it has a lot of ideas from TF2, and the commons perception that is very similar to Overwatch. I do not mind with any of those ideas, I play a game, no matter where they got the ideas.
Graphically, and as almost all the multiplayer PvP games, the game is not very demanding, since it has to be able to run in low end machines. Even so all is well designed maps are quite interesting and enjoyable. Colors are spot on, not over the top like in other similar games.


2- GAMEPLAY
We play in 5v5 teams.
There's 3 gamemodes. Payload, survival and siege. In the first one we have to capture the payload before we escort it, in the second one we play 5vs5, last team standing wins, in the third one we play in turns, one time escorting the payload, in the other attacking it.
We have a PvE mode, now called co-op. It's like a very hard weekly challenge, where a team of humans have to defeat a team of bots.
Teams have to be balanced to win. They will underperform if they only have champions from the same group, and you can't change your character in the middle of a round, so you have to choose wisely before the game starts.
We can acquire payloads to our champion. Cards that gives some buffs to the character previous to the match. During the match we can purchase perks to our champion, spending the earned round points. That gives some strategical aspects to your decisions, and they can change a round completely if chosen wisely.
It's common to see unbalanced teams, and poorly chosen perks during the rounds. Do not loose your temper, just try to teach newcomers.
There's no voice communications. You have to use chat or a set of predefined commands that have simple instructions to the team.
I've still experienced this game when he wasn't absolutely pay to win. Now we have a third currency, that cannot be acquired in any way. We win it with duplicates in a very slow pace. RNG is now back in full power. Even so, you can still progress, just not as quick, and it will be very hard to catch up older players.


3- CONCLUSION
So, what do I think? The game is free, I know, but if you want to play competitively, without spending any money, without a huge catch up to do, maybe this is not your game. In the other hand it's a great game, very fun, well designed, great gameplay. If you just want to have fun, be sure to give it a go.

This game is one of the worst walking simulator I played. The 'walking simulator' genre is one of my favourite (actually maybe my favourite) and I play most of them. I had heard from some friends that this game was no masterpiece, but when I saw it in a bundle for 1$ I decided I would take the risk.
Well, the game first of all runs horribly. Given that the graphics are far from beautiful, the performance has no reason to be this low.
Other than that, the game mechanics are quite boring. In a 'walking simulator' the atmosphere is what counts, you have to be involved somehow in the story, in the environment. It is a 'walking simulator' (not meant negatively, for lack of a better word) so there is no action, there is nothing to shoot at, and of course if you don't deliver a thick atmosphere and great voice acting or good lore, you are not offering much to the players.
The 'plot' is barely there and the whole apartment / city / civil war thing, which could have been a great basis for a good involvement in the atmosphere/environment doesn't deliver. You don't feel it, and the little lore you can get about the protagonist's life by sitting on a chair and letting her writing her diary is naive, simplistic.
Honestly I didn't find anything good in the game. The house (apartment?) itself is very badly designed, the proportions are weird, of course it's meant to be a big modernist expensive house with lots of big rooms, but the result is that it looks incredibly empty and out of proportions compared to the character. If you do more or less everything, the game will last around 5 or 6 hours. If you can resist that long and don't get bored after the first hour. Definitely in my worst 5 in the genre.

The set pieces are elegantly laid out, and wrapped up into a finely optimized game engine that can produce breathtaking visuals without ever dropping below 60 frames per second. Aside from a lack of content and potentially repetitive gameplay, Spintires is easily the most original and genuinely fun title I have played in 2014 thus far.
Few games can cause a player to feel genuine tension, and fewer still can invoke relaxation. Spintires has given me both, often simultaneously, for hours.

Champions are bought with gold. You have 8 champions and 12 + to unlock. It's great because you can train yourself to play on what you've got and master them!
Overwatch has 6 vs 6 battles, Paladins has 5 vs 5.
Here, you don't need teleporters, YOU HAVE HORSES. You ride horses everytime you respawn until you left click to get off. And before you ask, yes there's a pretty pank pony too.
Cards. You can modify your champion's stats. If you got the right cards, you increase your Champion's attack, lesser cooldowns, and more!
In-fight currency. There's this currency called credits, you buy and get them to use for ONE GAME ONLY. It can decrease your reload speed, be faster, get lifesteals, etc.
Nicer community. I come across the rare angsty teen but most times your team is good at cooperating with you! Make a plan and they'll usually do it to win!

TL DR version:
Loot boxes are absolutely not necessary to achieve a 100% completition in the game
+ The game is well optimized
+ Nemesis System
+ Combat System
+ Items/sets
+ Difficulty
- Story
- Lots of grinding at the endgame
Long version:
This game is awesome. If you liked Shadow of Mordor you will definitely love this. I recommend to play it in the hardest difficulty (Nemesis), then it will give you quite a challange. You will quickly learn who to avoid, and which fights to pick. The combat is basically the same as in the prequel with some tweaks here and there. The nemesis system is just awesome. Each ork that you kill/shame/whatever will have an influence on the future. For example, I have killed an ork by cutting him in half...later he ambushed me on a mission, and explained that his mates collected his parts and sew him back together. Then there is an orc that I killed with Fire damage. He keeps returning and he is mortally vulnerable to Fire damage (I killed him like 5 times already). He says that there is no point in killing him because he will return...maybe it is time for me to shame him. Then there are the sieges...the coolest part of the game. Recruit some badass orcs, choose your sige weapons and siege the enemy fortress. It really feels like I am on a real battlefield, which can get chaotic pretty fast when I am facing 4-5 captains at the same time. Defending and attacking are both entertaining and engaging. Another improvement to the previous game is that we can now equip items in 6 slots, and there are also legendary set pieces which offer different styles of play.
Lootboxes are not necessary to complete the game, but they definitely give you an edge if you want to participate in online sieges. The hardest part is to find good legendary followers to defend your fortresses. It can take hours to spawn a legendary orc in the world by playing the game, but you can easily get them from lootboxes. But if you don't care about reaching the top of the leaderboards you can do just fine by playing the game. It is fun hunting for these orcs, and you can still buy lootboxes with ingame currency.
Now the bad part. The story does not feel very interesting, sometimes it does not even make much sense. The charachters are not well developed, they feel one-sided and bland.
As I mentioned above, after you reach the endgame it becomes very grindy, and it can get too repetitive after a while. Hunt worms - get intel - shame captain - recruit - etc...ah yeah, your maximum level is 60, while Orcs can spawn up to 65 which means that you have to shame them to reduce their level to 60 or below, in order to be able to recruit them. But then there is a higher chance that he will betray you because you shamed him.

Natural Selection 2 has the elements of an FPS and RTS rolled up into one game, although it should be recognized as a different genre all together. On normal gameplay mode, there are two teams fighting each other, marines and aliens. Each team has a commander, which builds and decides the tech build order for the team. As commander, you have a top down view of the map. Which is similar to a RTS, except for one thing. Your focus isn't about micro managing combat units, because the bulk of the combat is done by the FPS players. Instead you're macro managing, which is mainly telling other players where to go, and adapting to your players instead of just focusing on a preset build order. Gameplay for the commander can get interesting allowing more micro management with several tech paths such as ARCs which are siege units, or creating illusions of fake alien units with a Shade.
As for the FPS side of the game, players on field are concerned about holding resource points and tech points so their commander can expand and provide more abilities to the team as a whole. The players also have their own personal resource which is gained from the same resource towers, which they can spend on buying temporary upgrades for themselves. Such as a marine could buy a shotgun, but upon death, it drops on the floor. An alien can evolve to a higher life form but when they die, they'll lose that life form.
Lastly, the game depends on teamwork and how well each individual player is. A game can easily be lost if the players are out matched on the field, or if there is an inexperienced commander in the seat.
