When you reach the end of the game it is really beautiful to see how far video games have come.  I feel like this game would have been perfect for 2002 when we were insecure about video games being a high art form.  Art is all about timing and today we just don't need a video game that is so dedicated to art that isn't traditionally fun.  Video games as art is working out just fine.  Games like The Last Of Us are combining art with reliably fun concepts.  We can have fun, beauty, depth.  We don't have to choose between the three anymore.
I really feel for the developers who rage quit when the game was critically panned.  A lot of people didn't really play the game and judged it too quickly as soon as they clicked on a chore.  It actually turns out there is fun to be had by establishing a routine for the main character and disrupting it by having a war happen all around you.  There is fun to be had through the immersion.  People didn't always give this game a fair chance and I apologize for them.
I must admit the major flaw of the game comes up immediately.  The narration.  It's kind of like the mostly unnecessary narration in Grey's Anatomy.  The way Sunset is designed the story has to be told to the player.  The actress just wasn't able to put on a convincing performance.  I found myself enjoying the immersion instead of the narration.  Great acting could have gone a long way in this game.
Recommended.  See for yourself how far games have come.  Admire how much effort was put into a concept that is no longer workable.

I can't really put into words why this game is so great. It just is.  The concept seems simplistic and repetitive; explore the map, find vehicles, unlock garages, get lumber, deliver lumber.  However its easier than it sounds as the challenge is actually doing all that when your 8 wheel drive vehicle is buried halfway deep in mud and your winch cable can't reach any anchor points.  Rescue your stuck vehicle to a garage of send another vehicle(s) to try and rescue it?  For me the challenge is to never have a vehicle rescued to the garage.  Stuck? Pull it out with another vehicle. Out of gas? Find a fuel truck and deliver some.  Extensively damaged and not drivable? Send a repair truck.  Just hope they don't get stuck too and make sure you know how deep that "puddle" is before you attempt to drive through it or how deep that river is before you attempt to ford it!
If you like driving games you may or may not love this game.  It's not fast paced, it's pretty slow and methodical but there is a lot of strategy involved and patience is definitely a virtue here.  The world is permanently damageable so if you dig up big ruts in the road and knock down trees you better believe it'll be the exact same way when you drive through there again hours later.  You'll know pain when you drive clear across the entire map with 6 loads of lumber only to tip the trailer and lose all of it only meters from your destination.  Yet somehow, turning around and getting more lumber to try it all over again, as frustrating as it may be, is a welcome turn of events.

is how I'd imagine "The Sims: Spaaaaace!" to work. The game involves managing crew members of a space ship, exploring the galaxy, and vanquishing foes. Visiting space stations allows you to obtain missions and new crew members.
Crew members have traits, moods and desires. They will automatically tend to their needs when your ship is not in an alert status. During alerts, however, crew members will faithfully remain at their posts and rely upon you to manually manage their needs. Crew members level up with experience and, upon their first promotion, specialize in a profession of your choosing: Security, Medical or Engineering.
Ship to ship combat is fairly straight forward.  Your ship is equipped with a basic shield for defense, and a machinegun and a torpedo launcher for offense.  In addition to slugging it out with ranged weapons, you may attempt to board the enemy by beaming crew members over.  Enemy ships may not be captured; however, ship equipment may be seized (or purchased) to upgrade your own vessel. You may upgrade your ship by purchasing a new one at a space station.
The game is in early access, and I experience the occasional bug - most do not seriously detract from my enjoyment of the game. I recommend Star Command Galaxies because it is fun. The current price (14.99 USD as I write this) is reasonable for what you get.

Shadow of war is a game of controversy. It has many good things in it and bad things in it. The things bad out number the things are good sadly and that is a real shame because as a tolkien/middle earth fan, I would of loved this game to have been good and have a lord of the rings game people can compare the future games to. I have almost 60 hours in, have completed the game 100% and almost got all the achievments as well. I am currently only missing 5 I think. I am gonna give an honest, review with indepth subjects. Lets begin.
GOOD THINGS:
1. Combat: is more polished and better than ever before. If you liked the first games combat, then you will love this combat system. I played on the hardest difficulty and you kinda have to with this game in order to get everything out of it. Only thing I don't like with the combat is how much orc captains, warchiefs and overlords have. It could just be the hard difficulty, but I ended up always freezing them with the B buttion if I could and kept spamming them till they were dead. Overall, combat is great.
2. Graphics: Graphics are amazing in this game. There is forsure no better lord of the rings game with graphics these good. You can look off into the distance and see Barad Dur (sauron's fortress) and just be amazed. With my gameplay, I did notice a few poppins in the distance but nothing too horrible, and framerate was steady at solid 60fps with my 1440p gaming experience. I only crashed once the whole time on a loading screen
3. Plenty of things to keep you busy: this game has plenty of things to do that will keep you occupied. Such as killing orcs, lvling up your fortesses and getting the best orcs to man them. Raiding other peoples fortresses, and so much more. It will keep you busy but this is personal opinion. Many people don't like the ubisoft type busy work in this game. It is starting to catch its toll on me but not yet.
4. Story is decent: While the story is no Witcher 3, the story is fairly average. It takes a different route on tolkiens lore which might upset some people but not me because I know this game is not cannon and Im not gonna ♥♥♥♥♥ about it. If you are a fan of the lord of the rings games or tolkien in general, than the story might interest you,. or simply watch all the cutscenes on youtube. its up to you. IF there is one thing, is that the story is not horrible. They tried, they really did and you can see it. Its just people expect a crazy good story now a days and this one does not try that.
5. Tons of in game lore you can read upon and appendices: if you like to read things then this is for you. There are tons of things to read about and collect. Each item you find has a back story in it in a voice and its great, Also, each character has an entry which is always a plus. I love it when games add things in like this. It really expandes the lore of the world.
BAD THINGS
1.Microtransactions: Everybody saw this coming. Microtranactions are a plague among the gaming community and if we don't stop it now, then it will be there forever and we lose as the consumers. Nobody like spending money in games, especially on single player games and when you already dropped 60 dollars on it too. They are just horroble and need to be stopped. its funny actually because if microtranactions were not in this game, it would of have more sales and WAY better reviews on steam and other websites in general. Bad move WB.
2. Music: The music in this game reminds me of a typical action movies type of music. You know what I am talking about. The music is not catchy or anything. Most of the time I don't even hear it because the other audio is so much louder.(Yes I had music up all the way.) In general, music is nothing special here, and in my OPINION, in order to have a good game, you need a good soundtrack. look at skyrim and other games. You would expect more from A middle earth game.
3. Story missions:While most of the story missions are repetitive, they're are the exceptional few missions that I enjoyed such as SPOILER: The fight with the balrog and sauron fight. I really wish they would of put better story missions in instead of the kill all orc in this area or fend off this area type mission.
4. Shadow wars: What a stupid mode. I bet that delay was for this mode and those dumb microtransactions. This is the worst part of the game in my opinion. The grind of defending and re-capturing fortesses over and over again. While you do not have to purchase anything it is still just annoying. Not one time I was tempted to buy anything which was good.
5. Lack of unique armor sets: While there are a few armor set I really like, most of the armor sets are just plain and doll. I laughed aloud when they shown me an armor set and the next one right next to it is the same armor set just a different color. that is lame. The only really good looking armor sets are some of the legendaries. all the others you just ware them for the stats not the cosmetics. Same thing goes for swords, daggers, and bows.
6. Talion: He is really pathetic. He seems like some generic dude with nothing interesting about him. Celebrimbor is alot better, but talion should of really been changed in this game. He has no emotion. I mean this guy witnessed his wife and son die right in front of him, but he still acts like a robot. I wish the game was all about celebrimbor instead of talion and while celebrimbor is not perfect, he is still better that talion the robot.
7. Some weird glitches: While I barely any crashes there were some weird glitches I encountered. One glitch I had was with the drake. It spawned outside of the map and I shadow dominated it to get on top of it to ride it. I was outside the map and I could not get in. so I decided to explore alittle bit. I was in seregost and flew all the way to sauron's dark tower you can see in the distance which made me LOL. There was another glitch when the overlord refuesed to fight me. Also there was this one Uruk I encountered which was immune to everything. Which might be a feature of the hardest gamemode so I am not 100% on if that is a glitch or not. If you buy this game expect some glitches.
So there are my Pros and Cons to this game.  I sadly do not recommend this game, even though I am a huge LOTR fan. If you are a huge fan of LOTR or The first game, than this is a buy. If you like repetitive grindy like games then buy this. It will keep you busy for 50 hours. In my opinion, buy it on sale. I was so hyped for this game when they released the first trailer for it but it just died.  This game is a 6/10 for me. Too many cons than pros.
I hoped you liked my review of shadow of war. Please remember this is my opinion and please forgive my spelling errors as I was typing this super fast without proof reading it.

Game Tags: Third-Person Action Adventure Stealth Game OpenWorld RPG DarkFantasy
Publisher: Warner Bros.
Developer: Monolith Productions
Released: 9 Oct 2017
Initial Response on Day One: Mostly Positive
Middle-Earth: Shadow of War is the sequel to 2014's Middle Earth Shadow of Mordor, and boy! is it a sequel in every meaning of the word. I enjoyed the heck out of Shadow of Mordor, on about two different platforms and recently three after purchasing it for my gaming laptop. But before I start, I'd like to say that Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor was GOTY and probably the best game that year, and it probably is going to always be on the top 40 list for: ''Top Forty Open World Action Adventure Games". After replaying Shadow of Mordor, I was really hyped for the sequel based on the video's shown on multiple gameplay demos. Is it similar to the gameplay demos? Yeah, in a way.
Story:
For my review of Shadow of Mordor, I thought that the story was a mess, it was trying to be loyal to lore while being loyal to gamers while trying to be fun. Was it fun at the end? Yeah, was it loyal to everything else? Yeah. But the characters were fricking boring af. Like, seriously, some of the orcs were more interesting that some of the main characters. That's different here though. The game takes itself as cannon and uses its right to Tolkien universe in a right manner. With Talion and Celebrimbor being way more interesting, but still 'Lorm the Twisted' and 'Stazgu the Twins' were better. This made the story, way better because of this. The rest of the plot flowed very well and didn't make me groan when I realized the story wasn't over. Though, as a LOTR and HOBBIT fan myself there are many mistakes in LOTR and HOBBIT lore, so just saying beware. Other than that the story feels better, but in no way will I compare this story to something like the Witcher 3, Skyrim or Batman Arkham City or not even near 'The Last Of Us'
Gameplay:
If you've played the first game, or even played Assassin Creed and Batman Arkham series, you'll catch up with the controls and movement system, in general fast. The Nemesis System is improved with a larger variety of Orcs, Olag Hai, tribes etc. Every Orc feels unique and different and each of them changes best on you and the environment. I remember "Stazgu The Twins" He basically had one head with a deformed extra head on the side. I made him apart of my army and I and he went through loads of hard times. But we had fun, at the end. That is until this backstabber, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ named Bruz killed me and captured all of them. I went on a rescue mission to save him and both of us went to reclaim our throne. Bruz killed Stazgu, well♥♥♥♥♥♥  I mourned his death and then teabagged Bruz for him. Well, guess what, when I was in the little forest thing in Sea of Nurn, I was ambushed by Stazgu, who cheated death. He kept killing me and got super powerful. I killed him in the end. Threw him off a cliff, I wasn't able to recruit him because of his 'Iron will' basically he has been so faithful to Sauron, that he can't betray him. So stories like this will last long, making Shadow of War very replayable.
Graphics:
A pretty looking game, just download the high-resolution pack, and if your pc can run it, the 4k pack, both of them are free. One issue I faced was the fact that I could play on High Settings 100 FPS, but on Ultra, which looked no different it ran at 5 FPS. It's an optimization issue, please fix it Monolith.
Loot Boxes:
I've never bought one, never intend too, don't buy one, play the game like its supposed to be played, trust me you'll enjoy it way more. Boycott it if you want, no one's forcing you to buy it though, so yeah.
End Verdict:
Middle Earth: Shadow Of War is a pure 7.8/ 10 or and 89 percent.

Cons
-A few of the add ons do not work. (Carrier Strike Force cannot launch 3wirex due to an issue on permissions on the application).

Game is awesome, lots of fun and well designed. I'm also part of the minority that enjoyed the story as well, but the reason I am not recommending this game is because of the application of the loot boxes in game as well as the DLC business model.
Back in the day when DLC first came around it was a bonus, the games we were getting were already finished and developers were giving us ADDITIONAL CONTENT. Now its jsut a gross pactice of chopping the game in two and selling each half for a full priced game and its no different here.
In regards to loot boxes, usually I am okay with them because unlike DLC content (where you don't get to experience to full game) loot boxes are completely optional, you aren't put in a position where you have to buy them to enjoy the full experience (unlike DLC). However, what they have done in this game is made the loot boxes contrusive to your experience in the game, unless you want to spend endless hours mindlessly grinding then loot boxes are virtually not optional here, I quit playing and as a result never got the "true ending" because the grind killed the game for me, it really felt like I wasn't getting anywhere, the time I was putting in was not equal to the progression/reward received.
So basically again, like I said, its a good game with lots of fun to be had but the business practices developed into the final product ruin it especially towards the end, plus the amount of game you get isn't worth $80 (Sidenote: I don't know why games seem to be getting more expensive every year, its ridiculous and this is probably the last time I will get a game on release).
Final Verdict: Wait until game of the year edition comes out, definitely not worth $80.

Wasteland 2 plays like a slightly less polished Fallout 2, but with a Wasteland setting (rougher and with less 60's nostalgia humor).  The gameplay is a throwback to the original western cRPGs; it's a cold RNG hell mitigated only by extensive save scumming.
Graphically it's a 3/4 down perspective 2.5D experience.  Unlike Fallout 2, the worlds aren't 2D drawings but are rather 3D rendered.  This is nice because it allows the camera view to be rotated between the 4 cardinal compass directions.  But, it adds the negative "feature" that sometimes important things (like loot or enemys) are obscured by the terrain, forcing you to constantly rotate the camera view to ensure you're not missing something.  It's also quite low res, especially in the character model department.
For what parts I've gotten through, the story is interesting and has numerous tie-ins to the original Wasteland storey.  But, it has enough explanation that people that didn't play (or can't remember anymore) the original Wasteland won't feel lost.  The game also alows you many different ways to complete most quests from diplomatic to violent and from good to bad.
So, as long as you don't mind reloading a lot (save early and often!) it's quite a fun trip back in memory lane.  This is very much how old school cRPGs were.  And, it's a blast!

A solid return for a beloved series and another title for 2014 that shows the turn based tactical RPG of old is making a comeback in a big way. The original game inspired the Fallout series and with this game they return the the spirit of Fallout 1 and 2 with a party based RPG with tactical turn based combat. Set about 20 years after the events of Wasteland 1 (Its not neccesary to play that game, Wasteland 2 is a stand alone story. Though fans who played it will see various call outs to the original)
You play a rookie in the desert rangers, a group of people dedicated to bringing law and order to the Wasteland. Surrounded by radiation from the war, a lot of people believe the rest of the world is completely destroyed, though a series of strange events that you are sent to investigate indicates that this is not the case and as the plot unfolds its clear that there are far greater threats in this ruined world that wandering bandits.

You have a lot of choice about how you go about things and you can either be a saviour or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ depending on the choices you make, though if you go to far down the dark side, be prepared for consequences. The world is huge and the large variety of skills you can master means that most situations will have various ways to overcome them, though be prepared to spill a lot of blood as not everyone can be reasoned with or manipulated. The plot is interesting and its fun to see how the designers portray the post apocalyptic world. It also has a suprisingly dark sense of humour and there are quite few moments that will make you smile or even laugh out loud. Despite being set in a Fallout type post nuclear world the game still manages to have its own identity and feel like its own game. I personally love both and highly recommend it to Fallout fans and fans of old school RPG's or post apocalyptic settings. If you are a fan of all three, just buy the game right now, you won't be disappointed!

While I really enjoy Wasteland 2, my recommendation would have to come with a huge dose of "your mileage may vary". It's a long, slow, burn, and if you like to jump straight into things, or find yourself easily losing concentration or focus, you may find yourself giving up on Wasteland 2 before it really begins to shine. But some patience will pay off, if the genre interests you. Of course, if you don't like turn-based strategy games, then you should be giving this a pass. The writing is really top-notch in this game, and I found it both enjoyable and rewarding to play through.
Focused on a team of 4 rangers (which you can create yourself, or use several pre-built characters), and using very detailed attributes and skills - the CLASSIC system (Coordination, Luck, Awareness, Strength, Speed, Intelligence, Charisma), it took me a while before I realised that some attributes and stats were extremely important, while others... could be passed over, especially depending on the followers (NPCs) you decided to acquire. Unfortunately, it can take some trial and error before you realise what you should be doing with your characters and what is important for them to have. Or... you could just forge ahead anyway! I quite liked that there were no classes, giving you the freedom to do whatever you wanted with your characters. You could have a guy carrying heavy weapons, while being a melee tank and also healing... for example. Though this can also be a negative, if you wanted to see class specialisation, perks, and so on.
And so, I was introduced to the fun (???) of character creation. And uhh... naming my characters, which proved to be a disaster... after an embarrassingly long time, I settled on "One", "Two", "Three", and "Four". Original, right. The vast array of skills can be intimidating at first, and leveling them up (especially at later levels) can become quite frustrating and very grindy, but it does add a lot of depth to the game. One thing I did not like as much though... how much time it took, and the animation, whenever you wanted to use a skill. Using a skill meant that your Ranger (or follower) would have to move to the location (clumping up your Rangers if you moved them all as a group makes this an exhausting chore), before an animation begins. With the vast amount of skill checks in this game, the checks do add up and can become very time consuming and therefore annoying.
Additionally, there is quite a lot of travel involved in this game, both in the larger world map, and also within smaller exploreable areas. Even if you're not in a rush, the travel can quickly become aggravating. I wished for quicker travel myself, despite the fact I don't mind slower paced games.
While you are limited to Arizona and California, one after the other, the world map is still pretty expansive, with secret areas to discover dotted around the place. Travelling isn't worry free though - not only are there standard enemy encounters (which can become annoying quite quickly), but also some more welcome encounters, which is a bit different and somewhat refreshing in comparison to the usual fare where encounters in the wild just end up being endless fights. There are also two unique mechanics: water and radiation. Your team carries canteens, which can, and should be refilled at any well and oasis you find. Once you run out of water, your team starts to dehydrate and can die. Similarly, in the post-apocalyptic wasteland, nukes have left lingering radiation in various areas - so you also have to watch out for contamination... or again, you'll find your team dropping like flies.
The musical score, sound effects, and even the voice acting is all done quite well, and combines well with the graphics to provide a smooth and enjoyable spectacle. The graphics are not the best in the world, but they do set the tone of the game well, and are very appropriate to the game's setting - harsh, gritty, and unforgiving.
Combat is generally quite straight forward, with the standard turn-based combat fare reappearing here, though more in-depth compared to some other games due to the more extensive attribute and skill system. Your attributes and skills will determine in what order your characters go, and how much they can do in their turn. There are also crouch and cover mechanics, though some weapons can destroy cover. However... there is not much else. There are no real special combat moves, or combat specific skills - they increase your damage and hit percentage, and that's it. No executes, no cloak, etc. While there is headshot and ambush... they are honestly not that great. It's just point, click, hope to hit (the RNG seems to be a bit odd, with a lot of misses even on shots with a high hit percentage), rinse and repeat. There is no cover, no flush, no interesting and genuinely unique abilities.
Additionally, RNG can always turn around and give you a hard time. Or... adversely affect the enemies. Critical hits, critical misses, weapon effects, and weapon jams can all have a surprisingly large affect on the outcome of an encounter. I also like the emphasis on scarcity and the need for careful management of your resources, which is quite fitting for a game like this, especially the ammo. If you just blaze away, you'll be out of ammo before you know it, so you do need to think before you act. Vendors are limited too... The combat is decent, and I enjoyed it, but I will admit there could have been more to it.
While your team revolves around 4 characters, you are able to recruit a number of NPCs to join your team (3 followers for a maximum team size of 7). While you are nominally in control of them, leadership is important here as there is the chance your "follower" (only if they are in a good mood) will just decide to do their own thing in combat - running into cover, shooting something you didn't want shot, etc. Overall, the combat is fun and challenging, with a variety of enemies to conquer - both man and animal.
Despite there only being two areas to explore, Wasteland 2 boasts a wide variety of quests, many of which have a variety of ways to finish - but be careful, your choices do have serious and lasting consequences. Which is something else I really enjoy about the game - your choices DO matter. And have a ripple effect. This is not just limited to quests, there are some actions while just generally playing and moving around which could have an affect, especially based on which followers are with you. Do you dig up some graves? Do you disarm the alarm? Do you deliberately trip it off? Do you use strength or a grenade to break a wall? Do you help this faction, or the other faction? Mediate a ceasefire or shoot everybody up? The variety of ways to overcome things in your way is definitely a highlight of the game. I really enjoyed the varying options available, and weighing them up, based on what you want your team to do. Your decisions may cause followers to leave your party, or even turn on you. Not only does this create an interesting in-game dynamic where what you do will affect how other in-game characters interact with your party, but this also allows for extensive replayability, if you so choose. "What if" questions are plentiful in this game.
Finally, I particularly loved the odd references and humour. The Wasteland 1 disc was a particular highlight. While not particularly game-making, or breaking, it was something that I enjoyed. The grand adventure that plays out, in addition to the continued support and patching by inXile, make me give this game two thumbs up.

Extremely creative thinking behind this relaxing title, but it's not for everybody. This will likely only truly appeal to certain folks: daydreamers, stoners, trippers, and anyone else who likes to zone out for long periods of time.
-------------------------------
FULL:
Very interesting concept. Definitely not a flop, though I have a hard time getting into it, myself. While it is relaxing, t's just one of those things that isn't for everybody. Though it would be great, for example, if you just enjoy getting lost in thought and want something that soothingly inspires that kind of experience.
Or, alternatively, it would be great for those who love to zone out on it for a few hours while stoned or tripping (if you know what I'm talking about, that used to be me, so I'm not just speculating. Would have LOVED it if Mountain existed back then).
If either of those describe you, this would likely be very fun for you. Really not a "game" for everybody. Still pretty cool though, for what it is. The creator, David OReilly, was certainly thinking outside of the box! We need more of that kind of ingenuity and creativity in modern digital entertainment! For that, I give it a resounding
. I had thought such creativity had all but disappeared after the late 1990s or early 2000s. Glad to see I was wrong. :)

From (Creator Publisher): Firaxis / 2k games
Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $4.99
Total Time played: 60 minutes
Review:
I had been waiting for this game, and really I was surprised that it came up so quickly in the randomizer.  Now, I have been a fan of the civilization series for well over a decade and a half, since the first version came out on PC, and have played it in one form or another almost constantly between then and now, and on nearly every console or PC I have owned.  That being said, more often than not the versions I have played have either been first generation games or one of the many free clones, so it was a treat to be able to play one of  the games I haven’t played yet.
Now, I have to admit that spending only an hour on any civilization game isn’t quite enough to have an adequate run with the game, but I still intend to give it a review based on that limited experience.  The gameplay is solid, though Civilization has a steep learning curve, providing little in terms of understanding asset management and growth.  This version does allow workers to auto-update the surrounding areas around the cities, so some of the more mundane tasks of the earlier versions are removed ,at least to an extent, however the controls around individual units have been reduced to a sort of drag and drop system, which can get confusing, especially when requiring units to change direction mid order.  The graphics are about what you can expect from a fifteen year old civilization game, though units are easily enough distinguished from each other, there isn't much else there in terms of fancy looks.  But then again, that isn’t why you’re playing.  Instead, you’re playing to feel the inexorable crushing defeat of having your little peaceful civilization on the  corner of the map overrun by whoever is the aggressive one of the AI monsters.  You play to waste time clicking on your cities each turn to watch the build counters drop.  You play to try, and fail, to understand why your citizens in just that one city won’t shut the ♥♥♥♥ up about taxes.  I mean, come on, every other city is okay with it.  You really don’t have much to complain about.  So why riot?  I certainly wouldn’t know.
Game’s Fate: This one will remain, and probably take up all my spare game playing time, at least until another one of the series comes up in the randomizer to replace it.

: Overall, I'd give this game an 3/10 – I wouldn’t recommend it unless you like punishing difficulty and/or doing the same things over and over again, and even then, I’m sure there are better and more fun things to do over and over again.
A fast-paced, difficult, top-down shooter, with no easy-mode to get you going, and an obvious emphasis on making things harder just because.
Difficult games can be fun, but only when you feel like there is a point to the difficulty. Instead, this game is a bit like some of the original NES games, in that it’s difficult just because that was the only way they knew how to make a game with staying power. That is not the case in 2017. Some people might still enjoy that type of difficulty, but even for them, there are probably less boring choices out there. Also, the only rogue-like element is the unlocking of characters. I unlocked two in my hour of playing, only one of which was worth a crap. You don’t carry any other mutations or anything forward, which would be pretty cool.
Not much. The first few dozen times I did the first three levels filled me with a feeling of, “Meh, this is alright.” Then it got tedious really fast.
People who enjoy hard games with little reward, I guess.
$12 seems pretty steep for a game with retro graphics, that clearly hinges on repeating the same content. The levels that I did see (over and over and over again) were pretty small, too.
The fact that you’re playing as little mutated things is pretty cool. I wish I could’ve seen more of them.
Call them retro if you like, but honestly, they’re pretty bad. It’s also capped at 30 FPS, which gives me a headache, and seems unnecessary.
The music was a saving grace. Very fitting metal tracks for the bullet fest.
Definitely a high point, especially if you have decent bass.
It’s basically what you would expect from a top down shooter with WASD movement. Nothing special at all.
Polished enough, I guess. No crashes in the one hour that I played.
The game is over a year old, but still updated (I think, going by the forums).

TL;DR: Maybe it is because it got updated for Steam or maybe it is because so much time passed and so much was added to the core game since its launch... Either way, for a true Fallout fan like me, this game is fleshed enough to be a good stand alone game. And if you are worried about the microtransactions, which are still possible in the PC version, know that there is no incentive whatsoever to buy anything. This is NOT a pay to win game.
Long version:
I remember when this game came out. It was some kind of promotional stunt alongside the developer wanting to jump on the microtransaction wandbagon... But the game itself always interested me since I'm a Fallout fan. Never played it since it wasn't available for PC and I was quite salty about it... Until now!
In a nutshell, this is a Facebook game about building a Fallout shelter in the Fallout universe. However, unlike the very vast majority of Facebook games nowaday, this one is actually quite decent and well made. It shows that a lot of thought have been put in this project and that it has not been put together in a few days only to cash in on microtransactions.
The mechanics of the game are quite polished and the game itself shows the mark of gem games: very easy to play with and start on but hard to master. There is quite a few unexplained quirks going on in this game that you slowly catch on as you get more experienced and if you are the kind of person who want to know right away without waiting then you can simply go on the game wiki which, while kind of bland, is quite complete. Another nice touch is that the game timers continue to tick down when you are not actively playing the game either because you get bored or more likely because real life get in the way, which mean that once you have established your vault you can decide to simply leave and come back later while still progressing on your goals.
The strongest downside of the game is that its interface leave a lot to be desired. This is unfortunately completely expected since this is a direct port from a version aiming for mobile users. There is no way around the fact that the game is built with touchscreen in mind and thus the controls completely suck to the point of being frustrating for a keyboard and mouse user. On the upside, you could play one vault on your PC in the comfort of your home and play the same game on your phone with another vault. Many guides also offer insight on how to copy one specific vault from one medium to another so technically it would also be possible to play a single vault if you are willing to cope with the extra work. This drawback can thus be either a curse or a nice addition to your playing experience depending of the direction you wish to take.
The nice thing about this game is that it is completely free. You just click install on the Steam store page and start playing. There is a tutorial for new players which gift you all what you need to start with alongside a decent amount of Nuka Cola, the "higher end" currency of the game. If you are intelligent about your spendings you can stretch that starting amount a long way and I have found that there is plenty to be found in the wasteland if you are patient enough for your explorers to find the stuff, which add to the "microtransaction available but you don't absolutely have to without being screwed" feeling. Meaning that yeah, if you go and buy a bunch of stuff you'll get going very fast and be "successful" very fast... But then again it is completely possible to play the game without it. And to be frank... The whole idea of the game is to be the overseer in charge of a vault. Waiting is part of the experience. If you're not willing to wait a tad then you probably already know this game is not for you and I'm left wondering why you are even reading this.
Good luck in the wasteland, overseer!

Now let me start with this - I am a massive Mafia franchise fan.
The first settlement has made me fall in love with computer gaming, it was a great design, missions were challenging enough and overall gameplay had me coming back for years to come. With the sequel coming up six years ago I was excited more than ever before because I was expecting a revival of that atmosphere I've once experienced. I was not dissapointed. The music, the humour, the shooting scenes + story telling was in my opinion spot on. You started from the bottom and worked your way up the mafia ladder. The game was so good in fact that I bought it 3 times, once on my PS3 then once as a disk for PC then following with a steam purchase, I must've played the story over and over again because it really made you feel like you were in those ages, you felt like vito.
Now let's get down to part three.
I've been following the release of this game for a long time, looking out for any footage available online to see what we are up against. Upon hearing the news that this settlement was going to take part in the later era I was very positively surprised but still had all of my hopes that the game would stay true to the roots and focus on hell of a good story and not the biggest map, amount of missions, collectibles to find etc etc...
I ended up with Assassins Creed: The Mafia.
The true Open World system is a plus because everybody loves a bit of freedom, however there is absolutely nothing to do, nothing to purchase, nothing to play around with. The story however good it may reveal to be further on, after just under 10h of gameplay I found myself thinking "god, this is boring". So far every single "mission" has been exactly the same - it consisted of:
- Wire Tap nearest junction box
- Scout the area
- Get rid of key enemies
- Stealth approach to take out as many enemies as possible
- Have a quick gun fight.
- Rinse
- Repeat
It is so repetetive that I already lost interest in the story, there's no push, there's nobody there with you (Like you had Joe alongside in Mafia 2 asking you every two seconds whether you've aquired such skills in the army) and I must say that having paid full price for the game I wish it was a bit more polished than that.
All in all it is still a half decent game, and when they've improved some of the aspects of the game (stealth kills, melee fight, world interaction) I'm still waiting to find out how fast I need to drive past a cop in order for them to start chasing me (that speedo must be there for SOME reason)
With the biggest regret (and a massive feel of disappointment from 2K Games) I would not reccomend it to anyone... Just get the much cheaper Mafia 2

Отличная РПГ, одна из немногих игр, которые я прошел несколько раз.
Видно, что заработав денег на первой части, авторы постарались вырасти и вширь, и вглубь во второй.
Плюсы очевидны:
1) Собственный движок, на момент написания обзора (май 2015) уже, конечно, не так поражает воображение (и не нагревает видеокарту =), но все еще радует бесподобными пейзажами.
2) Отличная локализация. Особенно стоит отметить титана отечественной озвучки Всеволода Кузнецова в роли Геральта - такое под силу, наверно, только ему. Лично для меня голос Геральта за пределами таланта Всеволода, скорее всего, не существует. Если отвлечься на игру прочих актеров, то ее уровень тоже очень вырос: в первой части они откровенно переигрывали и периодически говорили невпопад, не стыковались друг с другом интонациями, здесь такого нет. Впрочем, даже первой части Ведьмака далеко до Dragon Age Origins, в русскую озвучку которой попали неудачные дубли.
3) Вариативность и реиграбельность. Игру стоит пройти как минимум 2 раза: в зависимости от решения принятого в первой главе можно увидеть две совершенно разные вторые главы с разным сюжетом, действующими лицами, заданиями и концовками. Ветки развития тоже заметно отличаются, чего стоит только алхимическое направление, без которого некоторые эликсиры просто опасно употреблять. Ну и на сладкое - Темный уровень сложности, на котором есть чертежи уникальных доспехов.
4) Более быстрая и живая по сравнению с первой частью боевка. Да, это не Dark Souls, который каждые 5 минут показывает экран "You are dead", но и мы не за тем пришли. Тем кто хочет испытания просим пройти в хардкорный режим.
Минусы:
1) Инвентарь. Неудобный инвентарь в виде списка, видно, что игру параллельно разрабатывали и на консоли. Ну спасибо, что хоть максимальное разрешение не 720p.
2) Деревянная анимация. Как по мне, анимация передвижения Геральта какая-то... негибкая. На мой крестьянский взгляд корпус как-то неестественно неподвижен. Хотя моя девушка на это не обращает внимания и не замечает ничего.
Как видно, минусы скорее проходят как придирки, а вот плюсы, на мой взгляд, гораздо более фундаментальны. Игра однозначно стоит своих денег, особенно с учетом распродаж. И да, сейчас такого не делают. Вся надежда - на триквел.

Charming, funny, adorable, and insightful. Now that I played the full game, I felt the puzzles got harder at a reasonable pace. I was never frustrated, even while stuck, and when I solved a puzzle, it never felt like the solution was a cheat. Instead, the game itself gave me enough clues without being too obvious. It was really awesome to need paper and a pencil again to solve an especially difficult puzzle! I missed that from classic adventure games.
Visually, the game is beautiful. The soundtrack is a delight and fits the atmosphere. The characters are all funny and charming. I enjoyed the twists on the typical narratives for both Vella and Shay; they are truly the heart of the game, and I actually wanted to keep playing as them for a little while longer. That's actually my only complaint: that I can't spend more time in this world. The ending does feel a little abrupt, but the journey is worth it.
I also loved the themes explored by the story: teens and their relationships with their parents, one that isn't just of rebellion and lack of empathy, but genuine affection and growth on both sides. Adults and teens are both treated fairly and have reasonable reasons to act the way they do. This is something I don't usually see with teens as main characters. It raises interesting questions about tradition vs. change, security vs. conformity but never sounds preachy or black and white. It's kid friendly without being condescending.
Obviously, this is not Monkey Island, Psychonauts or Full Throttle (absolute favorites of mine). It lacks their biting/more meta humor, but by itself the game more than satisfied me. Definitely worth the money and the wait. I recommend for everyone who enjoys fairy tales with a twist, humor, and family themes.

I can't believe I'm writing a negative review for a game I've been wanting to play for a year, but that's what it gets. This game has almost the entire package. It's visually and musically pleasing. The core gameplay is very well done. The enemies and characters are very diverse, but still obey the game's structure as a twin stick shooter. If you play it you'll have fun for a couple of hours, guaranteed. But after that is where the fun ends, and you'll realize there is no way to naturally progress for either the player, the game, or the characters.
Firstly, the player. You'll grasp the game fairly easily, but when it comes to getting better at the game and moving forward, you'll get stuck. The way for you to "git gud" is by studying every aspect of the combat for each encounter. But this is a twin stick shooter, bullet hell-ish randomly generated game! This means you have to replay for hundreds of times, just to 'get everything right', and hope the RNG smiles on you. Or, you can look for help online, which misses the point entirely.
Repeating is not so horrible when done right, but in this case it's straight up grinding. This is because there is no overlapping progression system for the game. For at least 50 hours, it's fish\crystal with the revolver. All you can unlock is other characters, but since the only way to push forward is to grind, you can't switch characters, because you'll need to adjust to it's moveset and gameplay, which will take a lot of time. You might even get some extras through secrets, but that's only if you've read the wiki, and even then they're not really game enhancing.
The way your character progresses during a run, is by killing enemies and collecting "rads" that act as experience points towards leveling up. When you level up, you can't apply the reward until after you've beaten the stage. Then you are given four "mutations" and must choose one to enhance your character. This is a nice feature, but it's more of a twist on shop-like mechanics than level-up mechanics. There is a variety of weapons in the game, and as you advance you can get better weapons. But instead of replacing the old ones, they just get added to the pool, so you still have a chance of getting the games basic weapons even at the most advanced stages but not vice versa.
There are many ways to fix this problem without resorting to "nrf plz" or changing the games' essence. It will probably never happen, because it seems the developers have stopped working on this game last year.  Hopefully that'll change one day, but until then I can't recommend this game, despite wanting to do so.

Black Mirror II and III basically constitute one game, and let me tell you that it's an amazing adventure well worth playing.
It has almost everything to please: great atmosphere due to the amazing art, music and sound effects, great characters, great voice acting (with one notable exception). There's a lot of humor due to the main character's cynical remarks, but without making the whole thing goofy: in fact, there's a realistic feeling to it all rarely present in adventure games, and it's a very dark story which is not for the faint of heart. The game avoids most of the adventure game annoying features of the past such as pixel hunting and absurd puzzles, there's even an option to skip sliding-tile type puzzles if you play on easy.
Black Mirror I is in my opinion a much inferior game, and playing it is not necessary to play II + III. If you do play it first though, you'll notice a lot of playful and very well done references to it, and you'll have more background for everything that happens. The problem is that not everything is consistent with the first game, the studio that picked up the franchise after the first game did slightly modify the plot and lore, for the best I think, but if you play the trilogy you'll probably come out a bit confused about how things really work in this world. No such problem if you only play II + III.
There are some weaknesses: you'll probably see some plot twists coming far in advance, and the ending is ok but not as climactic as I would have wished. The games also shows you some interactive spots way in advance of when they're needed, but you can't interact with them or pick up the relevant item until the game decides you have a good reason to do so. I found that occasionally annoying and immersion breaking.
All in all though, play those games. You're in for many hours (my play time isn't accurate since you can play the game without Steam, I spent at least 15 hours on it) of very enjoyable, classic adventure gameplay, and the game's atmosphere will haunt you for a long time.

The original Black Mirror was an interesting bit of classic adventuring, a slow burn through the mysteries of an ancient British castle and its noble line. Personally I loved it but it's a tough sell in the modern era, with some questionable puzzles and practically glacial pace. Black Mirror II needs no such qualifications though, as it builds on the pedigree by improving virtually every part of the formula.
You play Darren Michaels, a young physics major out of Boston who's spending time with his mother in remote Biddeford, Maine. The appearance of a striking young woman in town sets off a chain of grim events that entangles Michael in the mysteries of Black Mirror, a storied castle in the English countryside. There's a lot of ground to cover between Maine and England but it's filled with tantalizing secrets, vicious machinations, and plenty of puzzles to solve.
The gameplay is standard point-and-click gameplay from the classic era, updated for more modern sensibilities. Double-clicking on a point of interest jumps you right to the action, bypassing the slow character plods and sometimes laborious animations. There's a highlight button to see all the interactables in a scene, and a very useful journal that includes optional clues for trickier puzzles. Most importantly, the bizarre left click/right click mechanics of Black Mirror I have been dropped for simple left-click interactions which progress through stages of discovery with every click. Keep this in mind, too... There's one object in the game you have to click five times; the first two clicks get you an item, and the next three reveal a key puzzle.
Your adventure is rendered in sharp detail, with 3D characters superimposed on 2D rendered backgrounds. I generally don't like this style but Black Mirror II has one of the better renditions of it, since the backgrounds almost match the detail of the characters and ONLY the characters are 3D, so no out-of-place polygonal items laying around. Everything is voice acted as well, and outside of some questionable European accents and a few weird word choices it adds greatly to the feel of the game (and can be freely clicked through for the impatient).
That feel of the game is really what helps set Black Mirror apart from other adventures. What I liked about Black Mirror I was the sense of forlorn decay as you plumbed the depths of Gothic ruins. That feeling is still around in II, but is mixed with a lot more detective work and scheming. You were fighting an expression of evil in the first game, whereas here you're contending with conspirators and villains, and the more active antagonism really helps keep the game fresh and engaging. Biddeford, Maine might not seem like an interesting setting at first, but mix in a murder and blackmail and it really starts to grab you.
There's not much negative I can say about the game, outside of Darren. He's an acquired taste to be sure, a hot-headded Boston youth who doesn't shy from getting in people's faces. I found him annoying early on but by the late game he mellows a bit as the stakes become clear. In fact, the overall game really improves as it rolls on, making more and more connections with the first game. That's something I really want to praise, too, how Black Mirror II builds off the first game without making it necessary. You can easily play this installment without having touched the first because Darren learns of the backstory as you do, and prior events are only used as solid world-building for the story told here.
Black Mirror II really took the best parts of Black Mirror I and made a fantastic new experience out of them. The gameplay is more streamlined, the puzzles are more challenging but also clearer, the story builds on the original while standing tall on its own, and the graphics and polish are a huge step up. It's still on the slow burn side of the adventure spectrum but is even more worthwhile than its predecessor. I would absolutely put this one near the top of any adventure or horror list for how well it handles both genres.

While I really enjoy Wasteland 2, my recommendation would have to come with a huge dose of "your mileage may vary". It's a long, slow, burn, and if you like to jump straight into things, or find yourself easily losing concentration or focus, you may find yourself giving up on Wasteland 2 before it really begins to shine. But some patience will pay off, if the genre interests you. Of course, if you don't like turn-based strategy games, then you should be giving this a pass. The writing is really top-notch in this game, and I found it both enjoyable and rewarding to play through.
Focused on a team of 4 rangers (which you can create yourself, or use several pre-built characters), and using very detailed attributes and skills - the CLASSIC system (Coordination, Luck, Awareness, Strength, Speed, Intelligence, Charisma), it took me a while before I realised that some attributes and stats were extremely important, while others... could be passed over, especially depending on the followers (NPCs) you decided to acquire. Unfortunately, it can take some trial and error before you realise what you should be doing with your characters and what is important for them to have. Or... you could just forge ahead anyway! I quite liked that there were no classes, giving you the freedom to do whatever you wanted with your characters. You could have a guy carrying heavy weapons, while being a melee tank and also healing... for example. Though this can also be a negative, if you wanted to see class specialisation, perks, and so on.
And so, I was introduced to the fun (???) of character creation. And uhh... naming my characters, which proved to be a disaster... after an embarrassingly long time, I settled on "One", "Two", "Three", and "Four". Original, right. The vast array of skills can be intimidating at first, and leveling them up (especially at later levels) can become quite frustrating and very grindy, but it does add a lot of depth to the game. One thing I did not like as much though... how much time it took, and the animation, whenever you wanted to use a skill. Using a skill meant that your Ranger (or follower) would have to move to the location (clumping up your Rangers if you moved them all as a group makes this an exhausting chore), before an animation begins. With the vast amount of skill checks in this game, the checks do add up and can become very time consuming and therefore annoying.
Additionally, there is quite a lot of travel involved in this game, both in the larger world map, and also within smaller exploreable areas. Even if you're not in a rush, the travel can quickly become aggravating. I wished for quicker travel myself, despite the fact I don't mind slower paced games.
While you are limited to Arizona and California, one after the other, the world map is still pretty expansive, with secret areas to discover dotted around the place. Travelling isn't worry free though - not only are there standard enemy encounters (which can become annoying quite quickly), but also some more welcome encounters, which is a bit different and somewhat refreshing in comparison to the usual fare where encounters in the wild just end up being endless fights. There are also two unique mechanics: water and radiation. Your team carries canteens, which can, and should be refilled at any well and oasis you find. Once you run out of water, your team starts to dehydrate and can die. Similarly, in the post-apocalyptic wasteland, nukes have left lingering radiation in various areas - so you also have to watch out for contamination... or again, you'll find your team dropping like flies.
The musical score, sound effects, and even the voice acting is all done quite well, and combines well with the graphics to provide a smooth and enjoyable spectacle. The graphics are not the best in the world, but they do set the tone of the game well, and are very appropriate to the game's setting - harsh, gritty, and unforgiving.
Combat is generally quite straight forward, with the standard turn-based combat fare reappearing here, though more in-depth compared to some other games due to the more extensive attribute and skill system. Your attributes and skills will determine in what order your characters go, and how much they can do in their turn. There are also crouch and cover mechanics, though some weapons can destroy cover. However... there is not much else. There are no real special combat moves, or combat specific skills - they increase your damage and hit percentage, and that's it. No executes, no cloak, etc. While there is headshot and ambush... they are honestly not that great. It's just point, click, hope to hit (the RNG seems to be a bit odd, with a lot of misses even on shots with a high hit percentage), rinse and repeat. There is no cover, no flush, no interesting and genuinely unique abilities.
Additionally, RNG can always turn around and give you a hard time. Or... adversely affect the enemies. Critical hits, critical misses, weapon effects, and weapon jams can all have a surprisingly large affect on the outcome of an encounter. I also like the emphasis on scarcity and the need for careful management of your resources, which is quite fitting for a game like this, especially the ammo. If you just blaze away, you'll be out of ammo before you know it, so you do need to think before you act. Vendors are limited too... The combat is decent, and I enjoyed it, but I will admit there could have been more to it.
While your team revolves around 4 characters, you are able to recruit a number of NPCs to join your team (3 followers for a maximum team size of 7). While you are nominally in control of them, leadership is important here as there is the chance your "follower" (only if they are in a good mood) will just decide to do their own thing in combat - running into cover, shooting something you didn't want shot, etc. Overall, the combat is fun and challenging, with a variety of enemies to conquer - both man and animal.
Despite there only being two areas to explore, Wasteland 2 boasts a wide variety of quests, many of which have a variety of ways to finish - but be careful, your choices do have serious and lasting consequences. Which is something else I really enjoy about the game - your choices DO matter. And have a ripple effect. This is not just limited to quests, there are some actions while just generally playing and moving around which could have an affect, especially based on which followers are with you. Do you dig up some graves? Do you disarm the alarm? Do you deliberately trip it off? Do you use strength or a grenade to break a wall? Do you help this faction, or the other faction? Mediate a ceasefire or shoot everybody up? The variety of ways to overcome things in your way is definitely a highlight of the game. I really enjoyed the varying options available, and weighing them up, based on what you want your team to do. Your decisions may cause followers to leave your party, or even turn on you. Not only does this create an interesting in-game dynamic where what you do will affect how other in-game characters interact with your party, but this also allows for extensive replayability, if you so choose. "What if" questions are plentiful in this game.
Finally, I particularly loved the odd references and humour. The Wasteland 1 disc was a particular highlight. While not particularly game-making, or breaking, it was something that I enjoyed. The grand adventure that plays out, in addition to the continued support and patching by inXile, make me give this game two thumbs up.

I feel this is the best in the 8 bit series.
The invader faction's units are more varied than previous games.
This is because most units have some unique qulities to bring to the table as well as having designated roles. Examples include Harpy infantry being able jump over clifs to reach areas. Cranioids tripod being able to see above all elevations giving you a range advantage when fighting on higher or lower ground. The Shriker unit being a designated anti-air superiority fighter and many more examples.
The resource gathering mechanics is also much simplifed. You build a harvester and it locks into a resource point and just collects. That means no drop off points or building creeping needed. It kind of gives that control point feeling like in dawn of war where you just secure a specific area rather than worring about destination A to B.
The Campaign objectives are better too. The sliver and gold objectives in previous games were commonly do X in X time. Whilst that still present here, it is not so common which means get objectives that let you take your time in doing which i feel is great to vary things up.

The choices you make in game make you wonder if you've made all the right ones as they affect what happens to you later on in the series. The roller coaster of events that unravel hold you in suspense and keeps you interested. A little slow at times but overall a great game.

Here's the bare bones report for what you need to know about this game right now.
Is the game fun? Yes, for a little while until the issues with early-access show up. (Bugs, unbalanced features, etc)
Is it worth the money? Yes. This game has AN EXTREME AMOUNT OF PROMISE, and all you need is faith, and patience.
Is the price point FAIR? Yes. You're supporting a game developer I have had a lot of experience with in the past, they won't steal your money.
Should I buy the game? Yes. You'll kick it around for a few hours and then come back to it every update and enjoy it, reminds me of old school minecraft alpha days. You'd play for awhile and then stop until the new update comes. Eventually there's enough content to create an extremely enjoyable game. Have faith.
With all of this being said, here's what you REALLY need to know, in greater length. Star Command Galaxies is a game that like many early-access titles, is riddled with bugs, unimplemented features, major balance issues, and deprivation of content, but what makes this game different is something we REALLY need to consider. What makes this game different is how the developers are operating.
A long time ago in the golden age of gaming, companies had no need to constantly stay in contact with the public, they kept their heads down, and took as much time as they needed (within reason) to create a product that the consumer would feel extremely happy with. Believe it or not, this is still in practice today, and large development studios/companies just announce a game, maybe throw you a few features to pique your interest, and then buckle in to get some work done. For some reason, when the concept of early access was created, that then created some kind of unspoken rule that "if I buy the game early the developers better listen to what I have to say and if they don't they're idiots". This is commonplace nowadays and we see lots of games and studios that have lots of promise get beaten down by terrible reviews based solely on how a developer stays in contact, which makes no sense. You purchase an early access copy because you believe in the developer and the vision for their game.
That being said, the REASON you SHOULD PURCHASE THIS GAME, is because this is a developer that while they might not stay in constant contact with you, you can rest easy knowing a competent group of people have their heads buried deep in their work, taking their time with a game that truly and honestly has the potential to be one of the all-time indie game greats, and I mean that with as much emotion as I can show. If you don't believe me, there is an iOS version of this game "Star Command" (it's not the same game, but a simplified mobile game version). That game is an Editor's Choice app on the iTunes store, which just goes to show their prowess for developing games. This is an extremely competent company, with good developers, and a AAA style of developing. Purchase this game and have the knowledge and confidence that these folks will take your money and use it to create something that will in the end make you extremely happy and proud of your purchase.
Warm regards and happy gaming,

If you like first person shooters and real time strategy games, Natural Selection 2 is the best attempt at bridging the gap between the two genres. Asymmetric sides, which aren't balanced to perfection but the striking differences creates depth and allows you tatics that just haven't been seen before in games. So the question is do you want a casual experience? If you answered yes, then you should probably go somewhere else.

To the point: I would not reccomend this game, at least not in its current iteration. A patch was released a few days ago that fixes numerous bugs, which is always good, but worries of how many are still rampant. Beyond that, 'balance' is a foreign word in this game, with Assault Rifles reigning supreme, Handguns, Bladed and Blunt weapons being a complete joke, and doing more sustained damage by PUNCHING GIANT METAL ROBOTS than using live ammo. If you haven't done research prior to actually playing this game, you won't get very far, with many attributes and skills being virtually useless; this leads to either frustrating gameplay with your characters not possessing the correct skills, or starting from scratch (again and again) until you get it right. Hardcore players aside, most of us just want to jump in without having to worry about using a day calendar to make sure we can electronically unlock and unwire the explosives from a trash bag with...4 shotgun shells. Also, forget upgrading to cool armor like in Fallout and becoming a walking tank: more armor = bad in the Wasteland universe once enemies start using energy weapons.
With that rant out of the way, let's focus on the good: Excellent atmosphere, funny characters, and a system, that if you ENJOY in-depth theoretical number-crunching, will last you hours, days, maybe even weeks and months. For most of us, however, that time investment just isn't worth it.
Final Verdict: This game is...decent, for a Kickstarter title, but certainly not worth the $40USD pricetag. Find it on sale or get it from somewhere other than Steam to consider a refund if you find it lacking.

Let me just start out by saying that I bought this when it first appeared on Steam a year ago. I played through the first act then replayed it when the second act was released.
The visual style of the game is quite outstanding. It gives you a sense that you are on the inside of a comic book. On top of this you have the quite smooth and flowing animations with both foreground and background objects. You will also note slight references within the game towards films or certain things.
The game uses several voice actors for the characters within the game. You have Elijah Wood Voicing the main character (Shay), Jack black For Harm'ny Lightbeard, Will Wheaton for the Lumberjack and Jennifer Hale as Mom. As some of these are quite big names the budget for the game was quite high. The ambient sounds and effects throughout are quite calming and nice to accompany the animations.
This is a point and click game in which brings in some standard elements from that type of game. You have an inventory area in which at some points you use to combine objects. For the use of finding something that you can interact with is an easy thing to do, as if you hover the mouse over the area it will change allowing you to click and interact. As with any point and click game it also adds the element of clicking and dragging.
Puzzles are always a huge aspect of point and click games. I have always felt that nowadays puzzle games tend to lack any sense of difficulty to them and instead just hand you stuff on a platter for you to scoop up. I feel this game doesn't do that and serves up some top rather intriguing puzzles. Some of the puzzles may seem difficult and impossible to pass however the game gives you hints and clues through dialogue or things within the scene. These help the player push towards getting the right set of things in order to complete the solution.
For me this was a worthwhile investment as I felt that the game offered me more entertainment time wise for the amount that I paid. As very rarely do I see a good point and click game that isn't from Daedalic.

You're going to need:
Kosher salt
12 Ounces whote-wheat penne
1 28-ounce can whole plum tomatoes
1 Tablespoon unsalted butter
2 shallots, minced
1 clove garlic, minced
1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
1/2 cup vodka
2/3 cup heavy cream
1/2 cup freshly grated parmesan cheese, plus more for topping
Handful of fresh basil leaves, torn, plus more for topping
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the penne and cook as the label directs. Reserve 1/2 cup cooking water, then drain the pasta. Empty the tomatoes into a bowl and crush with your hands.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the shallots and cook, stirring occasionally, until slightly softened, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, 30 seconds. Remove from the heat and stir in the vodka, tomatoes and salt to taste. Return the skillet to medium heat and simmer, stirring often, until the alcohol cooks off, about 7 minutes. Stir in the heavy cream and cook until the sauce thickens slightly, about 3 minutes. Stir in the parmesan and basil.
Add the pasta to the sauce and toss to combine, adding some of the reserved cooking water to loosen, if needed. Season with salt. Serve topped with more parmesan and basil.

This game is a trainwreck. I wanted to like this, I thought it was supposed to be a good, artsy game. Instead, its a cynical cash in. The writing is atrocious, and the game didn't even get a copy-edit. The voice acting sounds phoned-in half the time. Game is set in the fictional world of South Amerca, in fictional 1972. Why would you set a story in a real continent and year but not use real events or country names?
Sunset tries to be Gone Home, but the exploration is so underwhelming and it pretty much plays itelf. There's no real game here, as 'cleaning the floor', for example, means clicking the broom once and watch time tick past. Story items are only explained a little bit, one sentence or two for each, and the character you play as doesn't even need to see items to comment on them the next day. You get achievements for looking at the books scattered around the house each day, but why should I care if this guy reads Brave New World? You look at Life is Strange, and they tell you why the pop culture it references is worth looking into. Sunset's just like 'here's a book one of the devs likes'.
I don't know if the people who made this have ever done anything physically before in their lives, but, I'm sorry, a young woman isn't going to assemble a 500 pound mobile scuplture suspended 20 feet in the air with no tools and no ladder. What were they thinking? The only thing that I got any sort of kick out of was the space station chairs from 2001 A Space Odessy, and man is that a random thing to add.
The game bombards you with trite poetry, rife with spelling errors and ridiculous statements like 'fire, a symbol of comfort.. and destruction'. Really? The color pallet in the house is more abstract and less on-the-nose than the writing. And then, in the story, they just randomly introduce elements into the mythos. I decoded a document because I was snooping around, and so for whatever reason I now have a brother who's a resistance leader. Why didn't we mention anything about this before it was of major relevance to the 'plot'? There's absolutely no incentive to explore the game's story, anyway. And the character doesn't even know herself. She's black, so obviously she would refer to her own school as 'the black school', right? Riiight.
Oh, and the game performs horribly on my machine. They even have a setting where you can reduce the graphics to look like Journeyman Project (1992). I kid you not, the lowest graphics setting looks like the Sega CD and it still runs like garbage. And why do the carpets at the begining look like snow, even in the advertised screenshots, but in the sunset 'levels' the rugs are gone?
Stay away from this boring, unthoughtful title. The developers obviously wanted to have as little to do with it as possible, too. I'd just like to thank them for dispanding before they had a chance to make a sequel.

The puzzles of the first act is pretty easy, perhaps too easy. In the second act some of the puzzles were of the try-and-experiment sort that was fun to solve, but most of them were rather obscure with rather hilarious solutions, similar to Monkey Island. I really liked the part where I got stuck on a puzzle for a while and the main character started drawing up a table as a hint.
The story wasn't in-depth or thought provoking, and in fact had some plot holes, or twists that were quickly brushed aside. The big bad felt rather signle dimensional, and you couldn't even visit the big-bad-evil's lair, only watch cutscenes from it, making chunks of the game feel like a missed opportunity. Some of the object interactions were pretty verbose but that's more of a relic from old-school games. Now, that said, the writing was filled with junevile fun with heaps of jokes that didn't feel particularly wooden. Voice acting was phonomenal too.
The visuals were pretty and hadn't noticed/encountered any graphical glitches since the second act update. Animations ran slick as butter and had graphics had a well drawn painterly style. Music was subtle and well made, which helped set the tone of the scenes and set up an enjoyable environment but were hardly memorable.
So, now, you're wondering why despite the critisms I'm giving it a positive review? That's because I went into the game expecting a light-hearted and cheerful game, and got what I wanted. To me the great bits of the game outweighed the bad bits.
Is it perfect? No. Is it good. Yes.
There aren't many games like this and the only one I can think of is the Deponia series, but that game relies on being mean and offensive all the time, which just leaves a bad taste the further you go. Broken Age is *the* game you should pick up if you are looking for a light-hearted, point and click adventure game.

In Sunset you play Angela Burns, an American living in a fictional Latin American country under an oppressive regime. Angela is the housekeeper for Gabriel, a powerful man in the government. Though the backdrop of civil unrest and revolution is potentially interesting, the game itself often isn't.
Each day you take an elevator up to the posh penthouse. While Angela narrates some thoughts you are presented with the list of tasks to do, though you can do more (or less) if you'd like. The main mechanic of the game, is that you can perform tasks warmly or coldly. How you perform these actions affects your relationship with your absent employer. I didn't even notice there were options on how to perform tasks until a few days in. Then all of a sudden, after choosing to paint a wall red instead of blue, leaving some lights on, and moving some slippers, Angela and Gabriel were on the cusp of a romantic relationship.
The idea of romancing your boss, especially given the nature of the working relationship, wasn't one I was entirely comfortable with. The fact that Gabriel wasn't even present in the game, and Angela never met him, made it even more strange. However, once I was started, I continued down the romantic path to see where it went. After a while, Angela and Gabriel start communicating via notes left around the apartment, though the content of these notes don't seem to affect Angela's narration of the world events.
Sunset started out on rocky terrain by making the gameplay about housekeeping. That's not really something I want to do in my own apartment, never mind choosing to pretend to do it in a video game. The story isn't strong enough to make up for this. It takes a long time for anything interesting to happen. Days and days went by before the gameplay started integrating into the story of civil war. About an hour in, I was quite bored. Eventually, some interesting tidbits of information start appearing, but they were spread so thinly throughout the game.
The game isn't completely without charms. The voice acting is good, the music is great, and I enjoyed the increasing focus on art in the latter parts of the game. But it's just not enough. There are good things in this game, they are few and far between. Had the game been 2 hours instead of 4, I think some of the issues could have been solved, but as it is, Sunset just wasn't an engaging experience.

After 50+ hours of playing, I'm happy to recommend this game as a decent sequel to Shadow of Mordor but with some reservations.  The combat is great; the nemesis system is awesome, although can be a bit odd when an Orc you've killed comes back for the third or fourth time (although, to be fair, they will normally be missing limbs or have some impressive scars).  The story is ok BUT, like many others I recommend you stop playing after the third act and avoid the infurating grind of act four.
Once you are defending your forts there are so many attackers, combat is no longer fun/enjoyable as you'll spend your time being constantly interupted and targetted skills are almost pointless.  If things start to go sideways, expect to see a constant stream of intro and death cut scenes (that, up until now I'd enjoyed) which will cancel anything you were currently doing and force you to face in the direction of the "event".
I've completed two of the sieges but I'm struggling to find the motivation to do the rest having cleared almost all other quests.
As for the loot boxes... I don't really see them as an issue.  The game doesn't exactly push them on you and I haven't felt the need to buy any.  You can level up your Orcs by sending them to the fight pits but, like the rest of act four, this becomes a bit of a grind after a few.  They might help you complete act four but they won't make it fun.
TL;DR: Play acts one to three and watch the end game cutscene on your streaming video site of choice.
