Black Mirror II is probably not a very good adventure game, but I'm going to recommend it anyway as it does a lot of things well.  I'm going to break this down into categories of puzzles, voice acting, atmosphere/setting/graphics, and narrative as that's all that really makes up an adventure game.  Obviously, I'm going to be spoiling this game, so don't read if you want to play Black Mirror II.
Voice Acting:
My god the voice acting is atrocious.  It got to the point where I just turned on subtitles and wanted to turn off the voices.   Dialogue is pretty crucial in adventure games, having bad voice acting is just unacceptable.  This is definitely the worst voice acting i've ever encountered in any adventure game I've played.  Gemini Rue basically sounds like they did the voice acting in some guys apartment, even that was far superior to this.  I've heard the German voice acting on youtube videos and it's quite good, so as far as I can tell it's whoever they hired out for the English translation that just completely blew it.  I looked everywhere online to see if I could use German voice acting with English subtitles and as far as I can tell there is no way to do this.  When I played the Witcher 2 they had a fantastic option allowing me to use the original Polish voice actors with English subs, its clearly something that can be done and really should have for this game.
Even more unfortunate the main character (Darren) has a particularly terrible English voice actor.  It's just incomprehenisbly bad.  I can't fathom why they even paid this voice actor for this work.  He attempts to use a Southie Boston accent for the game.  It's offensively bad.  European studios should never attempt to hire voice actors that aren't from America and then ask them to do such specific American accents.  It hurt my ears everytime he talked.  I would just quickly read the subtitles and skip most of his acting.  I strongly considered not recommending the game based on this alone.  The rest of the voice actors are also terrible, but at least far better then the main character.
Puzzles:
These are some of the hardest puzzles I've ever encountered in any adventure games.  They are "The Dig" levels of difficulty.  Most of the time they are just completely obtuse.  I am ashamed to admit it, but I don't think I even solved half the puzzles in this game.  They have an auto solve button and I had to use this for almost every single puzzle (I didn't even realize this was an autosolve button until halfway through the game and had been constantly hitting it thinking you had to just to let the game know to check your solution).  This game also has an absurd amount of puzzles, more then I've seen in any adventure game and this game is a good 20 hours long too.  Narrative wise it got a bit ridiculous the amount of puzzles the game was asking you to solve.  So quite frankly I would say this game has many terrible puzzles.
For example in "Black Mirror Castle" at one point I had literally searched everywhere in the entire Castle for a password I needed for a lock.  Literally, everywhere.  The game has a hint system so I used it and it told me to check the mailbox.  That seem absurd as I had checked it and it was empty.  I checked again and a letter was inside with the password.  This letter only appears once you start solving the puzzle.  It's not as if the game showed you the passage of time, or as if this was a new chapter in the game that might indicate the passage of time.  No commend was made of the mail arriving.  You were just supposed to randomly check the mailbox again which had been empty moments ago.  Instances like this constantly came up in the game, where examining objects would reveal one thing and then seconds later the description would change.  It makes it so every single time you find any item in the game you then have to reclick every single icon on the screen to make sure the descriptions haven't changed as the character may well give you completely new information about an icon.  It's just extremely bad design.
Atmosphere/Setting/Graphics:
I enjoyed the art direction immensely for this game.  Sometimes I felt the 3D look was quite bad, characters move awkwardly a lot.  "Gray Matter" does it far better, however it's not abysmal.  The backgrounds are all very nicely rendered.  The game takes place in a seaside town in northern Maine, a decrepit English town, a castle in Wales, and a Castle in England.  During these journeys the game constantly has a dark foreboding look.  Everyone of these locations has dark skies and pouring rain.  I think the sun literally only comes out once in the game while you are in Maine.  It sets the mood perefectly.  The soundtrack is similarly fitting, but it needs to be far more expanded.  I think their was basically one song the whole game, even "Gray Matter" had about 3 songs!  The game predictably has a lot of grey's/browns/dark green, everything appears very creepy.  The flashes of constant lightning while in the decaying "Black Mirror" Castle was particularly nice.  If you are going to have a murder mystery can't go wrong with having a constant lightning storm through the game.
Narrative:
It's an adventure game, so narrative is pretty much the game.  This is why I'm recommending the game, despite it's absurd problems with voice acting and sometimes atrocious puzzle design.  The narrative is very good, certainly wouldn't put it above "Gray Matter" or any of the "Laura Bow" games.  It's a very competent murder mystery.  The bodies stack up at a nice pace, it's a slow burn which is how murder mystery's should be.  I will say I was disappointed that  solved the murdery mystery after act 1 (the game has 6 acts).  It was just painfully obvious who the murderer was.
The main problem imo is not that it's an easily solveable murder mystery though, but that the main character is atrocious (this is voice acting aside).  I guess people in Germany think Americans are obnoxious idiots, because my god the main character of Darren is probably the worst character in all of videogames.  He makes Geron from "Dark Chains" look like the most normal person in the world.  Darren is stupid, abrassive, obnoxious, insane, rude, violent, basically just use any negative adjective and it would fit Darren.  This is who you play as.  I don't know why the developers would think you'd want to embody such an awful person.  It's incomprehensible that anyone even talks to this person.  He will just go up and outright insult people and threaten to murder them...like constantly.  He even acts this way to the police.  I was so taken aback by every single bit of dialogue that came out of this characters mouth that I almost turned it off.
In Act one the main love interest "Angelina" is arrested for murder and your job is to find evidence to show she is innocent.  Now you basically easily know who the real murderer is and could even lead the police to the evidence that proves shes innocent.  Instead of this, Darren says the police are all incompetent and simply want to arrest some foreigner and it's up to him to get the evidence himself.  Besides saying this internally he straight up says this to the chief of police despite the fact the chief of police is extremely reasonable and courteous to you and clearly wants to solve this murder.  This is how Darren acts to all characters he will straight up call the person an idiot and most times threaten to murder them.  Except of course "Angelina" who he is creepily sexually obsessed with...and this is a woman he's known for about an hour in the game.  All his internal dialogue is pretty much how much he wants to have sex with her immediately. It's quite disturbing.
In the end though it's a fun murder mystery which I would recommend on the cheap. However, although Black Mirror 1 is not really connected, Black Mirror III is a must play as this game literally has no ending. So  #Worth $2.50!

Firstly, this review is independent of any opinons I have of the developers and their opinions.
I feel like this game is somewhat under appreciated. It's a game that you have to value and appreciate for its mood, story, and the methods in which they tell this story. I'm not the type to be into games that are overly preachy, which this game's dialog can be a little more of, but I found the way in which you unveil the story to be a lot of fun. Every day you're given a set of chores that you can do in different manners: warmly or coldly. The choices you make affect how your employer, Ortega, feels about you as a housekeeper and a person.
SPOILERS PAST THIS POINT
The story of the revolution and political climate is expressed through the entire environment. Nothing about this game is explicitly spoonfed to you. You listen to the gunfire, watch the skyline fill with smoke, observe the newspaper headlines scattered around the apartment, and so much more. It's a complete experience that isn't for people who are waiting to have a story thrown in their faces.
I rather liked the writing in the game, as it felt personal and the way someone of that era and background would be talking. I never had any problems with doing the chores, except for one day in which it was actually impossible to do everything listed (this is intentional, as Ortega will note the following day). I was even able to do more than what was asked of me by actually being a housekeeper and maintaining the home, such as changing the date on the calendar and turning on the lights every day.
Overall I thought this game delivered everything I expected it to when I kickstarted it. Yes, it is not a game for everyone, but I loved it anyways. I played it twice over: once doing whatever the heck I wanted and second to actually try to romance Ortega through my chores and replies to his notes. I wouldn't hesitate to play it again and take the time to explore more of Angela's thoughts and narrative.

A beautiful game that will put you in the main character's skin more tangibly than most games i've played. Beautiful story, original mechanics (being a housekeeper/bystander during a revolution) and interesting message.
The game really shines in its atmosphere. You'll arrive each day before sunset to clean the apartment and the apartment would naturally evolve, like any apartment after a week. You'll grow to really love that apartment. Know its rooms, its nooks and crannies. You'll get to know your employer and his habits, his interests and concerns. The story will really begin when he'll leave you your first note thanking you for your hard work. You spent most of the game alone in that apartment eager to read his notes to find out what he wants to tell you or what he was thinking.
I admit, the social justice themes get old after a few hours into the game. Yeah, war is bad, we get it, but it gets really stale. Luckily, you can avoid all that by avoiding writing the diary. I think the criticism this game has been getting is unfair - the game is quite good.
The story is disjointed at times though... some things don't make any sense and will leave your head scratching. Clearly written by amateurs. Nonetheless, it's a better story than a close equivalent Gone Home for example.
Overall, it's definitely worth it if you're looking for a different game like Gone Home and are interested in some social justice/anti war monologues.

After playing the game for around 20 hours, I like Spintires but it could be more. After 3-5 hours of playing the game, I started to wish Spintires was a road construction game. Delivering logs could have been more of a plot point. Some logging company sets up shop, they need to set up a decent road network before logs can be moved. They hire you to build the roads. You go from area to area picking up materials and dropping them off where the road construction is. You drive various vehicles and construction equipment to mark the routes, flatten the ground, and remove rocks. Once the road is done, the logging company is able to move logs and you win. You can either deliever logs on your fancy road and enjoy your work, or move on to the next map.
I'm still going to recommend this game, but only to gamers who enjoy choose your own adventure games. What you do and how much fun you have is pretty much up to you. Its a fun game and definitely a techical achievement, but it could have been more. It feels like this is a tech demo with a sprinkle of game added to it. Hopefully the devs land a nice contract for a new game using this tech.

This isn't a good game, even when you come at it with an open mind. As a hidden object Gone Home-like, it fails on many parts due to its poor communication/UI and limited, shallow level. As a narrative experience, I'm finding myself constantly confused by the flip-flopping protagonist and the seemingly random thoughts that don't have much of a link to what's happening outside the window. Coupled with some very long and grating diary entries and a LOT of filler content to artificially increase its length, this isn't going to get recommended.
At its full retail price it's insanely overpriced, even on a 50% sale it was overpriced. The quality is just not good enough.
As a side note, when you look at the developer's dev diary and subsequent Twitter reactions to comments about it, I just can't support Tale of Tales no matter how much they've apparently 'given' to the indie scene with their pioneering art games. They disrespect an entire medium and audience because their game flopped. It flopped because it's a poor quality game and the marketing was abysmal (a significant amount of comments say they didn't know it was out).

is really one of the best adventure games I've played in a while. The music, ambientation and graphics are very great. The voice acting is pretty good too. There are many characters who are complete and well created, and the game really feels, in many ways, quite realistic.
Darren's sarcasm is quite amusing and refreshing, although occasionally it gets a little annoying!
The best part about the game is that it is very long (many hours of gameplay), and the story really catches your attention, making you want to progress more and more. There are many things you need to do, ranging from the mundane to the mysterious. Many of the puzzles are inventory based, but there are also other kinds of very interesting puzzles.
Despite being a "horror" game, it is really not horror. It has an eerie atmosphere, like in the first Black Mirror.
The only critique I have is that, like most of these games, the ending was a little unsatisfying. But then, it immediately left me wanting to play Black Mirror III, which was probably the point.
Verdict: I highly recommend this game! But go ahead and buy Black Mirror III as well, because when you finish 2, you'll want to play it!

TLDR: Don't buy it.
It has an interesting combat system and play style that is not unlike that of Assassin's Creed. Combat is very action-packed and requires a lot of focus if you want to get counters and dodges off on multiple enemies and keep your hit-streak rolling. Unfortunately combat is continuously interupted by uneccessary cut-scenes of your orcs dying or killing off other orcs, taking you straight out of your focus and getting you killed over and over again. This right here is a very very big minus for the game because it pretty much ruins play. It makes me wonder if the developers ever played the game themselves before they released it.
Fortunately you can't die. You just lose 2 hours or more that you've invested into building your army, because if you get wacked, everyone else on your side also does. And you do get wacked if you lose focus for just one second.
The Nemesis system is entertaining but requires you to die for it to get interesting and let's face it, you don't play this game to die all the time. This Nemesis mechanic would be the sort of thing that makes a good game amazing. Unfortunately, this is not a good game and the Nemesis system is just a fun gimmick because of it.
Don't get me wrong, there are a lot of good sides to the game: graphics are amazing, character development system is kinda nice, and the playstyle and controls combined with certain character upgrades are exceptionally fluid and can make you feel like a one man army, something I personally find very attractive in this genre of games. However, all this is ruined by the cut-scenes you get when some insignificant orc gets cut down, interrupting you in the middle of combat with 20 other orcs, either causing you to die right there or be forced to flee. The problem is that this doesn't just happen ocassionally but depending on how you roll, can happen about 15-20 times in one fight and is some seriously game-breaking stuff.
One last note, Shadow of Mordor also features a store where you can do micro transactions and contribute to ruining gaming. Shame on you. Stop this madness please.

I really want to give this game a good review, the nemesis system is a step up from the previous game and has provided some truly memorable encounters, combat is generally fun, and the environments are diverse, if a little bland.

However, a number of factors prevent me from being able to recommend the game. Firstly, the story is generally bland, with a lot of the missions feeling like a task to complete so you can get back to hunting orcs and capturing fortresses with the entire first act just feeling like a drawn-out tutorial. As for the actual content of the story, whilst I was never expecting a lore abiding experience the extent to which Shadow of War butchered it was at times hard to believe.
Story aside the game is riddled with bugs, I was unable to complete the final mission after slogging through it as a skill broke. If this bug had happened only once then I could accept it, but it had already happened on a number of occasions causing me to fail a number of missions.
Another issue is the difficulty, or more accurately the fact that the game was not designed with the harder nemesis difficulty in mind. The mechanics of a number of encounters and the ranged units in general turn playing on nemesis mode from an enjoyable challenge to an infuriating nightmare being killed for reasons beyond your control such as bad camera angles preventing you from seeing, generally overpowered ranged units and an infuriating targeting system (especially from stealth) making it a gamble as to if Talion will attack the orc you intended.
Overall, yes, the game is a lot of fun and if you enjoyed the nemesis system of the first you will enjoy it here but be prepared to have that enjoyment tempered by some poor mechanics, game breaking bugs and whilst it may not bother everyone a butchering of the lore beyond belief.

This game is dated, and while it does run on the more modern OS's out there, it isn't well optimized.  I found the game running at a steady 8 frames per second on my old Windows 8 machine.  However, most gamers here use PCs powered by 32 gigs of ram and NVIDIA's latest graphics card which requires the heat of the sun to forge properly, so it might run better on your Windows 7 or 8 computer.
The game itself was a staple in my childhood.  I had many hours of fun with it, even though I sucked at it as a kid.  Now, I can lay out a strategy, and retaliate easily when the enemy declares war.
The game itself has quite a bit going on.  You have to balance your gold economy, which can be a challenge as you progress in scientific research, military power, and additions to your city.  You have to make use of the terrain around you, which itself can be a gamble.  You might get everything you need under one generated map, and then get completely ♥♥♥♥ed by another generated map.  There is a lot to cover, most of which I'll leave you to see for yourself.
In the end, there's a lot of content, and for its current price, its a great game.  If you like strategy games, then you'll probably love this game.  9/10.

It may seem a bit anemic compared to the later installments but I find CivIII is still worth picking up to at least try if you're a Civ fan.
While not deep, this 4x experience is very refined, you really do have to play exactly to your Civ's strengths if you want any hope to succeed in the higher difficulties- there is no real catch all method. People may have complained about bombardment and bombers being Op since they can straight up kill units but I find this adds a lot more tactical complexity to war, especially in the mid Ind. age where it really reflects how much warfare at that time was based around defensive positions.
The campaigns within are straight up the best of any vanilla Civ game, Rise of Rome, the Middle Ages and the Age of Discovery are excellent, and hell the Pacific Theatre almost could've been its own game!
Finally, it may be a personal thing, but I've always preferred the isometic display here to the 3d graphics of 4, 5 and Beyond.
And as a small side note, because of how cheap this game is now it can be an effective litmus test to see if you'll even enjoy Civ games, so there's that.

Alright, after playing it for 40+ hours and near completion... I have a better understanding of the game.
The Good: Cutscenes, voice acting, story, gun battles,stealth, driving, collectables and size of map, violence, blood, it's all really good... I love it, 5/5
The Bad: choppy graphics (especially when calling in favors), controls, movement can be bad at times (needs a polish). All the good stuff doesn't get unlocked until the near-end unless you go 100% with 1 or 2 uberbosses, which is pointless... no customisable vehicles, clothing, weapons, no direct access to gang members (can't bring 3 fellas with you on a driveby...) missions are interesting, but revolve around the EXACT same thing.... destroy this, kill that, chase him. Story missions are unique however. Few bugs here and there, driving into twig has impact damage... as does driving into (supposed to be over) a bush does the same, Melee is not very good (for PC at least).
I would have liked to seen a Criminal Enterprise system like Scarface and The Godfather, where you have like 1000 different businesses to extort/purchase, gang areas/safehouses to retreat to whenever you're being chased by a horde of enemies (massive gun battles would be cool). Would have liked to have you're own "Family", with a nemesis system like Shadow of Mordor (except for the player to recruit from).
Would also like to seen more variety in vehicles, guns and actually being able to customise my character, his weapons, his car, his gang, etc... would have been nice...
Anyway... my final take is, it's a good game, that kept me busy for a week, couldn't stop playing it, but after that, it got boring as I realised the grind was long and boring, and didn't get me what I wanted. I enjoyed the story and some of the gameplay (gun fights :D). Loved the characters and the environment, the feel of the age, etc... was great. But if you're looking for a game with ENDLESS gameplay, quick fun or an in-depth Gangster game... this isn't for you.
It is a good, long story.... with a lot of pages to get through and it does get boring after a while.

Broken Age is so unbelievably unsatisfying that I can safely say that Tim Schafer will never bring back point and click adventure games to any previous level of grandeur. Vella's voice acting is atrocious, but the main problem is that after the first, semi-decent "setup" of a first act, the second act retreads old grounds, literally, constantly. Puzzles involve running back and forth in areas already explored, testing player patience with puzzles that require some setup and then backtracking multiple times to solve. Broken Age's final puzzle is the distillation of everything the could be considered backtracking. It's backtracking incarnate. It's apex backtracking. It's so extraordinarily dry that it is only trumped in unpleasantness by the extremely terrible story. Many assets are not really "high res", and often in closeup shots things are pixelated, but that's the least of the game's problems. You spend more time requiring robots than you do exploring this tiny, miniature slice of the "world" they've created, which honestly is not really delved in to much, which is probably a good thing considering anything they attempt to explain or justify makes no sense, but for some reason seems "logical" to the participants in the story. Many of the jokes are okay, but the majority of the show is stolen by sentient silverware and other bit characters with excellent voice actors; it's more delivery rather than what they are saying, which is derivative most of the time of Tim's other works, collaborative or otherwise. It's not bad, but it's not an amazing experience (Day of the Tentacle) or what I'd call his magnum opus.
I made a terrible, terrible mistake backing this game. I regret ever suggesting that donating to this was a good idea. It was a three and a half year blueballing. Double Fine's been coasting on the critical success of Psychonauts for a decade now, and honestly they really need to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and beg Ron Gilbert to join them if they ever think of making another point and click again. All of these old point and click games had teams of designers and writers that made them great, and Tim's not able to fill that position on his own, obviously.
I've paid more for less.
Feels like I've gone backwards with the game.

A captivating, incredibly detailed adventure game that builds upon the shreds of mythos presented in the first game and weaves a tale that will keep you hooked from beginning to end.
I must admit, I began this game with some reservations, having suffered through the tedium of the first game and it's bland presentation. But as soon as the game began, it dropped twists, turns and plot bombshells, and never relented until the very end, keeping me on the edge of my seat while presenting an expanded world with deep characters and a merciless deconstruction of the Black Mirror Mythos. All questions brought up by the first game are answered, and more questions are posed that kept me guessing until the very end.
The puzzle design in this game is top notch, with enjoyable puzzles that make sense, and the protagonist's exhaustive notes and little flairs of genius don't feel like they come out from the void, but rather from his own character. Each solution feels natural and like it is part of a believable progression of his character arc. I particularily enjoyed the non-item based puzzles, as they were often layered and presented with a code to break before the mechanical part of the puzzle even began. Richness of puzzles like this are incredibly rare, and should be valued. The puzzles, also, felt well rooted in the world, and even the most arbitrary sliding puzzle becomes a charming character trait for one of the many well-developed characters.
The game's aesthetic is a huge step up from the previous game, creating lively and deep locales to explore that straddle the line between photorealistic and oil painting. The lighting effects, in particular, are fantastic, lending an authentic spookiness to what could otherwise be a bland set. The effects are simple, often just a alpha channeled overlay or a translucent image, but the game does marvels with what it has.
My only criticism of the game's aesthetic would be the relatively stiff and mannequin like character models. Though an improvement from the last game, a lot of the models seem to look rather dull and lifeless, especially when viewed from close up. There isn't much in the way of expression, though the game goes out of it's way to find alternate means to portray the characters, such as novel camera angles, good cinematography, and dramatic body movements that don't rely on facial expressions. In all it wasn't distracting.
The game's writing is fantastic, though suffers from occasional translation weirdness, as the characters refer to things in esoteric or crude ways that a native speaker would not do (such as referring to thermite as "welding powder", which, while accurate, is not the way a native english speaker would refer to it). Mostly, the voice acting covers for the minor typographical errors in the text, but this is not really a problem.
I couldn't recommend this game enough, though in order to fully appreciate it, you'd need to play the prequel, Black Mirror. Black Mirror II relies on a lot of callbacks, and references to gameplay mechanics, and story elements that would be sorely missed if you didn't play Black Mirror. So if you can suffer through the original game, you will be rewarded immeasurably by this sequel. That alone is worth the price of entry.

A lot of people are going to be including the question "was it worth the wait?" in their reviews of Broken Age so I think I'll start by saying that I don't intend to answer that. This game will be around for a long time and I want this review to reflect what I thought of the game, not the zeitgeist.
Let's also discard the obvious: Broken Age is a beautiful game and the music is excellent. The art design along with the superb voice acting is one of the best parts of the game. You won't find a single sour performance or disinterested NPC in the entire game, I promise you that.
Is it a good adventure game, though? Well, yes. Is it GREAT? No. You better keep reading, though, because the "why" behind that answer is more important than the answer. Puzzle design in the "Act 1" area was genuinely good if not a bit easy. I didn't find myself ever having to ask online for a hint and I didn't get stuck to the point of frustration. It was a very smooth ride all and all. "Act 2" shatters this perception and introduces puzzles that, while somewhat logical, are terribly designed.
One example of this is the tube puzzle at the beginning of Vela's second chapter. The puzzle itself makes sense, but the way one interact with objects is wonky. Often I found that clicking on something to move it required me to hold down the button and drag, oftentimes I only needed to click and move. The worst part of the puzzle is that the entire thing could have occupied one screen, but it was  split in half which make moving pieces between the two halves awkward. Luckily, the solution to the puzzle is apparent very quickly so it's really only the wonky interface blocking your progress.
This seems to often be the case. The game's final puzzle is huge and intricate, and seemingly involves time-based maneuvers when, in actuality, it uses very illogical movement triggers instead. Instead of giving the feeling that characters are working together to solve a puzzle, it becomes a tedious trial and error affair long after you figure out the entire solution. Sadly, I think the poorly designed puzzles would often dampen my enjoyment of what was otherwise a funny or emotional moment.
The good news, though, is that puzzle design is my only gripe. It's not insignificant. There is one mechanic that was NEVER used in the first game that gets used a few times without any subtle prompting, but I won't spoil it because I consider it a puzzle solution in and of itself.
After all this, why should am I recommending that you buy Broken Age? Simple, because those things I just described were present in Grim Fandango, they were present in Day of the Tentacle, and they were in Full Throttle as well. This game feels old school in the best and worst ways. Plus, the characters are fantastic. Every one of them is so well-written and bursting with personality that I would easily drop money on a Broken Age 2 right now just to see more of them. The story reminds me of Schafer's Full Throttle. It has an excellent flow, but just kind of ends. Not in a BAD way, mind you, but in a way that says, "this story isn't over" without sequel baiting.
Fans of adventure games old and new owe it to themselves to play this game. As long as you understand that it's not a flawless puzzler then you will find beauty and comedy that will make you laugh out loud at time. It captures that mix of wit and almost fatalistic mirth that makes Tim Schafer one of my favorite video game writers (and Doublefine such a fine team). It's a flawed gem, but still a very valuable one and well woth playing.

I watched the ad and thought.. this is right up my street as far as weird indie games go.
I feel.. as other critical members have said.. it dragged on in places, however I disagree with them on the point the UI was awkward, it was simplistic and I feel like the devs must have.. this immersred you into the beautful love story the experiance became.
I'm torn whether or not to recommend this game.. the slow chunks, the painfully frustating confusion about small nothing puzzles.. but the opposite is true.. there were moments of delight for me, seeing their love blossom ever so delicately, touched me in such a way, I might think it was real when I forget about playing this game ten years from now. The voice acting of Tina Marie Murray was excellent, delicate and emotive. But again.. I experianced many glitches in my copy, like the controller wouldn't look properly with the right thumb stick, and then would for no reason. That kind of glitch undoes the beauty of the interface, that you are telling a intimate interactive story, when so much thought's been put in deep immersion, and then broken. This game NEEDED everything to be competently coded, not that it was bad/bad, just it need to be *perfect* to keep those vibes going/flowing I also had 'wild textures' and no outside at one point. But I turned some settings off and it seemed to fix it.
The art is superb.. the styling, the lighting was odd, too much haze and neon in there, that obscured too much of the game.
The plot.. is a spoiler fest but.. on the whole I enjoyed it, I didn't like the scribbling noise she made in her diary, this would have been much better voice acted, as we are ment to be hearing her thoughts as no one else is there when she speaks, so logically this is her mind. It would have eased me.
I dont know what to say.. the bad bits were *bad* and convserly those slim moments.. touched you with lasting delight, As a love story.. I think it was much better than the swash of love films that are out there, as 'a one woman play'.. *this* medium of game is far better showing the great story than a play or a movie.

Glad I played it - but also now glad I've finished it.
I'll try to keep it short, as others have covered many of the points I wanted to make below.
Some positives I took away from it:
1) You play the entire game in a flat. By yourself. And it makes you feel part of something.
No cut scenes, no narrative, you're just in the flat - but manages to give a fantastic sense of 'world' outside.
2) I've no idea if what I did mattered. Normally in a game you're popped into a world and told to change it.
My world here definitely changed - but I've got absolutely no idea if *I* changed it.
I 'did things' from turning on hundreds of light switches to faxing off secret plans - and 'other things' happened as I did so.
I'm reasonably sure some of my actions influenced my employer, but the impact of that, on the world he inhabits - I've genuinely no idea.
That's actually quite an impressive mechanic, managing to give me a sensation of layered influence over a stack of things, I never see.
My negatives:
Really just concerned with that last point. I turned on so so many light switches. I developed my own routines of how I'd go through the flat. I got obsessed with ensuring lights were on  and the calendar was updated each day - and got genuinely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off when I realized I'd not updated it, prior to starting a job that would run out the clock for that game-day.
I've come away with the feeling the devs were trying to make a point (maybe they weren't and it's a gaming Rorschach test, but I digress). However, I feel they made their point, but in doing so they overlooked my enjoyment.
Bluntly, for better or worse, most of us play games to feel empowered in some way. It's intellectually interesting to demonstrate this doesn't have to be the case - but maybe takes away from the enjoyment of the paying subjects.
I imagine there's a spreadsheet, or stack of post-its on a board, where the "story" was plotted out in abstract, and dutifully mapped into the game day by day - but then nobody with fresh eyes gave feedback.
Games it reminded me of *opens list of Indie-hits from last couple of years* were:
Gone Home, for the solitary exposition in a fixed environment - although think there's still a sweet spot to be found between the magnificent lack of environmental-progression in Sunset, and Gone Home's "you've unlocked a room"
Stanley Parable, for messing with tropes - just Stanley gave you a quick pay-off on challenging them, Sunset lets you indulge and simply leaves you hanging. Conversely though, Stanley never felt it had any depth.
Lifeless Planet, for me loving the concept and execution - but having got the point, just wishing there'd been an editor involved in the process to wrap it up sooner.
Papers Please, this is a late edit, but finally worked out what it's missing is what this game had - the balance between the mundane job, and allowing you to make exceptions. PP didn't quite have the world, but the mechanic was less obtuse.
Re-reading, I feel the review comes across as negative, which wasn't my intention.
It's a unique game I'm glad I played, but just can't help feeling it could have been a bit better. Just a slight bit more "gamier"

Perhaps you heard of Sunset, even backed it on Kickstarter, and imagined life as a houseworker in a hot climate with fierce political tensions. You'd work for this man, cleaning his house, making many choices and experiencing a riveting narrative throughout. You will be disappointed.
Creators always have to think of the best medium for any creation, be it music, art, games, fiction. In this respect, Sunset's a token videogame. It should have been a web app or mobile game. You walk through a 3D environment and click your buttons just like a videogame, but the connection is so minimal that it's clear you're here for the story: which is just only passable. You're expected to search the apartment for clues as to what's going on, but the process of doing so just isn't enjoyable.
I set my walk speed to high so I could breeze through the chores. This renders Angela as a high-speed automaton responding binarily (two choices) to each action -- and this wasn't even communicated well. Where you'd expect to hover over an object and hit Y or N, (yes or no for positive/negative? sure!) you apparently have to move your cursor north and south of the object? Anyway, it took me a good few minutes to figure out how to water the plants one Day. I'd prefer to just tick an optional setting of, "highlight all important objects" so we can do away with the illusion that the game should be immersive.
The 1970's filter over the screen held charm for about 30 seconds. It's annoying in the day. At night, the apartment can become hard to see, and damn if I'm going to waste my precious (and pointlessly timed) minutes turning on each light so I can see. Another optional toggle for the filter would be appreciated, and I have a suspicion that it's cause of a few performance issues people have.
On that note, it is presently a little jittery in regards to performance. War games employ explosions, many NPCs everywhere, intense calculations, reflections, etc. and they still run better than Sunset, which takes place in a single apartment.
I will await a patch for further play. But no patch will avert the reality: they could have dedicated significantly more time to writing more options for these notes and other choices in the game, if only Sunset weren't a videogame. It plays like a web app could.

I am an Overwatch player with almost 400 hours logged on it. I enjoy that game tremendously and the polish is great. But Paladins feels like it has a ton of momentum and potential to be a great game. The mechanics of each Champion in Paladins is somewhat similar to Overwatch (Primary & alt abilities, agility ability,  and ultimate) but does allow each game to feel different and customizable given the in-game RPG-esque card system.
This makes the game unique every time, but difficult to keep up with. I found that I didn't love this aspecft since it felt too complicated to keep up with. The training and education for each Champion is inaccessible from outside of the Champion specific tab (rather than being able to see an overview of each hero whenever... same with each ability). There's so many card possibilities and combos that it makes it difficult to truly understand the game and learn it fast to begin mastering. It felt that I was constantly having to relearn everything every match rather than focusing on getting better.
I do think though, as an early access game, it will eventually iron out some user experience issues and probably cut down on some abilities and complexities to keep it much more accessible and easier to absorb. I definitely recommend the game to try and I think you will ultimately enjoy it.

I really want to give this game a good review, the nemesis system is a step up from the previous game and has provided some truly memorable encounters, combat is generally fun, and the environments are diverse, if a little bland.

However, a number of factors prevent me from being able to recommend the game. Firstly, the story is generally bland, with a lot of the missions feeling like a task to complete so you can get back to hunting orcs and capturing fortresses with the entire first act just feeling like a drawn-out tutorial. As for the actual content of the story, whilst I was never expecting a lore abiding experience the extent to which Shadow of War butchered it was at times hard to believe.
Story aside the game is riddled with bugs, I was unable to complete the final mission after slogging through it as a skill broke. If this bug had happened only once then I could accept it, but it had already happened on a number of occasions causing me to fail a number of missions.
Another issue is the difficulty, or more accurately the fact that the game was not designed with the harder nemesis difficulty in mind. The mechanics of a number of encounters and the ranged units in general turn playing on nemesis mode from an enjoyable challenge to an infuriating nightmare being killed for reasons beyond your control such as bad camera angles preventing you from seeing, generally overpowered ranged units and an infuriating targeting system (especially from stealth) making it a gamble as to if Talion will attack the orc you intended.
Overall, yes, the game is a lot of fun and if you enjoyed the nemesis system of the first you will enjoy it here but be prepared to have that enjoyment tempered by some poor mechanics, game breaking bugs and whilst it may not bother everyone a butchering of the lore beyond belief.

I didn't really think I would enjoy this game, since I've watched episode 1 once, and I was bored. Sadly, later I also got some spoilers about the ending, and again, I was not amused. Then, I decided to give it a try, and that was one of my best decisions ever.
I thought it was some simple teen drama with some love, crime and time travel, but it was so much more. It is a masterpiece - with the cover of a teen drama, including love, crime and time travel. It is like a telltale game, you have to make decisions to continue, and they are not easy at all. Almost all of them have consequences, even if you find it out only later. As the game goes on, the story gets dark, darker, yet darker, sometimes even disturbing and creepy, which I did not expect at all, and the choices make you think about some serious moral questions, sometimes for long, long minutes before you can decide. It makes you think about "What might have happened, if...?", "Why did that happen?", "Could I have done anything to prevent this and that?" in the game and in real life, as well. It makes you question if you really know those who are around you, and to think about their backstory, so I also found it a bit of a psychological experience.
Other than the brilliant story, the characters are amazingly detailed, they are like actual human beings, not just some random people in a game. It has pretty, kind of cartoonish graphics, perfectly fitting soundtrack, great voice acting. It has many twists, just like interesting moments. It might seem boring at first, because it's chill at the beginning in ep1, but it gets deep really quickly, and I stayed up all night just to finish the whole game - even if I knew what the ending was. Then I replayed it just to see what other choices do.
This is easily one of the best games I have ever played. It gives you so many feels and thoughts. And what makes life strange? The fact that so many things can happen in so little time, that will change someone's life forever.
It is definitely worth a try.

"Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures" These are the first words of The Iliad by Homer; the substratum of all western culture, and its first words vividly and eloquently describe the horror of war. It is human nature to fight. Violence is unfortunately an unstoppable force in our world. But the sooner we can admit that we come from brutal animals, the sooner we can let go of our animalistic brutality, and video games are a new and exciting medium that let us explore that dark part of ourselves without causing harm to anyone. We might not be able to get rid of that malice within every human, but there are ways to keep it away from others, and release that darkness peacefully and safely. One of those methods of harmlessly releasing it is with a violent video game like Dark Souls, Bioshock, Dishonored, and almost all other AAA games. But some games aren't just violent, they're sadistic. Hatred is a great example of not only an awful game, but sadistic without reason or meaning, and only rewards acts that are disgusting and cringeworthy. I'd argue that expressing sadism this way holds absolutely no artistic merit, with one exception that I know of. There is only one game that I've played that thoughtfully and tactfully explores the effects of sadistic actions performed by the player with little consequence, and even shows you a side of yourself that you didn't know was there. That game is Hotline Miami, and it's a great example of high-art in video games. Hotline Miami can seem like just a game about committing stylized crimes, but I think there's more to it. (Spoiler warning if you haven't played the game, and if you haven't, you should play it now) Hotline Miami is a small look into the life of a man (who happens to be constantly suffering from schizophrenia and liberally uses LSD) who gets mysterious messages on his answering machine telling him to kill everyone at a certain address. At first it seems like it's just another simple game where you kill people to add to the absurdly long list, except it's not.
There is a moment in Hotline Miami that may be breaking the 4th wall; a single line of text that has made me completely reconsider its purpose. "Do you like hurting other people?" It's a simple enough question with an obvious answer: no. I'm not a fighter, I'm a war-hating liberal pacifist by nature (I respect all other political beliefs as long as good intentions behind them. Please, I'm not looking for a fight). But then I thought about the game I was playing... Just minutes later I was bouncing along in my chair to the extremely catchy, throbbing, and encouraging synth music as I cracked digital skulls with a bat, slit simulated throats with a knife, and emptied the contents of a large automatic rifle into several 8-Bit Russian mobsters from bird's-eye-view, and realized how much fun I was having doing it. Then the music stopped.
Everything was silent save for the faint electronic hum of some insignificant device in the digital background. The walls and floors that were colored neon green and pink just seconds-ago were now red, and a collection of pixels lay dead on the floor. I felt... dirty. Like I had done something that I could never undo. It was at that moment that a small part of myself that I never knew existed responded to the question that broke the 4th wall. It uttered only a single word: "Yes." I finished the game soon after, and that small part of my mind disappeared, full and satisfied from the buffet that was Hotline Miami.
Is Hotline Miami attempting to show the dark and ugly sides of humanity and our society? Is Hotline Miami trying to show us a part of ourselves we didn't know was there? Is Hotline Miami the video game equivalent to Stanley Kubrick and Anthony Burgess's unbearable classic: A Clockwork Orange in the way it used violence to reprimand a society that uses sadistic violence for entertainment? Is Hotline Miami making all of these statements? Is Hotline Miami making any of these statements? I'm not sure. But although Hotline Miami was so brutal that I never want to play it again, it forced me to confront an extremely uncomfortable truth, I wouldn't wish for a second that I never played it. It is with scaleless eyes that I write this, and although those scales blurred things I didn't want to see, seeing those things leaves me wiser and more thoughtful than ever, so I find it impossible not to recommend Hotline Miami, even to the faint of heart. No, especially the faint of heart, because their heart will likely get several shades darker by the time those credits roll...

First, let me say that I LOVED the original Fallout games (fallout 1 and 2), and enjoy the occasional turn-based strategy game (X-com, for instance). However, this game just fell a little short. I'm not saying it's a bad game, but I probably wouldn't recommend it, especially at its current price.
Pros:
- The graphics are good enough for this genre.
- The sound is okay
- The setting is great, and the overall storyline seems kind of interesting.
Cons:
- THE CAMERA. Ugh. Unfortunately, the camera does not seem to expand far enough in any one direction, and the overall size and spacing of the terrain means you will constantly be heading into dead ends because the camera didn't let you see far enough ahead. It's not a game breaker, but is consistantly annoying.
- Too many skill options. I understand that maybe this eventually improves replayability, but it's frustrating to make it through a couple of quests, level up a couple of times, and still be level 1 in most of the skills you've chosen for your character.
- Controls and gameplay are annoying. I don't know of a better way to describe it then that. They are not bad, they are not game breaking, but it is constistantly a nusance to come up on an enemy unexpectedly, and all 4 of your squad members are clustered together and are immediately getting shot at.
In summary, it's not a bad game, but so much of it is frustrating and cumbersome that it becomes kind of annoying to play. If it's available on sale, maybe try it out, otherwise pass.

For the sake of this review, let's pretend I didn't suck at this game to an embarrassing extent.
Hotline Miami showcases a neon-drenched, colorfully visceral depiction of 80's Miami in a vivid art direction that sells the game almost by itself. This is complemented perfectly by a pulsating soundtrack of electronic and synth-wave songs that only occassionally becomes repetitive but always serves to enhance what you'll be doing a lot of in this game: killing.
For better or for worse, the game's bleak plot centers around killing, and lots of it; it's best left unspoiled, but suffice it to say you'll be confused at times and mildly intrigued at others. The narrative is very cryptic, it ultimately doesn't have a satisfying payoff, and a lot is left up to the player's interpretation. Fortunately, the story is merely a side element to the actual game.
That actual gameplay centers around a brilliant, madcap trip into insanity. Hotline Miami's addictive but criminally difficult levels utilize a top-down view of various layouts guarded by scores of armed and adequately intelligent AI. You control the protagonist as he beats fools to a pulp using a wide variety of guns and melee weapons. Enemies react violently to your attempts at wreckage, and one hit kills you, so you'll find yourself gleefully mashing the restart key, ready to try again after your guaranteed instances of failure. Progressing through each level becomes an artfully choreographed, deeply tactical dance to the end marker; if you get careless, you'll quickly get turned into a sad pile of garbage. Unlockable weapons, gameplay styles, and a secret ending are great excuses for few replays.
A few notable faults here and there: the whole package of levels is expertly designed and gets better with each progression, but individual levels become forgettable. The aforementioned story wraps things up alright near the end, but mostly peters along during the main chunk of the game. I also encountered several crashes and start-up issues; this may not apply to everyone, but I had to go to my File Explorer each time I wanted to start the game. But it stands as a testament to Hotline Miami's greatness that I was able to forgive these faults just to enjoy the incredibly, indescribably satisfying gameplay time and time again.
Hotline Miami gets a nice pat on the back and a well-deserved 8 broken keyboards out of 10.

Loot boxes, loot boxes. But what about the game?
I won't pretend they aren't there, this is a Mobage gacha game dressed up in it's preqel's armor. You'll aim for 5* orcs, and get 3*'s in the process. Same for weapons. You'll collect coins from fallen foes, and spin that wheel of chance once more. It's a huge interruption to gameplay. But what /about/ that gameplay?
First, let's talk about controls. There's a lot of improvements from Shadow of Mordor. There's also those same, glaring problems that lingered upon it like a festering wound. In homage to Assassin's Creed, your sprint will often find you clinging to walls within 100 feet as if they were Tallion's family. This can make navigating around mid combat or rushing through Orc camps a frustrating endeavour. On the bright side? The refinement. There's a double jump that aids with the distance you can leap, limiting your time spent climbing and an even faster run than before (or at least it feels it). Jumping up walls can be sped up by mashing space, leaping hundreds of yards in a single leap to turn an hour long climb into just a brief passage of time.
Controls, controls, controls. PC controls for this game are garbage. They're not awful enough for me to defer from using them entirely, but the default control scheme, or perhaps the mechanics themselves lead to again, some frustrating moments. You'll on occasion end up crouching aimlessly for no particular reason to the occasional onlookers during a fight, unbeknownst to them my goal was to hold/tap shift and execute one of their dazed brethren. Only to find, shift is also the stealth button, an essential part of the game; both features. Having them mapped to the same button leads to the obvious conundrum I previously mentioned. You could, /could/ bind them to a different button. However, many commands use the same button, control and shift in particular, and that means rebinding many features to different keys and one hell of a confusing mess. You're better off playing this one with a controller, or perhaps assigning a few things to a mouse button if you've the luxury.
What about those lootboxes? Can I get everything inside them without ever opening one? Yes, and no. You could, but you're going to be sinking about as much time into the game as Monster Hunter. The game gives plenty of freemium currency to use on the F2P lootboxes, use them and worry about your fun more than your pride. Though, I won't deny encountering a better general on the field rather than from the inside of a box, and conquering him myself is an amusing adventure. You'll also be given plenty of lootboxes containing some of the best gear from your online contributions.
Online is simple. It's nothing fancy, someone kills a player, you kill them. An orc a player struggles with constantly ends up showing up on your map every so often, you go and stab that orc 57 times in the chest, and a lootbox explodes from his innards. You will not escape these lootboxes. They are your God now. All you can do, is embrace them and try to enjoy yourself in the process.
Weapons range in rarity, I don't need to go into detail about this I'm sure, most people are familiar with the concept. The rarer, the better the weapon is. Each weapon comes with a unique(ish) task, do the task, unlock your weapon's true power. Could you complete the game on normal or hard with the default gear? Absolutely. You can completely ignore the spewing coins and shiny gems from your fallen foes and still have an amusing time, should that be your goal to 'stick it to the man'.
How's the story? It's got it's ups and downs. There's a lot more characters than the previous time we were in Mordor, and with them comes a geniune sense of dread and opressive depression that fits the atmosphere of the series; the voice acting is on point and I can find myself easily believing the characters presented to me are real people; if a bit cliche at times. You won't find yourself lacking immersion when you play, provided you're one capable of such things. There's a few changes some fans may not be happy to, involving Shelob particular, but if you're not overly fanatic or hardcore canon defending about the Lord of the Rings series, you're going to enjoy your time spent engaging with the story, and most likely, it's open world.
Combat? It's about what you'd expect, with some new abilities as proof of our hero's previous exploits. Counter, counter, attack, perhaps retreat to the shadows for a scond attempt while their first wounds are still fresh. How you engage your enemy is entirely up to you. Fire, poison, the local wildlife or perhaps throw some bees on them. Pick off everyone but the captain so that when he engages you, he finds himself alone, or jump into at times, 50+ orcs at once and let the fields run red.
There's a lot of collectibles. While it's not enough to slog down the game or take away the fun by making you want to focus on them, they're still a bit jarring to see in a game like this, though not out of place in the series. Artifacts of Gondorion lore, and elvish poems to open gates long hidden from Sauron's gaze.
Glitches? Some. Here and there. Nothing that breaks the game, just the occasional moments of thinking perhaps your sound has gone out when one character is speaking in a cutscene and the other isn't, and suddenly the first begins speaking again and you realize for some reason, the second character's voice is just..Missing. Only for that scene mind you, but it's still amusing to behold some of the things that can happen within an open world game; where every detail cannot be perfected.
It's an extremely good game, and I don't have a problem reccomending it to my friends, or the people here curious if it's worth the buy. I would say wait until it's on sale perhaps, or try your best to rent it from various outlets if possible.
What's here now is worth a purchase if you're a fan of the previous game, or the Lord of the Rings series, but others may find it lacking as a game on it's own.
I may sound critical of the game, but it's only because Shadow of Mordor was such an amazing stand out experience that paved the way for future games afraid to use an IP and write their own story with it. What they've done with this one is a shame; but it isn't ruined. Beneath the mobage elements remains an amazing game that a lot of love was put into.
Overall, I'm giving it a 7.0/10.00.

has arrived for PC, as a
. It’s still a Bethesda game and it’s still Fallout, but can a mobile fallout game work on steam??
First of all the game is free to play, so yes you guessed it, it has micro-transactions in it, but I will write about that a little later.
The grafix in the game is very true to Fallout and that pleased me when I saw that, it’s very well made and you actually get the feeling that you are playing a Fallout game.
Now the game starts of as you been a manager of a Fallout shelter and you give it a name. Then you are taken through a tutorial of some of the basics and then you are set and go for the rest. The problem is though you still don’t know half of what you can do in the game, or what the game later will introduce you to. There is a help section, and I can only recommend you reading it, because it gives you valuable information on how to management your dwellers into the right places, so you get faster resources.  And this is where the problems really start in my opinion, and where it shows that it is a mobile port. The waiting time you have to wait for resources are pretty long when you really can’t do much else. 2-4 minutes to be allowed to press a button to get resources is a long time. The first 30 mins you are pretty occupied with the game because everything is new, but then it starts getting boring. There are small events that happens like animal infestations or attack on your vault but that’s pretty much it. I am missing a more eventful game, maybe earthquakes or something else than a fire that can happen because you tried to be greedy with rushing resources.
The game has different items, armor, guns and pets in it, that makes it more interesting, and it is cool having your dwellers running around looking different. A way to increase your population is to make love and produce baby’s and that is a funny feature, again though it takes soooo long time to actually produce a new dweller and have it grow up to be able to work in your rooms. Now if you get passed the waiting time, and play it as a normal pc game, you will eventually get enough dwellers to unlock the Observere room, where the more interesting part of the game opens up. Being able to send your dwellers on quests is a nice feature, but yet again the time it takes to do something is brutally long. Ranging from 30 min to 5-6 houres for your dwellers to get to a location is something you just wont sit and wait for. This is yet again a place where the mobile part of the game shows, because you are more inclined to close down and look at it again later when you are on your mobile phone, than on a pc. You don’t want to open up a game, to play for 10 minutes to close it down again waiting for new things to do. When you actually get to play a quest, you get a new mini game where you have to kill something or answer questions about fallout. I like this part in the game, I just don’t like having to wait 1 hour plus to be able to do it.
Off course IF you use Nuca cola which is the real money currency in the game, you can get there instant, and now my rant starts. The starter pack is 4.99 Euro, which is fine, you seem to be getting a decent amount of things, but then the price goes up. 4-5 Euros for 6 Nuca-Cola when it cost maybe 8 to go instant is WAY overpriced. I am inclined to say that if you do not pay money for the game, you can’t play it as a PC game, and has to play it as a mobile wait game, and that is where I get annoyed.

If you port something to a specific console, you should really make sure that the game is still fun for none paying players, or ask a decent price for it and lower the time for things to finish.
Even minimising the game to try will eventually pause the game (having it to reload when you return), and if you haven’t bought the starter pack you don’t have the handy auto loot machine running around picking up loot for you. Yet again you are losing out when you don’t pay.
The sound in the game is standard for a mobile game, it’s not great but it’s all right, it works for Fallout Shelter.

Well that depends, if you want a game where you are occupied all the time, and having to wait for things to finish is a bother for you, without paying for it, then this game might not be for you. If however you don’t mind having a game you open up from time to time, and play for 10 minutes maybe 30 if you do a quest, then this can could be just what you needed in your life. :)

A really great point-and-click adventure game! Especially if you like Tim Schafer's flavor of characters and silly humor. In terms of puzzles and difficulty, the first half of the game is a little bit easy and (depending on your experience with adventure game puzzles) perhaps even a little boring in a few places, but the writing and characters are still excellent.
The second half of the game takes the puzzle difficulty up a notch! Some have complained that Double Fine overcorrected in the second half and made the puzzles too difficult, but I could not disagree more. The puzzles can be very difficult, and if you're not consulting a guide/walkthrough, you will definitely get stumped on a couple of occasions. Maybe if you're coddled by modern games and aren't used to the experience of not knowing what to do next, then you will find this frustrating or annoying, but back in the golden days of adventure games this was to be expected and was even desired! The great thing about Broken Age, though, is that even though you sometimes get stumped in terms of how to accomplish an objective, you always pretty much know what your next objectives are, and it's just a matter of fiddling with the environment and keenly observing your surroundings until you ultimately have an AH HA moment. It's sometimes slow to come, but it will come.
The genius of the puzzles in the second half is that they essentially come in two types: 1) Pure logic puzzles where, if you have heard the pertinent information in dialogue or seen it displayed somewhere, then simple logic and deduction gets you the answer you need; or 2) Intuitive puzzles that require you to think more laterally or metaphorically, and yet make enough sense that you can figure it out without consulting a guide. All you need to solve the most difficult puzzles in this game is a bit of lateral thinking, some patience, and excellent observation skils. (You won't be making any fake mustaches out of cat hair taped to a fence, if ye olde adventure gamers catch my drift.)
When the first half was released early, it seemed short and easy. As a full game, though, there is an upward-sloping curve to the difficulty that starts them at easy and raises them to very challenging.
Above all though, in this game, as in all Double Fine games, there is a unique and inimitible purity to the good-natured and good-humored characters and jokes and universe that just makes you happy. I'll take that over face stabbing any day.

Nuclear Throne is your standard roguelite game. It focuses on a variety of items, unlockable characters, and procedurely generated maps that have a set of "rules" depending on how far you have proceeded (such as weapon types, enemy spawn types, and map aesthetics). Though it will feel similar to other roguelites, it definitely has features that help it to stand out from the crowd.
What sets Nuclear Throne apart from many other roguelites is its large variety of characters. Coming from a game such as Enter the Gungeon, it is refreshing to have characters that are both greater in mumber and differ more fundamentally in Nuclear Throne. The gameplay is familiar, but that is fine, because it is spiced up a by the character variation. Each character plays very differently, giving the game a lot of replayability. A special ability for your character is executed by right clicking, and can vary from dodging, to blocking bullets, to eating a weapon, to dual wielding, and more. However, Nuclear Throne is also a much less polished game than some other roguelites. Its graphics are nothing too impressive. Though the pixel art is interesting enough and reasonably attractive, it is nothing compared to the sprite work put into Enter the Gungeon or Binding of Isaac. Its lack of polish can also be seen in how its framerate cap is 30 FPS, which is very disappointing. I have experienced the occasional bug and glitch, but it hasn't been intrusive for the most part. Nuclear Throne Together, a network-multiplayer mod I
recommend, introduced more bugs, but is well worth the ability to play with friends online.
What draws me most to Nuclear Throne is the amount of value and fun you get for the low price of $11.99. It is easily worth $20.00, and I am ecstatic that the developers have given us such a bargain.

Broken Age is a love letter to the classic adventure game by a classic developer, and it shows. If that's your bag, you'll enjoy this beautiful and quirky game. If you don't like adventure style games, your not gonna like it.
When it's strong, it's incredible. The dialogue and characters are memorable, the setting is unique, the duel story lines that criss-cross through two colliding worlds are legitimately interesting. When the worlds do collide, the different view points are interesting. 99% of the puzzles will make you think without being unsolvable. Here's a tip: flipping back and forth between the pair is essential to solve some of the later puzzles, and some hints apply to multiple puzzles.
When it's weak, it's still palatable. There are sections and background I would have loved to see more of, and a few parts that feel rushed. There are a few points where it suffers from 'clickitus', where you end up trying to use everything you have everywhere and with everyone to progress forward. While most of these appears obvious in hindsight, there are two cases where I was stupefied by the puzzle logic.
From my experience, I'd say it has around a 8 to 12 hour play time if you don't seek out any hints online, about 4 to 6 if your the type who just can't resist looking up hints when you get stuck. The inventory and controls are good, and the art is amazing.
TL;DR version: 8/10.
