A very pretty game but one that doesn't really merit a purchase or the whole debacle that has been it's development.
Two kickstarters and several years in the making, Double Fine finally finished Broken Age after splitting it into two development cycles.
The first half of the game could be finished in 2 hours without much issue. The 2nd half was dragged out by really un-intuitive puzzles that seemed only to exist because people compained how easy Part 1 was. The solution they had was to require some rediculous trial and error and puzzles that had their solutions hidden in the other persons section of the game.   sometimes the thing you needed to interact with really required almost no logical sense at all and had almost zero evidence pointing towards it that I can tell. I suppose this is true to old point and click adventure games, but that kind of logic probably was best left in the ancient era of Sierra games.
To re-interate how messy and nonsense the puzzles are in this game at one point you have to put a character in danger with very little hint that this is a thing you need to do. You have to do it for a while and even the character starts to discourage you towards the end, saying its time to stop. But if you stop you don't solve the puzzle, so you have to ignore common sense and everything the world and characters are telling you.
The characters constantly have to rely on knowledge they don't have and brush it off as "instict" that they figured it out after you found teh answer in the other persons story line. Sometimes you even have to do things that are presented as counter productive or perhaps make no real sense to do other than that you, as the player, are aware it needs to be done. And I don't mean stand on a pressure plate or pull a leaver. For a fictional example pretend a character of yours needs to stick a fork in a light socket to knock out the power. They as a character don't know hey need to do this. you as a player know that it will unlock a door down the block, but the character in this fictional example  just sticks the fork in there and knocks themself out in the process 'because reasons'. They have no reason to want to do it, and its presented as being detrimental, but you know better. Maybe.
The truth is there isn't much to this game. It has some funny dialog but even that is in short supply, if you were hoping for Tim Schafer's prime material then this isn't it. Plotwise it's a mess. At one point a character actually brushes off a major plot relevation as "oh yeah, I think i knew that but I kinda forgot" They have to have forgotten for it to work out as a big reveal to you, but then it's immediately deflated by the presenting it as your character just being that dumb they somehow forgot about this.
The game being made in two parts will also be quite obvious as it is a glarring jagged scar in terms of gameplay. You will breeze through the first half, then have the second driving you crazy. The final puzzle in the game requires you to do everything perfectly or it all resets back even further than it needed too, and in reality there is no reason it needed to reset at all other than to pad out the game time.
As for the ending, with no spoilers, this game has no real ending. It just kind of stops. You solve an annoying puzzle, there is a cutscene which tries to be epic but in the end it just does.. nothing. You accomplish nothing, you resolve nothing, you get no reward, no explination, and no resolution. It just ends. It might as well just pop a link to another kickstarter page saying "Yeah we ran out of money again, plz donate" Because honestly it feels like they burned through their cash and decided they had to just end it there. NO ENDING FOR YOU.
All in all if you already owned the first half, well you have the game already, if you were waiting for both halves to come out before buying, I can't recommend it.

Sunset is a fascinating and unique game of a type I wish we saw more of.  It's very much like reading a novel; I'd say it's one of the most elegant attempts at making a game be a novel that I've ever seen.
The graphics are fantastic.  As some have noted, performance can seem unexpectedly poor on a low end computer (reminiscent of "Tex Murphy: Overseer" back in the day, for me, on my weaker machine).  But on my newer system, the graphics are flawlessly smooth, delectably stylized, and I can't imagine wanting to change a thing.
The game is unusual in that it seems a bit as if you can do your job as poorly or disinterestedly as you please with absolutely no negative feedback.  This is unusual, and takes a bit of getting used to.  Eventually, the story begins to offer a plausible explanation for why this might be, but I didn't trust this concept for a good while.  I plan on doing a second playthrough shortly to test the theory that I am completely free to sociopathically disregard the work I am (theoretically) being paid to do at all times.  The game mechanics suggest that this is really how I was meant to be playing the game all along in the first place.
Really the only negative thing I have to say is that I have a suspicion that a few of the Steam Achievements might be buggy.  I definitely saw things that would make me assume I should have a few more of them than I do, and all of the ones I think that about show 0% of players successful.  Hopefully a patch will clear that up in the near future.

When it comes to traditional video games, there is no publisher/developer that is so out of the box as Tale of Tales. Their newest game Sunset reaffirms their place in their unconventional line of video games that rely far more on the narrative and what the player does with the information they are given rather than a set goal. Tale of Tales' games aren't meant for those who want to have a clear goal in mind or who prefer games to stick into the very restrictive bindings of what they think a game actually is. They are meant for those who want to experience just how interactive media can be used to tell a compelling narrative.
Sunset is told from the viewpoint of a housekeeper named Angela Burnes, who is cleaning the house for the wealthy Gabriel Ortega during a huge revolution in the fictional South American country of Anchuria. Every day, Angela comes to the apartment before sunset to do the tasks that Mr. Ortega has left for her. The player gets to choose whether or not they want to do everything or how they want to do it. These choices are what shape the games overall narrative. You never know what sort of impact your work will have until the day after you do it. Sometimes it takes even longer for Mr. Ortega to notice depending on what you did or didn't do.
The entirety of the game takes place in the apartment of Mr. Ortega, and the elevator to get there is the game's menu screen. It's a small setting that you're responsible for changing as the housekeeper. Everything you do affects how the apartment ends up looking. Whenever you come back there will be small items moved or new tasks for you to do that will change the place. It gives a sense of accomplishment or progress when you do these small things despite the game not having a set goal. Your job as Angela is to get through every day as a housekeeper as the world falls apart around her. The apartment is like a sanctuary, and while chaos explodes outside, which the player has the option of viewing, the apartment is the one place where Angela feels safe.

Sunset is about love, war and all the emotions in between that one could feel during those kinds of times. Set in a turbulent country you play Angela a foxy house maid who is curious about her employer. Gaberial Ortega. You will clean the house and accomplish menial tasks but more then that, possibly influence a country's fate.  The game is set during the 70's and captures the feeling and design of the times perfectly. From over the top wallpaper to Angela's bell bottomed pants. The house is designed beautifully with detail in just about every nook and cranny.
You become intimately familiar with this setting. When things change you know it. This is how the game mostly progresses. Small changes and small interactions over a long period of time. Giving you only one hour to explore the apartment and make or change the future. While this works for the first two acts of the game and fits the story up to that point. This losses its purpose and meaning when you reach the final acts. It becomes silly for Angela to leave and nonsensical. Also for her to be locked out of rooms. The story also tends to drag itself out a bit. Making some days feel like bread crumbs of character development or the story. Mind you this represents the passage of time. Which sometimes can be boring, however Sunset forgets its a game still. I felt some of the fat could've been cut off and still been a great story. The game itself suffers from some graphical issues and frame rate drops. This can be patched out.
Musically the game is stunning. Although the amazing soundtrack that was composed is somewhat lacking in the first two acts of the game. Making the game feel very quiet. However despite this, Sunset is a beautiful game with a deep message. You just have to be patient to get that message.

Sunset is a story based exploration game played in a single penthouse owned by Gabriel Ortega, a rich businessman. The game is set in a fictional latin american country lead under military dictatorship and shortly after the start of the game, riots begin occuring near the penthouse.
You are playing Angela Burnes, his housekeeper and you visit his penthouse once a week to clean up his♥♥♥♥♥♥ When cleaning up, you will be presented with 2 different choices. The blue choice will help you build a neutral relationship with Ortega while the orange choice will make him like you more than he should.
You have exactly one hour to complete the chores and leave the penthouse, before the sun sets.
As you clean Ortega's house, you will begin seeing notes left by Ortega himself, for you to respond to. You can choose to ignore his notes or write back. All decisions you make influence the further development of the story.
You can also do various different things in the penthouse such as sitting on your♥♥♥♥♥listening to music from his headphones or looking through the window and blabbering nonsense.
Sunset is a very interesting game that gives you the opportunity to create a genuine relationship between two people who have never even met. The most interesting parts of the game are the books that Ortega leaves around the penthouse and his behavior after you've done something special in the penthouse.
The books that you can find scattered across the rooms help you form opinions about Ortega, specifically zooming to read the name of the book. If you do not zoom and read the name of the book, that will not be a factor in your future opinions about Ortega. There is also the fact that he leaves classified documents in the open for you to see in case your relationship is leaning towards the orange color.
The other very interesting aspect of the game is the fact that you can do unusual things in the penthouse such as positioning his shoes in a circular pattern or building a pyramid of a few toy soldiers that you found. Ortega will not touch these creations. Even several weeks after doing this, it will stay intact while half of the penthouse items will change positions.
When playing Sunset, you really feel like every single choice you make, every book you read and every action you take during that one hour, matters and that the relationship between you and Ortega is changing.

I'd like to preface by respectfully requesting that anybody who plans to rate my review to please do so on the basis of if it gives a good or bad portrayal of the game. If you didn't like the game or if you are angry about lootboxes, please do not mark my review as unhelpful just for the sake of expressing your own disapproval. I put time and effort into my reviews and it makes me sad to have hard work ignored for the sake of wanting to show your own displeasure. Sonic Mania is a good example of this, with people marking any positive review as unhelpful simply because of their unhappiness with Denuvo. I expect a similar response from Shadow of War based on lootboxes. For consideration of my review, I have played for 55 hours entirely on the hardest difficulty (Nemesis). I have completed 95% of the ingame content (I didn't have the patience to finish the skill challenges) and at no point did I need to purchase a lootbox. I will discuss this towards the end.
I was writing an indepth review and discovered to my horror that Steam has a character limit. I can't really express my thoughts on the game in the manner I'd like, so I'm going to be concise. It is hard to discuss the game without heavily referencing Shadow of Mordor. If you haven't played Shadow of Mordor, it is well worth your time and a story completion can be done in less than 20 hours. It isn't necessary to understand the story of Shadow of War however.
The combat is instantly familiar from Shadow of Mordor. Fast paced, precise and satisfying. I found it to be a lot more intense in Shadow of War however, I'm unsure if this is from the Nemesis difficulty or just a change to mechanics. I had to make way more quick tactical decisions which kept me on my toes at almost all times. Looking for something to explode, an orc to Shadow Strike to heal myself with, a restock of arrows or even a route to escape. I never got bored, even after 50 hours of playing.
The skill tree allows a huge amount of customisation by having branching subabilities. Each ability has three unlockable variants, but you can only use one at a time. The best example is the beast summon. Do you want a very fast cargor that can be used indoors (great for Overlord fights), a gigantic graug that is slow and clumsy but has tons of hp and tons of damage, or do you want a (fully controllable) fire breathing drake which can get you around the map at rapid speeds but is vulnerable to ranged attacks? You'll find hard choices throughout the skills, but this ensures that everyone has a unique experience. There is no "right" build. You can change skills on the fly which is great for specific situations. I found myself needing a frost heavy build for a legendary overlord that was immune to all my other attacks and had olag grunts which I had to constantly dodge. Freezing them allowed me to finally get into the boss to damage him. This is a great system.
The open world is what you would expect. Five medium maps instead of two large maps, each with collectibles and challenges as per the norm. The different environments make absolutely no impact to gameplay, so they are basically an aesthetics change. Snow doesn't slow you, enemy variety doesn't change. Visually, the game doesn't seem that much of a step up from Shadow of Mordor, and I'm running the game in ultra, but it isn't ugly by any means. There is nothing about the open world aspects of this game that make it stand out, but it doesn't do anything poorly either.
The Nemesis system is expanded as expected. There are tons of different new additions and I'm probably likely to miss some. The same core system is here. Each map has an army of orcs and your goal is to make that army your own and ultimately conquering the map. There is a lot of randomness. Orcs will come from random tribes (which give them combat perks) and will have random names, random strengths and random weaknesses. Orcs may have bloodbrothers. Some orcs will be able to resist your domination. Some orcs will betray you (such as if you make an orc attack his bloodbrother). Ambushes happen regularly, necromancy is a thing and some orcs will return from the dead for revenge. The randomness of every orc is another means of ensuring that ever player will have a unique experience. I personally encountered very few bloodbrothers and was betrayed less than five times whereas others have been betrayed almost hourly. Captain orcs will always introduce themselves with a dialogue. It grows tiresome quickly however, especially as it is more of the same from Shadow of Mordor. Why is there no skip option? I will admit that the entrance of warchiefs is always cool though. The big bad orc with the daunting war theme and name being chanted. Overlords are a weird addition. They are basically just a type of boss in a restricted environment. They don't differentiate themselves from warchiefs outside of dialogue and an ingame generate cutscene. That said, some of the hardest fights will be against overlords so their inclusion is ultimately a good thing.
The story isn't special, but does contain interesting elements. The new characters vary between captivating and genericly boring. The introduction of Shelob as a story character is a pretty cool. It's not canon, but doesn't pretend to be. Many of the human characters are uninteresting and I struggled to care about them. I was genuinely taken aback at the end of the initial game ending, and I realised how invested I was in the characters that I actually cared about. But besides that, the story is bland.
The Shadow Wars seemed like a good idea on paper, but ultimately it is a dull, repetitive grind. I had a mentality of "I've started so I may as well finish". That's not a good mentality to have when gaming. There's also no indication that there is a "true ending" or that there is even a point. You are just thrust into it with no direction. I also found the true ending to be extremely underwhelming, but the final 30 seconds of cutscene was satisfying.
From start to finish I never once needed to buy a lootbox. If I so desired, I could have bought many with INGAME currency. There are also optional daily missions that award premium currency. The game rewards you to play it. I can imagine that the amount of people legitmately needing lootboxes with real currency to be a tiny minority. The option to pay with real cash ultimately seems unecessary given that you can earn everything you need just from playing naturally. It saddens me that the game reputation was negatively impacted as a result. The game is fantastic in many regards, with few flaws. Most importantly, it is consistently fun. The hard work of Monolith shouldn't be tarnished by the decisions of WB. It is my hope that with time, the naysayers will be prepared to give Shadow of War a chance, even if only because of future discounts. It is a game that is well worth your time and it is extremely unlikely for you to find yourself in a situation to need to spend a penny on lootboxes.

Vastly improved since release, originally titled ORION: Dino Beatdown. Don't let the Metacritic score fool you, this game is now a shadow of it's former terrible self. The constant updates and bugfixes have transformed this game from being a very bland and broken basic shooter, to a very fun co-op survival game. The amount of equipment, customization, and vehicles; combined with many months of simplifiing the games UI, game mechanics, and constant bug fixes make the entire package a very fun way to play.
The sheer scale of battles, and the fast-paced combat make it fun. If you get a bunch of friends in on it, you'll be coordinating air strikes, tank movement, and infantry battles all in one wave. It's really something just to see two VTOL's fly above you and reign down missle fire, as two tanks flank from both sides... with troops pouring from either side, engaging a T-Rex which is more then enough to take out everything around it.
The AI has been vastly improved, as well. When the game first came out, you would have raptors blindly rush you in a straight line... and pterodactyls swooping in predictiable patterns. Now, the enemies juke and run around, the pterodactyls are hard to shoot and become the bane of any VTOL pilot. Granted, don't expect any amazing AI here, it's still a horde game and horde AI still crowns... but the game is challanging, even if you have the credits and augments to last. Underestimate a triceritops, and it'll destroy your tank in two hits with its charge attack.
In fact, the best way to describe the feeling while playing this game is like living the movie 'Avatar', but instead of Navi... you have face-ripping dinosaurs.
The game has vastly improved on bug fixes, graphics, and optimization since it came out, as well. No longer do you have memory leaks crashing your game, or textures failing to load. No longer does the game lag on high-end systems, and the graphics looking akin to a grainy mess on your screen, hidden by lens flare. The style, while still basic, has been vastly improved; comparable to the style of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Lots of high bloom space colors, lasers, and heavy weaponary... with vechicles that look as much retro as they do futuristic; this game feels right at home... combining a 'Rad' vibe, high-tech space, and a cheesy 'B' movie feeling. The environments are lush, and the maps are large and immersive. A day-time/night-time cycle affects your visibilty and shifts your gameplay. For example, while playing on a tundra map the cold air at night will cause your visor to freeze if you stay outside in the dark for too long, requiring you to find someplace warm. Rainstorms and snowstorms can also hamper your vision, giving the dinos a leg up to ambushes.
The games three classes (assault, support, and infiltrator) have gotten a major upgrade since launch. No longer is the medic gun useless on the support toon... and no longer does the assault dominate maps. The classes seem very balanced, having their own weapons and play styles. An augment system is also in place, which allows you to purchase in-game upgrades with in-game credits you earn per round... allowing you to gain class specific upgrades like double jetpack energy for the assault, or that the support's medic gun can heal structures and vechicles. Later augments will even allow you to purchase and use other class specific weapons, like being a "boost-sniper" assault... or being a cloaked minigun assassin; as well as having the ability to canabalize raptors for health, earn more credits, or even cause the enemy who kills you to die as well. However, augments arn't permanent... and during rounds you have a finite amount of lives. Not only does dying during a wave cost you a life, but you loose all your augments that you've purchased; giving a larger penalty to death then most games do.
This game has the standard assortament of game modes like deathmatch, team deathmatch, king of the hill; along with having duel modes for both 1v1 and team. The standard horde mode exists as well, called 'survival'... but the meat and potatoes of this game is in it's conquest system, which will allow you to experience those large battles that you see on the screenshots. Players have to fight through waves of enemies, generating credits and protecting their power generator, then use those credits for upgrade, equipment, and vehicles. There's also a 'Rampage' mode that allows humans versus human dinosaurs... so you can live your dream of being a T-Rex and eating people.
The game also features an in-game store with microtransactions, using Spiral Coins:
1,000 Coins - $1.00
6,000 Coins - $5.00
13,000 Coins - $10.00
75,000 Coins - $50.00
Thankfully, this store is PURELY cosmetic with most items costing $1 dollar. No xp boosts, or in-game upgrades... the most you can purchase are hats and skins for your marine or dino. At most, I can see just spending a max of 6,000 coins to get a character the way you want him to look, unless you want to go deeper with customization.
The few things I can say bad about this game is that the maps and waves in conquest mode still seem too large. The amount of equipment, customization, and vehicles; combined with many months of simplifiing the games UI, game mechanics, and constant bug fixes make the entire package a very fun way to play.
The sheer scale of battles, and the fast-paced combat make it fun. If you get a bunch of friends in on it, you'll be coordinating air strikes, tank movement, and infantry battles all in one wave. It's really something just to see two VTOL's fly above you and reign down missle fire, as two tanks flank from both sides... with troops pouring from either side, engaging a T-Rex which is more then enough to take out everything around it.
The AI has been vastly improved, as well. When the game first came out, you would have raptors blindly rush you in a straight line... and pterodactyls swooping in predictiable patterns. Now, the enemies juke and run around, the pterodactyls are hard to shoot and become the bane of any VTOL pilot. Granted, don't expect any amazing AI here, it's still a horde game and horde AI still crowns... but the game is challanging, even if you have the credits and augments to last. Underestimate a triceritops, and it'll destroy your tank in two hits with its charge attack.
In fact, the best way to describe the feeling while playing this game is like living the movie 'Avatar', but instead of Navi... you have face-ripping dinosaurs.

No longer does the game lag on high-end systems, and the graphics looking akin to a grainy mess on your screen, hidden by lens flare. The style, while still basic, has been vastly improved; comparable to the style of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Lots of high bloom space colors, lasers, and heavy weaponary... with vechicles that look as much retro as they do futuristic; this game feels right at home... combining a 'Rad' vibe, high-tech space, and a cheesy 'B' movie feeling. The environments are lush, and the maps are large and immersive. A day-time/night-time cycle affects your visibilty and shifts your gameplay. For example, while playing on a tundra map the cold air at night will cause your visor to freeze if you stay outside in the dark for too long, requiring you to find someplace warm. Rainstorms and snowstorms can also hamper your vision, giving the dinos a leg up to ambushes.

No longer is the medic gun useless on the support toon... and no longer does the assault dominate maps. The classes seem very balanced, having their own weapons and play styles. Not only does dying during a wave cost you a life, but you loose all your augments that you've purchased; giving a larger penalty to death then most games do.

However, these are nitpicks for a game that really has been risen from the ashes of it's former self. Before starting my game: Avid SoM fan for nemesis engine and Monolith Productions
Me after completing 87% SoW: I much enjoyed this game, still playing at 40+ hours, but I have some concerns. THE GAME IS GREAT - the microtransaction direction Monolith took was my largest concern, as it's an innovative studio with fantastic developers, and I would loathe to see it fall into the same marketing trap as other large AAA studios.
This isn't a review of SoM, but let me start by comparing some aspects of the games. The nemesis engine largely works as a large picture the same across games, but it is vastly expanded upon in this game in the sense that there are new ways that consequences apply, new ways to battle new kinds of enemies, and a generally grander sense of involvement in the world's armies. The dialogues are kind of cheesy, some are creepy, some are eye-rolling content... it's easy to tell that a lot of love went into stylizing the NPC's, even when they start to feel like repeats (what wouldn't after so many hours, though?)
The combat is much more fluid than in the first game, feeling more akin to an assassins creed system, and the freerunning is much more controlled than in the first game. You are suprisingly mobile, making it easy to get anywhere on any map without much time spent while still experiencing the environment. You run past captains in quarrels, graugs fighting each other, caragors hunting Uruks, Orcs executing other orc war prisoners - all of these things without your influence.
My absolute favorite thing about Talion and Celebrimbor - and a nod to the devs for this - I can't really pick a favorite. In a character with two people inside, I still can't pick a side. They balanced the dialogues and relationship between Talion and Celebrimbor so well, and that takes some great writing.
That being said, I did not like the direction Monolith and WB took with implementing the microtransaction system. I did not like it when Mass Effect did it, I will never like it. Most consumers will not want that, but it makes an extra couple thousand dollars for the studios from the people with too much money and time to invest. It's more out of a sense of moral pride that I did not use the purchase boxes. THAT BEING SAID, You don't need to buy them. It just makes the endgame grind (the one I'm currently working on) go much faster. That alone is my largest complaint about the game, in addition to small mechanical things, like the fact that a good portion of the time when in combat, you're accidentally doing "something" just not quite right enough to get things like draining, executions or stealth to work properly, such as hanging from a ledge and attempting to stealth drain an enemy, only to drop into an entire roaming band of drunk Orcs that you then have to deal with. You just sit there and mash buttons and wonder what direction you wanted your life to go before video games.
End Point: I was a large SoM fan. If you enjoyed that game, you will enjoy this game. You can absolutely play the base game without the DLC first, and then add content later. It feels like they expanded the bubble more than reimagining the game itself, which I was half concerned about. You do not need to purchase additional content unless you really, really feel like it. It's smooth and runs well on my PC, but definitely look at the requirements before playing.

Alan Wake what an interesting game the overall ambiance of this game sucks you right into the story. The gameplay for the PC is a little lacking but the ambiance and the story made me forget all about that. The end to this game is not as rewarding and it feels something less desired. The main game is so much fun to explore and listen to all of the noises of the game. Bought this originally when PC games came out in those big square boxes, and to be fair it does show its age. The graphics aren't enivable at all because, well, it is nearly 14 years old. It crashes sometimes too. There is quite a learning curve, but after a while you do get through it. The AI is random or too predictable at times, if they plop a stack randomly into your territory and refuse to leave, they're 90% going to declare war. Playing on easier levels, outsmarting the AI is fairly formulaic, aggressive expansion for the first half, strategically stealing all resources and then ploughing through them all. Small maps are too small, and if you create a massive map (which you can do in the editor, which itself has a learning curve) there is a city limit of 450. The game reaches its limit, but by that point each turn is so long, why bother. Naval conflict is always a bit piddly too.
But really the base game has a simple enough format that its almost like a PC version of Monopoly. You can play it again and again, no fancy 3D experience or anything, the graphics really don't impede gameplay. 14 years later its still perfectly playable and, importantly, provides a fun and varied experience. Each game comes out wildly different from the last one, and every time you play a new challenge will arise. The randomized earths created offer nearly infinite variety and eliminate any boredom you could experience with similar games. I can easily play this game for hours and hours. Similar to Paradox games, once you start a campaign its hard to finish, there is enough variety in maps you always want to do something else. Games can easily go far into the future, and with some mods you can add some variety onto the existing game's timeline.

Vastly improved since release, originally titled ORION: Dino Beatdown. Don't let the Metacritic score fool you, this game is now a shadow of it's former terrible self. The constant updates and bugfixes have transformed this game from being a very bland and broken basic shooter, to a very fun co-op survival game. The amount of equipment, customization, and vehicles; combined with many months of simplifing the games UI, game mechanics, and constant bug fixes make the entire package a very fun way to play.
The sheer scale of battles, and the fast-paced combat make it fun. If you get a bunch of friends in on it, you'll be coordinating air strikes, tank movement, and infantry battles all in one wave. It's really something just to see two VTOL's fly above you and reign down missle fire, as two tanks flank from both sides... with troops pouring from either side, engaging a T-Rex which is more then enough to take out everything around it.
The AI has been vastly improved, as well. When the game first came out, you would have raptors blindly rush you in a straight line... and pterodactyls swooping in predictiable patterns. Now, the enemies juke and run around, the pterodactyls are hard to shoot and become the bane of any VTOL pilot. Granted, don't expect any amazing AI here, it's still a horde game and horde AI still crowns... but the game is challanging, even if you have the credits and augments to last. Underestimate a triceritops, and it'll destroy your tank in two hits with its charge attack.
In fact, the best way to describe the feeling while playing this game is like living the movie 'Avatar', but instead of Navi... you have face-ripping dinosaurs.
The game has vastly improved on bug fixes, graphics, and optimization since it came out, as well. No longer do you have memory leaks crashing your game, or textures failing to load. No longer does the game lag on high-end systems, and the graphics looking akin to a grainy mess on your screen, hidden by lens flare. The style, while still basic, has been vastly improved; comparable to the style of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Lots of high bloom space colors, lasers, and heavy weaponary... with vechicles that look as much retro as they do futuristic; this game feels right at home... combining a 'Rad' vibe, high-tech space, and a cheesy 'B' movie feeling. The environments are lush, and the maps are large and immersive. A day-time/night-time cycle affects your visibilty and shifts your gameplay. For example, while playing on a tundra map the cold air at night will cause your visor to freeze if you stay outside in the dark for too long, requiring you to find someplace warm. Rainstorms and snowstorms can also hamper your vision, giving the dinos a leg up to ambushes.
The games three classes (assault, support, and infiltrator) have gotten a major upgrade since launch. No longer is the medic gun useless on the support toon... and no longer does the assault dominate maps. The classes seem very balanced, having their own weapons and play styles. An augment system is also in place, which allows you to purchase in-game upgrades with in-game credits you earn per round... allowing you to gain class specific upgrades like double jetpack energy for the assault, or that the support's medic gun can heal structures and vechicles. Later augments will even allow you to purchase and use other class specific weapons, like being a "boost-sniper" assault... or being a cloaked minigun assassin; as well as having the ability to canabalize raptors for health, earn more credits, or even cause the enemy who kills you to die as well. However, augments arn't permanent... and during rounds you have a finite amount of lives. Not only does dying during a wave cost you a life, but you loose all your augments that you've purchased; giving a larger penalty to death then most games do.
This game has the standard assortament of game modes like deathmatch, team deathmatch, king of the hill; along with having duel modes for both 1v1 and team. The standard horde mode exists as well, called 'survival'... but the meat and potatoes of this game is in it's conquest system, which will allow you to experience those large battles that you see on the screenshots. Players have to fight through waves of enemies, generating credits and protecting their power generator, then use those credits for upgrade, equipment, and vehicles. There's also a 'Rampage' mode that allows humans versus human dinosaurs... so you can live your dream of being a T-Rex and eating people.
The game also features an in-game store with microtransactions, using Spiral Coins:
1,000 Coins - $1.00
6,000 Coins - $5.00
13,000 Coins - $10.00
75,000 Coins - $50.00
Thankfully, this store is PURELY cosmetic with most items costing $1 dollar. No xp boosts, or in-game upgrades... the most you can purchase are hats and skins for your marine or dino. At most, I can see just spending a max of 6,000 coins to get a character the way you want him to look, unless you want to go deeper with customization.
The game also has persistant stat tracking and a levelling system, however the system is very static... only unlocking set upgrades per each level.
The few things I can say bad about this game is that the maps and waves in conquest mode still seem too large. Gathering your entire army to move from base A to base B after you've spent 10 waves defending base A really doesn't make you feel like that base is 'yours'. Also, some weapons are more overpowered than others; and some items aren't that useful to invest your time into (IMHO, the flame turret). On top of that, dinos tend to 'pop in' if they're too far away... making a hunt for a large dino that you can idenifty close by a bit harder to locate. Also, the populations for game modes seem to be a bit low in my taste, with conquest allowing up to 5 people per server. Other modes have different population caps, but overall it feels small. The menu UI structure also is a bit hard to get used to... with the whole menu UI coming off a bit cheap. Granted, the old menu system from two years ago was DREADFUL, and this is an improvement... it's still not up to par with most games.
However, these are nitpicks for a game that really has been risen from the ashes of it's former self. The developers are very active in the games future, and this game does have the love and dedication of a passion project come to life. There's constant free updates to this game, and new features being added all the time; as well as having the team be very approchable with ideas and suggestions. With the changes I've seen with the past two years... and (at the time of writing) a new version of the game in development which will expand on this game, allowing for new features... including a persistant open-world game mode, ala Planetside 2... I can safely say that this game has a bright future.
If you had met me two years ago and asked about this game, I would have told you to never play it... to stear clear, and forget about it... If you had bought it, to try and ask for a refund.
Nowadays, I'd be asking if you wanna buddy up and kill some dino's in a APC. It's improved that much, and I'd be MORE than willing to give it a recommendation. It's cheap, it's fun, it's OOZING with Sci-Fi goodness, and there arn't many games out there like it.

Looks like lots of reviewers are already familar with this genre (like the classic fallout series). Well, as a newcomer, I'm writing this review for all rpg newbies like me out there.
- Background:
The world is destroyed by nukes, hundreds of years passed. Your home area is isolated by radiations, you don't know much about what's beyond them. You're(will be) a new member of the Rangers, an organization trying to keep order and peace of the area. It's not about the nukes(generations passed), but more about the post-apocalypse-world-people-sucks-thing-ness.
- Gameplay
Top view, you control four characters(Unless they're dead) + followers you picked up. You talk to people, get quests, get random abandoned loots yadi yada.
Annnd most importantly, the battle. it's turn-based. Every character gets a turn(some get more often than others - fast and smart ones). You can attack, move, ambush etc during that turn, each move using up your points for that turn.
...how do I explain this game...It's freakin' huge, for one. I don't know if this is the usual standard for this genre, but the devs thought of everything, really. For example, you can use lockpicking on a locked door, but if you fail...you can try again. Of course! I didn't even think that was possible for some reason the first time, but then I realized that it makes much more sense. But if you make a 'critical failure', the lock mechanism breaks and you can't lockpick it anymore. BUUUT you can repair it back with your 'mechanical repair' skill and try again. Also if all of that fails, you just smash the door by force(which also has a chance of critical failure).
Same vibe goes for the battle. I learned not to shoot enemies with sniper rifle when my teammate is in the way the hard way.
All your characters can die, and the game will keep going. Unless all of them are dead, of course. In that case, the game says, "Well, all of you died in the wasteland. We don't have fancy ending for that, few people will even remember you anyway...bye bye"
It's intended as a game where you're NOT supposed to reload after a failure, I think. It's like the game's saying, "Oh, you failed! Well, take your responsibility, live with the consequences from now on. We've already prepared another ending for ya...and it will affect your future quests as well"

I like Mountain. I definitely recommend it. However, it took me a while to really grasp. I opened Mountain the first time, watched it for 10 minutes, got bored, closed it, and then never opened it again. Why would I sit and stare at it any longer?
After over a year, though, I felt the call to Mountain once more. I opened it one day and did my coursework for a few hours while Mountain did its own thing in the background. During my study I occasionally would lose track of time or get distracted doing other things. However, Mountain sort of brought me back in with its occasional thoughts and its chorus hum. Mountain's ambient noise and sporadic thoughts helped me refocus and remember what the task at hand was. In this way, Mountain has actually become one of my biggest and most handy study/work tools.
After a few hours, Mountain had amassed quite the collection of knick-knacks and do-dads. There was a beach chair, a gun, a car, and a sewing needle, and since Mountain has gathered an even larger collection of fun stuff.
Mountain is something to open and let do its own thing. You can come back occasionally to look and appreciate it. When I do this, I get a lot of enjoyment out of Mountain. I feel connected to Mountain. In some ways it's a parallel for my life. When I'm frustrated and tired, I can just blow Mountain up and start anew, and when I'm feeling cheerful I can ask Mountain what it's thinking and appreciate its curiosity and simple splendor.
Mountain was well worth the very, very small monetary investment and now I hardly ever close it. There are countless other things I could've spent my $2 on. I'm glad it was Mountain.

I write this as someone who doesn't normally buy racing/car games, but was drawn to this because of the exotic real-world locale, the extreme trucking, the huge Soviet equipment, and the challenge.  It's a great simulation of offroad driving, but is also a puzzle game at heart -- how do you accomplish your goals with what you have at hand?
It plays well on older systems (mine is 5+ years old, with a budget vid card from 3 years ago), works well with existing and cheap controllers, and looks like it is selling well and will have more content in the future given the current success on Steam.  Definitely got my $30 worth so far, no crashes, and the challenge level has stayed very high.   This game, even in what is somewhat of a beta form, delivers on all counts and has been a great investment for my $ vs. other purchases I later regretted.   I will definitely be investing in any new content, and the updates promise even further improvement.
One note -- the learning curve in the beginning is steep, and you will fail often.  My advice, and I'm happy to write a separate guide -- Don't cross any major streams or get into super-deep mud until you have at least one very heavy truck in your arsenal, use teams in the beginning while scouting to help with towing out of trouble, and once you get to 3 vehicles, there will be little to stop you, even on Hardcore mode.  Don't be afraid to fail, learn, start again, and get better.  Don't rush to deliver the logs -- explore the map, unlock new options, and then set up a log run with the optimal equipment.  There's no rush, this is an open-world game without a time limit, just potential for each huge map (and there are around 6 right now, with many hours of gameplay involved to clear each map.).
Additionally -- first gear, and differential lock, is your friend.  As the game runs now, sometimes diff lock is more important than all-wheel drive (as it should be), and learning the gearshift is key to getting unstuck, in combo with the winch.  Look up some of this stuff on youtube (even those general topics, differential lock and offroad driving), and you will better understand what your truck is doing and why you use what gear.

Three years ago Tim Schafer's DoubleFine sold nearly 90,000 fans on the idea of making and an Old School Adventure game. And after all this time he finally gives us the completed Broken Age, which is a mess and one of the worst games this acclaimed studio has produced.
I've spent a whole day revisiting Broken Age, replaying Part 1 and playing Part 2, as per Mr. Schafer's advice. And that actually made the experience far worse because it made it all the more apparent how cheap this game feels. There's only three (well more like two and a half) locations you'll spend the majority of time exploring in this game, and man does it get boring. This game is supposed to rekindle the love of the LucasArts Adventure games but you aren't exploring a large and varied game world, you're just walking back and forth between the same backdrops OVER AND OVER AGAIN.
And it's not like the artwork does anything to alleviate this, the art as you can tell is awful, it belongs in a cheap kids book that Scholastic would produce.  It's not as interesting as the worlds the player explores in prior DoubleFine games or Lucasarts game. And the animation is absolutely barebones, the game is not nearly as fun to look at in motion as the Monkey Islands or Day of the Tentacle was. To be frank I feel like a loser playing this game, as the artstyle is so amatuer and childish I'm truly embarrassed to see it on my computer screen. I'd rather have friends catch me playing Hyperdimension Neptunia than Broken Age.
This would all be forgivable if yes this game were not for my demographic, as a man in my 20s I obviously understand that everything isn't made for me and Broken Age looks perfect for young children. But I would never suggest this game for children because it's not at all designed for novice or easily distracted players. There is no option for a "Goal" system to remind you what you're looking for or hints, if you forget what it is you're after in the game you just end up wandering around the environment till you find the right NPC. So yes in some ways Doublefine did indeed make an Old School Adventure game, while I can't speak for everyone this isn't what I loved Adventure Games for. I loved them because they felt like semi-interactive cartoons, with puzzles that made me scratch my head and then feel smart for solving them. Broken Age Puzzles are either ridiculously easy or ridiculously obtuse with no middle ground.
The amount of activity is also extremely low in Broken Age. Any of those old Lucasarts games allowed you to click around the environments and your character would say a funny little line, there's only a items in Broken Age that have the characters say anything out loud and it's usually just them stating the obvious with no fanfare. You don't even get a fun line by trying to use the inventory in ways you obviously shouldn't, for an example the character Vella doesn't react negatively to you suggesting you use a knife on her little sister.
The only compliment I can pay Broken Age is that the audio is nice. Tim clearly used a large portion of his 3.3 Million budget to rub elbows with celebrities and hang out with an Orchestra. As if the players really cared if the actor who played Frodo Baggins is the star of the game.
Do not buy this game for $20, hell I'd have a hard time saying it's worth $10. This is mediocrity and not even one that has lovable quirks. Doublefine put so little effort into it that I'm upset at how much time I've spent playing it. I only feel compelled to complete it because I gave them so much money in the Kickstarter.
Shame on you Doublefine and Tim Schafer, you went directly to the gaming enthusiasts and we might not give the cash a big publisher can provide but we allowed you full control on this project. And you squandered it on something completely unmemorable and spent most of that time partying and filming a self-fellating documentary.
Good luck ever trying to make a Kickstarter as popular as this first one was. Because I sure as hell am not pledging again and I doubt I'm an anomaly.
Before you buy this game I urge you to play through all the Lucasarts and Telltale Adventure games, after that play everything else Doublefine made. Trust me they are all better games.

Spintires is a game in which you travel over various maps utilizing realistic offroad driving ot deliver logs. This is not a game for those looking for an exciting time but rather a true(er) to life simulation of logging operations in a less developed country.
Good: The simulation is nearly spot on with only a few things missing for gameplay reasons. A promised feature was the ability to change the air pressure in the tire of the vehicles that has yet to be seen.
The maps are large and allow for a pretty interesting mechanic of scouting out the cloaking points that black out most of the map and vehicle and garage areas that can be used later on.
The vehicles are well modeled and react as a real vehicle would minus damage effects that could help the game along better.
An open world/Non-timed objective system allows for multiple strategies in completing the objective and a really fun exploration game.
Bad: The fun that you have with this game is wholly dependant on the person playing. This game has only the base amount of objectives of move logs from point A to point B and find all the garages and vehicles. You can also take the time to uncloak the entire map, but if you already learned the map previously you know your way already and it becomes pointless.
The map interface is a bit cumbersome and is a bit confusing. In order to map a route you must select the various points on that map for your waypoints, but in order for it to show your red navigation line you DO NOT click ok in the text box as this clears the waypoints from the map.
There are very few vehicles to play with.
A promised feature of variable air pressure in the tires is yet to be added to the game. The menu interface is easy enough to navigate and load times on even a mid-range PC are low but can still be a tad long to deal with.
While I do like the ability to just go right back into a session I was on previously I do wish it had multiple save slots to allow for more than one game at a time.
Overall: If you like simulators that actualy do a good job of simulating and you are able to make your own fun in an open world without guns and the like this game will be fine for you. If you are a more casual person this is not your game, especially for the price. I could'nt recommend this game to many of my friends, but I sure have had a fun time with it.

So, there it is.
is finally out. I haven't touched it before tonight (bought it sometime last year during a sale) and waited patiently for it to be ready for a full-on, one-session playthrough. The question is: Was it worth the wait?
The (spoiler-free) answer to that is: Yes it was, if you have been patient and didn't raise your expectations too high.
Now, something to say right away -
is not the adventure to end all adventures. It has its strengths and weaknesses. But what makes assessing them hard is that they switch around. In Act 1, the story was very strong and somewhat mysterious while the puzzles were mostly fairly easy. In Act 2, the story lost a lot of its pull (in my opinion) but the puzzles became more complex and challenging, some of them just the right amount to be satisfying, some pushing it a little (or well) into the realm of the frustrating.
But I will not blame Double Fine for experimenting with some of the concepts behind puzzles. The fewer developers keep recycling the same concept, content and game over and over, the better, so I can admit I was satisfied with that part of the game even though I eventually had to look up a hint or two.
The story left a somewhat bitter aftertaste, though. It's not that it's bad overall - The presentation is brilliant, the setup stellar (particularly Shay's Act 1 was great) and the cast of experienced and skilled (voice) actors add to it, as do the beatiful soundtrack and catching visuals. And the writing also doesn't leave a lot to be desired: It's witty, but not too over-the-top and just the right amount of educational to be played by all ages.
It does, however, suffer from what I would call the "Mass Effect 3" effect: By the end, it seems like nobody really knew what to do with it, so it was just wrapped up in whatever way they could. It's not as bad as Mass Effect 3 but I found the conclusion unsatisfying and the last few scenes made me wonder where the good writing with its surprises and twists had gone and why I was now watching a B movie.
I know that doesn't sound like a hearty recommendation but that doesn't mean you shouldn't pick it up.
is still a great adventure; it just isn't without faults, just like the story of its development.
Be aware, though, that you are probably only going to get one playthrough of 8-10 hours out of it (maybe another some years later). But during a sale, this is a good pick.

Sunset is a very... interesting game, to say the least. You play as Angela, a young woman who has apparently moved from her home to (what I think is) a fictitious Southern America country. The game is set in the early 70s and, as Angela, you are tasked with... doing chores?!
Yeah. Seriously. You'll spend the first parts of the game just doing chores for this man that you work for. As you do the items listed on the scrap of paper, you can also find different things to do outside of the list. The objective seems to be, "Do the items on the list while the story slowly unfolds."
The game looks interesting, in terms of its design. It looks really nice and has a great feel for the era, if not a bit artsy - in a good way, though. There's also some music that you can play (if that room is available) that's actually pretty nice to listen to. Unfortunately, it's not often that a record player will be available to use, which is a bummer - because there is no background music to listen to.
The game begins to feel "alive" around July 22nd, when things start to pick up. This is where I'm currently at, but I decided to stop and jot down some initial thoughts. I'll probably update this again once I get further and, eventually, complete the game.
Initial thoughts:
- Game feels real smooth
- Original setting
- The colors are very "vibrant" for the time/setting. It really feels like you're in the era.
- Game is very quiet. Feels perfect, but also makes you wish there was more music lying around the apartment to play.
It's not a Telltales-esque game; rather, it feels more like in the same circle as Dear Esther or The Moon Sliver. Very story-driven, not much action or much to do (early on, anyways).
As of right now, I'd be very cautious about purchasing this game. If you're a huge fan of games in this genre, then yeah - it's right up your alley & I think its setting and story-telling will be just as compelling as others. However, if this isn't your style and you may be interested in getting into this type of genre, I'd look for a cheaper game first, to get a feel for how these games flow. Spending $20 USD may be hard to swallow for some people who prefer more to do & finding disappointment here.

Here's what Broken Age actually is: a fantastic, indie-produced, community-supported point & click adventure. In a time where by & large, publishers control the games you get to play, Double Fine has created & shipped a rich, gorgeous game.
It's not long (maybe 8-9 hours total). There's a limited amount of replayability. That's the nature of the point-and-click beast.
But the art is wonderful, the narrative is fresh (not yet another Call Of Duty or GTA), the voice acting is excellent & the music is fantastic. It delivers on being a witty place, an interesting world, a living painting. IMO, it's worth your time & your money.
Well done, Double Fine. Well done.

When I first played this game, it had numerous issues. It crashed on startup, by which I mean the first 10 times I played it, it either shut itself down without an error message or froze and windows forced me to close it. It also made me physically sick, and didn't run well. It also had issues where if I zoomed in on an item (to collect an item), the game would crash.
There's been no patch but I have fixed some issues. Originally the game made me sick but that can be fixed by playing on Low Settings instead of Min and changing the FOV. No problems there.
The game does have frame rate issues. I've talked to a few people who had the same problem, some with a desktop computer. The games frame rate does dip below 20 at times. For me, it runs between 15 and 40 fps on low settings and changing the settings doesn't make a lot of difference.
You have to make choices in this game. This game is about choice. You get two options: a red or a blue option and you pick which one you think suits best for the way you want to play the game. There is also a lot of variety of your interactivity with the world. There are books to be found. Records to be played. Lights to turn on. There is a lot of it, and that's one of the great things the game has going for it.
The ambient noise is also really good. The crackling of records. Helicopters flying overhead. I love the ambient noise. There's nothing better than sitting down, and hearing the crackling of a record and some beautiful music. It's definitely one of my favourite moments of the game. The explosions actually scare you, as you have no choice but to..sort of hide from it. Same with gunfire. Although in other games it would terrify you, there's nothing you can do about it. You just live in constant fear that the next person to get shot/get blown up is yourself.
The game revolves around you, a Gringo housekeeper. As such, you get to know the nooks and crannies of the house very well. There are indoor and outdoor sections. But also as it is set in a house, there aren't a lot of variety to tasks "clean this", "mop that" so if you want a variety of activities, this isn't for you. However you can explore, crack codes, discover secrets, etc. and that's one of the things I love most about this game.
Would I recommend this game? Truthfully...I don't know. If you like so called "walking simulators" or you love indie games, then I'd say yes. If you can look past the issues I had at the start, then I would definitely recommend this game. But as the issues I had at the start, and still have seem to have ruined the whole experience for me. I can't. It takes me out of the world.

Fun enough. A little more grindy than I like, but not annoyingly so.
The part that interests me most is the combat system, learning to dodge the patterns of the enemies. But the game is a bit frustratingly linear, because next-level weapons do so much more damage; anything else is mostly irrelevant. The elemental weaknesses and strengths are not large enough to make much difference.
Armor is mostly irrelevant: a lot of the time I'm wandering in areas where getting hit at all is a one-shot death, and the best armor can do is maybe make it a two-shot death. So it feels like the best bonuses to go for are ones that increase move speed or add stun effects.
Combat gets really interesting when more than one enemy is attacking me. But it's a bit frustrating. The combined attack patterns seem like they should be fun to work with, but with so much of the game being one-shot death, it ends up being an exercise in endless dodging while my pet takes out the enemies. Bombs help some, but they're slow and don't really do enough damage; it's almost always better to use melee and dodge. Or better yet, avoid getting into multi-enemy fights.
In default difficulty, it's pretty easy to avoid multi-enemy fights. At higher difficulty, enemy generation is denser, making it harder to avoid messy fights, which is not really much fun.
The environments are kind of boring, in a fractal-noise way. Once I realized that it was fractal noise (with difficulty increasing from the center), I stopped trying to explore in detail. Generally, all that's necessary is head for the points marked for missions, or run continually in one direction to grind resources. The game lets you add map markers for things like rare resource spawn points, and I did that for a while, but I never bothered to revisit my marked points, because it's usually just a few units at each point. The map doesn't show respawn time, and walking to each of those points from the nearest teleport doesn't feel worth it. I usually grinded by just exploring outward more, especially when I knew what terrain type a resource is associated with.
Region 2 is much more interesting than region 1. It's kind of a shame it takes so long to get there. Maybe the game could have introduced it sooner, and done more cross-region questing, but switching regions is a brief but annoying stall. So it's good that it isn't necessary to frequently switch regions.
Region 3 is dull, unfortunately. I was hoping for something more different, but it's basically like region 1, with more water. And the enemy attack patterns feel repetitive, only minor variations of what came before.
The crafting, I mostly ignored except for the necessary items and some equipment. There doesn't seem to be much point to building a home with furnishings. It's just clutter that gets in the way of using the craft stations.
The pets are nice, but Vonma is so much better than the others, once I got it I didn't bother with anything else.
I played for a long time with a controller before I realized that there are parts of the UI that you can't trigger with the controller, like info bubbles. The info bubbles are not essential to playing, but it helps a lot to be able to see "what's that component I'm looking for again?"
It took a little while to adjust to combat dodging with mouse, but mouse and kb ends up being better than controller. Touch might be even better. There are a few things look like they'd be more convenient with touch.
The game shows some clear signs of being designed to be tablet-friendly, which is ok. I don't think it really hurt the overall design. I feel like the only way the limitations really show through is in compromises for a constrained amount of RAM, like the fractal-bland environments.
The story is so-so. The writing and humor didn't really work for me, no big deal. I mostly ignored the story and just quested.
I finished default "Adventure" difficulty and started a game in highest "Insane" difficulty, but I don't think I'll bother finishing Insane. It's been a lot of dying and grinding. I still like the combat challenge, but recovery after dying is tedious.

The reason i gave this game a thumbs up is because of the interesting story, It outweights the somewhat boring and repetitive gameplay.
-----------------------------------------------
- Really interesting story
- Overall unsettling atmosphere

I really liked the story, one of the better i have heard in a long time in a video game. while it's not a completely scary horror game it's unsettling enough to creep you out from time to time. While i liked that you could pick up your manuscript pages, it also kind of revealed what would happen later in the game. While the forests sure looks beautiful with lots of details and textures that's good enough, you can't help but think "Not another ♥♥♥♥ing forest" later in the game. Ohterwise, the game gots graphics good enough to deliver. And there's a few key moments that was intense and really interesting i won't mention here for the sake of not spoiling it for anybody.
-----------------------------------------------
- Linear and repetitive gameplay
- The same ghostmen over and over again (The variations is: Normal guys, Big guys and Fast guys)
- It's pretty predictable to spot when you will get ambushed
The game pretty quickly becomes linear and repetitive since you have to follow a path in the game and kill the same ghostmen the same way over and over. There's a couple of ways to deal with them, but it quickly becomes the same and you quickly learn how to deal with certain types of enemies. also like i mentioned.. you will get tired of forests sooner or later. When you're through the first episode, you will probably already know when to expect company by your best friends, the ghostmen.
-----------------------------------------------
- The ending
- Coffee collectables
The story itself was good, but the ending makes you think and i am still kind of lost. I still don't really know what the hell happened. (Maybe you'll get it) The coffee collectables... don't really know how i feel about them. They don't do anything and kind of feel out of place.
All in all, a good game with an interesting and unsettling story, but i don't want to play it again because of the gameplay. The only reason to play it again would be to play Nightmare mode to get all the manuscript pages, yes there is some manuscript pages you can only get by playing on nightmare mode.. which means you have to play the game twice. Now i'm off to play the Alan Wake's American Nightmare game.

text:
I wanted to like this game, but it stopped being fun. It's no fun when the 4th act is an endless grind. It's no fun when the game's camera angles suddenly change so you got blindsided by attacks, or miss the counter-prompts above attackers' heads, because they suddenly jump out of frame, as the game dances around trying to make itself look "epic". Its no fun when your bodyguards don't follow or defend you, but just sit waiting for a scripted moment while you're repeatedly attacked.
It would be fun if the devs designed a decent AI next time. It's no fun that you vault on every single pole or tree nearby, regardless of where you're actually trying to go. It's no fun when I can't dominate the broken enemy captain right next to me, because the game assumes I'm trying to 'redominate' my already dominated bodyguard, over and over again. Its no fun when my war graug attacks my own castle gate rather than the enemy captain standing right in front of it, because the game can't distinguish the two. Why would I ever want to do that?
Most of all, it's no fun that I can only run vengeance missions when my friends are actually online and instead I always have missions for a bunch of random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s I don't know or care about. Why would anyone want that? What if your friends live in different time zones or have different schedules? Do you never get to avenge them? What's with this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of being transferred "into their world"? It's never any different than mine and only adds unnecessary long loading times.
This really adds nothing to the later half of Shadow of Mordor, which was simply a more fun game. What a fail all around, Monolith and WB.

Vastly improved since release, originally titled ORION: Dino Beatdown. Don't let the Metacritic score fool you, this game is now a shadow of it's former terrible self. The constant updates and bugfixes have transformed this game from being a very bland and broken basic shooter, to a very fun co-op survival game. The amount of equipment, customization, and vehicles; combined with many months of simplifiing the games UI, game mechanics, and constant bug fixes make the entire package a very fun way to play.
The sheer scale of battles, and the fast-paced combat make it fun. If you get a bunch of friends in on it, you'll be coordinating air strikes, tank movement, and infantry battles all in one wave. It's really something just to see two VTOL's fly above you and reign down missle fire, as two tanks flank from both sides... with troops pouring from either side, engaging a T-Rex which is more then enough to take out everything around it.
The AI has been vastly improved, as well. When the game first came out, you would have raptors blindly rush you in a straight line... and pterodactyls swooping in predictiable patterns. Now, the enemies juke and run around, the pterodactyls are hard to shoot and become the bane of any VTOL pilot. Granted, don't expect any amazing AI here, it's still a horde game and horde AI still crowns... but the game is challanging, even if you have the credits and augments to last. Underestimate a triceritops, and it'll destroy your tank in two hits with its charge attack.
In fact, the best way to describe the feeling while playing this game is like living the movie 'Avatar', but instead of Navi... you have face-ripping dinosaurs.
The game has vastly improved on bug fixes, graphics, and optimization since it came out, as well. No longer do you have memory leaks crashing your game, or textures failing to load. No longer does the game lag on high-end systems, and the graphics looking akin to a grainy mess on your screen, hidden by lens flare. The style, while still basic, has been vastly improved; comparable to the style of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Lots of high bloom space colors, lasers, and heavy weaponary... with vechicles that look as much retro as they do futuristic; this game feels right at home... combining a 'Rad' vibe, high-tech space, and a cheesy 'B' movie feeling. The environments are lush, and the maps are large and immersive. A day-time/night-time cycle affects your visibilty and shifts your gameplay. For example, while playing on a tundra map the cold air at night will cause your visor to freeze if you stay outside in the dark for too long, requiring you to find someplace warm. Rainstorms and snowstorms can also hamper your vision, giving the dinos a leg up to ambushes.
The games three classes (assault, support, and infiltrator) have gotten a major upgrade since launch. No longer is the medic gun useless on the support toon... and no longer does the assault dominate maps. The classes seem very balanced, having their own weapons and play styles. An augment system is also in place, which allows you to purchase in-game upgrades with in-game credits you earn per round... allowing you to gain class specific upgrades like double jetpack energy for the assault, or that the support's medic gun can heal structures and vechicles. Later augments will even allow you to purchase and use other class specific weapons, like being a "boost-sniper" assault... or being a cloaked minigun assassin; as well as having the ability to canabalize raptors for health, earn more credits, or even cause the enemy who kills you to die as well. However, augments arn't permanent... and during rounds you have a finite amount of lives. Not only does dying during a wave cost you a life, but you loose all your augments that you've purchased; giving a larger penalty to death then most games do.
This game has the standard assortament of game modes like deathmatch, team deathmatch, king of the hill; along with having duel modes for both 1v1 and team. The standard horde mode exists as well, called 'survival'... but the meat and potatoes of this game is in it's conquest system, which will allow you to experience those large battles that you see on the screenshots. Players have to fight through waves of enemies, generating credits and protecting their power generator, then use those credits for upgrade, equipment, and vehicles. There's also a 'Rampage' mode that allows humans versus human dinosaurs... so you can live your dream of being a T-Rex and eating people.
The game also features an in-game store with microtransactions, using Spiral Coins:
1,000 Coins - $1.00
6,000 Coins - $5.00
13,000 Coins - $10.00
75,000 Coins - $50.00
Thankfully, this store is PURELY cosmetic with most items costing $1 dollar. No xp boosts, or in-game upgrades... the most you can purchase are hats and skins for your marine or dino. At most, I can see just spending a max of 6,000 coins to get a character the way you want him to look, unless you want to go deeper with customization.
The few things I can say bad about this game is that the maps and waves in conquest mode still seem too large. Gathering your entire army to move from base A to base B after you've spent 10 waves defending base A really doesn't make you feel like that base is 'yours'. Also, some weapons are more overpowered than others; and some items aren't that useful to invest your time into (IMHO, the flame turret). On top of that, dinos tend to 'pop in' if they're too far away... making a hunt for a large dino that you can idenifty close by a bit harder to locate. Also, the populations for game modes seem to be a bit low in my taste, with conquest allowing up to 5 people per server. Other modes have different population caps, but overall it feels small. The menu UI structure also is a bit hard to get used to... with the whole menu UI coming off a bit cheap. Granted, the old menu system from two years ago was DREADFUL, and this is an improvement... it's still not up to par with most games.
However, these are nitpicks for a game that really has been risen from the ashes of it's former self. The developers are very active in the games future, and this game does have the love and dedication of a passion project come to life. There's constant free updates to this game, and new features being added all the time; as well as having the team be very approchable with ideas and suggestions. With the changes I've seen with the past two years... and (at the time of writing) a new version of the game in development which will expand on this game, allowing for new features... including a persistant open-world game mode, ala Planetside 2... I can safely say that this game has a bright future.
If you had met me two years ago and asked about this game, I would have told you to never play it... to stear clear, and forget about it... If you had bought it, to try and ask for a refund.
Nowadays, I'd be asking if you wanna buddy up and kill some dino's in a APC. It's improved that much, and I'd be MORE than willing to give it a recommendation. It's cheap, it's fun, it's OOZING with Sci-Fi goodness, and there arn't many games out there like it.
