Vastly improved since release, originally titled ORION: Dino Beatdown. Don't let the Metacritic score fool you, this game is now a shadow of it's former terrible self. The constant updates and bugfixes have transformed this game from being a very bland and broken basic shooter, to a very fun co-op survival game. The amount of equipment, customization, and vehicles; combined with many months of simplifiing the games UI, game mechanics, and constant bug fixes make the entire package a very fun way to play.
The sheer scale of battles, and the fast-paced combat make it fun. If you get a bunch of friends in on it, you'll be coordinating air strikes, tank movement, and infantry battles all in one wave. It's really something just to see two VTOL's fly above you and reign down missle fire, as two tanks flank from both sides... with troops pouring from either side, engaging a T-Rex which is more then enough to take out everything around it.
The AI has been vastly improved, as well. When the game first came out, you would have raptors blindly rush you in a straight line... and pterodactyls swooping in predictiable patterns. Now, the enemies juke and run around, the pterodactyls are hard to shoot and become the bane of any VTOL pilot. Granted, don't expect any amazing AI here, it's still a horde game and horde AI still crowns... but the game is challanging, even if you have the credits and augments to last. Underestimate a triceritops, and it'll destroy your tank in two hits with its charge attack.
In fact, the best way to describe the feeling while playing this game is like living the movie 'Avatar', but instead of Navi... you have face-ripping dinosaurs.
The game has vastly improved on bug fixes, graphics, and optimization since it came out, as well. No longer do you have memory leaks crashing your game, or textures failing to load. No longer does the game lag on high-end systems, and the graphics looking akin to a grainy mess on your screen, hidden by lens flare. The style, while still basic, has been vastly improved; comparable to the style of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. Lots of high bloom space colors, lasers, and heavy weaponary... with vechicles that look as much retro as they do futuristic; this game feels right at home... combining a 'Rad' vibe, high-tech space, and a cheesy 'B' movie feeling. The environments are lush, and the maps are large and immersive. A day-time/night-time cycle affects your visibilty and shifts your gameplay. For example, while playing on a tundra map the cold air at night will cause your visor to freeze if you stay outside in the dark for too long, requiring you to find someplace warm. Rainstorms and snowstorms can also hamper your vision, giving the dinos a leg up to ambushes.
The games three classes (assault, support, and infiltrator) have gotten a major upgrade since launch. No longer is the medic gun useless on the support toon... and no longer does the assault dominate maps. The classes seem very balanced, having their own weapons and play styles. An augment system is also in place, which allows you to purchase in-game upgrades with in-game credits you earn per round... allowing you to gain class specific upgrades like double jetpack energy for the assault, or that the support's medic gun can heal structures and vechicles. Later augments will even allow you to purchase and use other class specific weapons, like being a "boost-sniper" assault... or being a cloaked minigun assassin; as well as having the ability to canabalize raptors for health, earn more credits, or even cause the enemy who kills you to die as well. However, augments arn't permanent... and during rounds you have a finite amount of lives. Not only does dying during a wave cost you a life, but you loose all your augments that you've purchased; giving a larger penalty to death then most games do.
This game has the standard assortament of game modes like deathmatch, team deathmatch, king of the hill; along with having duel modes for both 1v1 and team. The standard horde mode exists as well, called 'survival'... but the meat and potatoes of this game is in it's conquest system, which will allow you to experience those large battles that you see on the screenshots. Players have to fight through waves of enemies, generating credits and protecting their power generator, then use those credits for upgrade, equipment, and vehicles. There's also a 'Rampage' mode that allows humans versus human dinosaurs... so you can live your dream of being a T-Rex and eating people.
The game also features an in-game store with microtransactions, using Spiral Coins:
1,000 Coins - $1.00
6,000 Coins - $5.00
13,000 Coins - $10.00
75,000 Coins - $50.00
Thankfully, this store is PURELY cosmetic with most items costing $1 dollar. No xp boosts, or in-game upgrades... the most you can purchase are hats and skins for your marine or dino. At most, I can see just spending a max of 6,000 coins to get a character the way you want him to look, unless you want to go deeper with customization.
The few things I can say bad about this game is that the maps and waves in conquest mode still seem too large. Gathering your entire army to move from base A to base B after you've spent 10 waves defending base A really doesn't make you feel like that base is 'yours'. Also, some weapons are more overpowered than others; and some items aren't that useful to invest your time into (IMHO, the flame turret). On top of that, dinos tend to 'pop in' if they're too far away... making a hunt for a large dino that you can idenifty close by a bit harder to locate. Also, the populations for game modes seem to be a bit low in my taste, with conquest allowing up to 5 people per server. Other modes have different population caps, but overall it feels small. The menu UI structure also is a bit hard to get used to... with the whole menu UI coming off a bit cheap. Granted, the old menu system from two years ago was DREADFUL, and this is an improvement... it's still not up to par with most games.
However, these are nitpicks for a game that really has been risen from the ashes of it's former self. The developers are very active in the games future, and this game does have the love and dedication of a passion project come to life. There's constant free updates to this game, and new features being added all the time; as well as having the team be very approchable with ideas and suggestions. With the changes I've seen with the past two years... and (at the time of writing) a new version of the game in development which will expand on this game, allowing for new features... including a persistant open-world game mode, ala Planetside 2... I can safely say that this game has a bright future.
If you had met me two years ago and asked about this game, I would have told you to never play it... to stear clear, and forget about it... If you had bought it, to try and ask for a refund.
Nowadays, I'd be asking if you wanna buddy up and kill some dino's in a APC. It's improved that much, and I'd be MORE than willing to give it a recommendation. It's cheap, it's fun, it's OOZING with Sci-Fi goodness, and there arn't many games out there like it.

I funded this game at Kickstarter. I have mixed feelings about the result, as much as I try to like it:
+ Size of game: Large world, much to explore, long play time. Lots of different, quite large (larger than in Fo1) cities/places. Often they have some politics with each other but usually most quests are done right at the location you are, and some quests are generic get-and-return or talk-to-and-return quests.
-  Random encounters: Only fights and traders. Fights, if in the same area, take place on the same single map, same enemies. Traders can sometimes be found, nothing special. Better to skip everything if possible.
o Only limited freedom. No real sandbox. No real open world. The game is mostly seen to be linear because you are always locked out of new places unless you progress in the story, a story which is very linear unless you take the "bad path" leading to an early-on bad ending. Along the storyline you just do whatever the Ranger HQ tells you to do, at least when it comes to the main quests. You got more freedom to do whatever you want when it comes to how you solve disputes and such, which is nice in turn.
+ NPCs: A diverse selection of followers can be selected from to join your team throughout your journeys. Practically no interaction possible with them or between them. They do however often make comments, and rarely cause an event.
-- Bugs: The game is definitely playable, but after Patch 4 there are still a lot of major bugs. Especially in the California half of the game. This game was released too early and clearly had obvious issues left at release, and the developers must have been aware of its state. Releasing a game as "finished" when it in reality is riddled with bugs, that's a BIG no-no for me!
++ Bug-Fixing and Support: The feedback on bug report is fast and they still improve the game a LOT.
o Story: While the story is in its essence very interesting, the dialogs are often not. The writing could be improved upon a lot. Aso Vargas is annoying.
- Gameplay I: Quite weak attributes and skills system. It seems they did not think this design through well enough. Some skills were also dropped pretty late in development (sneaking). Negatives: Skills are not tied to attributes at all (brute force skill 10 works as well with strength 1  as it does with any other stringth. charisma and intelligence dont affect speech or dialogue options and dont affect the 3 speech skills (smartass,kissass,kickass) in any way, etc.)  Some skills should probably have been combined into one. Over all they tried to reinvent the wheel with their system and the wheel turned out to be cubic and clunky rather than more useful and efficient. Also: each player characters needs a lot of skill points to be spent on a weapon type to hit well wit hit but then a grenade or rocket launcher has 100% accuracy on any character by default. There are also two skills written as "???" without description in the character window, and that still after 4 patches.
-- You want to open a box or safe or pick up some poo? Well, bad luck for you: Boxes, safes, doors,  poop; everything explodes in your face when touched. And the real bummer: disarming bombs, safecracking and lockpicking is extremely time-consuming even if skilled at maximum possible levels. Try a whole mine field... Medic and surgery also takes forever. It often feels like wasting my time waiting for bars to fill up when playing. It felt like this took a large part of my playtime. Even unlocking a door with a key (!!) takes about 5 seconds. Pure nuisance. At some point I started to just triggers bombs, mines and traps and eat the damage instead of defusing them because even if skilled to the max, it still takes too long to defuse everything in the game. What is also very time consuming is the movement inside locations. If entering rooms, all characters will be teleported, so you can't even split up your team leaving one character at an area's exit to shortcut running back all the way.
o Gameplay II: The fights are not overly tactical. Formations are not supported. You often have to manually position each character 1 by 1 without being able to utilise the actual grid used in fights, meaning the characters will be moved unpredictably a short distance when a fight starts. Taking cover is practically useless, yjust shooting the enemy is often better than wasting action points running around taking cover. Fights are overall fun though. Just don't expect a Jagged Alliance here.
++ Gameplay III: Lots of weapons and weapon types available in this game and weaponsmithing is fun.
o Dialogs: while you get different options in dialogs, most are just serving you some general info, repeating almost the same batches of text. When it comes down to actual choice, I often felt a bit limited despite having skilled all 3 speech skills to the necessary levels to have all options present. The skills are pretty useless because you only get to use each of them maybe 5 times in the entire game, and often they do not even lead to better results but to WORSE results which really sucks after having invested valuable points...
++ Lots of quests and lots of things to do in this world. Often you have choices to solve quests differently, but ...
-  ...the quests do however still converge to an unwanted ending in a lot of cases no matter how you approach it. Sometimes places and people cannot be saved against all logic.
-- Graphics: The art direction feels uninspired / heartless and forgettable. Generally too many saturated vivid yellow/green/brown colours, subpar shading (where is the specular lighting?), terrible AA (some bad version of FXAA was chosen whyever), sometimes random blobs of colours. It overall looks very "meh" to me, they could have done a lot better. The low-poly modeling is generally fine for third person, but unfortunately they made mistake of letting the character portraits (optionally) be zoomed-in screenshots of the character. These captures look quite awful and you would normally not even see your character that close-up so why enforce making this flaw apparent?
- Character portraits:  For your own characters, instead of the 3D snapshots, 2D portraits can be chosen. But the selection is small and some can be encountered in the game again on NPCs. However, you can add custom portraits to the game if you want. A lot of NPCs in the game unfortunately share the exact same portraits. Often the portraits are contrary to the 3D model. The character portraits repeat even on important characters creating great confusion in anyone who would try for recognise them by looking at the portrait. The descriptions given in the text can often conflict the 3D model's looks which also is contrary to the 2D portrait. Three impressions which do not go along with each other. This killed the immersion for me at times.
- Many quests have to be solved in an unintuitive and sometimes unsatisfactory way (your actions may have an effect contrary to your goal), some relevant spots inside areas are weirdly hidden (Alexey in Highpool) which took me a lot of time to find in order to solve quests. Also I often encountered situations that weren't solvable (with the outcome I wanted) with logic and speech skills (Railroad Nomads conflict). Some quests were also bugged, but this was solved now. Personally I preferred the quest-solving in Planescape or Fallout. It seemed more straight-forward there, meaning that my actions lead to the results that I wanted to achieve.
All in all I feel like this game didn't get as much love from the developers as it should have and also was released prematurely with unfinished design aspects all over the place. Some issues i mentioned might be resolved in future patches but most won't because they would require redesigning big parts of the entire game. Overall it was okay fun to play, but the buggy release make me give thumbs down.
Beat it on Legendary, but i still come back to play it.

None of the suggested workarounds on the internetz worked for me (.hof file didn't have any read only restrictions, tried changing the victory video file, switched to game's default resolution etc.). I reloaded the last save and went for domination this time, and boom - crash on the victory screen again. 80+ hours now, and while I will admit it was fun while I was learning the game, the lack of the satisfaction from registering any victories is seriously disappointing.

Now that i finished the game the review can be more accurate.
This is NOT worth it's price in any way.
It is just a watered down version of the first two Mafia games with a lot more grinding so it seems longer.
There are several issues with this title, first of which. is the fact the beginning is packed with action. and you will not be eligible for a refund when you figure out what is really happening.
If you can see pass the bugs and graphical issues, the game itself is worth playing, Not worth the whole price, but you might get it reduced.
Here's my two cents without spoiling too much:
Story:
- The main story itself is pretty good, awesome cutscenes and acting, however, Lincoln is not a very memorable person, you don't really feel the character as you did with Vito and Tommy Angelo in the first games.
- Secondary missions are a bore, you get a very limited number of activities that you have to grind through all the game.
- Main character is quite over powered.
Environment:
The city is very well designed, it is a shame i can't say the same about the textures and lighting used.
Mechanics and AI:
- Bugged missions (In the main story there are a few, but some workarounds can be used).
- A LOT of clipping, teleports and NPCs remaining stuck.
- Driving has a very arcade feel to it, even on simulation.
- Car crashes are a joke, cars barely deform and the characters receives almost no damage.
- Most objects are indestructible, even tree branches.
- NPCs teleport and animation becomes corrupt.
- NPCs are dumb, they don't really do much and when they do, they tend to glitch.
- Police doesn't really do anything (Oh look, the black man that constantly kills people just machine gunned a car full of people. Let's honk because the car full of dead people is in our way).
- Crashes (Rare, but still annoying). On the up side the game saves constantly so you will not lose much progress.
Graphics:
- Low resolution texture. It's really a shame, the city is awesome.
- Cars look like plastic, all of them.
- The neat looking rendering will glitch (elements flashing on the screen, visible collision boxes whie raining, etc).
- Lighting will glitch (Characters and object with weird glows, day/night cycle is weird and glitchy).
Sound:
- Awesome music.
- Car sounds are not realistic at all.
- There are some sound bugs and glitches (but nothing that bad).
TL:DR
Overall the game has a lot of bugs but it is playable. It is very poorly built but it can be enjoyable.

I absolutely love this game but it's not for everyone. Its essentially a simulator, but the physics are actually great unlike most simulators. The goal is essentially to pick up and deliver loads of lumber. But theres map to reveal, garages to unlock by delivering supplies, and repair and gas trailers to service your trucks (which you will need to do). Theres lots of (functional) customization to do and each truck has its own options. Including having a fully controllable crane!
The game mechanics include deforming mud. So as roads are driven on the roads will degrade visibly as you leave your ruts in your wake. Trucks have lockable differentials and all wheel drive for when you need to get through the really tough terrain, which is most of the time. Trucks that are carrying loads feel considerably heavier than empty trucks. The physics are just awesome. My gf laughs at me but I swear, I've been driving down a rough road at about 3mph, and I've been literally on the edge of my seat because I'm afraid I'm going to tip the truck and lose my load after a long trek.
If you enjoy Ice Road Truckers or watching Bonecrusher drive the muddy Maine logging roads in American Loggers, or you just love trucks like me then you're going to enjoy this game.
My one complaint, and I am not alone in this, is the camera. It is pretty unweildy but I got mostly used to it. But there are times that you just can't get the view you need. The developers claim they are going to fix this in an update but that hasn't happened yet at the time I'm writing this.
Other than that, the game delivers exactly what they say and they do it well. Highly recommended.

The game is still charming, the art is still great and the voice acting is still superb.
But it's a frustrating mess.
Honestly, I got fed up with it one hour into the second act. The story's slow and predictable progress simply gave me no incentive to trudge through the sheer tedium of solving the puzzles.
The puzzles in act 1 weren't great and have been a major point of critique from the start. You'd expect Double Fine to do a better job in act 2.
Instead, puzzle solutions are unintuitive to the point of being arcane. And when they are obvious, they are tedious.
I gave up when I had to solve a certain knot-related problem. The solution becomes obvious quickly. But so does the realization that it involves mind-numbingly slow backtracking across several screens (ALL recycled from act 1) over and over again until a certain permutation of choices is made.
If this is any indication for the remainder of the puzzles, then I'd rather watch a Let's Play. I don't know how the story ends and frankly I don't care anymore.
Which is a shame, because it looked so promising.
This is not a bad game. But it's still a disappointment and simply not worth its price. I expected more.

A great adventure game from Tim Schafer and his team, which I would recommend to every fan of the genre. For non genre fans; if you can enjoy a well made family movie with a deeper underlying story you'll certainly like the game.
The characters and the world are fantastic and quirky as you would expect it from a writer who worked on the legendary Monkey Island series. Though for a true masterpiece the game is too short and has too few locations. The puzzles are well designed, need some creativity to be solved and fit well into the presented world. The musical score by Peter McConnell is held in a modern romantic style and fits the game well, it lacks, though, a memorable main theme or motive kept throughout the score. This is admittedly difficult in such a short game with few location changes and though solid the music doesn't achieve more the being background music. The art style of the game is creative and functional at the same time and fits the story, characters and world well.
The main story, if looked at bluntly, is quite brutal. It is, however, told in a very family movie like, innocent way. It works in the game, but, in my opinion, only because the end is not completely conclusive. I would love to see the same story in a more sinister and real world like game with a closed ending. I like the degree to which the parallel story of both main characters was intertwined in the puzzles, not too much, not too little.
Overall I really enjoyed the game, including the non evitable moments when you're stuck and don't know what to do and their resolutions, as they're part of the game.

Video games critic “Yahtzee” once remarked that he didn’t understand single-player RPGs. What is the appeal? With their emphasis on story over gameplay, why not just read a (good) book? Why interrupt the (maybe good) story with some of gaming’s weakest gameplay?
Since then he’s likely discovered that there ARE good RPGs, and that good RPGs don’t emphasize story over gameplay; rather they emphasis both.
In fact, the only key difference between an “RPG” and, say, a shooter like Half-Life is that in an “RPG” the development of your avatars’ virtual skill is emphasized (via leveling up, getting more powerful items, etc.) over your muscle memory skills.
And here we have Wasteland 2, and like most old- AND new-school RPGs, it manages to emphasize neither gameplay nor story.
You may at first find this hard to notice if isometric (“old-school”) RPGs are new to you. Even I was smitten. So turned on was I that, a dozen hours into the game, I donated $30 to InExile’s Torment project (OOPS!), to be followed an hour later by Wasteland 2’s depressing emptiness finally crashing down on me (♥♥♥♥!!!). Its gameplay proved to be just drudgery. To get a picture of it, imagine XCOM, but not anywhere as good, and with the saving angel of “reloading the last save” always being available? Now consider that to play without the reload function would render the game impossible to win within a lifetime, OR SO easy (because you can change the difficulty at any time) that there’s hardly any drama at all. Now add to this an inventory system that demands so much of your “play” time (a time-destroying chore similar in fun to data entry, except you don’t get paid). Then throw in the various versions of locked doors and chests and whatnot that all have their own skill trees. I want to underscore the fact that this last feature is neither fun nor intellectually stimulating, and that you need to do it to win the game. If, InExile, you are going to make your players spend a lot of time deciding where to invest their skill points, then at least make the payoff’s worth it. Make it so there are AWESOME rewards for opening stuff—a cool joke, a sexy weapon or armor set that you won’t find from enemies or shops—not just , soon-to-be-forgotten items.
[There are also bugs, which, to their credit, they’re continuing to address.]
Now for some almost good news. The writing is almost good.
Because of the setting—a nuked one—they, like Bethesda, have gone the mostly-serious tone route. There are moments of cruelty in the game that invoke the horrors of real, demonic human beings, atrocities that happen in, say, Syria and the Congo. And sometimes it’s effective. For example, there’s a scene where a character died a horrible death, and as he or she lay dying, he or she told my party to deliver something to another character in some town. Well, I went to this town and got distracted.
And many hours later, across the Arizona map away from the town, I thought, “Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I forgot to deliver that object!” And I trudged across the game world back towards that town, knowing that it would put me in boring battles with weaker enemies. That is a moment of video game art that taught me something about myself.
Moments like these are rare in the game, and the writing is mostly grim for no other reason than to remind players that nuclear holocausts are bad.
As for strong characters; I think the leader of the Desert Rangers is named General Vargas. There’s also the Matthias guy. Aaaaand those are all the names I remember from my 50+ hours of playing.
As for the plot, it’s an uninspired, boring cliché. To give you an idea of how zero it is, consider this. During the first half of the game, in the Ranger HQ, there’s this nuclear weapon in a museum. And when you press the wrong button, the place explodes and you get a Game Over screen that says, due to there being no Desert Rangers, Matthias and his Robot Army conquer the human race. In other words, InExile do not care about their own story enough to make a truly mysterious (or at least funny) enemy; this of course explains why the plot twists are so pathetically predictable that they basically don’t exist.
The NPCs talk a lot of “who is this Matthias person” emptiness, to which I respond, “OH C’MON, HE’S OBVIOUSLY A BORING ROBOT HITLER!”
[Robot Hitler, by the way, would be a more compelling, entertaining villain than Matthias.]
So if the intellectual bits are rare, and the characters are boring, and the plot is boring, then is it funny?
Nope. There’s at least one homage to a famous comedy. But basically that’s it. Visually they could have done many funny things—this is a 3D computer game, after all—but basically we got nothing. What missed opportunities…..To underscore how much these devs missed the mark, consider this: early in the game there’s a place you can opt to rescue from a giant flora infestation. What the developers could have done with this was pit your Rangers against, say, killer salads, aided by giant, banana-toting bananas. But what did InExile do? ZOMBIES! They made it so the plants infected the local fauna, turning them into zombies. Jesus Cliché Christ.
As for the graphics in general, it’s black, brown, green and grey. There’s some red for blood.
I do like the bullets flying and the body parts falling, especially when said body parts fall because someone hit the person with a blunt object. I also like some of the lasers. And the large robots look cool. Mostly I like the fact that you can dress your group like the Three Amigos. That was fun for twelve seconds.
The game also features sound.
SCORE: 3/10

I used to own this game on my X-Box awhile back, and I loved playing it on my XBox just as much as I did replaying it on my computer. Looking forward to playing it again to find all the manuscripts and thermoses I missed. Anyway, here's what's good and what's not so good:
Pros:
Awesome story. If you love horror games with a solid storyline behind it, or you just love great plotlines in general, then this game is for you.
The use of a flashlight to mortalize your enemies was something I hadn't seen before in gaming. Granted, I don't play a whole lot of horror games, but I always admired how they combined using a light source and guns into combat.
The atmosphere of the game changes and grows increasingly menacing as the story advances, just like any good game should. As you progress through the story away from society, you get exposed to the horror aspect of this game, especially in the later episodes of the game.
Cons:
The camera control can be a giant pain a lot of the times. That's the only major issue with the game. Eventually, you learn to live with it and avoid issues with the camera, but sometimes it just happens.
Overall, the game is awesome. Not as big on horror as other games like Outlast or Amnesia, but it's still worth it for the story. May be the nostalgia talking from playing it years ago, but I love it now just as much if not more than I did then. Definitely worth buying during the summer sale...

It's still plenty fun, but I felt like I did a TON of rolling around to try and avoid uncounterables, and any lengthy time spent rolling around kinda takes the fun out of the combat. The biggest issue with this is that combat is still pretty easy. If you get low on health, run 30 yards away, drain some unsuspecting orc...and go back to the area where you were fighting the captain and use your bow. I just don't want it to be that kind of easy. I want to slay armies upon armies of orcs without my combo being broken because of annoying uncounterable stuff. I didn't buy this to finesse my way around Mordor.
That being said, this game is still great, and those issues are easily countered by the myriad of additional gameplay elements introduced. Sieges are a lot of fun, and the story is awesome. (SPOILER: I actually really liked the twist.) There are more abilities that make things interesting. Having to choose from among certain abilities actually adds an element of strategy to the game and coupled with the equipment, means that you develop multiple builds and play styles depending on the mission at hand. It works better than everyone playing the same Talion as in the previous game.
Other minor gripes:
No skip for the intro speeches from the captains. This is paramount if they're going to offer an endless mode. No one likes being interrupted in the middle of a X40 combo only to listen to 5 different orcs tell you how much you suck and how much they want to kill you. We need an option to turn off the intros or more interesting options like perhaps interrupting them with an attack. Even better...multiple interrupt options (bow, dagger, melee, etc).
I get they tried to make the zones look a bit different this time around...but things still end up looking and feeling the same. I'm not sure how they could fix this. The last game that wowed me with its zones was...well...WoW. The color palette is still rather limited (I get it...it's Morder), so it might behoove them to take things out of Mordor for the follow-up.
I'm not a canon-freak...at all. But some stuff is a tad too much. I won't spoil anything. Shelob is probably my biggest gripe. Some decisions were actually really cool...most of those surround the twist I alluded to earlier.
I feel like some abilities were absent from this game...that kinda bummed me out. I also never seemed to have enough health or focus, and I felt like I could combo runes out of those issues in the last game, and I could never find the right equipment/ability combo to avoid those issues in this one. It only takes the orcs a few hits to put you in trouble no matter which gems you choose. Focus combos are just a tad too short, because focus is in dreadfully short supply.
I'm not suggesting Talion be unstoppable...but...I might like him to be a tad more badass.
I feel like I'm just complaining. I loved this game. That's what I'll say. I couldn't stop playing it. Everyone should buy it.

The Binding Of Isaac is a game I have been playing a lot recently.  Picture running through the dungeons of Legend of Zelda, with one constant item and one item you can switch around and you have the basic setup of the game.  You start off by selecting a character which controls your starting stats and items.  Then you enter the first level of the dungeon to start your quest.  Along the way you'll collect money, bombs, and keys which you can use to get into treasure rooms, shops, arcades, secret rooms and more.  At the end of every level is a boss.  What gives the game its great replay-value is that the levels are randomly generated, as are the items you'll encounter, and the bosses are randomly picked from a group of monsters who can show up in the given area.  With over 100 items you'll end up playing through the game very differently depending on what items you can get your hands on.
The controls are very simple: shift to drop a bomb, space to use an item (if you find one that needs activation) and Q to eat a pill/use a tarot card.  Killing all the monsters in a room will give you Tarot cards, bombs, keys, pills, hearts, money, and if you are really lucky a chest.  The tarot cards have mostly good effects.  Pills can add or take away from any of your stats, so be careful with them unless you have the lucky foot or the Ph.D.  Silver chests can contain any of the above pickups including another chest.  Gold chests need a key to open, but can give you an item or a heart container in addition to what a silver chest can hold.
On every floor there should be a treasure room, represented by a crown on the map.  Make sure you save a key to get in because the items are free, and a lot of good items can only be found here.  There is also a shop on every floor, but I'd only enter if you have plenty of keys and at least 15 cents.  The good items cost 15 cents unless they are on sale.  Be prepared going into the shop, because the mini-boss Greed can be waiting inside.  If he shows up, you'll be locked into a fight with him, and will not be able to buy items when you are done.
One of the dangers you can run into are the seven deadly sins.  Acting as mini-bosses they'll randomly show up in an unexplored room to ambush you.  Luckily they aren't that difficult to defeat once you know their moves.  The hardest of them is probably greed, who shoots 3 shots in a spread somewhat randomly and tends to hang out in the shop when you need to buy something the most.
You'll also find secret rooms, challenge rooms, arcades and other interesting rooms and creatures on your journey.  Although the game is simple on the surface, there is a lot going on underneath.  Take money for example.  On the surface you can spend it at the store or gamble in a slot machine.  You'll also find a beggar who you can give it to.  Low on money?  Drop a bomb on the slot machine (or the beggar) to get some money back (hopefully).  Item Synergies are another fun thing to explore as you try and find a working strategy to get past the final bosses.  There are a few items that can instantly kill some troublesome bosses.  The trick is figuring out which ones work where and finding them.
Expect to die many times while you figure out how to get past the monsters, traps, and bosses.  And expect to have a great time doing it.  As you progress further the enemies can get pretty nasty.  But hey, there is a great item that unlocks from dying 100 times, so get to it.
Once you figure out the game, completing the entire game will only take you an hour or so(Before you figure out the game, your games will be much shorter!), but it is still very enjoyable to load up again and again, finding new items every time.  I think a lot of the reason I love it is because I know one game won't be a huge time commitment.
Pros:
List of items that might appear.
The game works on Steam.
Lots of built-in and steam enabled achievements.  The achievements will unlock new items, bosses, and areas, so they are actually worth getting beyond bragging rights.
Multiple characters and a ton of items you can find give a lot of replay value.  There are also a lot of different bosses to fight.(I'm over 60 hours myself and haven't unlocked the last bonus area yet.)
Small time commitment - Completing the entire game will only take an hour or so.
Entertaining references to many other video games such as Super Meat Boy, Legend of Zelda, and more.
Great Soundtrack!  I spent the extra dollar to have the soundtrack.  (You have to go to the steam game folder to find it.)
The game is very reasonably priced at $4.99 when it is not on sale.
Cons:
There are a few bugs with the DLC which cause the game to slow down a bit between levels.  Nothing critical or that caused me to lose my game.
As you might be able to tell from the picture above, the game has disturbing imagery.  It didn't particularly bother me, but I could see it bothering people.
The game is done in Flash and so it doesn't quite work with the steam overlay, meaning you can't upload screenshots directly into steam.
Final Thoughts:
This game is great, and well worth buying at full price.  You can usually get it much cheaper during a steam sale and the winter sale is currently going.  The Best deal for this game right now is at the humble bundle site. Pay whatever you want for BoI and the DLC and other games!
There is a DLC available for this game and it is also great and inexpensive, however, it does make the game harder.  I'd wait until you have beaten the game a few times before adding the DLC.

Putting the boring arguments about the FPS lock (it really doesn't matter) aside, I have to say that it's probably one of the most linear open world games I've played in a long time. There's barely anything to do, and it does become very repetitive very quickly.
The acting is superb, the animation is very well done, the story is fantastic - but when you just want to take a moment out and play a game - there's not much to be found.
I understand the reasoning behind wanting all activities to be story driven, or contextual, but that isn't always why players play open world games. They want escapism, they want to leave a little of themselves in the game.
There's no character customisation, that's fine - but there's also no clothing, no car modification, absolutely nothing to do with any of the money you earn. This poses an issue - what's the point?
What's he point in seeing this young gangster and his crew become richer if it changes nothing? If you can't actually use it?
The developers have stated they'll be adding 'outfit swapping' and some cosmetic car modifications in future updates - but things like this are basic for an open world game. That's the beauty of it being an open world - you can immerse yourself in it completely. With Mafia III, you can merely dip a toe in the water.
As an interactive story, it's great. As a game, it falls short on so many levels.
Of course, this is just my opinion. Many will share it, many won't. Whatever you take from the experience is your own.

Broken Age is an adventure game by Double Fine that was initially funded via Kickstarter in 2012. Now in 2015, the game is finally fully released! But the question is: does it deliver?
The story describes the coming of age of a boy (Shay) and girl (Vella). You get to play with both characters by alternating their storylines, which are interwoven in a clever way. After a certain point, alternating between characters becomes essential for progressing in the game. I found the story compelling and it motivated me to keep playing the game.
The puzzles in the game use the classic object manipulation and character interaction staples from the adventure game genre, which are executed in a appropriate and traditional way. Unfortunately, some puzzles do suffer from being too easy or having an unclear context. A bit more polish here and there would have definitely made all puzzles great. Overall, I enjoyed solving the puzzles.
From a visual perspective, Broken age has a unique and nice art style, which is definitely a selling point. Animations are crisp and the world feels very much alive thanks to a quirky cast of characters with great voice actors. The ambience the game breathes is great and it is an enjoyable environment to walk around in.
The soundtrack is also very enjoyable and it always suited the mood for the story.
In conclusion, from the perspective of an adventure game player, Broken Age might feel underwhelming, since it never tries to go beyond the classic adventure game mold. What remains is a charming game that any gamer with an open mind can appreciate, given its sense of adventure and positive spirit.

Nuclear Throne is a top down twinstick shooter simalar to The binding of Isaac or Enter the gungeon.
Your main goal as the player is to reach level 7-3 and destroy the nuclear throne!
there are many chracter unlocks weapons items secrets and progression to keep you busy.
there is also a daily mode where you can compete against people all over the world to see who can get the most amount of kills and how many loops you can do! (1  loop is being the nuclear throne once)

the largest strenght this game has is the "one more go" mentality i feel like i open nuclear throne around 15-20 times a day just to get my fix of killing alot of things with a huge selection of weapons.
each character has their own abilities that make you play each character very differently
eg. crystal can withstand bullets and doesnt need to hide to avoid damage. if you run our of ammo with most characters it become useless but with robot and chicken you can throw your weapon (chicken) or eat your weapon to gain ammo for something else (robot)
Overall there is something here for everyone looking to have a quick blast of exitement and for people looking to buy this game but arnt too sure about the price wait for a sale because at any reduced price this game is worth every penny!
The only issues and gripes i have with NT is that deaths feel too sudden and really underwhelming the game is sometimes down to luck depending on what mutations you get and weapon finds and sometimes i dont even know how i died or how to imporve.
for new players looking for tips i would reccomend sticking with one chraracter until you beat the game a few times it took me around 40 tries to kill the throne might take a bit more for you since i record and see my mistakes which is also reccomend doing!

*DISCLAIMER*
In this review, I'm going to assume you have already seen enough footage to get what the game is about and what it contains. I'm not going to explain what the game is about, what the end goal is, etc.
Ok, so I'm going to go on a limb here and say that Nuclear Throne has been and still is my favorite game of all time. However, I have a soft spot for rogue-lites like this one, so I'm going to try and be as honest as possible. First, a list of pros and cons for easy viewing.
PROS:
+Amazing replayability
+Variety in weapons, mutations, etc.
+Incentive to keep playing with weekly and daily challenges
+Unique characters
+Neato soundtrack
+Smooth learning curve
+This game gets me hard
CONS:
-Late game becomes cluttered and confusing
-With enough playtime, getting new unlocks becomes extremely tedious
-You have to rely on RNG for a really good run
My only severe problems with Nuclear Throne is that the late game can become extremely confusing, and when your run ends it seems to come out of nowhere. Other than that, if you are a sucker for fast paced action games, or rogue lites such as Enter the Gungeon, you are going to have a blast with this game. And even if you don't, you will still enjoy the experience. This game's got excitement out the wazoo, and anyone will have fun with it. I give this vidya game a solid 4/5.

There's a lot of gore, but the game's cohesiveness, both in tone and visual style, make it so it's actually acceptable and not tasteless. The arcade gameplay, designed to have you try all options and strategies, works wonderfully thanks to the absence of death penalties ad the quick restart; the controls are simple and immediate, yet manage to make you do crazy stuff, like ricocheting weapons and enemies against each-others. The level design and missions are the main drawbacks of the game, they're too samey, with not enough new mechanics added as you progress and lacking a balanced learning curve: at a certain point the game simply starts throwing heaps of enemies after you and making the levels longer and longer. The plot keeps you interested throughout the game, even though it's a little confused at times; the twists are unexpected and the ending is pretty out there (maybe a little too much). The setting and acid coloured artstyle, which are a very unique take on the genre, together with the incredible soundtrack and the dirty, bloody hallucinations sprinkled through the game, create an immersive dream-like experience.

I used to own this game on my X-Box awhile back, and I loved playing it on my XBox just as much as I did replaying it on my computer. Looking forward to playing it again to find all the manuscripts and thermoses I missed. Anyway, here's what's good and what's not so good:
Pros:
Awesome story. If you love horror games with a solid storyline behind it, or you just love great plotlines in general, then this game is for you.
The use of a flashlight to mortalize your enemies was something I hadn't seen before in gaming. Granted, I don't play a whole lot of horror games, but I always admired how they combined using a light source and guns into combat.
The atmosphere of the game changes and grows increasingly menacing as the story advances, just like any good game should. As you progress through the story away from society, you get exposed to the horror aspect of this game, especially in the later episodes of the game.
Cons:
The camera control can be a giant pain a lot of the times. That's the only major issue with the game. Eventually, you learn to live with it and avoid issues with the camera, but sometimes it just happens.
Overall, the game is awesome. Not as big on horror as other games like Outlast or Amnesia, but it's still worth it for the story. May be the nostalgia talking from playing it years ago, but I love it now just as much if not more than I did then. Definitely worth buying during the summer sale...

10/10 not a point less.

The Binding Of Isaac is a game I have been playing a lot recently.  Picture running through the dungeons of Legend of Zelda, with one constant item and one item you can switch around and you have the basic setup of the game.  You start off by selecting a character which controls your starting stats and items.  Then you enter the first level of the dungeon to start your quest.  Along the way you'll collect money, bombs, and keys which you can use to get into treasure rooms, shops, arcades, secret rooms and more.  At the end of every level is a boss.  What gives the game its great replay-value is that the levels are randomly generated, as are the items you'll encounter, and the bosses are randomly picked from a group of monsters who can show up in the given area.  With over 100 items you'll end up playing through the game very differently depending on what items you can get your hands on.
The controls are very simple: shift to drop a bomb, space to use an item (if you find one that needs activation) and Q to eat a pill/use a tarot card.  Killing all the monsters in a room will give you Tarot cards, bombs, keys, pills, hearts, money, and if you are really lucky a chest.  The tarot cards have mostly good effects.  Pills can add or take away from any of your stats, so be careful with them unless you have the lucky foot or the Ph.D.  Silver chests can contain any of the above pickups including another chest.  Gold chests need a key to open, but can give you an item or a heart container in addition to what a silver chest can hold.
On every floor there should be a treasure room, represented by a crown on the map.  Make sure you save a key to get in because the items are free, and a lot of good items can only be found here.  There is also a shop on every floor, but I'd only enter if you have plenty of keys and at least 15 cents.  The good items cost 15 cents unless they are on sale.  Be prepared going into the shop, because the mini-boss Greed can be waiting inside.  If he shows up, you'll be locked into a fight with him, and will not be able to buy items when you are done.
One of the dangers you can run into are the seven deadly sins.  Acting as mini-bosses they'll randomly show up in an unexplored room to ambush you.  Luckily they aren't that difficult to defeat once you know their moves.  The hardest of them is probably greed, who shoots 3 shots in a spread somewhat randomly and tends to hang out in the shop when you need to buy something the most.
You'll also find secret rooms, challenge rooms, arcades and other interesting rooms and creatures on your journey.  Although the game is simple on the surface, there is a lot going on underneath.  Take money for example.  On the surface you can spend it at the store or gamble in a slot machine.  You'll also find a beggar who you can give it to.  Low on money?  Drop a bomb on the slot machine (or the beggar) to get some money back (hopefully).  Item Synergies are another fun thing to explore as you try and find a working strategy to get past the final bosses.  There are a few items that can instantly kill some troublesome bosses.  The trick is figuring out which ones work where and finding them.
Expect to die many times while you figure out how to get past the monsters, traps, and bosses.  And expect to have a great time doing it.  As you progress further the enemies can get pretty nasty.  But hey, there is a great item that unlocks from dying 100 times, so get to it.
Once you figure out the game, completing the entire game will only take you an hour or so(Before you figure out the game, your games will be much shorter!), but it is still very enjoyable to load up again and again, finding new items every time.  I think a lot of the reason I love it is because I know one game won't be a huge time commitment.
Pros:
List of items that might appear.
The game works on Steam.
Lots of built-in and steam enabled achievements.  The achievements will unlock new items, bosses, and areas, so they are actually worth getting beyond bragging rights.
Multiple characters and a ton of items you can find give a lot of replay value.  There are also a lot of different bosses to fight.(I'm over 60 hours myself and haven't unlocked the last bonus area yet.)
Small time commitment - Completing the entire game will only take an hour or so.
Entertaining references to many other video games such as Super Meat Boy, Legend of Zelda, and more.
Great Soundtrack!  I spent the extra dollar to have the soundtrack.  (You have to go to the steam game folder to find it.)
The game is very reasonably priced at $4.99 when it is not on sale.
Cons:
There are a few bugs with the DLC which cause the game to slow down a bit between levels.  Nothing critical or that caused me to lose my game.
As you might be able to tell from the picture above, the game has disturbing imagery.  It didn't particularly bother me, but I could see it bothering people.
The game is done in Flash and so it doesn't quite work with the steam overlay, meaning you can't upload screenshots directly into steam.
Final Thoughts:
This game is great, and well worth buying at full price.  You can usually get it much cheaper during a steam sale and the winter sale is currently going.  The Best deal for this game right now is at the humble bundle site. Pay whatever you want for BoI and the DLC and other games!
There is a DLC available for this game and it is also great and inexpensive, however, it does make the game harder.  I'd wait until you have beaten the game a few times before adding the DLC.

I wish I could give this a neutral rating. But having to choose positive or negative, I'd say positive in the end except for some complaints / bad design decisions:
1. Monotonous grind in Act 4. You're going to be doing the same thing over and over again defending your fortress, or if you fail, attacking numerous times in order to get the best ending.
2. RNG. You might come up on a warlord that has the worst immunities/strengths possible and you're going to have to kill him somehow in order to capture a fortress and progress. Maybe you should visit the in-game store and get some loot chests? *bleh*
3. Betrayal system. This shouldn't even be there in my opinion. If you recruit someone they should stay in their ranks, it doesn't add any value to gameplay, only to lengthen the game time.
4. Sticky controls. What I mean when traversing rooftops or other objects, the character sticks to ledges too easily. Sometimes the simplest tasks such as jumping off or trying to climb down are a pain.
5. No Chance. Sometimes you might get stunlocked by an enemy and a captain with No Chance finishes you off. It happens and its /facepalm time. Also, the extra talent to give you second chance at come back gets negated by it.
6. Balancing issues, this is both be a curse and a blessing. As you keep defending you fortress in Act 4, the enemies obviously get stronger. There's a tactic that I have been employing to get through Act 4 easily, yes it cheapens the gameplay, by then again, when you're doing the same thing over and over again without any reward, mind as well do it.I don't want to spoil it but it simply makes the gameplay stale. I`ll just say that some skills are overpowered such as the "blink" dominate.
7. No dialogue skip. This one is by far one of the most enraging aspects of the game. You cannot skip a dialogue from a captain/commander/warlord. Its kinda sad to see some low level captain ambush and taunt you for 30 seconds just to be slaughtered in the next moment. In the sieges later on, you will be sitting and waiting for the dialogue to finish for over a minute when the enemy gets into your fortress and 3-4 captains show up at once (multiply that by the number of waves incoming). This simply bad game design in my opinion. Also, you'll hear the same taunts over and over again as you progress through the game...
8. "War Chests" I could care less about someone else wanting to spend money for in-game items. Yes, in my opinion its dumb, but then again, it's their money. The reason I categorize it as a con is that many games are implementing this and along with DLC it just shortens/ruins gameplay in the end.
With DLC, you usually have content cuts. And with loot boxes, using Shadow of War as an example, you have game design decisions that center around them (RNG strengths/weaknesses, monotonous grind, overlords level up if you fail to overtake the fortress). The mindset around designing games lately has been in the wrong direction with some major releases (Cow Doody WII, Shadow of War, Assassin's Creed: Origins, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided) to name a few. Hopefully this might change in the future.

I'll try to keep this review short but with a valid and simple core to help you understand why
haven't enjoyed this game too much.
For me games should be an adventure, you know, depth, pace, experience, twists, surprises and this game for the most  part was. Anyone who knows how to screw around, have fun but still be efficient orc slaying machine would know that 70-80% of the skills and "upgrades" were below "optional". Why go with an ability that increases your might from Stealth kills, that hardly really matters when you have to fight 90% of the game 1.vs.legion, than with an ability that triples your Might generation from successful attacks, that works well with chain executions that you can almost every 4th or 5th attack (2-3 crits, which also comboes well with crit abilities) chain to kill and stack your hit-streak on multiple orcs, instakilling them and giving you an instant edge in the battle? Or you can use that might to insta drain/dominate orcs, or deal different types of aoe dot effects and wiping that army down instantly. I dont understand, it hardly lets you be creative with your builds and playstyles.
Lets talk about gear, which is also a good part of the game... And it bored me. Early Legendaries are boring, leveling them up is like going to the gym... but already exhausted for banging your neighbors daughter. Legendaries a re supposed to be Legendary, tho you seem to find 1 legendary orc after 3 turns... Wheres the "legendary" in that?.. WoW's combat and the feeling of success when you finaly get that one Achievement, even tho it doesnt do jack...) I cant say that this game grindfest satisfying at all... Either sitting there for 3 minutes to Pokemon your orcs, or babysitting them on an ambush is just boring, not rewarding...

Shadow of War has improved on almost everything from Shadow of Mordor (besides a few bugs) and then ruined it all with their loot boxes.
As you probably know, loot boxes give you weapons, orcs, orc powerups and XP boosts.
You can buy the low level loot boxes with the in game Silver you get, and you get a lot of it. You can also pony up and spend real money on Gold to buy high level loot boxes (you can also get some Gold from daily challenges).
And the result of the loot boxes is that
.
In Shadow of Mordor, the only way to get loot was killing captains. Getting a powerful weapon was an achievement. You would send death threats to the most powerful captains, making them more powerful, learn their weaknesses, then have a really tough fight to beat them. Now I can spend some of my free in game silver money to get a loot box which gives me 2 fairly decent bits of loot. The sense of acheivement is gone completely, there is literally no incentive to kill captains now, its always better to recruit them.
Then there are the orcs. It seems like they have decided to make the game massive and grindy near the end to encourage you to fast track some of that by buying orcs loot boxes. So they made the end of the game super boring and repetitive because of the loot boxes.
The very fact that loot boxes are in a game means they will want to provide incentives to buy them, which results in creating time consuming elements to encourage people to skip them. Its the same as what happened to mobile games, but now we are seeing it in full priced AAA games and it is resulting in a game that is boring as hell in the second part.
I, like other reviewers, haven't finished the game, because it is not fun to play after a certain point.
I loved Shadow of Mordor and prepurchased Shadow of War, and yes I thoroughly enjoyed the short time I have played, but I am sad that loot boxes turned this game from a gem into a turd. I honestly looked forward to this since the first game and I am bitterly disappointed.

Review Update: 17.Jan.2017:
________________________
Greetings spacefarers!
It's been quite a while since I have updated this review and after Warballoon asking me to look into it again at christmas, I did.
One thing is for sure: They improved the games a LOT. I remember it being a pile of massive bugs and while the game is not "perfect" in its current state, I really have to say that the Devs did an amazing job.
The game runs a lot smoother, the interface has been polished, the station is more than a decoration and a safe haven and the Crew actually is doing jobs... more or less.
Ship-Combat finally feels like it's going somewhere and the missions as far as I've seen them are diverse. Of course this is just the foundation and I hope in time there will be different ways to win a battle.
CQC still is a mess though. Apparently weapons have ammo (Vanishing pistol of two crew member), and your Crew is unable to even hit a barn door with it. With no cover-system, weak weapons and quite an overpowered healing ability, battles are not challenging.
Overall: The game is progressing in a way that is recommendable, that is if you are interested at looking at ALPHA-Gameplay and helping Warballoon out. If you are interested in enjoying the game for a longer period of time, do not buy it yet! For this it's way too unfinished at the moment.
Since we don't have a middle way for recommending games, I'll try to go with the perception of the common gamer and stay at "No".
Review Update 13. December 2017:
_____________________________
I really gotta say, the game came a long, long way.
I've seen several design updates and a lot of polishing.
Gotta say that the HUD is working nearly perfectly and I figured out most of the stuff by myself.
The station has some nifty shops that you can use to replenish supplies or buy new stuff, though I gotta say that a lot of stuff is imbalanced yet, including prices for stuff.
What I really, really dig is the perk-system, though it needs some polishing too.
Only perks that are available for the class of the crewman/woman should be visible.
Sadly as before the game really lacks when it comes to combat:
The fact that you have to destroy "hull tiles" makes is really difficult sometimes to destroy a ship, especially if an indestructible generator or other object blocks the path.
Combat on ships feels really lacking: Either you have good equipment and a large or advanced Crew or you'll get killed.
A further huge minus is the inability to disable a ship by taking their crew out, making it impossible to tackle a fight differently.
I'm really looking forward to seeing more updates, especially gameplay wise.
Zargul out~

Where it falls down are puzzles requiring information found in the other character's quest. On more than one occasion I found myself stumped my an impossible puzzle and having to resort to the internet for hints only to find out that the answer lay at the end of the other character's story.
Overall it's a well presented if flawed adventure game that's well worth your time if you enjoy adventure games. With a similar difficulty curve to Monkey Island, you'll find yourself retracing your steps over and over until you realise you've thought too logically about a puzzle.
Recommended, although bring a notepad and a stress reliever.

Man, I hate giving this game a negative review. I really wanted this♥♥♥♥♥♥to be awesome. I never really played adventure games before Broken Age's kickstarter happened, and the genre just seemed to explode in popularity.
The first Act of the game was great. Superb. Loved it. Interesting world, interesting puzzles that made me go DOH!, fun characters (even if they could be a bit one dimensional sometimes). The tone of the game was calm despite what drove the two main characters.
Then Act II came out. And... eeeeeh.
The big chunk of Act II for both characters is a very long fetch quest. Or at least it feels that way. A very, very long segment that prevents the story from progressing. In Act II, each puzzle pushed me closer to the next grand environment. In Act I, I was running around all the environments I'd already gone to, and it just wasn't as fun.
Both stories blow their big twists very quickly, which are ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Problem is that I consider them the climax, as the game feels like it just wants to end after that, but feels like it needs to live up to what I hear are 'classic adventure game puzzles', which to me just felt obtuse and forced me to get hints online.
Everything just began to feel rushed after the twists. Knowing Double Fine's budget problems behind the scenes, I understand why this is the case, but the game's still unsatisfying.
I'm a bit bummed by the lack of Merek at the end. The conversations you get to have with him are awesome. But I wanted more of him. He's my favorite character in a cast of characters I really enjoyed (outside Vella's family, which I don't think got enough screen time to feel important like Shay's 'mom' and 'dad').
So when you get to the end, it feels like everything is on a timer and death is soon to come if you don't act NOW. I understand putting a timer on the game would pressure puzzle fans, and I don't want a timer. But I would have enjoyed if the characters seemed more stressed out. There is an entire gang of characters sitting around and doing nothing. I know they can't really do much, but they just seem grumpy or otherwise docile.
The ending is weak. Won't get into it, but I considered it weak.

Don't normally do reviews, but I had to do one to counter the numpties who are posting about the Take 2 / GTA 5 issue.
To compare GTA 5 and KSP is, quite frankly, beyond ridiculous. GTA 5 is a massive AAA title with a budget over $200 million. KSP was made with shoestring and a piece of chewing gum. GTA 5 is a game with a massive online component. KSP is a purely single player experience (unless you use the unreliable multiplayer mod). GTA 5 is a game that is enhanced by mods, but mods aren't a necessity. KSP is a game where mods are a necessity.
KSP is a game that thrives on the mod community. Is KSP likely to end up with paid DLC, micro-transaction and a multiplayer component? No. KSP 2 would be the game that ends up with all those things. Will Take 2 get things right with a KSP2? Who knows. If they mess up KSP 2, then so be it. Under Squad, there would never have been another KSP, guarenteed.
However, this is about KSP, the first one. KSP will not undergo major changes. Maybe we'll get some DLC packs (such as the historical missions pack that is in the works), but major changes won't happen. It's not worth it. The game is too much of a hodge-podge, a legacy of the way it was created.
To make this relevant - KSP is a fun, challenging and sometimes downright frustrating game. It has a steep learning curve and you could spend hundreds of hours and still not master everything. 200 hours in and I still consider myself a newbie. Don't let the numpties put you off.

I'm about 50/50 on this game. It's meant to be a Butterfly Effect style game, like Until Dawn, for example (Which I highly reccommend). But the problem is, there's not too many "Drastic choices". In other Butterfly Effect games (Once again, I will be using Until Dawn as a comparison because I'm currently playing through it and I love it) there are actual game changing decisions, ***SPOILERS*** For example, when Chloe gets her leg stuck in the train track, you have to save her. In a game like Until Dawn, a true butterfly effect game, if you don't get someone out of those train tracks they're gone. No "Mission Failed". They're dead.. Pretty much the only game changers is when Kate may or may not die (Depending on the choices you make) and the end. But the end doesn't matter that much since it's the end. No direct sequel, no playing after it, nothing. So the ending doesn't change the course of the game really. ***SPOILER END*** What I'm saying is this is a fun game, cool characters, good story, some good twists at points. But I don't see it as a butterfly effect game, since the choices don't really matter. You want a true butterfly effect game? Play Until Dawn. The choices actually matter, it has a good plot, (Minor Spoiler****) It has some good curveballs to it.. I listed that as a spoiler so it doesn't really ruin anything and so you don't expect them. That's the point of twists and stuff afterall, even though it will seem very cliche at first. (****Minor Spoiler END) To wrap up, A) This is a good game, just not a good Butterfly Effect game, if that's what your looking for. B) Suggestion, if you're looking for a butterfly effect game, PICK UNTIL DAWN! And if your a good graphics lover like me, it is an incredible game in that aspect, and really in all aspects. Variety of character personalities, hundreds of different ways the game could go. By that I mean there are so many small choices that could catch up to you later, even the smallest of things, which is the point of the Butterfly effect.. you know.. "Go back in time, step on a butterfly, go back to the present and it's World War V and half the population is dead" kinda thing. This turned into an Until Dawn review very quickly.. Verdict: Good game. Reccommendations: Get Until Dawn instead. Life Is Strange is still good, but Until Dawn is better :/ And cheap. And awesome. I need to shut up now.

Please note that this negative review isn't to say that the game was bad or to discourage people from buying it.  I'm giving this a negative review in hopes of telling Tim Schafer and Double Fine to not repeat the painfully irresponsible methods they took to release this game.
Don't get me wrong, I loved this game.  The art is great, the characters are interesting, the world is interesting and the story is compelling!
Those are the reasons this should be my favorable, most memorable gaming experiences of all time ... but it isn't, it can't be.  Because for the longest time, it was unfinished, it was only half a game.
I am a fairly impatient guy, I can admit, but this goes beyond the need for patience.  I have become unimaginably frustrated with this recent "release by episode" phase that games have been going through ever since telltale games made it big.  I'm not mad just because I have to wait, but because companies have been using it as a method for being lazy and inconsistent with their work.
In this case especially it was basically "You want an amazing new point and click adventure?  Well here's half a game, hope that tides you over for awhile."  The deadline for "awhile" kept being pushed back further and further until and entire year and a half went by for the 2nd half this game to be released, a game that had already had over two years for planning and developing, and over 3 MILLION dollars of crowd sourcing behind it's back.
Long story short there was a unbelievable amount of support and motivation for this game, and yet somehow Tim and Double Fine seemed all but motivated to finish it.
But I've ranted long enough already.  Again I hope i haven't discouraged you from buying this game, it truly is an amazing story ... but it could have been SO much more if Tim and Double Fine had the ability to follow through with their promises and actually plan out the development of a game.

I would recommend Spintires to anyone with an interest in off-road driving. If you don't like driving and getting stuck in the mud, stick to Forza or truck simulators. Spintires will certainly not appeal to everyone, and so I would highly suggest to check out the Tech Demo at
if you think you're not sure.  I have been waiting a long time for a game like this and I knew I'd enjoy it from the time I viewed the screens and trailer.  I feel like I speak for many others when I say that Spintires has filled a pretty big hole in our video gaming realm.  A hole that some games had only dreamed of filling but didn't have the fluff.  There has been an absolute absence of off-roading games that actually portray the idea of being OFF the road.  We've played the games in which the dirt roads may as well be a mall parking lot, sure you might see your tread marks left in the dirt but you would never really have any trouble traversing the trail.  When you start playing Spintires you will find within minutes that you are far from that well kept highway or state road and become very skillful at planning your route to always be within range of a sturdy tree to winch yourself out WHEN you get stuck.  Each time you drive the same road your own tires dig the ruts deeper to make it more difficult the next time you pass.
If you're looking for a racing game, this is not for you.
If you're looking for a game with a in-depth story line, this is not for you.

Add one or two fixed camera modes and leave the current one as a preference.

There's a lot of gore, but the game's cohesiveness, both in tone and visual style, make it so it's actually acceptable and not tasteless. The arcade gameplay, designed to have you try all options and strategies, works wonderfully thanks to the absence of death penalties ad the quick restart; the controls are simple and immediate, yet manage to make you do crazy stuff, like ricocheting weapons and enemies against each-others. The level design and missions are the main drawbacks of the game, they're too samey, with not enough new mechanics added as you progress and lacking a balanced learning curve: at a certain point the game simply starts throwing heaps of enemies after you and making the levels longer and longer. The plot keeps you interested throughout the game, even though it's a little confused at times; the twists are unexpected and the ending is pretty out there (maybe a little too much). The setting and acid coloured artstyle, which are a very unique take on the genre, together with the incredible soundtrack and the dirty, bloody hallucinations sprinkled through the game, create an immersive dream-like experience.

Interactive stories like these are a few, but man is this a treasure. If you like these kind of games even a little. Do yourself a favor and play it. I hope it makes you cry. Best cry I've had in years.

I wish I could give this a neutral rating. But having to choose positive or negative, I'd say positive in the end except for some complaints / bad design decisions:
1. Monotonous grind in Act 4. You're going to be doing the same thing over and over again defending your fortress, or if you fail, attacking numerous times in order to get the best ending.
2. RNG. You might come up on a warlord that has the worst immunities/strengths possible and you're going to have to kill him somehow in order to capture a fortress and progress. Maybe you should visit the in-game store and get some loot chests? *bleh*
3. Betrayal system. This shouldn't even be there in my opinion. If you recruit someone they should stay in their ranks, it doesn't add any value to gameplay, only to lengthen the game time.
4. Sticky controls. What I mean when traversing rooftops or other objects, the character sticks to ledges too easily. Sometimes the simplest tasks such as jumping off or trying to climb down are a pain.
5. No Chance. Sometimes you might get stunlocked by an enemy and a captain with No Chance finishes you off. It happens and its /facepalm time. Also, the extra talent to give you second chance at come back gets negated by it.
6. Balancing issues, this is both be a curse and a blessing. As you keep defending you fortress in Act 4, the enemies obviously get stronger. There's a tactic that I have been employing to get through Act 4 easily, yes it cheapens the gameplay, by then again, when you're doing the same thing over and over again without any reward, mind as well do it.I don't want to spoil it but it simply makes the gameplay stale. I`ll just say that some skills are overpowered such as the "blink" dominate.
7. No dialogue skip. This one is by far one of the most enraging aspects of the game. You cannot skip a dialogue from a captain/commander/warlord. Its kinda sad to see some low level captain ambush and taunt you for 30 seconds just to be slaughtered in the next moment. In the sieges later on, you will be sitting and waiting for the dialogue to finish for over a minute when the enemy gets into your fortress and 3-4 captains show up at once (multiply that by the number of waves incoming). This simply bad game design in my opinion. Also, you'll hear the same taunts over and over again as you progress through the game...
8. "War Chests" I could care less about someone else wanting to spend money for in-game items. Yes, in my opinion its dumb, but then again, it's their money. The reason I categorize it as a con is that many games are implementing this and along with DLC it just shortens/ruins gameplay in the end.
With DLC, you usually have content cuts. And with loot boxes, using Shadow of War as an example, you have game design decisions that center around them (RNG strengths/weaknesses, monotonous grind, overlords level up if you fail to overtake the fortress). The mindset around designing games lately has been in the wrong direction with some major releases (Cow Doody WII, Shadow of War, Assassin's Creed: Origins, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided) to name a few. Hopefully this might change in the future.
I'd say go ahead get this if you like spending 30+ hours in a game and if you liked the first one. Otherwise be preppared to rage if you're not used to the series.
