I did a review that touched on the strengths and weaknesses of this game a while back. It falls short on a lot of things.

First things first, I do believe this game is definitely similar enough to Overwatch. But it isn't a direct copy. And if I were to call it a direct copy, it's a GOOD direct copy.
Here are some great things to say about this game: There are several different game modes to play and several different characters to choose from. It has a competitive scene already forming. It is still being updated with big content updates. This game compared to other free to plays isn't very pay to win. And many more.
This game does have some problems though. I have encountered some bugs, and it definitely needs some balancing. Certain characters are clearly better than others, so much so that they are generally on every team you are going to face against / play with. I also dislike the fact that characters are variable, so you can make your character be good at the things you want. So one player can be totally different from another player playing the same character just based on the cards and skills they chose. I personally would prefer if they just added more characters instead of making each character variable. Overwatch does not have this problem.
That being said, this game isn't bad at all. It's a great alternative to Overwatch especially if you aren't willing to pay the $40 for Overwatch. And I definitely expect it to become much better and more balanced in the future.

Wasteland 2 is finally here, courtesy of Kickstater, and for all the good it does to the genre, it's still a mixed bag.
//Contains spoilers//
It opens up really nice, with a live-action intro, thrusting you into the unforgiving, post-apocaliptic setting as you bury a fellow ranger. A scene later and you notice a unique shotgun straped to the hip of a nearby guard, all thanks to your perception skill, and with a little bit of convincing (another skill) you can make it yours. Across the bridge you can charm yourself a butt-kicking goat companion, which raises one of your ability scores by 1. And all that's in the very first, small area.
It's a great start, I found myself thinking, and if this reflects the rest of the game, I'm sold. Love me some world that actually reacts to my character build.
Unfortunately it isn't so. Perception soon becomes mainly a mine/trap finding tool, and truth be told, at some point it's simply better to detonate the explosives and accept the blast directly, then to try disarming any of them. There goes role-playing. Try watching the same disarming animation over and over and over again, and you will know what I mean. You are better off using a healing skill every once in a while. You can still find some buried junk using it, but it gets somewhat underwhelming after the initial shotgun surprize.
Taking about junk, You will easily find yourself at weight capacity carrying around all the junk you just found, hoping that someone somewhere may want it. And they do, but the game gives no hints as to just who may be interested in baby wipes. You may just as well gather all you can before you leave Arizona, and re-visit every single npc in the world looking for dialogue cues. And did I mention there are regular junk tems, and shiny junk items? Yeah. And when you use the Sell All Junk button at stores, the UI is hell-bent on selling the shiny ones too, even after you specifically flag them as not junk.
Item management in Wasteland 2 is a game on its own. You can't see your character's weight capacity on the merchant screen, you can't compare weapons with the ones you have in second hand slot, and you can't compare trinkets. All the clothing items look the same in the inventory screen, so unless you want to spend additional time trying them on and seeing what they actually look like, you will just sell them, like me. Armor does nothing to change the way you look, and the merchants screen gets really laggy when there are a lot of items.
The game has its moments, but they seem very few and far between. There is one giant robot fight, well three if you count fighting the same robot model again, and then its flame-throwing cousin. Yep, no huge mutant creatures, and no big♥♥♥♥♥bosses for you. The combat works at the bare minimum, and may get stale pretty quick. There is little excitement to be had on that front, and 95% percent of enemies can be taken out by a single shot from an RPG-7 if you get the enemies to clump together. Imagine my dissapointment when I finally got to fight Dugan, one of the few uniques bosses, and he went down in a single rocket blast. True, you can tune up difficulty, but as far as I know it only decreases your damage and incresases enemy's. And the last thing I wanted was to have weapons which don't do the damage they have in their description. How about more enemies? Or more hp for them at the very least. Ehh.
Random encounters have all the same flavour. Fight enemies, fight enemies. I got some barbecuing cannibals once, which seemed like a unique encounter, but the excitement was gone as soon as they attacked. In the end I just raised my outdoorsman skill, and tried to skip them alltogether. Had enough of the simplistic combat in other areas.
I found two different merchants braving the wastes, but they didn't even seem to re-stock. Curiously enough, one of them actually attacked me when I refused to buy anything, and it was a nice little way to spice things up. But still – Fallout 2 had it in spades and done better.
Then there are...bugs. Visual bugs, dialogue bugs, and of course quest-breaking bugs. Take your pick. There are whole forum threads on how to complete the Hollywood questline. There are people who spent hours on end, saving and reloading, trying to finish up quests in the correct order just to get the quest log cleaned up. Hats off to them. Personally, I could not get to finish the quest where Heidi asks my rangers to help her take over the Bastion of Faith. Hell, I could not even talk to her anymore. Her dialogue screen went blank. No “Hello”, no nothing. At this point I just said ♥♥♥♥ it and rushed to the ending. I don't know perhaps I talked to someone I should not have.
If that's all that could be achieved with nearly 3 million dollars, I shiver to think what the game would feel like if the devs got only what they asked for - a mere 900k. The games gets patches regularly, so there's hope. But for any potential buyer, I would suggest to wait a few months (and I thought I did that...) and try it then. Hopefully your experience will be better than mine.
Do I regret buying it? No. Am I planning on re-playing it? No.
The game's a good effort, and has some heart, but the brain is just not there yet. And just because it's a long-awaited sequel, it should not get a free pass.

Alan Wake had a huge name before I even knew what it was about. Rumours and small spoils motivated me to play it for myself. On 1 May 2015 I finally set out on this adventure as a well known, cocky, used book writer who went on a retreat to Bright Falls in Washington, USA. It sets off on a slow pace and introduces you to all basic concepts and details.
The main goal of Alan Wake was to create an immersive movie or story with little effort needed from the viewer, they achieved this with simple controls and an easy difficulty to play on. Do not be fooled and think that the entire story is all fun and games, at the end of each episode everything would get intense, hordes of taken would appear leaving you to fight or flee for your life.
Categorised as a thriller I back the entire game, dwelling in silence with illuminating glare from the moon evolves slowly into a suspenseful walk with atmospheric music setting the tone of every scene. Even the classic jump scares are included, strolling through a home when suddenly a taken busts through the door charging you with al there is. Some were predictable and some were not, but balanced and not worn out.
Physical gameplay felt unnatural and sloppy but to be fair it was a conversion form Xbox to PC. Minor glitches like getting stuck on something or jumping and getting stuck but no big problems.
Graphics….. This was hard, reviewing in 2015 vs back in 2010 is quite a difference seeing that my GTX 760 made mincemeat of any graphical requirement it threw my way. Certain unpleasantness struck me in cinematics due to visible comers and edges, Alan’s Face his hands ect.
BUT
Comparing to other titles released in 2010 it seems like the quality of visuals were up to standard, titles like Mass Effect 2, Just Cause 2, Assassin’s creed Brotherhood also had some of these characteristics that feels unpleasant to the eyes.
This story was amazing and immersive…
At first they make you compare yourself to Alan, at this stage you would feel all his pain. Then they drop an unravelling bomb on you where you start to hate our Hero, after a while you start agreeing again and feel his drive, anger, hatred and determination to finish his adventure.
At the very end the unthinkable happens and they leave you on the biggest cliff-hanger ever created by mankind.
They later on released special episodes 1 and 2 which continues the story after the story, these were not as good as the main story but also deserves your attention.  It does not really enlighten you about happenings after and if you can shut off your entire brain and only receive entertainment through playing games, I would implore you to do this as the FINAL
did not give any closure and generated more hope than was needed.
Unfortunately it seems that Alan Wake 2 will not make an appearance in the future, Quantum break releasing exclusively to Xbox one will receive this title. Producers and directors feel that it is not within the age or time to make a new Title to this extremely awesome piece of art and creative immersion.
My next game would be Alan Wakes American Nightmare.
Hit the review section up to see may say in a months’ time.
FINAL VERDICT: ABSOLUTE YES, Add it to your rich-story category in your library.

Great action adventure with a fantastic story! The story alone is what kept me playing for 15 hours. The visuals and audio were beautiful, and the presentation of the content in a movie-like fashion was brilliant and fit the game perfectly. The NPCs in the game are VERY well done and helped lighten the mood in a dark game. Not to mention, I don't think I ever heard a repeated phrase by a character and I loved that about this game.
The actual game play however was very poorly done for my taste. The fights were repetitive, predictable, intrusive, and unnecessary. Every 15 steps the game would interrupt my progression with a slow-motion introduction of a "new" set of enemies, and all I could think was "just let me play the game". It made enemies too familiar which took away any of the horror feel that they were supposed to bring to the game.
There were a few pieces of actual game play that were fantastic and stood out from the rest in my eyes. The battle on the stage at the farm was the most enjoyable out of all of the combat scenes in the game. The music and the rock-and-roll stage scene made me feel like a boss killing all of the Taken, and having Barry there to cheer me on made it feel like I was fighting with a friend. Nuclear Throne is perhaps one of the finest top-down shooters ever made. The characters and weapons are well-balanced and varied, and the small quirks and easter eggs scattered along the way add to the charm and personality of this game.
That said, it's also a very unforgiving and difficult experience, due mostly to the procedurally-generated levels. Without the benefit of memorization, you can only prepare yourself mentally for a given environment... and the random nature of the game can feel downright cruel sometimes. It takes a little while (and a bit of luck) to figure out how to "work" the game to your benefit and survive given the stingy weapons and health drops.
Most frustrating of all is the fact that when you die, you must start over from the very beginning rather than at the start of the level. This is a game where you'll throw the controller in anger after a particularly tragic death, but then pick it up and immediately give it another go. Few games are as aggravating but also as fun and addictive as this one.
For anyone new to the game, or to anyone who is on the verge of giving up, here's some advice that I wish I had many hours ago when I started playing it:
- Only rush through the very first level to see if you get a good random seed (in other words, a good weapon + lots of rads). But for everything after that...
- Be patient! Really, really patient! I can't stress that point enough. Above all else, the key to this game is resisting the urge to charge ahead, and instead to carefully and slowly clear each level with care.
- Do not play as Crystal. With her, it's too easy to become lazy and stop dodging and rely on her special skill. This game is all about defense: survive first, kill second. Crystal reinforces bad habits that will bite you later on.
- I like to take a warm-up round with Melting before playing as anyone else. While it's nearly impossible to beat the game with him, he's good for putting you in the right mindset (which is, again, caution and patience). My goal was to play as Melting until I at least cleared the sewer level... then I knew I was warmed up and in the right state of mind.
- Finally, the Nuclear Throne wikia page is great. They have lots of essential info there which helped to hone my tactics in the game.

If you enjoy sliding around a track in the latest piece of Italian exotica, this is not the game for you. If, however, you like the sound of crawling along at single digit speeds in an old Soviet truck that gets stuck easily, then look no further.
In summary, Spintires won't be for everyone. If you're like myself and enjoy a good sim then I highly recommend you give this game a chance. The one (and currently only) objective on each map is to deliver 8 pieces of lumber from one end of the map to the other. Where the fun begins is how the maps react to your vehicles. The mud is the star of the show, without a doubt. If you repeatedly use a particular track, it will get more and more churned up and become increasingly difficult to use. There are further obstacles to contend with such as fast flowing rivers, steep adverse cambers and narrow forested tracks.
The vehicles are lovingly modelled and all of them offer some benefit over the others. You don't start a level with all the available vehicles for that map unlocked. They are often hidden in the wilderness. And then when you do find them, they will regularly need repairing or fuelling, or sometimes even both.
The multiplayer makes completing the objectives a lot easier as you can move in convoy and help each other out but some maps are still very difficult.
While this game still has a long way to go to being called complete, I love it already. Completing a level is very satisfying and the physics are modelled beautifully. I'd highly recommend you give it a shot.

Crashlands is an extremely repetitive action RPG with dull crafting elements and some completely pointless Minecraft/Terraria-esque base-building. The writing is funny and the game has some interesting idea, but ultimately the tedium was too much for me.
The combat mechanics seem interesting and deep at first. Each enemy type has a different attack animation and you have to dodge the attacks or you'll die pretty much immediately. But in the 4 hours I played, I only came across 3 types of enemies. They all consisted of moving out of a red circle/square/rectangle on the ground, waiting for the attack animation, and then poking the enemy once or twice before the animation repeats. And of those 3 enemy types, one had way too much HP to kill in a reasonable amount of time.
The game would benefit greatly from more depth in the combat. Your only options for attacking are: 1) clicking on dudes for a basic attack; 2) stunning dudes for a couple seconds, on a relatively long cooldown; and 3) throwing limited-use bombs at dudes, which take tons of resources to craft. I understand these limited options result from Crashlands' origins as a touch-only mobile game. But the game would be way more fun with a dodge roll and some standard ARPG abilities/spells. With such limited options, the combat gets super tedious.
As a final complaint, the controls aren't great. You're really supposed to control your character with a mouse, MOBA style. But the interaction of that control method with collision detection and animations leads to a lack of precision in your movement. Since you ideally want to dodge enemy attacks by standing just outside of the red circle/rectangle, I found myself often getting hit with stuff I thought I should have dodged due to imprecision in the controls.
If you just want a game to fill lots of time, I'm confident Crashlands can do that. But as a timewaster, I didn't find it much more engaging than leveling woodcutting in Runescape.

There are some things in life that, whilst, for whatever reason it may be, a decent game is a let down. Well, for me, this is the reverse. When I  first saw Spintires I didn't believe it would be any good. Then I tried the tech demo they released and was pleasantly surprised.
Obviously this game is not a standard fare AAA title from the likes of Electronic Arts, Codemasters, Valve, even RAREWARE* for the Xbox. It is built around off-road physics and the ability to drive, off-road. Sounds simple, but alas the engine running the game needs to be capable of correctly calculating every nuance in the road surface, each dip and lip of hill or rock. I never thought they would be able to do it, but yet here I am.
The vehicles in any game like this, can make or break it. This game has a few vehicles, including the mighty MAZ. But it may leave a distinct taste in the mouth of people who love having a decent selection on offer. Although you should stop there and ignore that taste left by the lack thereof, and continue on and really get to grips with the physics of the game itself. It is true, it is not a game for everyone, but where this game fails, it delivers in almost atop fashion by capturing your every thought pattern.
The main reason for this game, is the physics and the ability to take what you believe you know, off-roading, and put it to the test. The basic premise of the game is to take a delivery from one part of the map, to the other. Simple enough, but then you also have to worry about damage and your fuel, because as we all know, roaming about hills takes it's toll on your fuel reserves. The maps themselves, have a "fog of war" to them. In-game it is known as "cloaked", and by "de-cloaking" areas you open up more of the map that you get to see when you are driving. Otherwise you have to play it by feel alone, trusting in your compass. Added is the ability to lock your diff's on the various vehicles as well as enabling and disabling All-Wheel drive. Although I must point out, that using a locked diff, your vehicle's turning radius is less, than when off. Both your diff locks and All-Wheel drive's will consume more fuel, so proper planning is needed for that. The rest, I feel is best left unsaid and left to the player to find and enjoy.
Along the way as you try to get your cargo from one location to the next, are various hazards you must negotiate. Whilst it is an off-roading game, it never feels like I have to race from one location to the next, but simply to take it at my own pace, and maximise my uses of the vehicle I am currently driving.
The camera in the game itself, is rather odd in it's own unique way and composition. It moves differently to how another game may implement.
Of course all this has been said before. So I shall take my leave, leaving this one last comment and score.
If you are unsure about the game, as it will only appeal to a certain few, try the free demo from the official site, and if you need more content, the game is moddable, and many mods exist.

I would say don't buy this with some qualifiers.  IF you loved Wasteland 1, do not realy care about a "real" squad tactics game, or just want to kill some time, then by all means, purchase.  I did get some enjoyment from this game, and while the gameplay was linear, I expected it to be due to the emphasis on the story, and following that story.  Approach it like a book you get to play instead of read and many of the complaints reviewers express are put to rest.
HOWEVER, if you wanted X-Com, JA, FOT, then this game is a weak sister by comparison.  Almost all my combat was to make a skirmish line just outside the enemy's engagement range, shoot a bad guy/thing/animal, then wait for all them to run at me one at a time to get shot up.  Stab the few melee jerks who get through (because the ranges of firearms is pitiful) and then loot. Almost no tactical skill needed.  Just draw them in, shoot them up, rinse and repeat.
And they get GUNS WRONG!!  Augh!  I have so much hate for lazy guns when you have a combat game.  M-14's take 7.62x51 (I would have been ok with .308, but I digress).  M1 Garands take .30-06.  I am sure that for simplicitys sake they assigned weapons by class, and assigned one ammo type per class (of course, classing a full size rifle like the 14, Garand, G3/HK 91, or the FAL as an "assault" rife is an insult anyway).  Granted, in game some pistols/smg's took 9mm, but some took .38......  .38? WTF! Name one smg that was ever chambered for .38.  I know of one, ONE, auto-loading pistol that ever took .38 (special) and that is the Coonan.  Granted there is the .38 Super round that is an auto rim design, but let's face it, they were talking .38 Special in this game.  I could go on, but I'll quit here......  LAZY!
The story was fine, but the decision process was very scripted.  There was little choice other than to go from A-B-C.  I am not really complaining about that, like I said, it is like you are reading a book, only playing it.  I could have handled a bit more of the "find your own adventure" style though.  It was nice to see what happened to the "original gang" from WL1.
This game was like that "Sir Robin" from Monty Python's Holy Grail.  It was a story of almost.  They almost made a tactical game like JA, FOT, X-COm.  They almost made a FO 1-2 RPG, they almost made the post apocolyptic game I was expecting as a follow up for WL1.  What we got was WL1 (basically a text game) with animations for combat and you could see the whole party at once instead of a single character, with 3D instead of 2D.
It is like wanting to eat Italian, but going to Olive Garden instead.

Good game, buried under questionable mechanics.
I have mixed feelings about Wasteland 2: first of all, I've backed it on Kickstarted and I really happy about its success. Also, I used to like this game for about 1/3 of my walkthrough, and had some really good moments in it - good enough to not regret time I spent there. However, at one point I've realized this game has fundamental flaw, what will prevent me from completing it - and that exactly what just happened. I'm in the middle of LA region, and significant part of plot is ahead of me, but I just can't stand it no more. I know, for any quest left, for any encounter there will be 100 useless actions I'll be required to perform.
Wasteland 2 is a good example why nobody should try to implement gameplay from 1990-x now. From 37 hours I've spent in this game I feel like about 30 were about opening boxes, crates and other various containers, disarming alarms and cracking safes. Not only that, this game is full of character skills for every occasion. Healer and surgeon. Heavy weapon and automatic weapon. Kiss a-s-s and smart a-s-s, and some other a-s-s - all related to one thing - dialogs. There is even special skill for toaster repair (not related to regular repair, of course). But having too many skills is just part of the problem. Another, biggest issue, most of this skills take real time to perform. It's 15 seconds or so to open a lock. 15 seconds of staring into the screen, it's not interactive. It's not much, but consider 5-10 safes per location - it's 2-3 minutes at best, more if you fail. Rinse and repeat it on the next encounter. You also might be really lucky to have 10 landmines begging to be disarmed - another 2-3 minutes of your priceless lifetime. Add alarms, healing, and whatnot - I'm surpised reloading weapons does not requires time! - and here you go.
I clearly don't have The Skill to master all these skills. If you do - play it, it's rather good.

God, this game is good. When I backed this at kickstarter I was doubtful if they can deliver on a promise of an old-school-ish RPG in a setting everybody loves (if you didn't play Wasteland, you must've played at least some of the Fallouts!) in this age. And yet they delivered fully.
This game to my taste played exactly like fallout 1 or 2 with maybe a little more fighting focus then I'd want, but that's ok. The setting, while being so familiar at the same time is all-new. The "factions" are ridiculous but actually make a lot of sense =) Mad monks worshipping a nuclear warhead? Religious people worshipping some ridiculous over_the_top_insane person based on some videocassete? A society of MANNERED people? :D I mean this all sounds bogus but it actually works very well for the story-telling purposes. The atmosphere is amazing.
RPG-systems again, while seeming pretty close to what we expect to see in a fallout game are not quite the same. They are neat, understandable and functional though. No problems with them.
This game has incredible amount of well-written dialogue and text. It's immense really. Very fair share of my 70-80 hours of walkthrough were spent reading. And I love it =)
Overall course of story is enjoyable and while it's nothing new (you're rangers, you save the world, duh) it still has some interesting twists and bits to it that were pretty good.
The gameplay holds up, the variety of ways to accomplish things are there and you can totally skip like 30-40 hours of content if you wish to do so (I didn't and my walkthrough was as close to full as I could possibly imagine, though I still guess I missed some things).
The music and sound design are very fitting to the atmosphere and are impeccable.
I have some problems with some particular systems like weapon-salvaging or the randomness of loot in chests, or too many chests too loot (which can become tiresome for a loot-hoarder like myself), but those are most likely just my own problems really, more than the problem with the game =)
Overall, I wholeheartedly recommend this game, thank Inxile for not failing me and waiting for Wasteland3 (Yes, I've seen the IBM AT and I 'shiver with anticipation'! :D)
Also the title song is incredible.

This game barely gets a yes from me. The nemesis system is great, but the expansion of it has led to some cracks in the system. I first have to ask why this system is in a Lord of the Rings game. Imagine Batman taking down gang leaders who grow based off of player encounters into super villains. There are a ton of WB properties that this would fit better. We're stuck with a Lord of the Rings game that is forced to butcher the lore in order to make it's systems woek. I will commend them for prioritizing gameplay. My biggest problem with this game is the gambling aspect. Yeah, sure there's loot boxes but the bigger gambling scandal is Talions controls. When I push A on my 360 controller will he sprint, will he jump will he catch on a small ledge, will he climb a wall. There is a combat mode and stealth mode triggered with RT that changes some of the controls which could help if the animation to transition was so spotty and took so long. This is a fast paced game and half of the animations don't fit that frantic pace. This leads to Talion peering over a ledge rather than jumping down at the perfect time to assassinate the target. The controls are so spotty and there are so many times I died because the game interpreted my controls in the complete wrong way I intended. I spent a siege attacking allies the whole time because the lock on would not point me toward the enemy I wanted to kill. The animations and controls gives this game a stop and start feel. The previous game was so smooth and fast moving and all the added bloat this game adds breaks that up. There are some frustrating enemy abilities too. This really crops up in the climactic duels at the end of sieges. Infinite grunts will spawn in that just pad out the fight. You can plan and adapt and fight tooth and nail for 30 minutes chipping away at this captain and then he will curse you and stun lock you. Then you die in a couple hits and have to try again. This game is just too big for its own good and these systems are starting to hurt each other. The story is so disappointing too. It is so cliche and completely blows the potential of the Lord of the Rings license.That's why I wish they would use a better suited license. This is a good action game with interesting mechanics, but a terrible LOTR game. They have no understanding of building tension and developing compelling characters which makes playing Talion a chore. It tries to tackle the LOTR theme of power corrupting but it is too little too late. All the cool looking fan service moments like the balrog fight and interaction with shelob fall flat by using generic action game and fantasy tropes. The best part of the game is the sieges and those make it worth getting. Just wait for a sale. It starts out rough but just stick with it until the first siege.

From the very beginning, every mainline edition of the Civilization series has gotten an average of a 90-95% user approval rate which is a greater approval rate than that normally ascribed to civilization itself. This could be due to the fact that the Civilization seies simply soars while civilization itself seems to soar and stink in equal measure. Then again, it could be that the game of Civilization simply appeals to the inner narcissist lurking somewhere within us all. After all, how often is it you can be elected ruler of your nation by popular acclaim, rule them in a governmental form of your choice, eventually rise to rule to world, establish Earth's first off world colony, and live for centuries. I have to admit that is slightly more ambitious than my own real world expectations, but I do have an eye on the North American continent. Consider yourself warned.
Now don't get me wrong here. I am not trying to say that Civilization is the best turn based, civ building, strategy game ever. That would be unfair to all those games I have not gotten around to trying. What I can say is that it is by far the best I have ever played, and narcissist that I am, I will try most anything that gives me a shot at world domination.
The Civilization series is up to Civ-5 at this point, but Civ-3 is a game which endures the times, remains comparable to like games of more recent production, and holds a special place in my heart when compared to the newer versions of this long running classic. Later editions of this game introduce elements which alter the play style and base strategy of the game, but while I believe that Civ-4 & 5 remain true to the original construct to a large degree, it is Civ-3 which most closely  resembles the original. In fact, it is exactly like the original, but with greater user options, and smoother game play.
If you have been thinking about giving this series a try, Civ-3 is a great place to start. With the release of Civ-5, the Steam price for Civ-3 is a mere $5.00 which in my opinion makes it one of the best bargains in the entire Steam Library. Just one run through of this game will keep you occupied for longer than the run time of a long movie, and when was the last time you got into a movie theatre for &5.00 eh? I began playing this game when it first came out for PC in the 90's, continue to play it to this day, and played Civ-1 & 2 before that. How's that for a testament for long term replayability? I simply could not recommend another game of this type more highly.

I bought this game without any prior knowledge of the kickstarter origins of Broken Age, and I feel that this title supports my arguement for NEVER backing a game through kickstarter, unless you like throwing money at something which may never happen. There is always a risk when giving money to someone for something that doesn't exist, and I think a lot of people have unrealistic expectations, and unfortunately in this case, it was the people making the game that didn't plan and budget ahead.
I bought this game in a steam sale not long after it was offically realised, which was the best choice at the time, as I had heard a bit about the game and was excited to play it myself. I played through act 1 and expected a few months wait for act 2, as this is the norm with most multi-part titles. How wrong I was. Over a year later, I am still waiting for act 2. I can't imagine how annoyed people must be from backing this game from the start! However, the signs for problems ahead were there from the beginning.
Having only just bought the game, I started looking through sites to see if there was an expected release date for act 2, only to find an article which stated that the profits from act 1 meant they could go on and fund act 2. I was horrified! I had no idea that this game was not even funded for the second part. I had no idea that this game wasn't even supposed to be split into 2 acts in the first place. But I thought to myself, oh well, it might take a little bit longer but I can wait. Update after update, deadlines came and went for act 2 to be released. I think this is what really got to most people. The waiting wasn't the problem, it was the promises that were broken that made people upset and lose faith in Double Fine as a developer. How can you trust someone with your money if you don't believe they know what they are doing? If someone who has 30 years experience in the games industry can't budget for a full game, then we are all doomed! Unfortunately for us, its too late to take back our money or get back our trust. This is the true lesson to be learned from this experience: Research, research, research! If something looks too good to be true, then it probably is!
I feel that some of the fault in my buying this game has to fall at Valve's door. The steam page for Broken Age is very misleading, as it gave me no indication at the time that this game is kickstarter funded and may never have been finished. And, even now, it is impossible to tell from the steam page that this game is not finished! This is why I have written this review, to give people the knowledge of the situation surrounding this game, so that someone else can make an informed choice over whether to purchase this game, I choice I didn't have.
So, I guess you want to know a bit about the game, huh? Other reviews can tell you more, but the basics are: It's a point and click adventure that follows two very different main characters, with the option to switch between characters whenever you wish. Its a pretty looking game, with amazing voice-acting and simple puzzles.
Is it worth almost £20? No. Act 1 took me about 3 hours (I got stuck for about 30 minutes because I'm bad at video game logic :P), with act 2, if and when it appears, to take another 5 hours. I'm honestly not sure I will play act 2. It has been so long since I played act 1 that I will have to replay it all from scratch. And really, there are SO many other games I could be playing, I may never experience this game as it was supposed to be played. My advice: Wait until both acts are out and grab it in a sale. As the second act is currently not out, I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

Crashlands is a simple game about simple fun. I personally enjoy it quite a bit but if you are looking for a more robust combat system or thorough crafting system, you should probably look elsewhere. This game does its best to keep out of your way by having simplified systems. There are tons of activities which you are encouraged to chip away at. In that regard it is not a game to spend hours playing but something to toss a half hour at every now and again. The combat isn't enthralling, the pet raising is simplified, and item crafting is grindy but it is all designed to be something you can do for a small chunk of time and feel tanglible progress.
What it does offer is that because of that simple tangible progress, it becomes a confortable game you can settle into without too much thought and hop out of at will. The progress also comes in the form of items that randomie their quality (much like Terraria) to create lots of special effect for your attacking. In that manner you can craft items repeatedly to kit yourself out for a specific specialty in combat. I have yet to get juicemancy howver, which supposedly makes the item crafting more malleable later in the game
I'd be remiss to not also compliment the writing in the game as it feels snappy without trying too hard (most of the time) and the dialog is used as quest info in your quest tracker which mean you actually have to read the text to interpret what you are supposed to be doing (probably the only real casual unfriendly decision in here).
All in all, this is a good game. It is what I would call a 3 out of 4 star game but with a lot to offer and a chill feel that lends itself well to the gameplay and atmosphere.

This game does not deserve the positive reviews it gets. It's a mindnumbing tablet game designed to be played with little concentration while watching TV or something.
The crafting and quests are 100% linear, there is no variation in the way the game plays, you don't really get very much choice in how you progress at all.
The combat is tedious, you hit the enemy and then move out of the red circle, wait for them to do their animation, then hit again. It takes a long time to kill even the basic enemies.
Acquiring resources is similarly needlessly time consuming. You click on a resource, wait for your guy to automatically hit it 4/5 times and then do it again, Each item crafted needs so many resources that it's a matter of minutes to craft simple stuff.
Controls and graphics are also bad and have received no special attention for the PC. The humour is all just trying too hard and not really managing. In a game that's clearly designed to be played without concentration, having millions of long and unfunny dialogues really only adds more to the tedious nature of the game.
This game may work if you're high and into casual tablet nonsense, but it has no place on the PC.

Did they pull it off?
I don't quite know what I was expecting when I first backed the Kickstarter. Wasteland was a beloved classic, my first proper PC game, and it showed me just what games were really capable of. Problems with more than one solution, missions that could be failed without forcing a game over, the player's responsibility to build a balanced team, the combination of descriptive paragraphs with the limited graphics to paint a more vivid picture; the experience blew my fragile little mind at the time. A contemporary title can do many or even all of those things, but whether they can match that feeling - the impression that I'm playing something truly groundbreaking - is a much more loaded question.
Many positive reviews of Wasteland 2 frontload the criticism, ending with some variant of "but I liked the game anyway because etc." It's easy to see why: bugs still being ironed out, a rather clunky interface, widespread locks and traps with long skill use animations, overuse of a limited pool of music, some weak story elements, large chunks of wasted space... you don't have to look too hard to see some serious flaws. The enjoyable aspects are likely to be subjective: how well the combat clicks for the player, whether they like the setting and overall fiction, the extent to which building a proper team is enjoyable, and so on. Indeed, in their bid to create a classic-sized PC RPG, it seems inXile could have made the game play better without sacrificing its hardcore appeal.
For instance, the locks and traps thing: consider the Baldur's Gate games, which also made use of frequent locks and traps on obstacles. Where BG has the advantage is that skill usage is practically instantaneous; the character moves to the trapped item and, if successful, the trap field simply disappears. WL2 added some needless visual flair to the process - your ranger rubbing their hands before working on the object, or kicking it repeatedly as a meter fills, or whatever - which adds a few seconds to each skillcheck. In a game with hundreds of them, those seconds start to add up. Little changes to things like that could have smoothed out a lot of reviewer complaints, with few if any adjustments to the core mechanics.  No doubt patches will address this and other issues over time, but the impression has set in nonetheless.
I'll be blunt: I put a fair chunk of change into the Kickstarter, and I can feel the little nagging doubts in the back of my head. Would I be fair if I saw something that bugged me, or read criticism? Would I go easy on the game, knowing that some of my own money was somewhere inside? Would my opinion be more biased than others? It's a reasonable question, and I never did come up with a good answer. Even putting that aside, I'm not gonna deny I was a little nervous when this came out. It's been a long time since the Infinity engine was king of the hill. Did I still have the stomach for a big PC game? What if my appetites had simply moved on? Doubts upon doubts upon doubts.
Did they pull it off?
Like putting up with the wizard fight at the Friendly Arm Inn while you're still level 1, the appeal persists: a game that won't pull its punches, that will try its best to bring me down. WL2 definitely has the spark of those classic RPGs, that hard-to-define something that makes them hard to put down once I start. Fights were tactical, kinetic affairs: cover got destroyed, enemies repositioned, backup weapons were handy, well-timed explosives turned the tide, and even a difficult encounter could be mitigated with the right preparation. Environments presented their own challenges, and with several ways through a given obstacle I was more often than not encouraged to work around a failed skillcheck rather than savescum. Uncooperative plot elements or even bugged out triggers could be answered by force-firing, and there was no problem that the right size bomb could not solve.
Arizona did drag and suffer from design problems - the Prison being chief among them - but it held its own curious charms, and it presents a neat contrast with California. At the start, you control a bunch of customizable scrubs whose mission rapidly spirals out of control. Echo Team starts in known territory and gradually pushes the boundaries, earning their stripes in the process. Water is precious, communities are scarce, and civilization is on the knife's edge atop a pile of late 80s-early 90s rubble. By the time I did get to California, Echo felt every bit the veteran ranger squad, doing what rangers do best: venture into wild territory and bring order to chaos. There, the script is flipped: water is everywhere, settlements are common, and it's on us to put our best foot forward. Every arrival the base, every interaction with the public, every time we stepped in to right some wrong felt like it mattered somehow, like it could have gone differently - and like everything we'd done before had shaped us for that encounter.
That's a key spice to those old titles: variety. What happens if I do this instead of that? What does this guy say or do if I mention this? What if I didn't have that skill, item, or party member? What are the consequences if we just kill everyone? Is there a way to get what I want peacefully, and if so how bad do I want it? I was constantly asking myself those questions during Wasteland 2, and it's for those reasons that I know I'll be back. There's more to see, even if I think I've seen it all; there's more to try, even if I've already sunk some 80 hours into the campaign. Old PC RPGs sometimes get a shot of life from modding communities, but even before I had heard thing one about mods, there were some games where I knew - just knew - that I'd be back, just to see what happened this time.
And god help me if I didn't get drawn in at times, just a little. I searched frantically during a hostage situation, wondering if there even was a third option between 'take down the enemy' and 'save the hostage.' I debated whether to intervene in a loophole-ridden religious dispute, and if so how. I paid attention to the radio broadcasts in LA, making mental notes of who's who in the neighborhood.  The villain was something of a one-note antagonist - there were moments of good writing, but his was a stock grand scheme - but there was a respectable sense that something was tracking Echo and the Rangers. There's a strange appeal to being stuck in uncharted territory, surrounded by potential enemies, with friends well out of reach and one hell of a longshot goal ahead of us. It's predictable in the end, but not without its highs; the trick of bringing back everyone you've made friends with for the final battle is an old one, but no less effective.
Sometimes it's not the game I'm after, but the adventure, the challenge. Sometimes it's the sense that I am probably going to lose if I play this game like I play every other game. So it was with games like Arcanum: flawed to hell and back, difficult to recommend, but special in a way that most games simply aren't for me. So it is with Wasteland 2.
Did they pull it off?
In my humble, flawed, biased opinion: yeah, I think they pulled it off.

I've had wasteland 2 since week 1 of early access on steam and the game has consistently been enjoyable, even with the bugs. Now that the game is finished I have finally returned to the wasteland to find that the bugs are fixed, the game runs 5 times as well on my computer, and that the user interface and turn based comabt is smoother and better than before.
The turn based combat is enjoyable and complex enough to be intresting and challenging throughout the game, without being difficult to understand or figure out as a beginner.
The choices and rpg elements are deep with real consequences, decisions need to be weighed carefully before choosing.
However I would have prefered more cosmetic customization options in the party/character creation even though there are plenty of options, in that respect more is always better, in my honest opinion.
To sum up this is a game I would definently recommend to people who have enjoyed fallout, or similar rpgs, those who like a deep narrative with interesting choices and those who enjoy tactical party based combat - e.g. XCOM.

Remedy Entertainment have a varied history on different platformer and a solid background of really polished, clean cut games with quirky/interesting takes on standard games. To me, Remedy Entertainment produce games that are like the interesting B-Side of the hit Pop record, and that's what Alan Wake is: Weirder and more interesting than the Triple A's, but with all the polish and production value you'd expect of one.
Suspenseful collectables and foreshadowing are layered around a very detailed world to produce some startling moments and encounters.
* A newer angle on combat and some survival elements which make sense in the world of Alan Wake.
* Quirky and interesting details to uncover in the world if you're inquisitive.
* Very polished and few bugs.
Alan Wake is often called Stephen King: The Game, which is meant as a good thing. Interestingly though, it suffers from the same problems as Stephen King novels and movie adaptations; almost silly story elements and inexplicable character motivations. Otherwise, on the whole, it's polished enough that it never lets you down in any one area.
* Easier than similar games and has a real lack of challenge.
* Often no variety of enemies and repetitive combat.
Gameplay comes in at a strong 11-14 hours play time and while it doesn't have much re-playability, it's a collector/achievement hunters dream. It's available on Steam at between £22.99/$29.99 and £29.99/$39.99 which, for a 4 year+ old game is simply overpriced. Fortunately it goes on sale very often for -80% and even comes up in Indie Bundles from time to time.
* The DLC is a waste of time. Instead, you can find the Developer Commentaries on YouTube here
and the Soundtrack on Spotify here
* ROW copies are cheapest from Japan.

I’m both an avid reader and a struggling writer. So to find a video game that looks at the perils and pitfalls of writing, albeit ensconced in a horror game, I decided to give it a shot. Ironically enough, I had read a novelization of
long before I even got Steam. But how would experiencing the game go?
Bright Falls, an isolated town somewhere in Washington State. It seems like the perfect getaway for accomplished writer Alan Wake, who is trying to get away from his increasingly turbulent lifestyle, and have a quiet holiday with his wife Alice at a cabin. But after an argument, Alice disappears, and after trying to save her from a lake, Alan wakes up, to find that a week has passed, a week he has no memory of, and that people are being turned into beings wreathed in darkness, the Taken. What really happened to Alice? What does it have to do with obscure writer Thomas Zane? And is Alan imagining these events, or are they part of a darker plot to turn his writings into reality? With few people to trust, Alan must deal with sceptical authorities and ancient entities in order to save Alice…
One thing that I definitely enjoyed in
more than anything else was the story. Even after reading the novelization, it felt like I came to it fresh and new. In fact, the TV-like ‘episodic’ format actually helps with the atmosphere, given that
was an influence. Of course, one of the biggest influences (and frequently acknowledged) is that of Stephen King. I’m reminded of
in particular. The atmosphere of the game is not unlike a more action-oriented version of
, albeit with not as much psychological unease.
Graphics are one of the complaints I do have about the game. Not because they are bad: for the most part, they’re pretty damned good. But on my computer, low frame-rate, especially during some of the more intense combat systems, plagues the game regularly, and I was lucky to be able to defeat some enemies partly because of that frustrating frame rate. This suggests that using standard onboard chips for this game isn’t a good idea, even with the graphics at a low setting. Get a graphics card if you don’t want the frustrating frame-rate. However, the graphics themselves, as I mentioned, are beautiful, my only big complaint being the design and animation of Dr Hartman. For a character who is meant to be a smug and manipulative git, his facial expressions frequently make him look like he’s taken too many happy pills, and whatever threat he has as an antagonist is lessened significantly.
Sound-wise, I enjoyed the voice acting fairly well. It does well for what this game is, and the voice processing for the Taken is actually quite eerie and frightening, even if it does sound at times like a Cyberman’s voice from
. Music, well, there’s plenty of good pieces, and there’s some interesting selections for the end credits for each episode. But I think the musical sting used whenever a Taken is within attacking range gets old real quick, and that it wouldn’t have hurt to have multiple stings to vary it somewhat.
Gameplay-wise, it seems to be the usual bit of action-shooter gameplay that horror games tend to be about nowadays. The combination of using a flashlight to render the Taken vulnerable and then shooting them is a novel one, but does wear a little, though using a flaregun and flashbangs as deadly weapons against the light-fearing creatures is enjoyable. But the camera controls for the mouse are too sensitive, even with the sensitivity turned down. The collectables do make it worthwhile, including reading manuscript pages that add to the backstory of the game, watching short episodes of a
-like TV show, and listening to radio shows that give some background.
Overall,
is a pretty damn good game, hampered only by its incompatibility with some machines, and a number of other small flaws. Fans of Stephen King, David Lynch, or
should give it a whirl.

This game is VERY different from your normal competative FPS.
The game puts two teams of players against each other in a mixed FPS / RTS environment, with one team as Space Marines and the others as a race of aliens.  The gameplay is unique in that the balance is highly asynchronous.  Marines have range with guns, but aliens have mobility.  Marines can build anywhere quickly but alien buildings construct themselves without the need for players present.  Any marines can repair buildings allied unit armor with a resource-cheap item, but for aliens only one expensive support unit lets a player heal or help build buildings.  This goes on and on, practiaclly nothing about the two teams is equal.  This makes for a very odd balance, and takes a lot to get used to.
The game doesn't do a great job of explaining to you how all these things work out when it comes to gameplay, but thats sor t of unavoidable here especially as a metagame and patches slowly shift how the game plays from its initial release,  Fortunately you can ask your teammates, and in this game cooperation is VERY important.  An un-organized team can lose the game or put the game in an unwinnable state within the first few minutes, and individual deaths and kills reall do impact this game more than most I've seen.
Its a pretty unique experience.  I'd reccomend it.

This Game wants you to take the body.
A lot of people are upset because it didn't match up with what they wanted.  Then again, this isn't a big budget title from a developer with decades of sports game experience and money for licensing.  And V7 isn't charging like it is, either.  Once you set aside your expectations, you'll find a fun little arcade hockey game that's long on atmosphere and is likely even better in local multiplayer than it already is in single.
The BHL is a fun little league.  Every logo and arena is thought out, clever, and makes me look forward to getting a sequel.  Controls reward going for the showy big plays like point-blank slapshots and open ice hip checks over subtle moves.  The goalies aren't designed to be good, and within a dozen hours you'll find it easy enough to beat them and easy enough that you are forced to play good aggressive defense because the computer is NOT going to bail you out.  One-timers would really be overkill.  Actually passing in the offensive zone is unnecessary.
The first team to send three opponents to the ice will catch fire, and how to use that fire is the strategy of this game.  On offense you cannot be knocked off the puck, you can deke, and your goals can anger the goalie (3 on fire goals make the goalie ready to fight).  On defense every opponent you knock over is going to be looking for a fight.  The choice is yours, and the risk in fighting is real.  I haven't tried multiplayer yet, but I imagine trying to get on fire will be the whole game.
Three strikes and you're out is not a hockey rule, until now.  First player to connect three times wins the fight.  Lose and your player will really play poorly afterwards and start subsequent fights on strike 2.  If a player can't land a punch, they're done for the night.  Especially in the playoffs, losing too many fights like that will cause that team to forfeit.  The fights themselves have an odd draggy rhythm that isn't that hard to pick up.
The humor in this game is puerile, but it did make me laugh.  There's some great easter eggs in the stadium signage.
For the price, this game is really fun, and I look forward to seeing OTH2 sometime in the future.

Old Time Hockey – Se Paciente Saltamontes
Como lo dice su nombre, Old Time Hockey es un título del rudo deporte de patines sobre hielo, ese donde probablemente nuestro recuerdo más fuerte sean peleas en la helada pista, ambientado en los años 70, Old Time Hockey pone a prueba nuestra habilidad, pero más nuestra paciencia.
Cuando recibimos el acceso a probar Old Time Hockey sentimos una gran alegría, desafortunadamente, lo bueno que se veía en los trailers no sería tan divertido como pensamos. Con muchos problemas de diseño y jugabilidad, que le vuelven demasiado frustrante para pasar un buen rato. Old Time Hockey fue creado bajo un enfoque donde simplemente pudiéramos empezar a jugar una vez instalado –con base en una serie de esquema de controles simples, pero nuestra experiencia de primera mano fue pura frustración.
Ni tan Noob Friendly
Incluso en el nivel de dificultad más bajo, los nuevos en el juego podrían no pasarla muy bien. La inteligencia artificial está llena de fallas, Tiene algunos problemas importantes, los defensores de nuestro propio equipo parecen estar en posiciones erróneas todo el tiempo, y lo menos que hacen es evitar que la CPU logre disparos fáciles, y para peores, los porteros son simplemente torpes. Claramente, el juego se vuelve más fácil conforme vamos acostumbrándonos y ganando experiencia que nos permite hacer uso de mejores estrategias. La cámara predeterminada es la de Acción, y es pésima -lo mejor es usar la cámara Classic.
Aunque no todo es jalarse los pelos hasta arrancárselos del colerón, marcar un gol te reconforta bastante después de haber movido mar y tierra para evitar que te marquen una anotación, es divertido que puedes golpear a los jugadores del otro equipo y todo eso, pero si quisiera pelear, me voy a jugar Street Fighter.
Para nuestro infortunio, Old Time Hockey no fue lo que esperábamos.
Pésimos Controles
La  “respuesta” en general a nuestras acciones en los controles es otro punto muy molesto, cambiar el jugador que estamos controlado mientras defendemos o cuando el disco está suelto toma demasiado tiempo, y muchas veces, nos hará controlar al jugador que menos queríamos.
Old Time Hockey tiene las famosas peleas entre jugadores de hockey, las cuales requieren un timing muy preciso, donde rara vez se gana, y es que ganar estas luchas es también un requisito para avanzar a través del modo de historia del juego, haciéndolo algo aún más tedioso. El modo historia es su punto fuerte, con una narración basada en texto a través de las pantallas de carga y con artes de recortes de periódicos.  A lo largo del modo historia, se desbloquean habilidades, esto proporciona algún sentido de avance. Old Time Hockey no cuenta con modo multijugador en línea (sólo local).
Los pésimos controles y jugabilidad le hacen una pesadilla.
Conclusion
A final de cuentas, algo de diversión se puede tener con Old Time Hockey, mínima, pero se puede, simplemente toma algo de tiempo llegar a alcanzar el disfrute. Old Time Hockey es desarrollado por el estudio independiente V7 Entertainment  con un precio de $12, disponible para PlayStation 4, Xbox One y PC.

This is a truly fantastic game, and shows why we should support the indie scene.
The Binding of Isaac's gameplay is pretty simple - it's a top-down dungeon crawler, very reminiscent of the early Zelda games, with randomly-generated dungeon layouts, random items to be picked up/bought, and so on. Your primary attack is firing tears, which can be upgraded and modified with different items. You also have access to bombs and special items which range from borderline overpowered to almost completely worthless. The random element of the game ensures that no two runs will be the same, so don't dismiss it because you had a bad first run. Try again, and you might end up with better items. It's mostly down to luck, but your ability to dodge attacks comes in handy!
There is a LOT of content in this game. Over 20 bosses, around 50 different enemy types, over 200 items to find... Not to mention deals with the devil, which give you powerful items at the cost of some of your precious heart containers.
To anyone who wants a fun, addictive, yet challenging game, pick this up. It doesn't even cost much, and the Wrath of the Lamb DLC adds a lot more as well. There's even a remake coming out with extra content!

While heaps of positive reviews are thrown at this game, I feel it is more because it was a labour of love and a good game to watch other people play than anything to do with the game itself.
The game is difficult without actually being hard which I realize requires explination but hard is when something tests your skills and leaves little room for error for example a good bullet hell game and difficult is when factors work against you that you might not have control over which is any game that has RNG with negative odds.
The stage layouts are randomized but you can always expect certain events to occour on specific stages, which I like as it lends better to retry attempts unlike FTL where you can get messed up and have zero control over it.
In that regard, when compared to its contemporaries Nuclear Throne is a game with good design.
However...
It is a buggy mess and updates are slow to the point of abandonware with an update being promised in early 2016 that still has not been deployed. Bugs and glitches add a forth dimension to the difficulty as you can die instantly or find yourself in bizaare situations and simply have to give up that run. These are events that are fun to watch such as during a twitch stream but not exactly fun to experience for yourself, infact they are downright antagonistic in a game that leaves little room for error.
On that topic, you have 0 recovery frames on hit so you can get cut down immediately if you are prone to moments of panic and some enemies seem to have a "♥♥♥♥ you" mode if left alive too long which might not be in your control to do anything about due to low ammo or a bunch of enemies you want to deal with in a controlled fashion so you feel punished for taking a careful approach.
No problem, just go gung ho right? well maybe don't! Actually, maybe don't do that. If you run out of ammo then tough. You do not get a melee attack, you will just have 2 guns with empty clips and if no ammo remains then thats too bad kiddo, time to kill yourself.
I'm not sure if that was intentional or an oversight and I am not citing it as a negative either way but the game never decides if it wants to be a bullet hell or a roguelike and so sometimes you can go nice, slow and cautious while other times you just end up going balls to the wall as you try to navigate a stage you have done countless times but this time RNG has not blessed you.
An arguement can be bad that it is the nature of these games and for a genre I claim to enjoy, I should know that however also par for the course for these games is minor progression. Sure you die over and over but you get some skill or trinket for future runs to make them more palatable however Nuclear Throne doesn't have that, instead you are expected to beat the game in order to hold on to goodies that will help you to, you guessed it, beat the game...Again.
This is difficult enough but we have a nasty bug that has become a "feature" at this point and its death. Or rather, the effects of death. If you die in multiplayer and are revived, you lose EVERYTHING and that includes
which I will frankly call a bug since you do not revert back to level one, you simply lose everything and get a middle finger in your face. This makes multiplayer bad, but the bad gets worse because if one person dies and you don't revive them fast enough, you also lose health until you die. You can both make it really far, die, and be stuck with no perks, too far in the game to get anymore and effectively be expected to win on "skill alone" which is a kick in the groin but not impossible however if I wanted such a """fun""" challenge there are actually better bullet hell games out that I could be playing that
have limited ammo.
My issue is that the game fails as a bullet hell because we, the player have limited ammo to retailiate with and it fails as a rogue-lite because the progression requires you to beat the game and thus misses the point and it fails as a co-op game because unless you are both godly at the game, having a partner is just adding an extra you lose condition so all we have left is a game that is fun to watch someone else play so you can enjoy all the action with none of the suffering.
Bluntly speaking, this game hasn't aged well and wasn't great when it did launch originally but it was a fresh foray into bullet hell rogue lites which as a whole, hardly has any titles. First impressions are also good so its easy to see why it sold as well as it did. Calling the game bad when it launched would get you beaten up but with the passage of time, better games have come forth and this is just a forgotten relic.
If you intend to play solo I can cautiously recommend the game but if you want to play with friends then here is a pro-tip, don't.

I'm going with Thumbs up because it's a solid game and I had fun with it for some hours, but there are a couple of issues that made me stop playing after a while and I'd like to talk about them:
1) The first one is related to the sense of progression. It's good at first, you start unlocking characters every time you reach a new zone or access to certain secret areas. They all have different abilities and bonuses, some of them more useful than others, which adds to the variety and replayability factors (despite the fact that they don't make runs feel so much different from others). The problem becomes once you need to reach a very far zone to unlock someone. As every time you die you start from the beginning, it's a very tall wall you have to climb, so you'll die and die feeling you achieved absolutely nothing.  It also doesn¡t help that all you can unlock are characters, nothing else. The other way to unlock them is by getting to some secret areas, which carries me to the next problem.
2) Secret areas are poorly designed. In pretty much any other rogue-like game I played, like Crypt of the Necrodancer, Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy, Spellunky, etc, you access secret areas by clever exploration of the maps. In Nuclear Throne, however, they are reached by doing specific things on a specific level. There's no clue about how to access them, you pretty much have to search a guide that tells you exactly what you have to do in the exact area. That isn't fun. Secret areas themselves aren't fun either. And neither it's the fact that you have to do the exact same things on every run if you want to get to those areas. No variation at all regarding that.
So, after some hours, the game became very monotonous to me. Runs didn't feel much different from each other, and the lack of sense of progression just made it more tedious. Why the good rate then? Because at least I had some fun, and  because I know that the things I found annoying may be fine for other players.

Being a game that begins with the letter "A", Alan Wake is constantly eluding my vision as I scroll up and down my Steam Library. Sometimes I forget I own it, and when I remember, I have to convince myself that I actually played it. When the memories all come back, Alan Wake slams me in the face and forces me to look down at that towering list of games it stands above, not only because it is alphabetically superior, but outwardly superior as well.
The narrative is so tight, so well-woven that it breathes in and out, heaves spit in your face, and so humid you can taste the ripe Stephen King inspiration on the tip of your lower lip, unless your lower lip decides to fall open for the mind-blowing finale and your mouth becomes vulnerable to the sweet juiciness it leaves on your tongue. Seldom can games be described as such.
However, I forget this fact. There it is, standing on a heap of otherwise sub-par games, escaping the "Top 10" lists I like to think up in my head, when it should be modeling at the forefront of story design for future games. The point is that it wasn't a wholly memorable experience. I really hate to admit this, considering how powerful a game it was in scope and atmosphere, but the game itself plays like a Stephen King novel: a single-dose experience that will likely be temporarily surpassed until it can come rushing back to your tongue. It's difficult that way. There's no dishonor in this; if anything, Alan Wake acts like a reality check, like a list of criteria all games must now meet before they can be truly commended for the features they present. Oftentimes I will come back and make sure I don't go overboard about loving a certain game until I pay my tithe to the king of all, if only a spiritual one: Alan Wake.
Buy it on a sale. Don't promise yourself to replay it, because you won't, but it offers an array of emotions that can rarely be captured. You won't ever fully appreciate how great it is, but that's okay, because it's still going to give you an impression you will HATE to see another games attempt to imitate.

What others have said is true:  This game misrepresents itself badly.  There are only 10 playable levels, the 11th one won't even allow you to make any moves, rendering it completely unplayable.  Once you unlock level 11 by beating level 10, you can't even select it from the menu to play it that way.  It feels as if the developer got bored or ran out of ideas and just decided to put what he had up on Steam to see what he could get for it.
Most levels are solveable in under a minute, giving you very little play time.  You will probably complete the game (as far as it can be completed) before the first card drops.  The physics on each level play out exactly same way every time, so once you figure out the correct box to click (and
to click it on some levels), there simply isn't a reason to ever play them again.
Exiting the game leaves some process running in your system, doing god-knows-what in there.  You can't kill it.  You have to log off Windows or restart your computer to be rid of it.  Worst job of coding I've ever seen.
A short, cheap-feeling, lackluster effort that feels more like a shell of what the game was supposed to be.  Don't bother with this one.

Overall, both acts of Broken Age left me disappointed. One might say, a double failed adventure.
The game has some things that work well, like the animation, the graphics and everything audio.
For those wondering where the multi million budgetdisappeared, I assume the famous voiceovers are partialy to blame. Is Jack Black's or Elijah Wood's voices essential to the enjoyment of this game? Not when it comes at the expense of the actual gameplay.
I've read on the forums some complaints about the difficulty of the puzzles. As a longtime adventure point and click aficionada, I thought they were of medium difficulty and if you really took the time to look for the solution, you would eventually find it (with one or two exceptions - like the wire puzzle). The main problem of the game is that it is tedious. The characters and the story are very unidimensional, there is no real substance, no nuances to them and the puzzles are there only so that you have something to do towards ending the game. There are so many loose ends, so many missed opportunities, you can only wonder how much thought they actually put in the game. In the end, you don't really care about any of the characters, you're glad it's over.
The cherry on top, after two years of waiting for a full game, you get an incomplete ending that seems to suggest there will be a third act. I see that as a slap in the face of everybody who ever payed for this game.

To all my bretheren out there and in here. If you have seen the advertisments for "SPINTIRES" and are considering investing in this game but not sure about spending your hard-earned $'s on a game that you're not sure if it's going to be a LEMON, or a SMASH-HIT. Just consider this. If you like simulation games or realistic driving games, this one is for you. I was really suprised at the level of detail in this game. The detail of the vehicles, and the muddy roads that have been rutted out by HEAVY MACHINERY is just awesome. And when you see trees snap at the ground, ruts cut into the soupy swamps, and mud accumulate on your tires and then seeing Rooster-Tails sling off your tires, or you just bury the truck that you're in up to the fenders. NOW YOU KNOW YOU'RE IN FOR A RIDE!!! The game seems simple enough, select your vehicle, your options for said vehicle, and you take off. Scout the flooded swamps for fuel stations or logging camps. Reach certain areas to unlock "CLOAKS" on your map. Put it in 4 low, set your differetial lock and slog your way to the top of the hill. Or if your in The 6X6 Kraz/Ural Soviet all Terrain Vehicle, attach the added fuel cistern and go for the long haul and refuel the trucks you've located. Got one of 'em stuck, hook on to it and whinch it out with The 8X8 Maz (BEAST) with the utility winch. Or you can tie off to a tree or a stump and winch out. That's if the tree you're tied to dosen't snap. This is a game for "Good 'Ole Boys" and "LadyRednecks" and those that love to Get Dirty!!! Try it out, because you're gonna have one HELL OF A GOOD TIME!!!. I know I did. The game isn't perfect by anymeans, but it is worth every $ I spent.
Mods are available, but not in the "Workshop". That's really the only downfall for me. Manual installation is just a little more time consuming and convenient. So in conclusion this is a game that I will continue to play for a long time. As long as it will run on my PC, I'm as happy as a pin in SHXT

Crashlands is incredibly fun game!
It's just as awesome as trailer shows.
Crashlands is a game about crafting. Craft Tool A to be able to gather from Resource B, which is a required to craft Weapon C and with it, you can kill Boss E to complete Quest F - and so on. It's extremely enjoyable cycle.
Many games I've played show everything they have to offer in the first hour.
I've been playing Crashlands for 30+ hours and I keep finding new stuff and even new mechanics.
That's why it's impossible to stop playing Crashlands - it stays fresh.
Many games I've played had a lot of things just copied from other games of the same genre.
Health potions, iron swords, fireball spells, dragons, etc.
Crashlands have none of those things, everything - items, locations, NPC's - is unique to the game, and everything has wacky names.
That's why it's impossible to stop playing Crashlands - it's filled with original things to discover.
Many games I've played are too easy or too hard.
Dark Souls/random retro platformers will kill you hundreds of times just for a bit of excitement when you actually succeed.
Skyrim/random casual AAA games will shower you in rewards, that doesn't matter because they are too easy.
Crashlands has a perfect balance between too hard and too easy.
It's challenging, but do-able, even in higher difficulty settings.
That's why it's impossible to stop playing Crashlands - it has many challenges that you'll really want to overcome.
There's base building, farming, legendary time-stopping items, fishing, savagery, GIANT AXES, alien frogs, treasure chests, bosses, great soundtrack, and so much more.
So yeah, if you're tired of looking for a satisfying game, get this one, because - give me your full attention - Crashlands is that AWESOME GAME you always wanted.

Counterstrike meets Starcraft:
Some people describe this game as a shooter with a supporting commander for each team. It is not! It is a fully grown RTS with real players as units. This is important to understand if you want to have fun with it.
I've seen my share of marketing claims asserting game X would really endorse team play. They all lied. Not so with Natural Selection 2. It doesn't "endorse" team play, it simply makes it a requirement for victory. You need your team, your team needs its commander and the commander needs the team to follow his orders. It's a symbiosis.
This is the strongest part of Natural Selection 2 and it's the feature that sets it apart from other games. In a way it could be seen as a game about leadership, and at the end of the day, when everybody knows the tech-tree and how to deal with opponents and the commander has learned the "best build order" and the countless possible strategies there is still work to do. Sometimes the biggest challenge seems to be to keep the team's morale up. This is where communication comes into play, an important part of the game. It is incredibly rewarding to overcome a worthy opponent and there are no achievements or unlockables in this game. Winning itself is the achievement.
And if there's no teamwork? Well, that's when Natural Selection 2 gets incredibly frustrating. Especially veterans can often tell how a game will end after 30 seconds. And it's always YOUR fault. See that NooB over there? YOU need to talk to him and make him follow you. It's impossible for the commander to take care of every single player.
If you just want to casually shoot some Aliens, this is probably not your game, but if you want to enjoy team play and are willing to commit to a degree: don't wait any longer.

When I was a Navy primary flight instructor, I made sure my students practiced with Microsoft Flight Simulator.  The program didn't teach them everything they needed to know to become pilots, but it did help them get the hang of basic flight maneuvers, local area navigation, and instrument flying.  I could tell which students used FS and which didn't: the ones who had practiced with FS consistently performed better in the real plane.
That was years ago.  Now, I have a child who has expressed an interest in aviation.  When I went looking for FS, I found it here on Steam.  I bought the program and a joystick, and today we worked on level turns.  He could turn to the assigned heading; he could maintain airspeed; he could hold altitude: he just couldn't do all three at the same time.  This is entry level, first-flight stuff, and I'd rather he get a feel for the three axes of flight for pennies at our kitchen table than for $250/hr for an instructor and a rental plane.  I'm thinking of this as $9.99 well spent!
I'm running the program using Windows 10 in a Parallels window.  My computer is a 2012 MacBook Pro with a 2.9GHz Intel Core I7 processor, 8 GB of memory, and Intel HD Graphics 4000 1536 M.  The program's running smoothly, with many of the performance sliders at or near maximum.
