Being a game that begins with the letter "A", Alan Wake is constantly eluding my vision as I scroll up and down my Steam Library. Sometimes I forget I own it, and when I remember, I have to convince myself that I actually played it. When the memories all come back, Alan Wake slams me in the face and forces me to look down at that towering list of games it stands above, not only because it is alphabetically superior, but outwardly superior as well.
The narrative is so tight, so well-woven that it breathes in and out, heaves spit in your face, and so humid you can taste the ripe Stephen King inspiration on the tip of your lower lip, unless your lower lip decides to fall open for the mind-blowing finale and your mouth becomes vulnerable to the sweet juiciness it leaves on your tongue. Seldom can games be described as such.
However, I forget this fact. There it is, standing on a heap of otherwise sub-par games, escaping the "Top 10" lists I like to think up in my head, when it should be modeling at the forefront of story design for future games. The point is that it wasn't a wholly memorable experience. I really hate to admit this, considering how powerful a game it was in scope and atmosphere, but the game itself plays like a Stephen King novel: a single-dose experience that will likely be temporarily surpassed until it can come rushing back to your tongue. It's difficult that way. There's no dishonor in this; if anything, Alan Wake acts like a reality check, like a list of criteria all games must now meet before they can be truly commended for the features they present. Oftentimes I will come back and make sure I don't go overboard about loving a certain game until I pay my tithe to the king of all, if only a spiritual one: Alan Wake.
Buy it on a sale. Don't promise yourself to replay it, because you won't, but it offers an array of emotions that can rarely be captured. You won't ever fully appreciate how great it is, but that's okay, because it's still going to give you an impression you will HATE to see another games attempt to imitate.

Nuclear Throne
Rating: 8/10
Overview: Bullet-Hell Rogue/ Isometric view
The Good:
+  Multiple characters each with their own unique skill and passive abilities. Each character plays very differently from each other.
+ Lots of weapons
+ Randomized levels and upgrades
+ Very addicting gameplay, it really has the “just one more time” element to it. Highly replay-able game.
+ Daily and weekly challenges
+ Good Soundtrack
The Average:
+/-  For a rogue game there isn’t a whole lot to unlock, other than the characters (you start with 2) everything is already unlocked right from the start
+/- This is a very challenging game, a typical run to the last boss is around 20-30 minutes, it took me 12 hours before I finally beat the game. Bad level layouts, and getting bad weapons usually result in a quick death. If you hate dying over and over again, this game may not be for you.


Conclusion:
This game is a lot of fun and very addicting. Despite my frustrating with the game I keep coming back to it from time to time just to see how far I can make it. Finding an awesome gun and getting good upgrades feels satisfying.

does exactly what it sets out to do.  It is an ambient, casual, silly game that is entertaining to mess around with for an hour or three… and I don’t see the problem with that.  I thought it was very fun.
This is a perfect game to combat boredom in a lecture, or a slow day at work.  You can mess around with it a bit and then let it run in the background, so you are free to only partially pay attention to it.  Not everybody at every time is available to get immersed in an epic game; sometimes it is nice to mess around with something light and casual.  This is where
shines brightest.
Of note: in order to truly and actively “play” the game, you should probably look up the songs (i.e.: codes) that you can use to force things to happen in the game.  I feel like many people who disliked this game weren’t fully informed of all the things you actually can do to make it more interesting.
I don’t normally focus on
in my reviews, because it is all relative.  Many people use Steam; people with a wide variety of incomes and who participate in very different economies.  I will make a brief exception here just to say that I think this game is very reasonably priced. Even at full price it costs less than a soda (at least where I live).  I mention this because I think it is important to recognize that the developers aren’t trying to rip you off; they acknowledge what the game is and what it isn’t, and have priced it accordingly.
And so, I believe
is a great little game which should appeal to those of you who may want to casually mess around with it for a few hours here and there.  It certainly isn’t some epic game, but it can be an enjoyable, quaint experience.

This is a fun little team based shooter which involves you, the player, gunning down... well, dinosaurs. Hundreds of 'em, in droves. If you ever get tired of shooting at dinosaurs, then there's a whole host of different modes to choose from, including several styles of PvP. The developers are very prompt about keeping this game up to date and adding new content, and have already released a huge update in the short time I've been playing it. Good work guys!
Pros:
- Caters to a range of different playstyles. You can play in first and third person, solo or in a group.
- Customisable characters provide a huge range of options.
- A range of vehicles to choose from. Ever felt like blasting hordes of raptors with a tank?
- Constantly updated with new maps, game modes and big fixes.
Cons:
- Currently a little buggy, though mostly minor stuff like sounds not playing properly and dinosaurs getting stuck.
- The music can be repetitive
- While the game
be played alone, it's noticeably built with multiplayer in mind. Most game modes are considerably more fun with friends.
TL;DR: This game is a lot of fun with a group of friends. Why not give it a try?

This game may have an ambiguous story, with plenty meant to be interpreted by the player... But the truth is none of that matters, does it?
The game shows you that the aforementioned plot doesn't matter, and you know that deep down, understanding what is happening isn't why you play this game... You play it for the rush of the kill, to feel the warm blood on your hands as another building is swept of life... You monster...
At first you feel uncomfortable with what you're doing, but by the end, you don't feel anything. It's all a game, it's just another level to be completed, what does it matter why you do anything? What does it matter who you're killing or what your motive is?
The blood is just gruesome enough to revolt without being cheesy like Mortal Kombat, the gameplay is fast-paced and challenging, the music puts you in a trance as you continue your homicidal rampage. This is what Hatred wishes it was, but the difference is THIS game actually makes a point in doing so. It doesn't matter who you are, or how "good" you think you have been, anyone can be a killer, including you.
Graphics: 9.0/10
The pixel art suits it well, and the colors are all incredibly pretty to look at. The art design is done very well, and all the sprites seem to pop out, like if the color scheme of the original Castlevania dropped acid... However, with the exception of the bosses, almost all the enemies look the same (You've got a white-suited standard mobster and a big, burly body-guard... that's about it). I get that that's to make the player feel that the cookie-cutter characters don't matter, and that they are only there as targets and obstacles with no real value to their life, but at least a little more variety would be nice.
Music: 9.5/10
The music is absolutely phenomenal, each track keeps you calm and focused rather than frustrated at the difficulty of the game. Only when the last man in the building dies, and the music stops do you realize what you've done... Until of course you stop feeling anything, and wading through every corpse in the building to get back to your car feels as mundane as going to the grocery store... You monster. My only complaint is that a few of the songs feel a little lacking sometimes. Maybe it's just my preference for less ambient genres, but I often felt like something was missing from the music.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Challenging gameplay that allows for multiple approaches to any scenario. You can charge forward recklessly like a maniac: kick down the door into a mobster, take his knife, slit his throat, throw it at the gunman around the corner, etc. Or you can play more tactical: survey the area, select a target, wait until he is isolated, go in for the kill, fire his gun to draw attention and pick off everyone as they run around the corner... However, my only complaint is that unlocking all weapons and masks depends on level score, which is incredibly difficult, and I'd prefer to feel like I can be rewarded for my own playstyle and still unlock everything, rather than rewarding a style of play that is unsuited for a more methodical and strategic killer such as myself (I want as many points for accuracy and bonus score for not dying on a level as the guy who kicked down the door, guns blazing and happened to get lucky on his 100th try after dying repeatedly got for his recklessness).
Story: 8.0/10
It is difficult to really give the story of this game a single score. As stated earlier, it is left up for interpretation, which to be frank, I really hate games that do that... Yet I'm willing to forgive this one because, also as stated earlier, it isn't the story that matters so much as it is the point the game makes by slowly turning you from an average person, with remorse and empathy, into a cold-blooded uncaring killer. The point the game makes by doing so is quite the impressive feat indeed, however, I cannot rate the story based on the merit of that alone. And if the story doesn't even matter due to that point being made, I cannot rate it higher than an 8.

Although my amount of time spent playing TF2 (900+ hours) currently dwarfs my time in Paladins (55+ hours), I feel qualified enough to provide a fair review. Overall, the game is very entertaining and great to play alone or with friends (as long as you do not bring more than four others). If one enjoys first person shooters/class-based shooters and is okay with a fantasy/sci-fi based world, I recommend at least trying Paladins. The game is currently free, so there is little reason to not hop in and play a few games.
First, I'll explain the gameplay briefly. Essentially, a player picks a character to play (after picking, one cannot switch untul the match ends). After this, the player plays whatever gamemode he/she has selected. The current options are Siege (starts with one control point, transitions into a cart-pushing game, and resets), Payload (try to push cart farther/faster than other team does), Survival (no respawn arena), and PvE (play against bots with special abilities). It should be noted that this game has two teams of five champions for a 5v5 format. Each champion has a specific role, which is damage, flank, front line, or support. However, these are not set roles, and one can often see healers flanking, damage champions being tanks, etc. Next, one must understand the mechanics of gameplay. Each champion has five main abilities. These vary depending on the champion, but most have one primary weapon, one secondary attack, an ability that does something unique, a movement ability, and an "ultimate" ability (must be charged to 100% over time, and is quite powerful). Each ability has a cooldown, with the exception of the primary, which usually has a reloading feature. Lastly, there is a system in each match where credits are earned by completing actions in that match. This allows the player to purchase buffs only for that match. In summary, Paladins is a class-based shooter, but it has many unique mechanics that separate it from the likes of TF2 and Overwatch.
To analyze the benefits, one must understand that all of these things are highly subjective, so you might not like what you hear as much as I do. The first positive thing I would like to mention is the amount of playstyles and customization players have. At the time of writing, 22 champions are playable in Paladins, and there should be about 30 (I have heard estimates of 35) by the end of 2017. While there are obvious balancing issues, all champions are viable to some extent. Furthermore, there are "loadouts," which are sets of cards used to alter a playstyle. For instance, a card might reduce an ability's cooldown or increase reload speed under a certain condition. A recent addition to the game is legendary cards. These provide major benefits to champions, and a player must pick one of three whenever he selects a champion to play. While it is not necessary to worry about loadouts and legendary cards, one will benefit from doing so, and I personally enjoy the customization to my style of play. Second, I will discuss the benefits of the purchase system during matches. This includes various buffs, including one that reduces the damage of direct attacks, and one that allows your attacks to deal extra damage to shields. This creates variety and adjustment to particular situations, but it requires gamesense. It allows players to choose what they would like to do better, and buy accordingly. These buffs are bought with credits that you earn in each match (they are separate in each match, so a player loses his buffs and credits at the end of each one). Lastly, this atmosphere or customization, multiple maps, multiple gamemodes, and many champions creates an entertaining game for casual and competitve players. Yes, this game also has a place in eSports. This atmosphere is often enhanced through the frequent updates the game receives. Also, do not worry about the game being "pay to win," as it truly is not. A player might have to grind a bit to obtain the cards he wants, but players who pay do not have a gameplay advantage over those who do not beyond perhaps getting cards they desire slightly faster. I have currently spent no real money on anything in Paladins, but one can do so for things such as cosmetic items.
Although this game has benefits, there are some clear downsides. As of writing, this game is currently in beta, so I believe many of these issues should be excused until the full release. Nonetheless, I will mention them. Firstly, there are a fair amount of bugs, some of which truly hurt champions. For instance, shots can currently pass through shields of certain champions when they are retreating. Second, there are balance issues, which lead to some champions being overpowered and some being underpowered, but regular updates adjust this often. These updates do not always benefit the game, however. For example. the Open Beta 44 patch added a new currency called "Essence," and most players feel it damages the economy of the game. Lastly, Paladins currently lacks many things, such as proper maps for aiming practice and a microphone-based communication system, and the toxic players found in any multiplayer game are sometimes present. As I said, however, most of these issues will hopefully be resolved before the beta period is concluded, and none of them are totally game-breaking.
Overall, I would recommend Paladins to any fan of class-based/first person shooters who has some time to spare. Although issues exist, it is a free game that is in a beta period, and the pros outweigh the cons to me. This game is far from an Overwatch clone (development actually started before Overwatch was announced, but that is besides the point) due to many mechanics, and its developers are usually decent or better in terms of communication and update speed. I hope you install Paladins and have a great time!

I have been playing hockey games since I began playing videogames. This may be the least fun and most disappointed I've been with any hockey game I've ever played, and that statement includes my experiences with the terrible NHL '94 port for the Game Gear and the recent 2K game on mobile.
When I saw the announcement for this game I was very intrigued. However, despite what it claimes, this game is not an old-school, retro arcade throwback. It is a low-rent,  unresponsive version of any recent EA hockey game but with cell-shaded graphics and a cheap 1970s attitude.
This game is slugglish at best. It was impossible for me to tell the difference between a player who had bad stats or was fatigued and the game's performance issues.  But it's true crime is the input delay. There is a half second pause between almost every input and the games animations beginning. At no point did I truly feel in control of the players. An arcade hockey game should be a balance between basic hockey instincts and fighting-game level speed with your fingers.  However, this game quicly deteriorated into me mashing a single button and hoping the players animation would trigger, and about half the time it did.
There appear to be no one timers. Perhaps they hadn't been invented by this point in hockey history. However, by 1994 they were well established in hockey video games, so I don't think this game has a good excuse not to have them as well. This means that the strategy of this game is basically to skate to the middle of the ice and shoot, and sometimes it goes in, and sometimes it doesn't. The players response time is not fast enough to be able to count on rebound goals either.  I also found the delay time on the passing to be bad enough that I stopped trying outside of the neutral zone. So, I would just skate backwards (because the game doesn't seem to anticipate that you will do that when you have the puck, and actually seemed faster than skating forward) and then try to take a shot. Which is to say, no actual hockey strategy is needed to be successful in this game.
So, I'm assuming this is actually a half hearted attempt to recreate Mutant League Hockey.  The hockey itself is secondary, and the true game is abusing the other team as much as possible and then debuffing them by winning fights. However, the fighting itself is terrible. It is slow, unresponsive, and - stop me if I'm repeating myself - feels somewhat random. It also suffers from a lack of animations, there are no satisfying knock out blows, when one player's health is gone, they return to their default grapple stance and then that player turtles and the other one gets to take meaningless shots at them on the ground. Every fight basically plays the same, you circle around and try to take free shots, then you lock into a grapple and punch or dodge, three punches and you're done.  But, it doesn't seems to matter when you hit the button, there is a cool down after each punch, so it will only throw the next one when its ready. And the dodge appears to be broken, except for the computer players.
I will conceed, fighting in hockey games is incredibly difficult to pull off. Blades of Steel was probably the best, because it was simple, reponsive and intuitive (high / low punch, high / low block). This is has basically been the only formula that has had any success: NHL Hits improved upon it, some of the new EA games also combined this system with a grapple to some sucess. But OTH fails. It is some of the least fun fighting in any game. It is exasperated by the fact that happens 10-20 times per game. Despite a wealth of clips of stick combat in their promotional video, it only happened once for me, and it was great, but only because it seemed to be a one shot kill and the fight ended immediatly afterwards.
I would like to apologize to the developers for this review, because I really wished this game was better. Maybe I came to it with the wrong expectations. I wanted a game that was fast and exciting. I wanted something with the NHL 94 speed boosts, 2-on-2 Open Ice Challenge and Wayne Gretsky 64 powerups, and NHL Hits fighting. But its not any of those things. It feels half baked. I will check back in with it in 3-6 months and I hope they have done significant work. If so, I will gladly change this review to reflect it. But at this point, take a hard, accurate pass on it (because none of the players in the game will).

Natural selection 2 is truly one of a kind, the graphics are good and there's in general an eerie misty atmosphere which makes you alert and keeps you staring at the screen looking for extra-terrestial movement,  however this can be demanding on your computer, so a proper gaming pc is prefered.
in al the hours i spend in this game i came across 1 person that was trolling so far , so i can say natural selection has an awesome gaming community who most of the times are happy to teach rookies and/or newbies the basics and tactics of the game. natural selection can be tough to learn and you defenately need to play some practise rounds or look up some tutorial video's before you start, especially for commanding as a team is fully relying on the commanders backup and upgrades.
it is a multiplayer only game and it  pits two teams (the human marines with an arsenal of weapons, and the brutal kharaa aliens who are living weapons) into combat with eachother in space -station like maps, there are plenty of maps and each map is different enough in style and form to be unique each.
you can play multiple roles on each team, for the aliens:you can take the roles of the basic melee infantry, the field medic/builder, assassin, support, or simply rampage into the enemy with an giant raging onos. the marines are more general, every marine can get each gun as you don't need specific classes, you can weld things up, use machine guns, shotguns, flamethrowers to clear enemy infestations, throw different types of grenades, place mines or use grenade launchers. you can buy jetpacks to make yourself more mobile or if you want to do some real damage you can suit up in minigun or railgun wielding exosuit. the commander can also decide to make mobile artillery called ARC's which ignore walls, but can't attack players so you need to defend these.
each match is different and its fun to discuss strategies with your teammates before attacking the enemy. this game relies alot on communication between the players, so for this game you need to talk alot to your teammates. either on textchat or ingame voicechat. you cant solo in this game as you will need your team, and the team needs you to do your part.
the soundeffects are also good, aliens sound fierce guns sound like they should. if you use headphones you can sneak around silently to hear aliens crawling on the walls behind or above you, or as alien you can hold still and hear marines running through corridors next to you. the music is also good, but you won't be hearing it during matches. especially if you want to be able to hear things around you, including possible aliens that try to sneak up on you.
so in short this game is great, the sound effects are good, and the gameplay is refreshing and unique, don't expect it to be like call of duty though, it's a true team game.also make sure your pc is good enough to run it, since this game can be real heavy. it got me addicted and if you like aliens or FPS games then you should take a closer look at this game!

It takes 528,000 essence to craft all the legendaries.
The prices for cards, didn't explain, cards are basically skill trees that you can use on your individual characters, each character has 16 cards,
common cards cost 500 essence and give back 250 for duplicates,
Rares cards cost 1250 essence and give back 250 for duplicates,
Epic cards cost 5,000 essence and give back 1250 for duplicates,
Legedary cards cost 12,000 and give back 4,500 for duplicates.
On average matches in this game are 12 minutes long. If you play 7 hours a day you can fit in 35 matches give or take.
At 7 hours a day you can make about 14,000 gold, which gives you about 5-6 chests.
In those chests there's an average of 1000 essence (assuming you have all the cards).
You can range however from 750(all commons/rares)- 3750(all epics which are around a 15% chance to drop each.)- 13,400(All legendaries, about 4-5% chance each.)
You may also get cosmetics from these chests which still have a small percentage they are more common than legendaries however.
Duplicate cosmetics are worth about 2k each.
Now for how long it takes to get legendaries, assuming your luck consists of all rares and commons.
If we go off of the above at 6 chests with all commons and rares you'll get about 4,500 essence for 7 hours of play.
Now say you wanted all 44 legendaries for whatever reason (I would like them incase the meta changes or they are nerfed/buffed.)
Now say you wanted all 44 legendaries for whatever reason (I would like them incase the meta changes or they are nerfed/buffed.)
It's around 16 chests for a legendary so 40,000 gold/20 hours for one, or 1,760,000 gold/880 hours for all of them.
Now for every card, if you wanted them now with 22 characters:
This is assuming you make 2,000 gold per hour from the number we got earlier on average match length and rewards.
Legendaries- 704 chests/1,760,000 gold/528,000 essence/880 hours
Epics- 293 chests/732,500 gold/220,000 essence/366.25 hours
Rares- 147 chests/367,500 gold/110,000 essence/183.75 hours
Commons- 73 chests/182,500 gold/55,000 essence/91.25 hours
So the total of all these are: 1,071 chests/3,042,500 gold/913,000 essence/1,521.25 hours (all of this assuming you already have all the cards)
(How I got these is by starting off with the amount of cards in each pool type, so 44-L/E, 88-R and 94-C. Then multiply them by the essence cost, once we have that we divide the essence cost by the minimum amount of essence per chest so 750, then we have the amount of chests, multiply by 2,500 take the gold, then divide by 2k.)
You could also knock these stats down a smidge based on the range that I gave, however 750 essence post having all cards is the most common.
These numbers are for just buying raw, I don't take into account mastery levels, bonus rewards and the like as to keep it easier to adjust and move from and will account for once we get 22 more characters probably sometime next year.
Now these numbers seem very grim. Especially if you have horrid luck like you need to get them, but considering that you get 5 chests for getting a character to
level 10 and there are 22 characters, you'll have 110 chests from leveling them all to 10. Not sure how long that takes.
You may also get any of these cards in your chest some with lower chances than others. By the time you open 1,071 chests you'll have all the cards from it anyway, but by the time 22 new characters come out, probably next year sometime considering their plan for 13 new characters later this year you'll need to invest somewhere around 1k hours to get everything for those 22.
What I'd suggest if you want all cards for all characters, if you're going to play a LOT. (Around 232 days of playing 7 hours of paladins each day.)
Save your chests for future characters and open a big bit once those come out of course if you already have all the cards.
In summary: The game is still not friendly for new comers especially if they want to be competitive/ a card collector. Taking over 1k hours to get all the cards for 22 characters. But on the other hand they should still be able to play casual with little problem for the earlier levels.

V7 Entertainment’s hockey video game is an ode to the beer-drinking, minor league tough guys battling both opposing goons and the post-industrialization of the 1970s. It’s essentially the 1977 film Slap Shot.
It’s also the first hockey game available on PC since EA Sports stopped porting over its NHL series back in 2009 — that’s if you don’t count the tremendous work done by modders to recreate NHL 04, but that’s a story for another day.
Fans looking for a simulation game akin to the NHL series will be a little disappointed. There’s no Sidney Crosby or Connor McDavid. There’s no Toronto Maple Leafs nor even a mention of the National Hockey League at all.
What you get is an arcade sports game with an over-the-top style like NBA Jamz and NFL Blitz. There’s blood on the ice, comic-book action booms come with big hits, and unconscious players have birds circling their heads.
Players accustomed to the NHL series can play Old Time Hockey with advanced controls that use both analog sticks, but there’s also an easier two-button mode made to replicate arcade games of yesteryear. There’s actually even a one-handed “beer mode” that allows you to evidently hold a beverage while playing.
Mechanically, you have the ability perform an array of defensive hockey moves, including: body, hip and poke checks, slashing, and hooking. Don’t worry, just like in today’s NHL, the refs won’t call much.
Laying big hits can give your team momentum and put them “on fire.” In this state, the players are difficult to knock off the puck, basically immune to penalties, and score easier.
Fighting obviously plays an important role in these rinks as well, and you’ll likely have chains of brawls to cycle through each game.
There are only two major problems with the gameplay, the first being the inability to one-time the puck. It’s an absurd omission for any hockey game and should be fixed in a patch. One-timers should be the starting point when designing a hockey video game.
The game’s AI is its other weakness. Your teammates are fairly useless at both ends of the ice, although their general lack of skill and awareness could be passed off as part of the minor-league level of hockey being portrayed. The real annoyance with the AI is the goaltending.
If the netminder makes a save, his only move is to pass it to the back boards. He won’t freeze it. He won’t pass it to the open teammate in the slot. The puck always goes behind the net. Always. This, of course, can too easily be exploited.
Despite the cracks in the ice, Old Time Hockey holds it own as a pretty good game. Where it really shines bright like a lit goal lamp is with its Story Mode. It’s a great touch to a sports game and V7 did a fantastic job setting a tone and atmosphere for the campaign.
You take control of the Schuylkill Hinto Brews, based in Pottsville, Pennsylvania (about 2 hours northwest of Philadelphia). The Hinto Brews are clearly based on another minor league hockey club based in an economically depressed Pennsylvania town — the Johnstown Chiefs, popularized by the aforementioned film Slap Shot. There also are flavors of the 1970s Philadelphia Flyers, nicknamed the Broad Street Bullies.
Like the Chiefs, the perennial-loser Hinto Brews struggle at the start of the season, and it’s your job to turn things around in order to bring a championship back to your struggling community and revenue back to your struggling team.
Each game on the schedule has different objectives that must be completed, such as score a goal while a teammate instigates a fight with the goaltender. Don’t worry, if an objective is too difficult, you can simply go back to the main menu and reload to change it.
V7 patched out a terrible feature that forced players to unlock controls as the season went along, allowing the Story Mode really showcase what the game is  — a goofy, sometimes crude experience fans of sport can enjoy.

I don't normally write reviews for games, but I felt obligated to do so for Alan Wake. This game is so good that I bought it TWICE (that's right, you read that correctly, TWICE). I bought the Collector's Edition for the Xbox 360, when it first came out. Then, a few years later I moved on to PC gaming and I knew I needed this game in my Library, so I bought the Collecter's Edition again. If you're looking for a multiplayer FPS, this game is not it. HOWEVER, that's how I categorize myself, a person who loves FPS, but this Campaign was by far the best story I have ever witnessed and I was glued to my chair playing this game until I finished it. Honestly, if it were a book series it should be on the shelves next to Harry Potter and Stephen King's books. Funny enough there is an Alan Wake book released of this game, THAT'S HOW GOOD IT IS!! I won't spoil the feels that I felt in this game, because no one should expect anything and honestly I think the best way to enjoy this game is to blindly jump into it and play it, that's how I did it (not looking at gameplay prior to playing)!
PROS
+ Great Story
+ Great Character Development
+ Great Music
+ Awesome Cutscenes and Scenery
+ No Bugs (Found by me on PC or X360)
CON
-Replayability
The replayability is the only CON I could think of. However, I sometimes comeback and play this game every odd month or so, because the game is so good and there are collectables, that really help with the background story, that I have missed. Plus, this game packs hours of gameplay to playthrough the campaign ( ~12 hrs on Average, if you try to find the collectables).
On another note, this game is best played on nightmare difficulty straight away in my opinion, it just adds that thriller feeling to the game, because of how vulnerable you are. To do so, right click on Alan Wake in the Steam library/Properties/Set launch properties and add -developermenu (with the hyphon). After launching the game, you'll find  developermenu in the game menu, click on it and then unlock nightmare difficulty.
It's worth the money. Hell of a game.

Nuclear Throne is a bullet hell Rogue-Like shooter with procedurally generated levels and enemies that will always keep you on your feet. You get through the game by collecting rads which are dropped by most enemies. Once you collect enough rads to level up you're given a choice of four mutations at the end of a level. These mutations will give you various buffs such as higher speed, higher health, less enemy HP, etc. Most mutations work well on their own, but some combinations are almost game-breaking. As such, there is a fair amount of theorycrafting behind the mutation system and it gives you a lot of room to try out different mutations and see which ones work for your character.
Speaking of characters, the game consists of 12 different characters including the 2 you unlock from the start. These characters are incredibly diverse in playstyle and I highly recommend that you try out all of them at least once to find out who works best for you. Each character has their own unique active ability, which is used by pressing RMB on PC. These range from shields to telekenesis to vine traps. These abilities can be upgraded with a mutation unique to your character called Throne Butt. Throne But generally makes your mutations even more powerful and allows you to synergize more mutations with your active.
Overall, this game is absolutely worth the price. I'd highly recommend this to player that enjoy games similar to Enter the Gungeon and other bullet hell games. However, be aware that this game has a very steep learning curve and you WILL be dying a lot. If you can get past that initial wall, you will spend hundreds upon hundreds of hours on this game topping your previous high scores and hunting for secrets.

If you think you will like this game, you probably will.
Many people complain about the mud being "too deep" and how the trucks react according to the enviroment, but they must not understand how large the trucks really are. Most of the hauling trucks surpass 6 tons easily, and are over 7 feet in height, if you don't believe me, search Russian loggingg trucks and just look.
Anyways, onto the review.
This game is really a peice of work, made by 2 people in Britian it takes place in Russia where you trade your time to deliver loads of logs to various objectives on 6 maps (more to come!). There is currently 2 gamemodes to choose from, casual and hardcore, both varying in features. In casual you can rescue trucks to a garage, in hardcore you cannot. Gas use in casual is little to none, in hardcore, you better have a fuel truck handy. Multiplayer is supported for 4-players at the time, and works best with people you know and can use a VoIP service with.
Some counter-arguements for peoples dislikes:
Camera: I honestly think the camera is part of the experience. And the views are some what odd, but you can toggle free view and lock it to where you like by clicking, and reset it by pressing "1". Could use some work, but if this is making you not buy the game, then your an a**hat.
Price: Yes, the $30 price can seem a bit steep, but I think you can seriously enjoy the game with your friends. I put in 8 hours the first day I got this game, and I do not regret it at all. You seriously can get sucked into this logging enviroment.
No 1st Person View: Seriously, is this keeping you from buying this?! Don't be such a panzy. Surely you have played a game with no 1st person view before, and it was just fine (GTA sound familiar). Like I said, don't be a panzy.
All-in-all, the game is really going well for less than 2 months on Steam, and being developed by 2 people, it's really just amazing to see this.
Do yourself a favor, buy the game, and don't be a panzy because there is no 1st person view, or something stupid of the sort.

I decided a while ago that I would write a short review when I would reach 1234 hours in the game, so here I am.
1234 hours over the course of 3 years and 7 months... that's almost 1 hour every day. It can also mean 1234 hours of nonstop playing for 51 days and 10 hours (that's how I did it).
There have been times where I spent 15 minutes doing math to make sure I had enough fuel for a mission... only to run out of fuel way before I was supposed to.
There have been times where I worked on a big project that took a few days... only to have it ruined by some stupid bug that I had no control over.
There have been times (one time actually) where a single outdated mod prevented me from being able to play the game for weeks, even after I got rid of it. I had to gather knowlegde on the stupid cfg file and mess around in it until It finally worked, which took dozens of attempts of opening the game to see if it worked (and for each one I had to wait 5 minutes for it to load).
And yet, Kerbal Space Program is my
. It scratches that itch of curiosity and exploration which resides deep within every human. That curiosity is what separated us from the animals, because we were the ones who wentured beyond our comfort zone just to see what was behind that hill.
That rewarding feeling of successfully landing on some random moon can't be explained using words. It's a feeling that traces back to when we were hunting our food, and accidentally stumbled upon a meadow with a nice little river. You didn't find anything of use, but hey, at least you know your surroundings a bit better now.
Or maybe I'm reading too much into this idk. It's a good game is what I'm trying to say.

Crashlands is a truely amazing game that really meets all of my expectations. When I bought the game, I expected to play this game casually, because, as a fan of games such as Terraria and Don't Starve, I generally wanted free reign in my survival games and disliked the idea of being controlled by a storyline. Let me just say, Crashlands blew those ideas out of the water.

I was immediately hooked on the game, with it's unique sense of humor, its music, it's diverse terrains and creatures, and most of all, much to my surprise, the storyline. The story seamlessy tied the game together, teaching you about the alien world you landed on, pushing you to create new and better crafting stations, armor, weapons, etc. The developers knew when to guide you and when to leave you alone, creating in my opinion, an almost perfect quest system, never leaving you lost and aimless.

There where very few things that I disliked or wished to see improved. Some of these are :
-Quests occationally repetitive
-Item discriptions sometimes do not describe how to obtain more of such item, making it difficult to advance
-Unable to plant things when a pet is in the area, even if the pet flies
Some things I would like to be added are :
-A game mode without the storyline. Even though I enjoyed it, it becomes repetitive on future runs,
so starting from scratch and not having to do quests to advance might bring something fresh for
veteran players
-A multiplayer mode, I would really enjoy playing this game with friends!
All in all, Crashlands is an amazing game that will appeal to fans of the survival, sanbox, and rpg genres. Enjoy the game!

Good game. Tickles a nostalgic nerve for older gamers and hockey fans. Instead of NHL teams, it features a fictional league with it's own lore. It looks similar to the EA hockey games you grew-up playing in the early to late 90's, but it lacks much of the depth and features. The controls cannot be re-mapped, but there are a few different pre-sets to choose from. I was able to pick-up the game and immediately outscore the medium level AI-competition just as if I was playing NHL '96 on Sega Genesis.  The game does not control as well as those old classics, but it's not as bad as most of the negative reviews claim. Although you can set-up and play exhibition matchs, the game focuses on it's 'story mode', which puts you in the shoes of a pre-chosen 1970's era failing bush-league hockey team. This mode is more interesting than it sounds, but having to playing the season with the same pre-defined team may not lend itself to replayability. Hopefully there are other unlockable modes, or the unlocklable ability to play the story/season with a team of your choice. Besides that, the game features nostalgic-looking fictional hockey cards to collect/unlock, and a surprisingly good soundtrack. I don't write my reviews in point-form. That's for people with 'attention deficit hyperactivity disorder'. If you read all this, you've earned yourself some pudding.

Ah, The Binding of Isaac, my guilty pleasure...
The Binding of Isaac is one of those games that stands out from the crowd in so many ways. It's a top down Roguelike game in which we play as a young child called Isaac (or one of a number of other biblical characters) as he travels through randomised dungeons located in his basement. The game takes a lot of inspiration from the story of the same name and provides us with a truly twisted, and in many ways disgusting, story.
The gameplay is great and despite having a steep learning curve it won't take too long for the player to get the hang of it (though if they will ever master it is a different question). The game has hundreds of unique and interesting items that have large effects upon gameplay, and even the many bosses are randomised to a degree. The numerous unlockables also have a wonderful effect upon replayability and the various endings will keep you coming back for more.
The soundtrack, which is composed by Danny Baranowsky, is one of my personal favourites and worth picking up, as is The Wrath of the Lamb expansion pack for the game which adds hundreds of new items, new levels, a new ending and a new character.
Overall, The Binding of Isaac is an absolute masterpiece and I cannot recommend it enough.

I love this game. Out of any of the Civ games, it is, in my opinion, the one with the best sense of scale. The combat is slightly unbalanced (Memetic mutation of a spearman beating a tank, after all...) and the interface isn't as perfected as in Civ 4, but these issues come up less often than you think. Its editor is simple to use and its modding community is huge even after all these years (possibly even the largest of the series from what I've seen). You can find mods and extremely well-done player-made campaigns about everything from the Reconquista and the Punic Wars to the Portuguese Colonial War. I especially recommend Age of Imperialism (the mod), and Escape from Zombie Island is another gem that shows just how much can be done with the game's relatively simple editor, completely transforming a game about empire-building into a game about zombie survival. But to be honest, even the vanilla, unmodded game is a blast to play and never really gets old.
In short, this is a game with endless value and honestly $5 is a steal. It's something I never get bored of and always come back to binge on every month or so. Fantastic game, a masterpiece. My favorite in the series, though I like 4 and 5 too.

Shadow of War is a worthly sequel to Shadow of Mordor, and a fantastic game in it's own right. Just about everything that was great in the first game has been improved, from the Nemesis system to the combat of the orcs. There are also several new abilities to play with, such as several "magical" attacks and revamped creature combat. The story, while nothing spectacular, was still pretty good in my opinion, as it had enough content to feel complete. Of course, the story really isn't important to me, as the true value of this game comes from the stories you create with the Nemesis system, such as the orc who chased me all across the ice region and nearly destroyed my army, only to be defeated when I assembled my last remaining captains in a final effort to finish him.
Now, quick note about the loot boxes. I've seen a lot of review which basically said "It's great, but thumbs down because loot boxes." Now, I can sympathize with this sentiment, but in my eyes, for that to be valid the game would have to suffer from said loot boxes. I played for hours and had everyone not made a giant fuss about them I wouldn't even know they exsisted. What's more, you can buy lootboxes with in game currency, and while only the lowest tier lootboxes are up for grabs, this game really isn't built for them, and I mean that in the best way. Any loot you could get from them is null because the game gives you much better stuff for playing it, and any captains you get from lootboxes can be found in the field. In fact, I found my self liking the lootboxes later in the game simply because they gave me a way to quickly replenish my army should I not feel like orc hunting. It's not like you'll ever be low on currency late game, as you will be selling basically all the loot you get. (Also lootboxes allow you to slightly improve existing orcs, which is nice.)
TL;DR Shadow of War is a fantastic game with great mechanics and a system that allows for organic stories to form as you play. Despite the outcry the lootboxes don't harm the game in any real way, at least not as I've seen.

Question: Do you like graphic adventure puzzle games, enjoy a good story told in an interesting way, can handle some slightly obtuse inventory puzzles, and can enjoy an atmospheric psychological horror experience?
If yes, then stop reading this and download this game.
It's free (not free-to-play, FREE. As in you don't pay for it.), it's got a really engaging story (the story is ostensibly a loose adaptation of Goethe's Faust, but the creators put some unique twists on it, even if you're familiar with the play you may still not see some of the plotlines coming), it's got some really clever puzzles, a fantastic art style, and even if you try it and it's not your thing, you literally have nothing to lose.
Anyway, I loved this game!
I found the story completely engrossing, I thought the aesthetic matched the tone the creators were going for to a tee, I found some of the more horror-y sequences very creepy (there are some parts of this game that legitimatly enter Silent Hill territory), and while I thought some of the puzzles fell into the trappings of old school adventure games (there was one involving a duck that I legitimatly don't think I'd have ever figured out without a hint), most of them are pretty straight-forward logic puzzles and even the ones that aren't you'll likely be able to figure out with a little trial and error (most of them anyway).
On that note, this game is still fairly obscure, even among enthusiasts (I only learned about through an acuantance on DeviantART), and as far as I know there are NO full walkthroughs available, I know of a few work in progress guides, and one incomplete Lets Play but that is it. There are a few hints floating around on the community discusion page, but by and large you are on your own. This game is uncharted territory in a way I havn't had the chance to experience in years, the feeling of really having to break out the pen and paper and figure out these puzzles, plus the resulting smug sense of self satisfaction I got when I did, was a very rewarding experience, and may have made up allot of what I really enjoyed about this game.
I have a feeling that at some point this game is going to get more exposure and there'll be more discussion about it (atleast I hope so), and there may indeed be a full guide up on GameFaqs or something by the time you read this, but I reccomend getting ahead of the curve on this one, I think you'll enjoy it all the more for it.
If you're familiar with RPGmaker games then you'll likely be acustomed to the UI already (also, Alt+Enter to fullscreen, this is not a game you want to play in a window), and the controls are pretty self explainatory.
As for the story, I wont discuss it too much, but it's a really creative take on the source material, and borrows not just from Goethe's Faust itself, but mixes in some elements from some of the literature and preformance art based or inspired by the original play(s), whilst also weaving together it's own narrative. The story, much like the rest of the game is kept as something of a mystery in and of itself until the very end when things start to piece themselves together, some things are left up for interpretation, it's hard to explain without spoiling anything but if you're a fan of unconventional stories told in unconventional ways (I am), then I think you'll enjoy this.
I don't really know what else to say about this game; I liked it allot, it's suprisingly long for a free game (I've paid full price for games that I've gotten far less enjoyment out of), and I hope it gets more exposure.
Play it late at night with all the lights off, bring a notepad and a nice cup of tea or coffee, and give it a go.

What can I say about this game?
I recommend it sure, but I have mixed feelings.
Why? Well sit down, relax and read my review.
Let me start off by saying that this game is a puzzle. The whole gameplay IS a puzzle,
and you will not find anyhting else other than a puzzle out of this game.
Both the gameplay and even the STORY is a puzzle on it self, and as you know
and if you don't know, I will tell you, that sometimes, puzzles can have a lot of entities/pieces that
you can use to solve the puzzle but just a bunch are the right one to actually solve the puzzle.
Also for that reason, you might need to wait for all the puzzle pieces to reveal,
to actually put some braincells to work, and solve the puzzle with what you have.
This mean, that things like the story, is ok if you don't understand them at first,
because really, around the end, things start to reveal itself in the story,
and the pieces start to fit together, solving part of that puzzle.
The only problem I have with many of the things regarthing puzzle on this game,
is that the game creator rely too much on being cryptic in both the progression
of the area, the puzzles and the story.
Things like this will make you get out of the game, and search the interwebs for some clues,
and that really is not good for a game in my opinion. You sincerly can get stuck in an area or chapter because
you haven't found a piece of something, just because you haven't trigger an event, or things turn
out different in some areas, because you didn't do the most cryptic outcome you never though you do
to solve the obstacle/event at the moment.
At the end of the game, in my opinion, just one bad ending, the true ending and the cryptic
hidden ending actually matters to me, to actually understand, what is wrong with the main character
and try to understand the experience from her perspective.
But yes, there are a lot of clues, hints, that give you insight on putting together
the puzzle that is the story, but there is also a lot of useless nothing that you don't
need to understand it.
That would be my analysis.
Have for the presentation.
1. The art/Aesthetics fit pretty well with the story and perspective, I like it.
2. The development of the dialog, need some work. I don't know if it because
of the translation barrier, or the way dialog is establish, you will sometimes, get lost
on what the character is talking, to who is she adressing to, and who is narrating.
This is a issue.
3. The music is great. I like the piano pieces/scores, good inspiration for the story too.
4. The story, well, you already know my opinion. What I can say here is that the story is heavily
inspire by Faust and the Goethe's Faust, but you don't really need to know about it,
the game will provide information to understand the story, regardless.
5.I love the puzzles, regardless of the cryptic moments in the game. The game will
tell you most of the clues needed to solve the puzzles, it does a good job on it.
There is even puzzles withing puzzles.
In the end, the best reward of this game is on the EXTRA section after you beat it
with the "true ending". If you want to understand more about the story, and read the diaries.

That true ending though, was underwhelming, the hidden one was better.
Good luck and have fun in the nightmare.

Nuclear Throne is a bullet hell Rogue-Like shooter with procedurally generated levels and enemies that will always keep you on your feet. You get through the game by collecting rads which are dropped by most enemies. Once you collect enough rads to level up you're given a choice of four mutations at the end of a level. These mutations will give you various buffs such as higher speed, higher health, less enemy HP, etc. Most mutations work well on their own, but some combinations are almost game-breaking. As such, there is a fair amount of theorycrafting behind the mutation system and it gives you a lot of room to try out different mutations and see which ones work for your character.
Speaking of characters, the game consists of 12 different characters including the 2 you unlock from the start. These characters are incredibly diverse in playstyle and I highly recommend that you try out all of them at least once to find out who works best for you. Each character has their own unique active ability, which is used by pressing RMB on PC. These range from shields to telekenesis to vine traps. These abilities can be upgraded with a mutation unique to your character called Throne Butt. Throne But generally makes your mutations even more powerful and allows you to synergize more mutations with your active.
Overall, this game is absolutely worth the price. I'd highly recommend this to player that enjoy games similar to Enter the Gungeon and other bullet hell games. However, be aware that this game has a very steep learning curve and you WILL be dying a lot. If you can get past that initial wall, you will spend hundreds upon hundreds of hours on this game topping your previous high scores and hunting for secrets.

Garry's Mod has almost no limitations with what is available to play. Heaps upon heaps of different gamemodes and such available, meaning there's so many different ways this game can be enjoyed. I personally played GMod Tower more than anything, but even now those servers aren't running anymore, I can still find tons of fun with DarkRP, Deathrun and just building things in Sandbox.
The only real downside to GMod is the need to own other games to have support for a lot of plugins and especially textures. This is quite annoying and makes having a truly enjoyable experience with the game more expensive than this listing seems, but even so it's definitely worth it.
It's not easy to sum up GMod in a short review. There's just so much on offer and a seemingly endless amount of games to play, and hours of fun to be had. Personally I feel GMod is a must-buy, but only really for those who are also willing to purchase the other games required to provide all the resources necessary.

I decided a while ago that I would write a short review when I would reach 1234 hours in the game, so here I am.
1234 hours over the course of 3 years and 7 months... that's almost 1 hour every day. It can also mean 1234 hours of nonstop playing for 51 days and 10 hours (that's how I did it).
There have been times where I spent 15 minutes doing math to make sure I had enough fuel for a mission... only to run out of fuel way before I was supposed to.
There have been times where I worked on a big project that took a few days... only to have it ruined by some stupid bug that I had no control over.
There have been times (one time actually) where a single outdated mod prevented me from being able to play the game for weeks, even after I got rid of it. I had to gather knowlegde on the stupid cfg file and mess around in it until It finally worked, which took dozens of attempts of opening the game to see if it worked (and for each one I had to wait 5 minutes for it to load).
And yet, Kerbal Space Program is my
. It scratches that itch of curiosity and exploration which resides deep within every human. That curiosity is what separated us from the animals, because we were the ones who wentured beyond our comfort zone just to see what was behind that hill.
That rewarding feeling of successfully landing on some random moon can't be explained using words. It's a feeling that traces back to when we were hunting our food, and accidentally stumbled upon a meadow with a nice little river. You didn't find anything of use, but hey, at least you know your surroundings a bit better now.
Or maybe I'm reading too much into this idk. It's a good game is what I'm trying to say.

Hotline Miami (Developed by Dennaton Games, Published by Devolver Digital - Released October 23rd, 2012) is an ultra-violent 16 bit game set in the 1980's. In the main storyline - the first one, you play as a psycopathic man known as Jacket. (None of the characters are ever explicitly given a name, and most names have been given by the fan community.)
-Summary- (SOME SPOILERS)
The game starts with the player in a dark area being talked to by some dirty looking person, who right off the bat, tells you that he is there to tell you how to kill people. After you finish the tutorial, Part One-Phonecalls begins with you in a dark room, with three people in it - excluding you - all wearing masks. An ominous base-line plays in the backround as these three people talk to you in what can be interpreted as a condescending tone. It is important to state that this is all implied to happen AFTER the events of the game. (discounting the optional BIKER portion) The man in the middle - Richard - asks if you remember the events of April the 3rd. The game begins. April 3rd, 1989 - Miami, Florida. You go to answer the phone, and are told by 'Tim' from the 'Bakery' that your cookies you ordered should be delivered by now. A list of 'ingredients' are included, be sure to read them. The person on the other line hangs up. Sure enough, there is a package outside of your apartment. Once opened, you find a Rooster mask inside with a list of instructions. "The target is a briefcase. Discretion is of importance." is all that is on the paper. You leave for the metro in your Delorean. Once inside, the massacre begins. Once you have cleared the area of any and all Mobsters there, you leave in the car that you arrived in. You drive to an alley. You put the briefcase in the dumpster, as instructed. After doing this, the dirty man from the tutorial calls out, having seen someone enter the alley which he probably lives in. He charges at you with a bat, and you have no choice but to kill him. Jacket vomits immediately afterwards. The chapter ends after he drives off. Most of the game goes on the same way. The player begins in his apartment and checks his answering machine to be told where to go. The player character then drives to the location and the player navigates the building while killing enemies and achieving any extra objectives. Early chapters end with the protagonist visiting a store or bar where his conversations with the employees (All the same guy, known to the community as 'Beard'.) serve to provide context and exposition for the storyline. He acquires a roommate after the chapter Decadence, when he decides on seemingly a whim to save a drug-addicted hooker. Over time, they seem to get together and his apartment becomes more tidy. Ultimately their separate beds are pushed together and other characters refer to her as the protagonist's girlfriend, implying that they have become romantically involved. In contrast to his apartment becoming more orderly, the protagonist's perceptions of reality begin to degrade. He revisits a decrepit room where three masked figures pose questions about the nature of his actions while never providing answers. His apartment and the locations around town become populated with gory figures resembling the mobsters he's murdered. And the various friendly shopkeepers are all replaced by a hostile man, who is later revealed to be the playable character's would-be assassin. It comes as a shock, when in the very beginning of Part Four, (Connections) when Jacket arrives back at his pad to find an intruder inside. His girlfriend is splattered on the floor. The man is sitting on his couch. "Ah, There you are. I was wondering when you'd get back. Well, let's get this over with then..." He then proceeds to shot you in the chest with a silenced pistol. The screen cuts to static. The ominous base-line from the beginning of the game starts up again. (Coconuts: Silver Lights) You are back in the game. The lights are out. The screen is periodically cutting to static. Richard is sitting on your couch. There is a yellow light on him. He goes to say "Looks like it's only you and me left now...I'm sure you know by now that this wont end well. Soon, you will be all alone. But that's okay. Before we say goodbye, I'll let you in on a secret...What you do from here on won't serve any purpose. You will never seen the whole picture...And it's all your own fault...Now it's time for you to leave. There's a warm bed across the hall from here...And you look like you could use some rest." You exit your apartment's front door...and sure enough, there is a new door. It looks like a hospital room. With you laying on the bed. Your head explodes. Chapter Eleven: Trauma. Tip: Wake up. July 21st, 1989, Miami Florida. You wake up in a hospital - pushed by rage and a need for vengeance, you sneak out of the hospital after overhearing what happened to your girlfriend...and hearing that the man that tried to kill you - the man who murdered your girlfriend - is sitting in lockup. You go back home after successfully sneaking out of the hospital. You tear through the police tape at the entrance of your apartment. You enter the bathroom - where your girlfriend was killed - and get your clothing on. Now, it's time to rock the heist. The rest of the game is about vengeance.
-Conclusion-
All in all, this was a great game. It's rage inducingly hard, but if you can look past that, the game has major artistic value. When the personas in the room ask questions like: "Do you like hurting other people?" They're asking the player. They're asking YOU if YOU like hurting other people. After each chapter is said and done, you have to go back to the beginning, and are forced to look at everyone you murdered. The game, in itself, is deep. There's a lot to interpret from the game if you simply look.
10/10

Though Broken Age acts as a return to Double Fine’s earliest adventure game roots, it’s also their largest and most ambitious project in years. But if anything, the added scope and possibility that exploded out of their hugely successful Kickstarter has only amplified their talents as a developer, giving birth to what seems easily capable of becoming the game that defines them as a studio.
But playing Broken Age, there’s never the sense that Double Fine has grown beyond the quirky, commercially unviable studio that I’ve loved for years. Broken Age as a game, is exceptionally simple and humble in its construction. It’s unmistakably a product of its creator: esoteric, humorous, and at times even a bit profound, but without the often rough mechanics and invisible cage of possibilities that shackled most of the studio’s prior games. It’s Double Fine in their purest, most unrestrained form, and if you’ve played anything the studio’s made I doubt I have to tell you how exciting that is.
It’s somewhat precarious to attempt to discuss Broken Age’s plot, both for fear of spoilers and for the fact it’s only half finished, but its themes are so strong and its writing on point that it’s deserving of more than a minor conversation. It follows the dual stories of Vella and Shay, two people stuck in vastly different situations but united by their shared lack of freedom, forced to blindly conform to the traditions and expectations of those older than them, unable to even question “why?”.
Shay is the sole human aboard a ship intended as humanity’s last chance at finding a new planet they can call home. Trapped in an endless isolation, he lives out his days following his computer mom’s orders, still treated as a child ignorant to anything outside his daily routine and sheltered existence.
Vella in contrast is a member of a village whose traditions dictate the sacrifice of several young women to the towering Mog Chathra during their annual maiden feast, or otherwise doom them all to its wrath. Vella is the sole person brave enough to propose they fight the beast, but is shrugged off as a silly girl who doesn’t understand the gravity of the situation.
These two plotlines fold into each other to form Broken Age’s main themes of rejecting the systematic lives their characters are placed in, and being brave enough to discover the world for themselves. It’s rebellion without anarchy; breaking out to find who you are, not out of distaste of the world, but a desire to make it better if only you’d be given the ability to think and act for yourself.
You could label Broken Age a coming of age story (in fact it itself does), but it’s so much more sincere than I feel that commonly implies. Its characters are delightful and lively and often absurd, but also fully developed in how they fit within their world. They fully embody their roles and proclaim them so effectively that it felt like I knew the people I was talking to, as if they had somehow taken on a life outside of the game. Even characters you see in only a single scene or who are given but a few lines of dialogue have so much personality and heart in their interactions that they transcend their small part into the larger world of the game.
Double Fine has always been a developer recognized for brilliant writing and characterization, but I’ve never felt as immersed in the worlds they created or as invested in their characters as with Broken Age. As bizarre as their circumstances become, I connected with Shay and Vella’s plight for freedom of their parental and societal shackles, and was as curious as them upon entering a new area and meeting its peculiar inhabitants.
For all I know act two could be a complete disaster. It could cause Broken Age to go down as one of the most disappointing games in recent memory and probably cause even me to think twice before checking out anything Double Fine puts out in the future. But for now, it’s sublime, beautiful, expertly pinned, and not afraid to wear its heart on its sleeve. As a huge fan of all things Double Fine, I’m finding it hard not to readily declare this their best work yet, which I consider no small praise.
Perhaps I expected too much.
It’s been more than a year since the first part of Double Fine’s Kickstarted nest egg first release, and since then the anticipation, unease, and in some cases legitimate anger have been steadily increasing to levels that beg the question just what this game means to people. It was one of the first hugely successful examples of using Kickstarter to fund games, as well as a callback to Double Fine’s earliest work and easily their biggest and most ambitious game in a long time (despite hav ing began as something far smaller). It was hard not to want to continuously give them the benefit of the doubt; to let them give it their all and assume Broken Age would come out the better for it however long it took. But for all the hype and impossible dreams of what Broken Age might be, we might have taken it too far. Or maybe Broken Age took it too far, and in my naive enthusiasm I went along with it. [...]
I said at the end of my act one write-up that I could see Broken Age being the game that defines Double Fine. I still think that to be true, but unfortunately it isn’t as glamorous an image as I had first imagined it to be. Broken Age isn’t a bad game, nor do I regret playing it or wish to advise others not to. It’s impossible to ignore though just how uneven and weird the first and second act are. Broken Age seems to reflect a lot on its extended development and the detriment its model of funding and community feedback may have had on it. It began with an eagerness you couldn’t escape and the feeling that this couldn’t be anything but an amazing, and yet by the end it has lost a lot of its drive. It’s tired and drained, seeking to provide closure for those who have been waiting so long, but being unable to do much more.

This is a fun arcade hockey game. The AI is challenging, well-placed hip checks are satisfying (with the added tension that if you miss the target you may be enabling a breakaway), you always get to pass to the intended player and you can score goals in many different ways (slap shots, wrist shots, off rebounds, semi-one timers after cross-ice passes, etc.). Gameplay can feel unresponsive at first, but after getting used to it (the game has a different rythm from other arcade or hockey games, even after a day-one patch) it is quite enjoyable.
The story mode introduces lots of humour as you progress mid-way through a season to try and make the playoffs. You can't take decisions on the roster (you just play the games), but events keep happening (reminiscent of the movie Slap Shot), adding context to your games.
Another plus is that the devs are approachable and involved with the community, with frequent updates and receptiveness towards feedback.
Downsides are that currently multiplayer is only local and that maybe its long-term value is questionable, although maybe the addition of new teams, events for story mode, dynasty features (contracts drafting, etc.), modding tools, etc. might solve this issue.
I definitely recommended it to all hockey or sports fans!

Once you discover that? You'll realize Old Time Hockey is a wonderful return to classic hockey games but not so much as to be a simple retread. It has its own identity and style that Hockey fans will come to adore.
This is a game I can highly recommend.

Life is Strange - an Action-Adventure, according to Steam.
While it uses well known mechanics of countless point&click adventures, it does so many things so well, that I was left sobbing at the end.
The story is mainly targeted at young adults, but certainly everyone can relate to at least one of the many topics the game touches.
Friendship, career choices, drug abuse and climate change, to only name a few, while the list goes on.
While the narrative feels a bit rushed at times, the game actively invites the player to just take in the scenery, live in the moment and think about all the ways life can be strange.
Carried by great artwork and a great soundtrack, I could not help but allow the main character, Max, into my cold heart.
It is the connection, the bond you form with Max, which draws you into the game and leads you through about 25 of the most intense gaming hours you have ever played through.
And the best part is: Even though the game has flaws, one of them being that it’s too short overall on top of some confusing quick time events, you are left with so many impressions and thought-inducing moments, that the flaws are easily overlooked.
Life is Strange is a game that everyone should have played, at least once.

Wasteland 2 is an amazing game and instant classic. It's very much like Fallout 1 and 2 (which were based off the first wasteland game), with lots of differences.
First of all, you start by creating a party of up to 4 people (and can have a party up to 7 from npcs recruited in game), there a tons of different skill to choose from for each character, ranging from mechanical repair, to computer science to assault rifles, pistols, shotguns, outdoorsman, smart♥♥♥♥♥hard♥♥♥♥♥kiss♥♥♥♥♥(3 dialogue skills that vary on attitude), etc.
There is also a decent attribute system, much like the SPECIAL from fallout, except this one is called CLASSIC (coordination, luck, Awareness, Strength, Speed, Intelligence and Charisma), and the attributes have a huge impact on characters and what they can do.
The battle system is much like DnD or any D20 system, grid turn based combat, using initiative to choose when people act. If you've played X Com then it's much like that, except more in depth (then the newest x com) in terms of mechanics and what you can do. As opposed to the two move system from x com or D20, this one is based off action points (like the original fallout games), you have so many action points (depending on your speed, strength, awareness and many more) that you can do in a turn. Walking 1 square requires 1 action point, shooting different weapons require more as well as other various actions.
Travelling the world map, again is very much like the original fallout games. You have the map, and your icon traverses across it as you may run into random encounters, there are oasises everywhere that give you water (as you gotta refill water to keep traversing the map), and you can run across various settlements this way. There are also radiation clouds that you must watch out for, you can go through them but you need radiation gear otherwise your party will get killed while walking through  it.
On top of the game mechanics and battle systems, the quests themselves are very intriguing, lots of side content and missions to do, and A LOT of choices to do in those missions. You can do missions so many different ways, from sneaking into a fort and killing some dudes to negotiating with them and allying them with you, to poisoning their food and killing them off.
The main big missions usually have various different outcomes in the missions, each giving you a drastically different faction running an area, or having you liked or hated by another faction, and even unlocking different potential companions depending on how you finished the mission.
The game itself sort of gears you to be a "good guy", in that you are a team of rangers that are supposed to be a police force in a post apocalyptic wasteland - but you don't have to be. Though the game would be MUCH harder being a bad guy, there's nothing stopping you and you can kill anyone you feel like for any reason. Though your NPC characters (that arent created by the PC) usually dont like when you go around double dealing guys, killing innocents and just failing to protect people (though there are other NPCs that don't mind you doing so, just dont expect the philantropist doctor girl to stay with your team when you betray a settlement or start murdering people indiscriminately).
Hell, you can even roleplay the morally gray ranger that is willing to sacrifice people and lives for the greater good if you so desired.
So far, i'm about over 100 hours in game (right now steam says im at 88, but after an update when i was about 20 some hours in, it reset my hours played for some reason), and I'm only about half way done the main game (though ive been doing any side stuff that i come across).
So far the game is amazing to me and im having a blast with it. Been waiting for a game like this for a long time, and definitely having a lot of fun with it and to me, this game will be a classic that i go back and play multiple times over the years, much like other classic RPGS such as Fallout 1 and 2, Knights of the old republic, Bauldur's gate, Neverwinter nights and Morrowind and so on.
I would recommend this game to any RPG fan, specifically hard core RPG fans, and this game is definitely worth the 40 dollars for the base game. Such an awesome game!

With Wasteland 2, inXile renews with the tradition that is best illustrated with the now defunct Troika (creators of the great RPGs Arcanum and Vampire Bloodlines): creating an amazing RPG, and releasing it broken and full of bugs.
Wasteland 2 is probably one of the best and most immersive RPGs I've played this year, and I would gladly recommend it to all RPG lovers, unfortunately it's also one of the most buggy games I've seen so far. From graphical glitches to an abysmal handling of the camera, the AI or various systems simply not working, most bugs aren't blocking the gameplay itself, and the game would remain great if it wasn't for the constant crashes. Despite two major patches already released on the title, it has been impossible for me to play more than an hour without a full game crash, and it's hard to love a game that doesn't let you play it.
Let's not be mistaken: Wasteland 2 is a truly great RPG, and I'm looking forward to being able to play it in decent conditions, at which point I will change my review. Here's to hoping inXile will continue fixing it.
