Wasteland 2 is a Kickstarter effort to bring back a classic RPG from the 1980’s.  I would recommend Wasteland 2 to anyone who enjoys turn-based RPG’s or anyone really.
What I liked:
--Graphics and artwork
Wasteland 2 looks nice and has a ton of little graphical details to keep players
engulfed in the post-apocalyptic world.  The artwork maintains the same quirky
“Mad Max” style that was evident in the original game.  I enjoyed the multitude of
character portraits that complimented the in-game characters.  As a nice little extra
you get a digital artbook that shows many of the conceptual designs and finished
artwork from the game.
--Nostalgia Factor
One of the main reasons I purchased Wasteland 2 is because of my experiences
with the original game.  I appreciated the humorous details put into the game.  Many
of the items you pick up as junk are reminders of the 80’s--Laserdiscs, Teddy
Ruxpins, 8-track tapes, etc.  I often found myself laughing at some ridiculous piece of
junk that I picked up.  Players of the original game will also appreciate that many of
the locations and characters from that game are present in the new game.  You
receive a copy of Wasteland with Wasteland 2 so you can revisit the original.
--Challenging Gameplay
I enjoyed the combat and exploration in Wasteland 2.  I found the combat challenging
and it was refreshing to have “critical failures.”  The realism of having things go wrong,
while annoying at times, felt different from a lot of games.  Guns jammed in the middle
of a fight, lockpicks broke, your demolitions expert triggered a trap while trying to
disarm it.  Too many times players are presented with a cakewalk of perfection and
Wasteland 2 really strays from that path.
--Choices
Players are given multiple choices in how to solve quests.  Maybe you’re a shoot first,
ask questions later type who opts to blow up all the Atchison’s rather than work out a
truce.  That’s a completely valid option.  Or you could attempt to negotiate a truce.
--Character Design Options
Your characters can have a multitude of different and random talents.  Part of the
challenge in Wasteland 2 is distributing abilities around your group for the maximum
benefit.  Toaster repair is something I skimped on and regretted. Go toaster repair!
What I didn’t like:
I really enjoyed Wasteland 2 and don’t have many complaints.  For a Kickstarter game
it’s really well done.
--Bugs
My first playthrough went really well for about 90% of the game.  It was when I got to
a later zone (won’t spoil it) that things got a little sketchy.  There is one area that will
not work if you do not complete the quests in a very specific order.  It also seems
somewhat unfinished--there are references to places in town that do not exist.  There
have been several major patches that have attempted to fix many problems, but this
one still persists.  It’s not unplayable, just mildly annoying.
I would recommend Wasteland 2.  If you have any frame of reference to the original game you will enjoy this immensely.  There are a lot of extras thrown in--artbook, the original game, and the soundtrack--which are fun.

I was like everyone awaiting this game with great anticipation and carefully planned my weekend to get some hours into Mafia III. The day of launch the game was an hour late. I didn't pay much notice to this and the game finally arrived to my game library. I clicked play and was hyped beyond belief but was greeted with a launcher that didn't work. I somehow managed to get to the play button and the game loaded in as it should. Then I realized 2K and Hangar 13 found it acceptable to put a 30 frames-per-second lock on the game. I immediately quit the game and turned my attention to their Steam community in hopes to find a bypass. Literally a few minutes before release they came out with an announcement and plead for inconvenience for the frames-per-second lock. This effectively fooled everyone who pre-ordered Mafia III in order for 2K and Hangar 13 to earn some quick money before announcing the bad news.
They write it like they have no idea what people expected in 2016 so they just released an unfinished game and now they want feedback on what to add. So to be frank we paid 50€ for an early access. The way 2K and Hangar 13 described 30 frames-per-second as
made the entire computer gaming audience have a royal cringe.
Two days later they finally decided to roll out the patch said to remove this lock giving us the option to pick unlimited frames-per-second. I gave Mafia III the benefit of the doubt and hoped for the best. Turns out to be the latter. Perhaps they removed the lock, but this introduced an unplayable below 60 frames-per-second pice of garbage. Mafia III doesn't render at your native resolution. There is some form of upscaling which is ruining the image quality. It appears the internal render is at 720p or 900p. This results in people playing in 1080p or above getting very blurry and stretched textures. As some reviewers already have made clear, even Zelda got a better looking skybox than Mafia III. This is obviously a straight console port where Hangar 13 simply had a hard-copy made and uploaded it to Steam and hoped for the best. This explains why the game was locked at 30 frames-per-second to hide the imminent performance issues and the horrible optimization.
I was running Mafia III on my couple of months old Zotac Nvidia GeForce GTX 1070 8GB GDDR5 AMP! Extreme, i5-6600K 3.9GHz Skylake and Kingston HyperX 16GB DDR4 2400Mhz after the patch and received no more than 40 frames-per-second on both medium, high an I even tried the low preset. And in addition Mafia III was using literally 100% of my resources including CPU, GPU and SSD. It ran so horribly unstable my computer started sounding like a vacuum cleaner. Eventually the game decided to crash on me. Which was probably for the best.
Unfortunately I got Mafia III from Green Man Gaming and they refuse refunds. I'm stuck with the game, but I have uninstalled the game from my library and will not touch it again. What genius at 2K came up with the brilliant idea to tell Hangar 13 to release the game capped to 30 frames-per-second in the first place? And how could a studio like 2K allow Hangar 13 to ruin an AAA title like this?
I recommend getting Mafia II instead and save the money for other upcoming titles. Mafia II is superior to Mafia III in pretty much everything. The driving physics is better, the optimization is flawless and the story don't force you doing the exact same thing over and over again.

Free to play is questionable.
You get for free 3 tutorial missions and 1 for each of the 6 races. You must to premium for all missions and access to somethings. Paying money helps you faster unlock more cards. To summon a hero you play their card and can have multiple. For beating a mission you get 1 hero coin. In missions when you take a settlement you have a chance to have a random hero of that race join you their. You can then recruit a copy of them for your deck.
You would have to grind lots to get enough of each card of each race you want.
The game works as a phone app. As such its a good game. As a full computer game its lacking.
Of the 6 races free mission 2 are unfair. 2 have the computer start with a boss lvl undead. Normally they only get them as punishment for allowing undead to take mana pools. In 2 missions they start with them or 2 squares away from them with no way possible to stop it. As such those 2 missions are extreamly hard. If they would get them on say turn 6 instead of 2 you would have a chance to do something.
The game is fun and strategy. You take settlements and mana pools and they earn you money and mp. Combat is just which ever side has more 100% will win but its the question of how many will live on your side. Heros often have an ability which is important. As such the game has many chess like mechanics. In single player time progesses when you tell it to. You move a unit to take a settlement and it takes time. Your ability is a on a cool down. Many things use differant amounts of time. You can decide how much time to pass for the next turn. Unfortunently they punish you for passing less than 6 hours of game time and reward you if its more than 6. I have mixed feelings about this because the computer does not "stop" and have to wait for the next turn to start an action. Only you.
This game has limited number of levels. They pretty much want you to buy the game at a high cost for low amount of content. It feels like a turn based fantasy top view management game but it lacking the complexity and content for the price they want. Im not giving them my money. The subscriptions or buy out right cost too much. Maybe 1/2 price would be fair.

On the harder difficulties, the feeling of using your heroes to fend off seemingly untenable hordes of zombies feels nothing short of heroic. The tactical depth is quite surprising -- if you've played a game like Neptune's Pride or Subterfuge, but you found it too social or too stressful, then as a cooperative game this one has no such problems, and as much, if not more depth to it.
The monetary system isn't bad. It doesn't feel like traditional grindy free to play, and you get "hero coins" pretty quickly through regular play. That said, you can be at a substantial disadvantage on the harder difficulties early on, because you'll go through the few heroes you have collected and put into your deck quite quickly (normal difficulty is fast enough you won't have the same problem, but the game shines on Hard). Buy lifetime premium for $24 and you'll get enough coins with it to, not quite finish your collection, but at least be guaranteed to have no issues with running out of heroes mid-game.
The real-time format (which is the best way to play, although the single-player is quite good) means it is definitely more of a mobile game than a PC one, but since your account is shared across devices, and you can get it on iOS and Android, this isn't a problem.

It plays in real time so everything takes ages to happen, most of the time the more interesting cards requires premium currency to get permanently, and its not exactly a visual spectacle. But if you can see pass all that, this game in its entirety is one of the most well-designed multiplayer co-op strategy games I have ever played, and because I feel like it here's a somewhat detailed look at the reasons why.
-
Lets get this out of the way first. This is a free game. But like most free games, parts of the features are unavailable unless you go 'Premium'. You get to play both multiplayer and single player modes for free, although in multiplayer the maps you are allowed to join are randomly selected and open to public, while in single player 1 scenario from each of the 6 races' campaigns are available. Special units/heros won't be available at first, but will pop up randomly as you play (more on this later).
In most free games out there you can expect a certain level of microtransactions, and this one is no exception.
If you didn't already instantly recoil from the M word hissing and spitting, then you will be glad to know that you don't actually HAVE to buy anything to enjoy the game. Premium currency (gold coins) are given out based on the number of people you manage to finish a multiplayer game session with (6 players, 6 coins) and how well you did in that session, as well as whenever you finish a singleplayer map (1 per map, maps are repeatable and can present a slightly different challenge every time). Plus, rarer and more interesting and/or powerful cards will appear in both game modes in the game itself, letting you use them immediately and giving you the option to add them to your collection permanently for 1 premium currency each, which you can then use again in all future games.
Simply put, the more you play, the better you play, and the more people you play with, the more interesting and fun the game gets. It's actually a really good way to ease players into the more advanced side of the game.
-
This game is perfect for the modern world of too little free time, requiring maybe 15 mins of attention tops before you can get back to what you were busy with. Even then, it's packed with just the right amount of strategy to keep you fully engaged and planning your every move, discussing and coordinating your actions with your buddies. My group often spend more time strategizing than actually playing, the discussion becoming part of the gameplay and makes it all feel like you are actually commanding an army in real life.
-
The single player mode is a whole different beast. Where in multiplayer everything happens in real time, in single player you can fast forward time, but the amount of time is preset unless you adjust it by paying up an ingame resource. This adds another dimension to the game and helps it stand apart from the multiplayer experience, but not so much that you have to relearn everything.
-
So lets get back to the whole Premium side of this game. To better understand it, here's how it works. At the start of each game, each race in the game starts off with a basic set of unit/hero summoning cards tailored for that map, and you can then throw in more cards of any race to add to your 'deck' that you will bring into the game proper. Where do you get these cards? Either you buy them from a lucky draw choose-1-of-3 style mechanic, or you wait for them to appear ingame as you play and you can 'recruit' them permanently for future games. These cards are really where the flavor of the game is at, with most of the combos-making and synergistic abilities reserved for these rare cards.
Its no surprise that a lot of people get turned off if they dont run into these cards early, so if you are eager to find these then definitely try out single player where you can fast forward time.

Let me start by stating this - I could recommend this game
when the second half is released or a big sale occurs. There are many reasons for this including playtime, replayability and puzzles, among others. I will be mentioning some scenes found in the game so if you haven't played it yet or don't like spoilers, skip to the conclusion at the bottom of this review.
Broken Age has an interesting premise; enter the lives of two teenagers worlds apart as you point-and-click your way through amusing dialogue, varying puzzles and vibrant locations. I really enjoyed the colours and art scheme, as they fleshed out the characters and created a unique atmosphere for the player to explore in. Upon entering the game, you will have the choice to select which character you would like to start with first, Vella or Shay. Out of the two, I preferred Vella's story because the puzzles seemed more varied and she was the only person to have a boss battle in the end of the first act, leaving me slightly disappointed in Shay's tale. The characters feel different and made me laugh quite a bit, especially a certain tree.
I feel that the main reason I prefer Vella is because the environments and characters in her story are more plentiful and vibrant than the secluded setting of Shay's. There was a lot of repetition in the levels aboard Shay's spacecraft. Sure, the repeated visits to his four missions had a certain charm to them, but the rescue mini-game felt repetitive and boring. One of his puzzles later on in the story requires the player to shrink their head to fit in a small helmet, but I only solved this by accident while trying to explore the spaceship. There was also a lot of backtracking involved, especially in Vella's plot, where I had to keep revisiting certain locations to retrieve items necessary for completing puzzles. I believe that DoubleFine not only needed to spend a bit more time increasing the difficulty of the puzzles (because some of them were too simple to solve) they also should have spent more time on Shay to balance out the two stories. Vella's is more unique and fun to experience because of the variety of characters, locations and overall aim of the plot. Would you rather slay a giant beast threatening towns with annihilation or avoid the AI aboard your ship?
Broken Age is what I would call an 'interesting game'. Not in the sense of challenging to complete, but more so being really conflicted in my overall opinion after finishing the first act. The way the stories of the two protagonists play out makes it feel like two separate games, but not entirely in a good way. The focus on character development feels unbalanced, as well as the amount of content and a certain boss battle only Vella experiences. I expected a lot from Broken Age, but instead of a sense of satisfaction I feel like my cup is half-empty. Once the second act comes out (if it ever does) I will add more content to this review but until then I will say this - a half-empty cup is not worth $25 to me.

In short, Wasteland 2 tells a story about what you cannot do - open doors, chests or safes, hit enemies or talk cunningly. Mostly at the beginning of the game to be fair, but even later on there are several objects to interact with that often cause you to fail critically when using a maxed out skill on them. You then either have to accept this and carry on or load a previous save game and try again.
Given the fact that the loot often is not worth the trouble, option 1 should be the way to go (or ignore the possible loot in the fist place), but that's not what I expect of a game. Reloading (and again and again sometimes) is a slow and tedious process. May be I'm not getting the point and Wasteland 2 then is not the game for me, but on the other hand this is a personal review and all about how I like it.
There's more boring stuff in it, like quests which have you to visit the same places a few times over without the possibility to quick travel. Given the size and layout of some areas and the way they are connected to other areas sometimes causes you to sit there for minutes and tell your team to go back and forth. That's a way of extending the play time. One I don't like at all. Especially if the quest giver sends you more often than needed to the same place when all that has to be done could have easily been accomplished on the first visit.
Personally I didn't care much for the story. Cannot really identify the cause though. I found myself mostly rushing through the dialog options, only scanning for relevant key words to get through quickly - which is a shame because I think the writing itself seems to be fine. But I couldn't connect the the world like I did when playing Fallout 1 and 2 for example. In the end I tried to solve all open quests and finish the story so I could mark this game as completed.
Technically I had severe performance issues in some (mostly indoor) areas on my Linux machine and encountered several bugs. The Linux version of Borderlands 2 for example runs much better here.
I'm not saying Wasteland 2 is a bad game. Most people seem to like it. But you have to tolerate a couple of things which just annoy me to the point the fun gets significantly spoiled. All in all I'm too disappointed to recommend this game.

With the risk of becoming a bit cheesy, it is hard to discuss Life is Strange and what makes it so good with someone who hasn't played it. I could describe it in general terms: that it has great characters with impressive voice acting, that it has a really well paced and well woven story, that the choices truly matter, that the timechanging mechanic is used pretty much perfectly and that the little world of Arcadia Bay truly sucks you in. I could tell my own story, that I played through the first episode and then waited to play the rest for way too many months and when I actually sat down to play episode 2 and onwards, I couldn't put it down for two full days. I could tell you that it's one of the best games I've ever played, but honestly, those words get thrown around a lot.
All of this doesn't quite tell the full picture, and it doesn't quite convey how I feel about Life is Strange, or necessarily how you will feel about it. The only thing I can say is that it is special, and if you buy it and get to the end. you will probably  feel a bunch of feelings. Wasteland 2 is a game that I really wanted to like, even though, it isn't a good game. I am sure that sounds confusing, so I'll explain what I mean.
To start off, I should mention that I really enjoyed Fallout 1 and 2 (am going to assume that you know what they are since you are looking at a wasteland 2 review, if for some reason you don't, you should spend a little time and look them up), and for the most part Wasteland 2 feels like it could be a direct sequel to those games. And that is one of its main problems with it, since Fallout 2 came out in 1998, and Wasteland 2 feels like it could have came out shortly after that.
The game's old school elements appeals to a part of me that really enjoyed the fallout games, however, another part of me knows that those elements are outdated, and that new and better game mechanics have been introduced since then.  One such example of these outdated mechanics is the lack of information and tutorials in the game. And while I do enjoy finding things out for myself, I do not like having to Google basic game mechanics (i.e. how to disarm mines) because the game does not provide this information. I know that there are games out there that promote a lack of information as a feature (am looking at you dark souls) but in a game where you have to create characters with a limited amount of skill points, this omission is damaging to the experience (since you might end up having to restart the game after a few hours, because you didn't invest any skill points into a stat that didn't seem to serve a purpose).
The game's basic design encourages the user to min/max their party, which results in the player picking side characters for the stats, and not their personality.  And for a RPG that all about story, choices and characters, this min/max system pulls the player out of the experience since they will no longer care about the characters they are using, but only about how they can use them. To put it another way, your squad doesn't feel like a band of brothers fighting through the wasteland, instead they feel like tools on your tool belt.
I did enjoy a few of the elements in the game which is way I wanted to like this game. Two things that they did right are the game's length and allowing the player to choose how to play the game.  This game is long in a good way. There is a ton to do, and most of it is interesting. I never really felt like the game was dragging out an encounter or experience just to pad its length.  And what made this experience so enjoyable was that player choice directly effects the game's flow. The player often finds themselves in a new environment with a little explanation and a lot of options.  There usually a main mission to a setting, for example bandits claiming to be the protectors of an area, that the player can deal with as they see fit (they can side with the bandit, wipe them out, or just leave them alone). And there are usually also several side objectives scatter about the area that influence the setting, provide items, or are just there to add favor.  These elements for the game are great, but all the other issues drag it down.
This game could have been something amazing, if they had taken the time to make a modern feeling RPG in the style of the older fallouts, however, they didn't. In the end this game will appeal mainly to a small niche community that enjoyed old PC RPGs and desperately want more of them.

I really wanted to like this game. I liked games like Fallout 1/2 and Fallout Tactics.  So the squad-based turn-based RPG is a category I like.  I also wanted to like this game to support indie designers, so against my better judgement I purchased the game shortly after release and at full price.  However, the flaws in this game are vary glaring and difficult to ignore.
1) If you haven't played Wasteland 1, this game is hard to follow.  It is more like a continuation of the story than a sequel set in the same world. Many of the clues dropped require some knowledge of the events in Wasteland 1.
2) The gameplay mechanics are just a mess.  The armor system is borked to the point of being pointless.  While the initiative system is interesting, there is no prevision for a character to delay his turn.  The effect of which is to create a log jam if a slower character is blocking a door.  Fortunately most of the combat is in wide open area -- probably for this very reason.
3)  Looting is similarly botched where crappy useless loot is stored in containers that require a number of difficult checks to open.  The difficult of skill checks is uneven through out the game as well.
I do like the three dimensional maps and the ability to rotate them (however they definitely do not rotate smoothly). The attitude and feel of the game seem to be done well.  The character models and animations however do not match the environment very well.  The in game character appearance does not change based upon the armor that is equipped. Clothing choices seem to be poorly matched to gender (I guess cross-dressing is a thing in the wasteland).
Overall, I doubt many people will get past part one in the game much less get into part 2 (Las Angels) where the writing and encounters start to fall apart.
This game will probably have to be saved by mods, which there does seem to be a few on the horizon to fix the mechanics.  However, I don't see the skill system being reworked with mods, which has a few issues as well -- mainly too many skills.  There are 29 skills in the game and at least 6 of them could simply be removed/combined with existing skills.
Overall, Fallout Tactics was a better game.  If you are really liking this type of game, wait for a steam sale.

I decided a while ago that I would write a short review when I would reach 1234 hours in the game, so here I am.
1234 hours over the course of 3 years and 7 months... that's almost 1 hour every day. It can also mean 1234 hours of nonstop playing for 51 days and 10 hours (that's how I did it).
There have been times where I spent 15 minutes doing math to make sure I had enough fuel for a mission... only to run out of fuel way before I was supposed to.
There have been times where I worked on a big project that took a few days... only to have it ruined by some stupid bug that I had no control over.
There have been times (one time actually) where a single outdated mod prevented me from being able to play the game for weeks, even after I got rid of it. I had to gather knowlegde on the stupid cfg file and mess around in it until It finally worked, which took dozens of attempts of opening the game to see if it worked (and for each one I had to wait 5 minutes for it to load).
And yet, Kerbal Space Program is my
. It scratches that itch of curiosity and exploration which resides deep within every human. That curiosity is what separated us from the animals, because we were the ones who wentured beyond our comfort zone just to see what was behind that hill.
That rewarding feeling of successfully landing on some random moon can't be explained using words. It's a feeling that traces back to when we were hunting our food, and accidentally stumbled upon a meadow with a nice little river. You didn't find anything of use, but hey, at least you know your surroundings a bit better now.
Or maybe I'm reading too much into this idk. It's a good game is what I'm trying to say.

An excellent combination of cooperative strategy board game and card game played out over an extended time. Whether you're playing it out in real time over days and weeks with a bunch of friends or strangers, or playing a solo turn-based game, it's difficult to overlook the genius behind Blight of the Immortals.
Finding a cooperative online game that nails the feel of a team-based tabletop experience is very difficult, but this game does so many things exactly right. I've played with my work buddies at the office, gamed with some friends from home, and the cooperative aspects of this game are a favorite for all of us.
Some benefits:
- Cooperative strategy gameplay.
- Board games are awesome.
- Card games are fantastic.
- The game's art is phenomenal.
- Multi-player and single-player options.
- Played out in long games in real-time or turn-based by skipping several hours.
- Premium content for paying customers felt fair when I was a free player (for 2 months, over 100 hours before Steam) and now that I'm a lifetime customer. Paying can unlock cards, but the true benefit is the fun of hosting your own game and tweaking the experience with changes to suit your group.
- The free experience is a ton of fun so you'll find yourself unlocking coins to purchase new cards, or come across new cards through regular play, without ever feeling you have to spend a single dime. I bought the game because I loved it and because I wanted to reward the developer for daring to reward even their free players with a TON of new cards just by playing normally (I unlock a new card roughly every hour in real-time games, much more than that via turn-based play).
- This could be a bonus for some who really like skill to determine combat results. The combat outcome (win or defeat) isn't random at all. The website shows the math that will affect you EVERY time. The stronger force will always win, and the game shows you the exact percentage chance of losing one of your own in every fight BEFORE the fight happens. Anyone who says otherwise hasn't read anything in the game's extensive combat breakdown resource (among other FAQs) found in the game.
- The developer is VERY responsive to feedback and new additions and improvements to the game come very regularly.

Blight of the Immortals is one of the most unique games I've ever played, blending the depth of a CCG with the clarity of a board game and the strategy of weeks-long cooperation. It's ambitious, addictive, and fun.
Before each game, each player assembles a custom deck of Heroes using cards in their personal collection. Heroes are impactful all game long, so building the right deck requires as much forethought as you'd expect from any other CCG. The game itself plays out as a real-time war against the undead, over the next several days or weeks.
The free-to-play experience includes all multiplayer content except the ability to host private multiplayer games. Free members may join as many (simultaneous) games as they can handle, so if you want to play with a bunch of friends, one of you will need a premium account. Or, just all join one of the public games at the same time.
A selection of the single-player maps are available each month for free players; these rotate so all are exposed over time. In addition, one map is selected each week as the Tournament scenario (availble to everyone), with prizes distributed to the players who perform the best (beating the zombies while saving the most mortal lives).
The community is plenty active enough that anyone looking to put together a particular game can quickly find a group to play with
. This is also a great place to find strategy guides, ask for advice, find replacement players if someone drops out, or contact the (very responsive) developers directly.

Really fun "semi-retro" hockey game that worked flawlessly with my Steam Controller. The developers are engaged and care about making this the best product possible. You can ignore most of the day one negative reviews because the developers had a story mode (which is awesome, by the way) and it blew the minds of a lot of people.
A word about the story mode - I've played hockey games on various systems for my entire life, going back to Hat Trick in the arcade or that Activision hockey for the Atari. Nobody -- before Old Time Hockey -- ever tried to create a feeling of running an awful team that seemed hopeless before these guys did so. I *liked* the fact that for my first three games the computer had access to moves that I didn't. I liked the fact that I slowly gained "powers", if you will, in story mode. Would I want all hockey games to be like this? No, but after 30 years of playing them it was AWESOME to see developed attempt to get a specific emotional reaction.
A reaction that unfortunately lead to a lot of kiddos embarrassing themselves on here.
Don't listen to them - the devs are taking all feedback and giving everybody what they wanted. This game is EXACTLY what indie games on Steam ought to be.
I have one last comment. In Old Time Hockey there are times where two fights break out at the same time. You play them serially, but  I have still never seen a hockey game where one fight broke out after another. So many sportswriters are weird about fighting in hockey, not understanding the role it plays and I love, love, love that this game is unabashed when it comes to the violence. OK, I have one additional comment, which is "Fire Gary Bettman" but that's not really about the game.

Love this game! I can't help but compare to Stardew Valley and to say that this game, for me, is everything I wish Stardew Valley had been. This game is fun. It has a great sense of humor - not only about the gaming industry, but about itself as well.
The crafting is easy, but still rewarding. Resource gathering is simple and fun, though near the end, some of the resources seemed a bit unnecessarily scarce.
Combat is easily mastered - mostly knowing how to move to avoid enemy attacks and to time your own attacks. Enemy attacks always highlight the area of danger before the attack occurs (in normal mode, anyway). Pets help quite a bit (My most used pet was the electrified, turtle-like creature, followed a close second by the flying, poison bug - sorry, forget their actual names).
Probably about 50% of the items you can craft are cosmetic in nature - lots of fun for those who like to decorate.
My only complaints/wishes:
Each new major workstation comes with new armor pieces and a new weapon. There were a few times when I had made one workstation and a set of armor and a weapon, then, a very short time later, made a new workstation and new armor and weapon. Maybe the resource gathering was a bit too easy.
It's somewhat late in the game when you finally get the workstation that allows you to alter the stats and quality of your weapons and armor. Would have been nice to have that a bit sooner - also, the speed with which armor and weapon types were replaced meant that I often felt as though I'd wasted a lot of my crystallized juice upgrading gear each time I had new gear available.
Hints:
Try to focus on one damage type - there are trinkets, gadgets, and armor buffs for each type (electrical, fire, cold, poison, physical). Near the end of the game, I was using two fire-related gadgets and one electrical. 2 fire boosting trinkets, one electrical boosting trinket and one cool-down reducing trinket. All of my gear had maxed "fire power", except for my weapon which had maxed crit chance. I could kill almost anything within a few seconds, and the final battle was almost too easy.

This game definitely won't be for everyone. However, if you enjoy old school grindy point-and-click ARPGs, you're in luck! Personally I am finding it a lot of fun.
The core gameplay consists of exploring each biome, taking quests, grinding kills and harvesting resources to build ever-better crafting stations. Each monster has its own attack style with a special attack every so often, so combat revolves around basically having to learn how best to tackle each one.
Whilst superficially the game bears some resemblance to Don't Starve, it is far more casual and forgiving. This may or may not appeal, depending on what you prefer. In Crashlands, death is not the end but rather a minor inconvenience; you respawn at your base, and get to retrieve your lost resources by visiting the site of your death.
The game has a very charming art style, a great soundtrack, and I find the dialogue funny and quirky. I can see why others might not enjoy it, though.
Crashlands has more content than I was anticipating; at the time of writing I have played about 45 hours and have just reached the 3rd biome, so I think I'll easily hit 60 before I'm done with the main plot arc.However, I would say that the repetitive combat mechanics and the fact that each biome is visually new but is basically a remix of the previous in terms of mechanics is starting to lose its novelty at this stage - I thought after the Bawg that'd be the end of the game and I was just about ready for a finale, so a whole other biome was a surprise!
Overall, if like me you enjoy ARPGs and don't mind stylised cartoony graphics, this game will give you hours of grindy fun. However, if you don't like the genre or find you prefer you games more with a darker, more serious setting and tone, then it's probably best to steer clear.

I never write game reviews but this game is just so bad I have to vent my anger somewhere.
Dont get me wrong, the first few hours of the game are OKAY but after these initial 5 hours or so your character becomes so overpowered that the game becomes far too easy and boring. The developers have taken the time to come up with multiple great techniques for taking down orcs but in the end all you need is one button. Roughly 20 minutes into the game I realised that the counter attack technique is all I needed to take down almost every normal type of orc in the game.
The randomisation of higher leveled orcs becomes stale after a couple of hours also. I was so close to pulling my hair out after the hundreth time of seeing an orc named Krimp or Bolg. And their strengths and weaknesses are just so similar I got through the game completely without ever needing to change anything drastic about my characters skills (Not that I could seeing as the menus are so clunky and painful to look at).
On top of all this the stealth system is so broken that it may as well be non-existent. As long as your holding down the sneak button you can LITERALLY walk right up in front of an orc and stealth kill them without them seeing you, EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. Even when your in the middle of an outpost with hundreds of orcs (who know your there because the alarm is going off) but all you have to do is climb a building jump behind the orc and boom... stealth kill.
And dont even get me started about how much this game breaks Tolkiens lore of Middle Earth. As someone who has read most of his books I can say its actually quite laughable. If your a Lord of the Rings fan just DO NOT buy this game.
Finally the last act of the game is just a complete and utter grind to get through. All you do is defend, defend and defend forts. Even if you do lose a fort its no biggie, just win it back and then defend it some more. Defending against oncoming waves of orcs becomes so insanely frustrating that I wanted to throw my controller through the screen roughly every 5 seconds. Especially if all the orcs ran to capture the same flag then I was unlucky enough to see the same mind numbingly boring cinematic screen for each orc which involved them taunting me or slating me for roughly 30 seconds each (Yes each!). Sometimes there was as much as 10 high ranking orcs meaning you may have to wait for about 5 minutes before you get to play the game again. And of course don't forget that you have to see a cinematic every time an enemy orc or even your own ally orcs gets scared, angry, retreats, dies or for some other ridiculous such things that I won't bother mentioning. I suppose your probably thinking "but that's fine I'll just skip these scenes". Nope, no you wont. Because these genius developers forgot to put in a command to enable you to skip these cutscenes. So then if you die you get to see all these cinematics all over again. How lucky are you!
At the end of the day I sank almost 50 hours of my life into this game that I will never get back. And I didn't even start to talk about the loot box system or online mode mode which take this mess of a game to an entirely new level of uselessness. Save your time and money and buy Shadow of Mordor instead. It's a much better game and you'll get it for a fraction of the price.  Rant over.

I usually don't write reviews, but this game deserves a review.
This might seem like nitpicking, but there are so many small things that are missing in this game. It seems unfinished, unpolished, badly ported and without the expected quality control. There are so many games that give you so much more in form of immersion, detail, precision, polish and depth than this game. I honestly did not expect this game to be bad on so many levels. This has the potential to become a really good game, only they didn't take the time to make it good. It seems more like a work in progress or a mod for an older game.
The good:
Excellent music
Beautiful world and interesting setting
Cutscenes and story
Potential
The bad:
The game is not finished
Poorly optimized for PC
The controls are extremely unpresise
The cars handle like bumper cars
Damage modelling is non existing
Lacking proper character animation during gameplay
No way to turn headlights on/off
No way to operate the roof on convertible cars
No way to lockpick cars
No penalty for speeding
Reflections pop in and out
Colors change from dark to bright and from chrome to matte
Cars are relocated after entering and exiting buildings
Car disappeared from garage
Vibration on xbox controller is nearly non existing (cobblestone, railroad tracks and so on have no feedback)
Things float around in empty space
Pedestrians are lagging in the distance
Pop-in distance is laughable and random (reflection, lights, car grilles etc.)
The hard setting is ridiculously easy, I've cleared areas in seconds by running and spamming q (melee and takedown)
The aiming feels off, both when emerging from cover and shooting in general
Menu inputs are conflicting (mouse and keyboard will interact with each others and prevent scrolling)
Backlighted keyboard turns on and off
Cars float in mid air
Nonsensical jumping mechanism (Character cannot jump, only scale a few obstacles)
No way of customizing character (hair, beard, clothes)
No way of fixing your car at a garage
No place to buy cars
++++++++

Alan Wake is a patchwork of a game. The influences are so obvious, it could have been titled Silent Peaks: The Stephen King Wet Dream. It does however, occasionally use these inspirations to create a strong indetity of its own.
Alan traverses the woods of the seemingly tranquil town of Bright Falls in search of his missing wife - who from all indication is actually a defective ventriloquist dummy - fending off the townsfolk corrupted by the Darkness. They are weakened by light, and fortunately Alan never leaves home without his trusty Energizer® battery powered flashlight. This light versus dark dichotomy is hardly original, but does make for a satisfying combat mechanic.
Alan is a writer. For all the plot related elements that brings, it must be said - the dialogue in Alan Wake is often weak. It's a TV movie melodrama script, and its often painfully cringey.
Despite taking place largely in the dense forest of Bright Falls, the game directs you well - I was never at a loss of where to go next. This keeps the pacing perfectly on beat, driving you to reach the next narrative development or gloriously designed set piece. However, elements of the level design are too simplistic. You'll often need to locate a power generator to turn on a lightpost or other equipment, and I'd often locate it before Mr Wake had even finished his sentence.
Where Alan Wake succeeds, is its presentation and atmosphere. Its highly engaging when at its eccentric, surreal, Laura Palmer loving best. The introduction to the Oh Deer Diner holds an unnerving and seamless tonal shift from the bizarre to the menacing, and back again. A park ranger consumed by the darkness, begs, in a desperate cry, "Please...." before immediately screaming in a demonic rasp "DO NOT FEED THE ANIMALS". Moments like this tell the story better than the mediocre dialogue.
An effective thriller served up with a generous helping of cherry pie, and a damn fine cup of coffee.

NS2 is NOT an easy game to master. The learning curve IS quite steep. You have been warned!
Still there? Great! Because once you get your head around some of the game's mechanics, it is a VERY rewarding experience.
NS2 pits a team of Marines against Aliens on various sci-fi maps ranging from planetary drilling sites to space stations. While most players experience the game from a FPS perspective, shooting, biting, burning or otherwise harrassing the enemy team, one player on each side acts as commander, viewing the map from an RTS perspective (think StarCraft, Command&Conquer, etc.), giving orders the the rest of the team, researching upgrades and placing structures that the players on the field have to build.
The commander mode is not just some gimmick that was tacked on - NS2 is a full featured RTS game. Taking out enemy players certainly helps winning a round, but if your team is not paying attention to the "economy", you risk being out-teched by the enemy. NS2's strategical depth makes it a very unique and rewarding experience for players that like to work as a team.
However, as said in the beginning, it also makes NS2 a game that is not as easy to get into as your annual "modern military shooter". A recently added tutorial introduces new players to some of the basic mechanics, and short hint videos give tipps and explain game mechanics while you wait to respawn. NS2 also has a very friendly community; most players are very helpful and will try to explain stuff to new players when asked - so don't be shy, if you have a question, just ask. New players are automatically flagged as "rookie" for the first couple of rounds they play by being marked in green on the score board, so other players know you might not have the hang of the game yet. I recommend playing on servers marked as "rookie-friendly" until you have a better understanding of all the game mechanics. Please note that "rookie-friendly" does NOT necessarily mean "low skill", but people will be a lot more forgiving about typical rookie mistakes.
So, if you are looking for an FPS with a lot of strategic and tactical depth, an emphasis on teamwork, a mostly friendly and helpful community, but WITHOUT the vices of "modern" games (like ranks, unlocking weapons, microtransactions, etc.) - then yeah, give NS2 a try.
PS: Modding tools. Steam Workshop integration. TONS of mods. From custom skins and crosshairs to completely new game modes like fast-paced "Combat".

The old version of this game was brilliant in its simplicity. The new features add what to the game, exactly?
Math was so simple in the old version. An army of zombies with 50 hitpoints meets an army of humans with 80 hitpoints. 80 - 50 = the human army has 30 hitpoints remaining and the zombies are all dead with zero hitponts. If the human army was cowering behind fortifications, then those would soak up say 40 points of damage and the human army would have 70 hitpoints remaining. This new version tries to keep track of individual soldiers and villagers, so you now get to do multiplication and sometimes even division when figuring out how much damage one army can do to the other, where the previous system was simply add-and-subtract.
The maps in the old version had movement for both sides limited to specific roadways. This made it easy to predict the movements of not only the zombies but your allies as well. The new version has open plains instead, which makes it harder to understand what happened in-between playsessions.
Can I have the old version of the game back?
On a more positive note, I was able to have a short chat with the developer of this. This is awesome and 5 years ago it would of been completely beyond expectations. Unfortunately, there is no option for a thumbs sideways and it does not ultimately change my opinion of the game.

I never imagined I would put nearly 50 hours into this game, especially considering how simple and repetitive the actual gameplay loop is. Make workstation -> find/earn recipes for it -> craft gear -> learn to make new workstation -> repeat! You're constantly replacing weapons and armor you might have made only minutes ago. You can build a base, but it's not at all necessary since you can carry anything and everything with you. There is a lot of grinding for crafting materials, so much so that you'll never stop smacking every plant and plucking every do-dad you walk past in a vast, procedurally-generated world that feels more like a chaotic soup of bizarre flora, fauna, and terrain types than a fully-realized place. Even the combat is simple and boils down to learning basic attack patterns and "staying out of the poop" while your invincible, embiggened pet does much of the work.
Those sound like complaints, right? They actually aren't. The quirky-yet-charming characters drive you and the story along at a brisk clip, and I enjoyed them and the genuinely funny writing so much that the simplicity of the gameplay itself never once bothered me. All the individual pieces fit together in just the right way to keep the experience fresh and fun from start to finish.

Crashlands is like other survival/crafting games, but without a lot of the mechanics that make the others annoying.
Infinite inventory means no having to go back to base to dump stuff, not running out of space so you don't have to decide what to dump if some new or rare item pops up.
Contextual tooling means you don't have to worry about switching between axe for chopping, pick for mining, weapon for fighting, etc.
You get recipes, so you know how to craft things! You don't have to figure out how to craft everything. You don't have to memorize all of the recipes. You don't need to have a wiki up just to be able to play the game.
Getting recipes as a result of crafting anything (couple with infinite inventory) means that unless you're going to an objective, it's never worthless to gather something.
Warping (but not when in combat) saves so much time.
There is much more that Crashlands does, but at the VERY least, by not doing the things that make other similar games unfun, it wins by default.

ORIGINAL REVIEW (Edits after updates are below)
As happy as I am to see a hockey game on Steam right now, I cannot recommend this game at the time of writing this review. Like others have said, there are a few key problems in this game. My review is solely based on my first attempt at unlocking controls in the campaign before I quit in frustration (see below):
-Lag/Control Response:
Oh my goodness, it is bad. Didn't want to believe it but the reviews are right. I try to switch to a player who's close to the puck but by time it switches, the AI has flown by and out of range again. Same with slap shots, the speed of which I try to take a shot isn't relayed fast enough. Sometimes it even thinks I tried to reset and only does a wrist shot. Few other examples are when the puck is sitting in open ice and my guy skates over it and still does not take possession of the puck but the AI just skates by it gives it possession. Another is I will hip check someone and the guy stays bent over after the hit and hits another player away from the play which draws a penalty. Have the puck, try to pass in a specific direction to an open player only to have the puck not go in that direction and right to an AI player.
-Objective based campaign:
Look, I really had no qualms with this campaign mode when I had read about it. But after playing it, I almost came on here and wrote a 'rage quit' review because I couldn't stand the constant issues detracting me from enjoying the spirit of the game. While I get the dev wanted to paint a picture of team the was in the basement when you take over, I didn't imagine having to sit there and go through all these games almost feeling forced into losing each time. I couldn't tell you what the story is about because I am so tired of repeating this stuff that all I want is the bloody advanced controls so I can ignore this mode and just play some exhibition games. But I cannot until I either struggle through the rest of these objectives or just use the very boring two button option.
-Other things that bother me
Switching to the right player is a chore. Every time I try to switch to a player on defense, I instead get stuck with the guy who is chasing the AI instead. This then leads me trying to hook, not making contact due to lag, AI going between the two defenders because they do nothing to stop the AI from crashing the net, and then scoring right on top of the goalie. Pro tip: don't hip check the AI if they are doing this. The puck goes straight through the five hole every time.
My team that is AI controlled also does not react to puck movement very well. Like if I try passing to a guy who is wide open but is coming up the right side and the game lags and does a straight pass that's in his direction but not directly at him, the winger still just skates his "route"  straight ahead and ignores the puck in open ice. Same with defenders. Goalie dumps the puck into the corner, my defense man does not chase it at all. By time I switch to the closest guy the AI has the puck and is shooting.
Also, chill with the tutorial screens popping up every time the puck possession is in favor of the tutorial I am trying to learn.  I understood how to do a slap shot the first 5 times it popped up. The problem isn't that I can't do one, the problem is that window pops up, detracting me from the goal of attempting the slap shot, I resume the game and then between lag/response time lose possession and have to then regain it. Especially if I am still in the defensive zone and surrounded by AI.
Finally, why the heck do I inherent a team that has 0 0 0 in all categories and play everyone who's at least got a 2 in each category??? I get that I have a basement team and they are supposed to be the laughing stock of the league but once again it detracts me from the game because I am constantly getting beat on both sides of the puck even on rookie.
-Final Thoughts
I want this game to do well. But I feel like these problems are something that first need to be addressed in some capacity. I love hockey and since switching to PC really miss having a yearly option to play the newest NHL game. But NHL games aren't fun like this has the potential to be. If it was a little faster, reduced lag/control response, focused on the fighting and ridiculous hits, and let you choose from the start which controls you want to give you a hockey experience, then I would change this review in a heart beat.
EDIT 3/30/17
After an update last night, the game now allows people to use the Advanced Controls from the start. I removed the issue I had in the review about not having this from the start. Also, I don't know if this was also in the update but I also removed the comment about the inverse controls based on which way your team was facing because I saw there was an option to change that. Both of these changes are steps in the right direction and I did have some fun (though still losing by a ton) playing a few Rookie exhibition games. (Tip: If you were having issues with the AI running away with the game, turn on at least BHL offsides. It stops the AI from completely rushing the offensive zone and gives your AI time to get back and make a defensive play)
As more updates come out, I will continue to update and comment on this review. I will say that this was a step in the right direction and I am actually looking forward to play more later today!

There's a lot to say about wasteland 2. Where to start...
This game is what I've been craving since I finished Fallout 2 and Tactics, and it's great to know some of the old people who made Fallout 1 & 2 are still alive and making games, with the same great writing and dark humor I loved them for.
Although I think Van Buren would've been just as good, this still great even though it's on a different storyline, if not better since it's not stuck on that 1950's-ish theme fallout's cursed with. Instead this game feels like it's 1980 forever.
As for the gameplay, the way speech types work is a nice but refineable edition, and the lack of quest markers give it an unneccisary amount of extra exploring for things you can't find. LIke when I spent 3 and a half hours trying to find planks to fix the holes in the walls of the ranger compund. That's 3 hours I'm never getting back. As for the combat, it feels fun, but not complex enough. I remember the old fallouts having mines, settable traps, and other things, as well as the possibility of today's technology to add prone, advanced bullet physics, and a lot more character customization. The level layout is very good, and gives the game a nice fair level of competitiveness, while the skill reasons and effects leave me disarming and unlocking every single box, door, and crayon box in the game.
Something that also really bothered me that had no real bad effect is how a lot of guns were rechambered to use really small or world war 2 ammo, and there was no difference between a .308 and 7.62x39 round, so AK-47s and M60s were using the same ammo. I guess I'll just be waitng until someone makes a mod where guns make sense.
Last but not least, the experience of the game. I really enjoyed listening to the soundtrack of the game over and over again, (Why? I don't know) and also looking at the digital art book that came with it. I wish the concept art book came with more in it, but what bothers me most of all is the style of most of the concept art was really really cool lookiing with raggedy worn down looking people and creatures living in a mysterious dying world full of dust, mist, gloom, grey, red, and radiation green skies that were all screaming "THIS IS THE END OF THE WORLD". However when you actually play the game, you say "HEY MOM LOOK, I'M PLAYING CELL-PHONE NEW VEGAS!" If only the designers of the game world actually took more inspiration from the concept art and ACTUALLY made it the chilling, spine shaking, teeth gritting, bullet biting, soul crushing, post-apocalyptic fantasy some (now) old people had wet dreams over when they played wasteland 1.
Overall, with this game's good and bads, I'm giving this game a 9.2/10, just because it's harder to find a good post-apocalyptic RPG/Turn based tactical squad based combat extravaganza than it is to find a cat who'll ride on the top of your vacuum while you're vacuuming while running down the sidewalk.
That, and this calmed my fallout 2 "real" sequel withdrawl.
Now I just need to wait for Wasteland 3!

I am not a fan of horror, but this game scratches an itch very few games do. It scratches a certain itch that usually comes with very well done psychological thriller movies, but it's stronger than that because of the nature of how games work. Being directly involved with the story of Alan Wake really creates a tension unlike any other. The way it uses suspense to create this tension is great, and while there are a few jumpscares in this game, that is not where the horror comes from. You'll find your heart rate beating at the times when you are alone, walking through a forest trail as the fog starts to creep in, politely letting you know that you are no longer safe.
The story is also fantastic and the way it pans out at the end will keep you thinking about it for weeks, maybe even years. I originally played this game when it first came out on the Xbox 360, and ever since then I think about this game regularly and recommend it at any chance I get, like now. And after a good few years without playing it I felt the need to go back an experience this once again to truly see if it holds up well now as it does in my memory. It definitely holds up, that is except the facial animations in the cutscenes. Those haven't aged too well, especially with the pixelated, low resolution that they are on. However, what truly makes this game special, the atmosphere, the story, the sense of a journey, and just the general horror of it all... Those have definitely held up. And other than P.T. on the PS4 Store (which uses atmosphere in a similar way, although P.T. is more jumpscare centred than AW), nothing has even came close to replicating this kind of horror game since, which is a shame because I really like this kind of horror, even though I'm not a fan of the overall genre across all mediums, I really hope Alan Wake gets a true sequel some day or at the very least a very good spiritual successor done in the same vein as this game.

This review was written long ago in the past, when only Act 1 (half of the game) was available & I didn't know when (or if) I will be able to play the rest of it. Act 1 was released on January 2014 and Act 2 just now (April 28, 2015), so as you can see it was a long wait for many people. I will rewrite this review as soon as I'll complete the second part of the game. :)
----------
Broken Age is a classical in nature point & click adventure game, that focuses mostly on the story, characters & dialogue. Puzzles themselves aren't challenging, although they are logical and support the narration nicely. Visuals are really charming - a distinct painted 2D art style. The setting (or settings, as there are two protagonists) is fresh and manages to grasp and keep the interest up.
Too bad this is just Act 1, or in other words - it's half a game, and ends with a cliffhanger. Certain parts of the plot are explained by the end, but not nearly enough & the ending scene just made me want to immediately play Act 2, which is unfortunately unavailable at this point.
The game itself is quite short. It took me 4h 20min to beat it and I certainly didn't rush it. I visited every location, talked with everyone about everything and tried to interact with every object.
Even though I would prefer to play both Acts at once & not wait indefinitely for 2nd half of the game, I'm still recommending this game :) It's charming, intriguing and enjoyable, provided one likes story focused adventures.

The game is £35, not £50 as many new games are, and it's well worth the money if you enjoy playing games as opposed to just criticising them based on what you read online.

After having completed the game a week ago, I decided to make on final edit of my review. Unfortunately, I will keep the thumb down. Mafia III is not a bad game, as a game. However, it does everything in its power to sabotage itself.
The PC port was and, as of time of writing this, still is terrible. Which particularly bad for a game that delivers sub par performance on consoles. On a GTX 1080 the game failed to maintain stable 60 fps at 1440p, with drops in the 30s, even though the visuals are ok-ish at best... sometimes, with upscaled textures and overall look that is definitely inferior to GTA V.
To make matters worse the game seems to sue some sort of temporal AA that makes everything super blurry even on low and it's impossible to completely turn off. The workaround is using SweetFX, but still - WTF. And using SweetFX to sharpen the image and battle the blur only reveals how low res the textures actually are.
However, the graphics are a relatively minor problem. On the technical side the game is horrible. Crashes, bug, broken missions, missing gamepad icons, absurd day/night cycle. I've seen sun during night time, I've seen sun during torrentual rain, I've seen day and night change in seconds and I've even seen different weather and time of the day in different parts of the city, just a few blocks away from each other.
Not to mention often at times and places the game is absurdly dark, to the point you cannot play it. I came to find that this happens at dusk and night time if there are clouds!!! Which is just... wow. And before you ask - yes, too bright is also an issue at time, though not as severe as the pitch black I've seen even in rooms with 4 separate light sources.
The game is easily as worse port as Arkham Knight initially was on the PC but I seriously doubt it will be fixed, as well as the last Batman game did.
And while Batman had a fun gameplay, despite the copious amounts of tanking around, Mafia III will have you repeat the same thing over and over and over and over and over again. There are only four types of missions - go kill, go interrogate, go destroy/burn some merchandise and deliver a truck/boat of goods. That is it. There is a bit more variety in the story missions, but to get to them you've to take over districts and that means doing the same four generic missions over and over again.
Combine all that with an idiotic AI and I found myself just shooting the place up more often than not, just to make the missions a bit more interesting and end them faster.  I did end up completing all optional missions, but do not mistake OCD and completionism with signs of good gameplay.
So is there anything actually good here? Yes - plenty. Sadly it is buried beneath a pile of glitches and repetitiveness.
For one the soundtrack is awesome. I'm not a music person and I knew little about late 60s music but the track list is amazing and I ended up bookmarking a lot of the songs on Spotify.
Second, the voice acting is simply amazing. Probably the best I've ever heard in a game. Combined with the brilliant facial animations of the characters the performance delivered is so good that it manages to make a generic mobster revenge story into something very compelling. If there is one thing that will make you endure Mafia III, it's the story.
Gunplay is also nice and makes shootouts overall satisfying. I also liked the collectibles.
So there you have it - one good game, that was destroyed by technical problems and artificially overblown game time. I don't blame the devs - they did good for a first game. I put all the blame on 2K, who obviously pushed the developers to go the GTA route and then did not allow them to finish the game and release it in a proper state. So now, by the time it gets fixed, most people, like myself, have already finished it. Pity, but between this and Battleborn I have completely lost faith in 2K and no longer respect them as a publisher.

Nuclear Throne is a rogue-like fast paced game created by Vlambeer. The game is currently available on Steam for GBP £8.99. At the current time, there are two game modes available to play: a single player mode and a Local Co-Op mode.
The games menu screen and settings are all easy and swift to go through. The game runs very well and feels smooth even when there are multiple enemies and projectiles on the screen. The game feels very well designed and there is enough variety in all the different map layouts, upgrades and weapons that the game never feels dull.
Nuclear Throne, like most rogue-like games has various different ways to enjoy playing. The game has twelve different characters which all have unique and special traits. You can play the game as a tanky character with a shield as an ability, or you can dual wield weapons and play as crazy and fast paced as you want.
Nuclear Throne is hard, it really is. It takes getting used to and learning enemy shooting patterns is extremely important if you wish to progress to some of the later levels. The game constantly pulls you back in with how different every single run can be. Sometimes you can wind up dead on the first screen and sometimes you can get to the end with barely a mark upon you.
If you are the sort of person who enjoys a challenge and gets a thrill out of fast paced rogue-like games, this is the game for you. My only negative feedback for this game would be that at the current time there is no official online multiplayer for the game which can make the game grow a bit stale over time unless you are lucky enough to play on Local Co-Op.
Overall, Nuclear Throne has been a fantastic purchase for me and has been worth every penny spent. I feel the price is great for how many hours of joy (or rage) you will get out of this well presented, well-made game.

The game features a story mode that follows a local hockey team’s tale of redemption. Each match has objectives requirements (either learning controls or achieving specific statistics) that are ridiculously difficult to meet; this results in extremely frustrating matches that must be replayed over and over until you luck out and roll easier semi-random objectives. In addition, the advanced control scheme doesn’t unlock until you have progressed far enough in the campaign, restricting your options in the exhibition mode. An easy solution would be to remove mandatory objectives and simply reward any achievements with experience points (a mechanic already in the game). The game also lacks custom seasons and online multiplayer. The control scheme (designed for a gamepad) involves somewhat complicated procedures for shooting, passing, defensive maneuvers (hook, slash, check, block), and fighting; more simplified control schemes are also available (though the story mode requires the advanced controls to be used). Player movement in the game is satisfying, and the hockey itself is entertaining to play. Line changes are automated, and penalties are rare. Momentum may be gained by leveling the opponent three times in a row or gaining a power play, which allows for more powerful shots and hits. The friendly players lack intelligence on defense, although this is possibly by design. Despite the generally solid gameplay, frustrating mandatory campaign objectives cast a dark shadow over the rest of the title.

CrashLands has some great ideas, but they are largely hamstrung by the slog:
Even if you choose just to create one armor/weapon set of each tier as it becomes available (disregarding any thoughts of re-rolling equipment or crafting leisure/decorative stuff), you will still be forced to grind out drops regularly. That's not always a bad thing, but in this game it sure feels like it.
The world is effectively infinitely scrolling, but with such extreme lack of diversity, there is little time for the joy of exploration before the experience degrades into exasperating saminess.  When you're out on your grind mission, it doesn't matter AT ALL which direction you travel; you'll encounter no surprises—just forever-scrolling sameyness.
The combat mechanics are satisfying for a while, but a lack of encounter-level design means that mostly you will be dodge-slap-dodge-slapping the same enemies over and over in one-on-one battles. The enemy attack patterns vary nicely, but they would have been more effective (and *were *in a few choice quests) in battles with prartially designed enemy group compositions and confined battlegrounds. The first-order optimal strategy gets tiresome fast.
This clearly borrows a ton from Don't Starve, and tries to improve on "tedium" re: self-managing infinite inventory and tool changing.  It's decidely *not* a survival game like Don't Starve, and I think this is largely why the borrowed mechanics fall flat. There's little-to-no penalty for death, and time is entirely your friend. In Don't Starve, spending time to gather drops has costs associated with it, namely: risk of death, growing hungry, rotting food, fading sanity, and the coming of Winter. In Crashlands, gathering drops is merely a gating mechanism for progression -> "spend enough of your time grinding for loot and we will dole out the story in little chunks". Crafting in Don't Starve took time, and time cost you in all sorts of ways. In Crashlands, the timers on crafting has no functional effect other than to waste your real-world time.  Perhaps it was meant to make crafting feel more substantial, but if that were the case, something interactive would have done much better than a timer.
TLDR: If Don't Starve wasn't a survival game, it wouldn't work nearly as well.

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and
rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax to the game I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about the story, about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

Natural Selection 2 is an amazing hybrid of a game which mixes some of the best elements from the strategy game Starcraft 2 and the fps and competitive elements from a game like say, Counter Strike. Natural Selection 2's graphics are beautiful, the gameplay is smooth and the mechanics solid. If you start a game and jump in the commanders chair, you play a strategy top down view comparable to Starcraft 2 where you play as either the terran or zerg race. You work to gather resources, nodes, upgrades, buildings, expansions and much more. But there's a twist, the units you control so-to-speak are real players who can think for themselves. Each player has different skill levels and strategies which keeps the game very diverse. If you're playing from the marine/alien fps point of view, you roam around the map killing enemy structures and nodes, group up for epic team fights and work together to achieve the ultimate victory. The thing that stands out most to me is the fact that the competitive side yet small, is purely brilliant. The mix of strategy and fps is done RIGHT and gives you some of the most epic and intense games. I feel like this game is nowhere near as popular as it should have been (regarding the competitive scene).

After having completed the game a week ago, I decided to make on final edit of my review. Unfortunately, I will keep the thumb down. Mafia III is not a bad game, as a game. However, it does everything in its power to sabotage itself.
The PC port was and, as of time of writing this, still is terrible. Which particularly bad for a game that delivers sub par performance on consoles. On a GTX 1080 the game failed to maintain stable 60 fps at 1440p, with drops in the 30s, even though the visuals are ok-ish at best... sometimes, with upscaled textures and overall look that is definitely inferior to GTA V.
To make matters worse the game seems to sue some sort of temporal AA that makes everything super blurry even on low and it's impossible to completely turn off. The workaround is using SweetFX, but still - WTF. And using SweetFX to sharpen the image and battle the blur only reveals how low res the textures actually are.
However, the graphics are a relatively minor problem. On the technical side the game is horrible. Crashes, bug, broken missions, missing gamepad icons, absurd day/night cycle. I've seen sun during night time, I've seen sun during torrentual rain, I've seen day and night change in seconds and I've even seen different weather and time of the day in different parts of the city, just a few blocks away from each other.
Not to mention often at times and places the game is absurdly dark, to the point you cannot play it. I came to find that this happens at dusk and night time if there are clouds!!! Which is just... wow. And before you ask - yes, too bright is also an issue at time, though not as severe as the pitch black I've seen even in rooms with 4 separate light sources.
The game is easily as worse port as Arkham Knight initially was on the PC but I seriously doubt it will be fixed, as well as the last Batman game did.
And while Batman had a fun gameplay, despite the copious amounts of tanking around, Mafia III will have you repeat the same thing over and over and over and over and over again. There are only four types of missions - go kill, go interrogate, go destroy/burn some merchandise and deliver a truck/boat of goods. That is it. There is a bit more variety in the story missions, but to get to them you've to take over districts and that means doing the same four generic missions over and over again.
Combine all that with an idiotic AI and I found myself just shooting the place up more often than not, just to make the missions a bit more interesting and end them faster.  I did end up completing all optional missions, but do not mistake OCD and completionism with signs of good gameplay.
So is there anything actually good here? Yes - plenty. Sadly it is buried beneath a pile of glitches and repetitiveness.
For one the soundtrack is awesome. I'm not a music person and I knew little about late 60s music but the track list is amazing and I ended up bookmarking a lot of the songs on Spotify.
Second, the voice acting is simply amazing. Probably the best I've ever heard in a game. Combined with the brilliant facial animations of the characters the performance delivered is so good that it manages to make a generic mobster revenge story into something very compelling. If there is one thing that will make you endure Mafia III, it's the story.
Gunplay is also nice and makes shootouts overall satisfying. I also liked the collectibles.
So there you have it - one good game, that was destroyed by technical problems and artificially overblown game time. I don't blame the devs - they did good for a first game. I put all the blame on 2K, who obviously pushed the developers to go the GTA route and then did not allow them to finish the game and release it in a proper state. So now, by the time it gets fixed, most people, like myself, have already finished it. Pity, but between this and Battleborn I have completely lost faith in 2K and no longer respect them as a publisher.
