I NEVER write reviews.  Ever.  However, after reading the plethora of negative reviews on this game, I felt it was necessary.  I would like to start off with a firm rebuke of those gamers who voted 'NO' about recommending this game.  Absolute nonsense.  I'm not sure why some of you actually play a game, but as far as Mafia III is concerned, the entertainment value is there, and more.
Graphically, (where most of the complainers reside) I would offer 8/10.  I'm 3 hours in and I have had zero complaints.  I have a decent rig: GTX 970 - Intel i7-3770 3.40GHz 16.0 GB RAM ASUS CM6330 // I have the settings all set to HIGH with everything turned ON - frame rate set to unlimited - No hiccups, no glitches, no CTD's thus far.  I honestly don't know wtf others are complaining about.  I haven't seen anything that stands out as a negative "OH MY GOD THESE GRAPHICS SUCK" moment. Now to the great stuff:  The story: 10/10  Oh, the story.  I'll start by stating I played Mafia I & Mafia II and enjoyed them both.  Mafia III does NOT disappoint.  It's Fan-F'n-Tastic, period.  The music draws you in, the characters are well developed, and the story is well written.
The mechanics: 9/10 I am using a dual setup with mouse/keyboard for gameplay & a controller for driving. It's perfect.  The combat responsiveness is perfect & the driving is smooth as silk.  I recommend turning the Aim assist off & setting the difficulty to no less than medium for a solid challenge.  If I could go into 1st person while walking I'd rate it a 10/10.
I should state that after initially reading these reviews, I almost didn't purchase the game.  Almost.  But I love the Mafia series, so I went online and really researched what others were saying.  Outside of Steam, there were many reviews that accurately reflected my experiences.  My conclusion: Steam is filled with arrogant, entitled, morons.

My time with this game, so far, has only been about an hour and a half, but I know I will be playing it much, much more!
Sometimes, with this game, it feels like luck is the only thing keeping you alive, and, in a way, it is.
Fast. Hard. Fun!
What more is there to say?
Your goal is to make it to the Nuclear Throne.
You use a variety of guns and characters to hopefully make it there, but it won't be any time soon. It's all in timing and accuracy, which you'll have to have in spades to win.
I love how quick the games are because of the difficulty! Got five minutes to kill? Play a game of Nuclear Throne!
One of my favorite parts of this game is the Daily and Weekly game modes. You have to play crazy versions of Nuclear Throne and compete for high scores on the leader board.
This week's was playing as Steroids with lots of weapons, but low ammo and no ammo pickups! Hard and fun, just like the base game!
I wish you could play Daily more than once, but it's still fun, none the less.
The pixel graphics in this game match the gameplay astoundingly. I couldn't imagine the game with any other art style. I feel that some of the enemies are a bit repetitive, but olny repetetive in the sense of Borderlands 1, where if you didn't suck so much you get past this part of the level and be done with it.
The characters in this game are all interesting are fun to play. Each one of them has certain special abilities to help them survive.
Fish, my personal favorite, has the ability to roll, putting distance between him and his attackers. Meanwhile, Crystal has the ability to cover himself in crystal for a few seconds to stop oncoming attacks. All of these are fun and open doors for a LOT of replayability.
One thing I don't like, though, is that you have to unlock characters by playing. I'm the kind of person who thinks all options should be available at the start of the game, but that might just be me.
I feel like the weapon choices in this game are a bit lacking, but I can barely get past the first boss, most games, so there might be some more later on in the game. I feel that no weapon is really "overpowered", but I feel some are often more useful than others.
For example, the grenade launcher is harder to use and aim, but a direct hit does a lot of damage, so you might want to save that one for boss battles. Meanwhile, the wrench is just as powerful, but you have to think and move fast enough to dodge bullets, while trying to ge close enough to the enemy to hit him.
This is where the luck really comes into the game, in my opinion.
Getting "Mutations", this game's version of perks, is all praying that you've got enough XP to level up, enough health to make up to the next level so you can level up, and then, the real kicker, you have to hope the mutation does anything good!
Sometimes you'll get full health or ammo! Sometimes you'll even get both!
But, sometimes all of your options seem useless. Better melee range? Possibility of regaining ammo if you kill something?
This seems like it would be bad game design, but it isn't! It works like a charm! The luck aspect is one of my favorite parts.
It's the driving force that pushes you to keep fighting, because if you can just kill that one enemy YOU MIGHT have enough XP to level up and YOU MIGHT get full health!
While some mutations are noticeably less useful than others, all of them are noticeable and do have an impact on the game.
Enter the Gungeon is probably the closest thing you could get to Nuclear Throne. It's a bit slower, but has more RPG elements and can be a bit more forgivable.
For me, pricing is very import. I, for one, did not pay full price for this game. I bought this game for $2.99 from a trader.
I will say that this game has never gone on sale, which is odd because it almost seems like a game that I imagine would have a much bigger audience if it ever went on sale and it feels and plays like a game that would go on sale CONSTANTLY!
It has had a recent price drop since it's release, which might be a sign of things to come and I've been told you can get it cheaper in bundles and on other sites, but still.
I'd like it to be cheaper and while it has it's flaws and could be a bit too difficult for the average casual gamer, I love this game and will enjoy playing it for a long time.

Fallout Shelter is a game I've put down MANY times, only to pick back up again when the developers announce seasonal updates. I didn't plan on writing this review, but given the amount of people giving it
a bad rap, I figured I had to step in and set the record straight as best as I can.
Firstly,
The graphics in this game aren't
it was originally ported from mobile, but even then it's simplistic design - being that of the cartoonish theme we have seen since the upbringing of the
franchise with it's iconic Vault Boy - is immensely appealing and vibrant, a stark contrast from the actual
games themselves, with the slightest exception of the recent installment.
is a resource-collection, spending, and maintenance game, simply put. You take the role of a Vault Overseer, your first initial task being that of naming your Vault. (There is a three-digit dial upon creation) During the early stages of the game, your objective is to have as many Vault Dwellers in your Vault as possible -- attaining Dwellers can be achieved by placing a male and female Dweller within the Living Quarters and letting them procreate, (it's best to choose the most high-SPECIAL Dwellers for breeding purposes) or attracting Wastelanders using a Broadcast Station you can build during mid-game.
The game takes a turn with the purchase of the
room which can be obtained with 1,000 caps. From then on, you are able to send your Dwellers out on missions of varying difficulty and with varying end-rewards. They take on the feel of the first two
games, even going as far as putting you in control of your Dwellers as they excavate buildings in search of loot, or to destroy a certain threat. Be sure to equip them with decent gear if you indulge in the option often. Missions alternate very frequently, and the developers are keen on dishing out holiday-related quests pretty often. (Saving Santa, anyone?) In addition to this, you can send a Dweller out on excursions from the very beginning by dragging them outside of the Vault. You can provide them with as many Stimpacks and Radaways as you see fit in the hopes they will survive long enough to  get some decent loot and return.
The game runs seamlessly, which is quite ironic given how broken some of the
games have been on PC, and yet somehow this game has yet to dissapoint me. During it's early release, however, I had to go about emulating an Android device on my computer in order to even play the game, which brought many headaches due to it still being in the later stages of development. However, they continued to port it to PC via Bethesda's official website, and now onto Steam.
This is where most of the negative reviews come in. Casual players of this game drawl on and on about how micropurchases affect the game to such a high degree and how it really isn't meant to be played often, the latter being the only
quarrel.
When you first enter the game, you are shown the variety of progress-boosting items you can buy for real-life cash, all of which you can go without. The boosters range from Lunchboxes which yield five cards, each card providing you with a different reward, (Special Dwellers, Resources, Weapons, Nuka Cola Quantum to speed up progress) as well as Mister Handy Boxes which allows you to place a single Mister Handy on any one floor of your Vault -- they will patrol, collect resources, and fight off Raiders or Deathclaws who dare infltrate your base when you are offline. Additionally, there are Animal Kennels you can purchase which contain a single animal you can give to any one Dweller to boost their attributes.
Ironically, if you
a reason to stop playing the game, then you indulge in the preoffered microtransations. Without them, you fare
and can even achieve Lunchboxes by completing quests found in your Pip-Boy menu. As I write this, I sit on over a few
caps, and have a storage partially filled with special weapons and outfits. It's all up to chance, but if you even bothered to give the game even 25% effort, you would
find yourself in a decent state. Additionally, as your Vault begins to increase in size, you will take notice of the iconic Mysterious Stranger beginning to make sudden appearances - with his well-known guitar entrance - finding him hidden in your Vault and clicking on him will reward you with an abundance of caps ranging from 1,000 and beyond.
This game is meant to be treated casually, like every other Cookie Clicker-esque game on the market. You can use it to wind down from an intense day of playing other things, or just have it in the background while you browse social media. I am currently going back and forth from writing this to collect resources and check up on my scavenging Dweller. Holding it in such high standards and giving it negative reviews simply because it isn't "your kind of game" or "the progression is outlandish and slow" is unfair and misleading.
I reckon I've written enough. I highly encourage anyone pondering to play this game to give it a try. It is a relatively small download, and if you don't enjoy it, you can delete it without a second thought. I assure you, however, you will find yourself coming back for more.

This game is fantastic, and frankly I'm disappointed with the highest rated negative reviews.
I will say that if you don't like crafting, or feel like Terraria, Starbound, or other survival / crafting games on Steam already satisfied your survival / crafting itch, then this isn't the game for you. However, for me I've found it has the most satisfying progression loop out of all of the survival / crafting games on Steam.
This game stands out from Terraria and Starbound (which I very much enjoy) by actually attempting to combine the random parts with the scripted parts. All of Crashland's NPCs and quests are based around landmarks that are blended into the generated world. The quests written for those NPCs feel more like a full-featured RPG because those NPCs have some interaction with the landscape. It's not full immersive-sim interaction, but characters and places do change during events, which is more than what happens in Terraria and Starbound.
This game is designed to work with mobile devices as well as PC, but that doesn't usually get in the way. The targeting system does occasionally prioritize resource gathering when I'M TRYING TO FIGHT THE ENEMY NEXT TO THE TREE, NOT CHOP THE TREE DOWN RIGHT NOW, THANK YOU, but I think this is mostly a problem with gamepads and not with mouse + keyboard. Other than the occasional targeting glitch, I really, really like this game.
While this games does indeed have a ton in common with other survival / crafting games, I'm going to say that right now it's my favorite out of all the ones I've tried so far. The NPCs feel like they're a part of the crazy, crazy world they're stuck on, and that really helps sell the idea that you're also wandering around an actual place with a story and not just procedural landscape #97648734653. Maybe the story doesn't hold up with repeated playthroughs, maybe it does, but either way I've already sunk over seventeen hours into this game and I've enjoyed every minute.
If you still enjoy classic 2D action-RPG combat, crafting, and reading NPC dialogue, this is the game for you. If you've had your fill of any one of those things, just consider yourself warned.

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and
rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax to the game I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about the story, about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

Hockey is my favorite sport, and it really saddens me that there aren't more hockey games floating around out there.  I find it hard to be enamoured with the NHL series because it really seems to take itself too seriously.  Many people are into the "realistic sim" sports games, but frankly, I'm not one of them.  I like the NFL Blitzes, NBA Jams, and Super Mega Baseballs of the world.  Games that feel realistic enough to be absorbing but ridiculous enough to be fun.  I'd been looking forward to Old Time Hockey for some time now, and I feel maybe a smidge disappointed.
The game is competently put together and certainly playable.  I like the idea of the game happening in a 70's minor/beer league where the teams are from relatively small towns in America and Canada.  Passes, though they never seem to go EXACTLY where you want them to, are crisp enough that you can transition from offense to defense quickly enough that you can get some nice back-and-forth action.  The game's controls are a nice blend of arcade-style mixed with the modern NHL series liberal use of the right analog stick, which is just sophisticated enough to allow you to pull off cool moves but simple enough that idiots like me can hop in and not feel we have to go though an 8-week educational course to be able to play without looking like a spaz.
I have plenty of niggles with this game though.  While I do like the 70's league idea, the visuals of the game, much like the actual 70's, is a little ugly.  Your teammate AI is pathetic.  Rule one of hockey defense: seperate your opponent from the puck so they can't score on you.  A regular situation in-game is your opponent streaking in alone with your two defensemen back and he casually skates between them and puts the puck top-shelf.  And because switching control to the player you actually WANT to control is an inexact science at best, situations where you are up 3-1 halfway through the 2nd period and let in 4 unanswered goals to make the score 5-3 are a little more common than I'd like them to be.
The "momentum" mechanic is shaky.  How it works is that during gameplay, landing 3 big hits before your opponent does OR drawing a penalty, gives you boosts.  Your players get harder to knock down, your shots get more powerful, and handling the puck is easier.  Meanwhile the other team gets pretty much kneecapped for about 20-30 seconds.  It's supposed to reward you by making it easier to create offense, but call me an awful player, but my success rate is less than 50%.  More often than not, I get scored on before I can take advantage of my momentum.
Old Time Hockey has a story mode, which is an interesting kettle of fish.  A sports game with some actual narrative is neat, and I admit, I have limited experience with it (only 4 hours at time of writing), but it's home to one of the most questionable  design choices the game has. In your first "story" you take control of the worst team in the league, and as you get better, so does the team.  I like this idea a lot, but now we get to the questionable part.  You unlock the 'advanced' control scheme bit by bit in the tutorial encased in the first story.  This, I'm guessing, is supposed to lend to the whole "crawling out of the basement" thing, and learning the game and getting better at it.  But it is frustrating as hell being schooled by the AI without being able to do half of what they can do.  It's a really long con, almost.  You have to complete objectives throughout a game in order to advance the story, and some of them can be a little unforgiving, especially when you have 2 tough objectives AND you have to win the game while the opposing team plays like a team full of Datsyuks and Crosbys.
But the worst part of the game is one of it's selling points in the advertising: the violence.  The checking is a little wobbly, but works well enough.  It's the fighting I don't like.  Fighting in hockey video games have been little more than button-mashers and stick-flickers, but this game tops it.  It's like rock-paper-scissors almost, and the first person to get hit three times loses.  Post fight, the player that lost gets "fatigued," which basically leaves that player virtually useless.  So if, like me, you really suck at the fighting, by the middle of the third period, your team is full of one-legged sloths that can't shoot or pass against a team who steamrolls your sorry♥♥♥♥♥

I found this to be well worth playing, but it left me somewhat unsatisfied in the end and wishing there had been far more content. After finishing one playthrough, I immediately started a new one but quickly realized that the game would not grab my interest enough for a second one any time soon, though it is partially my fault perhaps.
As you can see from my "hours on record", I finished the game in under 27 hours (subtracting the aborted second playthrough), so I'm not quite sure where they got the 80 hours of gameplay idea from. As noted below, I take shortcuts when playing, but I wouldn't expect those to shave 50 hours off of play time, more like a quarter at most.
As a casual gamer, I very much enjoyed the tactical combat aspect. I actually prefer a "heroic" gameplay approach in which my squad usually has the tactical upper hand, as opposed to more hard core players who prefer to have to struggle hard to reach objectives (I just don't have time for that - thus part of the reason play time was shorter, but not all the reason IMHO). As such, I tend to tweak player stats early on to give them a bit of an advantage (just a bit!). I actually found that this makes combat far more exciting for me at least. I would very much prefer a game in which one good shot will lay you, or the enemy, flat, as it would in real life, and tweaking stats can create such a situation (unfortunately for the player squad only). I find the concept of spamming heals on party members to survive an encounter to be *extremely* unrealistic and immersion breaking in anything but a fantasy setting, so the tweaked stats allowed be immersive roleplaying of a heroic squad versus more average opponents. I loved the increasingly effective gear replacements and the gun modification mechanics, as well as the various differences in the tactics required for the weapons, which also helped immersion greatly. Someone else here said that gun ranges seemed the same, but for me, the chance to hit was eliminated as a factor through tweaking, so I could see clearly that ranges were in fact quite important. This suggests to me that some tweaking of balance might actually make this game better for some people. Just for comparison, there are plenty of other RPGs I've played in the past, with tweaks/mods/God abilities etc., where long term playability was in no way effected by that. A truly good game should accomodate all sorts of play styles. Anyway, overall, I found the tactical aspect to be the most satisfying part of the game. Being able to preposition my squad and then draw the enemy into a shooting gallery was actually quite fun. Granted, that also points out the weak enemy AI others have mentioned. The AI does more typically rush into their weapon range and then end up unable to fire because they've run out of action points, making them sitting ducks out in the open. However, in situations where they are already in range and under cover, they will remain there, and they did seem to seek cover if it was close by.
I generally do not like scripted games at all. I prefer open world/sandbox almost exclusively, but I make an exception for this genre due to nostalgia from the original Fallout series. Others below have complained about the overall story and how it seems to be window dressing on the tactical combat experience. This was generally fine for me, and I was glad that it was perfectly possible to play encounters in a different order then the "standard story line" in many cases (but not all). At the least, doing things out of order did not seem to break anything for me (such as being unable to finish important objectives - with one noteable exception below).
On the downside, though, I found that navigation was slow and at times extremely confusing (and thus quickly boring). I found myself repeatedly referring to walkthroughs and the like to figure out what the criptic instructions of NPCs was meant to tell me. It was also very common for important instructions to quickly scroll by to be missed, so I was not even sure what I was supposed to be doing. The worst was a large map midgame where it is possible to get very, very confused and commit immersion breaking mistakes, requiring a reload to an earlier save.
The other immensely annoying aspect of the game was the constant lock picking, alarm deactivating, trap removal. Those activities actually took up a huge chunk of each map to the point that, considering that the contents of chests were often literally junk, I ended up skipping over only to miss the occasional important item. Thus, this became an extremely tedious negative experience which greatly subtracted from the overall fun. Also, the question of whether a given container was trapped/locked/alarm protected did not seem to follow any kind of logic.
Also, let's face it, this genre and the game mechanics that go with it are really becomming outdated, and this game, while providing a somewhat modernized and, IMHO, polished execution of it, still does not make up for the fact that the mechanics are artificially held back to a kind of simulation of 1990s technology. This to me is the greatest cause for the lack of depth in character development and other such aspects pointed out by others. While 3D rendered, this *is* really a glorified isometric game in presentation, and I found the low resolution of the characters to be a bit confusing in that it is not as if someone is going to be playing this on an Android phone (or is it?) I think they could have upped the resolution of the characters by a bit, and for instance have more of them appear to reflect what they were wearing.
Edit: While I'm on the subject of graphics, I have to say that the base model used for player characters is *UGLY*. There is really only one head shape each for male/female, with a few different skins slapped on seemingly slightly off center, and I had a really hard time coming up with characters that came anywhere close to someting I could identify with (this is an RPG after all). This is not a big deal, so I mention this only as a minor complaint.
The other thing I found to be *extremely* distracting was that the NPC portrait displayed on screen when conversing with that NPC invariably looked nothing like the 3D character, including clothing, colors, hairstyle, etc. This to me was just sloppy and incomplete. Rather than putting an emphasis on having portraits that would get lots of likes on Devient Art, they should have gone for volume and made sure that every unique NPC had a unique portrait.  Judging by some of the really bad portraits available in the initial character creation screen, my guess is that they hired an expensive artist to do these portraits and ran out of money. That was definitely a design mistake.
Certainly the game is visually beautiful to look at (when zoomed out), but after having played the Fallout reboot series and other Bethesda RPGs, which provide a relatively modern immersive 3D first&third person experience in a fully unscripted open world, it becomes increasingly difficult to be fully pulled in by this old-school, scripted, controlled viewport experience.
Not only that, but the freedom of the Bethesda approach has allowed very deep modibility which extends the playability of the games for many years, whereas this game ended up being just a minor distraction over a couple of weeks, sort of like a short TV miniseries.

I have all 5 episodes, but at this time of writing I just finished episode 4. I downloaded the game unenthusiastically because the first episode was free, and after beating the first episode I got the rest of them because I was invested in a story I really enjoyed, and now I can't wait to get home from work to get to the bottom of whats been going on at Arcadia Bay!
The game is set in a small Oregon town and you play as an 18 year old girl Max Caulfield who reunites with her childhood bestie Chloe. She randomly acquires powers that allow her to rewind time and change up things before they happen or use new knowledge you gained. The game plays like the Telltale Walking Dead games in that it is a 3d point and click adventure game. The pacing can get a little slow at times but thats probably my own fault because I keep running around and trying to make sure I talked to everyone and messed with everything. The music in the game is very solid and features real life artists like Amanda Palmer of Dresden Dolls. All the music is not my taste but in the game it is so fitting and perfect I really vibe with it as it sets the mood.
The game sort of feels like it was developed for a female audience as it focuses a bit more on clever humor and more drama while action takes a backseat... but don't let that turn you off for a second though because the setting feels refreshingly new and original and is a good break from all the games I normally play.
When I finish an episode I'm usually shocked and immediately want to fire up the next episode to see what happens next. The story is nothing short of amazing, the dialogue is incredibly clever, the voice acting is believable. The graphics are passable - I don't really expect amazing graphics from these types of games so thats fine with me. The graphics looked alright but it was more of the facial animations I thought were great.
The developers Dontnod also created Remember Me which was a pretty good game as well but it didn't sell well and nearly killed Dontnod. Life is Strange was sort of a hail mary on their part and this game is the title that put them on the map and is their flagship series at this point.
All in all, I highly recommend giving the first episode a download and if you don't like it, you can uninstall it.

If you are reading this then I'm certain you've read at least a couple of the other player reviews of this game, if not official reviews from IGN, PC Gamer & the like.  Many of the reviews equate this game as being a "tactical RPG",  I would classify it more as an RPG with
(
) tactical elements, there's a difference.
Like in the "golden age" of PC RPGs, you create your inital squad members, you can recruit up to 3 others, making a total of 7.  There are quite a few NPCs to recruit also, each has their own reasons for being on your team.  Depending on your actions it can be quite temporary how long a potential recruit stays on your team.  How you mix & match your PCs & NPCs can be quite interesting. Like the PC based RPGs of yesteryear, once a character dies, they're gone forever, so save often.  The game does not hold your hands on things, some of the clues in certain quests are down right obtuse & depending on the difficulty you set it at certain other things... well you'll see for yourself.
Is the game "pretty", nope.  Is the story something I've not seen before, nope on that also.  But this games
give me something I see too little of in RPGs these days: choice & consequence.  Most of the consequences based on the choices are also not readily apparent, they have a small ripple effect that may not be seen for hours down the road; are you
about to reload a save from 2 or 4 or more hours ago when the consequence of such a decision is happening so far down the line?  I seriously doubt that, which is another thing I like, you have to think on most of the choices here; "How will doing
bite me in the rear?" is something you should really consider.
I did one playthrough, it took me 120 hours to finish, I had a blast in exploring & finding things.  I intend on another.  Just 'cause I liked it though & felt it a fitting sequal to the original, it doesn't mean that I'm blind to the weaknesses of the game.  In most cases I hope what I wrote n the weakness column is considered & fixed for Wasteland 3, should the franchise continue.

This is, hands down, my favourite game ever.
Disclaimer: I'm a science nerd so I did have the advantage of having a good grasp of orbital mechanics before starting. The learning curve was still steep.
Luckily (or maybe skillfully), the game developers did an amazing job of several things: making the creation of a viable rocket intuitive, adding progression into the game so that your skills will always be challenged, and somehow having the game's mechanics handle how any combination of hundreds of different parts results in a flyable machine... mostly.
To illustrate the intuitiveness, my 6yo son loves building spaceships and does pretty well. But me, a 40 something year old scientist with nearly 600 hours of gameplay logged, will still stuff up... explosively.
It hits that sweet spot of being easy to learn and hard to master.
The game comes down to being all of the characters in the history of human spaceflight, Kerbalized. As Gene Kerman, you control the space programme, making management decisions about what facilities to upgrade and what contracts to accept. As Werner Von Kerman, you design and build the spacecraft. As Jebediah, you fly 'em.
Be careful. Some of those contracts are fiendishly difficult.
Now, this game is simplified insofar as you dan't have to worry about packing food or oxygen for your Kerbals. I have a theory about this - they're green, so I suspect they photosynthesize. If you want to add that realism... well, there are mods for that. In fact, there's a huge and thriving mod community out there.
KSP is about as realistic as possible given the processing limitations of desktop processors. The collaboration of actual rocket scientists from NASA probably helped. As such, I'd recommend this game to any teacher/professor of classical mechanics as a great way to teach orbital mechanics.
Now, after spending way too much time playing this game, I'm starting to wonder if "completed KSP Grand Tour" will look good on my application for a job at Rocket Labs.

An amazing tool for real-world flight training, WHEN MODDED. The base game itself is basically a bunch of dumbed down general aviation planes and airliners. Pretty much every plane in the base game has 2 steps to fly it. Throttle up, and take off. You don't even need to turn the engines on. So, the base game CANNOT be realisticly used as a simulator. HOWEVER, it's perfect for instrument practice. The ILS system in the game is pretty much spot on to the real deal, albeit still, a little dumbed down. But, the whole game is dumbed down, really. For example, to talk to ATC (Air Traffic Control) in real life, you look at the airport chart of the airport you are currently at, and find specific frequencies for the Ground Control and ATC Tower. Then, you input those frequencies into your radio, and switch the comms to make the new frequency your active frequency. You then pust the PTT (Push To Talk) button on your yoke, and state your intentions into your microphone to ATC. However, in FSX, you simply push a button that brings up all nearby frequencies that you choose from, and then choose your intentions. The ATC system in FSX is definitely outdated, but there are addons such as PRO ATC-X that tremendously improve the regular ATC. Now, good addons can get expensive. For example, I use the A2A Cessna 172 Skyhawk. It is an addon that costs $50. However, for that price, you are getting a professional level of simulation that is as close to a real Cessna 172 that you can possibly get on a home simulator. Everything, from physics, to instruments, to engine failures, radios, gps, (I could go on and on and on) are perfectly simulated. If you buy a yoke, throttle quadrant, and rudder pedals, than you can practice flying an actual Cessna indoors, as close as it gets to the real thing. I have many more A2A aircraft, and I highly reccomend them. Another type of addon aircraft is PMDG. They simulate Boeing arliners such as the 737, 747, and 777 very well. Once again, you can literally practice flying a real arliner from your home computer, something you can't even dream of doing in the base game. Although, learning how to fly a PMDG aircraft is very, very challenging and time-consuming, because it is essentialy an actual airliner. They are also expensive addons, but well worth it. The final type of addons are scenery addons, which improve the scenery of the game, and can make the game look photorealisic. They include SweetFX, REX 4, ORBX, and more. You can purchase the whole Earth to be modeled photorealistically or just a section, for obviously cheaper. You can also purchase specific, high quality airports to be added into your game, because the base ones just don't look very good (game came out in 2006). Anyway, I ranted for a while, and I wholeheartedly reccomend FSX. If you are just flying for fun and not on a pro level, or aren't a pilot in real life, then the base game is enough for you. However, if you are like me and fly aircraft in real life (I am a student pilot working to get my Private Pilot's License or PPL) and want a tool to help you practice at home, then addons are a must for FSX. One last thing, not all addons are payware. There are many, high-quality freeware aircraft, scenery, and tools available to download completely free, if you know were to look. Anyway, I hope I helped some of you out, and I reccomend you to get FSX. (also, my puny 42 hours on this game are only on the steam edition, I have the actual disc version with well over 500 hours in it.)

I'll make this quick:
1. Having to unlock advanced controls is a ridiculous design choice. You can unlock them by using the Konami code at the 'press A' screen (thanks to a guide in the community section), but still.
2. It feels slow and unresponsive. Considering this is supposed to be like the arcade NHL games, it honestly feels slower than the "simulation" ones. It's terrible when I'm trying to switch to a player closest to the puck, and the game decides to switch to two other players further away before finally getting me to the player I want.
3. The controls work in a weird way - when you are playing from the "upper" side of the rink, it's down, up on the right stick to do a slap shot, but playing from the "lower" side will result in you having to use up, down on the right stick. You end up messing up shots. However, it also seems that you can't properly aim shots either. It's a shoot and pray situation.
4. Resolution is capped to 1080p and framerate is capped to 60fps. I'm on 1440p and 144hz. The framerate I can deal with, but 1080p on 1440p looks bad, and will look even worse on 4k screens. The profile file is encrypted, so no manual editing available.
5. The commentary. The delivery isn't all that great, but what's worse is that you hear the same lines over and over again. Sometimes within a few minutes of each other.
6. The graphics. They could be so much better than this. Sure, indie team and all that, but the players look like they're out of the PS2 era. I get that they wanted the old school style of game, but that doesn't mean you should hinder the animations and player visuals.
In short, if you have a console, stick with NHL games. This has a bit of blood and is a bit more lax with the rules, but that's about it. Definitely far inferior to the NHL games in essentially every way. It's a shame, I was hoping for a fast paced violent hockey game with tight controls as an alternative to the NHL games.

Old Time Hockey is inspired both by classic NHL games like NHL ‘94, as well as hockey movies like Slapshot. The game brings back the glory days of the late 70’s, when helmets were optional (let’s be honest, no one wore them) and concussions were just excuses for wimps to get off the ice. With such inspiration, you might think that Old Time Hockey would be strictly arcade-like, with limited controls and game modes. Well, yes and no.
During a game you control all five skaters much like you would any hockey game, switching between whichever player will accomplish the task, whether that be hitting someone off the puck or ripping a slapper for the top shelf. The controls feel very comfortable, you can use the simple two-button approach or go for the advanced scheme. If you are familiar with the control scheme of EA’s NHL franchise, the advanced controls will feel right at home. Skating with the left thumbstick feels right, with the physics a little more on the heavy side and things like momentum and weight make an impact here, but you’re still able to skate accurately once you’ve had some experience.
The same story applies for shooting with the right stick, although it was a little hard to get used to in the two button scheme. In either case, you can aim your wristers and slappers, making it feel as if you are actually getting scoring chances instead of just pushing a button and pelting the goalie until the game decides you can score now. No matter which control scheme you choose, there is a slight delay between button press and action on screen. This will most likely lead to double pressing buttons or just mashing the button until your player does what you want him to, often times too late for that sick pass or sweet scoring opportunity. Because of this, it’s nearly impossible, as far as I can tell, to set up one-timers. Personally I would recommend playing with the advanced controls, since some new options open up to you on both the defensive and offensive side of the ice. Poke checks, dumping the puck, and protecting the puck all require you to use advanced controls, and you can bet a bag of pucks the opposition will be using these moves against you.
Speaking of opposition, let’s talk AI, starting with the opposing teams. Each team has a rating for offense, defense, and fighting, but as far as I can tell, these numbers don’t necissarily mean much out on the ice. When you play against the computer the other team will have no problem using poke checks, hooks and hits to get the puck from you, and the refs tend to fall on the side of “Let ‘em play!” but since this is the ‘70s era, it’s to be expected. It’s not odd to find only one or two penalties called per game, and some games will go by without even one! Just don’t lay the lumber on too much and you should be able to fend off the attempts for the puck.
As for your own team, I did notice a few things that I personally would have liked to see out of my team. Since you can’t control things like aggressiveness on the forecheck or your team breakout from your zone, you’re playing with your team as opposed to leading it. However, sometimes this means pulling a player out of position to pick up the puck in front of your net, frantically switching players until you get the one closest to the puck, player position be damned, or trying to set up a 2 on 1 only to have your teammate come to a dead stop at the blue line. It can be frustrating at times, but you’ll end up adapting your strategies and learn when you can and can’t pull certain plays off after logging enough time with Old Time Hockey. In fact, you will have to if you want to unlock the advanced controls. More on that in a moment.
It wouldn’t be a sports game without game modes, but if you’re looking for a general manager’s mode or even a season mode, the closest you’ll get is story mode. Story mode sees you playing as the epicly bad Schuylkill (skool-kill) Hinto Brews, the game’s version of the Chiefs, as you pull the team out of the dregs of amatuer hour in the Bush Hockey League. Starting with a cool zero stars in each of the three stats for overall team performance, it’s your job to turn the ship around and start winning and improving the team. However, you won’t do this by making trades or running practice drills, instead, you’ll play games in the scheduled season and learn how to play Old Time Hockey with mandatory tutorial objectives spread across mutiple games. So in your first game you might learn the basics of hitting and shooting, then three games down the road you’ll learn about dumping the puck and hip-checks.
Until you complete the entire tutorial, you will not have access to the full repitoire of moves in exhibition mode. Thankfully, as you unlock moves you will be allowed to use them in story mode, which is nice considering your rivals will be using moves against you that you might not be able employ at the time. It’s an odd choice considering many people who will be turned on to this game will already understand the basics of these skills and, like me I’m sure, will be frustrated that you cannot use them from the very first puck drop. Other than story and exhibition modes, there’s not much else to see or do in Old Time Hockey. As of yet online multiplayer is absent, the only multiplayer being local exhibition mode with up to four players.
The game looks and sounds unique, to put it nicely. Player models look about the quality of a Nintendo 64 game, albiet in HD. Jerseys are colorful though, and an outline effect over each player makes the action easily readible on screen. Fluid animation and a smooth 60 FPS also contribute to how clearly it’s all presented. The sound all works, skates cut the ice as you’d expect, shots ring off the crossbar, and players even yell at the refs, just like you’ll be doing when they don’t call a penalty! The music is licensed, and while I doubt you’ll be adding most of the songs to your playlist any time soon, there are a few that stand out. I’m just thanking the hockey gods that there doesn’t seem to be any generic, royalty-free stock music. You know what I’m talking about, the kind of stuff you hear on free mobile games. Old Time Hockey is presented in a package that actually conveys a sense of time (the 70’s) and gives you a bit more to bite off than “it’s a hockey game, press start to play hockey”.
When the final buzzer blares and the ice is cleared, Old Time Hockey is a good sports game, standing at the precipice of greatness and is extra special for those PC and Nintendo gamers, who’ve really got the high stick when it comes to hockey games on their favorite platform. It’s not without it’s faults, but with as much potential that exists here for future updates, such as adding features like a team creator, player creator, logo and jersey creator, online multiplayer, season mode, stuff like that, this game could really build a following, depending on how much support the game is given after release. It’s not beholden to the whims of the NHL or some large corporate entity that decides whether or not next year's iteration will be just another roster update. However, I can’t judge a game by what it could be, only by what it is today. The decision to lock the advanced controls is probably the biggest drawback I can think of right now.That said, Old Time Hockey is a good ol’ hockey game that bridges the gap between simulation and arcade sports title. It’s meant to be played for the fun of the game. I mean, it has a beer control mode so you can drink beer and play the game at the same time, for Gordie’s sake! If that’s not sports game innovation, I don’t know what is.

Finally a hockey game on PC!  Really fun game with lots of control options and love the stylized retro charm.  While it may not be for everyone, or 100% fulfill the want for real hockey on PC... it's well worth the purchase price.
Good :
- No NHL, No problem.  BHL brings fun smash mouth 70's hockey with great atmosphere.
- While maybe not for everyone, I really love the retro feel and art style.
- Multiple control options... two button, multiple button, dual stick (a loose version of the recent EA NHL titles).
- It's a new hockey game on PC!
Not So Good :
- Story Mode is very punishing to start, expect to lose your first few matches to the AI.  This is heavily because only very basic controls (wrist shot, pass, check) are provided to start.  As you progress through the story you unlock more controls (slap shot, hip check, poke check, etc).
- Only once you finish the Story Mode, can you play a season/career with any team of your choice.  Wish decision was up front.
- Animations could use some work... some very awkward moments.
- Some controls could be tightened up, such as slap shots and body checks.
Bad :
- No Online MP at this time, local only.
- Advanced (dual stick) Controls locked behind Story Mode progression... can't even try them in Exhibition until you unlock it in Story Mode.
I'd give it a 7/10.  Really hope the dev continues with future updates to address of a few of my concerns.  Overall happy with my purchase, even at full launch price ($15 CAD).  Look forward to having some friends over for some local multiplayer.

It's 5-on-5 arcade hockey, quick paced with short period lengths, big hits, and refs constantly looking the other way. It's good old arcade hockey gameplay wrapped up in a very unique 70s style. I love everything about the style with the small arenas, the soundtrack, the bluish ice, the sports cards you unlock, to just the art presented in the game in general.
The gameplay is a clunky, though. It all works, but it sadly isn't as responsive as you want it to be. There's noticeable delay you have to adjust to. It's not the hardest to learn, but it takes some time. The AI generally is fine, but I notice that they sometimes don't pursue the puck and it'll just sit there until you get it or your opponent wakes up from the nap your hit put him in. The goalies also never cover up the puck to stop play, they will always pass it away or behind/the side of the net. This is easy to predict, as well, so you can just keep regaining control of the puck pretty easily.
The only thing I dislike is that the advanced controls are locked for exhibition until reach a certain point in the story. Even in the story you only learn certain parts of the advanced controls and can't use other ones until you "learn" it later on. For example you can't do a slap shot until the game tells you that you can. Even if you looked up the controls and knew what to do, the game will not allow you to do it until you reach that point. It took about 3 hours or so for me to fully unlock the controls, that is way too long.
Overall, I find it quite fun and still do recommend it even with it's faults. I also will always support the effort to bring more sports gaming to PC.

10/10

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and
rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax to the game I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about the story, about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

This game is horrible. Do NOT buy it, even if it's on sale.
I was drawn in by the graphics and the genre (rouge-lite bullet-hell). So, I thought, this game cannot possibly be bad, given the forumla.
Unfortunately, I was wrong.
This game, other than the formula it follows, has almost no positive qualities. I am UNBELIEVABLY surprised by the fact that it is reviewed in such a positive light.
The variety of guns is lacking. You basically get fours types; guns that use bullets, energy, shells, and bolts (there are meelee type weapons too, like a screwdriver. How creative! Or, a wrench... wow! Double creative!).
The guns are all basically the same, except this particular gun shoots two bullets at a time instead of one, or this one shoots TWO bolts instead of one (mega creative!).
The difficulty is also quite high, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but sometimes you'll just be plopped down into a veritable warzone with little to no time to prepare, putting you at a HUGE disadvantage (which makes the game quite frustrating, especially when you consider two bullets can easily take more than half of your life, or just put an end to your run altogether).
The game also gives you the option to choose from different "mutants," with their own unique abilities. This sounds interesting, but some of the abilities are worthless. The "fish" character (one of the first available characters), for example, can "roll," but I never quite figured out what the purpose of this "ability" was. You don't become invulnerable, or anything; bullets and enemies still hit you. It was just kind of a "fun" way to move about the map.
Speaking of the map, the levels are all uninspired and boring.
If it is not part of your library already, just buy Enter the Gungon and play it instead. It is of the same genre, but excels at everything at which this game fails.
I've never tried to get a refund before, but it's going to be the first thing I do after writing this review.
TL;DR
This game is bad, bad, bad. Play Enter the Gungeon instead.

Well, I finally got off my♥♥♥♥♥and played Act 2, how long it took me should tell you how hyped I was after having to wait over a year.
While that fact shouldn't matter to those buying the full game now, you will no doubt notice some contrasts between the two halves. While the first half was quite easy, the second half is brutal at times. Pulling up a guide in the Steam overlay is at times REQUIRED due to how unintuitive the puzzles are sometimes. One such puzzle is almost literally a rorshach test, except its not open to interpretation. You have to get the correct interpretation, then give step by step directions in language that also sounds like it was pulled from a rorshach test. You COULD fiddle with it for an hour as you try to use just the right language, or, you could just look it up online because you ain't got time for that♥♥♥♥♥♥
Another such puzzle prevents you from so much as looking up the solution online, as you're forced to either gain clairvoyance or just guess at something for an hour.
Many noted that in Act 1, you could play either side of the story all the way through with roughly zero need to switch back and forth. Double Fine apparently saw this as a flaw to be corrected, because now you are forced to switch back and forth at times. No, you will not know when those times are. Yes, it is infuriating as you once again are required to have clairvoyance. Yes, you will just look it up on a guide.
Gameplay for the second Act can be summed up as "tedious". In any video game puzzle, completing it should make you feel smart. Like you did your work and gathered the clues, or you were able to follow a logical progression to the end, possibly even having some sort of epiphany. When completing the puzzles here, you just feel like you got lucky.
The story in the second half is still alright to good, but it does contain some moments where you'll think that the writers were "just pulling that out of their♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Aside from that, the ending is fairly unsatisfactory, with the feeling that there is a lot more that needs to be tied up. Normally that would have me hoping for a sequel, but we all know that Double Fine has never made a sequel. And after this, no one will ever give Tim Schafer money again for a project.
Speaking of money, let's get this out of the way. For a game with a 3.3 MILLION DOLLAR BUDGET, at no point do you feel the 3.3 million dollars and years of work that went into this. At its "best", the game only feels good. Nothing truly shines about this game. Yes the art is pretty, but its not 3.3 million pretty. Yes the music is nice, but none of it really wows you. The writing is good and has some twists, but it won't win any awards. The voice acting is good and they got some big names, but its
Actually, that might be the single aspect of this game that most reflects upon it as a whole. The voice acting is good, never bad exactly, but very few characters ever show strong emotions. Huge revelations are treated with minor surprise and then brushed off. Life changing events are also quickly brushed off. This is, hands down, my favourite game ever.
Disclaimer: I'm a science nerd so I did have the advantage of having a good grasp of orbital mechanics before starting. The learning curve was still steep.
Luckily (or maybe skillfully), the game developers did an amazing job of several things: making the creation of a viable rocket intuitive, adding progression into the game so that your skills will always be challenged, and somehow having the game's mechanics handle how any combination of hundreds of different parts results in a flyable machine... mostly.
To illustrate the intuitiveness, my 6yo son loves building spaceships and does pretty well. But me, a 40 something year old scientist with nearly 600 hours of gameplay logged, will still stuff up... explosively.
It hits that sweet spot of being easy to learn and hard to master.
The game comes down to being all of the characters in the history of human spaceflight, Kerbalized. As Gene Kerman, you control the space programme, making management decisions about what facilities to upgrade and what contracts to accept. As Werner Von Kerman, you design and build the spacecraft. As Jebediah, you fly 'em.
Be careful. Some of those contracts are fiendishly difficult.
Now, this game is simplified insofar as you dan't have to worry about packing food or oxygen for your Kerbals. I have a theory about this - they're green, so I suspect they photosynthesize. If you want to add that realism... well, there are mods for that. In fact, there's a huge and thriving mod community out there.
KSP is about as realistic as possible given the processing limitations of desktop processors. The collaboration of actual rocket scientists from NASA probably helped. As such, I'd recommend this game to any teacher/professor of classical mechanics as a great way to teach orbital mechanics.
Now, after spending way too much time playing this game, I'm starting to wonder if "completed KSP Grand Tour" will look good on my application for a job at Rocket Labs.

While I am marking this review as "Recommended", I want to say that it is NOT for every one.
I recommend this game for people that like slow paced games, strategic thinking and in-game physics, because that is all you will get. If you expect action, history, carrer mode, etc, this is not for you.
In this game your objective is to deviler wood logs from point A to point B. That's it. It may sound boring, but it is not. The challenge is choosing the right truck for the job, planning the best route and trying not to get stuck on mud. If you get stuck, you can use your truck's winch to pull itself out or bring another truck to help. If you flip your truck over, you can use a crane to collect the logs from the ground and repack your cargo to continue the journey.
There are currently 5 maps to choose from and 7 different trucks. In my opinion there should be more content for the price asked, but the DEVs are working on adding more content.
If you want to try how the game plays before buying it, there is a free Tech Demo available on the developer's website. I recommend doing that.

and now onto the review
Old Time Hockey is hockey game with a strong influence of NHL '94. It takes us back to the "good ol days" of Hockey where the rules were WAY more lax to say the least, and ruthlessness was encouraged as opposed to today's game.
-Gameplay-
Old Time Hockey has two game modes, Exhibition and Story Mode, unfortunately no online (as of now, I spoke with the devs and they told me if there was a ton of support for it, they would heavily look into it). Exhibition mode is a local multiplayer mode(for up to 4 players) with AI opponents included. We have 10 teams to choose all of which have very unique names, my personal favorite being the Long Island RumRunners. With a few different controller schemes, Classic. Two button mode. Beer mode (for one handed gameplay) and Advanced. Story Mode launches you into a failing franchise Hinto Brews, as you follow a classic from "last to champs" storyline. Afterwards you are rewarded with a "Career Mode" type of mode where you can play a full season with a team of your choosing.
-Graphics, Sound & Artstyle-
Old Time Hockey looks and sounds amazing. As soon as I started it up, I felt brought back to the days of my childhood as I blew on my SNES cartridge of NHL 94. The song "Old Time Hockey" along with the very retro soundtrack was just AMAZING to listen to.
-Price-
The retail price is 11.99 USD
-How many hours estimated?-
Honestly, I get lost in GREAT sports games like this. With inevitable DLC and hopefully WORKSHOP, I can see myself playing this game for HUNDREDS of hours.
-Buy it Now? Wait for Sale? Don't Buy?-
When I first a trailer to this game I was immediately sold, this was a much needed hockey game on Steam. One that delivered the retro mindless arcade feeling to it. I took a break from the NHL series and playing OTH made me feel so satisfied. There are some things I'd like to change about OTH, like the almost idiotic Defense AI, or the fact that you have to go through a vigorous tutorial on story mode, not having ADVANCED controls unlocked from the start. It has a heavy emphasis on hitting and sometimes it feels too easy to get some hits, but as told by Karthik, it's meant like that to give you the 70's Hockey feeling. The fights are a ton of fun too, although repetitive when doing line brawls but overall I've had tons of fun with the game. Will I recommend this game? HELL YES.

I was a bit scared when I picked up this title because of all the bad reviews it was receiving, stating that ORION: Dino Horde was one of the worst games ever made.
After I watched a rather hilarious german gameplay video, and the game was on sale for less than 2€, I finally decided to get this game.
First of all, we've got to set the record straight: ORION: Dino Horde IS NOT the same game as ORION: Dino Beatdown. This should be a no-brainer, but unfortunately many people will still post bad reviews mistaking the previous Dino Beatdown for Dino Horde.
Dino Horde is a mutiplayer action game in which you have to kill off waves of dinosaurs and defend buildings. Between those waves, you're able to upgrade your loadout and perks by spending money which is earned in a TD-like fashion by killing enemies. The general concept is rather simple as is the gameplay. When fighting on foot, the gameplay consists of rather monotonous gunplay. Because the dinosaurs are generally faster than the player, movement and celever positioning don't really play a role in fighting. The only real variation lies in the different enemy types of which some require different strategies to kill. The game also includes vehicles and vehicle combat, which is a pleasant relief.
The graphics are rather good considering this game is a low budget production, but the map design can be monotonous from time to time.
The strengths of the game lie within the co-op aspect and the frequently updated content. Since the launch of the title, the developers have included multiple new game modes, some of which deliver a rock-solid co-op experience, as well as other additional content.
This game isn't the next big multiplayer co-op shooter, but it definitely has it's moments and is generally enjoyable, especially when played with friends. The price of 13.99€ isn't worth the experience though. If this game goes on sale anytime soon, you might want to pick it up for some hours of multiplayer fun.

Crashlands is the most base game I've ever played, an impressive feat for an indie title. The best I can say is that it made me appreciate Minecraft more.
THE GAMEPLAY
Crashlands is split into 4 sections: building, crafting, gathering, and exploring. You won't be building that often since once you have a shack you realize that the walls and doors are just thick poles stuck into the ground at intervals and there's no way to make it look grand or amazing. You also won't explore, since if you beat the game you can name every naturally-occuring floor tile on your hands, and the map is an infinite flat plane with three biomes. You will not enjoy crafting either, since you know everything about the gear going in and I don't think that the Terraria-esque random buff feature has debuffs in the mix in this game, and the truly random element was a big reason why I tolerated it in Terraria. Gathering is the only fun part, since the enemies have very clever attack patterns adding a touch of bullet hell into the mix, but very few enemies have more than one attack.
THE STORY
The story in Crashlands is basic, but it gets the job done. Some people think that the game is bitter (you're pillaging a planet to make a phone call to your boss, after all), but I think it's just unfunny. The whole game has an air of unsuccesfully ripping off Behemoth (Alien Hominid, Castle Crashers, Battle Block Theater, Pit People) especially in terms of humor. The sawmill chase or volleyball game from Castle Crashers is strange and slightly immature, but the bit from Crashlands where you give a mother her son's remains is the joke you're imagining but now one of the actors is a generic giant fly.
THE EXECUTION
The controls in Crashlands are very strange, though they work. The arrow keys or mouse is how you move, while WASD + Q and E are hotkeys. You are expected to have your hand on the movement keys but not use them for move. It's strange, but functional. The artstyle is not such. Again, it looks like a half-complete Behemoth ripoff.
OVERALL
Don't play Crashlands. If you want the combat, play Dark Souls. If you want the exploration, play Minecraft. If you want the building, also play Minecraft. If you want the crafting, play Terraria.

I have just finished playing Alan Wake (I admit I was a bit late to the party!) and can honestly say it has the best story in any game I have played in the last 30 or so years of my gaming career. For me it is very rare for a story to actually engage me in a game, normally it is just something that serves as a narrative to explain why I am where I am doing something. Alan Wake is the first game I have played where the story was the star of the show and I played to the end to see the ending (good ending in a kind of "Wow, WTF!" sort of way).
I am not normally a fan of horror games, they normally bore me and/or stress me out, but Alan Wake was at my limit, it has some very creepy parts that made me have goosebumps, but nothing that made me jump out of my skin (one part tried, but failed).
My the only gripes I have with the game are some of the mechanics aren't as polished as other games (jumping is a bit of a lottery and the driving can be very frustrating), and the amount of combat that is liberally scattered throughout the game to pad it out. Personally I have to admit to using a dev mode cheat to give me loads of ammo so I could get through the combat with a lot less anguish and be able to savour the rest of the game.
Overall I would very much recommend this game, it is unique in having a story that would make a great movie or book, rather than the poor excuses for stories most games (and even a lot of movies) have.

I'm not a survival horror kind of guy. I'm not very much into action shooter types. However, I LOVE atmospheric adventure games, and hoped this would deliver on this front. It delivers on quite many fronts, and I found myself unexpectedly super invested in it, the story a page-turner in itself. I may not have been the best at it, and I may not have been particularly satisfied with the way it ended (both Episode 6 proper and the Special Features after), but the experience was well worth it.
This game pulls from pretty much every classic thriller it can think of, and doesn't pretend for a second that everything in it is completely original. Stephen King is name-dropped the second you boot it up, and if I had to sum the game up, it's basically more Stephen King than if Stephen King himself wrote this game. Author trapped in their own story, meta discussions about the nature of fiction and its influence on the real world, stuff attacking people that should not be able to do that... basically the only thing out of place is the town being in Washington and not Maine.
It's very good at creating a new and engaging world without distancing itself too much from reality. There are a few brand names present, mostly in places that make sense, only a few appearances by Verizon sticking out painfully towards the end. If anything, I more noticed when the batteries were suddenly off-brand in the Special Features, and the cars weren't recognizable makes and models. It works well for something in the style of a book / TV show, where these things would be present, and aren't forced like most games. I found myself stopping and listening to every TV and radio I could find, and the stories on Night Springs (an in-universe equivalent to Twilight Zone) made intriguing parallels to the main story.
The gameplay is strong enough to hold interest, and strikes a decent balance of giving you power, but not quite enough to face everything fearlessly. Enemies are shielded in darkness, and thus must have it burned away with a flashlight or other light source before you can attack them. Your flashlight serves as a targeting reticule for your gun, and the nature of your opponents leads to some creative variation from the standard weaponry. Revolvers and shotguns get the job done, of course, but you'll find yourself primarily hunting for flares and flashbangs that'll obliterate waves of Taken in a single blast. The Taken are pretty clever AI-wise, too, and you'll have to keep on your guard, because they WILL swarm around you. The camera often dramatically reveals them if no other warning was given, but not always. You can dodge with the sprint button, which doesn't seem to always work, but often can save your proverbial bacon, and you'll sometimes find it easier to give up on fighting and just run as fast as you can to the next light.
Long story short, 10/10, would risk my life for a coffee thermos again. But seriously, it's a pretty rad, very atmospheric game with some truly kickass moments. Good luck getting Children of the Elder God out of your head.

Alan Wake is an intriguing game with lots of interesting ideas and a compelling narrative. While the story is something that is sure to leave you thinking, the implementation may instead just leave you frustrated.
I was late to picking up this game. I finished it 5 years after its release and man…what a difference 5 years can make. Washed out colors and shoddy textures, lip syncing as bad as the PSX era and crazy amounts of clipping…but I had trouble leaving this game alone after I started playing it. Every time I would set the game down I would find myself speculating about the next twist and the impact of recent events/characters while I was away. The writing had me hooked, which was odd because often time the story would spoil itself through collectable items detailing events before they unfolded. This kind of mechanic sounds counterproductive, but it was used tastefully more often than not; giving you just a keyhole perspective into something yet to occur.
Tying directly into the narrative, the combat centers on an element of light vs darkness in the sometimes satisfying, sometimes intensifying use of a flashlight. Creatures of darkness (called “Taken”) cannot be hurt while in the dark, requiring the use of a flashlight in conjunction with all other weapons to defend yourself. This may or may not sound like a caveat in the combat, but it never felt cumbersome. Sure, it felt in the way while I was being rushed, but the flashlight never felt tacked on or pointless with such a strong tie in to the story…or perhaps it was just overshadowed by other elements of combat.
Combat, unfortunately, degrades and loses and real meaning about halfway through the second chapter of the game. Encounters and ambushes become textbook level predictable, there is very rarely a feeling of scarcity to supplies (flashbang galore!) and the game runs out of interesting ideas to keep combat as interesting as the story. In fact, the game seems to run so low on ideas halfway through the game that it introduces a new enemy type to mix it up: inanimate objects that levitate, jiggle then throw themselves at you. The points of the game that are heavy with jiggling inanimate objects are only slightly less woeful than the points in which Taken will ambush you and begin throwing random things at you from the forest.
At the end of the day, I greatly enjoyed Alan Wake (the story) but can’t help but feel like maybe I should have just watched a let’s play of it. The only mystery here deeper than the narrative here is why the developers thought a jiggling wheelbarrow made a good enemy, in terms of both gameplay and narrative.

Few people remember that the unfortunate X-Com spin-off, The Bureau, wasn't the franchise's first FPS; that honor belonged to Enforcer. Released in 2001, Enforcer was an even more ungainly fit to the franchise, being little more than an action-shooter that owed almost no similarity to the earlier titles of the series. But ignoring its unfortunate connections with the earlier games, the game was surprisingly fun.
Enforcer utilized the Unreal engine and - remembering this game is now 16 years old - quite good looking. It lacked any spectacular set-pieces -  featuring instead rather humdrum locations such as trailer parks and city streets - but provided a good amount of detail and variety. I particularly enjoyed the number of things - cars, propane tanks, signs, garbage cans, doors, windows - that I could blow up with my guns. Even more impressive was the sheer number of enemies available to kill. While most games of its day struggled with five or six enemies on-screen at once, Enforcer managed twenty to thirty at a time, and by the time I reached the end of a level I usually had slaughtered my way through four or five HUNDRED of the villains. In many ways, the game was more akin to modern "horde shooters" than the scripted adventures of its contemporaries. Similar to horde shooters, killing enemies earned you resources ("research points") with which to upgrade weapons and abilities. While this encouraged "grind", I didn't mind that much; the weapons were suitably overpowered and a well-placed shotgun blast could take out five or six enemies at a time. (The AI wasn't too deadly on its own, but their numbers could quickly whittle down my health if I wasn't careful).
The game's biggest flaw - aside from its XCom lineage - was that it was played in third-person, and it had lousy targeting and camera control. The latter was even more problematic when it came to the occasional jumping puzzle or navigating narrow ledges. It also was uneven in tone, never quite sure if it was an action-adventure, a horror game or a tongue-in-cheek poke at the whole UFO genre.
Still, as a quick pick-me-up shooter it was enjoyable, if simplistic, fun. I can recommend it to anyone under the caveat you ignore its unfortunate connection the other games of the franchise and go into it with the understanding this is a cheap shoot-em-up focused more on racking up huge kill-counts than offering sophisticated gameplay or world-building.

I bought this game during the Humble Winter Sale because I didn’t have the patience to wait for it to be bundled. I don’t regret buying it one bit - it was really well worth the money. For those of you who hate micromanagement in (A)RPGs and whatnot, Crashlands pretty much removes inventory management for you. Sometimes traveling in RPGs can be repetitive after you’ve seen all the scenery - in Crashlands, you discover these things called Telepads while exploring the region so you can teleport back to the telepads via the map when you want after you’ve explored the region - no repetitive walking! Also, this is weird for me to say, but I feel like Crashlands has the right amount of grind. Throughout much of the story, as long as you collect materials as you go and do a little bit of farming, you’ll be good to go - only near the very end of the game (and I do mean the very end) does it feel like a grind to get some materials. With a relatively recent update, the developers even made it so you could upgrade your gear to a higher rarity-level through the use of crystals (before, you had to rely on crafting RNG). Moreover, the side quests and main quests are interconnected exceptionally well. In Crashlands you can’t breeze through the main storyline without doing any side quests; more often than not, side quests provide important recipes you need for your main quests. Give or take 1-2 hours idle, it took be around 34 hours to finish the main storyline and side quests (with the exception of 2 side quests) at a laid-back pace. It took around 40 hours total to complete the reasonably-attainable achievements and the rest of the side quests. Overall, the game was really enticing. The other definitely had a sense of humor that appealed to me and it got rid of a lot of features that made RPGs tedious to play for me. The combat might have been one of the few downers for me. I’m just not a fan of the whole click-to-attack and move-to-avoid concept, just not my cup of tea. This is a unique game in that if you own this game across multiple devices, it allows for cloud saving via a BScotch account - it works pretty seamlessly. One of my few complaints was that the display settings when played on mac is glitchy; it’s not hard to fix, just toggle it a few times and click the green expand window on Mac to play in fullscreen again - but it’s just extremely annoying when you have to do it every time. I played on the game on normal mode, and it felt great to complete it - I probably won’t be going back and replaying the game in Challenge or Insane modes for the last few achievements, but if there are any major updates or if I just feel nostalgic…who knows ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
