I will list off the pros first before the cons of this game, Civilization 3 is a different twist of the game than you may be familar with 4 and 5. Go in understanding this switch:
-Its an old game, if you can run the actual game, there should be no real issues.
-Graphically, it's a sound experience and not many real issues, the modding community can find you bug fixes or new skins. Its pleasing regardless and you won't really be let down by this game.
-Combat is similar to Civ 4, simple dice combat where units have health bars going between 3-6, strength and defense stats play their parts and very simple to understand. There are Offensive Units, Defensive Units and Manovuer units, no exceptions and combat is based on these theorectical roles.
-31 Civs that each have 1 unique unit, unless mods are involved. Civ bonuses are general in that they have two traits which give them bonuses which are shared by others, Militaristic, Religious, Industrists, etc.
-Diplomacy is sound and reliable, techs can be traded directly as well as maps, I will faults soon
-Happiness is based per city, with simple factors involved including conscription
-Civfanatics Community and its modding community are lovely and its still alive and well, just no Workshop
The Cons:
-Civ 5 has a prediction based combat, units do no die with one attack on even matches. Not the case for this game, they fight till they die unless they are manovuer units against inf. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t can and will happen, don't cry.
-The AI Diplomacy is very defensive and almost always cautious, wary or spiteful towards you, no exceptions.
-Its really easy to find yourself fighting half the world because of one war, tech trading is enabled so you can find yourself backwater as they maintain amiable relations and trade those tech with one another while they fight you.
-Multiplayer is old, the members are not exactly nub-friendly, I myself was 3 years old when this game came out.
-Game doesn't work for you, you're ♥♥♥♥ed, not much anyone can do for you.
-In my opinion, the hardest Civilization I have every played, it will humble you many times over.
In the end it is a Civ-game, you can't really go wrong with trying. It is the game that personally got me into Civilization and its unique-ness will likely find you some memorable gameplay. This game is a flawed masterpiece.  The first two-thirds of the game are excellent, ranking up there with the original Baldur's Gate and the Icewind Dale games.  For me the threads started to unravel quickly during the last third of the game.  Numerous quests such as stopping an underground slave trade are introduced and then dropped without a clear resolution.    Playing the game through twice, I still can't tell if these latter quests are broken or if I simply screwed them up; there is no clear feedback from the game's denizens, which is different from the first half of the game where everyone is saying "Yea!  You're my hero!" or "F$%k you!  Our lives are ruined now!"  If you've played Vampire: the Masquerade - Bloodlines or Neverwinter Nights 2 or Knights of the Old Republic II, you've seen these kinds of problems before.  Content seems to be cut in order to meet a release date, and the overall quality of the game suffers for it.
On the plus side, the combat is excellent and the skill system is the best one I've seen since Deus Ex.  I think this skill system should become a standard for any game developer that wants to balance combat with stealth and diplomacy.  The game is also not short; I would estimate it takes 40 to 50 hours to play through every significant section.
In conclusion, this is not as good as Dragon Age: Origins or Baldur's Gate II, still the gold standard by any measure, but it measures up pretty well to some of Obsidian's early games such as Knights of the Old Republic II and Neverwinter Nights II.  Flawed but fun.

Like your average Choose Your Own Adventure, your choices affect the outcome of the story. Like most recreation of the Choose Your Own adventure in gaming, your choices are frequently on rails and have minimal overall impact to the total plot. (Whether you choose A or B, C will still happen. But, your A/B choice will result in D or E variation on the outcome of the unavoidable C event.) This may cause some feel a loss of overall control (especially with replays) but the illusion of choice (especially for a first playthrough) gives you a powerful sense of agency.
And, because many things in these kinds of games are set behind choices you make about where to go and what order to do things (and subsequent time spent engaged in dialog with other characters in the story)-- Life is Strange can end up feeling like a movie or serial miniseries-- and take about as long as a serial miniseries (if not longer). So it ends up being well worth the cost of entry.
The themes in Life is Strange resonate with my childhood. Isolation. Discovery. Tragedy. (Yea, my life wasn't rosey, but you don't really want to hear about that.) These themes are masterfully mixed with the fantastic.

General - 8.0
Sid Meier's Civilization is one of the greatest game franchises ever, it's a landmark for every turn-based strategy game. The name itself tells what the game is about, you pick one civilization, select a location to start, select CPU controlled civilizations and settings for that specific map. Your job is to make your civilization meet any of the victory conditions, which can be through science, military, culture, diplomacy, points, etc. The first game of the series I played was Civ II, back in 2001, which instantly made me a fan since then. However I skipped Civ III at its time, and that is what made me buy it many years later. I paid around 1USD for the game just to see what I missed, and unfortunately, not much. Don't get me wrong, it's a great game, but if you played Civ IV, in my opinion, there is nothing in Civ III that will be better than in the later game. It's only worth playing for saudosism purposes. It's heavily outdated.
Content - 8.5
Steam version is a complete version, which includes both expansion packs released. You have a vast number of civilizations to pick and you can adjust some major settings for a location, like temperature, umidity, geological era, water level, etc. You can also chose the victory conditions for a game, which you can fit into your play style, along with difficulty level. The Civilopedia is a tool of great educational value, it contains real data about the civilizations, technologies, unities and almost everything you can find in the game. There is a highest scores table too, but I believe it only displays single-player scores. I don't know if steam is providing some sort of multiplayer support at this time.
Gameplay - 4.0
Like most Civ games, you start with a settler, a worker and/or a warrior in most cases, from this you have to build your city and administer it's growth with the resources gathered around it, which can be selected in the city radius. Each unity you create in a city has a better use, and through the years (turns), as long as your cities and citizens are productive you'll eventually discover technologies which improve your unities and your cities buildings. You can focus your whole civilization in a few aspects or diversify your knowledge. Every civilization on the map have it's own personality and choices, from warmongers to pacifists. What you have to do is to secure your civilization a place in history. But why I give 4.0? It won't help you get started at all. I'm not asking for a strategy guide, I just wanna learn the basics of the game, what's unique to it, what options I have and what they do. I couldn't find a tutorial or at least a checkbox to display tooltips, even the options in the main menu don't have a basic description. It's one of the less intuitive game I've ever seen, unlike it's predecessor ou sucessor. Of course after sometime you'll start to get used to the controls, but they still feel weird. The UI is not friendly even for games older than it is, Age of Empires II is older and has a much more friendly interface and controls.
Graphics - 2.5
The game looks very bad even for its generation, Age of Wonders and Medieval Total War had much better visual quality. Civilization III looks so bad that if affects gameplay, you need to often take a closer look to identify some terrains and unities. There are no options for good graphic enhancements, you can not adjust resolution, it's based on desktop resolution, and even tweaking can't get satisfactory results. I know it's an old game, but the ones I cited are old too and are from the same genre. At least the game showed an improvement compared to the previous title, texture quality is better and there are movement animations for the unities.
Overall - 5.8

I'm not a survival horror kind of guy. I'm not very much into action shooter types. However, I LOVE atmospheric adventure games, and hoped this would deliver on this front. It delivers on quite many fronts, and I found myself unexpectedly super invested in it, the story a page-turner in itself. I may not have been the best at it, and I may not have been particularly satisfied with the way it ended (both Episode 6 proper and the Special Features after), but the experience was well worth it.
This game pulls from pretty much every classic thriller it can think of, and doesn't pretend for a second that everything in it is completely original. Stephen King is name-dropped the second you boot it up, and if I had to sum the game up, it's basically more Stephen King than if Stephen King himself wrote this game. Author trapped in their own story, meta discussions about the nature of fiction and its influence on the real world, stuff attacking people that should not be able to do that... basically the only thing out of place is the town being in Washington and not Maine.
It's very good at creating a new and engaging world without distancing itself too much from reality. There are a few brand names present, mostly in places that make sense, only a few appearances by Verizon sticking out painfully towards the end. If anything, I more noticed when the batteries were suddenly off-brand in the Special Features, and the cars weren't recognizable makes and models. It works well for something in the style of a book / TV show, where these things would be present, and aren't forced like most games. I found myself stopping and listening to every TV and radio I could find, and the stories on Night Springs (an in-universe equivalent to Twilight Zone) made intriguing parallels to the main story.
The gameplay is strong enough to hold interest, and strikes a decent balance of giving you power, but not quite enough to face everything fearlessly. Enemies are shielded in darkness, and thus must have it burned away with a flashlight or other light source before you can attack them. Your flashlight serves as a targeting reticule for your gun, and the nature of your opponents leads to some creative variation from the standard weaponry. Revolvers and shotguns get the job done, of course, but you'll find yourself primarily hunting for flares and flashbangs that'll obliterate waves of Taken in a single blast. The Taken are pretty clever AI-wise, too, and you'll have to keep on your guard, because they WILL swarm around you. The camera often dramatically reveals them if no other warning was given, but not always. You can dodge with the sprint button, which doesn't seem to always work, but often can save your proverbial bacon, and you'll sometimes find it easier to give up on fighting and just run as fast as you can to the next light.
Long story short, 10/10, would risk my life for a coffee thermos again. But seriously, it's a pretty rad, very atmospheric game with some truly kickass moments. Good luck getting Children of the Elder God out of your head.

This is the closest thing to Fallout 1 and 2 you can get today. On the pro side it has that perfect signature blend of dry Fallout-grade humor, atmospheric locations and a healthy pinch of postapocalyptic madness. Some NPCs and factions are just awesome (MAD monks surely the best), your own team sometimes makes epic remarks about locations you are on, and the thousands of small details scattered around make it a living, breathing world. Another hallmark feature of Fallout, its famed non-linearity, is implemented in nearly every single quest here, though as a Ranger you don't get a chance to become a really bad guy. Your actions really matter, and your inaction matters too, sometimes. And if you read lots of bad press concerning its flawed, bug-ridden state during the release, fear no more: there are a few minor bugs left for sure, but none of them will ruin your play, the developers did a great job of patching the game.
But there's a contra side. Combat sucks. It sucks like hell. In 2014 one would expect at least some degree of tactical thinking on the side of AI enemies. Come on, guys, Jagged Alliance - even the first one! - did a better job of maneuvering twenty years ago. And even a scripted ambush is better than no ambush. Mowing down rushing mobs gets old as soon as you develop some reasonable firepower and deal with initial ammo shortages, i.e. on your second day.
And there's the balance problem at last. At some point in the game you simply stop getting better firepower and armor because there are no bigger enemies to kill. I realize that this issue was caused by the need to let everyone finish the story, but there are many reasonable ways to solve this particular problem, starting with adaptable level of enemies. Instead the game chooses to punish meticulous players - basically its core audience - with arrested development and infinite boredom during its last chapters.
In the end I believe this game deserves to be played and enjoyed once. Just once, though. These days you don't get anything better anyway.

Alan Wake is an intriguing game with lots of interesting ideas and a compelling narrative. While the story is something that is sure to leave you thinking, the implementation may instead just leave you frustrated.
I was late to picking up this game. I finished it 5 years after its release and man…what a difference 5 years can make. Washed out colors and shoddy textures, lip syncing as bad as the PSX era and crazy amounts of clipping…but I had trouble leaving this game alone after I started playing it. Every time I would set the game down I would find myself speculating about the next twist and the impact of recent events/characters while I was away. The writing had me hooked, which was odd because often time the story would spoil itself through collectable items detailing events before they unfolded. This kind of mechanic sounds counterproductive, but it was used tastefully more often than not; giving you just a keyhole perspective into something yet to occur.
Tying directly into the narrative, the combat centers on an element of light vs darkness in the sometimes satisfying, sometimes intensifying use of a flashlight. Creatures of darkness (called “Taken”) cannot be hurt while in the dark, requiring the use of a flashlight in conjunction with all other weapons to defend yourself. This may or may not sound like a caveat in the combat, but it never felt cumbersome. Sure, it felt in the way while I was being rushed, but the flashlight never felt tacked on or pointless with such a strong tie in to the story…or perhaps it was just overshadowed by other elements of combat.
Combat, unfortunately, degrades and loses and real meaning about halfway through the second chapter of the game. Encounters and ambushes become textbook level predictable, there is very rarely a feeling of scarcity to supplies (flashbang galore!) and the game runs out of interesting ideas to keep combat as interesting as the story. In fact, the game seems to run so low on ideas halfway through the game that it introduces a new enemy type to mix it up: inanimate objects that levitate, jiggle then throw themselves at you. The points of the game that are heavy with jiggling inanimate objects are only slightly less woeful than the points in which Taken will ambush you and begin throwing random things at you from the forest.
At the end of the day, I greatly enjoyed Alan Wake (the story) but can’t help but feel like maybe I should have just watched a let’s play of it. The only mystery here deeper than the narrative here is why the developers thought a jiggling wheelbarrow made a good enemy, in terms of both gameplay and narrative.

Pros: Gameplay is fun and addictive. I died, on average, once every 53 seconds I played this game, but the checkpoints are fair and restarts are quick. Most deaths were my own fault, either through poor planning or slips of the finger navigating with the WASD keys. Interesting storyline helps justify game's gruesome subject matter. Soundtrack is spectacular. 80s neon pixel art design was great. Mask perks were fun. Weapon variety was enjoyable.
Cons: Grading system and point accumulation seemed arbitrary, which locks away different masks that could be useful. Did not see a guide explaining what scores to hit on which levels to unlock different masks. Occasionally encountered bug that allowed bad guys to share same space as me, so would waste entire clip trying to shoot threat that was impervious to my bullets. Also the Spacebar "ground kill" move was super inconsistent about when it wanted to work, and the kill animation was very long, which exposes you to needless risk using it. Often better to let the guy stand back up and stab him then. Most levels were constructed so your repeated deaths could teach you the layout and improve your next attempt, but some levels, especially the "Boss" levels, included insta-kill events that happened so quickly it was near impossible to discern a better way to approach the level in next attempt. Usually ended up having to consult youtube. The Boss levels were particularly frustrating because the checkpoints forced you to rewatch the cutscene every time. So it'd be 25 seconds of frantic clicking to bypass the dialogue, followed by ~3 seconds of gameplay trying to find a way around the insta-kill attack, only to start back at the beginning of the cutscene.
Note: I had to play the Original version. The game includes an updated version but I could not get it to open past the load screen. Maybe the new version fixes some of the bugs/frustrations I encountered.

First off I would like to congratulate the guys at Oovee for a great launch.  Unlike some big name developers both the single player and multiplayer worked nearly flawlessly at launch.  While Spintires is not perfect it is nonetheless an awesome and very enjoyable game.  I say game because the game mechanics turn this into more of a puzzle game with truck and mud skins than a simulator.  More on that in a sec.
This is truly a sandbox (mud pit) environment.  You are presented with a few vague goals to deliver logs to one or more objectives.  While this is the obvious objective the game often creates more objectives of its own.  You can choose to just deliver the logs (no easy task I might add) or make up your own objectives.
Those that complain that there is not enough variety are playing the game wrong.  If you keep rescuing your vehicle to the garage you miss some of the most enjoyable missions / puzzles the game has to offer.
The graphics, environment, deformable terrain are fantastic.  Pavel has done an amazing job creating a fantastic environment in which to experiment.
Mission types.
Exploration. Can be varied by forcing yourself to use a particular vehicle.
Expansion.  Activating new garages.
Rescue. Seems I have spent nearly half the game rescuing an overturned or swamped vehicle.
Repair and Refuel.
Race. Against other players or against the clock.
The game can be frustrating in many ways.  It took me a day or so to figure out how to activate other garages.  It took even longer to figure out the crane controls.  These are not very well documented in the manual.  Of course this is made even more infuriating in that key customization / mapping is very poor.  The crane controls should not share keys with the vehicle control keys.
Here are some issues that added to the entertainment (frustration).
The winch is unrealistically powerful.
There is no way a simple winch is going to pull a fully loaded logging truck up a steep incline through the mud.  It is also impossible for a winch to right a fully loaded tractor trailer laying on its side down a 45 degree slope.  Tone down the winch.  Unless the pulling vehicle is fitted with spade anchors a lighter vehicle will not be able to pull a heaver vehicle.  The lighter vehicle will pull itself to the load.  That does happen in game but the pull strength is still too much.  I would suggest the addition of a wrecker module that can be mounted on the truck chassis; a module that includes spade anchors, an adjustable boom and a high pull strength winch.
Winch points.
The winch points in game are not always realistic. Can’t winch to stumps but can winch to fallen trees, sometimes saplings.  Kind of funny to pull a huge mastodon loaded with logs by winching to a small fallen tree.  Winch points should be on stumps and the fallen trees should be movable.  Been a few times I’ve gotten the trailer trapped on one of these fallen sapling and had to dump load  and lift the trailer over the sapling with the crane.  I don’t know if the engine can support it but it would be nice if trees had a load limit at which point the tree would snap.
Logs can’t be winched.
Seems obvious.  Having worked around the logging industry this is a common practice.  Smaller vehicles can winch logs through dense areas to clearing for loading on larger trucks.  Also logs are often winched up from inaccessible areas to a loading position.  This also adds additional mission types where logs have to be pulled to a collection area.  Also the logs can be used to form obstacles that need to be cleared.
Enough with the mud.
Yes the mud provides a formidable obstacle but I feel it is overused.  Steep inclines, sand, rocks, logs, ditches, and abandoned vehicles are also suitable obstacles that are under utilised or not present at all.
Damage model is off.
I can double roll my vehicle down a steep rocky incline and receive less than 100 points of damage.  Yet if I put any speed down a dirt track I can accumulate 300+ points from just a few bumps in the road.  Come on these are off road trucks.  I can see receiving damage from large bumps and hitting rocks at high speed.  Surly rolling a vehicle more than 360 degrees should do more damage than a few dirt bumps.
Logs have no collision modeling.
When loading the logs in a wooded area I discovered that I could swing the logs through the trees like they were not there.  This made loading easier but not very effective as a simulation.
Fuel is a bit contrived.
I get that the fuel adds an additional mechanic to the game but since the maps are so small at 1km/1km I find it impossible to believe any of the vehicles can’t get across the map without needing fuelling.  This is another example of the puzzle mechanic at play.
Map is too small.
I can not understand why the game is limited to one square kilometre.  I like the map exploration portion of the game.  Unfortunately the area is so small and the cloaking points so few exploration is a short objective.  I would like to see 10km / 10km maps!  Also make the cloaking points smaller and drop the black tornado looking thing.  If the map were bigger the fuel issue above would not be as obvious.
The Camera.
By far my biggest frustration.  While I’ve become comfortable with the camera setup for driving in most cases, for loading logs manually the camera is impossible.  Enough has been already said of the camera by other.  I will wait and see what the next patch brings.
Key mapping.
I have a whole keyboard.  Every function should be assignable to a key. Start engine, and crane controls should have their own completely mapable controls.
Additional feature I would like to see.
Larger maps 10km / 10km.
Key mapping for all controls.
The aforementioned wrecker attachment.
Road repair and bridge building.  I would like to see the addition of concrete and steal culverts / pipes and gravel building material.  Dump truck, dozer and loader.  Maybe a flatbed trailer to carry the dozer.  I can see a goal where before the logs can reach the objective a road has to be repaired, a bridge constructed and perhaps a fresh cut made in a hillside to cerate a safe path for the logging trucks. I don’t want to see a full up road building sim.  Just enough to simulate the effort sometimes required to get the logs and then get them to the objective.  This engine is suppos to support deformable terrain so why not add the additional deformation objectives.  I`m sure Pavel can great an amazing mechanic to simulate the effect of rocks and gravel dumed in flowing water.

I remember Bethesda's announcement for Fallout Shelter, it was originally meant for mobile, and it worked perfectly.
On PC? I'm definitely enjoying it, but there are some cons, as well as pros
Pro's:
- Off the bat, it's fun, there seems to be a lot less waiting around than when I played on mobile.
- For what it is, it's graphically pleasing, each room has it's own feel to it, and you can upgrade and merge the rooms, and they change their look. It's had the thought put in and it's aethetically pleasing.
- I never experienced quests on mobile... I feel there is more content being added, or has been added since I last played the game.
- It's fairly addictive, and there's lots to do. It's obviously not the perfect game for PC, but it does still work.
Con's:
- It feels like a mobile port, lots of the dragging, either through your menu's or vault, it's very jumpy and it feels like it would work better with a touch screen (which mobiles obviously have these days)
- Local saving is a let down, you've probably read it already, but it makes micro transactions a bit of a waste, as they're solely on that save and only that one, along with your vault.
- Feels in leagues with like 'Clicker Heroes', it's definitely more of a background game, you don't sit there and play for hours, you have it open in the background and come to it every now and then. (Maybe not a con, but not a pro either)
All in all though, I'm enjoying it, it's fun, addictive, 8/10

The game is designed around fast paced twitch gameplay with mostly melee and weak aliens vs marines with guns. However the resource system is designed around being really slow and punishing you for deaths by forcing you to play as a skulk for 90% of the game while you're learning.
The game is abysmally unoptimized, so unoptimized that its not even funny, loading times are seriously minutes long, not even kidding. I actually have to turn settings down to run a bot server with the default amount of bots, and I bet you're saying "OH well you should get a better computer!" the truth is I can't, there is exactly one better processor and more powerful graphics cards do not exist outside of tri or quad sli setups.
The commander job is fantastic on paper, really innovative! Ingame it is a *expletive removed* that overshadows the rest of the entire game. The problem with NS2 is that you are entirely dependant on your commander, and your commander is entirely dependent on you. In theory this is fine, in practice it makes learning the game a *expletive removed* *expletive removed* *expletive removed* pile of zit puss.
Because the commander doesn't have much agency on their own, so nobody wants to play the commander for long, its a job that is nessasary but not engaging enough to be something that enough people actually want to specilize in to keep the game going. Its a core mechanic of the game and its frankly a janitor job, and only "strategy" in a broad sense, in a more specific and accurate sense its herding randoms on the internet around.
Think about that for a moment, think about how many random people on the internet are willing to follow orders, and how many of them you would trust to give orders. Now narrow that list down to people who bought this game, are willing to sit in the commander chair, and are willing to attempt the massive learning curve for the alien side of things. Now throw in a team of toxic people who can grow impatient with a bad commander.
Thats what I think is the biggest problem with natural selection since the player and commander are entirely codependent you need a good team to make things work and there is very little that you can do to help out a bad team. This could have been avoided by giving the commander something fun to do, like traditional ai controled soldiers to bring in more rts elements, or the ability to zoom out and see any decent portion of the map. Or something, anything to make the commander more interesting and easier to play in the face of their own incompetence or the incompotence of their team.
As it stands your enjoyment of this game will depend entirely upon your tolerance for other players and your willingness to get stomped into the ground for an entire round anytime you have a subpar team.
This is not even an X-COM game.

SPINTIRES is one of the best driving games I have ever played, and that is saying a lot because it beats out some of that in Forza and Need for Speed. While not part of the same type of game, where Spintires is a offroad games and the latter are Racing games, I still consider it a driving game. That aside, even with my computer not having a dedicated graphics card, the game still runs at about 40 FPS on my computer at medium graphics, and the game still looks great. The best thing about this game, though, is the physics. Your truck can sink into the mud, get washed away by raging water, and the trucks do not weigh too much or feel like they have too much power. Also, the sounds just add to the game in such a good way, because it sounds as I actually am driving a truck through the backroads of eastern Europe. This is one of the best driving games I have played, and also one of the best games I have played ever.

Overall, this game is very fun to play. There are many servers running at all times and finding one with players is no hassle. Warmode combines the mechanics of CSGO and CoD very well. While it has the kill-for-money system like CSGO, it also has fast paced action and relatively low recoil like the CoD franchise. There is only one game mode which is a team deathmatch to 150 kills.
The amount of content in this game is surprising. There are lots of maps and familiar weapons like the AK, M4, MP7 and the AWP make an appearance, and it is all included in the initial 250-ish MB download. Loading times are very fast, even for an extremely outdated rig. If you want more frames per second, go to the video tab in the options menu and play around with the settings a little bit.
Coming to the gameplay, you get $2000 at the start of the match along with a knife and a G17. Each kill adds $300 to your balance. I would recommend you to save money and play with the G17 for a while and then buy an AK47 or an AsVAL. They're definitely worth the wait. Also, try to run with your knife out as it increases your speed.
I would highly recommend this to anyone looking to have a lot of fun without spending any $$$.

A great roguelike game. Quick, fast, responsive, it feels much more satisfying than the Binding of Isaac (for me personally). It's bullet hell, but you will often find yourself in a trance-like state, no time to think, just dodging and shooting. Great soundtrack and sound effects. Unique and cool weapons, nice assortment of perks. A small amount of bugs, and unfortunately the game does not seem to be getting any new patches or updates. Secret areas and unlockable characters. There is more to this game than meets the eye. Looping allows you to loop back through a harder version of the game with more characters and new bosses.
This game is difficult, but it is immensely satisfying and for that reason gets an 8.5/10.

This game suffers from a lot of problems mainly being that this is a combat based comedy story game with jokes that really aren't all that funny and a combat system that feels extremely clumsy. You cant move with wasd by default but you can enable wasd movement in the menu, there is no keybind list or for that matter a list of all controls in the menu. The only way to attack something is by clicking it at which point your character walks towards it until in range and attacks but if you walk away with wasd for like .5 seconds then you lose target and this leads to a clumsy balancing act of clicking on what you want to kill and trying to walk around. The enemies aren't even hard and most of them have the same attacks but the combat is tedious especially on harder difficulties and the enemy will often hit you for around 4x your hp fighting things you're supposed to so youe health doesn't even matter and you have to hit them like 20+ times so you can either just run around in circles forever or risk getting 1 shot by going for 2-3 hits instead of one. There are also hitbox problems on many of the attacks where you will be out of the enemy's attack box which it displayed on the ground and they still hit you.
I can't recommend this game in it's current state but if they added the ability to set custom controls and also be able to freely attack then it might be ok but still not great.

To say that I was skeptical about playing this game would be an understatement. I've avoided it ever since it came out, despite its popularity. I was pretty much convinced that the game revolved around teenage drama with a bit of a twist, and truth be told, that didn't really speak to me. I know, I know - don't judge a book by its cover, right?
Alright, about the game. You could definitely describe the game in a way that I did at the beginning - in its core Life is Strange IS a teenage drama with a twist, but in a good way. There's not a lot you can say about it without spoiling too much, so I'll try to keep it short.
It's a story-driven adventure game, much like the Telltale library of games. Most of the gameplay (if you can even call it that) revolves around dialogue, walking around and collecting clues. What adds a little bit of diversity to all of this, is that you have the ability to reverse time. This is obviously situational, you cannot just reverse the whole game, but it definitely adds a bit more structure to how it plays.
But it's not the gameplay that matters in a game like this - it's the story, the characters and the urge to solve whatever mystery there is behind all of that. In the end, Life is Strange went from a game that I stayed away from, to something that's gonna stay in my memory as one of the best stories I've ever experienced, and rightfully so. When it finally finished, I was speechless and with no shame I can admit that I was holding back tears.
So if for some reason you are as skeptical as me about trying this one out - don't be. Give it a try. I can't promise that you won't be disappointed, but there's a chance that you might get the same thing out of it as I did, and that is a good enough reason to give it a shot.
Only one question remains: Did I beat the game, or did the game beat me?

What an amazing journey it's been, exploring the world of Wasteland 2. I bought into early access for the game due to how promising it looked during the kickstarter fundraising, and I was not disappointed when the game delivered on nearly every point it set out to do. You throw in a bit of imagination throughout the game, and you're immersed in a world that feels incredibly reactive to the player, and completely welcoming of choice.
The characters I made were each custom tailored to their respective roles, given custom portraits, backstories, and eventually came to have little moments which had me growing rather attached to them. Firefights took a twist when I pictured battles in more gruesome detail than was shown ingame, and really helped make my characters that much more exciting to play with. The combat mechanics are fairly well polished and offer a satisfying turn based combat system with different aspects which you can use to influence how a battle goes, and there's a multitude of systems that are incorporated into it. The world design was well enough that I knew what was going on, but also simple enough that through reading the flavour text descriptions of everything around me - it came alive.
Everything I did in the game seemed like it had alternatives that would be just as if not more successful than my choices, and world navigation whether through conversation or skill usage was so damn versatile I was consistently impressed. Break a lock when trying to pick it? It's a good thing you've got a mechanic on your team to fix that for a second attempt. Break it again? Try brute force on your bruiser and see if they can smash it open. Fail a third time? Looks like those sticks of dynamite you were carting around will come in handy all of a sudden - let's hope the loot is worth a valuable commodity! Have you been speaking with an NPC and find a particular speech check has come up? It's a good thing you've got a party member who just so happens to have a way to influence them in a special way. Are you lacking in that aspect, or not proficient enough in the one you need? You've got plenty of other ways to go about finding your way through the world, it just might take a bit of searching. A good deal of challenge was offered at varying intervals throughout the game, and it felt quite fair on normal difficulty - save for a couple fights which really ramped up the difficulty suddenly. A well rounded team and proper use of what is at your disposal will allow for you to pull through however, and you'll feel good in the end.
Sound design felt like it had some nice character to it, and the soundtrack to the game ended up being stuck in my head for days when I wasn't playing, making me wish I was back with my Rangers and roaming the wastes. Graphically, well, this was probably where the game lacks the most in its current state - and likely to be a good candidate for improvement. While I appreciate the fact things were kept a bit more on the simplistic side so that my imagination could take over, there were times where certain areas looked a little cheap and hokey, effectively breaking immersion. More options for character customization would always be a plus too.
All in all, I spent over 70 hours for a single playthrough of this game, and I enjoyed every second of it. Coming from somebody who's about as jaded as they come with modern video games, this is an impressive feat and I give my praise to the team for doing such an amazing job. This has to be one of the best cRPG titles I've played in a long time, and one which I've been highly recommending to friends. Can't wait to see what's in store for us next, whether with updates or DLC for this game, or a third game some time down the road!

Wasteland 2, by inXile Entertainment, puts you in the shoes of a group of trainees trying to prove their worth to an organization called the Desert Rangers. You see this group is about the closest thing you have to a police/military force that is out of Arizona and is willing to try to help all of those who are in need of help. The thing is there's a little something extra that is going on, that you are going to be thrusted into, and if you have the right people in your party, and you make the right decisions, you might be able to figure out what the hell is going on.
Graphically this game reminds me a lot of Baldur's Gate, except in a post-apocalyptic, highly radioactive, world. That's not to say that the graphics look dated, its just that the feel, the look, and the camera angle reminds me of BG. Now let me talk about the camera real quick, before I forget. I fought many a battle with the camera when it came to trying to keep the camera centered on my characters when in combat where the terrain was uneven. This was by far the most frustrating thing about this game.
Now lets get back to the graphics of the game, I did like the personalized photos of the characters that you interacted with, throughout the game, I just wish that it carried over, EVEN A LITTLE BIT, to the character models that you interacted with. The thing is that the majority of the character models where the same for specific type of gender in a specific area, so I understand the need to personalize them with the conversation system, but it constantly made me double take on who I was actually having a conversation with. Speaking of conversation system, I did really like the way it worked. Not only were you able to click on a selection, but you could also type it in. Now there were a couple of cases where when give the conversation prompt you HAD TO type in an answer, and that to me actually made me feel good about paying attention to what might have been a nonsense conversation that I had.
Now lets get into the voice acting, or mismatch of voice acting. This of course is one of my biggest pet peeves, if you are going to voice a character, voice them all the way. Don't half♥♥♥♥♥it and have some of the dialogue choices voiced and others you just had to read. I understand that it is a huge undertaking to voice everyone, and with such a vast amount of characters you could talk with, I can understand the enormous cost that could incur if you were to voice them all, but if you are voicing a character, just voice them completely.
The controls in the game are very straight-forward, you are going to point and click. You will also have some hotkeys for special abilities, that you will definitely need to employ. One HUGE recommendation that I have for any gamer that takes on this game, is make damn sure your entire party is selected when you are exploring over great distances in an area, and make damn sure you have all your party gathered together right at an entrance/exit before you go through. First you might be screwed because you will enter combat solo, and there's no way to come to your rescue, and second off the game doesn't do well with finding your other characters if they are in a slightly different area, even if you are not in combat.
So this is a very nice, layered, RPG. You will have tons of skills to master, weapons to upgrade, and of course things to find. I wouldn't call this an open world game, but its pretty damn close to it. There's definitely a story you need to stick with, if you are going to advance the game, but for the most part, as long as you have water in your canteens (VERY IMPORTANT), and a rad suit (to fend off the radiation), you can go wherever you please. Now I will admit that you might want to pay a bit closer attention to the conversational choices, or prompts that characters give you, otherwise you might end up accidentally massacring a TON of people that really didn't have to die, but ended up dying because you accidentally didn't heed a warning, or were trying to hard to advance a quest.
This game utilizes a five person party system, and I will tell you this right now, make sure that all your characters have their weapon of choice, and make sure its different. Ammo is hard to come by and it really sucks if you have two characters highly proficient in a specific type of weapon, and you seem to be running through bullets at an alarming rate. The problem is that you have to be at least level 1 proficient with a weapon, otherwise its basically useless in the game. I learned that one the hard way when I had not only two, but three people using pistols. There's also some other skills that will definitely come in handy. Make sure you have a weaponsmith, it is actually very interesting how many weapons you come across, and of course if you are not careful you will encumber your party members, so why not try to scrap it and see if you can't get a couple of upgrades to use on your parties weapons. Another thing that you will want to have, in combination, is a shovel and perception. The shovel is a hell of a tool to have and will allow you to dig up a lot of good items, and if you are interested, it can also dig up graves. The perception part is to make sure that there's no booby traps, I can't tell you how many mines blew up my characters for serious damage.
There's one last thing that I want to give you a heads up about in this game. Early on, at least for me, I found that I was collecting a ton of clothes. Well don't sell them, store them at the Ranger headquarters, there's a certain weapon that gets introduced in the game that will literally blow all your clothes (minus undergarments) away.
So I guess the final thing is this, should you get this game? Well that all depends, if you are looking for an RPG with depth, in a post-apocalyptic setting, then yes get this game. If you yearn for the days of old (Baldur's Gate-esque) get this game, as long as you are comfy with the guns instead of bows and crossbows. If you are looking for a game that gives you hand holding when it comes to the story, this is NOT the game for you. There is a portion of the game that if you miss the radio transmissions the first time, it becomes damn near impossible to figure out, until you start going over EVERY inch of the world. This game, even though it has its flaws, its ramping difficulty (yeah it gets pretty hard as it goes), and camera issues, its still a solid game, and I'm sure that it would be a nice addition to gaming collections. This game gets an 8.3 out of 10.

Pros: Gameplay is fun and addictive. I died, on average, once every 53 seconds I played this game, but the checkpoints are fair and restarts are quick. Most deaths were my own fault, either through poor planning or slips of the finger navigating with the WASD keys. Interesting storyline helps justify game's gruesome subject matter. Soundtrack is spectacular. 80s neon pixel art design was great. Mask perks were fun. Weapon variety was enjoyable.
Cons: Grading system and point accumulation seemed arbitrary, which locks away different masks that could be useful. Did not see a guide explaining what scores to hit on which levels to unlock different masks. Occasionally encountered bug that allowed bad guys to share same space as me, so would waste entire clip trying to shoot threat that was impervious to my bullets. Also the Spacebar "ground kill" move was super inconsistent about when it wanted to work, and the kill animation was very long, which exposes you to needless risk using it. Often better to let the guy stand back up and stab him then. Most levels were constructed so your repeated deaths could teach you the layout and improve your next attempt, but some levels, especially the "Boss" levels, included insta-kill events that happened so quickly it was near impossible to discern a better way to approach the level in next attempt. Usually ended up having to consult youtube. The Boss levels were particularly frustrating because the checkpoints forced you to rewatch the cutscene every time. So it'd be 25 seconds of frantic clicking to bypass the dialogue, followed by ~3 seconds of gameplay trying to find a way around the insta-kill attack, only to start back at the beginning of the cutscene.
Note: I had to play the Original version. The game includes an updated version but I could not get it to open past the load screen. Maybe the new version fixes some of the bugs/frustrations I encountered.

The Witcher series is, in my opinion, the best written and realized pair of roleplaying games of the last decade.  The characters are engaging and believable, the monster-hunting is highly detailed, and combat is simultaneously fluid, visceral, and tactical without becoming overly complex.  The settings are detailed and feel alive, and the conflicts within them are never simple enough that there is one apparent "good" or "bad" choice.  The Witcher 2 is about moral ambiguity and consequences that matter within the game, and it fully delivers.  Some rpg enthusiasts may balk at having to play as one character, Geralt, but the player has almost complete freedom to choose who Geralt really is and how the story turns out.
This is an absolutely fantastic game.

I thought i should write a short review about this game.
I have played a couple of hours (50) and i can confirm that this game
is despite the public opinion against lootchests very good.
I was wondering about the good scores even though this game has loot chests.
In a matter fact the loot chests are just an addition to the gameplay.
There is no need for buying these because its just like a normal game shop like in animal crossing.
To be honest in animal crossing you dont need to pay with real money and here you do neither.
During all the gameplay i never felt once forced to buy any of these chests.
After explaining the chest system in my point of view, i will continue with list of postive and negative.
Positive
+ beautiful graphics, really detailed
+ personality of the orcs
+ new and better nemesis system
+ really difficult
+ more fluently fighting system
+ good story start
+ Dragons (come on that are dragons!)
+ all skills
+ you probably get enough XP and all skills until the end of the game
Negative
- good graphics needs good PC
- sometimes you dont really realise the different personalites of the orcs due to short conversations
- unprecisly hitbox when running or jumping (Especially with dragons it feel uncomfortable)
- ending which does not really meet my expectations
- XP are only given from quests or bosses
- skill system makes the beginning too difficult because even in late game the difficulty is worse.
- Not skipable sequences (activites from orks, conversations, fast restart button in some cases are missing)
- skills which should be activated simultaneous cannot be activated simultanous
- every item needs to get dismantled one by one
- the forcing of doing castle thingies if you wanna level higher, otherwise its really difficult to get more level
- Orks can have a higher level than you which means they cannot be recruited
- If you wanna have Legendary items over lvl 60 you need to find a legendary ork over lvl 60
Feedback/wishes from my side
- For Pc players an hotkey for changing the skills would be nice, it was really annoying opening this menu first bevor changing skills. (Example if i wanna summon a dragon, i need to switch from summon a caragor first)
- just make the castle conversations skipable
- easier menu to dismantle things
This is all the feedback i have.
Although there is a lot of negative feedback its just fine adjustmend which would make the game more fluently in my opinion

I was one of the intial Kickstarter backers who helped it reach that magical 3.3 million funding bux.
I had high hopes for this game after remembering Grim Fandango and recently replaying a lot of adventure games myself, as well as new the new ones.
First I must say, for 3.3 million, I expected a lot more. The game when I played it had glitchy animations, graphics and overall felt rushed and unfinished. I can't even remember the music, or the voices. The level of polish and attention to detail I expected from the creator(s) of Grim Fandango just wasn't there. I can still recall Manny Calavera's voice, Glottis, the festival theme, the little jingles, and the rest of the strong characters in that game. That game made an impact on me which lasts to this day. Somewhere along the line, something got lost.
Regarding the gameplay, the puzzles were a bit on the easy side, but at least they were a bit more straight forward and logical than some of the puzzles in Grim Fandango (The Petrified forest driving sequence almost broke the experience for me in comparison). Still, I was not pleased when I saw that this was it. I expected more.
So for the price you are seeing, I will not recommend this game, and since it is only half the game still, I don't think I will ever recommend the game based on the fact that I was promised a full game and the developers backed off from that.

X-COM: Enforcer is a third person shooter developed by MicroProse and released in 2001. The controls can be a bit of a pain in the butt, the way you move the camera is changing the way you face, this game has a serious case of the early 2000's. It's still playable, but there are a lot of negatives about the game which will drive away most to far better games within the 3rd person shooter genre.
Oh if only I had a bit more time to finish this review, Enforcer, hello Enforcer? Can you hear me? You are trapped in my simulation and need to listen to my obnoxious voice repeat the same 4 lines of diologue throughout the whole game. Enforceeeerrr are you liiistening? Go that way Enforcer! Follow my transponder Enforcer, it's why I created it!
There ya go, you can turn off dialogue and sound now, because I basically gave you almost all recorded voice dialogue. This is a game where I was actually praying for an option to put on subtitles so I could spare myself the agony of his annoying voice.
You play as the Enforcer, basically an android-robot-thing which has been programmed for one purpose: the eradication and destruction of the alien threat. you will fight your way through the hordes of aliens, all of which are very familiar seeing as many have been seen in the previous X-COM games.
The camera stays at an almost always fixed angel behind the main character; you cannot tilt the camera up or down, but you can turn your character. so it works. However there are a few levels where the camera is at a stupid angle where you can't see anything in front of you.
General movement was fairly straightforward, as with the previous x-com games I played them on my windows 7 laptop which has aged, but that means I played completely without a mouse, I rebinded the keys to let me strafe with Q and E, and turn with A and D. Pretty standard movement controls for most video games. The game would move most smoothly with a keyboard AND mouse though
.
The rest of the controls are inconsequential: you move, you shoot, you adjust depending on your gun, you grab data chips, upgrade your character after you complete the mission, it's not rocket science most of the stuff introduced in this game is very straight forward and explains itself.
There are a couple ways to gauge your progression through the game, the first and least effective way is to judged it based on the levels themselves... That's not very effective, since I felt like they were all bleeding into eachother.
Next you can kind of gauge how far you are into the game based on the Aliens you encounter
. This is fairly effective because you can kind of get a handle based on how far you are into the game once you start fighting bosses and regularly see larger and larger Aliens.
Lastly and the most effective way is by seeing the various upgrades you unlock throughout the game. As you progress you will find special items, when these are collected and brought back to the nerd who is constantly repeating himself in your ear, you unlock new upgrades, weapons, and power ups. As you progress you will unlock more and more of these, and this helps you get a feel for how far you are into the game.
Here's the real question
, that's very difficult to answer. If it's in your steam library you should definitively give it a shot! -- And don't give up after the first few levels. If you're considering purchasing the game I'd suggest getting getting an X-COM bundle deal.
The game's reception is very mixed, and for good reason. The game isn't even close to what the original IP stands for
It's not a particularly good looking third person shooter, and who likes being shouted at every 5 minutes "ENFORCER GO THAT WAY, ENFORCER GO MAKE ME A SANDWITCH".
But here's the funny thing... I really enjoyed playing this game. I don't really know what it was, but I think part of it is that I just wanted to play something different, and this game was just that; different. I played through and beat the whole game once, and after beating the game I could probably play through a second time and try to find all the secrets to unlock more weapons.
As always, thank you for reading my review, and hopefully it has been some use to you. If you have any question or comments feel free to leave them below.

You've probably either played this game already or read a ♥♥♥♥♥on of reviews, so I'm just gonna say that the game is nice and write a few things that I think could either make the game better or are just a bit of a bummer for me.
First off - the art style for the environment is 3D, but the art style for dwellers, mobs, and anything alive is 2D. This is a bit of an issue for me - either make both 3D or both 2D, I hate the inconsistency.
Secondly - Either nerf the quests or buff the wasteland. It's pretty much pointless to go explore the wasteland if the rewards for quests are fifteen times as much rewarding, give more xp and even nuka colas.
Also - Mr. Handys are the most overrated things in the game, they can't be repaired, fixed, healed or anything and just wander the floor you assign them to... meh
Another thing is the themes - why would you add a new mechanic to the game, more than fifty recipe fragments to collect on quests and in the wasteland - only to add just 6 themes? Summary: Buy. Binge. Now. Life is Strange tugs at the heartstrings. Life is Strange can be summed up with
(two movies which spoil the entire 5 episode plot.) Max Caulfield is a touchingly awkward teen. She gains
Like your average Choose Your Own Adventure, your choices affect the outcome of the story. Like most recreation of the Choose Your Own adventure in gaming, your choices are frequently on rails and have minimal overall impact to the total plot. (Whether you choose A or B, C will still happen. But, your A/B choice will result in D or E variation on the outcome of the unavoidable C event.) This may cause some feel a loss of overall control (especially with replays) but the illusion of choice (especially for a first playthrough) gives you a powerful sense of agency.
And, because many things in these kinds of games are set behind choices you make about where to go and what order to do things (and subsequent time spent engaged in dialog with other characters in the story)-- Life is Strange can end up feeling like a movie or serial miniseries-- and take about as long as a serial miniseries (if not longer). So it ends up being well worth the cost of entry.
The themes in Life is Strange resonate with my childhood. Isolation. Discovery. Tragedy. (Yea, my life wasn't rosey, but you don't really want to hear about that.) These themes are masterfully mixed with the fantastic.

I was waiting until I finished the game to post this review, but it seems the (probable) final battle is a bit too hard.
Spoiler:
You are Flux, a (female, yay!) space trucker who is waylaid in space and crashed on a remote planet.  You have to harvest resources and craft items to survive, contact your bosses, and get off the planet.  With you is your trusty, if sadly non-combatant, robot pal JuiceBox, and the resident sentient species of the planet.
The best part of the game by far is the copious text, from wacky names, to funny descriptions of EVERY item, to especially all the funny dialogue.  The banter between Flux and Juice alone is great.
Controller support is quite good.  I don't think I've seen a game that assigned separate functions to the D-pad as well as both joysticks before getting Crashlands.  My only complaint here is that the button designations on the control scheme are only either Nintendo's XYAB style, or the Playstation shapes.  I have a Logitech gamepad, with numerical designations.  (Only the Lego games use my pad's labels properly.)  Controller works fine with the game, of course; the lack of proper labels just makes it a bit harder at first until I memorized what button did what.  Some buttons are mapped to a handy hotbar.
Maps are HUGE!!!  One each for the three biomes you need to visit.  Loading is quick.  Fortunately, you can easily find many teleport locations around, and there is an auto-map feature.  (Better be, what with a robot AI sidekick and all.)  Also, quest locations are given, either as specific points or wide circles to investigate.  Only a handful of times do quests require you to find and kill a specific critter who is "wandering about."
Crafting is done at various workstations, which, of course, themselves need to be crafted.  Each workstation focuses on items made with components harvested off one of the planet's critter species.  Some crafting recipes are given to you upon creation of a workstation, but others must drop randomly or be granted as part of a quest.
You can mark a recipe to be tracked, just one at a time in the corner of the screen.  The game flags how much you have and how much you need, and even calculates how much you can already make.  That calculation is done for every recipe you know in the workstation.
The workstations also allow you to view the individual items needed so you know where to go to harvest them.  Item names and descriptions generally are clear as to what they drop from.
Inventory is infinite, no need to juggle items in chests.  Unfortunately, there's no raw inventory count.  The only way to know exactly how much you have of a raw component is to either check with a recipe that has it, or watch the status updates as you collect components and hope the one you are watching for drops.
There's some furniture items, including beds that move the day-night cycle and heal you.  But other than the floors for bridges and to place stuff upon, nothing else is needed apart from fetch quests.
Critters and most plants drop multiple items at once.  The larger the critter, the more powerful it is, but also the more items it drops.  Higher risk, higher reward.  Also, the two largest versions of a species drop special essences, vital to upgrading your pets and some other good items.
Plants that do not drop anything else can be farmed in pots, once you receive the recipe.  Farmed plants respawn much faster than the random spawns out in the world.
Finding specific plant and creature types becomes much easier once you realize how the procedurally-created maps are laid out.  Your starting position is a safe zone, and the difficulty increases with distance from it.  Creatures and plants spawn on specific tile types in an eligible zone.
Weapons and armor builds come with Diablo-style random rolls of the status effects and resistances in the game.  Halfway through, you also receive a way to enhance your armor from those initial rolls.  On Normal difficulty, there were no negative effects, just losing a good effect as you otherwise upgrade to a new weapon.
Harvesting plants and rocks is the usual as in these games.  You need to craft various tiers of harvesting tools to progress.
Killing the critters . . . is a bit of a pain, especially at first.  Battles devolve into a rhythm of hit-dodge, hit-dodge.  The dodging part is eased somewhat because every attack zone is telegraphed a few seconds before they even start the attack.
Once you get beyond your initial ranged weapon and get ones that inflict status effects, and raise your first pet off an egg-type item drop, battles become easier.  Then, you only have to attack from afar, and your pet will attack your last target for a while.
You can also craft and fling bombs at enemies, but these are best saved for boss battles and the rare epic-level creature.
If you can handle the battles both big and small, this is a great game to check out.

Writing is the most important part of a role playing game like this, and the writing in Wasteland 2 is quite good (although a little shy of greatness). The world feels big and rich, and you feel as if you have quite a bit of freedom. The game mechanics are good and feel fair, although there are a few important things that are by no means intuitive. (For example, anything that comes out of a toaster will be a minor or major plot point and clothing, despite having detailed inventory slots, is entirely cosmetic with no in-game impact.) The user interface is pretty good, although one could make some nitpicks. Sound is handled quite well and this is one of the very few games where I never felt the urge to turn the music off, despite playing for 100 hours. Graphics are never a high priority in this type of game, and while Wasteland graphics are state of the art for the genre they would be someone primitive looking in other contexts. I have to say the art one area where the game really falls down because, despite looking quite good most of the time, there just wasn't enough of it to do what the game was trying to do. Hand painted images rarely matched descriptions which rarely matched 3D avatars, often to bewildering effect. Paintings would have the wrong hair color, build, clothing, and race. 3D avatars would sometimes even be the wrong gender. Surprisingly, this level of mismatch even extends to the player character images. Few character paintings have 3D avatars available that even vaguely match. Even more disconcertingly, the low number of paintings means that they are re-used many times in game so you will occasionally come across an NPC using your character's portrait.
But all in all, this is a very impressive game, easily worth its full, original sale price. I personally feel it is a seminal work, which will be referenced for decades.

Oh what a mess. Looking through this game's history is quite the nightmare, and makes me glad I have nothing to do with Spiral's PR team (if one even exists). I think the most important thing for anyone looking at this game to note is that it is not at all what it used to be. Over the past couple of years this game has been nurtured and cared for with an obvious love and dedication that I don't often see these days from developers. While the original ORION: Dino Beatdown was a buggy mess, Dino Horde has grown out of that messy goo into something I think plenty of people will enjoy for hours on end.
I recently acquired this game while it was on sale for ~$1.00 thinking I would have a good time playing it with my friends, not expecting a whole lot based on steam reviews and such. My goodness was I pleasantly surprised.
The first thing that grabbed my attention when I loaded up the game was the depth of the options menu. The sheer amount of UI customization and graphical tweaking available is phenomenal. And they scored major points for allowing me to turn off bloom and motion blur. However I will note that I have not yet found a way to change the controller look sensitivity, which is quite the downside if you prefer to play this with a controller, and stands in stark contrast to the quality of the rest of the options menu.
After tweaking controls and graphics options to my heart’s content, my friend and I jumped into a game of survival. Honestly, this is where I think the game suffers the most. We had absolutely no idea what we were doing, and there is very little help to be found online in the forms of wikis or guides. What we did know, was to follow the on screen prompts to turn on our generator. After we managed that, enough help popped up to lead us back to our base to buy weapons and augments (purchasable buffs that last until you die). With the starting money we grabbed a few SMGs and headed outside to kill us some dinos. Once they finally spawned we started frantically murderizing every giant reptile in sight, and they in turn began chewing on our faces. Seems dinosaurs don't appreciate bullets being hurled at them. We quickly discovered that setting the difficulty to medium for your first go might not be the best idea, and we were promptly turned into dino-chow. So we went back to the lobby, turned the difficulty down to easy and tried again. This time we were able to hold our own against the horde of angry reptiles bent on human consumption. Well, at least until wave 7.
After we finished playing a few games of survival I found that I craved more, and dino horde was happy to oblige, allowing for an "open world" mode they dubbed conquest. In this game mode you can choose from one of two huge maps to play on. One in the arctic and one in the recently added plains. When you load this mode up you are presented with a vehicle or two for traversing the world, and a couple generators you can head towards. When you go to one of the generators and turn it on, you begin a very similar wave driven experience as survival mode, however, if you manage to last the ten waves and secure that outpost, you are rewarded with a load of cash, and the opportunity to go work on securing another outpost. I will admit that I do not know what happens if you secure more than one outpost (I saw three, but didn't have the time to play 30+ rounds).
The biggest thing that stands out to me about this game is the fact that the more I play it, the more I discover about it and enjoy it. I have only played two of the twelve (yes, twelve) game modes and already I feel that this game is worth the money they are asking for it. Admittedly it has its share of issues such as no FoV slider, a lack of pertinent help documentation (took us forever to find out how to get more ammo) and a slightly overwhelming number of game modes that have no description. However, even with these things in mind, nothing beats the thrill of fighting a horde of raptors, a t-rex, a stegosaurus, two triceratops, and a deinosuchus all at once in the middle of a rainy night while trying to capture an outpost. I felt like a kid again, and there are so few games these days that give me that thrill and excitement. Definitely give this game a try.

If you loved the classic Fallout 1 and 2, you'll thoroughly enjoy this game. The post-apocalyptic setting was masterfully executed - not too recently ruined, just enough that civilisation is attempting to rise from the ravages of a bygone age. The characters you meet are colourfull and interesting enough to entertain but still maintain that seriousness that forged survivors need to continue living.
Combat is satisfying, its simple and straightforward. It does encourages specialisation, but with a party of 4-6 rangers, you can cover for each character's weaknesses. There's also the custom character option which is nicely implimented, with option to choose from a set of pre-made kooky characters to wander the wastes. The skill system is gratifying - you'll get that wide grin when you realise that one skill that you first thought off as useless, (Toaster Repair... Seriously?!?!) suddenly has relevance when you encounter it.
Only downside to such a good game is the length. Its a solid 10 hours if you like to explore and immerse yourself on the story, possibly less than double that amount if you explore all the nools and cranies of the game. But ultimately, it leaves you wanting more - In a good way mind you. Wild West post-apocalyptic Rangers never sounded so cool, untill now.

Let me make an analogy here: I guess some of you out there may remember that old Spongebob Squarepants episode, where Bob gets the magic pencil that brings everything it draws to life. Well, Alan Wake is kind of like that Spongebob Squarepants episode, although this time, it is our writer protagonist Alan Wake that brings dark things to life through the touch of his pen on the paper. The kind of things that want to kill you, for no apparent reason. Your only means of survival is light, be it environmental or the one coming from your handheld torch.
The game is quintessential horror at its best, and a quite psychological version of it as well, which only goes to show that you don't need bloody gore and meat cleaving left and right to build tension (I AM LOOKING AT YOU, EVIL WITHIN).
The engine gives a memorable experience and runs flawlessly, while the soundtrack rounds off the whole package in a very neat fashion (look out for the EPIC track "Children of the Elder God" by Old Gods of Asgard).
All in all, a fantastic experience, which, to be honest, hasn't had a match or even a competitor to this day.

Because the add stuff(resourses, land, better gear, etc)

Abosolutly nothing.

Overlords.
The entire game is all about getting that edge over your target.
Making sure everything is in your favor before you strike.
Execpt overlords.
They are just sitting in there throne room.
You have to enter there throne room.
Do a boss battle in a small room without any ability to weaken the overlord or bring in reforcemence.
So we basicly got this one orc who we have to kill in a location we cant in anyway manipulate.
Doesnt mather if you have an entire army of orcs outside able to easly zerg him to death.
Speaking forts.

All it take is one lucky ork to kill you and boom.
You lost your entire fort.
Despite the fact the you defeated 99% of the enemy attack and your orks shoud be able to hold them off by sheer numbers alone.

Let just say:
But tho must behave like a compleet moron is the only reason half of the story even work.
Then there is the manditory: Repesation of minnorties story be dammed if they mather.
Basicly.

A: Like me quit from sheer boredom.
B: Reach the mandetory number to see ending.

TL;DR - Good solid game if you can ignore the bad launch.
Okay let's first talk about the 30fps issue before we properly start. Yes what they did was bad in this day and age while also serving to highlight the proper porting of PC games however if you can look past this the game is very good.
I personally bought it from the first day without the patch and the game was more than playable at 30fps. Yes it wasn't silky smooth but I enjoyed the game either way!
The gameplay it'self is in a way refreshing, instead of going around and activaing towers (ubisoft style) you wiretap an areas phones meaning you can see all the enemy's and collectables however to do this you need 3 scrap electronics. Now unlike other games where if you didn't have the 3 scrap you were screwed and had to find the collectables via sight only this game has a radar proximity where if your passing close bye to one of them it will pop up on the mini map making exploring the map that much easier.
The gun play is very solid, unlike in some Third person games where shots from a pistol take multiple hits to kill a person this game get's it right. The starter pistol, the 9mm equivilant does feel like a firearm should, three shots to the chest and dead. However the sound and general animation behind the firearms make them feel all that more powerful, plus sniper rifles and shotgun tend to take enemy's down in one hit as you would expect them too!
All in all i would recommend this game if you can get past the little hump that the developers accidentally created.

Ultimately, for a game to be more than just good, it has to provide something that sticks with the player. It can be something new or unexpected. It can be the developing on, or the perfection of, a preexisting genre, mechanic or idea. It can even be a single transient inconsequential moment when a game made you laugh, cry or – dare we hope? – think.
When writing this review, BROKEN AGE invoked words like “well-presented”, “pretty”, “excellent voice-work” and “interesting.” What it failed to invoke was anything that I will be referencing or discussing one year from now. The paper cutout design is a high-point and should be praised, but I feel that the developers could have done more with it if they had not been aiming for a  smooth “nostalgic” style, originally imposed from technical limitations rather than artistic thought. The obligatory challenges are extremely easy, sometimes appearing more as parody than puzzles. The story is decent, but heavily telegraphed. As for the characters, they are well-rounded, with some witty dialogue and funny back-stories.
In the end, BROKEN AGE can probably serve as a very good example of a archetypical point-and-click adventure, tempered by the 2010s decreased focus on puzzles (and accompanied puzzle-related frustration) in favour of story and charm. If that is what you are looking for, BROKEN AGE will most likely suffice. But if you are looking for something 'more', you will not find it here.
ADDENDUM for Act 2:
Frustrating backtracking through the locals and people of Act 1, with the added addition of what I think is some kind of overlay graphic bug (not present in the ipad version) that makes two puzzles practically unsolvable.

Not really an X-Com game, it's only tangentially related, this game is a freakish frankenstien's monster of mashed together resources from cancelled X-com games of the era. They gave them to a few unrelated developers and said, make something we can sell out of this.
I don't recommend you buy it as a stand alone, but if you bought the complete pack you might have some fun with this if you don't look at this as a serious X-Com sequel.
What I recommend in this game is the shear sense of excess and abandon. This game is like the master levels in Doom II, except more so. At some point the level bosses become the regular enemies and they begin to fill up the smoldering remains of humanity in areas the size of the parking lot at disney world, and then they take more than one shoulder launched nuclear missile to kill.
Don't get me wrong, critically speaking, there is no story to speak of, the mechanics are basic, options limited and the exploration is limited to trying to find glowing letters that spell out B-O-N-U-S in semi open levels, but this game is like Smash TV meets Contra meets Doom meets Chex Quest.
When you're running 120 mph laps in a shopping mall with a helicopter blade strapped to your arm vertically, the aliens flying apart in front of you as if they've been thrown into a blender on the liquify setting, an effeminate lisping scientist is yelling something about "BIG BONUSES" in your ear and your robot avatar says "Back off space freaks" and you're only to the half point in the game you'll understand what I'm talking about.

The good: Fantastic art direction, amazing voice talent, engaging story, simple gameplay.
The bad: Frustrating 'use object with everything you can think of' gameplay, overly obtuse puzzles, breaks off before delivering on story.
It may be that I'm getting old and no longer have the patience for puzzle games, but I can't help but feel that Broken Age's strengths are the fantastic story, art and characterization, and that the puzzle mechanics actually get in the way and detract from that experience (I had to resort to a walkthrough a couple of times, which broke the immersion somewhat) and there are a few sections of the game that feel a bit rushed or, rather, too hastily progressed through.
The cliffhanger ending will hopefully be resolved in part 2, but as it stands it can feel a little unsatisfying as there's no real resolution provided for the situations the characters have created.
Those points aside, it's still an interesting experience and one I'm glad I had.

Legendary orcs you can get by doing Online Conquests or finding them and everything else you can get by buying normal boxes with ingame currency.
4) The game is about 55 hours long. Not once have I thought this game is forcing me to farm for something. All 55 hours were a blast to play.
In the end, if you loved Shadow Of Mordor then you'll love this sequel even more. It is improved in every aspect of the previous game and this time a lot more challenging, a lot more open and a lot more free.
